title: Open ultrasound foundation model for robust segmentation and clinical measurement across heterogeneous settings
comment: The PDF includes the Supplementary Information
summary: Ultrasound is the most widely deployed imaging modality worldwide, yet clinical AI remains fragmented into narrow single-task models that fail when device, operator, or anatomy changes. Here we present SonoCorpus, an open resource unifying 456,963 images and 1,626,085 expert masks from 53 public datasets spanning 24 clinical applications and 17 countries, and SonoBase, an interactive segmentation foundation model pretrained on it. Across fifteen evaluation datasets introducing new organs, devices, operators, and geographies, SonoBase outperforms SAM2, MedSAM2, and the concept-promptable MedSAM3 on every dataset and matches per-dataset specialist models trained on the same data; on fully external data it exceeds the accuracy these baselines achieve on their own in-distribution benchmarks. Ejection fraction derived from its segmentations falls within inter-observer variability (6.63\% error), with fewer misclassifications at the defibrillator-candidacy threshold than either promptable baseline (13\% versus 18--42\%); fetal head-circumference (1.81~mm) and gestational-age (1.2 days) errors fall below inter-observer variability. Where a baseline fails outright, one in four test cases, SonoBase recovers a usable segmentation in 81\% of them, including on handheld probes operated by minimally trained users in two low- and middle-income countries (Sierra Leone and Tanzania). Five labeled examples can help the model adapt to a new setting, and the identical training protocol transfers well to newer models such as SAM3, locating the advantage in ultrasound-specific pretraining rather than any single architecture. To ensure reproducibility and enable the community to build on SonoBase as a platform, we release all checkpoints, optimizer states, data-split indices, deduplication hashes, and starter code.

AI.tldr: SonoBase is a ultrasound segmentation foundation model trained on SonoCorpus (456,963 images, 1,626,085 expert masks from 53 public datasets) that generalizes across devices, operators, and geographies, outperforming promptable baselines on 15 external datasets and rivaling specialist models; it supports 5-shot adaptation and releases data/code for reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Clinical ultrasound AI is fragmented into narrow, device- or operator-specific models; a unified, adaptable segmentation foundation model is needed to improve generalization and accessibility.
AI.method: Assemble SonoCorpus from 53 public datasets across 24 applications and 17 countries; pretrained segmentation foundation model SonoBase on this data; evaluate on 15 external datasets with new organs/devices/operators/geographies; compare against SAM2, MedSAM2, MedSAM3; assess clinically relevant metrics (EF from segmentation, defibrillator candidacy misclassifications, fetal head circumference, gestational age); test 1:1 generalization on handheld probes with minimally trained users in LMICs; five-shot fine-tuning; transfer protocol to newer architectures; release all checkpoints, optimizers, splits, dedup hashes, code.
AI.result: SonoBase outperforms the baselines on every evaluation dataset and matches per-dataset specialist models; on fully external data it surpasses their in-distribution baselines; EF errors 6.63% within inter-observer variability; defibrillator misclassifications reduced to 13% vs 18–42%; head circumference error 1.81 mm; gestational-age error 1.2 days; in 25% of baselines' failures, SonoBase recovers usable segmentations in 81% of them; extends to handheld, low-resource settings; five-shot adaptation; protocol generalizes to SAM3; data and code released.
AI.conclusion: A dedicated ultrasound-pretrained foundation model yields robust, generalizable segmentation across devices and operators, enabling broad clinical utility and reproducibility; a five-shot adaptation path and full data/code release facilitate community uptake.

title: RAUL: Reference-Assisted Ureteroscopy Localization for Skill Assessment
summary: Objective: Incomplete navigation of anatomy during ureteroscopic kidney stone surgeries can contribute to repeat interventions. While skilled surgeons have lower reintervention rates, there are no objective metrics to quantify scope-navigation performance to evaluate when a trainee becomes skilled. This work aims to recover ureteroscope trajectories from endoscopic video and derive navigation metrics to quantify differences in skill. Methods: We propose RAUL, a reference-assisted reconstruction framework for recovering ureteroscope trajectories from ureteroscope videos only in phantoms. For each phantom, we use a slow, high-quality reference exploration video to generate a reference reconstruction. We localize subsequent exploration videos against this reference. We evaluate localization accuracy against electromagnetically tracked scope pose. We compute navigation metrics from phantom exploration trajectories to compare surgical residents across experience levels. Results: The proposed reference-assisted framework achieves a mean translation root mean square error of $0.5 \pm 0.1$ mm across 9 phantoms. Compared to standard Structure-from-Motion (SfM), the proposed pipeline increases frame-wise localization coverage from $50.5 \pm 14.9\%$ to $86.1 \pm 7.2\%$ of all video frames. The reconstructed trajectories revealed significant differences between high- and low-experience trainees in established navigation metrics. Conclusion: RAUL enables substantially more complete recovery of ureteroscope trajectories from videos compared to standard SfM pipelines, enabling trajectory-based skill assessment without additional tracking equipment. Significance: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first use of video-only recovery of ureteroscope trajectories without external tracking sensors for skill assessment, supporting scalable automated assessment of ureteroscopy navigation skill.

AI.tldr: A novel video-only trajectory recovery method (RAUL) for ureteroscope navigation in phantom phantoms that enables objective skill assessment without external tracking; significantly improves localization coverage and reveals trajectory differences between experience levels.
AI.motivation: Incomplete ureteroscope navigation during ureteroscopy leads to potential reinterventions. There is a lack of objective, video-based metrics to quantify navigation skill progression. This work aims to recover trajectories from endoscopic video and derive metrics for skill assessment.
AI.method: RAUL is a reference-assisted reconstruction framework. For each phantom, a slow, high-quality reference exploration video is used to create a reference trajectory. Subsequent exploration videos are localized against this reference, and localization accuracy is validated against electromagnetically tracked scope poses. Navigation metrics are computed from the reconstructed trajectories to compare residents of different experience levels.
AI.result: Mean translation RMSE of 0.5 ± 0.1 mm across 9 phantoms. Frame-wise localization coverage improved from 50.5 ± 14.9% (standard SfM) to 86.1 ± 7.2% with RAUL. Reconstructed trajectories showed significant differences between high- and low-experience trainees on established navigation metrics.
AI.conclusion: RAUL enables substantially more complete recovery of ureteroscope trajectories from video than standard SfM, enabling trajectory-based skill assessment without additional tracking hardware; this is claimed to be the first video-only ureteroscope trajectory recovery for skill assessment.

title: Can Vision-Language Models Judge Olympic Diving? From Reasoning to Scores in Zero-Shot Action Quality Assessment
summary: Automated action quality assessment (AQA) in Olympic sports remains a challenging task due to the complexity of human motion and the subjectivity inherent in expert judging. This work evaluates the capability of open-source Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to perform zero-shot action quality assessment on Olympic diving videos using the AQA-7 benchmark dataset. In this regard, a regression-based framework is pro-posed to leverage both the semantic reasoning and phase-level sub-scores generated by the VLMs, combining TF-IDF vectorization, dimensionality reduction, and ensemble learning to predict final competition scores. Experimental results show that standalone VLMs achieve moderate Spearman correlations below 0.32, while the proposed ensemble regression framework substantially improves performance in the reported evaluation, reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.67 with a four-model configuration. Textual reasoning features con-sistently outperformed raw numerical sub-scores, highlighting the richness of VLM-generated explanations for action quality analysis. These findings suggest that VLMs hold strong potential as assistive tools for explainable and semi-automated sports performance evaluation. The code is publicly available on GitHub https://github.com/hvelesaca/olympic diving judge vlm

AI.tldr: Zero-shot action quality assessment for Olympic diving using open-source Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with a regression ensemble. Textual reasoning from VLMs plus TF-IDF, dimensionality reduction, and ensemble learning yields strong correlation with expert scores (Spearman 0.67) on the AQA-7 benchmark; textual explanations outperform raw sub-scores.
AI.motivation: AQA in Olympic sports is hampered by complex human motion and subjective expert judging. The work investigates whether open-source VLMs can provide explainable, semi-automated action quality assessments in a zero-shot setting, leveraging their semantic reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: Use open-source VLMs to obtain semantic reasoning and phase-level sub-scores for diving videos. Build textual features (e.g., from explanations) and numerical sub-scores, apply TF-IDF vectorization, apply dimensionality reduction, and train ensemble regression models to predict final competition scores. Evaluate correlations with expert scores on the AQA-7 benchmark; compare standalone VLMs versus ensemble regression; assess the contribution of textual reasoning versus raw sub-scores.
AI.result: Standalone VLMs achieve moderate Spearman correlations below 0.32. The proposed four-model ensemble regression framework yields a Spearman correlation of 0.67, significantly improving performance. Textual reasoning features consistently outperform raw numerical sub-scores.
AI.conclusion: VLMs have strong potential as explainable assistive tools for semi-automated sports performance evaluation. The approach demonstrates effective integration of semantic reasoning with traditional scoring, and the code is publicly available for replication and extension.

title: Open-vocabulary 3D object detection with promptable segmentation
summary: Three-dimensional object detection for autonomous driving is dominated by detectors trained on large corpora of human-annotated 3D boxes. Such a detector learns a fixed category list, and everything outside it is invisible. This paper asks whether the task can be solved training-free and open-vocabulary. A promptable segmentation model (SAM3), queried with class names as text prompts, supplies instance masks in the vehicle's six surround-view cameras, and the masks are turned into metric 3D boxes using the geometry of the scene. The core is a controlled three-stage comparison on nuScenes in which 2D detection is held fixed and only the source of 3D geometry changes. Geometry predicted from images alone reaches 0.183 mean average precision (mAP) under the official protocol; fitting boxes from raw LiDAR points inside the same masks with training-free rules reaches 0.298 mAP / 0.348 nuScenes detection score (NDS) at zero labeling cost; borrowing supervised box geometry at inference time lifts the same detections to 0.413 mAP / 0.555 NDS, which locates the pipeline's largest deficit in measurement precision rather than 2D detection, while class confusion and confidence calibration survive that substitution. Reversing the direction, a three-state camera-witness rule built from the same masks improves a supervised LiDAR-only detector from 0.596 to 0.630 mAP, roughly half the gain of fully supervised camera fusion, with no training. A coverage analysis shows that SAM3 finds 84% of in-range objects with a correctly named mask; the classes that fail in the official metric are misnamed or geometrically unforgiving, not unseen.

AI.tldr: Prompts a training-free, open-vocabulary 3D detection pipeline using SAM3 masks and scene geometry; shows promising results on nuScenes with different geometry sources; identifies measurement precision as bottleneck and reveals that 2D detection isn't the main problem; open-vocabulary approach offers training-free gains and can enhance LiDAR-only detectors via camera cues.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of fixed-category detectors by exploring training-free, open-vocabulary 3D detection leveraging segmentation prompts and geometry-based box construction.
AI.method: Three-stage controlled evaluation on nuScenes: (1) geometry from images alone with fixed 2D detections; (2) fit LiDAR points inside segmentation masks to derive boxes using training-free rules; (3) use supervised 3D box geometry at inference. Also a camera-witness rule and coverage analysis using SAM3 masks.
AI.result: Metrics: image-only geometry yields 0.183 mAP; training-free LiDAR-point fitting yields 0.298 mAP / 0.348 NDS; using supervised geometry yields 0.413 mAP / 0.555 NDS. A camera-witness rule improves a LiDAR-only detector from 0.596 to 0.630 mAP. SAM3 achieves 84% in-range object coverage with correct naming; performance drops are due to misnaming or geometric difficulty rather than invisibility.
AI.conclusion: Open-vocabulary, training-free segmentation-driven 3D detection can substantially bridge the gap with supervised methods, but measurement precision and robust naming remain key bottlenecks; best strategy may combine strong 2D segmentation with geometry-aware fusion.

title: AthenaZero: A low-inertia, bimanual robot for dynamic manipulation
comment: Videos attached as ancillary. Cover article to September 2026 issue of Science Robotics
summary: AthenaZero is a bimanual manipulator designed to minimize inertia without compromising control authority. By utilizing quasi-direct drive actuation and transmission remotization techniques, the system achieves an effective endpoint mass comparable to that of a human---about an order of magnitude less than conventional robot manipulators. This characteristic, combined with its inherent torque transparency, makes AthenaZero exceptionally well-suited for dynamic manipulation. We describe the methodology} that led to this design and demonstrate the robot's capabilities on three baseball-inspired tasks: throwing, catching, and batting, which showcase complex interactions on human-comparable timescales where milliseconds matter. AthenaZero was capable of throwing at speeds in excess of 30 m/s, with catching and batting at speeds in excess of 14 m/s over a short 7.3 m distance. Batting practice and a game of catch were subsequently performed in robot-to-robot and human-to-robot variations, showcasing the efficacy and adaptability of our system in tasks that require high acceleration.

AI.tldr: Low-inertia, torque-transparent bimanual manipulator enabling high-dynamic baseball-like tasks; achieves human-comparable end-effector inertia and speeds (>30 m/s throw, >14 m/s catch/bat over 7.3 m).
AI.motivation: Enable dynamic manipulation with human-like inertia and control authority by reducing endpoint inertia while preserving torque transparency, addressing limitations of conventional robotic manipulators.
AI.method: Adopt quasi-direct-drive actuation and transmission remotization to minimize endpoint inertia while maintaining torque transparency; develop a bimanual platform and validate on throwing, catching, and batting tasks, including human-robot and robot-robot interactions.
AI.result: End-effector mass comparable to humans and about an order of magnitude lighter than conventional manipulators; demonstration of fast, dynamic tasks with throws over 30 m/s and catches/bats over 14 m/s within 7.3 m; successful robot-to-robot and human-to-robot demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: AthenaZero shows that low-inertia, torque-transparent, quasi-direct-drive systems can achieve high-dynamic manipulation and close human-robot interaction gaps, with potential extensions to broader dynamic tasks and control strategies.

title: Regularized Emphatic Temporal-Difference Learning: Stability under Constant Stepsizes
summary: Emphatic temporal-difference learning (ETD) stabilizes the expected off-policy TD update and changes its projection geometry, but neither property determines constant-stepsize sampled dynamics. We construct an ergodic two-state counterexample in which the ETD mean map contracts while the sampled product has a positive top Lyapunov exponent. Regenerative-cycle analysis separates this sign from the infinite variance of the follow-on trace. We introduce regularized emphatic TD (RETD), a normalized first-order post-shock repair that leaves the trace and importance ratios unchanged, stores the emphatic TD signal in a leaky scalar state, and releases a delayed correction. RETD's raw equilibrium is an affine shift of the ETD equilibrium; single- and two-regularization readouts recover the ETD fixed point exactly. We prove almost-sure convergence for harmonic diminishing stepsizes and a conditional constant-stepsize moment-contraction result from a Markovian random-product bound. RETD has certified negative exponents on the two-state construction and one Baird point, whereas the positive Baird ETD sign remains numerical. Paired 10,000-run experiments validate both separations, fixed-point recovery, a nonmonotone stability region, and task dependence. RETD changes post-shock dynamics; it does not reduce the shared follow-on-trace variance.

AI.tldr: ETD stability and projection geometry under off-policy updates; introduction of RETD, a regularized, post-shock repair that preserves ETD signals while altering post-shock dynamics; rigorous convergence analysis and fixed-point recovery; experimental validation; still does not reduce follow-on-trace variance.
AI.motivation: Understand why constant-stepsize ETD behaves poorly under sampling; create a repair that stabilizes dynamics without changing the essential emphatic signal; provide theoretical guarantees and empirical validation.
AI.method: The authors construct an ergodic two-state counterexample; use regenerative-cycle analysis; introduce RETD with leaky scalar state, normalized post-shock repair; analyze equilibria as affine shifts; prove almost-sure convergence for diminishing stepsizes and a conditional constant-stepsize moment-contraction bound via Markovian random-product; conduct large-scale experiments (10,000 runs).
AI.result: RETD achieves negative exponents for the problematic constructions and a standard Baird point, while standard ETD sign remains numerical; fixed-point recovery by regularization reads; nonmonotone stability region; task-dependent performance; post-shock dynamics altered; follow-on-trace variance remains unreduced.
AI.conclusion: RETD provides a principled stabilization and fixed-point-preserving alternative to ETD with provable convergence; however, it does not mitigate follow-on-trace variance, pointing to fundamental variance challenges in emphatic methods.

title: Generative Query Suggestion via Intent Coverage and Query-Level Credit Assignment
summary: Generative query suggestion aims to enhance user engagement by anticipating user intents and recommending relevant follow-up queries. A central challenge is to generate slates whose individual queries are useful while the slate covers distinct intents. We propose an Intent-Driven Query Suggestion Framework with dual-stage optimization. First, intent-aware diversity modeling constructs intent-aligned supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data and uses an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward to optimize intent coverage. Second, query-level credit assignment routes individual quality signals to the corresponding query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the slate. Experiments on a large-scale production dataset, including online A/B testing and offline evaluation, show improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage.

AI.tldr: A dual-stage Intent-Driven framework for Generative Query Suggestion improves both slate-level intent coverage and per-query quality by combining an intent-aware diversity reward with query-level credit assignment, validated by production A/B testing and offline metrics (CTR, query quality, intent coverage).
AI.motivation: To address the trade-off in generative query suggestion between making each suggested query useful and ensuring the slate as a whole covers a diverse set of user intents.
AI.method: 1) Intent-aware diversity modeling to create intent-aligned supervised fine-tuning data and optimize intent coverage via an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward. 2) Query-level credit assignment that distributes quality signals to individual query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the slate.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on a large-scale production dataset with online A/B tests and offline metrics shows improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-stage optimization effectively balances per-query usefulness with slate-wide intent diversity, yielding measurable gains in CTR and intent coverage and demonstrating the practicality of intent-aware diversity rewards and token-level credit assignment for production systems.

title: LinePilot Digitizer: Line-Plot Recovery with Manual and Automatic Calibration
summary: Recovering numerical series from line plots requires accurate axis calibration and reliable curve extraction. We present LinePilot Digitizer (LinePilot), which combines continuous color-based curve recovery with three calibration modes: LinePilot (standard), LinePilot (enhanced), and LinePilot (OCR). We also introduce DigitizerBench, the first dedicated benchmark for systematically evaluating digitizer performance, using an orthogonal design spanning signal, rendering, and plot-structure factors with complementary automatic and human-guided evaluations. We evaluate performance using failure-penalized capped normalized root-mean-square error (FPC-NRMSE), which assigns unit loss to missing, unusable, or catastrophically inaccurate outputs. On DigitizerBench-Full, LinePilot (OCR) achieves the lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.672) and highest trusted usability (38.2%) among the tested automatic pipelines. On DigitizerBench-Lite, LinePilot (enhanced) achieves the lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.081), 100% output success, and highest trusted usability (93.3%). The orthogonal benchmark design further enables factor analysis to identify the factors that most significantly affect digitizer performance. Together, the three calibration modes provide a practical trade-off between automation, user control, and accuracy within a shared curve-recovery workflow.

AI.tldr: LinePilot digitizer with three calibration modes (standard, enhanced, OCR) and DigitalizerBench benchmark; shows trade-offs between automation, user control, and accuracy; enhanced mode excels on Lite benchmark, OCR mode best on Full benchmark.
AI.motivation: Recover numerical time-series data from line plots with reliable calibration and curve extraction; quantify digitizer performance and provide a dedicated benchmark for systematic evaluation.
AI.method: LinePilot uses continuous color-based curve recovery; three calibration modes (standard, enhanced, OCR); DigitizerBench employs an orthogonal design over signal, rendering, and plot-structure factors with automatic and human-guided evaluations; performance measured by FPC-NRMSE with failure penalties.
AI.result: On DigitizerBench-Full, LinePilot (OCR) has the lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.672) and highest trusted usability (38.2%). On DigitizerBench-Lite, LinePilot (enhanced) has the lowest mean FPC-NRMSE (0.081), 100% output success, and highest trusted usability (93.3%). The orthogonal design enables factor analysis to identify performance drivers; three calibration modes offer a practical trade-off among automation, user control, and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Three calibration modes provide a practical workflow that balances automation, control, and accuracy in curve recovery; the new benchmark enables systematic evaluation and factor analysis of digitizer performance.

title: DITTO: Dexterous Interface for Transparent TeleOperation
summary: Collecting data for manipulation with high-DOF hands is challenging, as interfaces must capture rich hand motion while rendering the contact interactions essential for precise manipulation. Existing data collection approaches face a trade-off: teleoperation ensures deployment consistency but lacks force feedback, while handheld (in-the-wild) systems provide natural force transparency but introduce a visual embodiment gap at deployment. We present DITTO, a Dexterous Interface for Transparent TeleOperation, which resolves this through the anatomically informed co-design of a dexterous 7-DOF robotic hand and a kinematically equivalent motorized exoskeleton. A 1-to-1 actuator mapping between the exoskeleton and robotic hand enables handheld (in-the-wild) data collection and bilateral teleoperation with joint-level force feedback unified in a single platform. We demonstrate that the DITTO exoskeleton spans the operator's natural index-to-thumb workspace, and showcase DITTO's dexterous capabilities via learned policies on contact-rich tasks.

AI.tldr: DITTO combines a 7-DOF dexterous hand and a motorized exoskeleton with 1:1 actuation to enable handheld in-the-wild data collection and bilateral teleoperation with joint-level force feedback, validated by workspace coverage and learned policies on contact-rich tasks.
AI.motivation: Data collection for high-DOF manipulation faces a trade-off between teleoperation (consistent deployment but lacking force feedback) and handheld operation (natural force transparency but misaligned embodiment). A unified platform is needed to capture rich hand motion and contact interactions.
AI.method: Anatomically informed co-design of a 7-DOF robotic hand and a kinematically equivalent motorized exoskeleton with a 1-to-1 actuator mapping, enabling seamless handheld data collection and bilateral teleoperation with joint-level force feedback in a single platform. Validation includes demonstrating the exoskeleton spans the operator's index-to-thumb workspace and showcasing dexterous capabilities via learned policies on contact-rich tasks.
AI.result: The DITTO platform enables in-the-wild data collection and teleoperation with force feedback, achieves wide operator workspace coverage, and supports learning-based dexterous manipulation on contact-rich tasks.
AI.conclusion: A unified dexterous interface effectively resolves the trade-offs in data collection for high-DOF manipulation by providing natural force feedback during teleoperation and embodied, naturalistic data capture during handheld use.

title: BioPhys-Bridge: A Benchmark for Interdisciplinary Scientific Reasoning in Physics-Grounded Biological Research
comment: Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing 2026, 11 pages, 3 figures
summary: Language models face unique challenges in analyzing interdisciplinary scientific research literature. In biophysics research, faithful answers require grounding observed data in source evidence, interpreting it through a quantitative physics model, and linking it to a biological mechanism. To address this challenge, we introduce BioPhys-Bridge, a novel benchmark dataset for evidence-grounded scientific reasoning over biophysical literature. Each case contains evidence blocks, stable evidence IDs, quantitative values, units, equations, assumptions, mechanisms, and next decisions as grounding targets for question answering (QA) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The initial release contains 500 cases, 1,517 agent-facing tasks, and covers six biological domains and nine physical model families, including three sparse families reserved for future expansion. We enforce strict quality gates for all cases in schema, evidence-integrity, quantitative-grounding, source-license, duplicate, unit-normalization, with domain expert review and annotation for 81 cases. Preliminary evaluations show that DeepSeek-V4-Flash obtain the highest evidence-ID $F_1$ score (0.360), followed by Qwen3.7-Max (0.316) and GPT-4o-mini (0.294). BioPhys-Bridge is an interdisciplinary benchmark for evaluating attribution, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, and biological experiment design with complex, multi-step scientific reasoning. Future works will increase the size and complexity of the dataset and perform comprehensive evaluations. Code and data are available in the GitHub repository and on Hugging Face.

AI.tldr: BioPhys-Bridge is a rigorous evidence-grounded benchmark for interdisciplinary biophysics reasoning, with 500 cases and 1,517 tasks across six biological domains and nine physical model families, enforcing strict quality gates; initial baselines show moderate evidence-ID F1 scores; aims to evaluate attribution, faithfulness, and RAG design; code/data on GitHub and HuggingFace.
AI.motivation: LMs struggle to ground observations in source evidence and integrate quantitative models with biological mechanisms; there is a need for a benchmark to evaluate evidence-grounding, unit normalization, and complex multi-step reasoning in biophysics.
AI.method: Assemble dataset with evidence blocks, IDs, quantities, units, equations, assumptions, mechanisms; tasks for QA and RAG; enforce quality gates (schema, evidence-integrity, quantitative-grounding, source-license, duplicates, unit-normalization); expert review of 81 cases; initial release with 500 cases and 1,517 tasks; coverage across six biological domains and nine physical model families, with three sparse families reserved for future expansion; provide baseline evaluations with models; open-source release.
AI.result: Preliminary evaluations show DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieves highest evidence-ID F1 = 0.360, followed by Qwen3.7-Max 0.316 and GPT-4o-mini 0.294; the benchmark enables assessment of attribution, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, and experimental design.
AI.conclusion: BioPhys-Bridge provides an interdisciplinary benchmark for grounding and multi-step reasoning in biophysics; future work to scale data and conduct comprehensive evaluations; code and data available on GitHub and HuggingFace.

title: Layer-wise Curriculum Learning for Efficient LLM Compression
comment: Accepted by the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) 2026
summary: In this paper, we introduce layer-wise curriculum learning for efficient LLM compression. The proposed method facilitates the knowledge transfer from the teacher model to the student model, utilizing a curriculum learning approach that begins with easier optimization tasks and progressively tackles harder ones. In order to adopt the layer-wise learning in LLM compression, we partition the whole model into multiple segments consisting of layers, thereby enabling more computationally efficient knowledge transfer for LLMs. Based on our theoretical analysis of cumulative error phenomenon, layer-wise curriculum learning accelerates convergence while stabilizing the knowledge transfer process. In addition, we present a feature caching method with a multi-threading strategy to efficiently address feature misalignment across layers, maximizing GPU utilization. Consequently, our method exhibits advanced model compression performance, as well as high computational efficiency in terms of minimized memory usage and short training hours. Experiments on multiple datasets show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing GPU memory usage and training hours by more than 50\% on BERT and GPT-2. Moreover, it outperforms the other pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen models under the same training hours, with a lower GPU memory footprint.

AI.tldr: Layer-wise curriculum learning for LLM compression enables knowledge transfer from teacher to student models by progressively harder tasks, partitioning the model into layer segments for efficient transfer. It improves convergence and stability, with a feature caching/multi-threading approach to reduce misalignment and maximize GPU utilization. Empirically, it achieves state-of-the-art compression with substantial memory and training time reductions, outperforming pruning on LLaMA/Qwen under the same compute.
AI.motivation: Reduce training cost and memory during LLM compression while preserving performance; address cross-layer misalignment and convergence challenges in teacher-student transfer by introducing a layer-wise curriculum.
AI.method: Partition the model into layer-based segments and apply curriculum learning from easy to hard optimization tasks for knowledge transfer from teacher to student. Introduce a feature caching strategy with multi-threading to mitigate feature misalignment across layers and improve GPU utilization. Provide theoretical analysis of the cumulative error phenomenon to justify faster convergence and stabilization of knowledge transfer.
AI.result: State-of-the-art compression performance with significant resource savings: GPU memory usage and training hours reduced by over 50% on BERT and GPT-2. Outperforms other pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen under the same training hours, with a lower GPU memory footprint.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise curriculum learning is an effective approach for efficient LLM compression, achieving fast convergence, stable knowledge transfer, and strong compression performance with reduced resource requirements; shows promise for broad applicability to large-scale models and various pruning strategies.

title: Riemannian--Lorentz Fusion of Vision Transformers and State-Space Models
summary: Scaling deep learning faces critical bottlenecks: data exhaustion, exponential training costs, and resource concentration. Model merging combines pre-trained checkpoints without gradient descent, offering orders-of-magnitude savings versus retraining. Combining independently trained vision models is difficult when their architectures and parameter shapes differ. Existing weight-space merging methods generally assume aligned, shape-compatible checkpoints, whereas a Vision Transformer (ViT) and a state-space model (SSM) implement token mixing with different operators. We study a hybrid Heterogeneous merging setting that retains both architectures while aligning parameter groups by semantic role. Our proposed Riemannian--Lorentz Parameter Fusion (RLPF) method projects aligned groups to common coordinates, lifts selected coordinates to the Lorentz hyperboloid model of hyperbolic space, computes a regularized geodesic barycenter, and decodes the result into the two branches. A learned gate then combines branch logits for each input. Component groups use fixed curvature values, with normalization parameters treated as Euclidean. In the results available in this manuscript, the fine-tuned system obtains 82.37\% on CIFAR-10, 75.04\% on Oxford-IIIT Pet, and 78.58\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K; the corresponding best-parent accuracies are 76.54\%, 71.42\%, and 76.42\%. On ImageNet-1K, the reported pre-fine-tuning initialization reaches 77.80\%. These results support further study of geometry-aware heterogeneous fusion, but not a training-free single-checkpoint merge: RLPF is a two-branch hybrid whose gate and reported final models are trained.

AI.tldr: A geometry-aware, heterogeneous model fusion (RLPF) aligns semantically corresponding parameter groups across ViT and SSM, lifting selected coordinates to hyperbolic space to compute a geodesic barycenter, yielding a trained two-branch fused model with a gating mechanism; results show improvements on CIFAR-10, Pets, and ImageNet but require training (not a zero-shot merge).
AI.motivation: Scale deep learning by merging pre-trained checkpoints without gradient descent, addressing data exhaustion, training costs, and resource concentration. Heterogeneous architectures (ViT and SSM) complicate weight-space merging due to misaligned operators, prompting a geometry-aware solution.
AI.method: Align parameter groups by semantic role across two architectures. Map aligned groups to common coordinates; lift a subset to Lorentz hyperboloid (hyperbolic) space with fixed curvature; compute a regularized geodesic barycenter; decode back to both branches; use a learned gate to fuse branch logits. Normalize some groups in Euclidean space; curvature fixed per component. Resulting in a two-branch fused model that is trained (gate and final model).
AI.result: Fine-tuned system achieves 82.37% CIFAR-10, 75.04% Oxford IIIT Pet, and 78.58% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy; best-parent baselines are 76.54%, 71.42%, and 76.42% respectively. ImageNet-1K pre-finetuning initialization: 77.80%. Indicates potential of geometry-aware fusion for heterogeneous architectures but not a zero-training-free single-checkpoint merge; the final deployment relies on the two-branch composition with a trained gate.
AI.conclusion: RLPF demonstrates that geometry-aware heterogeneous fusion can yield performance gains over independent pre-trained checkpoints, but it remains a training-based fusion method rather than a training-free single-checkpoint merge; geometry (hyperbolic) spaces and semantically aligned parameter groups are key to enabling cross-architecture fusion.

title: ULOHA: An Underwater Bimanual Robot System for Robot Learning
summary: Underwater visuomotor policy learning has focused primarily on single manipulators, while bimanual imitation learning has been studied largely in air. We present ULOHA, an underwater bimanual robot learning platform that combines custom-designed leader--follower hardware with software extensions to LeRobot, integrating teleoperation, multi-view sensing, demonstration collection, policy training, and autonomous deployment. Real-robot experiments demonstrate a range of coordinated underwater bimanual behaviors, including inter-arm transfer, shared-object manipulation, and buoyancy-driven interception. We evaluate ACT, Diffusion Policy, and the vision--language--action model SmolVLA on the platform. We investigate how learning methods and execution strategies developed for manipulation in air perform underwater, examining bubble disturbances, buoyancy-driven object motion, action-execution horizons, and real-time chunking. A separate single-arm study examines policy transfer between air and water and shows that demonstrations spanning both media support execution in both under the tested conditions. ULOHA provides a unified experimental platform for studying underwater bimanual robot learning under the coupled perceptual and physical effects of underwater environments. Additional material: https://mertcookimg.github.io/uloha/

AI.tldr: ULOHA introduces an underwater bimanual learning platform combining leader–follower hardware and LeRobot extensions to enable teleoperation, demonstration collection, and policy training; real-robot experiments show coordinated bimanual behaviors and cross-media transfer studies, with evaluation of ACT, Diffusion Policy, and SmolVLA.
AI.motivation: Underwater bimanual manipulation is underexplored, and air-to-water transfer is nontrivial due to bubble disturbances, buoyancy, and perceptual challenges; a unified platform is needed to study and compare learning methods under underwater physics.
AI.method: Hardware: leader–follower underwater manipulators; software: extensions to LeRobot; capabilities: teleoperation, multi-view sensing, demonstration collection, policy training, autonomous deployment. Evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA on bimanual tasks; included a single-arm air–water transfer study and reference to additional material link.
AI.result: Real-robot experiments demonstrate coordinated inter-arm transfer, shared-object manipulation, and buoyancy-driven interception. Investigated bubble disturbances, buoyancy-driven motion, action-execution horizons, and real-time chunking. The single-arm study shows demonstrations spanning air and water support execution in both media under tested conditions.
AI.conclusion: ULOHA provides a unified platform for studying underwater bimanual robot learning under coupled perceptual and physical effects of underwater environments, enabling cross-media analysis and benchmarking of modern learning approaches.

title: What Do We Expect from LLMs? Mapping the Design of LLM Benchmarks
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Data and code: https://github.com/xxcg322/LLM-Bench-Map
summary: Benchmarks are central to how progress in large language models (LLMs) is assessed and communicated. Yet model rankings alone reveal little about how evaluation requirements themselves are changing. The expanding variety of benchmarks offers another perspective: what researchers expect LLMs to do, and what they count as successful performance. We systematically map 14,767 papers introducing or updating evaluation resources from arXiv submissions between January 2022 and August 2026. Using staged screening and automated full-text coding, we examine changes in target systems and domains, evaluation materials and conditions, and scoring mechanisms. The collection shows growing emphasis on action, interaction, and professional applications, while established and newer design elements frequently coexist. Model participation also develops unevenly: LLM-based scoring grows within both agent and non-agent groups, whereas model-generated materials show no comparable sustained increase in recent cohorts. These findings illuminate how public research translates capability expectations into concrete tests and criteria for success. As AI participates in constructing tests, performing tasks, and judging responses, they also raise a question: does expanding evaluation provide more independent evidence, or risk reproducing the preferences and blind spots of its participating models?

AI.tldr: Systematic mapping of 14,767 arXiv papers (Jan 2022–Aug 2026) on LLM evaluation benchmarks reveals evolving expectations: increased focus on action, interaction, and professional applications; benchmarks coexist with established designs; LLM-based scoring expands across agent and non-agent groups, while model-generated materials do not show a sustained rise; raises concerns about independence of evidence and bias in test construction.
AI.motivation: To understand how evaluation requirements for LLMs are changing, what researchers expect models to do, and how success is defined, and to assess whether expanding benchmarks yields independent evidence or reproduces the preferences of participating models.
AI.method: Systematic mapping with staged screening and automated full-text coding of 14,767 arXiv submissions (Jan 2022–Aug 2026) to examine changes in target systems and domains, evaluation materials and conditions, and scoring mechanisms; analyze participation by model-based scoring and model-generated materials across agent and non-agent groups.
AI.result: Findings show growing emphasis on action, interaction, and professional applications; established and newer design elements frequently coexist; model participation is uneven: LLM-based scoring grows in both agent and non-agent groups, while model-generated materials do not show a sustained increase in recent cohorts.
AI.conclusion: Expanding evaluation provides more evidence about capability tests, but risks reproducing the preferences and blind spots of participating models as AI participates in test construction, task performance, and judging responses; highlights tension between independence of evidence and the influence of AI in evaluation.

title: Block Parallelism For Efficient Distributed Long-Context Diffusion Language Model Training
summary: Block diffusion language models (BDLMs) combine autoregressive dependencies across blocks with parallel denoising within blocks, but long-context training is constrained by distributed attention communication and activation memory. Conventional context parallelism (CP) shards the combined clean-plus-corrupted sequence by position, communicating shared clean K/V together with block-specific corrupted K/V and their gradients. We observe that the BDLM objective separates over target blocks. We introduce block parallelism (BP), a new distributed parallelism dimension that assigns each corrupted-block computation to one rank. To scale BP to long contexts, we introduce context-sharded block parallelism (CSBP), which also shards the shared clean sequence across those ranks. CSBP keeps corrupted K/V and gradients local, avoids replicated clean prefixes, and preserves BDLM training semantics. On 16 H200 GPUs at 256K context, CSBP improves throughput over the best baseline by 1.18-1.45x for supervised fine-tuning and 1.27-1.33x for conversion of autoregressive models to BDLMs, while matching or reducing peak HBM. Full-model speedup reaches 1.61x at 512K. On eight H100 GPUs, CSBP accelerates DFlash2 speculative-decoder training by 2.48x at 512K and 7.59x at 1M. In matched 12-hour DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B SFT runs, CSBP achieves higher pass rates at every trained checkpoint on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench Lite. Code: https://github.com/ScalingIntelligence/Turbo-dLLM

AI.tldr: Introduces block parallelism (BP) and context-sharded BP (CSBP) to scale BDLMs to long contexts. By assigning corrupted-block compute to individual ranks and sharding the shared clean K/V, CSBP reduces cross-rattice communication, keeps corruption/local gradients, and preserves BDLM semantics, yielding substantial throughput and speedups across GPUs and long contexts while maintaining or reducing memory usage.
AI.motivation: BDLMs enable long-context modeling but suffer from high communication and activation memory costs due to distributed attention across long sequences. Conventional context parallelism (CP) replicates clean prefixes and shards sequences by position, causing inefficiencies at scale. A scalable BP/CSBP framework aims to improve throughput and memory efficiency for long-context BDLM training while preserving BDLM semantics.
AI.method: Introduce block parallelism (BP): each corrupted-block computation is assigned to a dedicated rank. Extend to context-sharded block parallelism (CSBP): shard the shared clean K/V across ranks handling corrupted blocks; keep corrupted K/V and gradients local; avoid replicating clean prefixes; maintain BDLM training semantics. Validate via large-scale experiments on H100/H200 GPUs with long contexts (up to 1M tokens), comparing throughput, memory (HBM), and performance on supervised fine-tuning and model-conversion tasks; also report DiffusionGemma SWE-bench pass rates.
AI.result: CSBP delivers 1.18–1.45x throughput gains for supervised fine-tuning and 1.27–1.33x for autoregressive-to-BDLM conversion at 256K context on 16 H200 GPUs; peak HBM is matched or reduced. Full-model speedup up to 1.61x at 512K. On 8 H100 GPUs, DFlash2 speculative-decoder training speeds up 2.48x at 512K and 7.59x at 1M. In 12-hour DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B SFT runs, CSBP achieves higher pass rates at every trained checkpoint on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench Lite.
AI.conclusion: CSBP enables scalable, memory-efficient BDLM training for very long contexts by localizing corrupted-block compute and distributing the shared clean K/V, preserving BDLM semantics and delivering substantial throughput and speedups across diverse hardware and tasks.

title: WZPlanner: Safe End-to-End Path Planning for Autonomous Driving in Work Zones
summary: Work zones alter lane geometry through temporary traffic controls and closures that may be absent from on-board maps, challenging autonomous vehicle (AV) perception and planning. Generalization is also limited by scarce public datasets with structured geometric supervision. We present WorkZonePlan, a dataset comprising 149K+ synthetic and 5K+ real-world multimodal samples with 3D annotations for lane boundaries, work zone boundaries, and driving trajectory options. It also provides 76 closed-loop CARLA scenarios replayed under three weather conditions, yielding 228 Bench2Drive-format evaluation routes. We introduce WAVE (Work-zone-focused AV data generation in Virtual and rEal Environments), a semi-automated pipeline for creating the dataset, and BoundaryFormer (BF), a transformer-based model that jointly predicts lane and work zone boundary polynomials and driving trajectories. BF uses slot attention for boundary prediction. Ablations show that a separate trajectory decoder using boundary slot features substantially improves trajectory prediction over a slot-attention-only approach. Building on this finding, BF++ offers Camera and Camera+LiDAR variants with metric ground-plane encoding, typed boundary/trajectory queries, long-range point anchors, image-space curve refinement, and conservative gated LiDAR fusion. On the 211 routes common to all four models at the evaluation freeze, BF++-Camera and BF++-Camera+LiDAR achieve Driving Scores of 63.0 and 64.4, respectively, compared with 59.3 for SimLingo and 26.1 for TransFuser++ (TF++). BF++ is 40 times smaller than SimLingo and more than 10 times smaller than TF++, while achieving higher Driving Scores. These results support jointly predicting lane boundaries, work zone boundaries, and driving trajectories as a promising direction toward safer AV operation in work zones. Code and dataset: https://github.com/Nishad-Sahu/WZPlanner.

AI.tldr: Jointly modeling lane boundaries, work zone boundaries, and driving trajectories in a unified framework using a dedicated WorkZonePlan dataset, WAVE data generation, and BoundaryFormer (BF/BF++) yields strong, compact models for work-zone AV planning.
AI.motivation: Address safety and generalization gaps in autonomous driving within work zones due to lack of public datasets with structured geometric supervision and the absence of work-zone awareness in onboard maps.
AI.method: WAVE: semi-automated synthetic/real data generation for work zones; BoundaryFormer (BF): transformer with slot attention to predict lane/work zone boundary polynomials and driving trajectories; BF++: enhanced variants with metric ground-plane encoding, typed boundary/trajectory queries, long-range point anchors, image-space refinement, and gated LiDAR fusion; ablations show separate trajectory decoding using boundary slot features improves trajectory prediction.
AI.result: Dataset: 149K+ synthetic and 5K+ real samples with 3D annotations; 76 CARLA scenarios and 228 evaluation routes (Bench2Drive format). Evaluation on 211 routes common to all models shows BF++-Camera 63.0 and BF++-Camera+LiDAR 64.4 Driving Scores vs 59.3 (SimLingo) and 26.1 (TF++); BF++ is ~40x smaller than SimLingo and >10x smaller than TF++; ablations indicate benefits of a separate trajectory decoder using boundary slot features.
AI.conclusion: Jointly predicting lane boundaries, work zone boundaries, and driving trajectories is a promising direction for safer AV operation in work zones. The BF/BF++ family achieves strong driving performance with compact models, and the WAVE-generated data supports scalable evaluation; code and data are publicly available.

title: REACT: A Fully Spiking State-Space Model for Real-Time Event-Driven Temporal Perception
summary: Robotic systems operating in dynamic environments require visual perception that evolves continuously with the incoming sensory stream. Event cameras provide microsecond temporal resolution and asynchronous sensing, but most learning-based methods accumulate events into frames or temporal bins, introducing an integration delay that can limit fast reaction. Here we propose REACT, a fully spiking state-space model for event-driven temporal perception that processes raw events one by one, without temporal accumulation. REACT uses a complex-valued spiking neuron, C-SiLIF, whose continuous-time dynamics are driven by the physical inter-event interval, allowing its internal state to evolve at the temporal resolution of individual events. We evaluate REACT on gesture recognition and time-to-collision (TTC) estimation from full-field event streams, without a target bounding box or localization input. On EvTTC, REACT achieves a 9.59% relative TTC error with 4.6 ms end-to-end inference latency, within 0.15 percentage points of the best learned method while requiring no target prior. At the dataset's mean approach speed, this latency corresponds to only 4 cm of vehicle motion, compared with 1 m for the fastest competing learned method. REACT further supports anytime TTC prediction, zero-shot transfer to a different driving sequence, and INT8 quantization, reducing the estimated energy consumption from 18.5 to 2.8 mJ per 32,768 events. These results show that event-driven spiking state-space dynamics can provide low-latency, continuously updated temporal perception for reactive robotic systems.

AI.tldr: Fully spiking, event-driven temporal perception with no frame/binning, enabling low-latency TTC and gesture tasks via complex-valued spiking neurons (C-SiLIF) and state-space dynamics.
AI.motivation: Overcome integration delay and information loss from frame-based event processing; enable continuous, low-latency perception for dynamic scenes.
AI.method: REACT: a fully spiking state-space model that processes events one-by-one; uses C-SiLIF neurons whose dynamics follow inter-event intervals; no temporal accumulation; end-to-end inference; evaluations on EvTTC for TTC and gesture recognition; supports INT8 quantization and anytime TTC; zero-shot transfer.
AI.result: TTC error 9.59% relative; end-to-end latency 4.6 ms; within 0.15pp of best learned method; at mean approach speed, latency equates to 4 cm motion vs 1 m for fastest competitor; zero-shot transfer; INT8 energy reduction from 18.5 to 2.8 mJ per 32,768 events.
AI.conclusion: Event-driven spiking state-space dynamics can deliver low-latency, continuously updated temporal perception for reactive robotic systems; competitive with learned methods without target priors.

title: Position: It is Time to Virtualize Foundation Models with a Self-evolving Operating System Layer
summary: AI applications have shifted from single, monolithic foundation models (FM) to compound agentic systems. Yet today's stacks remain fragmented: even as protocols (e.g., MCP, A2A) ease tool/agent connectivity, each framework embeds an implicit runtime for state, memory, budgets, and guardrails, making behavior non-portable and governance brittle. It mirrors computing before operating systems, when every program re-implemented basic services. This position paper argues that the field now needs a Foundation Model Operating System (FMOS) -- a system layer that virtualizes FM interactions analogous to how virtual machines abstract physical hardware, giving applications the illusion of dedicated, trustworthy FM instances with effectively unbounded capabilities. Internally, the FMOS orchestrates knowledge across memory tiers, model selection and resource allocation, and verification and policy enforcement. Like the human brain switching between fast intuition and slow deliberation, the FMOS learns when to intervene and when to let inference proceed directly and continuously adapting its policies based on operational experience.

AI.tldr: FMOS: a proposed OS-like layer for foundation models to virtualize interactions, manage memory/model selection, resources, verification, and policy enforcement, enabling portable, trustworthy FM instances akin to virtual machines.
AI.motivation: Current AI stacks are fragmented: protocols connect tools and agents but embed implicit runtimes for state, memory, budgets, and guardrails. This brittleness hinders portability and governance. An FMOS aims to provide a unified, OS-like abstraction for foundation models to improve interoperability, safety, and scale.
AI.method: Conceptual/position-paper architectural design. Proposes FMOS as a system layer that virtualizes FM interactions, with components for memory management across tiers, model selection and resource allocation, verification, and policy enforcement. Emulates human-like control via fast vs. slow thinking, with adaptive, experience-based policy updates.
AI.result: No empirical results; offers a blueprint and rationale. Identifies benefits (portability, trust, scalable governance) and challenges; outlines evaluation directions such as correctness, efficiency, isolation, safety, and governance compliance.
AI.conclusion: FMOS could unify FM interactions, enabling trusted, portable FM instances with effectively unbounded capabilities under managed governance. It acts as a foundation for future agent stacks, balancing responsiveness and deliberation through adaptive policies.

title: Randomized SVD Approximations for Spectral Co-Clustering of Word-Document Matrices
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (ICMLA)
summary: Spectral co-clustering is a useful tool for discovering latent structure in word-document matrices, but its reliance on singular value decomposition (SVD) can make standard formulations expensive on high-dimensional data. This paper presents two randomized approximations for normalized spectral co-clustering of bipartite text data when the numbers of document and word clusters may differ. The first method uses randomized SVD through random projection, while the second combines partial SVD with element-wise random sampling. Across real-world and synthetic datasets, both methods reduce runtime relative to the full-SVD baseline, but their behavior depends on matrix sparsity. The random projection method is the more reliable approximation across the tested settings, whereas the sampling-based method is most useful on denser matrices and provides limited benefit on already sparse text data. These results show that randomized approximations for spectral co-clustering should be selected according to the underlying structure of the data.

AI.tldr: Two randomized approximations for normalized spectral co-clustering of bipartite text data reduce runtime relative to full-SVD; one uses random-projection-based randomized SVD, the other uses partial SVD with element-wise random sampling. Performance depends on sparsity: random projection is more reliable; sampling helps mainly on denser matrices; method choice should align with data structure.
AI.motivation: Spectral co-clustering relies on SVD and can be computationally expensive on high-dimensional, sparse text data. There is a need for fast, scalable approximations that handle differing numbers of document and word clusters.
AI.method: 1) Randomized SVD via random projection for normalized spectral co-clustering with potentially different document/word cluster counts. 2) Partial SVD combined with element-wise randomized sampling. Both aim to approximate the co-clustering solution with reduced computation.
AI.result: Both approaches reduce runtime compared to a full-SVD baseline in experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets. Their performance depends on matrix sparsity: random projection is the more reliable approximation across tested settings; sampling-based method is more beneficial for denser matrices and provides limited gains on already sparse data.
AI.conclusion: Randomized approximations for spectral co-clustering should be chosen according to the underlying data structure, particularly sparsity, to balance speed and accuracy.

title: RGS: Reflection-aware Gaussian Splatting via Learning Geometry Continuity for Reflective Objects
summary: Gaussian Splatting has significantly improved the quality of novel view synthesis with explicit Gaussian representation. However, we observed that existing 3D Gaussian Splatting methods (3DGS) often suffer from surface collapse issues on reflective regions, and thus produce inferior geometry and low-quality specular. In this work, we propose a physically-based deferred rendering framework, named Reflection-aware Gaussian Splatting (RGS), that can accurately model specular regions and improve novel view synthesis performance. Specifically, we found that a powerful 3D foundation model can provide a strong 3D geometric prior to foster correct geometric modeling. Based on this, we propose a cross-view shape consistency regularization to regularize the geometry surface with the large model prior and cross-view constraints. In this manner, our RGS can produce smoother geometric surfaces on reflective regions while reducing geometric hollows. To further improve rendering results on reflective regions, we present a reflection-aware densification strategy that is designed to capture specular variations across various views. With this strategy, our RGS is able to render novel views of objects in higher quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate our method consistently renders high-quality reflective objects, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: Reflection-aware Gaussian Splatting (RGS): a physically-based deferred rendering framework that uses cross-view shape consistency with a large 3D foundation model prior and a reflection-aware densification strategy to improve geometry and specular rendering in 3D Gaussian Splatting, achieving state-of-the-art results for reflective objects.
AI.motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting methods (3DGS) struggle with surface collapse and poor rendering in reflective regions, leading to degraded geometry and low-quality speculars. There is a need to robustly model specular regions and leverage strong 3D geometric priors to improve novel view synthesis.
AI.method: Propose a physically-based deferred rendering framework, RGS, that: (1) incorporates a strong 3D foundation model as a geometric prior; (2) introduces a cross-view shape consistency regularization to align geometry with the priors and cross-view constraints; (3) adds a reflection-aware densification strategy to capture specular variations across views, enabling higher-quality rendering of reflective objects.
AI.result: RGS produces smoother geometric surfaces on reflective regions, reduces geometric hollows, and renders high-quality reflective objects across novel views, achieving state-of-the-art performance on experiments.
AI.conclusion: Integrating a strong 3D prior via a foundation model with cross-view regularization and a reflection-aware densification strategy enables accurate specular modeling in 3D Gaussian Splatting, improving geometry quality and novel view rendering for reflective scenes.

title: 4D Radar Perception Algorithms for Autonomous Driving: A Review
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to IEEE Sensors Journal
summary: Research on 4D millimeter-wave radar perception algorithms has flourished in recent years, extending from signal processing and object detection to semantic segmentation, motion estimation, occupancy prediction, and dynamic scene reconstruction. This review organizes the field according to the evolution of perception tasks and algorithms. It first introduces radar fundamentals, data representations, and quality-enhancement methods, and then reviews object-level perception, motion and localization, local and dense spatial perception, and dynamic scene understanding. Across these directions, we compare radar-only learning, multimodal fusion, and cross-modal supervision and knowledge distillation. Particular attention is paid to how elevation, Doppler measurements, and radar physical priors are exploited across tasks. We further summarize the task coverage, input data, annotations, and evaluation protocols of existing datasets, clarifying the empirical support for different research directions. Finally, we discuss the common challenges and future directions of 4D radar perception for autonomous driving. This review provides a task-oriented perspective on the transition from sparse object perception to dynamic spatial understanding.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive task-oriented survey of 4D mmWave radar perception for autonomous driving, spanning fundamentals, data representations, perception tasks, fusion strategies, datasets, and future challenges.
AI.motivation: To organize the rapidly growing 4D radar literature by perception task and algorithm, clarify data/annotation protocols, and chart future directions.
AI.method: Literature review structured along perception tasks (object-level, motion/localization, local/dense spatial perception, dynamic scene understanding); compare radar-only, multimodal fusion, cross-modal supervision/knowledge distillation; summarize data representations, priors (elevation, Doppler); catalog datasets and evaluation protocols; discuss challenges and future directions.
AI.result: A unified taxonomy and synthesis across tasks; emphasis on how elevation, Doppler, and radar priors are exploited; detailed dataset/annotation/evaluation landscape; highlights gaps and roadmap for future research.
AI.conclusion: The field is transitioning from sparse object perception to dynamic spatial understanding; suggests task-oriented research directions and standardized benchmarks to advance autonomous driving applications.

title: What Do Current Systematic Generalization Tasks Miss? A Reasoning-Centered Analysis
summary: Systematic generalization, the ability to solve novel problems by recombining known atomic elements, is central to human intelligence but difficult to study rigorously under controlled settings. Existing studies therefore rely on simplifications such as approximately linear action composition, productivity-based tests, and action-explicit goals, which make systematic generalization easier to study but omit some essential aspects of this capability. To characterize what these simplifications miss, we adopt a reasoning-centered lens and introduce TranSGrid, a testbed that brings deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning together within a unified task. Experiments with seven Transformers on 4,800 TranSGrid instances show that all models perform much worse on TranSGrid than on a held-out test set: the largest model solves 79.6% of the test set, but only 55.3% of TranSGrid and 15.8% of the hardest subset. The gap remains within the training length range, showing that productivity alone is not sufficient to evaluate systematic generalization. Additionally, we reintroduce the other two simplifications into TranSGrid: one variant makes actions compose almost linearly (reducing the inductive demand), the other makes goals action-explicit (reducing the abductive one). In both, solve rates return to roughly the test set level, showing that either simplification alone is enough to reduce TranSGrid to an ordinary held-out test set. Together, our results show that existing tasks reduce either or both of the inductive and abductive demands, and that comprehensively measuring systematic generalization requires a task that involves all three forms of reasoning.

AI.tldr: Introduces TranSGrid, a reasoning-centered testbed combining deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning to assess systematic generalization; Transformers struggle on TranSGrid despite strong test-set performance, and simplifying any single reasoning demand reduces it to ordinary generalization, underscoring the need for comprehensive evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing systematic-generalization benchmarks rely on simplifications (linear action composition, productivity-based tasks, and explicit goals) that mask inductive and abductive reasoning demands. A unified framework is needed to quantify performance when all three reasoning forms are required.
AI.method: Construct TranSGrid to integrate deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning in a single task and evaluate seven Transformer models on 4,800 instances. Analyze performance gaps versus a held-out test set. Introduce two variants that relax inductive (almost-linear action composition) or abductive (action-explicit goals) demands to assess their impact.
AI.result: On 4,800 TranSGrid instances, the largest model solves 79.6% of the held-out test set, but only 55.3% of TranSGrid and 15.8% on the hardest subset. The performance gap persists across training lengths. When either inductive or abductive demands are relaxed, solve rates revert to near the test-set level, indicating that each simplification alone is sufficient to align TranSGrid with standard generalization.
AI.conclusion: Existing benchmarks tend to undertest inductive and abductive reasoning; a comprehensive measure of systematic generalization requires tasks engaging all three forms of reasoning (deductive, inductive, abductive). TranSGrid reveals substantial generalization gaps and shows how simplifying one reasoning form erodes the challenge.

title: Radio-Frequency Convolutional Neural Networks
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary Information: 50 pages, 31 figures, 1 table
summary: Running artificial intelligence (AI) models directly on edge devices such as smartphones, wearables, and drones offers low latency, pervasive scalability, and data privacy, but these devices rarely carry the computing capability that modern neural networks demand. Edge accelerators have been developed in response, yet each adds computing hardware to devices already constrained in size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C). An alternative lies in what these devices already carry: the frequency mixer in every wireless radio multiplies signals in time, natively performing convolution in the frequency domain. Here we introduce radio-frequency convolutional neural networks (RF-CNNs), which repurpose existing communication hardware for CNN inference. Multi-channel convolutions are mapped onto frequency tones for a passive mixer to execute in a single pass. We experimentally demonstrate that RF-CNN runs deep CNNs up to 26.4 million parameters and nine layers from classification of wireless signals and images to controllable image generation, close to full-precision performance. Because the weights arrive over the air and the analog hardware is shared with communication, the edge device spends energy only on data preparation and readout-down to 0.72 femtojoules per multiply-accumulate, two orders of magnitude less than it would cost on an added digital processor. These results suggest that deployed wireless infrastructure can bring efficient, state-of-the-art AI inference to the billions of devices it already connects.

AI.tldr: RF-CNNs repurpose existing radio frequency mixers to perform CNN inference directly in the frequency domain, enabling ultra-low-power edge AI by leveraging shared communication hardware.
AI.motivation: Edge devices suffer SWaP-C constraints; adding dedicated accelerators increases size, weight, power, and cost. Using the radio front-end for computation reduces extra hardware and energy consumption.
AI.method: Map multi-channel convolutions onto frequency tones; use a passive mixer to execute convolution in the frequency domain; weights arrive over the air; inference performed on deep CNNs (up to 9 layers, 26.4M parameters) across wireless signals and images, plus controllable image generation.
AI.result: Performance is close to full-precision; energy per MAC is about 0.72 femtojoules, two orders of magnitude lower than a dedicated digital processor; demonstrates viability on diverse tasks.
AI.conclusion: Deployed wireless infrastructure can enable efficient, state-of-the-art AI inference on billions of devices by repurposing existing communication hardware for CNN execution.

title: Seeing Abnormal from Normal: Glomerular Abnormality in Representations of Normal Renal Morphology
summary: Fine-grained evaluation of glomerular pathology must distinguish normal glomeruli from abnormalities such as global and segmental glomerulosclerosis, obsolescent, ischemic, solidified, disappearing, and atubular glomeruli. Supervised classification requires labeled examples of every category, which is impractical when subtypes are rare or absent from the training cohort. One-class anomaly detection offers an alternative by modeling normal data and scoring deviations, allowing previously unseen abnormalities to be detected. We use the frozen residual U-Net backbone of Omni-Seg, pretrained to segment structurally normal renal primitives without abnormal-subtype labels. We propose NoRDeC (Normal-Reference Detection and Characterization), a framework combining Mahalanobis normal-reference scoring with layer-wise representation analysis to determine whether and where glomerular pathology is encoded, how spatial aggregation affects detection, and whether abnormalities alter inter-layer relationships differently. Using glomerular images from two institutions, we evaluate backbone layers and aggregation strategies, compare NoRDeC with PaDiM and PatchCore, and analyze representations using centered kernel alignment (CKA). Layer 4 with Center-70 aggregation achieved a pooled AUROC of $0.926\pm0.013$. NoRDeC achieved the highest AUROC in six of seven abnormality categories and in the pooled analysis, while CKA suggested subtype-dependent changes in inter-layer relationships not captured by anomaly scores alone. The normal-reference model is fitted using only normal glomeruli; abnormality labels are used for configuration selection, evaluation, and grouping in the representation analysis. These results show that a frozen renal feature extractor can support both detection and representation-level characterization of glomerular abnormalities without using abnormal examples to fit the detector.

AI.tldr: NoRDeC: one-class, normal-reference detector for glomerular pathology using a frozen Omni-Seg backbone; Mahalanobis scoring and layer-wise analysis; achieves AUROC ~0.93 and often outperforms PaDiM/PatchCore; reveals subtype-specific inter-layer changes via CKAs.
AI.motivation: Supervised classification requires abundant abnormal labels, which are rare; need to detect unseen abnormalities using normal data only.
AI.method: Use frozen residual U-Net backbone from Omni-Seg, trained on normal renal primitives; fit Mahalanobis normal-reference in feature space across layers; evaluate with Center-70 aggregation; perform representation analysis with centered kernel alignment (CKA); compare with PaDiM and PatchCore on multi-institution data.
AI.result: Layer 4 with Center-70 yields AUROC 0.926±0.013; NoRDeC highest AUROC in 6/7 abnormalities and pooled; CKA shows subtype-dependent inter-layer changes not captured by anomaly scores.
AI.conclusion: A frozen renal feature extractor can enable both detection and representation-level characterization of glomerular abnormalities without abnormal labels.

title: Grasping by interconnection: robust closing motions from coarse object templates
summary: Dexterous robot hands must often grasp objects whose shape, size, and pose are known only approximately. Grasp planners typically require accurate object models or correct errors with feedback, but how much inaccuracy a closing motion can tolerate on its own remains unclear. To address this question, we designed a motion planner based on four principles: a coarse template of the object, human grasp types, an object-centric interaction, and compliant, sliding contacts instead of prescribed contact points. This paper presents the planner, implemented through virtual model control, and its evaluation on a Shadow Dexterous Hand. Without feedback, the planned closing motions tolerated size errors of about 1cm and pose errors of several centimeters and tens of degrees, a wider range than a state-of-the-art data-driven planner in 25 of 27 tested conditions. They also grasped 82.5% of 80 everyday objects and succeeded within an autonomous pipeline. Robustness can thus be designed into the closing motion itself, rather than left only to feedback. This planner opens a path toward reliable manipulation in uncertain settings, which we will pursue by combining it with adaptive feedback control on the physical hand.

AI.tldr: A planning framework for dexterous in-hand grasping that tolerates object size/pose inaccuracies using a four-principle, contact-based closing motion; demonstrates robustness without feedback on the Shadow Hand, outperforming a data-driven planner in most cases and achieving 82.5% success on 80 objects; argues for designing robustness into closing motion and future adaptive feedback.
AI.motivation: Quantify the tolerance of a closing motion to object inaccuracy and reduce reliance on precise models/feedback in dexterous manipulation.
AI.method: Four design principles: coarse object template, incorporation of human grasp types, object-centric interaction, and compliant sliding contacts; implemented via virtual model control; evaluated on Shadow Dexterous Hand; no external feedback during planning.
AI.result: Without feedback, size tolerance ~1 cm; pose tolerance of several cm and tens of degrees; outperformed state-of-the-art data-driven planner in 25/27 conditions; 82.5% success on 80 objects; autonomous pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Robustness can be embedded in the closing motion itself; plan to combine with adaptive feedback control on the physical hand; supports reliable manipulation under uncertainty.

title: Characterizing Web Search by Conversational LLM Agents: From Search Decisions and Strategies to Results and Responses
summary: Conversational LLM agents increasingly rely on Web search, yet the end-to-end lifecycle of agentic search remains poorly understood. We present the first study of Web search across four major conversational platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and DeepSeek), combining real-world user interactions (invivo) with controlled experiments using the same platform's models by their APIs (invitro). We investigate the quality of agentic decisions to invoke Web search, their strategies to formulate queries, the potential domain preferences in the search results they receive, and the choices they make when transforming search results into grounded responses. We find that Web-search decisions vary substantially across platforms and models, while more frequent Web-search invocation does not necessarily yield better response quality. We further show that conversational agents employ different complex querying strategies and that platform specific search engines return search results from their preferred domains. Finally, although responses are largely grounded in search results, some claims rely on uncited search results, raising concerns about attribution and reliability. Our findings have important implications for the design of future AI agents and Web search tools optimized for conversational retrieval.

AI.tldr: Across four major conversational platforms, this study analyzes how agentic web search is invoked, how queries are formed, and how results are transformed into grounded responses, revealing platform/model heterogeneity, non-monotonic search benefits, domain biases, and reliability concerns.
AI.motivation: To understand the end-to-end lifecycle of agentic search in conversational LLMs and to assess differences across leading platforms.
