AI.method: Combined real-world interactions (invivo) with controlled invitro experiments using each platform's API; examined decision to invoke search, query strategies, domain preference in results, and grounding of responses.
AI.result: Web-search behavior varies substantially by platform/model; more frequent search does not guarantee higher quality; complex querying strategies observed; platform-specific search engines bias results toward certain domains; most responses are grounded but some claims rely on uncited results; attribution reliability concerns.
AI.conclusion: Findings inform design of future AI agents and conversational search tools, emphasizing handling of platform biases, attribution, and reliability; suggests need for better provenance and evaluation frameworks.

title: Learning-Induced Dynamical Transition in Recurrent Neural Networks
summary: Learning in recurrent neural networks can fundamentally reshape their underlying dynamics, transforming initially chaotic activity into stable task-dependent behavior. We develop a non-equilibrium dynamical mean-field theory(DMFT) to describe this transition during learning. We show that a slow feedback-driven learning process generates an evolving effective feedback strength that drives the network through a transition from chaotic to stable dynamics defined by a bifurcation of the DMFT solution. By deriving the two-time correlation function throughout learning, we identify a critical feedback strength and a corresponding learning rate dependent critical time separating these regimes. The transition arises from the progressive deformation of an effective dynamical landscape by the growing learned feedback structure. Starting from the untrained state, the theory predicts the time evolution of the network output during training and shows quantitative agreement with numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: Non-equilibrium DMFT captures learning-driven transition in RNNs from chaotic to stable dynamics; identifies a critical feedback strength and a learning-rate dependent critical time, and predicts output evolution in agreement with simulations.
AI.motivation: Bridge microscopic learning processes and macroscopic dynamical states by modeling how slow feedback during learning reshapes the network's effective dynamics, driving a bifurcation in the DMFT description.
AI.method: Develop non-equilibrium DMFT for learning in recurrent networks; compute two-time correlation during training; track evolving effective feedback strength and identify bifurcation and critical time; validate with numerical simulations.
AI.result: Slow, feedback-driven learning deforms the dynamical landscape, causing a transition from chaos to stability via a DMFT bifurcation. The two-time correlation reveals a critical feedback strength and a learning-rate dependent critical time. Output during training is predicted from untrained state and matches simulations.
AI.conclusion: Learning reshapes network dynamics through growing feedback, yielding a predictable transition and providing quantitative predictions for training dynamics, consistent with numerical experiments.

title: Efficient Unified Multimodal Understanding (EUMU): Winning Solution for the MUMU Track at the 8th LSVOS Challenge
summary: The Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding (MUMU) Challenge requires a single efficient model to jointly perform multi-concept image tagging, open-vocabulary object detection, and image captioning. We present Efficient Unified Multimodal Understanding (EUMU), the winning solution for the MUMU Track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge. EUMU builds on a shared pretrained multimodal model, using its prompt-based capabilities for detection and captioning and training lightweight heads on shared visual features to predict quality, scene, and event tags. Rather than treating the three tasks independently, EUMU applies task-aware inference refinement by reusing task outputs as cross-task cues. For detection, caption cues help recover objects missed by the initial detection. For captioning, detection cues help refine the caption to better reflect the detected objects. For tagging, image statistics refine quality predictions, while caption and detection cues refine scene and event predictions. This design unifies all three tasks within a single model while satisfying the challenge's resource constraints. EUMU contains 239.169M parameters, requires 23.947 GFLOPs, uses 4.5 GB of peak inference memory, and achieves a final challenge score of 17.3409. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Dayoung-Kil/EUMU.

AI.tldr: Efficient Unified Multimodal Understanding (EUMU) delivers a single shared model for multi-concept image tagging, open-vocabulary object detection, and image captioning in the MUMU challenge, using cross-task cue refinement to achieve 17.3409 score with ~239M parameters and modest compute/memory.
AI.motivation: Unify three related multimodal tasks within a single, resource-efficient model, leveraging prompt-based capabilities and cross-task cues to improve accuracy without isolated task-specific models.
AI.method: A shared pretrained multimodal backbone with lightweight task-specific heads predicting quality, scene, and event tags. Prompt-based detection and captioning are used, and task-aware inference refinement reuses outputs as cross-task cues: captions recover missed detections; detections refine captions; image statistics refine quality; cues refine scene/event predictions.
AI.result: Final MUMU challenge score of 17.3409. Model has 239.169M parameters, ~23.947 GFLOPs, 4.5 GB peak memory. Code and models released at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that a unified model with cross-task cue refinement can perform across tagging, detection, and captioning under tight resource constraints, offering a practical solution for integrated multimodal understanding.

title: Learning Safe Humanoid Navigation from Reduced Order Models
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, under review for ICRA 2027
summary: Research in humanoid robotics has achieved rapid progress in locomotion, and recent results have pushed the boundary on autonomous navigation. We demonstrate that a standard single-stage RL navigation pipeline struggles to scale to multi-level and multi-story terrain, limited by the difficulty of complex humanoid terrain interactions such as stairs. To overcome this challenge, we decompose the navigation problem into two pieces. First, we train a policy operating on the reduced order dynamics but with full 3D LiDAR observations to navigate complex, multi-story terrain. We then utilize this navigation knowledge to kickstart a policy operating on the full-order humanoid dynamics, with a frozen locomotion policy in the loop. Additionally, we demonstrate that applying a Poisson safety filter to the navigation policy output recovers safety in the presence of out-of-distribution obstacles, without dropping navigation success rate. We demonstrate the resulting RoM-Nav policy on a Unitree G1, accomplishing mapless multi-floor navigation covering trials with over 10m of vertical displacement and over 100m of path length. Project page with videos https://wdc3iii.github.io/rom-nav/ .

AI.tldr: Two-stage RoM-Nav: reduced-order navigation with full 3D LiDAR to scope multi-story terrain, then bootstrap a full humanoid policy with a frozen locomotion policy; Poisson safety filter preserves safety against OOD obstacles; hardware validation on Unitree G1 achieving 10m+ vertical, 100m+ path
AI.motivation: Single-stage RL navigation struggles to scale to complex, multi-story humanoid terrain (e.g., stairs); need to decouple navigation from full-body locomotion and ensure safety under out-of-distribution obstacles.
AI.method: Stage 1: train a navigation policy on reduced-order dynamics with full 3D LiDAR observations to handle multi-story terrain. Stage 2: leverage this navigation knowledge to initialize a policy for full-order humanoid dynamics, with a frozen locomotion policy in the loop. Apply a Poisson safety filter to navigation outputs to improve safety against OOD obstacles. Hardware validation on a Unitree G1 for mapless multi-floor navigation.
AI.result: RoM-Nav enables mapless multi-floor navigation with over 10 m of vertical displacement and over 100 m of path length on a Unitree G1; Poisson filter maintains safety without sacrificing navigation success rate.
AI.conclusion: A two-stage decomposition plus safety filtering scales RL-based navigation for humanoid robots in complex multi-story environments and demonstrates practical hardware deployment.

title: Do AI Agents Understand Computer Architecture?
summary: Agents are increasingly asked to design hardware, and increasingly reported to succeed. Such reports establish that a design improved; they cannot establish why. An agent that improves an accelerator may be reasoning about the machine, or may be searching competently over knobs whose meaning it never recovers -- and only the first transfers to the next architecture. Existing evaluations cannot tell the two apart, because they vary the agent while holding the framing of the problem fixed. We do the opposite. AutoTuring hands the same agent the same 15-dimensional accelerator space twice: once as named architectural knobs with simulator counters, once as anonymous variables on [0,1], with the evaluator, the legal space and the reachable optima held identical, so that the only thing that varies is whether the problem means anything. The gap between the two is the measurement. On a nine-kernel FP16 GEMM basket, meaning pays: the architect beats a modeled H200 by 5.4% and its blind counterpart by 12.3% on average, with 70.1% fewer simulator calls. It does not pay uniquely: a critic loop recovers most of that gap for the blind agent and buys the architect nothing, so architectural knowledge and structured critique behave as substitutes rather than as complements. We report these as preliminary findings -- five to six runs per condition on a single modeled accelerator -- and take the comparison itself, not the accelerator, to be the contribution.

AI.tldr: AutoTuring compares an agent's performance under two encodings of the accelerator space to separate meaning from knob-search; preliminary results indicate architectural knowledge yields modest gains over a modeled accelerator and larger gains over blind search, with critique able to recover much of that gap; the contribution is the comparison framework, not the accelerator.
AI.motivation: To determine whether improvements arise from reasoning about the machine's semantics or from exploring knob space that lacks recoverable meaning; traditional evaluations confound this; propose a controlled experiment by presenting the same agent with two encodings that differ only in whether the problem has semantic meaning.
AI.method: Instantiate AutoTuring with two encodings: (1) named architectural knobs with simulator counters; (2) anonymous [0,1] variables; keep evaluator, space, and reachable optima identical; compare performance gaps to measure meaning.
AI.result: On a nine-kernel FP16 GEMM basket, the architect outperforms the modeled H200 by 5.4% and the blind counterpart by 12.3% on average, with 70.1% fewer simulator calls. A critic loop recovers most of the blind gap and negates the architect's advantage, suggesting architectural knowledge and structured critique are substitutes rather than complements. Findings are preliminary: five to six runs per condition on a single modeled accelerator, and the comparison itself is the contribution.
AI.conclusion: The paper emphasizes that it's the comparison framework that provides insight into whether improvements reflect real architectural understanding; meaning matters but is not unique; the method is the contribution.

title: Personalized Federated Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Privacy-Preserving Modeling of Heterogeneous Distributed Systems
summary: We present Personalized Federated Hierarchical Gaussian Processes (pFedHGP) for probabilistic regression and classification when data are distributed across heterogeneous clients. Each client's latent function decomposes into (i) a shared global component, (ii) a client-specific deviation that shares the global kernel structure, and (iii) a flexible local residual. Sparse inducing-variable approximations and federated variational inference keep raw data local while the server synchronizes only low-dimensional statistics for the shared component. Full predictive distributions support uncertainty-aware decisions. In application studies, pFedHGP attains perfect fault classification in press tonnage monitoring using 13.77% of labeled cycles and recovers geographic zones in federated air-quality modeling without centralizing station-level time series. An Instantaneous Linear Mixing Model viewpoint links the hierarchy to multi-output Gaussian processes for correlated sensors.

AI.tldr: Proposes pFedHGP: a federated hierarchical Gaussian Process with a global, client-specific, and local residual latent structure, enabling privacy-preserving probabilistic regression/classification and uncertainty-aware decisions; validated on fault classification and air-quality zoning.
AI.motivation: Need for privacy-preserving probabilistic learning across heterogeneous, data-distributed clients. A hierarchical GP framework allows sharing structural information via a global kernel while preserving data locality through federated inference.
AI.method: Latent function decomposes into (i) a shared global component, (ii) a client-specific deviation sharing the global kernel structure, and (iii) a flexible local residual. Uses sparse inducing-variable approximations and federated variational inference; server aggregates only low-dimensional statistics for the shared component; full predictive distributions are produced. An Instantaneous Linear Mixing Model viewpoint links the hierarchy to multi-output GPs for correlated sensors.
AI.result: In applications, achieves perfect fault classification in press tonnage monitoring using only 13.77% of labeled cycles and recovers geographic zones in federated air-quality modeling without centralizing station-level time series; provides full predictive distributions for uncertainty-aware decisions.
AI.conclusion: pFedHGP enables accurate, uncertainty-aware probabilistic learning in federated settings without centralizing data and connects the hierarchical setup to multi-output GP frameworks for correlated sensor data.

title: ParticleSplat: Self-supervised Object-centric Latent Particle Splatting
summary: We present ParticleSplat, a self-supervised object-centric learning method that decomposes scenes into a set of latent ''particles'' representing semantic entities through feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting. Building on the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework, which represents images as a set of particles with attributes such as position, scale, and visual appearance, we address a key limitation of DLP: its inherently 2D nature, which prevents explicit 3D spatial and geometric reasoning that are critical for downstream tasks such as robotic manipulation. Leveraging the structural similarity between latent particles and 3D Gaussian primitives, we introduce a 3D latent particle space trained with a novel view synthesis objective. Our model jointly encodes multiple views with camera poses into a shared 3D object-centric latent space, then transforms particles into particle-aligned 3D Gaussians whose composition reconstructs the full scene. On simulated and real-world datasets, we show that this formulation inherently learns object masks without supervision and supports controllable 3D scene editing, such as moving objects by modifying particles in the latent space. We further establish that the learned 3D representation improves downstream performance on robotic manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: ParticleSplat extends Deep Latent Particles to 3D by using a latent space of 3D Gaussian particles; learns unsupervised object masks and enables 3D scene editing; improves robotic manipulation performance.
AI.motivation: DLP is inherently 2D and lacks explicit 3D spatial reasoning needed for manipulation tasks; a 3D latent particle representation can facilitate perception-to-action in 3D scenes.
AI.method: Encode multiple views with camera poses into a shared 3D object-centric latent space; convert particles into 3D Gaussians aligned with particles; use a novel view synthesis objective to reconstruct the scene; latent space supports manipulation of particles to edit the scene.
AI.result: Empirically, learns object masks without supervision, supports controllable 3D scene editing (e.g., moving objects by editing latent particles), and improves downstream robotic manipulation tasks on both simulated and real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Three-dimensional latent particle representations via 3D Gaussians provide a robust, editable, unsupervised object-centric scene representation that improves 3D reasoning and downstream robotics tasks.

title: OHRID-Retail: An Open Multimodal Dataset of Human Activity in Retail Environments
summary: Open datasets describing human behavior in environments shared with mobile robots remain limited, particularly for retail activities that combine locomotion, reaching, object handling, and robot guided movement. This paper introduces OHRID Retail, an open, human centered multimodal dataset collected from 16 healthy adults performing a simulated shelf picking task under three within participant conditions: no robot, low speed robot guidance, and high speed robot guidance. Each participant completed two trials per condition. Whole body kinematics were recorded using 17 Xsens Awinda inertial sensors and muscle activity was measured at 10 locations using Delsys Trigno surface electromyography sensors. Descriptive analyses demonstrate variation in whole body movement intensity and muscle activation across robot interaction conditions and body locations. OHRID Retail provides openly available raw recordings, processed measures, documentation, and reproducible analysis resources. The dataset can support research in human activity recognition, multimodal sensor fusion, occupational biomechanics, ergonomics, human aware robot navigation, and human robot interaction in retail and related shared environments.

AI.tldr: Open multimodal dataset (OHRID Retail) of 16 adults performing simulated shelf-picking with three robot interaction conditions (no robot, low speed, high speed). Includes 17 Xsens inertial sensors and 10-location EMG; provides raw and processed data, docs, and reproducible analysis resources to support HRI, activity recognition, biomechanics, and ergonomics in shared robot-enabled retail environments.
AI.motivation: Addresses the lack of open, human-centered multimodal datasets in shared, robot-guided environments—especially retail tasks combining locomotion, reaching, and object handling—hindering progress in human-robot interaction research and related fields.
AI.method: Experimental data collection with 16 healthy adults performing a simulated shelf-picking task under three within-subject conditions: no robot, low-speed robot guidance, and high-speed robot guidance. Each participant completed two trials per condition. Data captured with 17 Xsens Awinda inertial sensors for whole-body kinematics and 10-location Delsys Trigno EMG sensors. Descriptive analyses examine movement intensity and muscle activation across conditions and body locations. The dataset includes raw recordings, processed measures, documentation, and reproducible analysis resources.
AI.result: Demonstrates variation in whole-body movement and muscle activation across robot interaction conditions and body locations. The dataset is openly available and supports research in human activity recognition, multimodal sensor fusion, occupational biomechanics, ergonomics, human-aware robot navigation, and human-robot interaction in retail/shared environments.
AI.conclusion: OHRID Retail provides an openly accessible, multimodal resource with rigorous documentation and analysis tools, enabling validation and development of HRI approaches and sensor fusion methods in realistic, shared environments.

title: MAGS: Multi-agent Auto-formalization Guarantees Safety for Agentic Outputs
summary: LLM coding agents now generate complex programs at a scale that makes thorough human review increasingly difficult, raising the risk of safety and security failures. Common approaches, including fuzz testing, static analysis, and LLM-as-a-Verifier, can detect many failures but struggle to cover all possible edge cases. Formal verification addresses this by providing machine-checkable guarantees over specified properties, but traditionally demands substantial manual specification and proof engineering. We introduce a unified multi-agent framework, MAGS, that generates executable programs with formal safety guarantees, using Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation where safety properties can be mechanically checked. MAGS formalizes and freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, translates generated code into Dafny, repairs violations using verifier feedback, and compiles verified programs back into executable code. We evaluate MAGS on 100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, and 20 robotic-arm tasks. Across all 220 examples, it achieves a 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against frozen specifications. Independent safety and functional evaluations further show strong performance across all three domains, while revealing failures when the auto-formalized semantics do not fully capture the target behavior.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent system (MAGS) uses Dafny as a verification-aware IR to generate executable programs with formal safety guarantees across CUDA kernels, terminal scripts, and robotic-arm tasks, achieving 100% success against frozen specs; failures occur when auto-formalized semantics miss target behavior.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated code in high-stakes domains risks safety/security failures; existing testing and verification approaches cover only a subset of edge cases; formal verification can provide machine-checked guarantees but traditionally requires heavy manual effort.
AI.method: MAGS formalizes and freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, translates LLM-generated code into Dafny, repairs violations using feedback from the verifier, and compiles verified code back to executable form. It operates as a unified multi-agent framework with Dafny as the intermediate representation for safety properties.
AI.result: On 220 examples (100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, 20 robotic-arm tasks), MAGS achieves a 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees relative to the frozen specifications. Independent safety and functional evaluations corroborate strong performance, while exposing failures when auto-formalized semantics fail to fully capture target behavior.
AI.conclusion: MAGS demonstrates that combining LLM-driven generation with verification-aware intermediate representations can yield executable programs with formal safety guarantees across diverse domains; the approach relies on well-defined, frozen specs and Dafny-based verification, though gaps remain where the auto-formalization does not align with real-world semantics.

title: How to Guide Your Language Flow
summary: We introduce a new method to guide flow matching models. Our approach, which we call probe guidance, uses the frozen internal states of an existing diffusion model to construct a guidance signal. This works using a similar principle as autoguidance, but eliminates the need for an additional forward pass at inference time and provides a reliable path to ensure that the weak and strong model share similar dynamics. We apply and benchmark this method on continuous diffusion language models, where probe guidance sets a new state-of-the-art performance on unconditional generation. When applied to a 1.7B diffusion language model, probe guidance consistently improves on multiple choice question answering benchmarks. Using our probes, we study the traditional autoguidance setting where the strong model is a weak checkpoint, and find that the weak model must come from a low-entropy region of training. These findings both provide a practical way to improve diffusion language models and shed light on the actual mechanism behind autoguidance, which is currently poorly understood.

AI.tldr: Probe guidance is a zero-cost, state-aware regularization for diffusion language models that uses frozen internal states to align weak and strong models, achieving SOTA unconditional generation and improved QA benchmarks, while revealing that autoguidance’s effectiveness hinges on weak checkpoints from low-entropy training regions.
AI.motivation: Improve diffusion language models efficiently (no extra inference Cost) and gain insight into the mechanisms of autoguidance by understanding how weak/strong model dynamics can be aligned.
AI.method: Construct a guidance signal from the frozen internal states of an existing diffusion model (the probes) and apply it to guide diffusion language models without requiring an additional forward pass at inference time. Evaluate on continuous diffusion LMs for unconditional generation and MCQA, and study autoguidance by comparing strong/weak models.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on unconditional generation for continuous diffusion LMs. Improves multiple-choice QA benchmarks on a 1.7B diffusion LM. Finds that in autoguidance experiments the weak model must originate from a low-entropy region of training.
AI.conclusion: Probe guidance provides a practical method to improve diffusion language models and offers empirical evidence about the autoguidance mechanism, specifically that weak checkpoints from low-entropy regions are crucial for effective guidance.

title: SCOUT: Sim-to-Real Text-Based Person Retrieval by Embedding-Space Prediction over Frozen Video Features
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on AI City Challenge (Track 4). Code and annotations: https://github.com/abtraore/SCOUT-ECCV
summary: Text-based person retrieval under a sim-to-real gap (synthetic training data, a real-image gallery) is usually tackled with costly fine-tuned cross-encoders. We ask whether a frozen-encoder system can compete. We present SCOUT, which casts cross-modal retrieval as prediction in embedding space. A trainable predictor maps the patch tokens of a frozen video encoder into the embedding space of a frozen text encoder under a bidirectional InfoNCE objective, and no encoder is fine-tuned in the base model. The video encoder is V-JEPA, the text encoder is EmbeddingGemma, and the predictor is initialized from a Qwen3.5-0.8B decoder. We make three findings. First, the best frozen text encoder is simply the one whose geometry best matches the video features. A training-free alignment score ranks three candidate text encoders in the same order as their retrieval accuracy on our held-out split (Spearman $ρ= 1.0$); a fourth, LLM-based encoder shows the rule is metric-dependent, holding for a neighborhood-overlap score ($ρ= 0.8$) but not for a linear probe ($ρ= -0.2$). Second, two precision-targeted levers, parameter-efficient ExPLoRA adaptation of the video encoder and a training-free attribute-decomposed reranker built on a vision-language model, improve the top-rank precision that otherwise limits the frozen system, adding 2.2 points of leaderboard R@1. Third, a local-versus-public calibration study explains which interventions transfer to the real domain. On AI City Challenge 2026 Track 4 the full retrieve-fuse-rerank system reaches 84.25 mAP@10 on the final leaderboard, while a single frozen model submitted alone reaches 60.63. Our trained components cost about 95 GPU-hours. CMP, the dataset authors' fine-tuned cross-encoder that trains for sixteen GPU-days, is one fusion member of the full system, not an alternative. Code and annotations: https://github.com/abtraore/SCOUT-ECCV

AI.tldr: Frozen-encoder cross-modal retrieval (video-to-text) via SCOUT uses a trainable predictor to map video patch tokens into a frozen text-embedding space, achieving competitive results with minimal fine-tuning and low compute.
AI.motivation: Reduce the sim-to-real gap and training cost in text-based person retrieval by avoiding fine-tuning of encoders while maintaining retrieval accuracy.
AI.method: A predictor is trained to translate video patch tokens into the embedding space of a frozen text encoder under a bidirectional InfoNCE objective, with both encoders frozen. Video encoder: V-JEPA; text encoder: EmbeddingGemma. Predictor is initialized from Qwen3.5-0.8B. Three strategies are proposed: (1) model selection for the best frozen text encoder via a training-free geometry-alignment score; (2) two precision-focused levers—ExPLoRA parameter-efficient adaptation of the video encoder and a training-free attribute-decomposed reranker built on a vision-language model; (3) a local-versus-public calibration study assessing transferability to real data. The full system uses retrieval, fusion, and reranking; CMP is a fine-tuned cross-encoder considered a fusion element, not an alternative.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) The frozen text encoder that geometrically best matches video features yields the best retrieval; a training-free alignment score orders text encoders in the same way as held-out retrieval accuracy (Spearman ρ = 1.0) for a metric like neighborhood-overlap; a fourth, LLM-based encoder's order depends on metric (ρ = 0.8 for neighborhood-overlap, ρ = -0.2 for linear probe). (2) ExPLoRA adaptation of the video encoder and a training-free attribute-decomposed reranker add 2.2 points to top-rank precision (R@1). (3) Local-vs-public calibration studies explain transferability to real domain. On AI City Challenge 2026 Track 4, the full retrieve-fuse-rerank system reaches 84.25 mAP@10, versus 60.63 for a single frozen model; trained components cost ~95 GPU-hours, and CMP (a fine-tuned cross-encoder) remains a fusion member, not an alternative.
AI.conclusion: A frozen-encoder retrieval framework with a trainable predictor can approach or match strong baselines at reduced compute, provided the text encoder geometry aligns with video features. The approach benefits from geometry-based encoder selection, lightweight video-adaptation, and a calibrated reranker. Some gains depend on metric choice, and the method is sensitive to calibration between synthetic and real data; overall, the method demonstrates practical efficiency and competitive accuracy with a fraction of the training cost.

title: GAVEL: Graph World Models for Verified and Efficient Long-Horizon LLM Task Planning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for long-horizon robot planning, but generated plans often fail to respect embodiment constraints, recover from planning errors, or reason effectively under partial observability. We present GAVEL, a framework for verifying and repairing long-horizon LLM planning built around an explicit graph world model. The graph represents relevant object-relations, action pre-conditions and effects, and probabilistic beliefs over unobserved object locations. This model can predict the consequences of LLM-generated actions before execution, detect violations, and repair those whose corrections follow directly from the world model. This method also reserves LLM replanning solely for errors requiring semantic reasoning. For multi-task instructions, GAVEL reasons over distributions of possible object locations to reorder remaining subtasks and minimize expected search cost. We evaluate GAVEL on BEHAVIOR-1K across 100 single long-horizon tasks and 500 multi-task instructions. With Qwen3-8B, GAVEL improves single-task success from 41.2% to 91.8% and multi-task success from 19.9% to 92.6%. Distributional belief reasoning also reduces travel distance by approximately 5.4% compared with a static variant. These improvements show that an explicit graph world model harness can substantially improve the reliability and efficiency of long-horizon embodied planning across compact and frontier hosted LLM capabilities.

AI.tldr: GAVEL uses an explicit graph-based world model to verify and repair long-horizon LLM plans, predicting consequences, detecting violations, and reordering subtasks under uncertainty; it greatly improves success rates on BEHAVIOR-1K across single- and multi-task settings.
AI.motivation: LLMs enable long-horizon planning but plans often violate embodiment constraints, fail to recover from errors, or struggle under partial observability; a model-based verifier/repair mechanism and selective replanning can improve reliability and efficiency.
AI.method: Construct an explicit graph world model encoding objects, relations, action preconditions/effects, and probabilistic beliefs over unobserved locations. Use it to simulate consequences of LLM actions prior to execution, detect violations, and repair those corrections that follow from the world model. Reserve LLM replanning for semantically challenging cases. For multi-task instructions, perform distributional belief reasoning over object locations to reorder remaining subtasks and minimize expected search cost.
AI.result: BEHAVIOR-1K evaluation: single-task success rises from 41.2% to 91.8%; multi-task success rises from 19.9% to 92.6%. Distributional belief reasoning reduces travel distance by ~5.4% versus a static variant.
AI.conclusion: An explicit graph world model can substantially improve reliability and efficiency of long-horizon embodied planning with LLMs, with GAVEL achieving significant gains on both single- and multi-task tasks across different LLM backbones.

title: Closed-World Resolution Against Tool Hallucination in LLM Agents
summary: Tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents fail in a way no tool-selection or tool-security method addresses: they call tools that do not exist and pass arguments no schema declares. Existing defenses either pick the right tool (selection) or constrain what an agent may do with real tools (gating), both of which presuppose the emitted call refers to a real tool at all. We show this is a structural blind spot: a hallucinated call is by construction not a decision any gate made, so no gate can reject it. This paper is primarily a measurement and benchmark study. We give a five-class taxonomy of tool hallucination (H1-H5) and, as a reference point, the Resolution Rung: a training-free, closed-world resolver (registry membership plus a signature check) whose interest is where it must sit, not what it computes. We prove hallucination defense must precede any causal gate, and characterize the one irreducible residue (borrowed arguments schema-indistinguishable from a valid call). Across ten hosted models under two invocation surfaces we measure 322 genuine hallucinations; fabricated-tool calls concentrate on the unconstrained raw-JSON surface (34 vs. 3), and model scale does not help (a 675B model matches a 7-8B one). We then extend to the Model Context Protocol, where merging several servers into one namespace creates hallucination surfaces a single registry cannot express (a second taxonomy, M1-M5); on the live MCP surface we measure 154 hallucinations, including from frontier models that were clean on the single-registry surface, because collisions and shadowing are structural to the merge. We release the versioned Hallucinated-Tools Benchmark (HTB) so any resolver is comparable across submissions.

AI.tldr: A measurement/benchmark study of tool hallucinations in tool-augmented LLMs, introducing a five-class taxonomy (H1-H5) and a second taxonomy (M1-M5) for the Model Context Protocol, plus the HTB benchmark. Findings show hallucinations persist across model scale and surfaces; fabricated calls cluster on unconstrained JSON surfaces; defense must precede gating; releases HTB for cross-submission comparability.
AI.motivation: Tool-augmented LLMs can emit calls to non-existent tools or with ill-formed arguments, and existing tool-selection or gating defenses fail because a hallucinated call is not a decision made by a gate. A measurement-driven taxonomy and benchmark are needed to understand the landscape, quantify hallucinations, and provide a common evaluation framework.
AI.method: Empirical measurement across ten hosted models and two invocation surfaces; taxonomy-based labeling of hallucinations (H1-H5); analysis of a reference resolver (Resolution Rung) and its placement; evaluation on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) via merging multiple servers into one namespace (M1-M5); comparison of single-registry vs multi-registry surfaces; quantification of hallucinations (e.g., 322 genuine hallucinations across all tests, 154 on MCP live surface); analysis of where hallucinations concentrate (raw JSON surface) and how scale affects results; release of Hallucinated-Tools Benchmark (HTB) for comparability.
AI.result: Identified a structural blind spot: hallucinated tool calls are not gated decisions; a one irreducible residue exists where borrowed argument schemas appear indistinguishable from valid calls; fabricated-tool calls concentrate on unconstrained surfaces (34 vs 3 in a certain split); scale does not suppress hallucinations (675B vs 7-8B shows similar rates); on live MCP, 154 hallucinations observed, including frontier models clean on single-registry surfaces due to merge-induced collisions and shadowing; HTB released for benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: Defense against tool hallucination must precede any causal gating; a comprehensive taxonomy (H1-H5) and a second taxonomy (M1-M5) are necessary to understand surfaces introduced by multi-namespace contexts; measurement benchmarks like HTB enable fair comparisons across submissions; future work should integrate prevention mechanisms upstream and develop registries/solvers that can be verified before gates are applied.

title: Smart Insole Human Activity Recognition for Continuous Monitoring in Elderly Care
summary: Falls in older adults are often preceded by changes in mobility, balance, and postural transitions. This paper presents a wireless smart insole platform and machine-learning workflow for recognizing sitting, standing, walking, and unstable walking from plantar-pressure and inertial signals. Each insole integrates 16 active pressure-sensing locations and a six-dimensional IMU stream consisting of tri-axial acceleration and angular velocity. Data were collected from 15 healthy adults at 80~Hz and segmented into overlapping windows. Window length and candidate model families were first screened with stratified 10-fold cross-validation; the primary performance estimate was then obtained with participant-independent 5-fold Stratified Group cross-validation, ensuring that all windows from a participant remained in a single fold. Under this protocol, Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.954 and 0.959 for the left and right feet, respectively, and 0.980 with bilateral sensing. A compact 1D-CNN evaluated with the same participant-independent folds did not significantly outperform HGB ($p=0.0625$). The results show that low-profile footwear sensing can infer activity state from pressure and IMU measurements for participants unseen during training, establishing a basis for activity monitoring and fall prevention in elderly care.

AI.tldr: A wireless smart insole with pressure sensors and IMU can classify sitting, standing, walking, and unstable walking with high accuracy in unseen participants, using Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting; a 1D-CNN offered no significant gain. Bilateral sensing improves performance, supporting fall-prevention monitoring in elderly care.
AI.motivation: Falls in older adults are often preceded by mobility and balance changes. A portable, noninvasive sensing platform is needed to infer activity states to support monitoring and fall-prevention strategies.
AI.method: Insoles with 16 active pressure sensors and a 6-DOF IMU collected plantar-pressure and inertial data from 15 healthy adults at 80 Hz. Data were windowed and evaluated with stratified 10-fold CV to screen window length and model families, followed by participant-independent 5-fold Stratified Group CV to assess generalization (all windows from a subject in one fold). Compared approaches: Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) and a compact 1D-CNN. Performance was reported for left, right, and bilateral sensing.
AI.result: Macro-F1: left 0.954, right 0.959, bilateral 0.980. The 1D-CNN did not significantly outperform HGB (p=0.0625). Bilateral sensing yielded the highest accuracy, indicating complementary information from both feet improves state recognition.
AI.conclusion: Low-profile footwear sensing from plantar pressure and IMU can generalize to unseen participants and supports activity monitoring and fall prevention in elderly care; HGB is a strong, efficient classifier for this task.

title: AMB3R-SLAM: Kilometer-scale SLAM with Hierarchical Backend
summary: We present AMB3R-SLAM, a real-time monocular SLAM system capable of reconstructing kilometer-scale trajectories over 10k frames on a single consumer-grade GPU. Our model couples a lightweight front-end for low-latency online tracking with a hierarchical backend that progressively enforces local, mid-level, and global consistency. By avoiding bundle adjustment that relies on the static world assumption, our system naturally handles complex dynamic scenes out of the box. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be extended to leverage stereo, RGB-D, and LiDAR as additional inputs. AMB3R-SLAM achieves strong camera tracking performance across 9 datasets, reducing the absolute trajectory error (ATE) of previous state-of-the-art methods on VBR and Oxford Spires by over 70%. With additional LiDAR input, our model further reduces ATE to sub-meter level on KITTI and VBR datasets.

AI.tldr: Real-time monocular SLAM (AMB3R-SLAM) reconstructs kilometer-scale trajectories on a consumer GPU, with a hierarchical backend and dynamic-scene handling; extends to stereo/RGB-D/LiDAR and achieves major ATE improvements.
AI.motivation: Address the static-world assumption of traditional SLAM and the need for long, real-time trajectory reconstruction on consumer hardware, while handling dynamic scenes and enabling multi-sensor inputs.
AI.method: A lightweight front-end for low-latency tracking paired with a hierarchical backend that enforces local, mid-level, and global consistency. It avoids bundle adjustment that relies on a static scene. The system can fuse stereo, RGB-D, and LiDAR inputs.
AI.result: Performs on 9 datasets with kilometer-scale trajectories (over 10k frames) in real time on a single GPU; reduces ATE over prior SOTA by >70% on VBR and Oxford Spires; with LiDAR, achieves sub-meter ATE on KITTI and VBR.
AI.conclusion: AMB3R-SLAM demonstrates robust real-time, large-scale, dynamic-scene monocular SLAM with multi-sensor extension, suggesting strong practicality for real-world navigation and mapping tasks.

title: A Morphing Aerial Robot With Thruster-Integrated Flexible Continuum Links for Shape Adaptive Aerial Manipulation
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
summary: In recent years, aerial manipulation has attracted increasing attention as a key to expand the application of aerial robots. In this work, we focus on two major research directions for achieving versatile aerial manipulation: (i) acquiring high environmental adaptability using soft manipulators, and (ii) expanding the feasible wrench space by distributing thrusters along the manipulator. However, no aerial robot has simultaneously satisfied these two requirements. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a morphing rotor-distributed aerial robot with flexible continuum links that achieves both high shape adaptability and an expanded wrench space. The flexible continuum links function as soft manipulators, passively conforming to the shape of the environment, while the thrusters distributed along the continuum links expand the feasible thrust wrench space and enable the end-effector to exert large interaction forces. To realize the proposed robot, it is essential to suppress vibrations of the lightweight continuum links. Thus, we develop a composite leaf-spring structure that provides both high torsional and vertical stiffness, and vibration-suppressing control methods. Using these implementations, we demonstrate stable flight and a variety of aerial manipulation tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to realize aerial manipulations using flexible links with an integrated thruster.

AI.tldr: A morphing rotor-distributed aerial robot uses soft continuum links as manipulators with thrusters along the links to expand wrench space, paired with a leaf-spring vibration-damping structure; demonstrates stable flight and manipulation, claimed to be the first integration of flexible links with integrated thrusters for aerial manipulation.
AI.motivation: Aerial manipulation is limited by rigid manipulators with small feasible wrench space and poor environmental adaptability. There is a need to achieve high shape adaptability and an expanded wrench space to enable versatile interactions with the environment.
AI.method: Introduce a morphing rotor-distributed aerial robot architecture that incorporates flexible continuum links acting as soft manipulators and with thrusters distributed along the links to broaden the allowable wrench space. Develop a composite leaf-spring structure to provide high torsional and vertical stiffness and implement vibration-suppressing control strategies. Validate through flight experiments and manipulation tasks.
AI.result: The robot achieves stable flight and performs a range of aerial manipulation tasks. It is presented as the first work to realize aerial manipulation using flexible links with integrated thrusters.
AI.conclusion: The proposed design successfully combines high shape adaptability with an expanded wrench space via distributed thrusters along soft links, enabling large interaction forces during manipulation and broadening the capabilities of aerial robots.

title: The syntax and semantics of goals
comment: To appear in Topics in Cognitive Science, special issue on Goal-Centric Perspectives in Cognitive Science
summary: In both cognitive science and computer science, goals are conceptualized as cognitive states that flexibly combine with world knowledge to organize and specify purposeful behavior. In this way, goals are compositional representations whose content relates to rational behavior. We here draw attention to goals as representations and their content because it highlights a parallel with other areas in cognitive science - in particular, the syntax-semantics interface in linguistics and logic - while also foregrounding foundational questions about the expressivity, design, and efficiency of different goal representations. For example, goals are typically taken as fixed and imposing constraints on desirable behaviors, but we can also identify constraints on goal representations themselves, such as whether a particular goal language is sufficiently expressive to capture behaviors of interest, or whether different goal representations capture the same behavior. Here, we synthesize work that aims to characterize the properties of different goal representations and suggest these are points of a broader design space. We close by discussing how distinguishing the form and meaning of goals can elucidate the implicit assumptions we make about goals, inform the study of interactions between higher-level cognition and motivation, and isolate axes of variation for different conceptions of goals.

AI.tldr: Goals are treated as compositional representations that intertwine with world knowledge to drive behavior; there is a design space of goal representations with varying expressivity and efficiency, and distinguishing form from meaning clarifies assumptions and guides the study of cognition-motivation interactions.
AI.motivation: To foreground goals as representations and explore their content, drawing parallels to the syntax–semantics interface in linguistics/logic, while probing expressivity, design, and efficiency of goal representations.
AI.method: Literature synthesis and conceptual analysis across cognitive science and computer science; compare how different goal languages capture behavior, and analyze constraints on representations and their expressivity.
AI.result: Identifies a design-space perspective on goal representations: not only fixed goals constraining behavior but also constraints on the representations themselves; different representations can capture the same behavior; trade-offs exist between expressivity and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Distinguishing the form and meaning of goals clarifies underlying assumptions, informs interactions between higher-level cognition and motivation, and provides axes for comparing differing goal-conception frameworks, suggesting directions for future work.

title: Stiefel Attention: When the Geometry of Transformer Projection Matrices Dominates Optimizer Choice---and When It Does Not
summary: The query and key projections $\WQ,\WK$ in attention are almost always trained by Euclidean optimizers with no constraint on their geometry. We constrain them to the Stiefel manifold and optimize them there with a Riemannian Adam that carries one scalar second moment per frame, caps its step by a trust region, and retracts polarly. Four propositions prove this update is steepest descent in the embedded metric, independent of gradient scale, well conditioned, and exactly $\mathrm{O}(d)$-equivariant, each certified numerically in \texttt{float64}. A fifth supplies the mechanism: weight decay has \emph{identically zero} Riemannian gradient on $\St(d,r)$, since $W = W I_r$ lies in the normal space, so the learned attention geometry survives the collapse cycles that decay drives through the rest of the model. On modular arithmetic grokking, a single run holds $97.0\%$ validation accuracy at epoch 20\,000 against the baseline's $61.1\%$---an unstable endpoint we report as evidence for the mechanism rather than as an effect size. On CIFAR-10 patches the same rule gains $\mathbf{+8.98}$\,pp over 12 paired starts ($t{=}60.6$, $12/12$), and the gap widens with data rather than eroding. The step rule earns this: a fixed-step Riemannian update is degree one in the gradient, so it moves $24$--$40\times$ less per step than an identically shaped AdamW matrix---its frames barely leave their initialization, and freezing them outright costs only $0.28$\,pp. An ablation credits the whole gain to making the step scale free, and nothing measurable to the projector or to equivariance. A negative result sharpens the account: gauge removal cannot motivate the method, because a direction along which the loss is invariant carries no gradient at all.

AI.tldr: Constrain attention projections to the Stiefel manifold and optimize with a Riemannian Adam that uses a scale-free, trust-region update. The approach yields steepest-descent-style updates on the manifold, is O(d)-equivariant, and preserves learned geometry (weight decay has zero Riemannian gradient on St(d,r)). Empirically, it dramatically improves performance on modular arithmetic grokking and CIFAR-10 patches, with ablations attributing gains to the scale-free step rather than the projector or equivariance; a negative result shows gauge removal cannot motivate the method.
AI.motivation: Standard query/key projections are trained in Euclidean space with unconstrained geometry, which can lead to unstable updates and collapse cycles. Constraining them to the Stiefel manifold aims to enforce a fixed-geometry constraint that preserves learned structure, improves conditioning, and provides a principled, equivariant optimization framework.
AI.method: Restrict W_Q, W_K to the St(d,r) manifold. Optimize with a Riemannian Adam variant that uses a single scalar second moment per frame, enforces a trust-region-like cap on step size, and retracts polarly to the Stiefel manifold. Prove four propositions: (1) update is steepest descent in the embedded metric, independent of gradient scale; (2) well-conditioned; (3) exactly O(d)-equivariant; (4) numerically certified in float64. A fifth mechanism: weight decay has identically zero Riemannian gradient on St(d,r) since W = W I_r lies in the normal space. Experiments include modular arithmetic grokking and CIFAR-10 patches; ablations compare to standard Euclidean optimization and gauge/removal arguments; negative result: gauge removal cannot motivate the method since invariant directions carry no gradient.
AI.result: The update on St(d,r) behaves as steepest descent in the embedded metric and is scale-invariant and well-conditioned; the method is exactly O(d)-equivariant and numerically certified in double precision. Weight decay does not affect the Riemannian gradient. Empirically, on modular arithmetic grokking a single run achieves 97.0% validation vs 61.1% baseline at epoch 20,000 (though endpoint instability is noted); on CIFAR-10 patches, the method gains +8.98 percentage points over 12 paired starts (t=60.6, 12/12). The fixed-step Riemannian update moves the gradient by 24–40× less per step than a similarly shaped AdamW, and freezing projections costs 0.28 pp. Ablations indicate the gains stem from a scale-free step rather than the projector or equivariance; a negative result shows gauge removal cannot motivate the method (directions with invariant loss have zero gradient).
AI.conclusion: Constraining attention projections to St(d,r) with a scale-free Riemannian optimization yields stable, well-conditioned, and equivariant updates that preserve learned geometry against collapse. The gains appear to arise from the scale-free stepping rather than the specific projector or equivariance, and weight decay does not perturb the Riemannian gradient on the Stiefel manifold. The work provides both theoretical guarantees and empirical evidence supporting the geometry-aware optimization of attention components.

title: PerSeM: Persistent Semantic Memory for Long-Horizon Open-Vocabulary UAV Mapping
summary: Open-vocabulary segmentation enables rich semantic perception for UAVs, but frame-wise predictions can remain temporally inconsistent across repeated observations and changing viewpoints. We present PerSeM, a training-free persistent semantic memory framework for long-horizon open-vocabulary UAV mapping. PerSeM associates frame-wise semantic observations with persistent world-space voxels and constructs a majority-based semantic memory, which is conservatively refined through history-preserving spatial refinement, trust-aware replay, and context-guided verification. Experiments on the Forest and UAVScenes benchmarks show that persistent 3D memory provides substantial gains in semantic correctness and temporal stability over frame-wise predictions. Beyond this strong persistent-memory baseline, PerSeM provides consistent additional improvements, improving both semantic accuracy and temporal stability across all five evaluated UAVScenes sequences. Analysis using regions identified independently of the final PerSeM predictions further shows that these gains are concentrated in semantically difficult and temporally unstable regions, where majority-based memory is most likely to remain uncertain. These results demonstrate that persistent 3D aggregation provides a strong foundation for long-horizon semantic mapping, while conservative refinement of uncertain memory states can provide additional improvements without retraining or additional neural-network inference.

AI.tldr: PerSeM is a training-free persistent semantic memory framework for long-horizon open-vocabulary UAV mapping that fuses frame-wise observations into a persistent 3D voxel memory, uses majority-based semantics and conservative refinements to improve semantic correctness and temporal stability without retraining.
AI.motivation: Open-vocabulary 3D perception for UAVs suffers from temporal inconsistency of frame-wise predictions across views and time; persistent memory stabilizes semantic maps over long horizons.
AI.method: Associate per-frame semantic observations to world-space voxels to build a majority-based semantic memory; refine memory via history-preserving spatial refinement, trust-aware replay, and context-guided verification; training-free; evaluate on Forest and UAVScenes; analyze region-independently to identify unstable regions.
AI.result: Significant gains in semantic correctness and temporal stability compared with frame-wise predictions on Forest and UAVScenes; persistent memory baseline improves further with conservative refinements; gains concentrated in semantically difficult and temporally unstable regions; no retraining or extra neural-network inference required.
AI.conclusion: Persistent 3D memory provides a robust foundation for long-horizon open-vocabulary UAV semantic mapping; conservative memory refinement yields additional improvements without retraining; suitable for integration into UAV pipelines to produce stable semantic maps.

title: SemSafe-3DGS: Semantic Risk-Aware Active Navigation in Uncertain 3D Gaussian Splatting Maps
comment: Accepted to be presented at the SeMaNa 2026 Workshop at IROS 2026
summary: Autonomous robots operating in partially observed environments must navigate safely while acquiring observations that improve future planning. Existing safety formulations generally reason primarily about geometry. Consequently, geometrically similar scene elements may induce comparable control responses despite having different semantic consequences. We present a semantic risk aware safe-active perception framework for navigation in attributed 3D Gaussian maps. Semantic attributes modulate an Average Value-at-Risk collision clearance model through class dependent risk weights, allowing safety-critical Gaussian primitives to receive greater influence in the composite barrier. The resulting weighted clearances are aggregated into a control barrier function, while a trajectory-relevant active perception barrier promotes observations that reduce geometric map uncertainty along the robot's anticipated motion. Both objectives are integrated in a unified CBF-QP that enforces semantic risk-aware collision avoidance as a hard constraint while relaxing information acquisition when it conflicts with safety or task progress. Experiments demonstrate efficient safety constraint, improved navigation through active perception, semantic dependent trajectory adaptation, and real-robot execution under Ackermann dynamics.

AI.tldr: Semantic risk-aware safe-active perception integrates semantic risk weighting into a CBF-QP framework for safe, information-rich navigation in attributed 3D Gaussian maps.
AI.motivation: Enhance safety and exploration efficiency by differentiating semantics in risk assessment, addressing geometry-only limitations in existing safety formulations.
AI.method: Compute class-dependent risk-weighted Average Value-at-Risk collision clearances from attributed Gaussian primitives, form a weighted clearance barrier; create a trajectory-relevant active perception barrier to reduce map uncertainty; solve a unified CBF-QP hard-constraining semantic risk-aware collision avoidance while allowing information gathering when safe.
AI.result: Showed efficient safety constraint enforcement, improved navigation via active perception, semantic-dependent trajectory adaptation, and real-robot validation with Ackermann dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating semantic risk into safety barriers enables priority to semantics, enabling safe, perceptive navigation under uncertainty.

title: Compositional Reasoning in Language Models under Reinforcement Learning Post-Training
summary: Compositional reasoning is critical for real-world problem solving: since training data is necessarily limited, models must generalize by composing learned skills in new ways. While post-training methods such as reinforcement learning (RL) have substantially improved the reasoning abilities of language models (LMs), their effects on compositional reasoning remain less well understood. We propose a dependency-graph framework to formalize compositional reasoning, yielding three levels of compositionality with increasing complexity. Empirically, we instantiate this framework with data-structure tasks, which provide deterministic reward computation and clear compositional structure. We find a consistent decomposed-to-composed asymmetry: decomposed-skill training does not reliably transfer to composed tasks, whereas composed-task training transfers more readily back to decomposed tasks. We provide theoretical explanation for this asymmetry, and further evaluate compositional generalization under length extrapolation, structural distribution shift, and transfer to tasks requiring unseen skills. Finally, we present a pilot study on real-world tool-calling benchmarks, showing preliminary evidence that the decomposed-to-composed asymmetry can extend to practical settings.

AI.tldr: Introduces a dependency-graph framework for formalizing compositional reasoning and identifies a consistent decomposed-to-composed transfer asymmetry across tasks; supports findings with data-structure experiments and a pilot real-world tool-calling benchmark; analyzes robustness to length, structure distribution shift, and unseen skills; offers theoretical explanation and practical training implications.
AI.motivation: To enable robust compositional generalization under limited data by formalizing compositional reasoning and understanding how training on decomposed versus composed skills transfers across tasks.
AI.method: Proposes a dependency-graph framework with three levels of increasing compositionality. Empirically evaluates on deterministic data-structure tasks to study transfer directions between decomposed and composed skill training; develops theoretical explanations for the observed asymmetry; extends evaluation to length extrapolation, structural distribution shifts, and unseen skills; includes a pilot study on real-world tool-calling benchmarks.
AI.result: A consistent decomposed-to-composed asymmetry is observed: decomposed-skill training does not reliably transfer to composed tasks, while composed-task training transfers more readily back to decomposed tasks. A theoretical explanation is provided. The asymmetry persists under extrapolation, distribution shifts, and unseen skills; pilot real-world benchmark results suggest the effect extends beyond synthetic settings.
AI.conclusion: Training for compositional generalization should emphasize learning composed-task structures, as this transfer benefits broader skill repertoires, and the dependency-graph framework offers a structured lens to analyze and guide such training across both synthetic and real-world tasks.

title: Machine-Learning Assessment of the Predictive Value of Inflammatory Biomarkers for Cognitive Impairment in an Older Hispanic Adult Cohort
summary: Small clinical tabular datasets require interpretable machine learning because deep learning is often impractical and ensemble models can be difficult to inspect. A key pitfall is that statistical significance does not necessarily imply predictive utility. Using data from the Panama Aging Research Initiative--Health Disparities (PARI-HD) cohort (n=165), we implemented a leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes (BNB/CNB) classifier. Within every training fold, each continuous predictor was reduced to a supervised chi-square-derived state, while income entered the model through a categorical likelihood. All data-dependent steps were performed within repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 30 repeats. The demographic baseline achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.630 +/- 0.017. I-309 (CCL1) was the dominant incremental feature, increasing AUC by 0.110, with paired DeLong tests yielding p<0.05 in 100% of repeats. In the pre-specified primary analysis, I-309 produced a fixed-partition DeLong p=0.0018, with robustness assessed across 200 random partitions, where the median p-value was 0.0011. Within the exploratory family of 18 candidate markers, I-309 achieved a Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted q=0.032 on the frozen partition and satisfied q<0.05 in 85% of random partitions, whereas no other marker demonstrated reliable incremental predictive value. Because the fitted model is an inspectable table of thresholds and class-conditional probabilities, these results identify I-309/CCL1 as an interpretable candidate feature for tabular prediction of cognitive impairment, pending external validation.

AI.tldr: Small, leakage-safe, interpretable Naive Bayes approach on n=165 shows I-309/CCL1 as a robust incremental predictor for cognitive impairment; emphasizes interpretability and proper cross-validation; external validation needed.
AI.motivation: Address the need for interpretable models on small clinical tabular datasets where statistical significance may not translate to predictive utility; provide leakage-safe, inspectable predictor framework.
AI.method: Leakage-safe Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes with thresholded continuous predictors via supervised chi-square discretization; income modeled as categorical likelihood; training within repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 30 repeats; evaluation using ROC-AUC and DeLong tests; primary and exploratory analyses with multiple partitions.
AI.result: Baseline ROC-AUC 0.630±0.017. I-309 (CCL1) adds 0.110 to AUC; DeLong p<0.05 in all 100% repeats. In primary analysis, I-309 p=0.0018; robust across 200 random partitions (median p=0.0011). Among 18 markers, I-309 had BH-adjusted q=0.032 on frozen partition and q<0.05 in 85% of random partitions; no other marker showed reliable incremental value.
AI.conclusion: I-309/CCL1 is an interpretable candidate feature for predicting cognitive impairment in this dataset, with consistent incremental predictive value across partitions; external validation is required.

title: A Multi-Modal Generative Model for Tomato Disease Leaves Understanding
comment: In submission to Computers and Electronics in Agriculture Journal
summary: Artificial intelligence for plant disease analysis has advanced from task-specific classifiers to multi-modal models capable of jointly interpreting visual and textual information. However, practical deployment in precision agriculture remains limited because most existing approaches treat disease understanding as isolated prediction tasks, failing to capture the complementary relationships among symptom recognition, severity assessment, and question-driven diagnostic reasoning. In tomato pathology, accurate interpretation of diseased leaves requires more than label prediction; it demands integrating visual symptoms with semantic context to support a comprehensive and explainable understanding. Here, we present SOLAR, a multimodal generative model that understands tomato disease spanning six question-answering tasks. SOLAR learns to align visual features with task-aware language representations by Fusion Expert module based on mixture-of-expert, enabling it to generate contextually relevant answers across diverse diagnostic tasks. By formulating tomato disease analysis as a generative Visual Question Answering (VQA) task, SOLAR provides a flexible framework that supports multi-task inference within a single model while improving performance and cross-task knowledge sharing. We evaluate SOLAR on $41,677$ images, including $216,209$ Question-Answering (QA) pairs to understand tomato leaf disease under both closed and open-ended QA settings. Experimental results show that SOLAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art vision-only, vision-language, and task-specific models across all tasks, demonstrating superior accuracy, robustness, and multimodal reasoning. These findings highlight the potential of generative multimodal modeling as an effective direction for understanding of plant disease. The code for this study is available at https://github.com/EnalisUs/SOLAR.

AI.tldr: SOLAR is a multimodal generative model for tomato disease understanding that unifies six question-answering tasks under a single framework using a mixture-of-experts Fusion Expert to align visual symptoms with task-specific language, achieving state-of-the-art results on a large tomato leaf dataset and enabling open-ended QA.
AI.motivation: Move beyond isolated disease prediction by capturing complementary relations among symptom recognition, severity assessment, and diagnostic reasoning; provide a flexible, explainable, multi-task VQA framework for plant pathology.
AI.method: SOLAR uses a multimodal generative architecture with a Fusion Expert module based on mixture-of-experts to align image features with task-aware language representations. Tomato disease analysis is cast as a generative Visual Question Answering task across six QA tasks, enabling shared knowledge and cross-task transfer. The model is trained and evaluated on a large dataset of tomato leaf images and QA pairs.
AI.result: SOLAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models across all six QA tasks, in both closed and open-ended settings, demonstrating higher accuracy, robustness, and multimodal reasoning. Evaluation conducted on 41,677 images with 216,209 QA pairs.
AI.conclusion: Generative multimodal modeling is an effective direction for plant disease understanding, enabling flexible, multi-task diagnostic reasoning in tomato pathology and showing promise for practical deployment in precision agriculture.

title: Dynamic-LIVO: A Dynamic-Aware LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry System Using Spatio-Temporal Normals
summary: This paper proposes Dynamic-LIVO, a dynamic-aware LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry (LIVO) system for robust state estimation and static colored mapping in dynamic environments. Dynamic-LIVO employs Spatio-Temporal (S-T) normal analysis to identify dynamic LiDAR points and propagates the resulting classification to both LiDAR-inertial and visual-inertial updates, preventing dynamic LiDAR measurements and their associated visual observations from affecting state estimation and mapping. However, S-T normal estimation can be unreliable in newly observed and spatially sparse regions due to insufficient spatio-temporal observations. To address this issue, we introduce a time-delayed S-T normal estimation strategy that defers the classification of insufficiently constrained points and re-evaluates them as additional observations become available. This strategy improves dynamic classification reliability while preserving valid static points for map construction. Extensive experiments on public and self-collected datasets with diverse sensor configurations demonstrate that Dynamic-LIVO improves localization accuracy and produces cleaner static colored maps in challenging dynamic environments. The source code and self-collected dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: Dynamic-LIVO introduces a time-delayed Spatio-Temporal normal analysis to robustly classify dynamic LiDAR points and propagate this information to LiDAR-Inertial and Visual-Inertial updates, improving localization and static colored mapping in dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: Dynamic environments corrupt state estimation in LIVO systems. Spatio-Temporal normal analysis can misclassify points in newly observed or spatially sparse regions due to limited observations; a delay strategy aims to improve classification reliability without discarding valid static points.
AI.method: Propose Dynamic-LIVO, a dynamic-aware LIVO framework that uses Spatio-Temporal normal analysis for dynamic point identification and propagates classifications to LiDAR-inertial and visual-inertial updates. Introduces a time-delayed S-T normal estimation that defers classification for under-constrained points and re-evaluates as more observations become available, preserving static points for mapping. Evaluations on public and self-collected datasets with diverse sensor setups.
AI.result: Dynamic-LIVO yields improved localization accuracy and cleaner static colored maps in challenging dynamic environments across varied datasets and sensor configurations.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively enhances robustness of LIVO in dynamic scenes and enables cleaner static mapping; code and a self-collected dataset will be released upon acceptance.

title: Safety Beyond the Interface: Detecting Harm via Latent States in Large Language Models
summary: Autonomous systems increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) yet the safety infrastructure surrounding these models introduces latency and compute overhead. This limits utility in resource-constrained, time-critical deployments. Existing external guardrail models remain blind to the model's internal workings, creating a fundamental assurance gap. We ask: does the model already know when the content is harmful? We extract activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP classifier probes (12.6M parameters) to detect harmful prompts. Evaluated on WildJailbreak, Beavertails, and AEGIS 2.0, our probes achieve F1 scores of 99%, 83%, and 84%, respectively competitive with 1000x larger guard models while cutting latency and compute costs.

AI.tldr: Small, lightweight probes detect harmful prompts by analyzing activations of LLaMA-3.1-8B, offering a low-latency safety alternative to large guardrails.
AI.motivation: Reduce latency and compute overhead of external safety guardrails while preserving assurance that prompts are harmful, especially in resource-constrained, time-critical deployments.
AI.method: Extract hidden activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP probes (12.6M parameters) to classify prompts as harmful. Evaluate on three jailbreak/safety datasets (WildJailbreak, Beavertails, AEGIS 2.0).
AI.result: Probes achieve F1 scores of 99% (WildJailbreak), 83% (Beavertails), and 84% (AEGIS 2.0), competitive with 1000x larger guard models, while reducing latency and compute.
AI.conclusion: Internal activations of the LLM contain signal for harmful content; small, on-model probes can provide effective safety discrimination at much lower cost, potentially closing the assurance gap without large guardrails—but may have limitations in generalization across tasks, prompt types, and model architectures.

title: FCx: An algorithm for finding Feasible Counterfactual Explanations
summary: Counterfactual (CF) explanations identify changes that alter an input's classification. While existing methods produce realistic and low-cost CFs, they often fail to ensure feasibility, by suggesting non-constructive modifications or incompatible with future changes (e.g., changing an individual's race to secure a job offer). We introduce a refinement of CF explanations that explicitly enforces feasibility. Our approach is the first to efficiently generate CFs that are realistic, low-cost and feasible. We accommodate both hard feasible constraints, specified by domain knowledge users, and soft feasible constraints, inferred automatically via causal inference from the dataset. Our method, Feasible Counterfactual Explanations (FCx), is based on a modified Variational Autoencoder (VAE) optimized with a multi-factor loss function. We measure the cost of a change based on the absolute change in values (proximity) as well as the number of features changed (sparsity) while realism is measured based on the LOF for density estimation, guaranteeing that CFs reside in densely populated regions. Extensive experiments on four public datasets show that our approach matches state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while guaranteeing feasibility.

AI.tldr: Feasible Counterfactual ExPLANATIONS (FCx) refine CFs to be feasible by enforcing hard domain constraints and soft, causally inferred constraints, via a modified VAE with a multi-factor loss to yield realistic, low-cost, sparse CFs. LOF-based realism; proven on four public datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing CF methods produce realistic/low-cost explanations but can be infeasible (e.g., non-constructive changes or changes incompatible with future context). There is a need for CFs that are both actionable and feasible under user-specified or data-inferred constraints.
AI.method: Introduce FCx: a modified Variational Autoencoder trained with a multi-term loss. Enforce hard feasible constraints from domain knowledge and soft feasible constraints inferred via causal inference. Change cost is measured by proximity (abs value changes) and sparsity (few features changed); realism is enforced by LOF-based density to keep CFs in dense regions, ensuring plausibility.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on four public datasets shows FCx matches state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while guaranteeing feasibility.
AI.conclusion: FCx delivers an efficient, scalable approach to generate feasible, realistic, and low-cost counterfactual explanations, accommodating both hard and soft constraints and enhancing the practicality and actionability of CFs.

title: Selective Cotton Boll Localization for Robotic Harvesting: Evaluation of Deep Learning Vision Models Under Field Conditions
summary: This study developed and evaluated a deep-learning-based perception framework for selective robotic cotton picking. The dataset contained 1,008 annotated field images collected using three cameras under varying natural lighting and weather conditions. Object-detection models from the YOLOv8 through YOLOv13 families were evaluated using their default configurations, while segmentation performance was assessed using YOLOv8-seg, YOLOv11-seg, YOLOv12-seg, the Segment Anything Model (SAM), SAMv2.1, FastSAM, and Grounded-SAM with the Recognize Anything Model (RAM). Among the detection models, GELAN-s achieved the most favorable balance between mean average precision (mAP) and inference speed, obtaining an mAP of 86.1%, precision of 81.6%, recall of 76.6%, and an F1-score of 79.0%, with an average inference time of 42.3 ms per image. Among the direct segmentation models, YOLOv12-m-seg provided the most favorable balance between AP@0.5 and FPS, achieving a segmentation AP@0.5 of 83.7% with an inference time of 20.4 ms per image. In the detection-prompted segmentation approach, bounding-box prompts generated by GELAN-s improved the localization of cotton bolls for SAM and SAMv2.1, while SAMv2.1 Tiny consistently outperformed FastSAM and Grounded-SAM with RAM. In the area-based evaluation against manually annotated segmentation masks, YOLOv12-m-seg achieved an $R^2$ value of 0.966, compared with 0.860 for GELAN-s + SAMv2.1 Tiny. Field experiments conducted using a UR5e robotic manipulator, a custom end-effector, and a ZED2i stereo camera further validated the effectiveness of the YOLOv12-m-seg model for real-time cotton boll detection, segmentation, and selective picking under varying confidence levels. These results demonstrate that YOLOv12-m-seg provides an efficient perception model for robotic cotton harvesting and has strong potential for field deployment.

title: ViLoMan: Learning Visual-Proprioceptive Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation Skills for Humanoid Robots
