To overcome these limitations, we leverage instruction-based Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), which can interpret entire images and follow complex textual instructions. We propose a simple yet effective single-stage multi-face forgery detector, called IMFD (Instruction-based Multi-face Forgery Detector), which is trained end-to-end to jointly localize faces and predict per-face forgery labels. Rather than treating face box prediction only as a joint objective, IMFD explicitly integrates predicted face bounding boxes into the instruction as visual cues that enhance instruction grounding and forgery detection. To support the training and evaluation of IMFD, we convert existing multi-face forgery datasets into an instruction-based format. Experimental results and analyses show that IMFD improves multi-face forgery detection by integrating face bounding boxes into the instruction, and consistently outperforms various state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes IMFD, a single-stage LVLM-based multi-face forgery detector that uses predicted face boxes as visual cues in the instruction, converting datasets to instruction format; achieves state-of-the-art multi-face forgery detection.
AI.motivation: Traditional detectors crop and verify each face, ignoring context and inter-face relations, leading to suboptimal detection.
AI.method: End-to-end single-stage detector IMFD that localizes faces and predicts per-face forgery labels; integrates predicted face bounding boxes into the instruction as visual cues to improve instruction grounding; datasets converted to instruction-based format.
AI.result: Experiments show improved multi-face forgery detection and consistent outperformance over various SOTA methods.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating face bounding boxes into instruction grounding with LVLMs enhances multi-face forgery detection.

title: From Wizard-of-Oz Human-Robot Dialogue Collection to a Taxonomy of Robot Response Decisions: A Retrospective Analysis of Assistive Pilot Interactions
comment: Accepted at the Human-Robot Dialogue (HRD) Workshop, held by the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Robots that follow natural-language instructions in everyday indoor environments must act on incomplete human utterances. Instructions often omit essential information, such as the identity of an out-of-view object, an intended destination, or the user's goal. Existing datasets contain little real-world situated dialogue and provide few practice-grounded criteria for deciding when a robot should act, confirm, clarify, or refuse. We retrospectively analyze a pilot Wizard-of-Oz study in which five participants performed everyday indoor tasks, including door opening, drawer opening, feeding, drinking, and cleaning, with a wheelchair-mounted mobile manipulator while the wizard responded without a formal communication policy. This preserved authentic user behavior but produced inconsistent robot-side decisions, motivating an explicit decision scheme. From 40 episodes, we derived a hierarchical taxonomy of six response modes (ANSWER, REPORT_DONE, REFUSE, CONFIRM, CLARIFY, ACT) and four ambiguity types (intent, referential, spatial, intelligibility). Two human annotators and an AI annotator applied the scheme to the pilot data. Clean-label rates were 91% and 89%, and Cohen's ranged from 0.72 to 0.95 across decision-point, mode, and ambiguity levels for both human-human and human-AI comparisons. Fine-tuning LLaVA-1.6-7B on taxonomy-derived labels for ACT and CLARIFY indicates the feasibility of training vision-language models using annotations from our taxonomy. Remaining boundary cases in decision-point identification and REPORT_DONE motivate a constrained protocol for more consistent dialogue collection.

AI.tldr: A pilot Wizard-of-Oz study identifies a six-mode response taxonomy and four ambiguity types to guide robot follow-up in incomplete natural-language instructions, showing high annotation reliability and feasibility of training vision-language models on taxonomy-derived labels.
AI.motivation: Address incomplete human utterances and the lack of real-world, practice-grounded criteria for when robots should act, confirm, clarify, or refuse in everyday indoor tasks.
AI.method: Retrospective analysis of 40 episodes from five participants using a wheelchair-mounted mobile manipulator with a Wizard-of-Oz setup lacking a formal dialogue policy; derivation of a hierarchical six-mode taxonomy and four ambiguity types; dual human annotators and an AI annotator applied the taxonomy; evaluation with Cohen's kappa; fine-tuning LLaVA-1.6-7B on ACT and CLARIFY labels.
AI.result: Six response modes: ANSWER, REPORT_DONE, REFUSE, CONFIRM, CLARIFY, ACT; four ambiguity types: intent, referential, spatial, intelligibility. Clean-label rates ~91% (humans) and ~89% (AI); Cohen’s kappa 0.72–0.95 across decision-point, mode, and ambiguity for human-human and human-AI comparisons. Demonstrates feasibility of training vision-language models with taxonomy-derived labels; boundary cases in decision-point identification and REPORT_DONE suggest a need for a more constrained dialogue-collection protocol.
AI.conclusion: Taxonomy-guided annotation enables reliable, scalable training of dialogue policies and supports building datasets for consistent robot dialogue behavior; future work should refine the decision-point boundary cases and implement a constrained protocol for data collection to improve consistency.

title: Agentic AI Networking for Heterogeneous Unmanned Aerial Systems in Low-Altitude Wireless Networks
summary: Low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs) are emerging as a key infrastructure for heterogeneous unmanned aerial systems that support concurrent services within a shared three-dimensional airspace. Their coexistence creates strong coupling among mobility, connectivity, and shared network resources, while heterogeneous services impose distinct and time-varying requirements. These interactions naturally form a dynamic non-cooperative game in which both operating conditions and coordination objectives evolve over time. Conventional optimization and learning-based controllers typically rely on predefined objectives, limiting their ability to adapt autonomously to changing service requirements and resource priorities. To address this challenge, we propose a hierarchical hybrid large language model (LLM)- multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) architecture organized as a dual-loop structure. Specifically, an outer adaptation loop employs LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent, and reconfigure objectives and resource priorities, while an inner loop executes decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game. A logistics-monitoring case study illustrates how the proposed framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services, adapting to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies. Finally, we discuss key challenges and research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs.

AI.tldr: A dual-loop LLM-MARL framework for low-altitude wireless networks enabling adaptive, game-theoretic coordination among heterogeneous services without retraining MARL policies.
AI.motivation: LAWNs exhibit dynamic, time-varying requirements and strong coupling among mobility, connectivity, and resources; conventional optimization/learning struggles to adapt autonomously.
AI.method: Outer loop uses LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and reconfigure objectives/priority weights; inner loop runs decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game.
AI.result: Logistics-monitoring case study demonstrates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services and adaptation to evolving operating conditions without retraining the MARL policies.
AI.conclusion: Discusses challenges and future directions for scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs.

title: Compressed Active Subspaces for Scalable Bayesian Inference
summary: Active subspace methods provide a framework for quantifying predictive uncertainty in high-dimensional models by identifying and performing inference along parameter directions that have the greatest influence on the model output. However, the construction of active subspaces requires storing many full-dimensional model gradients, which becomes prohibitive as model size increases. We address this limitation by proposing Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS), a scalable approach that first maps the model parameters to a compressed space using a structured isometric embedding and then constructs the active subspace within this reduced parameterization. Our approach substantially reduces the memory required for active subspace construction and enables Bayesian inference for large models where standard active subspace methods become impractical. We demonstrate the scalability of CAS on neural networks of increasing size while maintaining predictive performance and robust uncertainty estimates.

AI.tldr: A scalable pipeline for active subspace analysis via Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS) using a structured isometric embedding to reduce memory and enable Bayesian inference on large neural networks.
AI.motivation: Active subspaces can quantify predictive uncertainty by identifying influential directions, but require storing large full-gradient vectors, which is prohibitive for large models; a memory-efficient method is needed for scalable uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: Introduce Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS): map parameters to a compressed space via a structured isometric embedding, then construct the active subspace within this reduced parameterization, enabling Bayesian inference with reduced memory.
AI.result: CAS substantially lowers memory requirements for active subspace construction and enables Bayesian inference on large models; demonstrated scalability on neural networks of increasing size while preserving predictive performance and robust uncertainty estimates.
AI.conclusion: CAS makes active subspace analysis scalable for large models, facilitating Bayesian uncertainty quantification in high-dimensional settings and broad applicability to neural networks.

title: Understanding and Exploiting Diagonal Attention Sparsity in Autoregressive Image Generation
summary: Autoregressive image generation has emerged as a paradigm for multimodal AI systems due to its compatibility with transformer-based LLM serving infrastructures. However, generating thousands of visual tokens per request makes decoding increasingly bottlenecked by KV cache accesses during attention computation. Sparse attention is particularly attractive for this workload because many visual generation applications tolerate moderate quality degradation in exchange for improved performance and efficiency. While sparse attention has been extensively explored for text-based LLM inference, it remains unclear whether its sparsity assumptions generalize effectively to autoregressive image generation. We present the first systematic characterization of attention sparsity in autoregressive image generation across diverse workloads and representative open-source models. Our analysis reveals several distinguishing properties, including a pronounced prefill-decode asymmetry, strong attention concentration on prompt and local tokens, and a unique diagonal attention sparsity pattern arising from the spatial locality of visual tokens. Motivated by these observations, we propose a diagonal-aware sparse attention mechanism that selectively skips KV entries along the diagonal attention direction within a recent window. Implemented on top of a GPU-based serving system using FlexGen, FlashAttention-2, and custom kernels, our approach achieves up to 3.1x throughput and 1.19x latency improvements with less than 2% quality degradation compared to dense inference.

AI.tldr: Diagonal-aware sparse attention for autoregressive image generation accelerates decoding with modest quality loss; first empirical sparsity characterization for image generation, followed by a diagonal-skipping KV approach implemented on GPUs, yielding up to 3.1x throughput and 1.19x latency gains with <2% quality degradation.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive image generation faces KV-cache bottlenecks in attention with thousands of visual tokens per request. Sparse attention is appealing but its effectiveness for image-domain autoregression is untested; need to understand sparsity patterns and tailor sparse strategies accordingly.
AI.method: Systematic characterization of attention sparsity across diverse image-generation workloads and open-source models. Identify properties: prefill-decode asymmetry, local/token prompt concentration, diagonal attention sparsity from spatial token locality. Propose diagonal-aware sparse attention that skips KV entries along the diagonal within a recent window. Implemented on GPU serving stack using FlexGen, FlashAttention-2, and custom kernels.
AI.result: Achieves up to 3.1x throughput and 1.19x latency improvements with less than 2% quality degradation compared to dense inference.
AI.conclusion: Diagonal-aware sparse attention is effective for autoregressive image generation, leveraging inherent diagonal sparsity from spatial locality to accelerate decoding with minimal quality loss; demonstrates practical gains on GPU-based serving systems and provides a framework for applying sparsity tailored to image tokens.

title: Winning a Won Game: Strict Reach-Avoid-Stay Control Barrier Functions for High-Dimensional Black-Box Systems
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Robots must complete their tasks and maintain the achieved outcomes while avoiding safety failures at all times. Strict reach-avoid-stay (sRAS) formalizes this requirement: safely reaching a target and remaining there indefinitely after first entry. We propose an sRAS Q-control barrier function (CBF) safety filter for high-dimensional black-box systems under bounded uncertainty. Our construction combines a stay value encoding safe permanent residence in a target subset with a reach-avoid value encoding safe reachability of this subset while avoiding target states from which safe permanent residence cannot be guaranteed. We prove that these values jointly yield a valid robust discrete-time CBF and lift them to state-action Q-functions for runtime intervention. For exact values and under a measure-zero condition, our filter preserves sRAS feasibility from almost every winnable initial state and keeps the system safely within the target after first entry, against all admissible uncertainty realizations. We adopt reachability-based adversarial reinforcement learning for scalable value approximation using only black-box interactions. Notably, neither synthesis nor deployment of our filter requires known dynamics, affine structure, value derivatives, or hand-designed barriers. We validate our framework in quadruped gap jumping in simulation and hardware, where the robot crosses the gap, lands safely, and remains safe afterward. Simulated F1TENTH races further demonstrate safe overtaking and lead retention.

AI.tldr: Proposes a robust, model-free sRAS safety filter for high-dimensional black-box systems by combining stay (safe permanent residence) and reach-avoid (safe reach while avoiding traps) values into a robust discrete-time CBF, lifted to state-action Q-functions for runtime intervention. Valid under bounded uncertainty with a measure-zero condition, and learned via reachability-based adversarial reinforcement learning without requiring dynamics models. Validated in quadruped gap jumping (simulated and hardware) and in simulated F1TENTH races for safe overtaking.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical robotics require guarantees to reach a target and remain there safely despite bounded uncertainty, especially for high-dimensional, unknown-dynamics systems where traditional model-based CBF design is infeasible.
AI.method: Define two value functions: a stay value encoding permanent residence in the target subset, and a reach-avoid value encoding safe reach to the subset while avoiding states from which safe residence cannot be guaranteed. Prove these jointly form a robust discrete-time CBF; lift to state-action Q-functions for runtime intervention. Use reachability-based adversarial reinforcement learning to approximate values with black-box interactions; no need for known dynamics, affine structure, derivatives, or hand-crafted barriers.
AI.result: Under a measure-zero condition, the filter preserves sRAS feasibility from almost all winnable initial states and maintains safety within the target after first entry against all admissible uncertainties. Demonstrations include quadruped gap jumping (simulation and hardware) with crossing, landing, and safe residual safety, and simulated F1TENTH races showing safe overtaking and lead retention.
AI.conclusion: The sRAS Q-CBF framework provides a scalable, model-free safety filter for high-dimensional systems under bounded uncertainty, enabling safe repeated operation without dynamics models or hand-designed barriers. It integrates two value components into a robust CBF and leverages adversarial RL for value approximation, showing practical efficacy in both real hardware and simulation.

title: Continual Enterprise World Model Discovery in Dynamic Systems
summary: In an enterprise system, updating one field can set another, create a record, or start an approval. These effects are produced by business rules that are not built into the platform but written by each organization and revised over time. An agent working in such a system cannot predict the result of its own actions without knowing these rules. We study continual enterprise world model discovery, where an agent starts without knowledge of these business rules and discovers them by interacting with records and observing the outcomes. From those observations it builds a world model, which it revises as the rules change. To evaluate this, we introduce EnterpriseWorldShift, built on a live ServiceNow environment with nine tables, 25 hidden rules and 600 evaluation actions. It presents four versions of the same enterprise world, with the tables and records held fixed while a rule is modified, then added, then removed, so that discovery, revision, extension and retirement are each tested in turn. Our Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) builds such a model and carries it from one world to the next. It predicts the effects of the hidden rules more accurately than looking them up for each question, the approach taken by prior work, by up to 8.98 IoU points, and it answers from its own model without querying the running system.

AI.tldr: Agent learns and updates a continual world model of enterprise rules; achieves improved prediction over lookup; validated on EnterpriseWorldShift with rule modifications in a live ServiceNow setup; Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) transfers models across rule changes and outperforms rule-lookup by about 9 IoU points.
AI.motivation: Enterprise business rules are dynamic and not fixed; agents require mechanisms to discover, revise, and transfer models of system behavior as rules evolve.
AI.method: Develop a Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) that builds a world model from observations of records and outcomes in a live enterprise environment. Evaluate on EnterpriseWorldShift with nine tables, 25 hidden rules, and 600 evaluation actions across four world variants where rules are modified, added, or removed, testing discovery, revision, extension, and retirement. Compare to a rule-lookup baseline.
AI.result: CDA predicts effects of hidden rules more accurately than lookup by up to 8.98 IoU points and answers from its own model without querying the live system.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of continual world-model discovery in enterprise settings, with successful knowledge transfer across rule changes and improved predictive accuracy.

title: FedFIbOS: Fisher Importance based Optimal Submodelling for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
summary: Heterogeneous federated learning requires clients with diverse computational capacities to collaboratively train a global model, where each client trains a capacity-constrained submodel. Existing methods select submodel parameters using heuristic importance measures---most prominently parameter magnitude---without theoretical justification for why these measures support convergence. We identify a fundamental gap: existing parameter selection criteria lack theoretical grounding in the convergence framework, partial client participation introduces additional estimation effects in the Fisher scores. We propose \textbf{FedFIbOS}: Fisher Importance-based Optimal Submodelling for heterogeneous federated learning, using Fisher Information in a principled criterion derived from minimizing submodel masking error. %We formally establish when magnitude selection is equivalent to Fisher selection fail under non-IID heterogeneous federated learning. We theoretically formulate submodel selection through a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate and show that the raw Fisher top-$k$ rule implemented by FedFIbOS solves this surrogate under a Fisher-dominant ranking condition. The resulting method retains the convergence structure of the underlying masked federated optimization bound. Fisher scores are efficiently estimated from empirical diagonal Fisher information using squared gradients, enabling stable and adaptive parameter selection without additional optimization overhead. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under pathological and Dirichlet non-IID settings show FedFIbOS achieves ${\approx}10\%$ higher accuracy than the state of the art, with improvements becoming more pronounced under stronger heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: Fisher Information-based submodel selection (FedFIbOS) provides a theoretically grounded criterion for selecting submodels in heterogeneous federated learning, addressing limitations of magnitude-based heuristics and partial participation. It uses a Fisher-weighted masking surrogate, estimates PCA-like Fisher scores via squared gradients, and top-k Fisher selection under a Fisher-dominant condition, preserving convergence properties.
AI.motivation: Existing submodel selection in heterogeneous FL relies on magnitude or heuristic criteria without convergence guarantees, and partial client participation introduces estimation effects in Fisher scores. A principled criterion derived from minimizing submodel masking error is needed to ensure convergence and robust performance.
AI.method: Derives a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate for submodel selection and proves that, under a Fisher-dominant ranking condition, the raw Fisher top-k equals the surrogate solution. Uses empirical diagonal Fisher information estimated from squared gradients for efficient, adaptive parameter selection without extra optimization. Maintains the convergence structure of the masked Federated optimization bound.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under pathological and Dirichlet non-IID settings shows FedFIbOS achieves approximately 10% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art methods, with larger gains under stronger heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Provides a theoretically grounded, efficient submodel selection method for heterogeneous FL that preserves convergence guarantees, outperforming magnitude-based heuristics, especially as data heterogeneity increases.

title: GAPrompt++: Multi-Granular Geometry-Aware Point Cloud Prompt for 3D Vision Model
summary: Pre-trained 3D vision models have substantially advanced point cloud analysis, yet adapting them to downstream tasks via full fine-tuning is computationally expensive and storage-intensive. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) offers a promising alternative by reducing both adaptation cost and storage burden. However, existing prompting-based approaches ignore the intrinsic geometric structures of point clouds, thereby limiting their adaptation capability. This limitation stems from their inability to encode both fine-grained geometric cues and coarse-grained structural semantics, as well as failing to propagate such information effectively through the model hierarchy. To address these challenges, we propose GAPrompt++, a multi-granular geometry-aware prompting method that provides richer geometric guidance for efficient 3D task adaptation. Specifically, we introduce a Point Shift Prompter that extracts multi-granular geometric features across different scales, enabling instance-specific geometric adjustments during adaptation. Next, a Keypoint Prompter adaptively generates point-level prompts to highlight local geometric saliency and fine-grained structural details. Furthermore, a Prompt Propagation mechanism injects these multi-granular geometric cues throughout the feature extraction hierarchy, strengthening the ability to capture essential geometric characteristics. Extensive experiments show that GAPrompt++ achieves state-of-the-art performance among prompting-based PEFT methods and even surpasses full fine-tuning across diverse benchmarks, while requiring less than 2\% trainable parameters. In addition, to address the saturation of existing evaluation datasets, we construct two more challenging benchmarks derived from 3D Gaussian Splatting and Multi-View Stereo reconstruction, offering diverse and realistic point cloud scenarios to promote future research.

AI.tldr: GAPrompt++ is a geometry-aware, multi-granular prompting method for PEFT in 3D vision that outperforms prompting-based baselines and even full fine-tuning with under 2% trainable parameters, by introducing Point Shift Prompter, Keypoint Prompter, and Prompt Propagation to capture and propagate fine- and coarse-grained geometry.
AI.motivation: To reduce adaptation cost and storage in 3D vision by leveraging parameter-efficient fine-tuning, while overcoming prompting-based methods' neglect of intrinsic geometric structures and hierarchical information flow in point clouds.
AI.method: 1) Point Shift Prompter: extracts multi-scale geometric features for instance-specific geometric adjustments. 2) Keypoint Prompter: adaptively generates point-level prompts highlighting local geometric saliency and fine-grained structure. 3) Prompt Propagation: injects multi-granular geometric cues throughout the feature extraction hierarchy. These components are integrated to adapt pre-trained 3D models to downstream tasks with limited trainable parameters.
AI.result: GAPrompt++ achieves state-of-the-art performance among prompting-based PEFT methods and even surpasses full fine-tuning across diverse benchmarks, while requiring <2% trainable parameters. The authors also construct two new challenging benchmarks derived from 3D Gaussian Splatting and Multi-View Stereo to promote future research.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware, multi-granular prompting with propagation effectively enables efficient 3D model adaptation, achieving strong performance with minimal trainable parameters and providing new benchmarks to push evaluation in 3D PEFT.

title: GLAMDRING: Gait Learning And Morphology co-Design via Reinforcement LearnING of CPGs
summary: Robots are moving out of the structured factory floor and into unstructured environments such as disaster sites, planetary surfaces, and agricultural fields, for which the right robot often does not yet exist. We present GLAMDRING, a framework that synthesizes the optimal robot for a locomotion task and, jointly, learns the controller that drives it. For the given specifications of forward-velocity bounds, a per-actuator power budget, an actuator library, and a payload requirement, GLAMDRING returns a matched quadruped morphology (link geometry and per-joint actuators) and a Hopf-oscillator Central Pattern Generator (CPG) gait policy. We rank feasible designs against a target design objective, viz., maximum speed, minimum Cost of Transport (CoT), or max Payload Margin. Because body and locomotion are coupled, the optimal morphology dictates how a robot is driven, while optimal gait depends on the physical body. We train a small number of CPG policies by reinforcement learning across the space of candidate morphologies, co-learning the gait with the underlying robot hardware. Link lengths and actuators are then resolved post-hoc from the policy's logged operating envelope, reducing synthesis cost to a small, fixed number of reinforcement-learning runs instead of one per candidate. Our experiments show three key findings: co-designing body and gait is necessary to satisfy locomotion constraints; actuator-envelope feasibility, rather than locomotion success alone, determines realizable payload capacity; and canonical animal gaits emerge naturally in most designs from morphology and constraints alone. A real-world demonstration further highlights the efficacy of our work.

AI.tldr: GLAMDRING jointly designs quadruped morphology and Hopf-CPG gait policies under actuator and payload constraints, using RL across morphologies and post-hoc geometry/actuator resolution, achieving emergent animal-like gaits and real-world validation.
AI.motivation: Robots operating in unstructured environments require adaptable morphologies and locomotion policies. Fixed-body designs limit performance under diverse tasks and payloads; co-design of form and function is essential to meet joint constraints (velocity bounds, power budgets, payload).
AI.method: Define constraints: forward-velocity bounds, per-actuator power budgets, a library of actuators, and a payload requirement. Use RL to train a small set of CPG-based gait policies across candidate morphologies, co-learning gait with hardware. The architecture yields a matched quadruped morphology (link lengths and actuator choices) and a Hopf-oscillator CPG. Post-hoc, solve link lengths and actuators from the policy's operating envelope, reducing synthesis cost to a fixed number of RL runs. Evaluate objective(s): maximize speed, minimize Cost of Transport (CoT), or maximize Payload Margin; compare feasibility with actuator envelopes instead of only locomotion success.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Co-design of body and gait is necessary to satisfy locomotion constraints. (2) Actuator-envelope feasibility, not just locomotion success, limits realizable payload. (3) Canonical animal gaits emerge from morphology and constraints alone. A real-world demonstration confirms efficacy.
AI.conclusion: GLAMDRING enables efficient co-design of morphology and gait for locomotion in unstructured environments, reducing synthesis cost and enabling real-world validation. The approach highlights the interdependence of body plan and locomotion, and shows emergent, biologically inspired gaits driven by physical constraints.

title: SIMLIFE: Pattern Understanding for Long-Horizon Human-Agent Partnership
comment: COLM 2026 Learning from Situated and Embodied Interaction Workshop
summary: Understanding humans over long horizons requires agents to infer not only what people need in the moment, but also how routines form, why they repeat, and when they change. We introduce SimLife, a scalable platform for simulating long-term household life with rich visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues with audio. Built on SimLife, SimLife-BP evaluates long-context pattern understanding: the ability to infer latent behavioral rules from weeks or months of everyday observations. The benchmark contains 106 episodes averaging 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days, and 1,439 question-answer pairs. Each task probes direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under different levels of rule hints. Evaluating frontier models and architectures, we find that current models often achieve surface-level prediction without comprehensive rule understanding, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning over evidence, and struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change. These findings suggest that long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents, while SimLife opens a broader space for studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction.

AI.tldr: A scalable long-horizon household-life simulation (SimLife) and a benchmark (SimLife-BP) to evaluate models on inferring latent behavioral rules from long-term observations, revealing current models rely on surface cues and struggle with rule-based adaptive reasoning.
AI.motivation: To study long-term human behavior understanding, including routine formation, change, and adaptation, through rich multimodal data and synthetic dialogues to push embodied AI beyond short-horizon prediction.
AI.method: Introduce SimLife platform with rich visuals, ground-truth action logs, and audio dialogues; develop SimLife-BP benchmark with 106 episodes (~15.5 hours; 38.57 in-game days) and 1,439 QA pairs. Tasks probe direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under varying rule hints; evaluate frontier models/architectures on long-context rule inference.
AI.result: Models currently achieve surface-level predictions, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then rule reasoning, and struggle when behavioral patterns change; long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents.
AI.conclusion: SimLife enables studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction, highlighting the need for models with robust rule-based inference and adaptability to evolving behavioral patterns.

title: The Complexity Kink: A Prompt-Side Structural Complexity Index for Code-Generation Reliability
summary: Complexity measured from generated code is failure-dependent: a difficult prompt can yield a short failing program and be assigned low output complexity. We introduce a six-dimension prompt-side structural-complexity index scored before generation and kept separate from correctness. We select 5,000 Python prompts across six bands of a preliminary single-rater rubric. Four out-of-panel LLM raters rescore the locked prompts, giving 19,997 score rows; composite inter-rater reliability is ICC = 0.872 on the 4,998 prompts with all four ratings. We evaluate 21 models per prompt, yielding 105,000 generations. In the unadjusted mean-pooled analysis, pass rate has a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite 13.75, with 79.9% at or below and 87.6% above. This is not a universal failure cutoff. Task-type fixed effects shift the breakpoint to 10.75 and cut the regime gap from 7.6 to 2.1 points. A construction-frame control shifts it to 8.50 with a raw gap of -3.5 points, and neither frame alone reproduces the pooled +7.6-point change. Model-specific fits include 16 upward and five downward changes. A 365-prompt audit-clean extension matches the original five-model estimates at bins 15 and 16 but adds only 14 prompts above bin 16. Among zero-pass generations with computable Lizard complexity, 28.5% pair a prompt composite above 8 with output complexity at most 10. Human agreement is moderate and rater-dependent on a disagreement-enriched calibration set; paraphrase and cross-language rescoring preserve score ordering. Overidentification tests reject the joint restrictions on the six dimensions, so we treat the composite as an index and make no causal interpretation of the 2SLS estimates. The contribution is a pre-generation measurement framework and a bounded observational analysis of reliability regimes.

AI.tldr: A pre-generation six-dimension prompt-side complexity index is proposed to predict code-generation outcomes, analyzed on 5,000 Python prompts across 21 models (105k generations). The study emphasizes reliability regimes and noncausal interpretation, using a large multi-rater dataset, frame-aware analyses, and a bounded observational approach.
AI.motivation: To understand how pre-generation prompt-side complexity affects downstream code-generation success and complexity, independent of correctness, and to establish a pre-generation measurement framework for reliability regimes in LLM-assisted coding.
AI.method: Develop a six-dimension prompt-side structural-complexity index scored before generation. Assemble 5,000 prompts across six bands; obtain four external raters who rescore 19,997 items; compute ICC = 0.872 on 4,998 prompts with full ratings. Evaluate 21 models per prompt (105,000 generations). Perform unadjusted mean-pooled analysis to locate a pass-rate breakpoint; apply task-type fixed effects and construction-frame controls; analyze model-specific fit (16 upward, 5 downward changes); extend with 365-prompt audit; examine zero-pass generations with computable Lizard complexity; assess human agreement and cross-language robustness; conduct overidentification tests and use 2SLS with no causal claims.
AI.result: Pass-rate breakpoint is nonuniversal and shifts with task type and framing (e.g., 13.75 overall, 10.75 with task-type fixed effects, 8.50 with construction-frame control). 16 models show upward changes, 5 downward. An audit-extension aligns with early bins but adds few beyond bin 16. Among zero-pass cases with computable Lizard complexity, 28.5% pair high prompt composites with low output complexity. Human scoring agreement is moderate and rater-dependent; paraphrase/cross-language rescoring preserves ranking. Overidentification tests reject joint restrictions on the six dimensions; the composite is treated as an index with no causal interpretation from 2SLS. Contribution is a pre-generation measurement framework and a bounded observational analysis of reliability regimes.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a pre-generation measurement framework to assess prompt-side complexity and document reliability regimes in code-generation, providing a bounded, noncausal observational analysis rather than causal claims about how prompts drive outcomes.

title: SeetaPsych v1.0: An Open-source Computer Vision Toolkit for Behavior-based Psychological Measurement
summary: Automated visual analysis opens new avenues for behavior--based psychological measurement. Nevertheless, existing technological modules are typically scattered across task specific systems with heterogeneous interfaces and disparate deployment requirements. In this work, we present SeetaPsych v1.0, an open source, unified and extensible computer vision toolkit designed to extract psychologically relevant signals from facial images and/or face based videos. The current release encompasses four major core modules aiming at behavior--based physiological perception: unified face based emotion analysis (simultaneous facial expression recognition, facial action unit detection, and valence--arousal estimation), camera based heart rate estimation, screen point--of--gaze estimation, and scene gaze following. A suite of auxiliary preprocessing modules for human centric visual analysis is also included, comprising face detection, facial landmark detection, and head detection. These functionalities are encapsulated within a modular Pipeline/Runner architecture that automatically resolves attribute dependencies, constructs computation graphs, and support intermediate result sharing among modules. SeetaPsych provides standardized Python APIs to facilitate reproducible, large scale analyses, alongside an interactive WebUI for rapid, code--free method evaluation. Overall, SeetaPsych offers an integrated and accessible visual measurement platform for research in psychology, behavioral science, human computer interaction, and related fields.

AI.tldr: SeetaPsych v1.0 provides an open-source, unified CV toolkit to extract psychologically relevant signals from faces/videos, featuring modules for emotion analysis, heart rate estimation, screen gaze, and scene gaze, plus preprocessing and a Pipeline/Runner for dependency management; includes Python APIs and a WebUI.
AI.motivation: To overcome fragmentation and heterogeneity of task-specific computer vision tools in behavior-based psychology by delivering a single, extensible, reproducible platform enabling large-scale analysis.
AI.method: Four core modules: (1) unified face-based emotion analysis ( FER, facial action unit detection, valence-arousal estimation ); (2) camera-based heart rate estimation; (3) screen point-of-gaze estimation; (4) scene gaze following. Auxiliary preprocessing: face detection, facial landmark detection, head detection. Implemented within a modular Pipeline/Runner that resolves attribute dependencies, constructs computation graphs, and enables intermediate result sharing. Standardized Python APIs and an interactive WebUI for rapid, code-free evaluation.
AI.result: An integrated, extensible platform that standardizes interfaces and deployment for behavior-based visual measurement. The current release encompasses the four core modules and preprocessing tools, with an emphasis on reproducibility and large-scale analyses through Python APIs and WebUI.
AI.conclusion: SeetaPsych offers a comprehensive, accessible visual measurement platform for research in psychology, behavioral science, human-computer interaction, and related fields.

title: Pose-aware Legged Robot Semantic Exploration with Omnidirectional Perception in Confined Unknown Environments
summary: Semantic exploration in confined environments requires both environment mapping and detailed observation of target objects. For ground robots, limited sensor vertical fields of view and restricted standoff distances can leave upper object surfaces unobserved from planar viewpoints. Body tilting can improve coverage, but additional observations and posture transitions increase mission time. To address this trade-off, we present POSE, a pose-aware semantic exploration system that exploits a legged robot's intrinsic body pitch and roll with omnidirectional camera-LiDAR perception. The proposed pose-aware viewpoint sampling module selects body postures from partial object maps according to expected coverage gain, while aim-aligned execution reduces unnecessary body reorientation. Further, we introduce an object-centric viewpoint pruning strategy assisted by a vision-language model (VLM), which uses persistent observation history and bird's-eye-view (BEV) maps to reduce redundant inspection visits. The resulting semantic viewpoints are combined with geometric exploration viewpoints in a global exploration planner. Simulations show that POSE improves final target-surface coverage by 8-10 percentage points over the planar planning baseline while reducing exploration time by 17-32%, and achieves the highest mean object coverage AUC among the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments with a legged robot carrying an omnidirectional camera-LiDAR suite in a machine shop further demonstrate the system's applicability. These results support adaptive body-posture planning for improving the coverage-efficiency trade-off in legged robot semantic exploration. We plan to release the code for community benefit in the future.

AI.tldr: POSE improves legged robot semantic exploration by using pose-aware viewpoint sampling and VLM-assisted pruning to increase target-surface coverage while reducing exploration time, combining with a global planner.
AI.motivation: Confinement and limited sensor FOV in planar viewpoints lead to incomplete visibility; increasing coverage through body Posture changes incurs time; need a balance between observation gain and mission duration.
AI.method: 1) Pose-aware viewpoint sampling based on intrinsic body pitch/roll to select postures from partial object maps; 2) aim-aligned execution to minimize unnecessary reorientation; 3) object-centric pruning aided by a vision-language model using history and BEV maps to reduce redundant inspections; 4) integrate semantic viewpoints with geometric exploration in a global planner; 5) validation via simulations and real-world experiments on a legged robot with omnidirectional camera-LiDAR.
AI.result: Simulations show 8–10 percentage points higher final target-surface coverage than planar baseline and 17–32% shorter exploration time; highest mean object coverage AUC among baselines. Real-world experiments demonstrate applicability in a machine shop. Code planned for release.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive body-posture planning effectively improves the coverage-efficiency trade-off in legged robot semantic exploration, with POSE offering a practical pathway for improved autonomous perception in confined environments.

title: From Intent to Action: Benchmarking LLM Safety in Vehicle Voice Command Authorization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into vehicle voice assistants. But linking natural-language requests to vehicle functions creates a safety-critical authorization problem. Before executing a command, the system must choose whether to execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, defer to manual control, trigger an emergency response, or make no tool call. To our knowledge, prior evaluations do not isolate this pre-action decision across speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability. We introduce a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions under a seven-class taxonomy. We evaluate two local open-weight models and three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics. Alignment ranges from 40.1% for Llama 3.2 3B to 89.1% for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. The API-based models score between 83.2% and 89.1%, with no statistically significant differences among them. Even these models produce two to three False Executes among 161 non-execution scenarios, and persistent errors remain in confirmation and manual-control decisions. A controlled Llama 3.2 3B ablation increases alignment to 40.1% under the structured authorization policy, versus 28.2-29.2% under schema-only and generic-safety baselines, but it does not eliminate False Executes. Structured LLM decisions are therefore insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism, and deployment requires an independent enforcement layer that verifies tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function.

AI.tldr: A 202-scenario benchmark reveals that structured pre-action decisions by LLMs in vehicle assistants achieve limited alignment and do not reliably prevent unsafe tool calls; API models perform best but still require external enforcement.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical authorization for vehicle functions; prior work did not isolate pre-action decisions across speaker role, auth status, vehicle state, and tool availability.
AI.method: Construct a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions under a seven-class taxonomy; evaluate two local open-weight models and three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics.
AI.result: Alignment: Llama 3.2 3B at 40.1% up to Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview at 89.1%; API models 83.2-89.1% with no significant differences; 2-3 False Executes per 161 non-execution cases; ablation shows structured policy improves alignment to 40.1% vs 28.2-29.2% for baselines but does not eliminate False Executes.
AI.conclusion: Structured LLM decisions alone are insufficient for safety; an independent enforcement layer is required to verify tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking vehicle functions.

title: A Policy Profile for Croissant: Refusal as a Property of the Dataset
comment: 23 pages. Reference implementation and conformance corpus archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22018156 and doi:10.5281/zenodo.22016112
summary: Croissant is the de facto machine-readable descriptor for ML datasets: JSON-LD over schema.org. Since version 1.1 it also carries data use conditions, recommending DUO and ODRL for them. What no version specifies is how any of them is evaluated: no decision procedure, no bound on evaluation cost, no outcome for a condition an implementation cannot evaluate, no record of what was checked, and nothing on composition with caller-side authority. We supply that half. An additive profile lets a dataset declare the operations it admits and the conditions under which it admits them, over a closed set of five operators whose decision procedure is given in full, so a gate decides from the descriptor alone and records what it checked. Two corpora evaluate it and their evidence is kept apart. Three descriptors that gated a real nf-core pipeline give the deployment result: decisions from a profile document match the gate's native descriptor record for record, stripping the layer leaves a valid Croissant document, and the added cost is 11.7 $μ$s against a 119 $μ$s decision. A corpus generated from the profile's grammar gives the breadth, covering every operator, refusal class and conformance clause. Across its valid cases, 552 complete decision records agree three ways -- native descriptor, profile terms, and the same policy as ODRL in usageInfo. The carrier is therefore not the contribution; the evaluation semantics is. Finally, caller-bound and data-bound policies range over non-overlapping state spaces, so neither permit set contains the other.

AI.tldr: Introduces verifiable evaluation semantics for Croissant via an additive profile with five operators and a full decision procedure; demonstrates cross-implementation agreement and low overhead across corpora; the evaluation semantics is the core contribution.
AI.motivation: Existing Croissant metadata specify data-use but lack a formal evaluation mechanism (decision procedure, cost bounds, outcomes for un-evaluable conditions, provenance, and caller/caller-side composition).
AI.method: Define an additive profile that declares admissible operations and conditions over five operators with an explicit decision procedure; gate checks are recorded; evaluate on two corpora with separate evidence; apply to three gated nf-core pipelines; generate a grammar-based corpus to cover operator/refusal/clause space; compare native descriptors, profile terms, and ODRL usageInfo; analyze policy-state spaces.
AI.result: 552 complete decision records agree across three routes (native descriptor, profile terms, ODRL usageInfo); a nf-core deployment example shows matching decisions and that removing the profile layer yields a valid Croissant document; overhead: 11.7 μs for profile decision vs 119 μs baseline; two corpora keep evidence separate; grammar-generated corpus achieves breadth; across valid cases, decisions align across all modalities.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is the evaluation semantics, enabling auditable, caller-bound and data-bound policy composition; profile and policy spaces occupy non-overlapping state spaces, ensuring clear separation and interoperability while Croissant remains the carrier.

title: Recency Forcing: Bridging the Long-Horizon Gap in Autoregressive Video Generation
summary: Autoregressive (AR) video generation degrades over long horizons due to an overlooked train-inference discrepancy we term KV eviction mismatch: models train on short clips where all context frames reside in the KV cache, but at inference, memory constraints force distant frames to be evicted from the KV cache - removing context the model was conditioned on. Rather than simulating eviction via context truncation - which discards temporal information the model still needs and degrades motion coherence - we keep the context but while progressively reducing the influence of distant frames, making their eventual eviction negligible. To guide this design, we introduce the positional response $R( Δ, \, t_{\text{denoise}})$, a perturbation-based sensitivity measure revealing that context influence decays steeply with temporal distance and varies systematically across denoising steps. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Recency Forcing, which applies a non-positive, timestep-dependent bias, termed Temporal Response Bias (TRB), on pre-softmax attention logits derived directly from $R$, closing the train-inference gap without modifying context length or training objectives. We further introduce Biased Attention Reparameterization (BAR), an exact reformulation that moves the bias outside the softmax, making TRB a standard FlashAttention call at zero overhead. Recency Forcing operates in both training-free mode and training-based mode. Experiments on VBench and VBench-Long demonstrate state-of-the-art long-horizon generation quality at no additional inference cost.

AI.tldr: Proposes Recency Forcing with Temporal Response Bias (TRB) and Biased Attention Reparameterization (BAR) to mitigate KV eviction mismatch in autoregressive video generation, improving long-horizon consistency without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: Train-inference discrepancy from KV eviction when long-horizon context cannot be stored; prior truncation harms motion coherence; need a way to reduce distant-context influence without changing memory footprint or training objectives.
AI.method: Introduce a perturbation-based positional sensitivity R(Δ, t_denoise); derive TRB as a non-positive, timestep-dependent bias on pre-softmax attention logits using R; reformulate via BAR to move bias outside softmax, enabling zero-overhead TRB within FlashAttention; apply Recency Forcing in training-free and training-based modes.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art long-horizon generation quality on VBench and VBench-Long at no additional inference cost; preserves context while attenuating distant-frame influence over time.
AI.conclusion: Addressing train-inference gap via bias-based recency mechanisms yields stronger long-horizon coherence without changing inputs or training objectives; BAR makes TRB practical within standard attention implementations.

title: FASA: Feedback-Aware Sampling Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion-Based VLA Models
comment: Accepted by the 18th International Conference on Networking, Architecture, and Storage (NAS 2026)
summary: Diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in embodied tasks, but their iterative sampling imposes heavy computational and memory-access cost, blocking real-time deployment on edge platforms. Existing acceleration methods either require expensive training (e.g., distillation, flow matching) or degrade perception via statically scheduled pruning and caching, ignoring the dynamic workload variance of robotic interactions. This paper presents FASA (Feedback-Aware Sampling Adaptation), a training-free runtime framework that treats real-time multimodal feedback as a control signal for the denoising pipeline: an interaction-driven range adaptor modulates the global sampling-step budget based on visual and gripper-force feedback, and a proprioception-aware step adaptor pinpoints the optimized step within the adapted range. This co-designed framework allows the underlying hardware architecture to adaptively match the workload demands of different execution phases. Comparative evaluations across several benchmarks show that the inference speed can be increased by up to 1.45$\times$ while maintaining competitive success rates, providing a novel dynamic runtime architecture paradigm for deploying heavy generative embodied AI workloads onto resource-constrained computing platforms.

AI.tldr: Training-free runtime adaptation for diffusion-based VLA models: dynamic, interaction-driven sampling control to enable real-time edge deployment with up to 1.45x speedup.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based VLA models are powerful but require iterative denoising, incurring high compute and memory costs; edge devices demand real-time inference. Existing accelerations are either expensive (training-time distillation, flow matching) or degrade perception via static pruning/caching that ignores dynamic workload variance in robotic interactions.
AI.method: FASA (Feedback-Aware Sampling Adaptation) is a training-free runtime framework that uses multimodal feedback as control signals for the denoising pipeline. An interaction-driven range adaptor adjusts the global sampling-step budget based on visual and gripper-force feedback, while a proprioception-aware step adaptor selects the optimal step within the adapted range. The framework co-designs the hardware runtime to adapt to workload variations across execution phases.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks show inference speed gains up to 1.45x with competitive success rates, demonstrating a dynamic runtime architecture for deploying heavy generative embodied AI workloads on resource-constrained platforms.
AI.conclusion: Presents a novel, training-free, interaction-driven runtime adaptation paradigm that aligns diffusion-based VLA inference with real-time robot workloads, enabling more practical edge deployment.

title: Reach or Solve? Attributing Agentic RL Gains with Checkpoint Handoffs
summary: Reinforcement learning now trains language-model agents that act over dozens of steps in live environments. The gains are large, and they are read as better decision-making. An agent in a closed loop writes its own inputs. Each observation follows from its own earlier actions, so the states it meets late in an episode are partly of its own making. An SFT checkpoint and an RL checkpoint are then scored from different states, even on identical tasks. Endpoint success mixes two changes: where the agent arrives, and what it does once it is there. Restricting the comparison to states both policies reach does not separate them. That restriction selects on an outcome, and in our data it flips the sign of the effect. We introduce checkpoint handoff, an evaluation protocol that clones a state one released checkpoint reached and hands it to another, with no retraining. Crossing a reacher role and a solver role over SFT and RL splits an endpoint gain into REACH and SOLVE. REACH is how often a policy arrives at a state the environment confirms is a fixed number of actions from success. SOLVE is how often it finishes from an identical cloned state. Across two benchmarks and two independently released pipelines, the reacher by solver interaction is positive in all five conditions. An RL history is worth more to an RL solver than the same history is to an SFT solver. On ALFWorld, RL improves both terms, and the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails. Independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the aggregate interaction. Handoff asks only that one checkpoint's history can be replayed under another, so long-horizon evaluation can report arrival and completion beside endpoint success.

AI.tldr: Checkpoint handoff decouples arrival to favorable states from solving from them, revealing that RL histories provide value to RL solvers and that REACH/SOLVE gaps predict overall performance across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: End-to-end endpoint success blends where an agent reaches a state and what it does thereafter, confounded further when agents generate their own observations over long horizons. A fair comparison of SFT vs RL requires separating arrival from solving to understand the true sources of improvement.
AI.method: Introduce a checkpoint handoff protocol: clone a state reached by one checkpoint to another policy without retraining; define REACH as the frequency of arriving at a state within a fixed horizon from success, and SOLVE as the frequency of finishing from an identical cloned state. Evaluate across two benchmarks and two pipelines, comparing RL vs SFT solvers and agent histories (reaching and solving) on ALFWorld.
AI.result: Across five conditions, the REACH×SOLVE interaction is positive when an RL history is used by an RL solver. RL history is more informative to an RL solver than to an SFT solver. On ALFWorld, RL improves both REACH and SOLVE; the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver does. Independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the overall interaction strength.
AI.conclusion: Checkpoint handoff enables reporting arrival and completion separately, revealing how long-horizon solving benefits from the agent’s history. Evaluations that decouple REACH and SOLVE provide a robust predictor of endpoint performance and clarify why RL histories outperform SFT histories in long-horizon tasks.

title: CoRe: Coherence and Relational Alignment for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
comment: Accepted at the International Conference on Neural Information Processing (ICONIP 2026)
summary: Direct forecasting has become a standard paradigm for multivariate time-series forecasting because it predicts the full future horizon in a single pass. However, its training objective is often still decomposed into pointwise errors such as MSE. Such objectives provide stable supervision, but they do not explicitly preserve the structure of the future trajectory: temporal coherence within each variable and relational consistency across variables can both be weakened. We propose CoRe, a model-agnostic learning objective for direct multivariate forecasting. CoRe replaces pointwise supervision with two output-space constraints: a frequency coherence loss that aligns predicted and target spectra, and a low-rank relational graph loss that matches sampled pairwise differences in a target-derived PCA subspace. The resulting objective introduces no trainable parameters and can be applied to existing forecasting backbones by changing only the loss. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that CoRe improves strong baselines, compares favorably with recent forecasting objectives, and remains effective across different backbones, datasets, and hyperparameter settings overall consistently.

AI.tldr: CoRe introduces a parameter-free, structure-preserving objective for direct multivariate forecasting, using a frequency coherence (spectral) loss and a low-rank relational graph loss to enforce temporal and cross-variable structure without adding trainable parameters; it improves baselines across benchmarks and backbones.
AI.motivation: Pointwise losses (e.g., MSE) used in direct forecasting neglect the temporal coherence within variables and the relational structure across variables, yielding less faithful future trajectories.
AI.method: Two output-space constraints: (1) frequency coherence loss aligning predicted and target spectra; (2) low-rank relational graph loss matching sampled pairwise differences in a PCA-derived subspace of the target. No new trainable parameters; can replace the loss in any forecasting backbone.
AI.result: Empirical results on standard benchmarks show CoRe improves strong baselines, competes with or outperforms recent forecasting objectives, and remains effective across various backbones, datasets, and hyperparameter settings.
AI.conclusion: CoRe offers a simple, general, parameter-free objective for direct multivariate forecasting that preserves temporal and relational structure, enhancing performance with minimal integration effort.

title: Federated Learning Framework for Privacy-Preserving Kidney Stone Detection
summary: Recent innovations in deep learning have significantly enhanced the diagnosis of medical images, although they are based on the use of centralized data storage that pose severe threats to patient privacy and medical data security. To address this issue, this research proposes a Federated Learning (FL) model that is coupled with an optimized YOLOv8 network to detect the kidney stones on a computed tomography (CT) image and at the same time, protect privacy of the patients. The suggested system can help various medical organizations to jointly train a common model without exchanging the information about the patients. This is to ensure that data protection laws like GDPR and HIPAA are adhered to. The residual feature fusion and DropBlock regularization among other architectural improvements are also included in YOLOv8 to enhance detection robustness and minimize overfitting. Experimental analysis carried out on a distributed CT dataset demonstrated that the federated YOLOv8 model has a mAP at 50 of 0.733 and is able to keep the data confidential. Moreover, its lean design facilitates fast edge deployment and real-time inference across a clinical setting. Altogether, these findings indicate that Federated Learning is a safe and efficient solution to AI-assisted diagnosis in contemporary healthcare when combined with the use of sophisticated object detection models.

AI.tldr: Federated learning combined with an optimized YOLOv8 detector is proposed for CT kidney stone detection, achieving mAP@50 of 0.733 while preserving patient privacy and enabling fast edge deployment for real-time clinical inference.
AI.motivation: Protect patient privacy and comply with data protection regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA) by avoiding centralized data sharing; enable collaborative AI training across medical institutions for accurate kidney stone detection in CT images.
AI.method: A Federated Learning framework is coupled with an improved YOLOv8 architecture. Architectural enhancements include residual feature fusion and DropBlock regularization to improve detection robustness and reduce overfitting. The model is trained on distributed CT datasets across clients, favoring edge deployment and real-time inference within clinical settings.
AI.result: On distributed CT data, the federated YOLOv8 achieves a mean Average Precision at IoU 0.50 (mAP@50) of 0.733 and preserves data confidentiality. The approach supports lean, fast edge deployment suitable for real-time clinical use.
AI.conclusion: Federated learning with an optimized object detector (YOLOv8 with residual feature fusion and DropBlock) is a viable, privacy-preserving solution for AI-assisted diagnosis in healthcare, enabling cross-institution collaboration without data exchange while delivering robust detection performance.

title: Self-excited actuation enables adaptive and resilient flapping-wing flight
summary: The muscles that power insect flight fall into one of two categories: 1) synchronous muscles that contract under direct control from the nervous system, and 2) asynchronous muscles which have an intrinsic stretch activation response that spontaneously generates wingbeats without the need for signaling from the brain. It is thought that the emergent nature of asynchronous wingbeats provides both adaptive and responsive capabilities for flight control. To date, most flying robots use synchronous actuation. In this paper we develop the first flight-capable flapping wing robot that uses asynchronous actuation. We demonstrate that asynchronous actuation allows wings to respond to changes in the resonant mechanics of the body without control input, and wings can react instantaneously to collisions with obstacles with no extrinsic sensing needed. Flight tests within cluttered environments demonstrate that asynchronous actuation significantly improves stability and performance when compared to synchronous actuation. In total this work demonstrates that a flapping wing robot actuation strategy that emulates the asynchronous muscles of flying insects can provide fast, reactive actuation responses before a control system would need to intervene. This partitioning of embodied control to both the low-level actuation dynamics and and high-level sensorimotor system provides a compelling blueprint for new flying robots.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates the first flight-capable flapping-wing robot using asynchronous actuation inspired by insect muscles; shows fast, collision-reactive behavior and improved stability without relying on high-level control for rapid wing responses.
AI.motivation: Synchronous actuation limits rapid, robust flight control in cluttered environments; biological asynchronous muscles offer emergent, fast actuation. The work investigates whether such embodied actuation can enhance robustness and reduce dependence on external sensing.
AI.method: Developed a flight-capable flapping-wing robot employing asynchronous actuation. Conducted experiments to test responses to resonant changes in body mechanics without control input, immediate reactions to collisions without extrinsic sensing, and comparative flight tests in cluttered environments against synchronous actuation.
AI.result: Asynchronous actuation enabled instantaneous responses to collisions and improved stability/performance in cluttered flight. Wingbeats could adapt to resonant mechanics autonomously, outperforming the synchronous-actuation baseline.
AI.conclusion: Emulating asynchronous insect muscles provides fast, reactive actuation and partitions control between low-level actuation dynamics and high-level sensorimotor systems, offering a blueprint for next-generation agile flying robots.

title: ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI
summary: Scientific discovery is defined by the ability to identify the boundaries of existing knowledge and venture into unexplored territory. The ultimate vision for AI in science is problem-driven autonomous research: given a fundamental challenge by a human expert, the AI independently navigates the scientific landscape, uncovers theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expands the frontier of knowledge. In this paper, we introduce ScientistTwo, a fully autonomous multi-agent framework designed to realize this vision. Specifically, ScientistTwo takes an initial problem as input, establishes state-of-the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to orchestrate an end-to-end discovery cycle without human intervention. Moreover, the framework rigorously conducts experiments using diverse datasets and metrics, refines methodologies through automated ablation studies, and validates research findings via a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine. To evaluate ScientistTwo's capabilities against the highest standards of human scientific achievement, we benchmark it across papers accepted at top-tier conferences such as ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS. As a result, ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models, and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents. These results show that ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery. Project website: https://scientist-two.github.io/

AI.tldr: ScientistTwo is a fully autonomous, multi-agent framework for autonomous scientific discovery that autonomously formulates hypotheses, runs experiments, performs ablations, and engages in simulated peer review to generate publishable papers and executable code, benchmarking against top-tier conference work.
AI.motivation: To realize problem-driven autonomous research in which AI independently identifies knowledge gaps, proposes hypotheses, and systematically advances science without human intervention, thereby pushing the frontier of knowledge.
AI.method: An autonomous multi-agent system that takes an initial problem, establishes strong baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to execute an end-to-end discovery cycle. It conducts diverse experiments, performs automated ablations, and uses a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine. It is evaluated by benchmarking on papers from top conferences (ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS) and producing expert-level, publishable manuscripts with verified codebases.
AI.result: ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers with fully executable codebases, achieving performance that surpasses human state-of-the-art models and receiving higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that autonomous scientific discovery is achievable at a high level, functioning not merely as an assistive tool but as an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of expanding the frontiers of human knowledge.

title: Conservation Buys Stability and Factoring Buys Counterfactuals in Physical World Models
summary: A learned simulator can reproduce its training conditions accurately yet fail in two distinct ways once those conditions change. Over long rollouts, small errors accumulate until the trajectory drifts away from physically plausible behavior; under an intervention on a physical parameter, the model may continue to follow the law seen during training rather than the intervened one. We show that these two failures require different structural remedies. Evolving a learned energy with a symplectic integrator preserves the geometry of the conservative dynamics and keeps rollouts bounded and physically meaningful for up to $100\times$ the training horizon, while equal-capacity predictors, an energy-regularized predictor, and a tuned neural ODE diverge. By contrast, encoding the physical coupling through an explicit linear factorization enables the model to follow a never-seen sign of that coupling, whereas an unrestricted parameterization remains locked to the training law. Crucially, the two mechanisms are separable: removing the structure responsible for long-horizon stability leaves counterfactual transfer intact, while removing the factorized coupling destroys counterfactual transfer without eliminating stability. This double dissociation, established with matched controls that remove or replace one structural component at a time, persists beyond the headline three-body system and remains visible when the physical state must be inferred from pixels rather than provided directly. The result is a concrete design principle for physical world models: long-horizon stability and changed-law generalization arise from distinct structural commitments, and each can be imposed deliberately without requiring the other.

AI.tldr: Long-horizon stability and counterfactual generalization in learned simulators arise from distinct architectural choices: symplectic-energy dynamics grant bounded, plausible rollouts; explicit linear coupling factorization enables transfer to unseen (intervened) laws. These two mechanisms are separable (double dissociation) and apply beyond simple three-body systems to pixel-based state inference.
AI.motivation: Understand why learned physical simulators fail under distribution shifts in two ways—drift over long rollouts and adherence to training laws under interventions—and identify architectural remedies that address each failure mode without compromising the other.
AI.method: Systematic ablation and control experiments comparing: (i) energy-evolving models with symplectic integrators vs baselines (equal-capacity, energy-regularized predictor, tuned neural ODE); (ii) explicit linear factorization of physical coupling vs unrestricted parameterization; matched-controls to isolate the effects; tested on a three-body system and scenarios where the state must be inferred from pixels.
AI.result: Long-horizon stability is achieved by evolving a learned energy with a symplectic integrator, yielding bounded and physically meaningful rollouts up to ~100× training horizon; baselines diverge under long rollouts. Counterfactual transfer (ability to follow an intervened physical law) is enabled by explicit, factorized coupling; unrestricted parameterizations remain locked to the training law and fail to generalize under intervention. Crucially, the two mechanisms are separable: removing the stability structure does not destroy counterfactual transfer, while removing factorized coupling eliminates counterfactual transfer without removing stability. The double dissociation persists beyond the three-body system and remains when states are inferred from pixels rather than provided directly.
AI.conclusion: A concrete design principle for physical world models emerges: long-horizon stability and changed-law generalization originate from distinct structural commitments, and each can be imposed deliberately without requiring the other.

title: Region-Level Policy Optimization for Fine-grained MLLM Perception
summary: Fine-grained visual perception in MLLMs is commonly improved by raising the resolution, but the added visual tokens inflate vision-encoding and language-model prefilling costs. We show that the two operations underlying fine-grained perception, localizing the region of interest (RoI) and recognizing its content, have different resolution requirements. In a controlled diagnostic, localization tolerates roughly 3 to 4 times stronger token compression than recognition, which motivates localizing from a coarse view and concentrating resolution on the selected evidence. Decoding coordinates with the MLLM can be trained end-to-end from answers, but costs a full model pass per query and depends on grounding ability. A lightweight proposal network distilled from the model's attention is fast, but inherits the noise of its attention targets. The RoI from the proposal network reaches the answer through a discrete region choice, so its faithfulness to the answer cannot supervise the network. We therefore optimize the proposal network with region-level reinforcement learning, which we call Vision-RL2. It treats coherent regions as actions, and a frozen MLLM reader scores each one by how its removal changes the answer likelihood. Complementary subtractive and additive objectives suppress distracting proposals and recover missing evidence, updating only the predictor without region annotations, response sampling, or reasoning trajectories. The refined proposal further enables a sparse encoding that magnifies evidence and excludes background tokens. Across six fine-grained benchmarks and four MLLM backbones, Vision-RL2 improves accuracy over the base model at every token budget and surpasses its largest-budget accuracy with about 4 times fewer visual tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/YuHengsss/VisionRL2 .

AI.tldr: Vision-RL2 trains a region-level RL-based predictor to select coherent RoIs for MLLMs, enabling sparse, targeted visual tokens and beating baselines at reduced token budgets.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained perception in MLLMs requires high visual resolution but increases token cost. Localization/recognition have different resolution needs; coarse localization with focused high-res evidence reduces cost.
AI.method: A lightweight proposal network distilled from model attention; region-level reinforcement learning treats coherent regions as actions; a frozen MLLM reader scores each region by how removal changes answer likelihood; complementary additive/subtractive objectives reduce distractors and recover missing evidence; update only the predictor; no region annotations or reasoning trajectories.
AI.result: Across six fine-grained benchmarks and four MLLM backbones, Vision-RL2 improves accuracy at every token budget and reaches the largest-budget accuracy with about 4x fewer visual tokens.
AI.conclusion: Vision-RL2 provides efficient, accurate fine-grained perception by RL-guided, sparse region proposals, enabling better token efficiency in MLLMs; code available.

title: PIVOT: Perception-aware Independent Viewpoint Online Optimization
comment: 9 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Yuyang Chen and Shekoufeh Sadeghi contributed equally to this work. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: A fundamental assumption in robotic perception is that the sensor's field of view (FoV) is fixed relative to the robot body.
