Motion-decoupled sensors, such as gimbal-mounted cameras and MEMS-based LiDARs, instead allow sensing direction to be controlled independently at runtime. This freedom creates a computational challenge: efficiently selecting useful viewing directions online in feature-dense environments. We propose PIVOT, a lightweight iterative method that optimizes sensor viewing direction along a fixed translation trajectory to maximize feature visibility. Under a conical FoV model, visibility depends only on the optical axis, yielding a two-degree-of-freedom optimization on the viewing sphere $S^2$. Coordinate-free $SO(3)$ exponential-map updates enable efficient continuous optimization without explicit angular parameterizations or exhaustive viewing-sphere search. Monte Carlo evaluations retain 98.1--99.6% of brute-force visibility with a 76--85x speedup. Photorealistic simulation and real-world experiments further demonstrate improved visual localization robustness and practical viewpoint control on a quadruped robot.

AI.tldr: PIVOT is a light-weight iterative method to choose the viewing direction of a motion-decoupled sensor along a fixed translation to maximize feature visibility, using a conical FoV model and SO(3) updates on the viewing sphere; it achieves near-brute-force visibility with large speedups and is validated in photorealistic simulation and real-world tests on a quadruped.
AI.motivation: Efficient online viewpoint selection for motion-decoupled sensors (e.g., gimbal cameras, MEMS LiDAR) is challenging in feature-dense environments due to the need to optimize orientation without exhaustive search or heavy computation.
AI.method: Treats the problem as a two-DoF optimization on the viewing sphere S^2 by focusing on the optical axis under a conical FoV. Uses coordinate-free SO(3) exponential-map updates to perform continuous optimization without angle parameterizations or sphere search. The approach is iterative (PIVOT) along a fixed translation trajectory and evaluated with Monte Carlo sampling.
AI.result: Monte Carlo experiments retain 98.1–99.6% of brute-force visibility with a 76–85× speedup. Photorealistic simulation and real-world experiments show improved visual localization robustness and practical viewpoint control on a quadruped robot.
AI.conclusion: Efficient online viewpoint optimization for motion-decoupled sensing is feasible; PIVOT provides near-optimal visibility with substantial computational savings, enabling robust perception and controllable viewpoint in real-world robotic platforms.

title: Replan, Repair, or Edit? A Unified Empirical Evaluation of Travel Agents for Itinerary Revision under Resource Disruptions
summary: Travel-planning agents generate itineraries that may become infeasible after acceptance because of flight cancellations, hotel unavailability, or attraction closures. Revising these itineraries involves full replanning, classical plan repair, and LLM-based travel-agent revision, whose differing task formulations and evaluation protocols hinder comparison. We conduct a systematic empirical study using two TREK-derived benchmark sets: 500 single-disruption cases, including feasible and infeasible instances, and 200 feasible simultaneous compound-disruption cases. We compare LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and an iTIMO local-revision adapter across effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost. LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest observed compound-disruption success. IPyHOPPER nearly matched that configuration's single-disruption overall success, while preserving substantially more of the accepted itinerary on successful repairs. Successful hierarchical and local repairs made fewer edits and retained more accepted commitments than full replanning. Computational profiles differed: IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference, the evaluated LLM-Z3 adapter used compact one-call inference, and the iTIMO adapter consumed substantially more tokens. The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost within evaluated settings.

AI.tldr: A systematic empirical study comparing three travel-plan repair/replanning approaches (LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, iTIMO local-revision) on TREK benchmarks, showing LLM-Z3 Gemini excels in compound disruptions, IPyHOPPER preserves commitments and performs well with fewer edits, and hierarchical/local repairs are more efficient than full replanning; guidelines for balancing feasibility, commitment preservation, and cost are offered.
AI.motivation: To enable fair, apples-to-apples comparison across different reformulation strategies for feasibility recovery in travel planning, and to illuminate trade-offs among success, stability, and computational cost.
AI.method: Systematic empirical evaluation on two TREK-derived benchmarks: 500 single-disruption cases (feasible and infeasible) and 200 feasible compound-disruption cases. Methods compared: (1) LLM-Z3 full replanning, (2) IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, (3) iTIMO local-revision adapter. Evaluation metrics include effectiveness (feasibility/success rate), plan stability/commitment preservation (edits retained), and computational cost (LLM inference, tokens used, etc.).
AI.result: LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest observed compound-disruption success. IPyHOPPER nearly matched that configuration’s single-disruption overall success, while preserving substantially more of the accepted itinerary on successful repairs. Successful hierarchical and local repairs made fewer edits and retained more accepted commitments than full replanning. Computational profiles differed: IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference, the evaluated LLM-Z3 adapter used compact one-call inference, and the iTIMO adapter consumed substantially more tokens.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost within evaluated settings.

title: Opinion Dynamics-based Coalition Formation for Federated Learning in Heterogeneous IoT Systems
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving, on-device training across heterogeneous Internet-of-Things (IoT) deployments such as smart-city water-metering networks, where each smart meter observes a household-specific consumption time series. Under such statistical heterogeneity, the standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg) aggregation averages dissimilar local models into a single global model that may fail to capture client-specific patterns. We address this by forming client coalitions directly in the local-weight space and aggregating at the coalition level. Extending a prior weight-driven coalition-formation scheme, we model coalition formation as a Hegselmann-Krause (HK) bounded-confidence opinion-dynamics process acting on the local weights, and develop variants of the HK interaction based on Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity confidence criteria. The framework is applied to short-term water-consumption forecasting with local Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models and evaluated against FedAvg, Per-FedAvg, FedProx, and FedAvg with Euclidean-distance or cosine-similarity coalition formation. Experiments on a real smart-metering dataset of water consumption show that the proposed HK-based coalition formation produces stable, endogenous coalition structures within at most ten inner iterations, incurs no additional client-side computation or communication compared to FedAvg, and reduces the average MAE by up to 54% relative to FedAvg, 39% relative to FedProx, and 24% relative to Per-FedAvg, while achieving the highest global accuracy (83-85%).

AI.tldr: A federated-learning approach uses Hegselmann-Krause bounded-confidence dynamics to form weight-space coalitions among clients, enabling local-pattern-focused aggregation for IoT time-series forecasting. It improves accuracy without extra cost compared to standard FL baselines.
AI.motivation: Statistical heterogeneity across IoT devices (e.g., smart meters) causes FedAvg to blend dissimilar local models, failing to capture client-specific patterns. The work aims to create endogenous coalitions in weight space to better align models with local data distributions, improving short-term water-consumption forecasting.
AI.method: Extend a weight-driven coalition-formation scheme by modeling coalition formation as a HK bounded-confidence opinion-dynamics process operating on local weights. Develop HK variants using Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity confidence criteria. Apply to short-term forecasting with local LSTM models in a federated setting. Compare against FedAvg, Per-FedAvg, FedProx, and HK-based coalitions using Euclidean or cosine criteria.
AI.result: HK-based coalition formation yields stable, endogenous coalitions within at most ten inner iterations, adds no extra client-side computation/communication beyond FedAvg, and substantially reduces MAE (up to 54% vs FedAvg, 39% vs FedProx, 24% vs Per-FedAvg). It also achieves high global accuracy (83–85%).
AI.conclusion: Weight-space coalition formation via HK dynamics effectively mitigates heterogeneity in FL for time-series forecasting on IoT data, delivering significant accuracy gains without extra cost and with stable coalition structures.

title: STAR: Structure-aware Test-time Adaptation for diffusion-based light field Reconstruction
summary: Light field (LF) reconstruction from limited and noisy focal stack (FS) measurements is a highly ill-posed inverse problem. Although the LF-to-FS imaging geometry is fixed for a given optical setup, LF spatial-angular structure---including within-view spatial details, cross-view angular dependencies, and disparity across views---varies across scenes. Consequently, a fixed pre-trained prior may not optimally capture the spatial-angular structure of each test LF. We propose Structure-aware Test-time Adaptation for diffusion-based light field Reconstruction (STAR), the first test-time adaptation framework for reconstructing an LF from FS. For each test LF, STAR freezes a pre-trained diffusion prior and fits three lightweight adapters to the observed FS to jointly adapt the three components of the LF's spatial-angular structure. STAR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both two- and three-focal-sheet settings, with shorter inference times than those with test-time parameter updates.

AI.tldr: STAR is a diffusion-based, test-time adaptation framework for reconstructing a light field (LF) from focal stack (FS) measurements. It freezes a pre-trained diffusion prior and fits three lightweight adapters to tailor the LF's spatial-angular structure, achieving state-of-the-art results with faster inference than test-time-parameter-update methods.
AI.motivation: LF reconstruction from limited and noisy focal stacks is highly ill-posed. LF structure (within-view details, cross-view angular dependencies, disparity) varies across scenes, so fixed pre-trained priors may not capture test-time variations.
AI.method: Freeze a pre-trained diffusion model and jointly train three lightweight adapters to adapt three components of the LF's spatial-angular structure to the observed FS. Applies to two- and three-focal-sheet configurations.
AI.result: STAR outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both 2- and 3-focal-sheet settings and achieves shorter inference times than approaches that update model parameters at test time.
AI.conclusion: STAR is the first test-time adaptation framework for LF reconstruction from focal stacks, enabling effective and efficient reconstruction by per-test adaptation of spatial-angular structure.

title: CoreSense: Traceable Failure Recall and Conflict-Aware Belief Gating for Auditable Robot Decisions
summary: Robots can recall prior failures without knowing whether recalled evidence remains valid, conflicts with current observations, or is sufficient to guide a decision. We present CoreSense, a robot-system integration architecture that combines traceable episodic evidence with a conflict-aware belief gate and bounded, auditable recommendations. The gate checks scope, provenance, time, contradiction, and support before it permits PROCEED, requests re-observation, abstains, or escalates. Evaluation follows three complementary layers without commanding a physical robot: offline public real-robot data, a frozen signal-level simulation, and a live cloud deployment path. On CableTrace-120 and BotFails-200, belief gating reduces protocol-defined unsafe proceeds from 20% and 40% to 0%. A disjointly calibrated raw-video policy also reaches 0% unsafe proceed, but overblocks every nominal episode. On public data, a ViFailback-BotFails visual detector reaches 0.778 AUROC yet remains all-blocking, whereas cycle-disjoint UR3 telemetry for protective stops yields 0% unsafe proceed, 36.1% overblocking, and 61.9% coverage; grip-loss transfer remains a negative result. Controlled physical corroboration yields 3.3%, 0%, and 42.0%, while conflict-aware fusion yields 4.7%, 0%, and 42.8%. Finally, 20/20 cloud recalls validate a CockroachDB Cloud-Amazon Bedrock deployment path. The evidence supports an auditable integration pattern, not autonomous recovery or certified safety.

AI.tldr: CoreSense provides an auditable, conflict-aware decision gate for robots that leverages traceable episodic evidence to bound and justify decisions, achieving near-zero unsafe proceeds across multiple benchmarks, while stopping short of autonomous recovery or safety certification.
AI.motivation: Robots often rely on recalled failures without validating whether the evidence remains valid, conflicts with current observations, or suffices to guide a decision. The work argues for an auditable integration pattern that gates decisions rather than enabling autonomous recovery or claiming certified safety.
AI.method: CoreSense combines traceable episodic evidence with a conflict-aware belief gate and bounded, auditable recommendations. The gate assesses scope, provenance, time, contradiction, and support before issuing PROCEED, requesting re-observation, abstaining, or escalating. Evaluation spans three layers (offline real-robot data, frozen signal-level simulation, live cloud deployment) using datasets like CableTrace-120, BotFails-200, and various detectors/policies (visual detectors, UR3 telemetry, grip-loss transfer) and a cloud deployment path (CockroachDB Cloud–Amazon Bedrock).
AI.result: Belief gating reduces unsafe proceeds to 0% on CableTrace-120 and BotFails-200. Other approaches range from all-blocking detectors (0% unsafe proceed but overblock) to nuanced metrics such as AUROC 0.778 with all-blocking behavior, 0% unsafe proceed with UR3 telemetry but 36.1% overblocking and 61.9% coverage, and mixed outcomes from grip-loss transfer (negative) and physical corroboration (3.3%, 0%, 42.0%; conflict-aware fusion 4.7%, 0%, 42.8%). Cloud recalls (20/20) validate deployment. The work supports an auditable integration pattern rather than autonomous recovery or certified safety.
AI.conclusion: The evidence supports an auditable, evidence-driven integration pattern for robot decision-making, showing strong reduction of unsafe proceeds, but it does not claim autonomous safety or certification.

title: When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks but exhibit systematic inefficiency: they often overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches based on uniform length penalties or rigid routing incur an efficiency tax, trading reduced computation on easy instances for accuracy loss on hard instances. We formulate efficient reasoning as an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem and propose When2Think, a post-training framework for hybrid reasoning that dynamically allocates computation based on problem difficulty. Our method introduces Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that leverages pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. When2Think encourages direct answering on easy instances while preserving extended reasoning on hard instances, thereby learning when to use System 1 (NoThink) versus System 2 (Think). Experiments on mathematical benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: on AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model, and on AIME25, When2Think achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.

AI.tldr: When2Think is a post-training framework for adaptive reasoning depth that allocates computation by problem difficulty, using IDAC reward shaping and verifier-based rewards to improve accuracy-efficiency on math benchmarks, enabling System 1 vs System 2 switching without learned reward models.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models suffer inefficient use of computation: they over-commit on easy tasks and under-invest on hard ones. There is a need for instance-adaptive computation to improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off without requiring expensive online queries or reinforcement signals.
AI.method: Introduce IDAC (Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control), a reward-shaping mechanism leveraging pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combine with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages to enable stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. Implement as a post-training framework that dynamically decides between System 1 (NoThink) and System 2 (Think) reasoning during inference, enabling direct answers on easy instances and extended reasoning on hard ones.
AI.result: Empirical results on mathematical benchmarks show improved efficiency: on AIME24, Pass@3 up by 10.0% with a 27.9% reduction in token usage relative to the base model; on AIME25, Pass@3 reaches 40.0%, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: When2Think demonstrates that instance-adaptive computation with IDAC can tighten the accuracy-efficiency frontier for large reasoning models by conditionally expanding reasoning depth; the framework achieves notable gains without reward-model training or online reference queries and supports a clear System 1/System 2 interpretation.

title: Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling: A Specification and Design Guide for Contrast-Based Multi-Armed Bandits
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables in the main text; 2 figures and 3 tables in the supplement. Reference implementation at https://github.com/sulgik/orts
summary: Batched multi-armed bandits update on a service's own schedule, and the usual implementation carries each arm's absolute reward rate from one update to the next. When the shared level moves between batches, that memory goes stale even though the comparisons between arms may not have. Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling (OR-TS) instead carries the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts and fits the common level afresh in every batch, marginalizing it out. This paper specifies that update, places it inside a Bayesian bandit agent with two controls, decay for how much past evidence survives an update and aggressiveness for how sharply belief becomes allocation, and evaluates it against absolute-rate memory. Across 86 public A/B series the level varies about twenty-five times more than the contrast. In prespecified synthetic environments a moving level costs absolute-rate memory five times the regret and leaves the best arm below a majority of traffic in 7 of 20 runs, against none for OR-TS. In a policy simulation built from 71 real experiments, where the contrasts are too small to resolve, expected-click differences stay within 0.1% for 58 of them, yet contrast memory still ends on the better arm more than twice as often. Where the contrasts themselves move, the bet fails, and that case is reported too.

AI.tldr: Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling (OR-TS) uses a batch-aware Bayesian update that freshens the level at every batch by marginalizing it out, contrasting log-odds contrasts instead of maintaining per-arm absolute rates. It introduces two knobs (decay and aggressiveness) to control persistence of past evidence and speed of allocation. Across extensive synthetic and real-world A/B sequences, OR-TS outperforms absolute-rate memory in environments with moving levels, but fails when the contrasts themselves move.
AI.motivation: Address stale memory in batched bandit updates due to cross-batch level changes. Absolute-rate memory preserves past rewards, which can mislead decisions when the shared level shifts. OR-TS aims to maintain relevant comparisons by modeling log-odds contrasts and re-fitting the level each batch.
AI.method: Embed OR-TS in a Bayesian bandit agent with two hyperparameters: decay (how much past evidence survives an update) and aggressiveness (how sharply posterior allocation reacts). Update the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts and re-estimate the shared level anew in each batch, marginalizing the level. Evaluate on 86 public A/B series with variable level/contrast dynamics, plus a policy simulation based on 71 real experiments. Synthetic environments vary level movements (level moves ~25x contrast movements).
AI.result: In moving-level scenarios, absolute-rate memory incurs roughly 5x higher regret and can starve the best arm of traffic (7/20 runs favorable to OR-TS vs none for OR-TS in that synthetic setting). In real-policy simulations where contrasts are too small to resolve, expected-click differences stay within 0.1% in 58 of 71 cases, but contrast-memory still more often yields the better arm (over 2x as often). The method fails when contrasts themselves move, and such cases are reported.
AI.conclusion: OR-TS provides a robust alternative to absolute-rate memory in batched bandits with drifting shared levels, especially when contrasts can be resolved; its efficacy diminishes when contrast dynamics dominate. The two-parameter control allows tuning the memory–adaptivity trade-off, but care is needed in environments with moving contrasts.

title: Benchmarking MLLMs via Cognitive Expected Scene Graph for Safety-Critical Visual Negation Understanding
summary: True machine intelligence requires transcending passive pixel registration to master top-down functional reasoning over absent information via visual negation understanding. However, unconstrained visual negation paradigms remain overly open-ended, and pervasive affirmation bias causes both existing Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and evaluation metrics to fail under negative semantics. To solve these intertwined challenges systematically, we first anchor the boundaries of negation reasoning within specific cognitive goals. Specifically, by focusing on safety as a highly pragmatic and critical cognitive dimension, we define the task of \textbf{S}cene \textbf{N}egation \textbf{U}nderstanding under \textbf{S}afety Cognition (\textbf{SNUS}). Under this framework, we construct a high-fidelity negative caption dataset mapping dense assertions of localized hazards. Concurrently, we propose the Cognitive Expected Scene Graph (CESG) Score, a structure-grounded, polarity-aware evaluation metric. Extensive experiments demonstrate that while current models struggle on the task, traditional metrics completely collapse under semantic reversals. Conversely, our framework delivers a solid benchmark for SNUS, providing a rigorous foundation to advance risk-aware situational comprehension and counterfactual cognition.

AI.tldr: Proposes SNUS: Scene Negation Understanding under Safety Cognition, a safety-focused framework for visual negation, with a negative caption dataset and CESG score to evaluate risk-aware scene understanding; shows current models and metrics fail under negation, establishing a benchmark.
AI.motivation: Address uncontrolled visual negation and affirmation bias in MLLMs by grounding negation reasoning in safety-oriented goals, enabling robust, counterfactual understanding.
AI.method: Create a high-fidelity negative caption dataset mapping localized hazards; introduce CESG Score, a structure-grounded, polarity-aware metric; perform extensive experiments comparing models and traditional metrics.
AI.result: Current models struggle; traditional metrics collapse under semantic reversals; SNUS framework yields a solid benchmark and baseline; demonstrates need for risk-aware evaluation.
AI.conclusion: SNUS provides foundation for safe, risk-aware visual reasoning and counterfactual cognition; sets stage for future research in negation understanding.

title: AURORA: A Natural Language-Driven Agentic Framework for Understanding, Reasoning, and Orchestrating Reliable Air-Ground Co-Simulation
summary: Air-ground transportation research increasingly relies on co-simulation, yet constructing scenarios remains labor-intensive and difficult to validate. More importantly, a generated scenario may execute successfully while failing to realize the spatial, temporal, communication, or behavioral relationships requested by the user. This paper presents AURORA, a natural-language-driven agentic framework that treats air-ground scenario generation as a process of compilation with verification. Central to AURORA is the Air-Ground Scenario Graph (AGSG), a typed intermediate representation that explicitly connects agents, aerial missions, events, communication links, success conditions, and their cross-domain dependencies. This shared representation enables simulator-grounded parsing, joint road-airspace grounding, temporal planning, pre-execution feasibility checking, trace-based runtime verification, failure localization, and bounded repair within a unified workflow. We further introduce AURORA-Bench to evaluate not only whether generated scenarios execute, but whether they faithfully realize the requested interactions. Experiments across multiple language models show that structured execution substantially improves reliability, while runtime verification exposes silent failures that completion-based evaluation overlooks. Localized repair further resolves many violations without regenerating the entire scenario. The results show that reliable scenario generation requires verifying realized behavior, not merely executable code, and demonstrate the value of explicit intermediate representations for verifiable and repairable language-driven co-simulation.

AI.tldr: AURORA provides a natural-language-driven framework for air–ground scenario generation using a typed intermediate representation (AGSG) to enable verification, grounding, planning, and repair, improving reliability and faithfulness over purely completion-based generation.
AI.motivation: Co-simulation for air–ground scenarios is labor-intensive and validation-dependent; generated scenarios can executable yet fail to realize requested spatial, temporal, communication, or behavioral relationships. A structured intermediate representation and verification workflow are needed to ensure fidelity and repairability.
AI.method: Introduce the Air-Ground Scenario Graph (AGSG), a typed intermediate representation linking agents, aerial missions, events, links, success conditions, and cross-domain dependencies. Develop simulator-grounded parsing, joint road–airspace grounding, temporal planning, pre-execution feasibility checking, trace-based runtime verification, failure localization, and bounded repair within a unified workflow. Propose AURORA-Bench to evaluate both executability and fidelity to requested interactions. Demonstrate across multiple language models that structured execution and runtime verification improve reliability and reveal silent failures; localized repair reduces need for full regeneration.
AI.result: Structured execution enhances reliability; runtime verification uncovers silent failures not detected by completion-based evaluation; localized repair fixes many violations without regenerating the entire scenario. Realizing behavior, not just executable code, is essential; explicit intermediate representations enable verifiable and repairable language-driven co-simulation across air–ground scenarios.
AI.conclusion: AURORA shows that verification-enabled NL-driven co-simulation using a typed IR (AGSG) yields more reliable, repairable scenario generation, with explicit intermediate representations enabling grounded, verifiable, and repairable co-simulation workflows.

title: FINSKILLOPS: A Self-Evolving Multi-Agent System for SEC Filing QA
summary: Financial QA systems are typically improved before deployment through better retrieval, prompting, or agent coordination, leaving their reliability behavior fixed thereafter. In practice, new SEC-filing questions repeatedly expose heterogeneous errors in period, entity, evidence use, and calculation. Existing self-improvement methods can turn failures into new behaviors, but offer limited control over where a correction should apply or which previously correct answers it may break. We therefore frame post-deployment improvement as controlled behavioral maintenance: recurring failures should become scoped skill patches, and each patch should earn deployment with- out introducing regressions. We instantiate this view in FINSKILLOPS, a multi-agent system for SEC filing QA. FINSKILLOPS derives reusable skills from evidence-grounded, typed failure diagnoses and governs them through targeted validation, protected-case regression checks, negative controls, and versioned replacement or retirement. Across six financial QA benchmarks, a single frozen skill registry achieves the highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency among the evaluated systems. Evolved skills raise correctness from 3.70 to 4.55 on our enhanced benchmark. In a separate 12-round operational study, only six of 33 proposed skills are promoted, while the monitoring non-correct rate falls from 20.0% to 12.5%. These results establish controlled skill scope, admission, and lifecycle management as the foundation for reliable self-improvement.

AI.tldr: Framing post-deployment QA improvement as controlled skill maintenance; introduces FINSKILLOPS, a multi-agent framework that licenses, validates, and version-controls reusable skills to fix SEC filing QA failures without regressions.
AI.motivation: Reliability issues in financial QA after deployment due to heterogeneous errors, and limitations of prior self-improvement methods lacking targeted, safe patching; need lifecycle management for skills.
AI.method: Develops FINSKILLOPS: a multi-agent system that derives reusable skills from evidence-grounded, typed failure diagnoses; uses targeted validation, protected-case regression checks, negative controls, and versioned replacement/retirement; maintains a frozen skill registry; evaluation across six benchmarks and a 12-round study with metrics.
AI.result: Highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency with frozen registry among six systems; evolved skills raise correctness from 3.70 to 4.55 on enhanced benchmark; in a 12-round study, six of 33 skills promoted; non-correct rate falls from 20.0% to 12.5%.
AI.conclusion: Controlled scope, admission, and lifecycle management are the foundation for reliable self-improvement in financial QA.

title: Learn Your Own Thoughts: Abstract Token Curriculum
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable reasoning capabilities by utilizing chain-of-thought (CoT) as a scratchpad for intermediate stages of thinking. However, CoT techniques require explicit supervision on thinking tokens, which requires rich, task-specific data. In this work, we propose Abstract Token Curriculum (ATC), a novel curriculum learning framework that elicits effective continuous intermediate representations without direct supervision or manual scratchpad design. ATC gradually increases problem complexity through a sequence of distributions, training the model to develop internal abstract ``thoughts'' in the continuous representation space. This paper provides both theoretical and experimental evidence for the benefits of ATC and its advantages over previous methods for training continuous thoughts. Theoretically, we show that for learning parity functions with single-layer softmax attention using ATC, attention naturally focuses on the CoT tokens in the context that provide the ``easiest path'' to predicting the next token. Experimentally, we show ATC's effectiveness on graph reachability and arithmetic learning tasks.

AI.tldr: ATC introduces a curriculum over problem distributions to elicit continuous internal representations as abstract thoughts without explicit scratchpads, supported by theory on parity with single-layer softmax attention and validated empirically on graph reachability and arithmetic tasks.
AI.motivation: Aims to remove dependence on explicit chain-of-thought supervision and manual scratchpad design, enabling models to cultivate internal reasoning representations in a continuous space.
AI.method: Proposes Abstract Token Curriculum (ATC): gradually increases problem complexity via a sequence of distributions, training the model to develop internal abstract representations in a continuous space. The work provides theoretical analysis showing that, in parity learning with a single-layer softmax attention, attention naturally focuses on the CoT tokens that yield the easiest path to predicting the next token, and reports empirical results on graph reachability and arithmetic tasks.
AI.result: Theoretically, ATC causes attention to attend to CoT tokens that provide the easiest path to next-token prediction under parity with single-layer softmax attention. Empirically, ATC improves performance on graph reachability and arithmetic learning tasks compared with baselines.
AI.conclusion: ATC offers a principled framework for training continuous thoughts without explicit supervision, supported by theory and empirical results, with advantages over prior CoT-supervision approaches.

title: AI Smart Glasses for Wearable Intelligence: From Egocentric Sensing to Agentic Personalization
summary: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping smart glasses from egocentric capture and display devices into platforms for wearable intelligence. Smart glasses increasingly serve as wearable AI systems that connect first-person observation with real-time assistance under strict form-factor constraints. We frame this transition through the lens of \emph{AI smart glasses} and define them as a system-level concept in which egocentric sensing, resource-aware computing, intelligent reasoning, multimodal interaction, and real-world application constraints are co-designed for personalized assistance in the physical world. To systematically study this perspective, we organize the survey around four connected dimensions. First, we examine the hardware foundation that bounds sensing, computation, feedback delivery, and sustained deployment. Second, we study wearable intelligence, where egocentric signals are transformed into perceptual, contextual, and agentic capabilities. Third, we discuss interaction design, through which users request, receive, correct, and regulate assistance during ongoing activity. Fourth, we analyze application scenarios across healthcare, accessibility, situated learning, daily life assistance, cultural tourism, and industrial support, showing how domain requirements reshape system design and evaluation. We further identify five cross-cutting research challenges for future AI smart glasses: next-generation hardware, trustworthy egocentric intelligence, lifelong personalized memory, proactive intelligence, and embodied foundation models. By centering smart glasses as wearable-intelligence platforms, this survey provides a unified framework for organizing technologies, applications, and open challenges in this emerging area.

AI.tldr: A survey that defines AI smart glasses as a system-level wearable intelligence platform and analyzes hardware, perception, interaction, and applications to map future challenges.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified framework for organizing technologies, applications, and open challenges in AI-enabled smart glasses and to advance wearable intelligence that tightly integrates sensing, computation, and real-world use.
AI.method: Systematic survey organized around four connected dimensions (hardware, wearable intelligence, interaction design, and application scenarios) and five cross-cutting research challenges; cross-domain analysis across healthcare, accessibility, situated learning, daily life, cultural tourism, and industrial support.
AI.result: Proposes a unified framework for organizing technologies, applications, and open challenges in AI smart glasses; articulates design constraints and evaluation needs; identifies gaps and directions for hardware, reliability, memory, proactive intelligence, and embodied foundation models.
AI.conclusion: Center smart glasses as wearable-intelligence platforms and call for advances in next-generation hardware, trustworthy egocentric intelligence, lifelong personalized memory, proactive intelligence, and embodied foundation models to enable personalized, real-world assistance.

title: SLAMSqueezeBench: Comparing SLAM Systems under Resource Constraints
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is one of the services running on an autonomous robot. It is typically run to assist other tasks such as planning, manipulation, etc. All these tasks are run on edge hardware and are subject to severe resource constraints. However, most SLAM systems are built and tested in isolation, and their performance is reported as if they are the only task running on a system. We observe that existing benchmarks lack a common mechanism for comparing SLAM systems under realistic resource constraints. To address this limitation, we have developed SLAMSqueezeBench, a framework that allows testing of SLAM systems under realistic workloads on edge hardware. It does so by imposing constraints on compute and memory resources available for the SLAM system during execution. It also simulates realistic camera frame acquisition with frame drops when a finite buffer is full. Using SLAMSqueezeBench, we compare nine SLAM systems spanning classical systems, learning-based systems, and approaches for Gaussian splatting. Our testing framework will be available for use by the community upon publication.

AI.tldr: SLAMSqueezeBench benchmarks SLAM systems under realistic edge-compute constraints, including compute/memory limits and frame drops, by simulating camera acquisition; evaluates nine SLAM systems across classical, learning-based, and Gaussian splatting; aims to standardize realistic resource-constrained benchmarking.
AI.motivation: Existing SLAM benchmarks assume dedicated resources and ignore co-run tasks; a need for realistic workloads to compare SLAM performance on edge hardware under resource constraints.
AI.method: Developed SLAMSqueezeBench framework that imposes compute and memory constraints on SLAM execution and simulates camera frame acquisition with a finite-buffer frame-drop model; uses this to run nine SLAM systems across classical, learning-based, and Gaussian splatting approaches; results will be published with the framework.
AI.result: A framework and study to test SLAM systems under constrained resources, enabling a fairer, more realistic comparison; includes comparison of nine SLAM systems spanning different paradigms; framework to be released to the community upon publication.
AI.conclusion: SLAMSqueezeBench provides a standardized, resource-aware benchmarking platform for SLAM on edge hardware and facilitates realistic cross-system comparisons; invites community use and validation.

title: LearnActCoder: Role-Aware Error Memory for Adaptive Clinical Coding Agents
summary: Clinical coding agents repeatedly encounter the same failure modes, including unsupported codes, missed documented conditions, specificity errors, and procedure-coding convention mismatches. We introduce Learn-Then-Act, an inference-time adaptation framework that converts errors from a small labeled LEARN batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database (MistakeKDB). False-negative lessons are routed to a recall-oriented Coder, while false-positive lessons are routed to a precision-oriented Judge. We instantiate the framework in LearnActCoder, a Coder-Judge clinical coding pipeline with lookup-table grounding where available. On 150 matched MIMIC-III notes, structured MistakeKDB improves CPT F1 by 5.9 percentage points, while raw-example and reflection-style memories remain near the no-memory baseline; the ICD-9 improvement is not significant. On a matched MIMIC-IV cohort, memory shifts ICD-10 coding toward higher precision at a recall cost, leaving F1 statistically unchanged. Applying the same memory to 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes maintains a stable ICD operating point, providing scale/stability evidence. Overall, the results are consistent with structured, feedback-derived error memory being useful for adapting clinical coding behavior across cases without weight updates or changes to the underlying workflow. Absolute CPT/HCPCS performance remains low, and the system is evaluated retrospectively rather than in clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: A memory-based Learn-Then-Act approach (MistakeKDB) improves CPT F1 on MIMIC-III by 5.9 points, with mixed ICD effects and no retraining, demonstrating stable, scalable error-driven adaptation; CPT/HCPCS performance remains low and clinical deployment is not reported.
AI.motivation: To address recurring coding failures (unsupported codes, missed documented conditions, specificity errors, and procedure-coding convention mismatches) by converting observed mistakes from a small labeled batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database (MistakeKDB) that guides future predictions without weight updates.
AI.method: Construct MistakeKDB from a small labeled LEARN batch of coding errors; route false-negatives to a recall-oriented Coder and false-positives to a precision-oriented Judge; instantiate LearnActCoder with lookup-table grounding where available; evaluate on MIMIC-III (150 notes) and MIMIC-IV cohorts; assess with 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes to test scalability.
AI.result: On MIMIC-III, CPT F1 improves by 5.9 percentage points; ICD-9 improvement is not significant; on MIMIC-IV, memory shifts ICD-10 coding toward higher precision at a recall cost, leaving F1 unchanged; 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes maintain a stable ICD operating point; raw-memory variants perform poorly and absolute CPT/HCPCS performance remains low.
AI.conclusion: Structured, feedback-derived error memory enables adaptation of clinical coding behavior across cases without weight updates or changes to the underlying workflow; results are retrospective with limited deployment; gains are dataset- and metric-specific and the approach does not yet achieve high absolute CPT/HCPCS accuracy.

title: Alliance Beats Isolation: Unifying Heterogeneous Allied Datasets Improves Classifier Performance
summary: In many application domains, such as student dropout, insurance fraud, loan approval, and machine failures, several labelled public datasets are available where (i) data is about the same type of objects but the set of actual underlying objects are disjoint; and (ii) the class labels are same; and (iii) the feature spaces of the datasets are largely distinct (heterogeneous), with a few shared features. We call such datasets as allied. A single classifier cannot be trained on both datasets together, and one classifier trained on one dataset cannot be tested on the other. In this paper, we propose a method to merge the feature-spaces into a single feature-space for a pair of given allied heterogeneous datasets. We then use a matrix completion method to create a unified dataset based on the merged feature-space. The hypothesis is that the merged representation facilitates the transfer of classification knowledge from one dataset to another. We conduct experiments on several pairs of allied, heterogeneous datasets and several classifiers to demonstrate that any classifier trained on the unified representation always outperforms classifiers separately trained on the constituent allied datasets on several pairs of allied datasets. This work provides an easy way to substantially improve classifier performance by unifying and using multiple allied datasets together.

AI.tldr: Merge heterogeneous allied datasets into a unified feature-space via matrix completion to enable cross-dataset transfer; the unified representation yields classifiers that outperform models trained on individual datasets across multiple pairs and classifiers.
AI.motivation: Several real-world domains have multiple allied datasets that share labels but have disjoint objects and largely distinct feature spaces. A single classifier cannot be trained on both datasets, and cross-dataset testing is ineffective without a common representation. A unified representation could enable transfer of classification knowledge between datasets.
AI.method: For a pair of allied heterogeneous datasets, merge their feature-spaces into a single space. Use a matrix completion approach to populate a unified dataset in this merged space. Train classifiers on the unified data and compare performance to classifiers trained separately on each dataset across several dataset pairs and classifier types.
AI.result: The unified representation consistently improves classifier performance over baselines that train on each dataset separately, across multiple allied dataset pairs and classifier types.
AI.conclusion: Unifying allied heterogeneous datasets through feature-space merging and matrix completion provides an effective, simple approach to enhance classification by leveraging cross-dataset information, with broad applicability to multi-source learning.

title: Absence is Presence: Understanding Visual Scene Negative Events Under Safety Cognitive Constraint
summary: Traditional scene understanding focuses on affirmative information objectively present in images. However, in safety-critical domains, comprehending key information that should exist but is actually absent is vital for risk mitigation. To bridge this gap, we focus on visual scene negative captioning with safety as the cognitive constraint. The core challenge is to convert physical absence into semantic negative events. Existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with this process because affirmation bias suppresses negative reasoning, while limited mental filling capability and representation bias further hinder the inference of absent information. To address these challenges, we propose a negative captioning framework based on counterfactual reconstruction and contrastive decoding (CRCD). Inspired by human cognition, CRCD reformulates the task as counterfactual latent change captioning to bypass affirmation bias. It contrasts a synthesized safe expectation with reality to identify semantic omissions. To address limited mental filling, we design a dual-branch counterfactual reconstruction architecture. The amodal completion branch restores defective objects, while the functional association branch infers completely absent safety objects. Concurrently, a multi-condition representation learning mechanism is integrated to mitigate representation bias by projecting universal features onto predefined safety criteria subspaces, thereby capturing information across more dimensions. By decoding feature-level semantic residuals between the reconstructed scene prototype and raw input, CRCD bounds the non-existence search space and activates the decoder's negative logic. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of CRCD, establishing a high-performance baseline for this pioneering task.

AI.tldr: CRCD introduces a negative captioning framework for safety-critical scenes by reframing absent information as counterfactual latent changes. It uses a dual-branch architecture (amodal completion and functional association) plus multi-condition representation learning to contrast safe expectations with reality and generate semantic negative captions, validated by extensive experiments.
AI.motivation: In safety-critical domains, recognizing information that should exist but is absent is crucial for risk mitigation. Existing VLMs suffer from affirmation bias, limited mental filling, and representation bias that impede inferring absent safety information.
AI.method: CRCD formulates negative captioning as counterfactual latent change captioning. It employs a dual-branch counterfactual reconstruction: (1) amodal completion to restore defective objects, and (2) functional association to infer completely absent safety objects. A multi-condition representation learning module projects universal features into predefined safety subspaces. Negative semantics are decoded by comparing feature-level residuals between a reconstructed scene prototype and the raw input.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate CRCD’s effectiveness and establish a high-performance baseline for visual scene negative captioning under safety constraints.
AI.conclusion: CRCD successfully enables semantic negative reasoning about absent safety information, addressing affirmation and representation biases and providing a robust framework for negative captioning in safety-critical vision-language tasks.

title: Navigate or Relocate? Planning Among Movable Obstacles in Unknown Environments
summary: Conventional robot planning methods seek collision-free paths to a goal but fail when all paths are blocked. In these cases, the robot must determine which objects to relocate, in what order, and where to place them to clear a path---a problem known as Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO). Most NAMO planners assume a known environment, while existing approaches for unknown environments typically reason locally about relocations and cannot plan interdependent relocation sequences. We consider NAMO in unknown environments revealed through onboard sensing, where the robot must decide whether a blocked route requires relocation or a feasible path may exist through unexplored space. We propose an online framework that addresses this ambiguity by selecting between navigation and relocation using shortest paths that treat discovered movable objects as obstacles or as removable. Navigation relies on existing motion planners, while relocation uses a sampling-based approach that, unlike existing approaches for unknown environments, searches over \textit{interdependent} relocation sequences and uses an LLM to bias sampling. Numerical experiments demonstrate scalability to cluttered environments requiring interdependent relocations and improved plan quality over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: Online NAMO in unknown environments: an approach that alternates between navigation and relocation, using a sampling-based planner for interdependent relocations guided by an LLM, showing scalability and improved plan quality.
AI.motivation: Conventional planners fail when all collision-free paths are blocked; unknown environments require deciding whether to relocate objects or explore unseen space, and existing approaches lack interdependency reasoning.
AI.method: An online framework that selects between navigation and relocation using shortest paths; navigation leverages existing motion planners, relocation uses a sampling-based method that searches over interdependent relocation sequences; an LLM biases the sampling process to guide exploration.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show the method scales to cluttered environments with interdependent relocations and achieves improved plan quality over baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables efficient, interdependency-aware NAMO planning in unknown environments, with LLM-guided sampling enhancing plan quality and scalability.

title: AutoData: Agentic Search for Pre-training Data Selection
summary: LLM agents have recently shown promise in automating machine learning engineering by editing model and training code under execution feedback. Data, however, remains largely outside this agentic optimisation loop. We frame pre-training data selection as heuristic engineering over per-document features, i.e., lexical statistics, categorical labels, and perplexity. We introduce AutoData, an agent that searches directly over executable selection algorithms. Unlike prior data mixture methods that optimise weights over a fixed set of domains, AutoData searches a richer program space of scoring, stratification, and stochastic selection rules, discovering feature interactions automatically by iteratively refining algorithms with validation feedback from a proxy model. Within an overnight search, AutoData discovers a selection algorithm that outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines. Despite being searched only on this small proxy, the discovered recipe transfers to larger scales and improves the downstream metric CORE. These results suggest that data engineering can be treated as an agentic machine learning problem, extending autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to the data.

AI.tldr: AutoData treats pre-training data selection as an executable program search problem, enabling an LLM agent to evolve data-curation algorithms (scoring, stratification, stochastic selection) that outperform hand-crafted pipelines and transfer to larger scales, improving CORE.
AI.motivation: Data curation is a critical, under-optimized component of ML training; prior work uses fixed data-weighting schemes and lacks automated exploration of data-selection logic. Framing data selection as heuristic engineering with executable policies allows agent-driven discovery of feature interactions.
AI.method: Define per-document features (lexical stats, labels, perplexity) and search an executable space over scoring, stratification, and stochastic selection rules. An agent iteratively refines programs using validation feedback from a proxy model, performing an overnight search to discover effective data-selection algorithms and automatically learn feature interactions.
AI.result: The discovered data-selection recipe outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines on the proxy model and transfers to larger scales, yielding improvements in the downstream CORE metric.
AI.conclusion: Treat data engineering as an agentic ML problem, extending autonomous optimization from models and training code to the data domain, enabling automated discovery of high-performing data-curation pipelines.

title: OceanMoE: Structured Conditional Sparse Computation for Long-Horizon Multivariate Ocean Forecasting
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Yishun Zhu and Jian Wang contributed equally to this research
summary: Multivariate ocean forecasting must exploit shared evolution in a coupled ocean system while adapting to the heterogeneous statistical and dynamical characteristics of different prediction variables and locations. Fully shared models may lack the flexibility to handle this heterogeneity, whereas fully independent models discard the common ocean context shared across variables. The key question is how to retain shared context in a unified model while allowing computation to specialize according to the prediction target and local state. We propose OceanMoE, a structured conditional sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework that combines sharing and specialization for multivariate ocean forecasting. OceanMoE fuses cross-variable information to construct target-specific local representations and uses them to perform content-conditioned sparse routing at each spatial location, with the number of active experts adapted to router confidence. In the decoder, routing is augmented with a learned geographic bias parameterized by spherical-harmonic spatial bases, while shared residual and seasonal pathways provide common cross-variable and month-dependent context. Experiments on long-horizon autoregressive ORAS5 forecasting show that OceanMoE lowers aggregate forecasting error in both evaluated settings and maintains lower geometric-mean normalized RMSE than the corresponding baselines over most later rollout months. Routing analyses further show that expert allocation varies with prediction targets and spatial locations. These results support structured conditional computation as a modeling strategy for balancing shared ocean context with adaptive specialization.

AI.tldr: OceanMoE is a structured conditional sparse Mixture-of-Experts approach for multivariate ocean forecasting that balances shared context and target-specific specialization through cross-variable representations, content-conditioned routing, and spatial biases, improving long-horizon forecasts.
AI.motivation: To capture shared evolution in a coupled ocean system while accommodating heterogeneous statistical and dynamical characteristics across prediction variables and locations; fully shared models lack flexibility and fully independent models discard cross-variable context, necessitating a method that preserves shared context while enabling specialization.
AI.method: OceanMoE uses a structured conditional sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework that (i) fuses cross-variable information to build target-specific local representations; (ii) applies content-conditioned sparse routing at each spatial location with the number of active experts adapting to router confidence; (iii) augments the decoder with a learned geographic bias via spherical-harmonic spatial bases; (iv) includes shared residual and seasonal pathways for cross-variable and month-dependent context.
AI.result: Experiments on long-horizon autoregressive ORAS5 forecasting show OceanMoE reduces aggregate forecasting error in evaluated settings and maintains lower geometric-mean normalized RMSE than baselines over most later rollout months; routing analyses indicate expert allocation varies by prediction target and location.
AI.conclusion: Structured conditional computation can balance shared ocean context with adaptive specialization, validating OceanMoE as an effective strategy for multivariate ocean forecasting.

title: SnapPhysics: A Physics-Aware Scene Graph from a Single View for Interactive Mixed Reality Scenes
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE ISMAR, 2026
summary: We propose SnapPhysics, a training-free framework that reconstructs 3D objects and estimates their physical properties such as mass, friction, and center of gravity from a single image. For physically coherent interactions in mixed reality (MR), such properties are as important as geometry. Prior approaches infer them by analyzing object dynamics in video, which is computationally costly, or by querying vision-language models (VLMs) on single images, which lacks geometric grounding and inter-object relationships. We address these limitations by combining instance-level 3D reconstruction and spatial alignment with a physics-aware scene graph that encodes these relationships and per-object metric geometry as structured context for VLM-based property reasoning. Experiments on 3D-FRONT show that SnapPhysics improves scene-level F-Score by 18.6% over the best learning-based method, and on real captured scenes with ground-truth mass, it reduces the mean absolute log difference error (mALDE) by up to 20.5% and improves log-scale correlation ($r^2_{\mathrm{ls}}$) by up to 19.6% over VLM-only estimation. SnapPhysics enables physically interactive MR experiences without manual parameter tuning. Project page: https://snapphysics-ismar2026.github.io/.

AI.tldr: SnapPhysics is a training-free framework that reconstructs 3D object geometry and estimates physical properties (mass, friction, center of gravity) from a single image. It uses a physics-aware scene graph to ground VLM-based property reasoning, improving scene-level accuracy on synthetic and real scenes without training.
AI.motivation: Physically coherent interactions in mixed reality require not just geometry but per-object physical properties. Prior methods either rely on video dynamics (computationally heavy) or VLMs on single images without geometric grounding; this work seeks to fuse geometry grounding with inter-object relationships to enable reliable property reasoning.
AI.method: Integrates instance-level 3D reconstruction and spatial alignment with a physics-aware scene graph that encodes per-object metric geometry as context for VLM-based property reasoning. The framework is training-free and uses VLMs to infer physical properties conditioned on structured context.
AI.result: On 3D-FRONT, SnapPhysics improves scene-level F-Score by 18.6% over the best learning-based method. On real scenes with ground-truth mass, it reduces mean absolute log difference error (mALDE) by up to 20.5% and increases log-scale correlation (r^2_ls) by up to 19.6% over VLM-only estimation.
AI.conclusion: SnapPhysics enables physically interactive MR experiences without manual parameter tuning, addressing limitations of prior approaches by grounding property reasoning in geometry and inter-object relationships.

title: VABench: Measuring Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Visual Demonstrations, Active Perception, and Metric Control
summary: Spatial intelligence requires more than describing object locations. Under incomplete observation, models must identify and acquire missing evidence, interpret it in a common spatial frame, and act on it. We introduce VA-Bench to evaluate the complete observe-reason-act-revise loop. General-purpose MLLMs learn procedural context from RGB-only demonstrations, actively select camera viewpoints, issue metric Cartesian commands, and revise them from execution feedback. Models receive no privileged object poses, oracle trajectories, or learned action heads. A fixed model-agnostic controller executes only model-specified targets. VA-Bench contains 14 base task families (11 single-arm and three dual-arm), seven held-out geometry/layout variants, and a long-horizon five-object composition track. We evaluate 12 primary model conditions in three independent runs over the same 20 physically verified seeds per base task, reporting terminal success, nine trajectory-level behavioral diagnostics, and subtask progress. First, the best-performing model scores 100.0% on target localization and 78.9% on spatial relations in the annotated run. Its three-run macro-average task success is only 53.93+/-3.17%. Second, active camera control significantly improves task success over passive multi-view observation. In one matched comparison, success rises from 27.86% to 57.50%. Third, held-out geometric transfer can reduce task success by over 30 percentage points. No model completes a strict long-horizon episode, despite substantial partial progress. VA-Bench thus tests whether general-purpose MLLMs can turn visual demonstrations and actively acquired evidence into successful embodied action.

AI.tldr: VA-Bench provides a comprehensive end-to-end benchmark to evaluate the observe-reason-act-revise loop for embodied visual reasoning using RGB-only, general-purpose MLLMs. It assesses active sensing, reasoning, and action with a fixed, model-agnostic controller across diverse task families, revealing strong localization but limited long-horizon success and sensitivity to geometry transfer.
AI.motivation: To move beyond static perception toward embodied agents that can acquire missing evidence, interpret it in a common spatial frame, and act under incomplete observations, without privileged object poses or learned action heads.
AI.method: A fixed model-agnostic controller executes model-specified Cartesian targets. VA-Bench comprises 14 base task families (11 single-arm, 3 dual-arm), 7 held-out geometry/layout variants, and a long-horizon five-object composition track. Evaluation uses 12 model conditions, 3 independent runs, and 20 physically verified seeds per base task, reporting terminal success, nine trajectory-level diagnostics, and subtask progress. Models learn procedural context from RGB demonstrations, actively select camera viewpoints, and revise commands from execution feedback.
AI.result: Best model achieves 100.0% target localization and 78.9% spatial-relations accuracy in the annotated run; macro-average task success across three runs is 53.93% ± 3.17%. Active camera control improves task success (matched comparison: 27.86% passive vs 57.50% active). Held-out geometry transfers reduce task success by >30 percentage points. No model completes a strict long-horizon episode, though substantial partial progress occurs.
AI.conclusion: VA-Bench effectively tests whether general-purpose MLLMs can close the observe-reason-act-revise loop with embodied action using visual demonstrations and actively acquired evidence. Results indicate meaningful gains from active sensing but highlight persistent challenges in long-horizon generalization and geometry transfer, motivating further work on planning, perception-action integration, and robust generalization.

title: Rethinking Multi-Agent Collaboration: When More Is Less
summary: The rapid advancement of large language models and single-agent harnesses has reshaped the landscape of autonomous systems, raising a critical question of when multi-agent collaboration offers genuine value. As individual agent capabilities continue to scale, multi-agent collaboration faces diminishing returns while incurring growing context overhead. Through systematic analysis, we delineate the capability boundaries of multi-agent collaboration relative to single-agent alternatives, showing that it confers systematic benefits specifically in long-horizon tasks with sparse dependencies, while single-agent harnesses remain superior in tightly coupled, sequential workflows. Building on these insights, we propose SAIGE, a lightweight multi-agent collaboration mechanism based on Semantic-Aware Incremental Graph Evolution. SAIGE models collaboration as a dynamically evolving graph, where nodes are agent instances spawned on demand and edges encode semantic dependencies established through content-based information retrieval. Experiments on long-horizon, complex task benchmarks show that SAIGE achieves a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance, and that scaling the agent pool or deepening the recursion level does not consistently improve outcomes. Our findings suggest that multi-agent superiority is bounded by task structure rather than universal, and that more agents do not necessarily make a system more intelligent.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent collaboration offers benefits mainly for long-horizon tasks with sparse dependencies; single-agent pipelines outperform in tightly coupled tasks. SAIGE introduces a semantic-aware incremental graph evolution mechanism to orchestrate agent collaboration, modeling it as a dynamic graph with on-demand nodes and content-based dependency edges. Scaling agents or recursion depth yields diminishing or inconsistent gains. Boundaries of multi-agent superiority depend on task structure, not universal capability.
AI.motivation: As LLMs and single-agent tools scale, it is unclear when adding more agents provides real value. The study seeks to identify the task structures where multi-agent collaboration yields systematic benefits and where it incurs overhead, aiming to guide design choices for autonomous systems.
AI.method: Systematic analysis of collaboration boundaries, followed by the proposal of SAIGE. SAIGE models collaboration as a dynamically evolving graph: nodes are agent instances spawned on demand; edges encode semantic dependencies via content-based information retrieval. Evaluation on long-horizon, complex task benchmarks, examining variations in agent pool size and recursion depth.
AI.result: SAIGE achieves a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance in long-horizon tasks. Increasing the agent pool size or recursion depth does not consistently improve outcomes, suggesting diminishing returns and context overhead can offset potential gains.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent superiority is task-structure dependent rather than universal. More agents do not automatically yield better intelligence; SAIGE offers a scalable, lightweight collaboration mechanism optimized for sparse, long-horizon tasks.

title: PhyRestore: Physics-Structured Latent-Factor Restoration
summary: Estimating temporal soil-loss change is challenging when physically meaningful input factors are noisy or corrupted, particularly because substantial changes are rare relative to the large number of locations exhibiting little change. We study this problem through the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) and introduce PhyRestore, a physics-structured latent-factor restoration framework. Rather than directly predicting soil-loss change or correcting a degraded physical estimate, PhyRestore restores corrupted physical factors and reconstructs temporal change through the known physical relationship. We evaluate PhyRestore in a watershed-scale bitemporal raster setting under isolated and simultaneous corruption of rainfall erosivity and cover management, comparing it with the degraded RUSLE estimate and Direct RF, XGBoost, MLP, and CNN models. Factor restoration improves high-magnitude recovery when the corrupted factors remain identifiable, but its advantage weakens under joint corruption, sparse positive extremes, and factor values outside the training support.

AI.tldr: PhyRestore restores corrupted physical factors in RUSLE to reconstruct temporal soil-loss change by leveraging the physical relationship, outperforming degraded RUSLE when factors are identifiable; its advantage diminishes under joint corruption and when factors are outside the training distribution.
AI.motivation: Temporal soil-loss change estimation is difficult when input factors are noisy or corrupted and significant changes are rare; a physics-structured latent-factor restoration approach can leverage known physical laws to recover meaningful changes.
AI.method: Introduce PhyRestore, a physics-structured latent-factor restoration framework that restores corrupted input factors (e.g., rainfall erosivity, cover management) and reconstructs temporal change via the RUSLE physical relationship. Evaluate in a watershed-scale, bitemporal raster setting, under isolated and simultaneous corruption, and compare against degraded RUSLE and standard ML models (Direct RF, XGBoost, MLP, CNN).
AI.result: Factor restoration improves high-magnitude recovery when corrupted factors remain identifiable; the advantage weakens under joint corruption, sparse positive extremes, and factor values outside the training support.
AI.conclusion: Physics-structured restoration is beneficial for recovering large changes when corrupted factors are identifiable, but its effectiveness declines with joint corruption and distributional shifts; robustness to extreme/out-of-distribution factors remains a challenge.

title: KoUniTalk: A Lightweight Articulation-Centered Korean-English 3D Talking Face Benchmark
summary: High-quality 3D talking face datasets remain largely English- centric, and Korean 3D facial motion data are difficult to combine with standard English benchmarks because of differences in mesh topology, spatial scale, coordinate system, and temporal sampling. We present KoUniTalk, a lightweight articulation-centered Korean-English 3D talk- ing face benchmark that retargets VOCASET and the released Korean speech-based 3D talking face data to a shared mesh topology using de- formation transfer. Rather than proposing a new deformation-transfer algorithm or a full-head identity-preserving avatar dataset, KoUniTalk provides an identity-neutral canonical output space for controlled speech- driven facial articulation training and evaluation across English and Ko- rean. The unified template contains 1,176 vertices and focuses on the mouth and adjacent lower- and mid-face regions, reducing the output dimensionality from 15,069 and 72,147 dimensions to 3,528 dimensions, corresponding to 4.27-fold and 20.45-fold reductions compared with VO- CASET/FLAME and the original Korean mesh, respectively. To exam- ine whether retargeting preserves speech-relevant motion, we evaluate semantic mouth-landmark trajectories, including mouth opening, mouth width, aperture ratio, and mouth-opening dynamics. Since the official test set of the Korean dataset is not publicly released, we additionally define a subject-disjoint Korean benchmark split. The processed matched benchmark contains 22 speakers, 4,978 sequences, and 642,781 frames, enabling Korean-English cross-dataset evaluation of speech-driven 3D fa- cial animation models in a single compact articulation-template space. Source-reported inventory counts are listed separately from these pro- cessed counts

AI.tldr: KoUniTalk: a lightweight Korean-English 3D talking face benchmark that retargets VOCASET and Korean 3D data to a shared, mouth-focused mesh, enabling cross-language articulation evaluation in a compact template space.
AI.motivation: High-quality 3D talking face data are English-centric and incompatible across languages due to mesh topology, scale, coordinates, and sampling; a unified articulation-centered space enables controlled speech-driven facial analysis across Korean and English.
AI.method: Retargets data to a unified mesh via deformation transfer onto a 1,176-vertex mouth-adjacent template; reduces output dimensionality from 15,069/72,147 to 3,528; evaluates semantic mouth landmarks (opening, width, aperture, dynamics); defines a subject-disjoint Korean benchmark; compiles 22 speakers, 4,978 sequences, 642,781 frames.
AI.result: Demonstrates preserved speech-relevant motion in the retargeted data through mouth-landmark trajectories; provides compact, identical-space data for cross-language evaluation; produces a processed Korean-English benchmark with 22 speakers, 4,978 sequences, and 642,781 frames.
AI.conclusion: KoUniTalk offers an identity-neutral, canonical output space for controlled speech-driven facial articulation training/evaluation across English and Korean, facilitating cross-dataset studies without introducing a new full-head avatar dataset.

title: Tele-Traversability: Rethinking Traversability for Teleoperated Ground Robots in Terrain Navigation
summary: Teleoperation, a human-in-the-loop control scheme, allows a human operator to remotely command and guide a mobile robot to navigate in off-road environments, yet fluent and user-friendly tele-navigation requires an alignment of traversability evaluation between human and robot. In the teleoperation system, the human operator typically utilizes off-site incomplete and delayed feedback via a human-machine interface to make a judgment of traversability, while the robot makes such an evaluation based on in situ onboard sensory information, which could cause divergent traversability estimation and thus generate mismatched decisions and actions. Existing approaches for traversability modeling, estimation, and prediction are mainly derived from the view of robots, i.e., robot-centric, and are practically suitable for fully autonomous mobile robots, but neglect the influence of human operators. To address this problem, this paper extends the concept of traversability from robot-centric to human-centric by accounting for the operator's cognitive states, such as attention, workload, and risk tolerance or awareness, termed tele-traversability. We first revisit the definitions and roles of traversability in robotics and then extend them to teleoperation settings. Finally, we highlight future trends and open challenges of tele-traversability toward human-centric teleoperation systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes tele-traversability: extending traversability concepts from robot-centric to human-centric in teleoperation by incorporating operator cognition to align human and robot assessments.
AI.motivation: To mitigate mismatched traversability judgments between delayed/incomplete human feedback and onboard robot sensing in teleoperation, enabling safer, more fluent tele-navigation.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis: redefine traversability for teleoperation, integrate operator cognitive states (attention, workload, risk tolerance), review existing robot-centric traversability, and outline future trends and open challenges.
AI.result: Formal definition and framework for tele-traversability; a synthesis of human-centric considerations in traversability modeling; roadmap for future research.
AI.conclusion: Tele-traversability is essential for effective human-in-the-loop navigation, with significant open questions in modeling, evaluation, and system design.

title: TorchCraft: Unified binder design by inverting an all-atom structure predictor
summary: All-atom structure predictors model diverse molecular interactions, but using their learned structural priors for binder design remains challenging. Here we present TorchCraft, a unified binder-design framework that optimizes sequence logits through a frozen all-atom predictor. Implemented in TorchFold, TorchCraft combines confidence, contact, geometric, and sequence-prior objectives within a shared optimization procedure for minibinders, framework-conditioned VHHs, cyclic peptides, and ligand-binding proteins. Using pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights, TorchCraft generated representative minibinders and VHHs with experimentally measured binding across four targets in each format, without post hoc sequence redesign. Computational benchmarks further demonstrated the framework's applicability to cyclic peptides and ligand-conditioned pocket design. TorchCraft extends predictor inversion to multiple binder formats and molecular contexts, providing a common framework for reusing all-atom structural priors in design.

AI.tldr: TorchCraft uses a frozen all-atom predictor to optimize binder sequences across minibinders, VHHs, cyclic peptides, and ligand-binding proteins, reusing AlphaFold-like priors without redesign.
AI.motivation: Leveraging learned structural priors from all-atom structure predictors for binder design remains challenging; a unified framework could extend priors across diverse binder formats.
AI.method: Implemented in TorchFold; optimizes sequence logits via predictor inversion of a frozen all-atom model; combines confidence, contact, geometric, and sequence-prior objectives in a shared optimization; applicable to minibinders, framework-conditioned VHHs, cyclic peptides, and ligand-binding proteins; uses pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights.
AI.result: Generated representative minibinders and VHHs with experimentally measured binding across four targets per format, without post hoc sequence redesign; benchmarks show applicability to cyclic peptides and ligand-conditioned pocket design.
AI.conclusion: TorchCraft generalizes predictor inversion to multiple binder formats and contexts, enabling reuse of all-atom priors for binder design across diverse molecular scaffolds.

title: Learning-Based Reconstruction of Optical Properties in Bilayered Media from Single-distance Time-Resolved Reflectance Measurements
