summary: The inverse problem of reconstructing optical properties, specifically absorption and scattering coefficients, in layered biological media from time-domain reflectance measurements remains a significant challenge for traditional analytical models. Inverse solvers based on the diffusion equation often struggle with structural heterogeneity, frequently yielding poor accuracy for superficial absorption and deep-layers scattering. In this work, we propose a machine learning framework as an alternative approach to reconstruct the optical properties of a bilayered medium, benchmarking its efficiency and accuracy against model-based algorithms. To overcome the intrinsic approximations of diffusion theory and inverse reconstruction, we generated a robust synthetic dataset of forward DTOF using exact Monte Carlo simulations at multiple source-detector distances. A machine learning pipeline was then trained on this dataset and validated against state-of-the-art model-based reconstruction methods. Besides the significant reconstruction speed-up, the machine learning approach achieves higher accuracy than model-based inverse solvers, further providing an estimate of the parameter space dimensionality without requiring any a priori information about the number of layers in the investigated geometry. Further enhancements in the reconstruction accuracy can be expected in future extensions of this work, by training the pipeline over multiple DTOF curves from the same medium, in a joint multi-distance reconstruction approach.

AI.tldr: A machine learning framework reconstructs optical properties of bilayer media from time-domain DTOF data, using Monte Carlo forward simulations for training and outperforming diffusion-based inversions in speed and accuracy, while obviating a priori layer-count assumptions and enabling potential joint multi-distance reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of diffusion-based inverse solvers in heterogeneous, layered media, where superficial absorption and deep-layer scattering are poorly resolved.
AI.method: Generate a robust Monte Carlo-based forward DTOF dataset for a bilayer medium across multiple source-detector distances; train a machine learning pipeline to map DTOF curves to layer properties; benchmark against state-of-the-art model-based reconstructions; discuss potential for multi-distance joint reconstruction.
AI.result: The ML approach achieves higher accuracy and faster reconstructions than model-based solvers and can estimate the dimensionality of the parameter space without prior knowledge of the number of layers; performance is poised to improve with training on multi-distance DTOFs.
AI.conclusion: A ML-based reconstruction framework is a viable alternative to diffusion-based inversions for layered media, removing the need for a priori layer-count knowledge and offering avenues for further improvements via multi-distance, joint reconstructions.

title: PACE: Precise AI Cinematic Expression: A Typed Specification for Script-Grounded Previsualization and Geometric Conformance
summary:
Between a screenplay and a film sits a planning problem that is spatial first: who stands where, and what a camera sees from where it stands. An image diffusion model asked for a shot in free text settles that plan by its own defaults. We present PACE (Precise AI Cinematic Expression), a typed representation for the plan: the screenplay evidence, the characters, props and locations it needs, where each subject stands, and what the camera does. A value is written once at the level it belongs to (script, scene, shot or panel) and inherited below it. A compiler turns the result into both the prompt sent to the diffusion model and a 3D scene built in metres, and a camera solver places the camera so that the declared framing is the framing built. Where a declared value becomes geometry, PACE measures, field by field, how far the compiled camera and the staged render sit from the declaration, rather than asking a model to judge.
  On the 11-scene Automatic Drive screenplay, every staged single-subject panel places its subject within 1.2% of frame width of its declared position; with two or three subjects one camera pose cannot satisfy every position, and the residual is reported rather than absorbed. On 204 external director-storyboard shots, delivered head height is 1.906 times the staged target from the director's words, 1.733 from the compiled prompt, and 0.955 with the greybox control; the condition that holds framing best draws the described action least. Declaring the pose on 30 shots raises the action drawn from 58.9% to 74.4% without moving the framing. Transitions, fitted motion and human review of the generated panels remain open. Code: https://github.com/StudioPiLabs/pace-core

AI.tldr: PACE introduces a typed, hierarchical representation for cinematic planning that binds screenplay elements to 3D geometry and diffusion prompts, enabling measurement of deviation between declared framing and produced imagery.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between narrative planning and AI-generated imagery by making composition explicit and verifiable, rather than relying on model defaults.
AI.method: Define PACE as a typed plan with values at script, scene, shot, panel; inheritance of values; a compiler outputs diffusion prompts and a metres-scale 3D scene; a camera solver positions camera to satisfy declared framing; measure residual difference field-by-field between declaration and compiled render.
AI.result: Empirical results on datasets: 11-scene Automatic Drive: single-subject panel positions within 1.2% frame width; multi-subject limitations; 204 external director-storyboard shots: head height differences (1.906x, 1.733x, 0.955x depending on mode); declaring pose improves action depiction from 58.9% to 74.4% without changing framing; some aspects (transitions, motion, human review) remain open; code available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: PACE provides verifiable compliance of composition with declared planning, reducing reliance on diffusion defaults, but requires further work on transitions, motion, and human-in-the-loop review.

title: Recovering Aggressively Pruned Vision-Language-Action Models with Offline Hidden-State Distillation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models let robots follow language instructions, but their language backbones of several billion parameters are the main obstacle to running them on robot hardware. Structured pruning reduces that backbone, and removing 63% of it from OpenVLA-OFT drops LIBERO-Long success from 93.2% to 0.8%. A recent approach restores such a model with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, which needs online rollouts and hundreds of GPU-hours. We recover most of the lost success entirely offline. Width pruning narrows the blocks but keeps the residual stream at its original size, so teacher and student hidden states have the same shape and are matched directly, without a projector. Training against a cache built in one teacher pass lifts the 63%-reduced student to within 3.5 points of the teacher in about 8 GPU-hours. A sweep over nine ratios locates where the recovery objective starts to matter. Up to 45% reduction the two do not differ significantly on OpenVLA-OFT. Hidden-state distillation then adds +2.1 to +4.5 points there between 63% and 87%, and +9.4 to +22.1 points on CogACT from 63% onward. At 81% on CogACT, a tripled recovery budget narrows the distilled student's gap to the teacher to 3.9 points on average, while supervised recovery stays more than 20 points below. At matched compression, width pruning yields higher success and depth pruning lower latency. On a 6-DoF manipulator, the distilled student at 72% reduction reaches 77.5% success against 59.5% for supervised recovery, runs 2.23x faster on-board than the teacher, and uses 62% less memory.

AI.tldr: Offline, hidden-state distillation with width pruning recovers most of the performance loss from large-prain VLA backbones, enabling near-teacher accuracy with offline training and faster on-board operation across OpenVLA-OFT, CogACT, and 6-DoF tasks.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational and hardware burden of billion-parameter language backbones in vision-language-action robots while preserving task success.
AI.method: Apply width pruning to transformer blocks while preserving the residual stream; train a student offline using a cache derived from a single teacher pass (no projector needed); perform hidden-state distillation; sweep pruning ratios to assess recovery objective; compare with supervised recovery plus reinforcement learning; evaluate on OpenVLA-OFT, CogACT, and a 6-DoF manipulator.
AI.result: 63% pruning alone drops LIBERO-Long success from 93.2% to 0.8%. With width pruning and hidden-state distillation, the student reaches within about 3.5 points of the teacher in ~8 GPU-hours; up to 45% pruning shows no significant difference from the teacher; hidden-state distillation adds 2.1–4.5 points (and 9.4–22.1 on CogACT). At 81% pruning on CogACT, the gap narrows to ~3.9 points; on a 6-DoF manipulator, 72% pruning yields 77.5% success vs 59.5% for supervised recovery, while running 2.23x faster on-board and using 62% less memory.
AI.conclusion: Offline width-based pruning paired with hidden-state distillation can largely recover teacher performance and yield practical efficiency gains for VLA robots; width pruning at matched compression outperforms depth pruning for latency, enabling effective on-robot deployment.

title: Integrating knowledge from case reports: a medical ontology based multimodal information system with structured summary
summary: Published medical case reports serve as a crucial medical information carrier, documenting discoveries in rare diseases, diagnostic methods, and innovative treatments. Despite the wealth of clinical knowledge in millions of case reports in the public medicine literature database (PubMed), accessing relevant information efficiently is hindered by the limitations of traditional keyword-based retrieval tools on unstructured and diverse case reports. To address the above issues, we introduce a comprehensive multimodal information system for case reports integrating structured clinical summaries of patients including medical images and biomedical named entities from 52949 open-access case reports published from 2000 to 2021. The multimodal essential information is organized in a well-structured medical ontology. Also, a powerful interface for searching and browsing case reports is designed to assist junior clinicians in retrieving cases effectively and improving the identification and diagnosis of rare diseases.

AI.tldr: Multimodal case-report information system aggregates 52,949 open-access case reports (2000–2021) into a structured ontology to improve retrieval of rare-disease cases.
AI.motivation: Traditional keyword-based retrieval on unstructured case reports is inefficient for accessing relevant information; there is a need for cohesive access to multimodal clinical data to support diagnosis of rare diseases.
AI.method: Build a multimodal information system that extracts/organizes structured clinical summaries, medical images, and biomedical named entities from 52,949 open-access case reports (2000–2021) into a comprehensive medical ontology, plus a search/browse interface for clinicians (especially juniors).
AI.result: An integrated multimodal information resource organized in a medical ontology with a user-facing search interface, aimed at improving retrieval of case information; no explicit performance metrics reported.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal, ontology-driven organization addresses limitations of keyword-based retrieval in unstructured case reports and facilitates efficient discovery of rare-disease information.

title: DeliveryGym: An RL Environment for Long-Horizon Embodied Agent Planning with Adaptive Curriculum
summary: Executable environments enable LLM agents to learn from the consequences of their actions. For embodied agents, those consequences extend beyond whether the current task succeeds: completing a delivery can consume the time, energy, or money needed for later work. Learning to plan therefore requires environments that preserve these dependencies and turn them into feedback across a complete trajectory. We introduce DeliveryGym, a 3D environment for evaluating and training agents on continuous courier shifts. It couples multimodal tool interaction with persistent world dynamics and computes trajectory rewards from simulator events, making the costs of an agent's decisions available for reinforcement learning (RL). The environment also adapts future training shifts to the policy's observed weaknesses while keeping evaluation fixed. Across six models and 13 city maps, evaluation exposes a gap between reliably executing assigned deliveries and choosing and sequencing work over a shift. On the fixed test suite, RL improves Qwen3-VL-4B's net income by 54.3%, showing that learning from complete shifts improves performance under these coupled constraints. Adapting the training environment improves test income by 16.5% over uniform sampling at the same rollout budget, indicating that which situations an agent practices also matters. DeliveryGym provides an executable setting for studying how agents learn to coordinate deliveries and preserve resources for later orders within an episode.

AI.tldr: DeliveryGym introduces a 3D executable environment for continuous courier shifts to study RL with trajectory-level rewards, coupling multimodal tool interaction and persistent dynamics, with adaptive training shifts; demonstrates improved performance across six models and 13 city maps.
AI.motivation: Address the need for environments that preserve resource-penalty dependencies across a full task trajectory, enabling learning from the consequences of actions in embodied RL settings.
AI.method: Introduce DeliveryGym, a 3D environment for continuous courier shifts with multimodal tool interaction and persistent world dynamics. Trajectory rewards are computed from simulator events. The training shifts can adapt to the policy's observed weaknesses while staying fixed for evaluation. Evaluation spans six models and 13 city maps.
AI.result: On fixed test, RL improves Qwen3-VL-4B's net income by 54.3%—evidence that learning from complete shifts helps in coupled constraints. Adapting training environments increases test income by 16.5% over uniform sampling at the same rollout budget, indicating that the choice of training situations matters.
AI.conclusion: DeliveryGym provides an executable setting for studying how agents learn to coordinate deliveries and preserve resources for later orders within an episode, highlighting the value of trajectory-aware feedback and adaptive training for embodied RL.

title: Socialized UAV Cross-Task Learning: Towards Cross-Granularity Collaboration through Hierarchical Interaction
summary: Joint learning across heterogeneous tasks is often treated as task coupling through feature sharing, distillation, or auxiliary supervision. However, in cross-task learning, mismatched representational and supervisory granularities make such coupling prone to interference, teacher bias, or unidirectional collapse. We argue that cross-granularity learning is fundamentally a problem of hierarchical interaction regulation rather than simple task coupling. This issue is particularly evident in UAV perception, where visual shifts and detection--segmentation objectives naturally form coarse- and fine-grained knowledge sources. To systematically study this problem, we introduce CrossUAV, a UAV benchmark for joint object detection and instance segmentation that provides a unified evaluation platform for cross-granularity task collaboration. To address these challenges, we propose Cross-Granularity Socialized Collaboration (CGSC), a progressive and adaptive framework that regulates when, where, and how tasks exchange information across network hierarchies. CGSC progressively activates cross-task interactions and adaptively adjusts the strength according to task contribution, suppressing harmful interference while exploiting complementary coarse- and fine-grained structures. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements on both tasks, validating hierarchical dynamic interaction as an effective mechanism for cross-granularity collaboration.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical cross-granularity cross-task learning framework (CGSC) with a UAV-specific benchmark CrossUAV, regulating feature/prediction exchange across hierarchy to jointly improve detection and instance segmentation.
AI.motivation: To address interference, teacher bias, and unidirectional collapse in cross-task learning due to mismatched representational and supervisory granularity; frame cross-granularity learning as hierarchical interaction regulation, particularly for UAV perception with coarse- and fine-grained sources.
AI.method: Introduce CrossUAV as a unified benchmark for joint object detection and instance segmentation in UAV imagery; propose CGSC (Cross-Granularity Socialized Collaboration) that progressively activates cross-task interactions and adaptively scales their strength based on task contribution, regulating information exchange across network hierarchies to suppress interference while leveraging coarse- and fine-grained structures.
AI.result: Empirical results show consistent improvements on both detection and segmentation tasks, validating the approach's effectiveness in enabling beneficial cross-granularity collaboration via hierarchical dynamic interaction.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical regulation of cross-granularity interactions is a promising mechanism for cross-task collaboration; the CrossUAV benchmark provides a standardized platform, and CGSC demonstrates robust, adaptive cross-task collaboration for UAV perception.

title: OmniCalib: Target-Free, Task-Structured Self-Calibration for Humanoid Robots
summary: Assembly, wear, and component replacement perturb the sensor extrinsics and joint zeros encoded by a humanoid CAD model. Existing procedures calibrate one sensor pair or require external fiducials. Using only robot-native motion and onboard sensing, we present OmniCalib, a target-free workflow that calibrates the full upper limbs---all 14 arm joint zeros and the extrinsics of both wrist and chest cameras---as well as lower limbs and the multi-camera head rig. Each module matches a robot-native task to a parameter block, checks observability, and writes only supported corrections to the CAD model. Our depth ICP method recovers all 14 arm joint zeros and calibrates all RGB-D camera extrinsics without any calibration target. Relative to CAD, the estimated extrinsic corrections are 10.56 mm and 1.74 degrees for the left wrist, 6.33 mm and 1.25 degrees for the right wrist, and 9.81 mm and 0.929 degrees for the chest RGB-D camera. ICP point-to-plane residual is 2.09 mm. On the same injected offsets, ICP and ArUco recover all 14 joint zeros below the 0.1-degree encoder-resolution reference. On an AGIBOT A3 Ultra humanoid, four static double-support stances recover all 12 lower-limb joint-zero offsets injected with an RMS error of 0.063 degrees. The head module combines multi-camera visual odometry with legged odometry and dynamic compensation through the live ROS transform tree. Using only planar walking, it attains a mean SO(3) error of 1.061 degrees across three sequences. The best sequence reaches 0.775 degrees, competitive with iKalibr at 0.902 degrees from rich 6-DOF excitation. Rig-relative angles repeat within 0.140 degrees. Injection recovery and held-out tests validate each observable block.

AI.tldr: OmniCalib offers a target-free, full upper- and lower-limb, and head-camera extrinsic calibration for humanoids using only onboard motion and sensing, achieving sub-centimeter pose corrections and sub-degree orientation errors without fiducials.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of existing calibration approaches that calibrate only one sensor pair or rely on external fiducials, by using robot-native tasks and onboard sensing to calibrate all joint zeros and camera extrinsics in a self-contained workflow.
AI.method: A modular, target-free workflow where each module maps a robot-native task to a parameter block, performs observability checks, and applies only supported corrections to the CAD model. Depth ICP recovers arm joint zeros and extrinsics for RGB-D cameras without targets; ArUco markers are used for injection/validation of some corrections; the head module fuses multi-camera visual odometry with legged odometry in a live ROS transform tree; lower limbs calibration uses static double-support stances; planar walking is used for head pose evaluation.
AI.result: Extrinsic corrections relative to CAD: left wrist 10.56 mm / 1.74 deg; right wrist 6.33 mm / 1.25 deg; chest RGB-D 9.81 mm / 0.929 deg. ICP residual: 2.09 mm. ArUco-based recovery of six- to fourteen joint zeros out to <0.1 deg vs encoder resolution. Lower limbs: RMS 0.063 deg for 12 joint zeros. Head: mean SO(3) error 1.061 deg across sequences (best 0.775 deg); rig-relative angles repeat within 0.140 deg. Observability validated via injection + held-out tests.
AI.conclusion: The approach delivers accurate, target-free calibration across a full humanoid rig with strong observability checks and modularity, competitive with iKalibr in angular accuracy, and suitable for ongoing self-calibration using only onboard sensing.

title: Contagion on the Trading Floor: How Adversarial Signals Spread in Multi-Agent Trading Systems
comment: Published in ECML PKDD 2026. 25 pages, including 7 pages of supplementary material
summary: Multi-agent trading systems built on large language models (LLMs) are beginning to appear in quantitative finance, yet their robustness to adversarial inputs is largely unknown. We study the vulnerability of LLM trading stacks to black-box, input-only attacks that enter solely via admissible social-media feeds. We introduce the Generic Multi-Agent Trading System (GMATS), a framework that captures modern multiagent trading architectures and instantiate a class of black-box poisoning attackers that treat an LLM as a post generator and inject budget-constrained, plausibly benign social-media content into the analyst's evidence stream. We define contagion metrics that trace how adversarial content propagates through the stack, including belief-shift scores at analyst and coordinator layers and attack-clean deltas on standard backtest metrics. Experiments on a safe offline benchmark with historical market and social data show that even simple input-only attackers can materially degrade risk-return profiles, sharply reducing Sharpe ratios. At the same time, we find that suitably designed multi-agent topologies and coordinator prompts can dampen adversarial shocks and improve average robustness under identical poisoning budgets.

AI.tldr: Black-box social-media poisoning can degrade LLM-based multi-agent trading performance; GMATS framework and contagion metrics reveal vulnerability and some mitigation via topology and prompts.
AI.motivation: Assess robustness of LLM-driven multi-agent trading stacks to adversarial, input-only attacks delivered through admissible social-media feeds; develop metrics to quantify contagion and backtest impact.
AI.method: Introduce GMATS framework for modern multi-agent trading architectures; instantiate black-box poisoning attackers that use LLMs as post generators and inject constrained, plausibly benign social-media content into the analyst's evidence stream; define contagion metrics (belief-shift scores at analyst and coordinator layers; attack-clean deltas on backtest metrics); perform offline experiments with historical market and social data.
AI.result: Simple input-only attackers materially degrade risk-return profiles, notably reducing Sharpe ratios; certain multi-agent topologies and coordinator prompts dampen adversarial shocks and improve average robustness under equal poisoning budgets.
AI.conclusion: GMATS exposes vulnerability of LLM-based trading stacks to input-only social-media poisoning and shows that architecture and prompt design can mitigate such risks; contagion metrics provide a framework for evaluating robustness and guiding defense design.

title: Beyond Flattened Tokens: Structure-Preserving EEG Decoding with Reusable TriDim Blocks
summary: Effective EEG decoding requires representations that preserve organization among channels, local waveform dynamics, and long-range temporal context. Existing EEG architectures often capture these structures using separate specialized modules or collapse them into a single token sequence, making it difficult to maintain their distinct roles and coordinate their interactions throughout the backbone. We propose TriDim, a reusable block that preserves the representation shape and keeps three EEG axes explicit: channel, sample position within each patch, and patch position across the recording. These axes correspond to spatial, short-term temporal, and long-term temporal information, respectively. Each TriDim block applies feed-forward transformations along individual axes and cross-axis attention to coordinate information exchange among them. By stacking TriDim blocks with a multi-level tri-axis readout, we construct TriDimEEG, a standalone EEG decoder. Under strict cross-subject evaluation on eight datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, motor imagery, and emotion recognition, TriDimEEG achieves the best overall performance among fifteen evaluated models, with a 4.3% relative improvement in average accuracy over the second-best model. Replacing Transformer blocks in three EEG foundation models with TriDim blocks yields an average relative improvement of 7.4% in downstream accuracy while reducing parameter counts by 17.0% to 47.3%. These results establish TriDim as an effective and reusable building block and TriDimEEG as a strong standalone EEG decoder. Code and parameters of TriDimEEG are available at https://github.com/ncclab-sustech/TriDim_model.

AI.tldr: TriDimEEG introduces TriDim, a tri-axis block preserving channel, short-term temporal, and long-term temporal structure in EEG, achieving state-of-the-art cross-subject performance and improving downstream accuracy while reducing parameters.
AI.motivation: Preserve multi-axis EEG structure (spatial, short-term temporal, long-term temporal) without collapsing into a single token sequence; enable coordinated interactions across axes.
AI.method: TriDim block applies feed-forward along each axis and cross-axis attention; blocks stacked with multi-level tri-axis readout to form TriDimEEG; code released.
AI.result: On eight datasets for clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, motor imagery, and emotion recognition, TriDimEEG achieves best overall performance among 15 models, 4.3% relative improvement; replacing Transformer blocks in three EEG foundation models yields 7.4% average improvement and 17.0-47.3% parameter reduction.
AI.conclusion: TriDim is an effective reusable building block for EEG; TriDimEEG is a strong standalone decoder; code available.

title: PART: Learning 3D Part Assembly and Retrieval with Transformers
comment: Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers. 11 pages, 12 figures. Project page: https://iambrc.github.io/PART-project-page/
summary: 3D assembly is fundamental to modern manufacturing and digital content creation. In this paper, we present PART, a unified transformer-based framework for 3D part retrieval and assembly: given a target shape and a part library, PART automatically selects the appropriate parts and predicts their 6-DoF poses to reconstruct the target. While prior work has achieved impressive progress on assembling a pre-defined set of parts, this more practical retrieval-based setting remains largely unexplored. The task faces three key challenges: (i) a combinatorially explosive search space that grows exponentially with library size; (ii) variable-length outputs, as different targets require different numbers of parts; and (iii) continuous 6-DoF pose estimation for part assembly. To address these, we formulate retrieval and assembly as a set prediction problem and design a novel transformer-based framework that retrieves parts and regresses their poses with variable-length output. Additionally, we exploit the duality between part pose estimation and target segmentation through joint training and a novel segmentation-enhanced optimization module. Finally, We curate a large-scale dataset of 80K+ shapes, and the results show that PART generalizes to scene layouts, image targets, and real-world scans. Project Page: https://iambrc.github.io/PART-project-page/.

AI.tldr: PART is a transformer-based framework for 3D part retrieval and 6-DoF pose assembly from a library, addressing combinatorial search, variable-length outputs, and continuous pose estimation; shows strong generalization on a large-scale dataset.
AI.motivation: 3D assembly is central to modern manufacturing and digital content creation. Prior work largely tackles assembling fixed or predefined part sets; a practical system requires retrieval from large libraries, scalable handling of varying part counts, and precise 6-DoF pose estimation.
AI.method: Formulate retrieval and assembly as set prediction. Introduce a unified transformer that retrieves parts and regresses their 6-DoF poses with variable-length outputs. Exploit a segmentation-pose duality via joint training and a segmentation-enhanced optimization module. Build a large-scale dataset with 80K+ shapes for evaluation.
AI.result: Empirical results indicate PART generalizes to scene layouts, image targets, and real-world scans, demonstrating effective retrieval and pose regression across diverse targets.
AI.conclusion: PART advances retrieval-based 3D assembly by enabling scalable part selection and continuous pose estimation, supported by a large dataset, and highlights segmentation–pose synergy for improved optimization.

title: Quantifying Mechanical Intelligence in Legged Robots with Information Theory
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 1 table, submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027 for publication
summary: Mechanical intelligence, loosely defined as the reduction in control burden afforded by a robot's physical form, has become a prominent concept in robotics, with instantiations in bioinspired robotics, soft robotics, robotic swarms, and many other areas. However, rigorous theoretical understanding and quantitative measures of mechanical intelligence have lagged behind the engineering systems that the community has developed. In this work, using modern legged robots as a benchmark and exemplar, we propose several information-theoretic metrics for quantifying mechanical intelligence. By viewing body dynamics as both a computational process and a communication channel, we show that several prior insights in legged-robot engineering can be described using information theory, and we quantify how bits are processed by mechanical modes and across robot coordinates. Specifically, we examine the trade-off between explicitly incorporating compliance through series-elastic actuation and using so-called proprioceptive, low-gear-ratio transmissions, and we explore how these mechanisms interact with control policies during locomotion. We develop these results on systems of increasing complexity: a simplified linear model of a robot-leg transmission, a nonlinear single-leg simulation, and simulated quadruped robots controlled by a learned policy while navigating challenging terrain. These results lay the groundwork for broader study of robot mechanisms and their role in embodied computation.

AI.tldr: Proposes an information-theoretic framework to quantify mechanical intelligence in legged robots and analyzes how morphology and control interact across progressively complex models.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous, quantitative measure of mechanical intelligence—the reduction of control burden by a robot's physical form—and connect engineering insights with information theory.
AI.method: Introduce information-theoretic metrics; model body dynamics as a computation and a communication channel; analyze trade-offs between compliant series-elastic actuation and proprioceptive low-gear transmissions; evaluate on linear transmission model, nonlinear single-leg, and simulated quadrupeds with learned policy on challenging terrain.
AI.result: Provides metrics for how information (bits) is processed by mechanical modes and across coordinates; demonstrates how mechanics and control interact; establishes groundwork for studying embodied computation in robot mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: A foundational framework for quantifying mechanical intelligence and understanding the role of physical form in computation, enabling broader analyses across robotic platforms.

title: Steering Equilibrium Selection in Regularized Self-Play via the Reference Policy
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Companion to arXiv:2606.28308 and arXiv:2607.17543. Fully reproducible: a single self-contained notebook regenerates every number, table, and figure
summary: Regularized self-play -- the family behind DeepNash's Stratego play -- drives a two-player zero-sum policy to a Nash equilibrium by best-responding to a slowly moving, entropy-regularized reference policy $ρ$. When the game has a polytope of value-equivalent equilibria, the regularizer silently breaks the tie: with a uniform reference it selects the maximum-entropy member, the I-projection of $ρ$ onto the Nash set. Can the reference be used to choose the equilibrium on purpose? On five exactly solvable games plus a 2-D polytope, with exact best responses and equivalence tests over independent seeds, anchoring the reference at a target member and refining steers self-play to that member with mean coordinate error 0.007 at median exploitability $5\times10^{-5}$, TOST-equivalent to the request within $\pm0.05$; the anchoring persists through refinement and follows the reference, not the initialization. Selection follows the reach-weighted I-projection (slope 0.969 [0.950, 0.987]). We report with equal emphasis where the story breaks: fixed off-manifold references cost 0.08-0.25 exploitability; stiff or flat families require a smaller mirror step, set by a pre-registered rule; boundary targets undershoot; curvature predicts where boundary saturation bites (rank correlation 0.90, p=0.037) while interior precision is curvature-independent. Table and MLP steering maps are equivalent within $\pm0.03$ at every target (30 seeds); matched control arms show attention's robust signature is excess seed variance, any systematic shift bounded at 0.018 and not significant. Against a best response the selection-robustness trade-off is degenerate: steering matters only against fixed, non-equilibrium opponents. The recipe -- anchor the reference at the desired member and refine -- reinterprets the KL anchor of RLHF-style RL as a selection knob, not only a stability leash.

AI.tldr: Anchoring and refining a reference policy in regularized self-play can steer the unique equilibrium among value-equivalent Nash equilibria in small zero-sum games, via the I-projection of the reference onto the Nash set. The method achieves close alignment to a target equilibrium and reveals systematic trade-offs and curvature effects; off-manifold references degrade performance and boundary behavior is governed by step size and geometry. The approach reframes the KL anchor from RLHF as a controllable selection knob, not just a stability constraint.
AI.motivation: To determine whether a slowly moving, entropy-regularized reference policy can be used to deliberately select a desired Nash equilibrium in regularized self-play, and to quantify the stability, robustness, and geometry of such selection across solvable games and a 2-D polytope.
AI.method: Empirical study on five exactly solvable two-player zero-sum games plus a 2-D polytope. Use exact best responses and seed-wise equivalence tests across independent seeds. Anchor the reference ρ at a target equilibrium member and perform iterative refinement to steer the self-play policy toward that member. Measure mean coordinate error, exploitability, and test equivalence (TOST) to assess target attainment. Analyze selection via reach-weighted I-projection slope, curvature effects, and boundary behavior. Compare fixed vs. anchored references, uniform references, and steering maps (Table/MLP); report control-arm comparisons for seed variance and sensitivity. Draw conclusions on robustness and trade-offs against best-response opponents.
AI.result: Anchor-and-refine successfully steers self-play toward a chosen equilibrium on the tested instances. Key quantitative results include mean coordinate error ≈0.007 and median exploitability ≈5×10^-5; TOST equivalence within ±0.05. Selection slope ≈0.969 (95% CI [0.950, 0.987]). Off-manifold fixed references incur higher exploitability (0.08–0.25); boundary targets undershoot; curvature predicts boundary saturation but interior precision remains curvature-independent. Table and MLP steering maps agree within ±0.03 across 30 seeds; seed variance dominates extrinsic shifts. The selection-robustness trade-off is degenerate against best responses: steering matters mainly against fixed, non-equilibrium opponents. The framework reframes the KL anchor from RLHF-style RL as a controllable selection knob, not merely a stability constraint.
AI.conclusion: An anchor-and-refine protocol can deliberately select among value-equivalent Nash equilibria in regularized self-play by projecting the anchored reference onto the Nash set (I-projection). The KL anchor functions as a tunable selector rather than only a stability device, enabling targeted equilibrium attainment in solvable games. However, performance is sensitive to reference placement, curvature, and step sizing, especially near boundaries; off-manifold references and overly stiff/flat families degrade exploitability. The approach yields a practical mechanism for controllable equilibrium design with predictable geometric behavior and a clear direction for extending to larger games.

title: Expected Hypervolume Maximization for Multiobjective Optimization under Uncertainties
summary: The problem of multiobjective optimization under uncertainties is often approached by taking the expectation of each objective. In this work, we propose instead to formulate this as a Bayesian decision problem and to rely on the expected value of the hypervolume, which is to be maximized with respect to a finite set of input points. We show that this can be performed using methods based on gradients in a stochastic optimization framework, provided that care is taken with respect to dominated points. Moreover, in the absence of readily available differentiable code, we propose to use Gaussian Processes as differentiable surrogate models, in order to perform the optimization. An additional contribution in this work are some active learning strategies, through acquisition functions which helps construct a surrogate model well-designed for the multiobjective optimization problem at stake. These strategies are compared on simple analytical problems to assess their performances.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian decision-theoretic approach to multiobjective optimization under uncertainty, maximizing the expected hypervolume. Uses gradient-based stochastic optimization with careful handling of dominated points, and Gaussian Process surrogates with acquisition-based active learning strategies; evaluated on simple analytical problems.
AI.motivation: Address uncertainty in multiobjective optimization and provide a principled decision framework beyond simply taking objective expectations; leverage hypervolume as a scalar quality measure and probabilistic models.
AI.method: Formulate optimization as maximizing the expected hypervolume w.r.t. a finite set of input points (Bayesian decision problem). Use gradient-based stochastic optimization; ensure proper treatment of dominated points. Employ Gaussian Processes as differentiable surrogate models when differentiable code is unavailable. Develop acquisition functions for active learning to build a surrogate tailored to multiobjective optimization.
AI.result: A structured framework is proposed along with differentiable GP surrogates and active-learning acquisition strategies. The various strategies are compared on simple analytical problems to assess performance.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a practical Bayesian framework for robust multiobjective optimization under uncertainty, leveraging GP surrogates and acquisition-based learning to optimize the expected hypervolume, with empirical comparisons on basic problems.

title: BINDER: A Latent Variable Model for Probabilistic Medical Image Registration
summary: We propose a new probabilistic model for general-purpose medical image registration that builds upon the mutual information registration criterion. It centers around a spatial interpolation technique that assumes latent voxel-wise correspondences between the images being registered. By exploiting these latent variables, we derive dedicated optimization and MCMC sampling techniques that only involve closed-form iterative updates. When applied to nonlinear registration, an efficient demons-like optimization algorithm is obtained that shows robust out-of-the-box performance across a variety of monomodal and multimodal registration tasks. We also demonstrate a corresponding sampler that can quantify, for the first time, uncertainty in multimodal registration scenarios with very high-dimensional 3D deformations. Our code, which we call BINDER (Bayesian INference for DEformable Registration), is freely available at https://github.com/ste93ste/BINDER.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian probabilistic model for general-purpose medical image registration (BINDER) that builds on mutual information, introducing latent voxel-wise correspondences to yield closed-form updates and a demons-like optimization. It provides a Bayesian sampler to quantify uncertainty in high-dimensional 3D deformable registrations, with an open-source implementation.
AI.motivation: To improve robustness and accuracy of image registration across monomodal and multimodal data while enabling principled uncertainty quantification in complex 3D deformable registrations, addressing limitations of traditional mutual information methods.
AI.method: Introduce latent voxel-wise correspondences and a spatial interpolation framework. Derive optimization and MCMC sampling procedures with closed-form iterative updates. Develop a demons-like nonlinear registration algorithm and a Bayesian sampler for uncertainty quantification. Name: BINDER (Bayesian INference for DEformable Registration).
AI.result: Demonstrates robust out-of-the-box performance on monomodal and multimodal registration tasks. Presents an efficient demons-like optimization routine and a sampler capable of quantifying uncertainty in high-dimensional 3D deformations. The method is implemented as open-source code at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a unified probabilistic framework for deformable registration that combines optimization and Bayesian sampling to enable robust performance and uncertainty quantification in multimodal, high-dimensional 3D scenarios; the approach is released as BINDER for public use.

title: WorldContact: A Contact-Centric World Model for Scalable Robot Learning
summary: Adapting robots to new objects and tasks requires interaction experience that can be costly to obtain. We present WorldContact, a contact-centric world model for deformable-object manipulation, constructed from a limited set of high-quality trajectories to generate additional training data efficiently. It predicts object dynamics using larger time steps than the source numerical simulator, which requires small integration steps to resolve rapid motion and prevent interpenetration. We evaluate WorldContact across 16 shopping-bag manipulation tasks. State-rollout measurements on a single H100 GPU show a $10\times$ speedup over the source simulator, excluding rendering and disk I/O. We use the generated data to fine-tune an existing vision-language-action policy and deploy it directly on a real robot. In bag lifting, the same policy achieves 65% single-attempt success when fine-tuned on source simulation data alone, compared with 95% when fine-tuned on the dataset expanded with WorldContact. These results support efficient data generation with WorldContact for robot policy adaptation.

AI.tldr: WorldContact is a contact-centric world model for deformable-object manipulation built from a limited set of high-quality trajectories. It enables faster data generation by simulating with larger time steps than the source simulator, achieving around 10x speedup on an H100 GPU and improving real-robot policy fine-tuning for bag lifting (65% to 95% single-attempt success).
AI.motivation: Adapting robots to new objects and tasks requires interaction data, which is costly to collect. A data-efficient world model that can generate useful training data for deformable-object manipulation can reduce data collection burdens and accelerate policy adaptation.
AI.method: Construct WorldContact as a contact-centric world model of deformable-object dynamics trained on a small set of high-quality trajectories. It uses larger integration time steps than the source numerical simulator to accelerate data generation and prevent interpenetration. The generated data augment a vision-language-action policy; the policy is fine-tuned with this dataset and deployed on a real robot. Evaluation across 16 shopping-bag tasks includes state-rollouts on an H100 GPU (speed measurements) and real-robot deployment.
AI.result: State-rollout computations on a single H100 GPU yield about a 10× speedup over the source simulator (excluding rendering and disk I/O). Fine-tuning an existing vision-language-action policy with WorldContact data yields 95% single-attempt success in bag lifting versus 65% when using only source-simulator data.
AI.conclusion: WorldContact enables efficient data generation for deformable-object manipulation, enabling faster and more reliable policy adaptation on real robots.

title: Dual-Axis Policy Optimization for LLM Agents: Bayesian Feedback Attribution and Trajectory Mass Normalization
summary: Reinforcement learning for LLM agents involves two distinct optimization di- mensions: how environment feedback is exploited within a trajectory, and how complete trajectories are aggregated across a batch. We formulate these dimen- sions as Intra-Trajectory Feedback Attribution and Inter-Trajectory Objec- tive Aggregation, and introduce BATON (Bayesian Attribution and Trajectory Objective Normalization), a dual-axis policy optimization framework. BATON instantiates the first axis with Bayesian Feedback Attribution, which constructs a feedback-conditioned posterior over sampled actions, and the second with Trajec- tory Mass Normalization (TMN), which assigns equal optimization mass to com- plete trajectories. Experiments with GRPO and GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA show that both axes provide independent gains and that their combi- nation consistently achieves the strongest overall performance across model scales.

AI.tldr: BATON is a dual-axis RL optimization framework for LLM agents that separately optimizes (i) intra-trajectory feedback attribution using a Bayesian posterior over actions, and (ii) inter-trajectory objective aggregation via Trajectory Mass Normalization. It demonstrates that each axis yields independent gains and together provide the strongest performance across task domains and model scales.
AI.motivation: To address two distinct optimization dimensions in RL for LLM agents: (1) how feedback within a single trajectory is attributed to actions, and (2) how complete trajectories are aggregated across a batch to form the objective. The work argues that addressing both dimensions jointly can improve learning efficiency and performance.
AI.method: Define Intra-Trajectory Feedback Attribution as a Bayesian feedback-conditioned posterior over sampled actions. Define Inter-Trajectory Objective Aggregation as Trajectory Mass Normalization, which allocates equal optimization mass to complete trajectories. Implement BATON by instantiating the two axes with Bayesian Feedback Attribution (for the intra-trajectory axis) and Trajectory Mass Normalization (for the inter-trajectory axis). Evaluate using GRPO and GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA datasets/tasks.
AI.result: Empirical results show that each axis provides independent gains, and their combination yields the strongest overall performance. The improvements are observed across different model scales, suggesting robustness and generality of the dual-axis approach.
AI.conclusion: BATON provides a principled, dual-axis framework for RL with LLM agents, enabling additive benefits from modeling intra-trajectory feedback and inter-trajectory normalization. The approach demonstrates consistent performance gains across domains and scales, indicating its potential as a general enhancement to policy optimization in LLM-based RL settings.

title: Pretrained Medical Representations for the Practical Screening of Drug Repositioning Candidates
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Representation learning from medical code sequences in electronic health records and medical claims data has been successful in various clinical applications, such as those regarding disease prediction. However, significant challenges remain in extending this approach to the discovery of scientific hypotheses. One reason is that many existing BERT-based models fail to adequately capture the hierarchical structure of medical codes and the complex interactions between diagnoses and treatments. To address these limitations, we propose a new unified pre-training framework that explicitly integrates hierarchical sub-token aggregation, partial masking, and cross-reference mechanisms. The proposed model consistently outperformed existing methods on both pre-training objectives and downstream clinical event prediction tasks, including the onset of dementia and hospitalization. We also conducted an in silico drug repositioning case study targeting Alzheimer's disease. In the hypothesis generation step, our approach successfully rediscovered known promising drugs in a data-driven manner without relying on such external knowledge sources as the literature. Subsequently, in the hypothesis prioritization step, we introduced a Task-Adaptive Representation Approach to alleviate the over-encoding of historical prescription information within diagnostic vectors, enabling the robust prioritization of generated hypotheses. This study establishes an exploratory screening workflow for hypothesis generation and prioritization based on observational associations. Importantly, this framework is not intended to provide causal evidence, but rather to identify promising candidates for subsequent rigorous causal inference. Overall, this study demonstrates that domain-informed representation learning combined with task-adaptive representation control can enable a practical hypothesis discovery workflow.

AI.tldr: A unified pre-training framework for medical code sequences that captures hierarchical information and cross-code interactions to enable hypothesis discovery; it improves pre-training and clinical task performance and demonstrates in silico drug repositioning for Alzheimer's, with a Task-Adaptive Representation Approach to prioritize hypotheses.
AI.motivation: To address limitations of BERT-based medical code models in capturing hierarchical sub-token structures and interactions between diagnoses and treatments, enabling robust hypothesis generation from observational data.
AI.method: Introduce a unified pre-training framework with hierarchical sub-token aggregation, partial masking, and cross-reference mechanisms; include an in silico drug repositioning case study for Alzheimer's; develop Task-Adaptive Representation Approach to prevent over-encoding of historical prescription information; propose an exploratory screening workflow for hypothesis generation and prioritization.
AI.result: Outperforms existing methods on pre-training objectives and downstream clinical event prediction tasks (e.g., dementia onset, hospitalization); rediscovered known promising Alzheimer's drugs in silico; Task-Adaptive Representation Approach enhances prioritization; demonstrates practical hypothesis discovery workflow.
AI.conclusion: Domain-informed representation learning with task-adaptive control enables a practical workflow for hypothesis discovery from observational data, with the caveat that findings are not causal and require further causal inference.

title: SlugTrails: An Egocentric Benchmark for Floor Plan Localization in Large Buildings
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Preprint. Code and data: https://github.com/Head-inthe-Cloud/SlugTrails
summary: Floor-plan-based indoor visual localization enables infrastructure-free positioning, but most methods are developed and evaluated in small residential environments unlike the large public buildings of real deployment. We introduce SlugTrails, a floor plan localization benchmark for large indoor spaces under realistic egocentric sensing: $30$ Hz Aria glasses recordings across three campus buildings and six floors ($22089$ m$^2$ of floor plan outline), CAD-derived floor plans with semantic classes and circulation space masks, and trajectories aligned into the floor plan frame using laser-surveyed anchors. One protocol covers three practical ways of gathering geometry under a limited field of view -- a single walking frame, a stationary multi-view sweep, and a walking stream with odometry -- so methods designed for different regimes are compared on the same buildings and ground truth. Evaluating five representative geometric and learned systems under their native sensing configurations, we find that stock checkpoints (official released weights) are near zero on SlugTrails (at most $0.004$ R@1m30$^{\circ}$ on walking single frames), while fine-tuning on SlugTrails improves every trainable family on all three tasks (e.g., F$^3$Loc $0.0 \rightarrow 0.141$ single-frame and $0.03 \rightarrow 0.66$ sequential), with gains compounding as observations accumulate. The same fine-tuned weights also improve cross-dataset generalization on LaMAR with no LaMAR training (sequential R@1m $0.048 \rightarrow 0.143$ for F$^3$Loc and $0.063 \rightarrow 0.127$ for UnLoc), whereas train-from-scratch on SlugTrails alone stays far below fine-tuning from stock weights -- evidence that floor plan localization is currently limited by indoor data rather than by architecture. We release the dataset, protocols, and tools at https://github.com/Head-inthe-Cloud/SlugTrails.

AI.tldr: A large-scale, floor-plan–driven indoor localization benchmark (SlugTrails) using egocentric 30 Hz wearable data across six floors in three campus buildings, with CAD floor plans and laser-aligned trajectories; evaluates multiple sensing regimes and shows fine-tuning on SlugTrails substantially improves performance and cross-dataset generalization (LaMAR), implying data limitations, not model capacity.
AI.motivation: To close the gap between small-scale residential datasets and real-world large indoor environments, enabling infrastructure-free localization under realistic egocentric sensing and providing a standardized benchmark with practical data collection protocols.
AI.method: Collect 30 Hz Aria-glasses data across three campus buildings and six floors (≈22,089 m^2), align trajectories to CAD floor plans using laser-surveyed anchors, provide CAD floor plans with semantic classes and circulation masks, and evaluate three data-collection regimes (single walking frame, stationary multi-view sweep, walking stream with odometry) across five geometric/learned systems. Compare stock pre-trained weights versus fine-tuned weights on SlugTrails and assess cross-dataset generalization to LaMAR.
AI.result: Stock checkpoints perform near zero on SlugTrails (R@1m30° ≤ 0.004 on walking frames). Fine-tuning on SlugTrails yields strong improvements across tasks (e.g., F^3Loc: 0.0 → 0.141 for single-frame; 0.03 → 0.66 for sequential). Gains compound as observations accumulate. Fine-tuned weights also boost cross-dataset generalization to LaMAR without LaMAR training (sequential R@1m: F^3Loc 0.048 → 0.143; UnLoc 0.063 → 0.127). Training from scratch on SlugTrails remains far below fine-tuned models, suggesting data limitations rather than architectural limits. The dataset, protocols, and tools are released at the provided URL.
AI.conclusion: Floor-plan localization in large indoor spaces is currently data-limited; architectural advances alone are insufficient. SlugTrails provides a valuable, realistic benchmark that reveals substantial gains from data tuning and demonstrates cross-dataset transfer, underscoring the importance of large-scale, realistic data for infrastructure-free localization.

title: TacSushi: Tactile-Grounded World-Action Modeling for Dexterous Sushi Manipulation
summary: Dexterous food manipulation requires control under deformation, occlusion, and uncertain contact. We present TacSushi, a tactile-grounded, Cosmos3-based world-action policy that learns from recorded future consequences while acting on current observations. The backbone encodes current RGB, language, and hand state, and feature-wise gated fusion incorporates fingertip tactile features into the action representation. During training, a decoder conditioned on demonstrated action chunks predicts logged future visual observations, task progress, relative contact risk, and tactile summaries; this decoder is removed at deployment. Failed trials provide consequence supervision, but their actions are excluded from imitation. We train TacSushi on 340 successful and 50 failed real-robot trials and compare six methods in 600 separate rollouts across three in-distribution tasks and two out-of-distribution ingredient variants. To assess food quality beyond a single geometric threshold, we score terminal outcomes using an anchored visual-quality protocol that equally weights five human ratings and three vision-language-model ratings per rollout. Full TacSushi achieves 68.3% average in-distribution success and 37.5% out-of-distribution success, compared with 36.7%/10.0% without future-consequence supervision and 25.0%/17.5% with direct tactile concatenation in place of gated fusion. These comparisons support complementary benefits of feature-wise gated tactile fusion and training-only predictive supervision.

AI.tldr: TacSushi: a tactile-grounded world-action policy that uses future-consequence supervision and gated tactile fusion to learn dexterous food manipulation from real-robot data, achieving strong in-distribution and moderate out-of-distribution performance.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation under deformation, occlusion, and uncertain contact is hard; leveraging tactile signals and predictive supervision can improve control robustness beyond purely imitation-based methods.
AI.method: A TacSushi architecture with a backbone that fuses RGB, language, and hand state; feature-wise gated fusion of fingertip tactile features; a decoder conditioned on demonstrated action chunks predicts logged future observations, task progress, relative contact risk, and tactile summaries during training (discarded at deployment); failed trials provide consequence supervision while excluded from imitation; trained on 340 successes and 50 failures across 600 rollouts in 3 in-distribution tasks and 2 out-of-distribution ingredient variants.
AI.result: Full TacSushi achieves 68.3% in-distribution and 37.5% out-of-distribution success; baselines: 36.7%/10.0% without future-consequence supervision; 25.0%/17.5% with direct tactile concatenation instead of gated fusion, indicating complementary benefits of both components.
AI.conclusion: Feature-wise gated tactile fusion and predictive supervision from logged futures jointly improve dexterous food manipulation, offering robustness to distribution shifts and a principled way to leverage failed trials for learning.

title: MetaRTL: Meta-path Attention Enhanced Relational Table Learning
summary: Relational table learning has gained increasing attention with the widespread use of relational databases. Existing methods typically rely on deep GNN or HGNN stacks, leading to high computational costs and limited performance on large real-world databases. We propose MetaRTL, a two-stage framework for scalable and expressive relational table learning. In the first stage, MetaRTL obtains initial table embeddings via lightweight pre-training. In the second stage, it performs non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features, which are then aggregated by an attention module, MetaAttn. By shifting computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation, MetaRTL captures rich relational semantics while maintaining high efficiency. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: MetaRTL proposes a two-stage relational table learning framework that replaces heavy deep GNNs with a lightweight pretraining stage plus non-parametric meta-path feature aggregation via MetaAttn, yielding scalable and expressive relational reasoning across 24 tasks.
AI.motivation: Relational table learning on large real-world databases is computationally expensive with deep GNN stacks and may underperform due to limited relational semantics; a scalable, expressive approach is needed.
AI.method: Stage 1: lightweight pre-training to obtain initial table embeddings. Stage 2: non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features, aggregated with an attention module MetaAttn. This shifts computation from deep message passing to meta-path aggregation, enabling efficient rich relational semantics.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks demonstrates effectiveness and efficiency, supporting scalability and improved performance relative to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage framework successfully balances scalability and expressive relational reasoning, offering a practical approach for large relational databases.

title: AURA: Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis for Email Threat Detection
summary: Email spam and phishing attacks remain a critical security threat. Adversaries increasingly exploit large language models to craft contextually convincing malicious messages, and existing spam detection systems often struggle to keep pace. Generalization across diverse and evolving attack scenarios is limited, which reduces effectiveness once these systems are deployed in practice. This paper introduces Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis (AURA), a multimodal email threat detection system that analyzes both the content of an email and its embedded URLs. AURA is built around two layers: the first quantifies prediction uncertainty from a URL classifier, and only ambiguous messages are escalated to a fine-tuned transformer encoder for semantic analysis. The system is evaluated on eight heterogeneous training corpora together with two held-out real-world corpora spanning a decade of adversarial campaigns. AURA reaches a macro F1-score of 0.9858 in-distribution, and on NazPhish-Eval and GuenterTrap-Eval it maintains 0.9502 and 0.9436, respectively, which is evidence of robust generalization under genuine distribution shift.

AI.tldr: AURA is a two-layer multimodal email threat detector that uses a URL-based uncertainty score to decide when to apply a fine-tuned transformer for semantic analysis, achieving strong in-distribution and cross-dataset generalization across eight corpora and two held-out real-world corpora over a decade.
AI.motivation: Generalization across diverse and evolving email threats (spam/phishing) is poor for existing detectors, which struggle with distribution shift and adversarially crafted messages leveraging LLMs. AURA seeks robust performance by fusing content and URL signals and deferring expensive analysis to uncertain cases.
AI.method: A two-layer system: (1) a URL classifier outputs an uncertainty score for each message; (2) only messages with high uncertainty are routed to a fine-tuned transformer encoder for semantic analysis of the email content. Multimodal features combine email content and embedded URLs. Trained on eight heterogeneous corpora; evaluated on two held-out real-world corpora spanning a decade.
AI.result: Macro F1 of 0.9858 in-distribution; 0.9502 on NazPhish-Eval and 0.9436 on GuenterTrap-Eval, indicating robust generalization under distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-based routing to a transformer for only ambiguous cases yields strong overall performance with efficient use of expensive modeling, and demonstrates robust cross-domain generalization for email threat detection across evolving campaigns.

title: BinoGen: Scaling egocentric binocular data for embodied visual perception and learning
summary: Embodied visual perception relies on temporally coherent visual experience accumulated through continuous engagement with the environment. However, collecting large-scale egocentric binocular observations together with dense annotations remains costly and difficult. Moreover, visual experience is shaped not only by the environment but also by the embodiment of the observer, including viewing height, field of view, binocular geometry, and motion through the scene. To address these challenges, we present BinoGen, an automated framework for generating large-scale, embodiment-aware egocentric binocular visual experiences in indoor environments. BinoGen jointly models environmental and observer variation through generative scene synthesis, probabilistic object instantiation, appearance randomization, stochastic trajectory generation, and configurable binocular camera setups. The framework produces synchronized binocular videos together with dense multimodal supervision, including depth maps, optical flow, surface normals, semantic maps, object coordinates, and camera poses. Using BinoGen, we construct a dataset comprising more than 20 million annotated images for supervised learning. We demonstrate two complementary utilities of BinoGen. First, incorporating BinoGen data consistently improves real-world visual perception, including depth estimation, object detection, and video object tracking. Second, paired human-inspired and mouse-inspired observations from the same environments enable controlled investigation of how observer embodiment affects perceptual learning. Embodiment-specific adaptation substantially improves performance, while joint training enables a single model to perform competitively across both embodiments. Together, these results demonstrate that large-scale, controllable visual experience can improve embodied perception...

AI.tldr: A framework to synthesize large-scale, embodiment-aware egocentric binocular data with synchronized multimodal supervision, enabling improved embodied perception and controlled study of observer embodiment.
AI.motivation: Collecting large-scale, annotated, embodiment-aware egocentric binocular data is costly; observer embodiment (height, FOV, binocular geometry, motion) affects perception, requiring study and adaptation.
AI.method: Generative synthesis of environments with configurable observer variation; probabilistic object instantiation; appearance randomization; stochastic trajectories; configurable binocular camera setups; outputs include synchronized binocular videos and dense modalities (depth, optical flow, normals, semantics, coordinates, poses).
AI.result: Created a dataset with over 20 million annotated images; data improves real-world perception tasks (depth estimation, object detection, video tracking); embodiment-specific adaptation enhances performance; joint training allows a single model to perform well across different embodiments.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale, controllable synthetic visual experience can enhance embodied perception and enable systematic study of how observer embodiment shapes perceptual learning.

title: EmbodiedMind: Adaptive Data Curation and Prefix-Tree Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Embodied Intelligence
summary: Training embodied foundation models typically requires massive-scale datasets and extensive computational resources, yet often suffers from three critical limitations: (1) inefficient sample utilization due to low-informative samples; (2) imbalanced gradient contributions across heterogeneous tasks; and (3) severe credit assignment problem in long-horizon planning, where trajectory-level rewards indiscriminately penalize all tokens. To address these issues, we propose an efficient training paradigm that achieves state-of-the-art average performance through strategic data selection and hierarchical policy optimization. Our approach consists of three synergistic stages. First, Rejection Sampling-based Fine-Tuning (RSFT) filters out low-informative samples to establish robust behavioral priors while preventing distributional collapse. Second, Iterative Rejection GRPO (IR-GRPO) employs task-specific queues stratified by difficulty to keep datasets balanced across reinforcement learning iterations, coupled with a hybrid reward mechanism for precise cross-task feedback. Third, to enhance long-horizon task planning, we introduce Trie-GRPO, a novel reinforcement learning algorithm based on action prefix trees, which enables step-level advantage estimation. This resolves the credit assignment problem by isolating intermediate correct decisions from downstream errors, while effectively balancing exploration efficiency and depth compared to conventional search trees. As a result, EmbodiedMind achieves a state-of-the-art average performance of 70.02% across 18 benchmarks, and significantly outperforms other embodied foundation models in long-horizon task planning accuracy. Our project will be released for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: Three-stage training paradigm for embodied foundation models: RSFT, IR-GRPO, and Trie-GRPO; aims to improve data efficiency, balanced multi-task learning, and long-horizon credit assignment; reports 70.02% average across 18 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address key limitations in current embodied foundation model training: (1) inefficient sample utilization due to low-informative samples; (2) imbalanced gradient contributions across heterogeneous tasks; (3) credit assignment problems in long-horizon planning where trajectory-level rewards penalize all tokens.
AI.method: RSFT filters out low-informative samples to form robust priors without distributional collapse. IR-GRPO uses task-specific queues stratified by difficulty to balance datasets across RL iterations and employs a hybrid reward mechanism for cross-task feedback. Trie-GRPO introduces action-prefix-tree-based RL for step-level advantage estimation, isolating intermediate correct decisions from downstream errors and balancing exploration depth versus efficiency.
AI.result: Claims state-of-the-art average performance of 70.02% across 18 benchmarks and significantly better long-horizon planning accuracy than other embodied foundation models.
AI.conclusion: Promises reproducibility via releasing the project/code and demonstrates that data selection and hierarchical policy optimization can yield strong performance in embodied agents.

title: A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents
comment: Preprint of a manuscript completed in November, 2025
summary: LLM-based GUI agents increasingly act on behalf of users in digital environments that were designed with human users in mind. These graphical user interfaces were designed to support, but also deliberately steer, the behaviour and decisions of users. While behavioural biases in the textual outputs of LLMs are well-documented, far less is known about how such influence operates when models act as agents that perceive interfaces and execute decisions---and, in particular, whether the reasoning capabilities increasingly built into these agents make them more robust to it. Drawing on Dual-Process Theory, we empirically investigate whether LLM-based GUI agents are susceptible to automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) digital nudges, and how their reasoning configuration moderates this susceptibility. In a randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents and a total of 21,600 simulations across six frontier models from three providers, we found that agents were vulnerable to both nudge types. Crucially, the reasoning configuration moderated these effects in opposing directions, reducing susceptibility to automatic default nudges while heightening it to reflective social influence nudges. Extensive reasoning therefore did not make agents more robust but redirected the route through which choice architecture takes effect. Exploratory analysis further showed this redirection to be systematically structured by model scale. Beyond establishing nudge susceptibility as a behavioural property of agentic AI, the study positions interface design as a governance concern for organizations that delegate decisions to autonomous agents.

AI.tldr: LLM-based GUI agents are vulnerable to digital nudges; reasoning configuration modulates susceptibility differently for automatic (default) vs reflective (social) nudges; larger models redirect nudging pathways but do not universally reduce vulnerability; interface design has governance implications.
AI.motivation: To understand how agents that perceive interfaces and act on decisions respond to nudge techniques, integrating Dual-Process Theory to distinguish automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) processes and how reasoning configuration affects susceptibility.
AI.method: Randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents and 21,600 simulations across six frontier models from three providers; tests automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) nudges; manipulates the reasoning configuration of the agents.
AI.result: Agents are susceptible to both nudge types. Reasoning configuration reduces susceptibility to automatic default nudges but increases susceptibility to reflective social influence nudges. The redirection pattern scales with model size, implying larger models shift the channel of influence rather than eliminating it.
AI.conclusion: Interface design constitutes a governance concern for organizations delegating decisions to autonomous agents. Nudging is a behavioral property of agentic AI, and model scale shapes how nudges are propagated through agent reasoning.

title: Uni-LaDiR: Latent Diffusion Unifies Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Multimodal reasoning requires models to draw on information from multiple modalities throughout the reasoning process. Yet existing methods often concatenate modality-specific thought tokens in a single sequence, leaving the model to bridge representational differences as it reasons across modalities. We introduce Uni-LaDiR (Unified Latent Diffusion Reasoner), a framework that brings these thoughts into a shared latent space for reasoning. A unified encoder maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into shared thought tokens, trained to preserve the information needed for later reasoning steps and the final answer or action. Because the same context can support multiple valid next steps, we use diffusion to predict the next block of thought tokens from the input and preceding blocks. Jointly training the encoder and diffusion reasoner with shared model weights encourages thought tokens to be both useful for the task and predictable from the available context. At inference, the model generates these tokens without teacher observations. Across eleven vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks and two vision-language-action (VLA) suites, Uni-LaDiR achieves relative gains over the strongest evaluated baselines of 7.3% on visual reasoning tasks and 6.1% on robot manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Uni-LaDiR unifies multimodal reasoning by encoding teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into a shared latent space and using a diffusion model to predict the next tokens, enabling inference without teacher signals and yielding strong gains across vision-language benchmarks and vision-language-action tasks.
AI.motivation: Bridge representational gaps in multimodal reasoning by aligning modality-specific thoughts into a single latent space, rather than concatenating tokens from different modalities.
AI.method: A unified encoder maps teacher reasoning steps from multiple modalities into shared thought tokens. A diffusion model predicts the next block of thought tokens from input and prior tokens. The encoder and diffusion reasoner are trained jointly with shared weights, and inference proceeds without teacher observations at test time.
AI.result: Across 11 vision-language model benchmarks and 2 vision-language-action suites, Uni-LaDiR achieves relative gains over the strongest evaluated baselines of 7.3% on visual reasoning tasks and 6.1% on robot manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Unified latent diffusion reasoning improves multimodal reasoning by aligning cross-modal thoughts and leveraging diffusion to predict future reasoning steps, enabling effective inference without teacher signals and yielding substantial performance gains.

title: GS-PI: An Optimization-Decoupled Appearance Decomposition Approach for Generating PBR Gaussian Assets
summary: Gaussian Splatting (GS) excels at novel-view synthesis but encodes baked-in radiance, tightly entangling illumination with geometry and preventing seamless integration into physically based rendering (PBR) pipelines. Existing inverse-rendering methods attempt to disentangle materials via joint optimization, but often suffer from competing objectives that cause severe ambiguities and residual lighting artifacts. To overcome this, we present GS-PI, a novel optimization-decoupled framework that casts PBR material generation as a geometry-conditioned diffusion process on 3D point clouds. By operating directly in the 3D domain, our method inherently guarantees multi-view consistency, sidestepping the severe pixel correspondence issues that challenge 2D diffusion approaches. We introduce a multi-scale cross-view conditioning mechanism that integrates three complementary components: a global semantic prior, source-anchored photometric cues, and an absolute spatial learned view-direction conditioning signal. This design efficiently compresses complex multi-view evidence, mitigating cross-view projection misalignment and successfully preventing specular highlights from baking into intrinsic colors. By extracting a point cloud from a pre-trained Gaussian model, predicting PBR attributes via conditional diffusion, and distilling them back through differentiable rasterisation, we yield a fully relightable PBR-GS asset. GS-PI outperforms recent inverse-rendering baselines while replacing per-scene joint illumination/BRDF optimization with a learned diffusion pass followed by a short target-driven distillation, without requiring proxy meshes.
