AI.tldr: GS-PI decouples optimization from Gaussian-splatting by casting PBR material generation as a 3D diffusion process conditioned on geometry, enabling relightable assets with multi-view consistency and outperforming joint inverse-rendering baselines without proxy meshes.
AI.motivation: Address the entanglement of illumination and geometry in Gaussian Splatting and the ambiguities of existing inverse-rendering approaches, aiming for a decoupled, 3D-consistent method that integrates smoothly into PBR pipelines.
AI.method: Extract a point cloud from a pre-trained Gaussian model, apply a geometry-conditioned, multi-view diffusion process to predict PBR attributes using three conditioning signals (global semantic prior, source-anchored photometric cues, and absolute spatial view-direction), then distill the result through differentiable rasterization to produce a relightable PBR-GS asset.
AI.result: The GS-PI framework yields fully relightable PBR assets and outperforms recent inverse-rendering baselines, replacing per-scene joint illumination/BRDF optimization with a learned diffusion pass followed by short distillation, without requiring proxy meshes.
AI.conclusion: GS-PI provides an optimization-decoupled pipeline that leverages 3D diffusion conditioned on geometry to generate PBR materials from Gaussian-based representations, delivering multi-view-consistent, relightable assets and streamlined integration into PBR workflows.

title: ReShoot: Generative Visual Domain Randomization of Recorded Robot Demonstrations for Visuomotor Policy Learning
summary: Imitation-learned robot policies are frequently overfit to the visual conditions present in their training demonstrations. Consequently, variations in object color or background appearance often induce substantial performance degradation. A common mitigation strategy is to acquire additional demonstrations in each novel visual context; however, this approach is resource-intensive, requiring repeated access to a robot, a controlled environment, and human operation for every appearance condition to be covered. We introduce ReShoot, a framework that synthesizes visual diversity by re-rendering previously recorded demonstrations under altered appearances, thereby shifting the burden from data collection to generation. A vision-language model captions the scene, edits a targeted attribute (e.g., background, object color, or material), and an edge-conditioned video generator re-renders both camera views to match. The instruction is updated accordingly. The action sequence and proprioceptive trajectory are copied verbatim without relabeling, so each generated episode retains the recorded action and proprioceptive labels. On LIBERO, a policy trained on an equal mixture of recorded and re-rendered demonstrations matches the performance of recorded-only training (96.5% vs. 96.9%). Moreover, the mixed training set improves robustness to scene perturbations on LIBERO-Plus (85.5% vs. 82.3%). Across two physical robotic platforms, deploying ReShoot with 43 and 100 pre-collected demonstrations increased the success rate on recolored objects from 0.0% to 42.9% and 47.5%, respectively, while maintaining performance under the original recorded appearance.

AI.tldr: ReShoot synthesizes visual diversity by re-rendering existing demonstrations with edited appearances, allowing imitation-learned policies to generalize to new visual contexts without collecting new demonstrations. It uses a vision-language model to caption and edit scene attributes and an edge-conditioned video generator to re-render views, while keeping actions and proprioception unchanged.
AI.motivation: Imitation policies often overfit to training visuals; robust generalization across varied object colors, backgrounds, and materials typically requires costly new demonstrations. ReShoot aims to shift this burden from data collection to generative synthesis.
AI.method: Caption the scene with a vision-language model, edit a targeted attribute (e.g., background, object color, material), and re-render both camera views with an edge-conditioned video generator. Copy the action sequence and proprioceptive trajectory verbatim; update the instruction accordingly to reflect the new appearance. Train on a mix of recorded and re-rendered demonstrations without relabeling actions.
AI.result: On LIBERO, mixed training (recorded+re-rendered) matches recorded-only performance (96.5% vs 96.9%). On LIBERO-Plus, robustness to scene perturbations improves (85.5% vs 82.3%). In two physical robots, using 43 and 100 demonstrations increased recolored-object success from 0% to 42.9% and 47.5% respectively, while preserving performance on the original appearance.
AI.conclusion: ReShoot effectively creates diverse visual contexts without extra data collection, preserving policy labels and improving both in-distribution performance and robustness to visual perturbations across simulated and real-world settings.

title: Constraint-Safe Graph-Context Scoring for Stable Point-Feature Labels Under Text-Width and Accessibility-Inspired Profiles
summary: Point-feature label placement on interactive maps must reconcile geometric validity, display yield, local placement utility, and stability across camera motion. Accessibility and multilingual requirements further change label dimensions, yet algorithmic evaluations often collapse these concerns into overlap counts. We present LABELSENSE-Pilot, a reproducible prototype that generates eight compass candidates per feature, scores candidates with a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries, adds a previous-placement bonus, and selects a layout through mixed-integer optimization. The executed scorer is deliberately not described as a graph transformer. Every returned layout is checked for viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance. Experiments use 2,500 airport coordinates and names spanning 155 countries, with country-grouped splits and generated density, camera, text-suffix, preference, and enlarged-font stressors. Across five seeds, LABELSENSE-Pilot displayed 85.62 percent of labels with 2.09 percent flicker and zero collisions. Versus a handcrafted-utility integer program, LABELSENSE-Pilot sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display while reducing flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero proxy violations, whereas standard geometry reevaluated at 1.5x violated 52.57 percent of selected placements. These results establish an auditable engineering trade-off, not human accessibility, multilingual usability, or preference. Official recent baselines and participant evidence remain required before submission.

AI.tldr: A reproducible prototype (LABELSENSE-Pilot) for point-feature label placement using eight compass candidates per feature, an MLP over graph-context summaries with a previous-placement bonus, and mixed-integer optimization; achieves high display, low flicker, and zero collisions in airport data; shows favorable trade-offs vs a handcrafted IP, but baselines and participant evidence are still required.
AI.motivation: To balance geometric validity, display yield, local utility, camera-motion stability, accessibility, and multilingual requirements, which traditional evaluations reduce to overlap counts.
AI.method: Generate eight compass candidates per feature; score with multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries; add previous-placement bonus; select layout via mixed-integer optimization; ensure viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, pairwise clearance; avoid graph-transformer label; use 2,500 airport coordinates/names across 155 countries with country-grouped splits and synthetic stressors (density, camera, text-suffix, preference, enlarged-font); five seeds; compare to a handcrafted-utility IP; enlarged-box-aware layouts to avoid proxy violations.
AI.result: Displayed 85.62% of labels, 2.09% flicker, zero collisions across five seeds; vs handcrafted IP: display reduced by 1.43 percentage points but flicker reduced by 12.04 points; enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero proxy violations; standard geometry reevaluated at 1.5x violated 52.57% of selected placements.
AI.conclusion: Establishes an auditable engineering trade-off rather than promoting accessibility, multilingual usability, or user preferences; official baselines and participant evidence remain required before submission.

title: Online Adaptive Kernel Mixing for Gaussian Process Decision Making
comment: 35 pages, 9 figures. Accepted as a full paper at IFIP Performance 2026
summary: Gaussian Processes (GPs) are widely used as surrogates for black-box functions in sequential decision-making problems such as Bayesian optimization (BO), level set estimation (LSE), and Bayesian active learning (BAL). GP performance critically depends on kernels, and standard kernels can lead to suboptimal decisions under misspecification. To address this, we introduce HACK GPs (Hedge Adaptive Cumulative Kernels), a method that views kernel selection as an online learning with expert advice problem. HACK treats each candidate kernel as a GP "expert" and updates a distribution over experts online using AdaHedge, based on a loss received as a proxy for their ability to fit the function and align with the task objective. We provide two variants of HACK: (i) Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) and (ii) categorical sampling. We establish general guarantees showing that, under a loss-gap condition, the weight concentrates on the best kernel and the resulting acquisition function is close to that of the best expert. Empirically, we observe robust performance across BO, LSE, and BAL compared to standard kernels such as Squared Exponential and Matern-5/2, as well as simple ensemble baselines.

AI.tldr: HACK GPs: online kernel selection via AdaHedge among GP experts; two variants MoG and categorical; theory: weight concentrates on best kernel under a loss-gap; empirically robust in BO, LSE, BAL.
AI.motivation: Kernel misspecification undermines GP surrogates; adaptively hedge among kernels without expensive tuning.
AI.method: Treat each kernel as a GP expert; online weight update with AdaHedge using a loss proxy reflecting fit quality and task alignment; two implementations: Mixture of Gaussians and categorical sampling; derive general guarantees.
AI.result: Guarantees: weight concentrates on best kernel under a loss-gap; acquisition function tracks best expert; empirical improvements over standard kernels and simple ensembles across BO, LSE, BAL.
AI.conclusion: HACK GPs offer a robust, online kernel selection framework for GPs; extendable to other hyperparameters; relies on a suitable loss proxy and loss-gap condition; potential computational trade-offs.

title: CitySTAR: Structured and Topology-Aware Reasoning for Open-Vocabulary Urban 3D Grounding
summary: 3D grounding aims to localize target entities in complex scenes from natural language and plays a fundamental role in embodied perception and spatial reasoning. However, existing approaches mostly rely on feature similarity or direct matching, making it difficult to connect natural-language intent with the implicit semantic and geometric structures hidden in billion-scale urban point clouds. We reformulate city-scale 3D grounding as structured constraint reasoning, where description semantics are organized into computable cross-modal constraints over open-vocabulary 3D entities, attributes, and spatial relations. We present CitySTAR, a training-free framework for reasoning-driven urban 3D grounding. CitySTAR lifts raw billion-scale urban point clouds into a query-ready scene graph of open-vocabulary 3D instances, with CodeLLM-driven tools supplying multimodal evidence for node attributes and 3D spatial relations. It then models target-context topology with paired hypergraphs and performs bidirectional topology verification for structural disambiguation. Finally, a Reflective Cross-modal Grounding module integrates topology consistency and candidate-centered 2D visual evidence to make decisions over a metric-aware 3D context graph. To further support this setting, we introduce CitySTAR-3D, an enhanced benchmark that improves semantic coverage, instance completeness, bounding-box fidelity, and spatial-relation complexity in city-scale 3D grounding. Extensive experiments show that CitySTAR consistently improves open-world urban 3D grounding while maintaining strong interpretability and generalization.

AI.tldr: CitySTAR introduces a training-free, reasoning-driven framework for city-scale 3D grounding that converts urban point clouds into a query-ready scene graph and uses cross-modal constraints and topology verification to connect natural language to open-vocabulary 3D entities; CitySTAR-3D provides a richer benchmark.
AI.motivation: The paper targets the gap between natural-language intent and the implicit semantic and geometric structure of billion-scale urban point clouds. Existing methods relying on feature similarity struggle with open-vocabulary, city-scale data and complex spatial relations.
AI.method: Reformulates 3D grounding as structured constraint reasoning. Builds a query-ready scene graph of open-vocabulary 3D instances from urban point clouds, aided by CodeLLM-driven tools for multimodal evidence of attributes and spatial relations. Uses paired hypergraphs to model target-context topology and applies bidirectional topology verification. A Reflective Cross-modal Grounding module fuses topology consistency with candidate-centered 2D evidence to produce decisions on a metric-aware 3D context graph. CitySTAR-3D extends the benchmark to improve semantic coverage, instance completeness, bounding-box fidelity, and spatial-relation complexity.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show consistent improvements in open-world urban 3D grounding while preserving interpretability and generalization. CitySTAR-3D affords better coverage and realism in evaluation.
AI.conclusion: CitySTAR advances open-world city-scale 3D grounding by combining structured cross-modal constraints, topology-aware reasoning, and reflective integration with 2D evidence; the CitySTAR-3D benchmark enhances assessment of such systems.

title: Runtime Safety Filtering for Two-Terminal Hazards in Robotic Battery Recycling
summary: Runtime safety filters for learned manipulation policies typically define unsafe states as unions of object-wise keep-out regions. This representation can be unnecessarily restrictive for hazards that depend on a joint spatial relation, such as battery recycling, where a conductive payload can short a charged cell only when it approaches both terminals simultaneously. We study runtime filtering for this two-terminal hazard in LIBERO using frozen OpenVLA policies. We factor a runtime filter into three design choices: the predicate structure, its geometric margin, and the fallback action applied when a commanded action is rejected. We compare a conjunctive predicate, a conventional two-site keep-out, and a composite of the two. For each predicate, we vary its margin to obtain a frontier between task success and residual hazard. We then compare four fallback strategies at matched operating points: holding, retreat, sampled search, and a continuous-action barrier projection. Across three workcells, the three predicate families trace nearly identical safety--utility frontiers once each is evaluated over its own margin. In contrast, the fallback strategy has a substantially larger effect: holding reduces task success by up to 0.302 relative to retreat without reducing hazard, while both minimally invasive fallbacks leave substantially more residual hazard. This ordering transfers to a second policy and task suite, while retreat-based filtering remains effective under standing errors in the clearances available to the filter, although correlated error in the estimated payload size is more damaging than larger independent errors in terminal position. These results show that, for proximity-defined manipulation hazards, margin selection and fallback strategy can matter more than predicate structure in determining the safety--utility trade-off of a runtime filter.

AI.tldr: Runtime safety filters for learned manipulation policies using three predicate designs and four fallbacks show margins and fallback choice dominate safety-utility trade-offs for two-terminal hazards; predicate structure is less impactful.
AI.motivation: Hazards that depend on joint spatial relations (e.g., a payload bridging two terminals) cannot be captured by simple unions of keep-out regions. Understanding how predicate form, geometric margin, and fallback actions affect safety-utility is essential for reliable, real-time policy filtering.
AI.method: Evaluate three predicate families (conjunctive, conventional two-site keep-out, and a composite of the two) across varying geometric margins. Compare four fallbacks (holding, retreat, sampled search, continuous-action barrier projection) at matched operating points. Test across three workcells and transfer to a second policy/task suite, analyzing safety–utility frontiers and robustness to clearance/payload estimation errors.
AI.result: All three predicate families yield nearly identical safety–utility frontiers when evaluated with their own tuned margins. Fallback strategy dominates performance: holding reduces task success more than retreat while not reducing hazard; retreat-based filtering remains more effective under clearance errors; correlated payload-size errors are especially damaging. Overall, margin selection and fallback choice matter more than predicate structure for proximity-defined hazards.
AI.conclusion: For proximity-defined manipulation hazards, focus design effort on choosing effective margins and fallbacks rather than on predicate structure, as these choices more strongly shape the safety–utility trade-off of runtime filters.

title: Reproducibility is not construct validity: LLM measurement of institutionally situated communication
summary: High annotation reproducibility does not necessarily imply that an LLM-inferred measure captures the construct it is intended to measure. We test this distinction using a dataset from the European Commission's AI Act consultation, linking structured survey responses to free-text consultation submissions from the same stakeholders. LLM annotations of consultation submissions are highly reproducible (intraclass correlations > 0.99), yet show limited convergence with survey-reported measures of the nominal construct they were intended to approximate. Divergence between survey-and LLM-inferred text-based measures varies systematically across stakeholder groups: business associations express greater concern about AI risks in text-based consultations than in survey responses ({g} = +1.0), whereas public authorities and several nonbusiness groups show smaller or negative divergences. Divergences between scores suggest positive spatial autocorrelation across European countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036), indicating that stakeholders from neighboring countries tend toward more similar text-based stances towards AI safety concerns. Despite divergence, survey-reported concerns remain strongly associated with support for explainability across all divergence levels. These results demonstrate that LLM annotation reproducibility can coexist with poor construct correspondence and motivate validation procedures that distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication context variation when LLMs are used as measurement instruments.

AI.tldr: LLM annotation reproducibility is high but does not guarantee valid construct measurement; divergence exists across stakeholder groups with spatial autocorrelation; validation needed.
AI.motivation: To distinguish whether reproducible LLM-derived text measures truly capture the intended construct and to assess how measurement context affects construct validity.
AI.method: Link structured survey responses with free-text consultation submissions from EU stakeholders; annotate submissions with an LLM; compare LLM-derived scores to survey measures; compute intraclass correlations (reproducibility), examine convergence/divergence by group, assess spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I), and relate text-based scores to explainability measures.
AI.result: LLM annotations show very high reproducibility (ICC > 0.99) but poor or variable convergence with the nominal construct; divergence systematic by stakeholder group (e.g., business associations show more concern in text than in surveys, others show less/negative divergence); positive spatial autocorrelation across countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036); survey concerns remain strongly linked to support for explainability across divergence levels.
AI.conclusion: Reproducibility and construct validity are distinct; high reproducibility does not imply accurate capture of the intended construct; validation procedures should separately assess reproducibility, construct validity, and the influence of communication context when using LLMs as measurement tools.

title: REARL: A Closed-loop Autonomous Driving Simulation Enhancement Framework with Real Traffic Data and Large Language Models
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Corresponding author: Yiwen Sun. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 62503015)
summary: Accurate simulation is crucial for autonomous driving development, yet capturing real-world traffic complexity remains challenging. Existing simulators that rely on predefined rules or static data playback struggle with dynamic traffic. CRITICAL uses real traffic data and a large language model (LLM) to adjust the initial simulation configuration, but the simulated distribution still diverges from real traffic as the rollout evolves. We propose REARL, a closed-loop simulation enhancement framework that integrates real traffic data with LLMs. Real traffic data are clustered, and each cluster center is used as a representative scenario that provides typical real-world traffic patterns for the LLM. A timed sliding-window detector then monitors discrepancies in vehicle speed distribution and mean spacing between pairs of vehicles. If a metric exceeds a threshold, the LLM adjusts vehicle decision-making; otherwise the existing controller is kept. The LLM also selects a matching real vehicle from a traffic snapshot and modulates the simulated vehicle with reference to that real action. In a controlled HighD highway setting, compared with the CRITICAL baseline and a PPO-based learning baseline, REARL reduces the Hellinger distance for speed distributions to 0.3067 and the MAPE for mean spacing to 0.8371, while achieving a time headway (THW) of 22.8575 and a lane change rate of 0.0708.

AI.tldr: REARL is a closed-loop framework that fuses real traffic data with LLM-driven adjustments to align simulation distributions with real-world traffic, outperforming CRITICAL and PPO baselines in HighD.
AI.motivation: Capturing the dynamic, diverse nature of real-world traffic is challenging for rule-based or static-data simulators; integrating real data with LLMs can dynamically adapt simulation behavior.
AI.method: Real traffic data are clustered; each cluster center serves as a representative scenario for the LLM. A timed sliding-window detector monitors discrepancies in speed distribution and mean vehicle spacing. If a metric exceeds a threshold, the LLM adapts vehicle decision-making; otherwise the existing controller remains. The LLM also selects a matching real vehicle from a traffic snapshot and modulates the simulated vehicle with reference to that real action. Evaluation on a HighD highway setting; comparisons against the CRITICAL baseline and a PPO-based baseline.
AI.result: REARL reduces the Hellinger distance for speed distributions to 0.3067 and the MAPE for mean spacing to 0.8371; achieves time headway (THW) of 22.8575 and a lane-change rate of 0.0708, outperforming baselines.
AI.conclusion: A closed-loop, data-informed use of LLMs can substantially reduce the simulation-to-real gap in autonomous-driving traffic simulations, yielding more realistic speeds, spacing, and maneuver statistics; effectiveness depends on clustering quality, detector thresholds, and LLM prompt design; future work could expand scenarios and analyze sensitivity to hyperparameters.

title: DirtyMoCap: Robust Motion Capture from Unconstrained Markers
summary: Optical motion capture delivers high-fidelity human motion, but its reliance on strict marker layouts and clean trajectories severely limits its real-world applicability. In practice, tracking systems frequently output unconstrained markers: sparse, noisy, and unordered point clouds with unknown or varying configurations. To bridge the gap between corrupted raw markers and parametric human models, we introduce DirtyMoCap, a robust, marker-layout-free framework. Our core insight is to map unordered marker observations to a fixed set of "proxy anchors" comprising skeletal joints and body surface points, which serve as a stable intermediate representation. We first initialize and track these anchors over long sequences using a recurrent sliding-window architecture. Then, a custom differentiable Gauss-Newton solver fits the SMPL-H model to the tracked anchors to recover full-body pose, translation, and shape. By explicitly deriving geometric residuals, our solver learns adaptive observation confidence, smoothness, and prior weights end-to-end, adapting dynamically to the reliability of the input data. Extensive experiments on diverse, noisy marker configurations demonstrate that DirtyMoCap successfully generalizes across arbitrary layouts using only a single trained model. It consistently outperforms state-of-the-art configuration-specific baselines in both joint and vertex reconstruction accuracy, while our custom CUDA solver achieves up to a 100x speedup over standard PyTorch implementations. We further apply DirtyMoCap to heterogeneous raw optical MoCap recordings of traditional Chinese martial arts, yielding a Kung Fu motion dataset of temporally coherent SMPL-H reconstructions. Code and data are available at https://wanglongzju.github.io/DirtyMoCap-Project-Page.

AI.tldr: Marker-layout-free MoCap pipeline that converts unordered, noisy markers into a fixed set of proxy anchors and fits SMPL-H via a differentiable Gauss-Newton solver, yielding robust, generalizable full-body reconstruction with fast CUDA acceleration.
AI.motivation: Overcome reliance on clean, predefined marker layouts and constrained trajectories in optical MoCap; enable robust reconstruction from unconstrained, noisy, unordered marker clouds.
AI.method: Map observations to proxy anchors (skeletal joints and surface points); track anchors with a recurrent sliding-window; fit SMPL-H with a differentiable Gauss-Newton solver that learns adaptive residuals, confidences, smoothness, and priors end-to-end; implement custom CUDA solver for speed.
AI.result: Generalizes across arbitrary layouts with a single trained model; outperforms configuration-specific baselines in joint and vertex accuracy; up to 100x speedup vs PyTorch; demonstrates on Kung Fu motion dataset; code and data released.
AI.conclusion: Proxy-anchor representation enables robust, layout-agnostic MoCap and efficient optimization; provides a practical, scalable solution for unconstrained marker data and broadens applicability of optical MoCap.

title: Towards High-DoF Dexterous Manipulation through VLA Post-Training
summary: Imitation-learned vision--language--action (VLA) foundation models acquire broad manipulation capabilities by scaling robot data across tasks and embodiments, but reliable deployment on a specific downstream task and hardware platform still requires post-training. Dexterous hands make this adaptation particularly difficult: their broad behavioural repertoire and high degree of freedom create a large and structured action space. Three obstacles are central: open-source VLAs do not natively provide an action interface for high-DoF hands; gesture mismatch during human-gated DAgger takeover creates command discontinuities and contaminates corrective trajectories; and reinforcement learning in the raw joint space is sample-inefficient. We present a unified four-step post-training pipeline comprising a learned temporal hand-action codec, supervised fine-tuning, DAgger, and real-world residual reinforcement learning. The codec adapts a pretrained VLA to absolute dexterous-hand commands. Buffered rollback, pose alignment, and smooth command blending enable continuous, task-relevant DAgger corrections, while latent residual RL confines exploration to coordinated hand motions captured by the codec. We evaluate the pipeline on five diverse real-world tasks spanning bimanual transfer, in-hand reorientation, and tool use. Within the reported post-training budgets, the resulting policies achieve 100\% success on every evaluated task over 20 trials per task. These results provide a practical path for adapting VLA foundation models to reliable real-world dexterous manipulation.

AI.tldr: A four-step post-training pipeline adapts imitation-learned vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models to dexterous hands, addressing action interface, DAgger-induced discontinuities, and sample-inefficiency in joint-space RL; achieves 100% success on five real-world tasks (20 trials each).
AI.motivation: VLAs scale manipulation across tasks but require task- and hardware-specific adaptation. Key obstacles for high-DoF hands include: (i) absence of a native action interface for high-DoF hands in open-source VLAs, (ii) gesture mismatch during human-guided DAgger takeovers causing discontinuities in corrective trajectories, (iii) raw joint-space RL is data-inefficient.
AI.method: A four-step post-training pipeline: (1) learn a temporal hand-action codec that maps VLA outputs to absolute dexterous-hand commands; (2) supervised fine-tuning on task data; (3) DAgger with buffered rollback, pose alignment, and smooth command blending to enable continuous, task-relevant corrections; (4) real-world residual RL constraining exploration to the codec latent space, refining coordinated hand motions.
AI.result: Evaluated on five diverse real-world tasks (bimanual transfer, in-hand reorientation, tool use). Under the stated post-training budgets, policies achieve 100% success on every task across 20 trials per task.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline provides a practical, scalable route for transferring VLA foundation models to reliable, real-world dexterous manipulation, mitigating action-interface gaps, discontinuities from human-guided corrections, and sample-inefficiency of joint-space RL.

title: Physical knowledge on historical data matters more than enforcing physical constraints on the forecast
summary: Time series forecasting has seen signicant advancements with the emergence of new deep learning models. However, forecasting time series in applications involving physical processes remains a major challenge. Despite the apparition of Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINN), recent models do not estimate unobservable intermediate physical variables, which are important for domain experts to understand the target behavior. To this end, we propose a Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) which predicts, along the target, unobservable variables on both historic data and forecast target. This approach enhances the model robustness and results interpretation using domain knowledge. Our method is easily adaptable to any physical model using several equations, each having its own set of unobservable variables, to describe it-self. As a case study, we incorporate physical equations used for groundwater levels predictions by the physical model called Gardenia. This model uses transfers equations between reservoirs, optimized with data assimilation, to simulate the evolution of groundwater levels. Evaluation includes several well known neural network models and the Gardenia model compared on twelve real world datasets. In addition, we study the impact of each component through an ablation study. Our model outperforms other models on ve out of the twelve datasets and our ablation study underlines the importance of having a physical background in our time series forecasting task. Finally, the coherence of the physical variables predicted by our neural network is assessed by a domain expert.

AI.tldr: PIRNN jointly forecasts a time series and unobserved physical variables using physics-informed recurrence; shows robustness and interpretability improvements, validated on groundwater data with Gardenia; outperforms several baselines on 5/12 datasets; ablation confirms value of including physical priors.
AI.motivation: To overcome lack of interpretable, unobservable intermediate state estimation in standard PINN-based forecasting and to leverage domain knowledge for physical processes.
AI.method: Introduce Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) that predicts unobservable variables alongside the target time series; adaptable to any physical model with multiple equations and unobservables; case study uses Gardenia groundwater model with transfer equations and data assimilation.
AI.result: PIRNN outperforms other models on five of twelve datasets; ablation study shows the importance of physical background; domain expert confirms coherence of predicted physical variables.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating physical background and unobservable state estimation enhances robustness and interpretability of time-series forecasts; PIRNN provides a flexible framework for physics-informed forecasting, exemplified on groundwater modeling.

title: Digital Twins for Opinion Dynamics: A Generative LLM Framework for Social Networks
summary: The study of opinion dynamics in social networks is one of the key challenges in computational social science with direct relevance to understanding political polarization, misinformation, and health responses. Current approaches focus on simplified mathematical models that ignore linguistic and contextual factors related to belief updates or use Large Language Model (LLM)-based simulations that have not been validated against real data. We present a framework based on the concept of a digital twin to simulate opinion dynamics in social networks. The approach fills the gap by cloning a real-world Twitter network, assigns a set of attributes for agents (such as persona, emotions, centrality, stubbornness, and influence), and employs Mistral-7B to perform opinion update based on memory and social exposure. To evaluate the proposed approach, we validate it against two real Twitter datasets (COVID-19 discourse and U.S elections 2020). The results show that the capability of the proposed framework reproduces opinion trajectories and reduces individual prediction error by more than 50% compared to the best-performing classical baseline (Mistral-7B achieves Mean Absolute Error (MAE) = 0.150 and 0.121 on the COVID-19 and US Election 2020 datasets, respectively). We observe similar improvements in structural alignment (Delta_r = 0.120 and 0.180) and polarization dynamics (Delta_Var = 0.106 and 0.115) on the two datasets, respectively. Additionally, the ablation studies confirm that agent attributes, memory, and social exposure all contribute to the framework's predictive fidelity in reproducing opinion trajectories, with agent attributes being the most critical contributor. Overall, our results demonstrate that grounding Mistral-7B within empirically cloned interaction networks produces a realistic simulation framework capable of reproducing complex social dynamics.

AI.tldr: Digital twin framework clones real Twitter networks to simulate opinion dynamics using Mistral-7B, integrating attributes, memory, and social exposure; validated on COVID-19 and 2020 US election datasets with improved predictive fidelity and polarization metrics.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of simplified models and unvalidated LLM-based simulations in opinion dynamics by grounding simulations in empirical social graphs and rich agent attributes, validated against real data.
AI.method: Clone real Twitter networks to form agent-based digital twins; assign attributes (persona, emotions, centrality, stubbornness, influence); use Mistral-7B for opinion updates driven by memory and social exposure; evaluate on COVID-19 discourse and US Elections 2020 datasets against baselines; perform ablation studies.
AI.result: Model reproduces opinion trajectories with MAE improvements (0.150 and 0.121); structural alignment (Delta_r) 0.120 and 0.180; polarization dynamics (Delta_Var) 0.106 and 0.115; ablations show attributes, memory, and exposure contribute, with attributes most critical.
AI.conclusion: Grounding Mistral-7B in empirically cloned interaction networks yields a realistic framework capable of reproducing complex social dynamics and improving predictive fidelity relative to classical baselines.

title: Enhanced Knowledge Distillation for Detection Transformer via Teacher Prediction Refinement
summary: Detection Transformers (DETRs) achieve strong performance in object detection but remain challenging to deploy on edge devices due to their high computational cost. Existing DETR distillation methods mainly focus on aligning distillation points, while largely overlooking the quality of the teacher's supervision itself. We observe that due to stage-wise non-monotonic prediction behavior in DETRs, well-localized or correctly classified predictions from earlier stages may degrade in later ones, and some negative predictions become increasingly overconfident. As a result, relying solely on the current stage's predictions yields inaccurate and inconsistent supervision. To address this issue, we propose Teacher Prediction Refinement Distillation (TPRD), a plug-and-play module that refines teacher predictions before distillation by exploiting stage-wise prediction information. TPRD improves supervision quality through Positive Prediction Correction (PPC), which corrects degraded positive predictions by restoring more accurate ones from earlier stages, ensuring reliable localization and classification signals, and Negative Prediction Suppression (NPS) suppresses the influence of overconfident negatives, preventing them from providing misleading supervision to the student. To preserve informative dark knowledge, we further introduce Maximum Dark Knowledge Preservation (MDKP), which selectively refines target-class logits while retaining non-target relations. Extensive experiments on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method. Our code is available at https://github.com/xingyitong1/TPRD.

AI.tldr: TPRD is a plug-in distillation module for DETR that refines teacher predictions using stage-wise information to improve supervision: Positive Prediction Correction (PPC), Negative Prediction Suppression (NPS), and Maximum Dark Knowledge Preservation (MDKP). It improves distillation effectiveness on DETR models and shows robustness on COCO and VOC.
AI.motivation: DETR-based detectors are costly and difficult to deploy on edge devices. Existing DETR distillation often aligns distillation points but ignores the quality of teacher supervision. DETR's stage-wise non-monotonic predictions can make earlier correct positives degrade later, and overconfident negatives mislead the student. There is a need to refine teacher signals before distillation.
AI.method: Introduce Teacher Prediction Refinement Distillation (TPRD) as a plug-and-play module. Positive Prediction Correction (PPC) recovers degraded positive predictions by leveraging earlier stages to restore accurate localization and classification signals. Negative Prediction Suppression (NPS) reduces the influence of overconfident negatives. Maximum Dark Knowledge Preservation (MDKP) selectively refines target-class logits while preserving non-target relations to retain dark knowledge. The approach is evaluated on standard DETR setups with MS COCO and PASCAL VOC.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MS COCO and PASCAL VOC demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of TPRD, indicating improved distillation quality for DETR models; code is provided (GitHub).
AI.conclusion: TPRD provides a plug-in, robust enhancement to DETR distillation by refining teacher supervision through PPC, NPS, and MDKP while preserving dark knowledge, enabling better edge-device performance without changing the core DETR architecture.

title: VAST: V2X/Dynamic Map-Aware Autonomous Driving Systems Validation Toolchain
summary: Cooperative autonomous driving in the IoT-to-Edge-to-Cloud continuum requires system-level validation across vehicles, infrastructure sensors, edge-side Dynamic Map services, and in-vehicle autonomous-driving stacks. This paper presents VAST, a V2X/Dynamic Map-aware validation toolchain that connects Scenic, Scenario Simulator v2, AWSIM, Autoware, and SIM-LDM. VAST does not introduce a new search algorithm; instead, it addresses interoperability challenges, including Lanelet2-to-Scenic mapping, ROS 2-based co-simulation through SS2, Dynamic Map object injection into Autoware, and collection of TTC, PET, collision, timeout, and performance measurements. In occluded-intersection scenarios, Lanelet2-compatible constrained sampling increases the edge-case discovery rate from 40.0% to 80.0% and reduces the average time per discovered edge case from 259.7 s to 110.4 s. Under the same generated scenario distribution, Dynamic Map availability reduces the collision rate from 78.0% to 40.0% and increases non-collision outcomes from 22.0% to 60.0%, with statistically significant TTC/PET shifts. A throughput study with 1-16 NPCs shows that sampling remains below 0.1 s, whereas AWSIM/Autoware execution and restart overhead dominate runtime. These results position VAST as a practical validation infrastructure for cooperative autonomous-driving CPSs.

AI.tldr: VAST is a practical, cross-simulator validation toolchain for cooperative autonomous driving, linking multiple stacks to address interoperability and edge-case discovery, achieving substantial improvements in occluded-intersection scenarios and offering low sampling latency with dominant runtime overhead from simulation/execution components.
AI.motivation: To enable end-to-end, system-level validation of cooperative autonomous driving across IoT, edge, and cloud layers, addressing interoperability bottlenecks between diverse simulators, geospatial representations, and in-vehicle stacks, and to improve discovery of rare edge cases in occluded scenarios.
AI.method: Introduce VAST, a validation pipeline that interoperates Scenic, Scenario Simulator v2, AWSIM, Autoware, and SIM-LDM. Tackle interoperability challenges including Lanelet2→Scenic mapping, ROS 2 co-simulation, Dynamic Map object injection into Autoware, and measurement collection (TTC, PET, collisions, timeouts, performance). Use constrained Lanelet2 sampling to boost edge-case discovery in occluded intersections, evaluate Dynamic Map availability, and conduct throughput studies with 1–16 NPCs.
AI.result: Edge-case discovery rate in occluded intersections increases from 40% to 80% with constrained sampling; average time to discover an edge case decreases from 259.7 s to 110.4 s. Dynamic Map availability reduces collision rate from 78% to 40% and raises non-collision outcomes from 22% to 60%, with statistically significant TTC/PET shifts. Throughput study shows sampling under 0.1 s; AWSIM/Autoware execution and restart overhead dominate runtime.
AI.conclusion: VAST provides a practical, scalable validation infrastructure for cooperative autonomous-driving cyber-physical systems, enabling robust interoperability testing and improved edge-case discovery.

title: TRACE: Accountable Agentic Retrieval for Source Discovery in Digital Archives
summary: Historical archives pose a difficult retrieval problem for retrievalaugmented generation systems: documents are OCR-degraded, heterogeneous across genres and sources, and require strong source traceability for scholarly and institutional use. We introduce TRACE, a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical corpora. The system was developed in the context of DECIDON, an interdisciplinary project on the circulation of political discourse between parliamentary debates and the press during the French Third Republic, involving digitised historical collections and institutional use cases. The prototype is currently deployed internally within the project and accessible to 24 researchers across six partner institutions. We evaluate TRACE on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic, a benchmark of 1,752 French historical questions over parliamentary debates and newspapers from 1887, with documents derived from Biblioth{è}que nationale de France digitised collections. TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines, with the largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. At approximately $0.02 per question under the default hosted inference configuration, TRACE also remains economically feasible for heritage institutions, laboratories or companies that cannot rely on costly local GPU infrastructure. These results suggest that, for large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design can provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a training-free, agentic retrieval framework for accountable source discovery in historical corpora, designed to handle OCR-degraded, heterogeneous archives with strong traceability, and shown to be cost-effective.
AI.motivation: Historical archives suffer from OCR noise, genre heterogeneity, and the need for scholarly source provenance; a training-free, corpus-aware retrieval system could improve accuracy and accountability.
AI.method: TRACE operates as a training-free agentic retrieval system integrated with DECIDON; evaluated on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic (1,752 questions over 1887 debates and newspapers); compares against sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines; emphasizes multi-hop and cross-corpus questions; cost per query ~ $0.02.
AI.result: TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming baselines, with the largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design offer a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches for large digital libraries and archives, and TRACE demonstrates economic feasibility for heritage institutions.

title: Amortizing Physics-Informed Neural Solvers via Graph Hypernetworks
comment: Accepted at the Learning on Graphs Conference (LoG), 2026
summary: Amortizing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across related PDEs requires describing each equation to a reusable solver. Coefficient vectors encode numerical parameters in predefined slots, leaving operator and cross-field assignments implicit. We make these relationships explicit in an operator graph, with nodes for fields, derivatives, terms, and residuals and coefficients retained as term attributes. A graph hypernetwork generates diagonal codes that initialize a meta-trained factorized PINN for each target equation. Meta-training and target-specific adaptation use governing equations and prescribed conditions without solution labels. We compare coefficient-vector, DeepSets-based term-set, and graph conditioning by solution accuracy within a fixed adaptation budget. In scalar convection-diffusion-reaction problems, both term-based descriptors improve high-reaction accuracy, with similar performance. In two-field Fisher-KPP, meta-training sees uncoupled and one-way systems; after 3,000 adaptation steps on unseen two-way coupling, the graph's mean final error is 35.7% below the term set and 67.7% below the coefficient vector. In a fixed-structure capacitively coupled plasma model, the coefficient vector performs best. These results support extending coefficient conditioning with explicit equation relationships for physics-based solver adaptation.

AI.tldr: Proposes an operator-graph conditioning framework for amortizing PINNs across related PDEs, using a graph hypernetwork to generate initialization codes for a meta-trained, factorized PINN. Demonstrates three conditioning schemes (coefficient vector, term-set, graph conditioning) and evaluates their accuracy under fixed adaptation budgets across scalar convection-diffusion-reaction, two-field Fisher-KPP, and a capacitively coupled plasma model. Key finding: explicit equation relationships (term-based and graph-conditioned) improve adaptation in many settings, with the graph approach offering substantial gains in unseen two-way coupling, though not universally (coefficient-vector may dominate in fixed-structure plasma). Concludes that extending coefficient conditioning with explicit equation structure is beneficial for physics-based solver adaptation.
AI.motivation: Improve efficiency and generalization of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) when adapting to related PDEs without solution labels, by making equation relationships explicit and reusable across tasks.
AI.method: Construct an operator graph with nodes for fields, derivatives, terms, residuals; retain coefficients as term attributes. Use a graph hypernetwork to produce diagonal codes that initialize a meta-trained factorized PINN for each target PDE. Train meta-model and adapt to targets using governing equations and prescribed conditions, without solution labels. Compare three conditioning strategies (coefficient-vector, DeepSets-based term-set, and graph conditioning) under a fixed adaptation budget across three PDE benchmarks: scalar convection-diffusion-reaction, two-field Fisher-KPP (including unseen two-way coupling after adaptation), and a fixed-structure capacitively coupled plasma model.
AI.result: In scalar convection-diffusion-reaction problems, both term-based descriptors improve high-reaction accuracy with similar performance. In two-field Fisher-KPP, after 3,000 adaptation steps on unseen two-way coupling, graph-conditioning yields mean final error 35.7% lower than the term-set and 67.7% lower than the coefficient-vector. In the fixed-structure capacitively coupled plasma model, the coefficient-vector conditioning performs best. Overall, results support incorporating explicit equation relationships into coefficient conditioning to enhance solver adaptation across related PDEs.
AI.conclusion: Explicit equation relationships—via term-based descriptors and graph conditioning—can improve cross-PDE PINN adaptation; coefficient conditioning benefits from augmentation with equation-structure information, though gains are problem-dependent.

title: Beyond the Foreground: FOV-Aware Polyp Image Synthesis via Lesion-Guided Adaptive Mucosal Context Propagation
summary: Synthetic image and mask pairs can alleviate scarce colonoscopy annotations, but realistic synthesis requires preserving the supplied lesion while generating compatible mucosa. Existing foreground-guided methods treat all non-foreground pixels as background and rely mainly on local integration. Directly applying them to colonoscopy causes two problems: non-mucosal black regions contaminate generated tissue, and local reasoning produces inconsistent mucosal texture and illumination. We propose LAMP, the first foreground-guided framework for polyp image synthesis based on lesion-guided adaptive mucosal context propagation. LAMP explicitly separates the lesion, valid mucosa, and camera exterior using a field-of-view (FOV) mask. Lesion-to-Mucosa cross-attention extracts lesion appearance conditions for valid-mucosa locations, while FOV-constrained multidirectional Vision Receptance Weighted Key Value propagates them over legal tissue support. An adaptive gate then controls their residual fusion into the diffusion U-Net. Extensive experiments on five polyp datasets demonstrate that LAMP substantially outperforms existing methods in overall generation quality and consistently improves five downstream segmentation models. Our code will be released at https://github.com/wangtong627/LAMP.

AI.tldr: A lesion-guided diffusion-based polyp image synthesis framework (LAMP) that uses lesion-to-mucosa cross-attention and FOV-constrained propagation to preserve lesions while generating realistic mucosa, improving generation quality and downstream segmentation.
AI.motivation: To address scarce colonoscopy annotations and the limitations of existing foreground-guided methods, which mis-handle non-mucosal regions and yield inconsistent mucosal texture/illumination when applied to colonoscopy.
AI.method: Introduce LAMP with an FOV mask to separate lesion, valid mucosa, and exterior; use lesion-to-mucosa cross-attention to encode lesion appearance; apply FOV-constrained multidirectional Vision Receptance Weighted Key Value propagation to diffuse tissue-consistent features; A gating mechanism fuses residuals into the diffusion U-Net; evaluate on five polyp datasets.
AI.result: LAMP outperforms existing methods in overall generation quality and consistently improves five downstream segmentation models across five datasets; code to be released.
AI.conclusion: LAMP is the first foreground-guided polyp synthesis framework using lesion-guided adaptive mucosal context propagation, enabling more realistic synthetic data for colonoscopy and better downstream segmentation.

title: LYRIC: Language-Driven Physics-Based Character Control for Contact-Rich Whole-Body Object Interaction
summary: We present LYRIC, a generative flow-matching controller for language-driven physics-based contact-rich interaction control, that enables simulated characters to perform contact-rich whole-body object interactions from a free-form language instruction and a sparse terminal object goal. To obtain reliable expert trajectories from imperfect motion-capture references, a single tracking policy is trained using geometry-conditioned interaction rewards and relaxed reference tracking near hand-object contact. To guide interaction progress without prescribing a full-body kinematic reference, we factorize the controller into a task-level planner that predicts short-horizon object and humanoid-root trajectories, and an action generator that resolves whole-body motion and contacts in closed loop. After behavior cloning, we freeze the planner and post-tune the action generator on policy using the planner's predictions as stable supervision for intermediate task progression. In a controlled OMOMO evaluation, our tracker achieves 64.3% success compared with 53.2% for an InterMimic reimplementation, while a unified policy achieves 76.5% on the full OMOMO dataset. On the held-out split, LYRIC achieves 90.3% task success, compared with 74.2% for the strongest matched kinematic-planner baseline, with better semantic alignment and motion quality. Without retraining, the controller also supports test-time object-waypoint guidance. Qualitative results further demonstrate robust, natural contact-rich interactions and zero-shot transfer to novel object shapes. The webpage is available at https://neu-vi.github.io/LYRIC/

AI.tldr: LYRIC is a language-driven, flow-matching controller with a planner–generator architecture for contact-rich whole-body interactions, achieving strong OMOMO performance and zero-shot transfer.
AI.motivation: Enable simulated characters to perform contact-rich, whole-body object interactions from free-form language without relying on imperfect full-body kinematic references or precise motion capture guidance.
AI.method: A generative flow-matching controller is factorized into a task-level planner (short-horizon object and humanoid-root trajectories) and an action generator (closed-loop whole-body motion and contacts). After behavior cloning, the planner is frozen and the action generator is post-tuned using the planner's supervision; training uses geometry-conditioned interaction rewards and relaxed reference tracking near hand-object contact; test-time guidance is supported.
AI.result: In OMOMO evaluation, tracker achieves 64.3% vs 53.2% for an InterMimic reimplementation; unified policy reaches 76.5% on full OMOMO. On held-out split LYRIC yields 90.3% task success vs 74.2% for best matched kinematic-planner baseline. Demonstrates better semantic alignment, motion quality, and zero-shot transfer to novel object shapes; test-time object-waypoint guidance is supported without retraining.
AI.conclusion: LYRIC provides robust, natural contact-rich interaction control driven by language, with a scalable planner–generator architecture that improves task success and generalization while enabling zero-shot transfer; a web page with details is provided.

title: From "Who Is This User?" to "What Does This Purchase Mean?": A Deployed Pipeline for Semantic User Profiling at Bank Scale
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, IEEE International Conference on Data Mining 2026 (ICDM)
summary: Per-user LLM inference on transaction histories binds the inference budget linearly to user count, which becomes prohibitive at applied scale. We re-cast attribute inference from per-user to per-transaction-pattern. The pipeline runs in three phases: Resolve abstracts item names with optional web grounding, Profile infers attributes for each frequent pattern, and Tag clusters free-text attributes into a queryable database. In Profile, a single LLM call per pattern emits predefined categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates. Because inference runs over patterns rather than users, the budget grows with the pattern count rather than the user count. On the public Open e-commerce corpus, the database is statistically indistinguishable from an LLM that reads each user's raw history directly in AUC across the evaluated attributes, and the prevalence estimates carry discriminative signal between positive and negative users. The pipeline is deployed at a major Japanese bank profiling on the order of tens of millions of users, with close to a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in LLM inference targets versus a per-user pipeline. The code is publicly available on https://github.com/CyberAgentAILab/profiling-agent-open-ecommerce.

AI.tldr: Recasts attribute inference from per-user to per-transaction-pattern, enabling scalable profiling with pattern-based LLM inference; achieves similar predictive performance to per-user reading while reducing inference targets by ~1000x; code released.
AI.motivation: Reduce inference cost and privacy risk for large-scale user profiling by aggregating signals at the pattern level rather than per user.
AI.method: Three-phase pipeline: Resolve abstract item names with optional web grounding; Profile: one LLM call per frequent pattern to emit predefined categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates; Tag: cluster free-text attributes into a queryable database; evaluation on Open e-commerce corpus; deployment at a Japanese bank with tens of millions of users; demonstrates effective profiling with orders-of-magnitude fewer LLM calls.
AI.result: Database performance is statistically indistinguishable from an LLM that reads each user's raw history in AUC across evaluated attributes; prevalence estimates carry discriminative signal between positive and negative users; deployment achieved ~3-order-of-magnitude reduction in LLM inference targets compared to per-user pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Pattern-based inference is a viable scalable alternative to per-user inference for attribute profiling, preserving predictive utility while dramatically reducing inference targets; code is publicly available.

title: One Intervention per Component is Enough: Towards Identifiability in Linear Stochastic Dynamics from Steady State
summary: We study the problem of recovering the parameters of a multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process from steady-state observational and interventional data. In many applications, such as large-scale gene perturbation experiments, only stationary "snapshot" measurements are available, making standard stochastic differential equation estimation methods that rely on time-series trajectories inapplicable. We first establish an identifiability result: one intervention per strongly connected component (SCC) of the drift graph suffices to recover all OU process parameters generically up to a global scaling factor. This holds provided that the SCC condensation graph is connected with a single root and certain spectral nondegeneracy assumptions hold. We propose a recursive learning algorithm that orders SCCs topologically and, for each component, isolates its marginal dynamics and solves a linear system derived from the steady-state moment equations, leveraging parameters recovered for upstream components. Building on this theoretical foundation, we propose a regularized least-squares estimator that jointly minimizes residuals of the steady-state mean and covariance equations across observational and interventional data. Experimental results validate our theoretical findings in recovering parameters of the underlying OU process.

AI.tldr: Identifiability of multivariate OU process parameters from steady-state observational and interventional data: one intervention per strongly connected component (SCC) suffices for generic recovery up to a global scale, with a recursive SCC-based learning algorithm and a regularized least-squares estimator; validated experimentally.
AI.motivation: In many applications (e.g., large-scale gene perturbations) only stationary snapshot data are available, making time-series SDE estimation methods inapplicable. The work aims to recover drift/diffusion parameters from steady-state data under interventions.
AI.method: 1) Prove identifiability under conditions: SCC condensation graph is connected with a single root and spectral nondegeneracy; one intervention per SCC suffices for generic recovery up to a global scale. 2) Propose a recursive algorithm that orders SCCs topologically, isolates marginal dynamics for each component, and solves linear systems from steady-state moment equations using previously recovered upstream parameters. 3) Introduce a regularized least-squares estimator that minimizes residuals of steady-state mean and covariance equations across both observational and interventional data.
AI.result: Theoretical identifiability and algorithmic framework are established, and experimental results validate the ability to recover OU process parameters from steady-state observational and interventional data.
AI.conclusion: A principled approach combining identifiability theory, a topological-SCC recursive learning algorithm, and a regularized LS estimator enables parameter recovery for multivariate OU processes from steady-state data, with practical applicability to settings like gene perturbation experiments.

title: An Event Preserving Velocity Invariant Representation for Event Cameras
comment: @inproceedings{ikura2026event, title={An Event Preserving Velocity Invariant Representation for Event Cameras}, author={Ikura, Mikihiro and Gava, Luna and Wu, Jiahang and Glover, Arren and Bartolozzi, Chiara}, year={2026}, booktitle={ECCV 2026 Workshop-Event-Based Multimodal Vision: From Imaging to Perception and Understanding} }
summary: Event cameras provide low-latency, high temporal resolution perception for real-time vision tasks such as robotics.The novel circuitry (i.e. asynchronous, independent pixels) that enables these advantages also introduces new algorithmic challenges. Velocity-invariant representations alleviate missing observations under slow motion and motion blur under fast motion, but most discard temporal information by converting events into image-like representations. We propose Set of Centre Active Receptive Fields (SCARF), a real-time velocity-invariant representation that preserves raw events while consistently handling fast motion, stationary scenes, and independently moving objects. SCARF achieves state-of-the-art performance in both computational efficiency and representation quality.

AI.tldr: Introduce SCARF, a real-time velocity-invariant event representation that preserves raw events and handles fast/slow motion and independent motion, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency and representation quality.
AI.motivation: Address the loss of temporal information in image-like conversions and the challenges of asynchronous, pixel-wise events; need velocity-invariant representations that robustly handle fast motion, stationary scenes, and multiple moving objects.
AI.method: Propose Set of Centre Active Receptive Fields (SCARF), a representation operating on raw events to maintain temporal information and provide velocity invariance; designed for real-time performance.
AI.result: SCARF achieves state-of-the-art performance in both computational efficiency and representation quality on relevant tasks/datasets.
AI.conclusion: SCARF offers a robust, efficient, velocity-invariant event representation that improves real-time perception for event-camera systems, enabling better handling of diverse motion scenarios.

title: UniExo: Unified Multi-Skill Policies for Musculoskeletal Locomotion and Co-Adaptive Exoskeleton Control
summary: Daily locomotion encompasses diverse activities and frequent transitions between them, yet most exoskeleton controllers are designed for a single activity or a narrow set of related movements. Changes in activity therefore typically require explicit mode switching and separately tuned or retrained controllers. Simulation-based learning reduces the need for hardware-based tuning but generally retains this limitation. Here we present UniExo, a framework that first constructs a multi-skill musculoskeletal human policy and then jointly trains an exoskeleton control policy with it. Four single-skill imitation experts for walking, turning, running and backward walking are distilled into a single network structured by a skill latent and subsequently fine-tuned through reinforcement learning on transition sequences. The resultant unified human policy achieves a mean tracking success rate of 94.7% on unseen clips of the four skills and exhibits greater robustness to perturbations than its constituent experts. A single hip exoskeleton controller (UniExo) is initialized from hip moment prediction of the human policy and co-adapted with it through multi-agent reinforcement learning across the four skills. This co-adaptation shifts the timing of the assistance torque and raises the fraction of positive work delivered to the hip. When deployed on a custom hip exoskeleton, the controller generalizes across four treadmill speeds in six participants and assists one participant through a continuous route of all four skills and their transitions, without skill labels or explicit mode switching. UniExo thus provides a step towards replacing activity-specific controllers with unified, user-specific controllers that support diverse locomotor activities and the transitions between them.

AI.tldr: UniExo unifies multi-skill human locomotion control with a hip exoskeleton by distilling four single-skill imitators into a latent-skills network and co-adapting an exoskeleton controller via RL, enabling seamless transitions without explicit mode switching.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation that most exoskeleton controllers target a single activity, requiring explicit mode switching and retraining; enable robust, continuous locomotion across diverse skills and transitions.
AI.method: Distill four single-skill experts (walking, turning, running, backward walking) into a single network parameterized by a skill latent; fine-tune with reinforcement learning on transitions between skills. Initialize the hip exoskeleton controller from the human policy's hip torque predictions and co-adapt with multi-agent RL across the four skills. Validate on a custom hip exoskeleton across unseen speeds and a continuous sequence of all four skills and their transitions, without skill labels.
AI.result: Mean tracking success rate of 94.7% on unseen clips of the four skills; greater robustness to perturbations than individual experts; co-adaptation shifts timing of assistance torque and increases positive hip work; generalizes across treadmill speeds in six participants and with one participant through a continuous route of all four skills and transitions, without mode switching.
AI.conclusion: UniExo demonstrates a path toward replacing activity-specific controllers with unified, user-specific controllers that support diverse locomotor activities and their transitions.

title: Beyond Depth Truncation: Controlled Evaluation of Depth Utilization in Recursive Language Models
summary:
Depth-recurrent language models iteratively apply a small layer stack, decoupling per-token compute from distinct parameter count. To determine whether such a model genuinely utilizes its depth, both recurrence and layer-pruning literatures rely on a shared evaluation: truncating depth at inference time, plotting quality against retained depth fraction, and reading off the slope. While cheap and training-free, this metric suffers from an unexamined flaw: it extracts a single scalar from an intervention that alters multiple model properties simultaneously. Depth truncation concurrently reduces the number of block applications, decreases the volume of distinct computation performed, and pushes the readout head onto an out-of-distribution residual stream. The observed slope conflates all three factors, yet is conventionally interpreted as reflecting solely the second.
  We propose the Depth Control Protocol (DCP), a diagnostic suite that disentangles these three quantities. DCP comprises three positive controls that isolate each factor while varying the others, a negative control applying the identical interventions to dense transformers to ensure the effect is not an artifact of the measurement protocol, and a controlled training intervention to verify causality. The linchpin control, running the full budget of block applications while executing only a single distinct iteration, is strictly realizable only in depth-wise weight-sharing architectures, since in a dense network repeating a layer yields an entirely different model rather than the same model in an alternative configuration.

AI.tldr: Proposes the Depth Control Protocol (DCP) to disentangle depth-related factors in depth-recurrent models from a common depth-truncation metric; introduces three positive controls, a negative control on dense transformers, and a training intervention to establish causality; the linchpin control requires depth-wise weight sharing.
AI.motivation: The usual slope-from-truncation metric conflates multiple changes triggered by reducing depth (fewer block applications, reduced compute, and reading from a shifted residual stream). A single scalar cannot identify which factor drives observed performance changes.
AI.method: Present DCP with three positive controls that isolate each factor while varying others, a negative control applying identical interventions to dense transformers to rule out measurement artifacts, and a controlled training intervention. The crucial linchpin control preserves the full budget of depth-by-depth iterations but runs only a single distinct iteration, achievable only in depth-wise weight-sharing architectures.
AI.result: The abstract articulates a diagnostic protocol (DCP) rather than reporting empirical results; it outlines the method and expected validation steps.
AI.conclusion: DCP offers a principled diagnostic for attributing performance effects to depth usage in depth-recurrent architectures, highlighting the insufficiency of standard depth-truncation slopes and the necessity of depth-wise weight sharing for the linchpin control.

title: Graph-Based Stochastic Power-UCT: Monte-Carlo Graph Search with Power Mean Estimation
summary: Tree-based Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) duplicates the same state when it is reached through different trajectories, which can waste simulations in stochastic MDPs. We introduce Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT), which shares states reached at the same planning depth while keeping separate values for states reached at different depths. This design applies to general stochastic MDPs, including problems with cycles. We prove that for a fixed planning horizon, the root estimate converges to the finite-horizon value at rate $O(n^{-1/2})$, matching tree-based Stochastic-Power-UCT while reusing samples across shared states. We also study two full-state variants: GS-Power-UCT-F, which stores one node per physical state to increase sample sharing but may mix values from different remaining horizons, and GS-Power-UCT-F$^+$, which uses an adaptive horizon to control this bias. The latter converges to $V^{\star}(s_0)$, the optimal infinite-horizon discounted value at the root state $s_0$, when the remaining cross-depth gap vanishes. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show improved sample efficiency over tree-based and graph-based baselines.

AI.tldr: Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT) shares states at the same planning depth in stochastic MDPs to reuse samples, while keeping depth-specific values; two full-state variants (GS-Power-UCT-F and GS-Power-UCT-F+) address horizon mixing; theoretical convergence guarantees; empirical improvements.
AI.motivation: Avoid duplicating a state reached by different trajectories in tree-based MCTS, which wastes simulations, especially in stochastic MDPs with cycles. Leverage graph structure to reuse samples without sacrificing depth-wise value distinctions.
AI.method: Introduce GS-Power-UCT that partitions the search graph by planning depth for shared states, with separate value estimates per depth. Analyze two full-state variants: GS-Power-UCT-F (one node per physical state; increased sample sharing but potential mixing of values from different remaining horizons) and GS-Power-UCT-F+ (adaptive remaining horizon to mitigate bias). Prove root convergence rate O(n^{-1/2}) to finite-horizon value; show F+ converges to V*(s0) as cross-depth gap vanishes. Provide experimental evaluation on stochastic planning benchmarks comparing against tree-based and graph-based baselines.
AI.result: Convergence rate: root estimate to finite-horizon value at O(n^{-1/2}); GS-Power-UCT-F+ converges to infinite-horizon discounted optimum V*(s0) when horizon gap vanishes; empirical results show improved sample efficiency over baselines.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based sharing with depth-aware values offers improved sample efficiency for stochastic planning with cycles; F and F+ provide trade-offs between sample reuse and bias; applicability to general stochastic MDPs; further work could explore larger-scale benchmarks and extensions.

title: QCPruner: Query-Conditioned Population Coverage for Visual Token Pruning
summary: The high visual-token load in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) motivates training-free pruning to reduce later-layer computation, but under a fixed budget, pruning must preserve query-relevant evidence while avoiding redundancy. Existing methods rank tokens, diversify selected subsets, or optimize coverage without using a shared per-visual query utility to weight both visual targets and candidate representatives. We introduce QCPruner, which makes both roles query-conditioned through bilateral utility weighting. Using keyword-matched query anchors, QCPruner fuses two cross-modal cues into utility and applies it to both visual targets and candidate representatives within visual-affinity-based coverage. The resulting nonnegative facility-location objective is monotone and submodular, retains the standard (1-1/e) greedy guarantee, and requires no model training or parameter updates. Across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-Video, and Qwen2.5-VL, QCPruner achieves the highest average relative performance among evaluated complete-system pruning methods at every reported token budget. At 32 of 576 tokens on LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 96.1% of unpruned performance, versus 93.9% for the strongest evaluated baseline. At 256 of 1296 tokens on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the corresponding values are 96.7% and 92.5%.

AI.tldr: QCPruner introduces a training-free pruning method for multimodal LLMs that uses query-conditioned bilateral utility weighting to select visual targets and representatives under a fixed token budget, framed as a nonnegative facility-location objective with monotone, submodular properties and a 1-1/e greedy guarantee.
AI.motivation: High visual-token loads in multimodal LLMs raise the need for efficient, training-free pruning. Existing methods lack a shared per-visual query utility to weight both targets and candidates, risking loss of query-relevant evidence or redundancy under a budget.
AI.method: QCPruner uses keyword-matched query anchors to fuse cross-modal cues into a unified utility. It applies this utility to both visual targets and candidate representatives within a visual-affinity-based coverage, resulting in a nonnegative facility-location objective that is monotone and submodular. The method is greedy with a (1-1/e) guarantee and requires no model training or parameter updates.
AI.result: Across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-Video, and Qwen2.5-VL, QCPruner achieves the highest average relative performance among evaluated complete-system pruning methods at every token-budget. For example, at 32/576 tokens on LLaVA-1.5-7B it retains 96.1% of unpruned performance vs 93.9% for the strongest baseline; at 256/1296 tokens on Qwen2.5-VL-7B it retains 96.7% vs 92.5%.
AI.conclusion: QCPruner is a training-free, provably effective pruning framework for MLLMs that improves token-budget efficiency by jointly weighting visual targets and candidate representations with a query-conditioned utility, and it demonstrates strong empirical gains across multiple models.

title: Decoupling Physical Speed from Path Parameterization in Singularity-Free Guiding Vector Fields
summary: The existing singularity-free guiding vector field (SF-GVF) with an additional virtual coordinate can eliminate singular points (i.e., points where the vector field vanishes) inherent in conventional GVFs and guarantee global convergence of robot trajectories to closed and self-intersecting desired paths. However, the desired speed given by the GVF along the desired path in the original lower-dimensional space cannot be arbitrarily specified but depends on path parameterizations. One possible workaround is to partially normalize the physical projection of the SF-GVF and assign a user-designed speed. However, we show that this workaround may introduce new singularities since the normalization denominator can become zero. To address this issue, we propose a new SF-GVF with prescribed physical speed (PPS). The integral curves of the new SF-GVF converge exponentially to the desired path from any initial condition in the higher-dimensional space (including virtual dimension); more importantly, the robot's physical speed converges to the PPS, while the path-error dynamics remain invariant under regular reparameterizations of the desired path. We further develop a saturated acceleration control law for second-order kinematic models.
