Finally, comparative simulations and 3D path-following experiments with a quadrotor under different PPS profiles validate the theoretical results and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: Introduces a SF-GVF with prescribed physical speed (PPS) that guarantees exponential convergence to the desired path in augmented space, with the robot’s physical speed converging to PPS and path-error dynamics invariant to path reparameterization; includes a saturated acceleration control for second-order models and validation via simulations and quadrotor experiments.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of previous singularity-free GVFs where the along-path speed in the original space cannot be arbitrarily prescribed and can depend on path parameterization, and where partial normalization to impose speed risks introducing new singularities.
AI.method: Develop a new SF-GVF with PPS in an augmented (including virtual) space. Prove exponential convergence of integral curves to the desired path, prove that the physical speed converges to the prescribed speed, and show invariance of path-error dynamics under regular path reparameterizations. Propose a saturated acceleration control law for second-order kinematics. Validate via comparative simulations and 3D path-following experiments with a quadrotor under various PPS profiles.
AI.result: Theoretical guarantees of exponential convergence to the path; convergence of physical speed to the prescribed speed; invariant path-error dynamics; a practical saturated acceleration control; empirical validation through simulations and 3D quadrotor experiments supporting effectiveness of PPS approach.
AI.conclusion: The PPS-based SF-GVF resolves speed-specification limitations while ensuring robust convergence and avoiding new singularities, with demonstrated effectiveness in simulated and real quadrotor path-following scenarios.

title: MaSCoD: A Multi-Agent Framework for Structural-Context-Guided Candidate Causal Graph Generation
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been applied to causal discovery, but candidate-graph generation rarely treats premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations as an explicit design objective. We propose MaSCoD, a multi-agent framework that organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment. We evaluate MaSCoD on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs using GPT-5.4 as the primary backbone and GPT-4o for replication. MaSCoD exhibits a dataset- and backbone-dependent retention-selectivity profile rather than uniform superiority. Across all six dataset-backbone settings, Full, which supplies structural hypotheses before direct-edge judgment, achieved higher mean Recall and F1 than No Phase 1, which instead constructs them within the judgment procedure, while also increasing false-positive rates. Additional reference-edge retention over all evaluated baselines was observed on DWD with GPT-5.4 and on Sachs with GPT-4o, rather than uniformly across settings. Partial ablations showed that supplying both information components did not always outperform supplying only one. For GPT-5.4, stage-wise analysis showed that the Full-No Phase 1 retention gap was already present after direct-edge judgment, while reconciliation introduced additional reference-edge loss for Full on Sachs. These findings support structural pre-organization as an explicit design and evaluation target for omission control and motivate evaluating context construction jointly with its utilization in judgment.

AI.tldr: MaSCoD is a multi-agent framework for causal discovery that emphasizes pre-organizing structural hypotheses to mitigate premature ommission of relevant causal relations; its effectiveness varies by dataset and backbone, with Full-phase pre-organization generally improving recall and F1 but at the cost of more false positives; results highlight the value of explicit omission-control and joint evaluation of context construction and its use in judgment.
AI.motivation: To address premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations in causal discovery by explicitly designing a pre-organization step that structures candidate variables and local patterns before edge judgment.
AI.method: MaSCoD employs a multi-agent setup that convenes candidate third variables and local structural motifs prior to direct-edge judgment. Evaluation is performed on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs datasets using GPT-5.4 as the primary backbone and GPT-4o for replication, comparing Full (with structural hypotheses supplied) vs No Phase 1 (constructed during judgment).
AI.result: Across six dataset–backbone settings, Full improved mean Recall and F1 relative to No Phase 1 but increased false positives. Additional reference-edge retention appeared on DWD with GPT-5.4 and on Sachs with GPT-4o. Partial ablations showed mixed gains; stage-wise analysis indicated retention gaps arising after direct-edge judgment, and reconciliation added reference-edge loss on Sachs with GPT-5.4. Overall, results support structural pre-organization as a target for omission control and suggest evaluating context construction jointly with its use in judgment.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that explicit pre-organization of structural hypotheses can enhance edge-judgment performance in certain settings, but benefits are not uniform across datasets/backbones; it advocates treating context construction and its application as a coupled design objective.

title: CellRFT: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling
summary: Predicting cellular responses to perturbations supports the study of gene function, disease mechanisms, and therapeutic strategies. Despite advances in single-cell perturbation modeling, existing models typically optimize surrogate losses that do not directly reflect the biological criteria used for evaluation, so better data fitting need not yield better biological predictions. To address this mismatch, we introduce \textbf{CellRFT}, a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that uses biological evaluation as direct training feedback. CellRFT uses policy-gradient optimization to learn from non-differentiable evaluations of generated cell populations and integrates multiple biological rewards through hierarchical reward aggregation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate CellRFT's applicability across different pretrained models and effectiveness in improving perturbation prediction, reveal that optimizing one biological criterion can help or hinder others, and show that complementary rewards can improve criteria beyond those directly optimized, offering a way to probe how biological metrics shape model behavior, with the potential to inform evaluation design. Code will be made available.

AI.tldr: A reinforcement fine-tuning framework (CellRFT) that aligns perturbation prediction models with biological evaluation using policy-gradient and hierarchical rewards; addresses mismatch between surrogate losses and biological criteria; shows improved performance and insight into metric interaction; code coming.
AI.motivation: Surrogate loss optimization in single-cell perturbation models does not guarantee biologically accurate predictions; need training signals that reflect evaluation criteria.
AI.method: Policy-gradient reinforcement learning; non-differentiable biological evaluations used as rewards; hierarchical reward aggregation to combine multiple biological criteria; applicable across pretrained models.
AI.result: Improved perturbation prediction across models; reveals that optimizing one criterion can help or hurt others; complementary rewards can improve criteria beyond those optimized; demonstrates potential to study metric influence and inform evaluation design.
AI.conclusion: CellRFT provides direct alignment between training objective and biological evaluation, enabling better biological predictions and a framework to study how metrics shape model behavior; code will be released.

title: AVTrace: Diagnosing Audio-Visual Temporal Reasoning in Omni Models
summary: Omni models can describe video content, but can they locate events in time, preserve event order, and judge audio-visual synchronization? We introduce AVTrace (Audio-Visual Temporal Reasoning Assessment and Capability Evaluation), a silver-standard diagnostic suite spanning onset and span grounding, synchronization, next-step prediction, cross-modal localization, chain parsing, and event-conditioned comprehension. It contains 34,114 training examples and category-balanced development and test splits of 3,500 and 7,000 examples. We evaluate five open omni models under their respective input configurations using reference-blind response normalization followed by deterministic scoring. All five off-the-shelf systems score below the test split's majority-label baseline of 0.556 on synchronization verification, and obtain low scores on chain parsing and event-conditioned grounding and comprehension. Development-set perturbations reveal task-dependent sensitivity in Qwen3-Omni-30B to modality removal and changes in visual input processing, without isolating their underlying causes. Parameter-efficient temporal post-training improves Gemma4-E4B-it on several benchmark metrics. On three external image benchmarks, task metrics change modestly, including some degradations, while teacher-forcing perplexity decreases. Together, these findings show that semantic reference-text overlap should not be treated as a proxy for temporal localization, and that AVTrace can identify task-specific weaknesses while providing a testbed for temporal post-training.

AI.tldr: AVTrace is a silver-standard diagnostic suite to probe temporal reasoning in video-language Omni models; it reveals limited temporal understanding, and supports targeted temporal post-training.
AI.motivation: Current omni models often rely on semantic overlap rather than temporal localization; AVTrace provides a broad, labeled benchmark across tasks to diagnose and guide improvements in temporal reasoning.
AI.method: AVTrace comprises 34,114 training examples with dev/test splits of 3,500 and 7,000. Tasks span onset/span grounding, synchronization verification, next-step prediction, cross-modal localization, chain parsing, and event-conditioned comprehension. Evaluations use reference-blind response normalization and deterministic scoring across five open omni models under their input configurations. Includes development-set perturbations to study modality/visual input effects; explores parameter-efficient temporal post-training; assesses transfer to external image benchmarks.
AI.result: All five models score below the 0.556 majority-baseline on synchronization; low performance on chain parsing and event-grounding/comprehension. Development-set perturbations reveal task-dependent sensitivity (e.g., Qwen3-Omni-30B to modality removal). Temporal post-training improves Gemma4-E4B-it on several metrics. External image benchmarks show modest metric changes with some degradations; perplexity decreases due to teacher-forcing. Overall, semantic reference-text overlap is not a reliable proxy for temporal localization; AVTrace identifies task-specific weaknesses and enables testing of temporal post-training.
AI.conclusion: AVTrace provides a robust framework to evaluate and diagnose temporal reasoning in omni models, highlighting significant gaps in timing and sequence understanding while offering a path to targeted improvements via temporal post-training and cross-task analyses.

title: Equivariant Filter Design for Acoustic and Depth Aided Inertial Navigation Systems
summary: Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) navigating without GPS typically fuse inertial measurements with acoustic Doppler Velocity Log (DVL) velocities and pressure-derived depth. Posing the navigation state on a Lie group improves accuracy and consistency. However, state-of-the-art filters based on the Invariant Extended Kalman Filter (IEKF) append the Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) biases as a Euclidean extension, which breaks the group-affine structure required for exact log-linear error dynamics, causing the reported covariance to degrade alongside the estimate. We apply the Tangent-Group (TG) symmetry, which carries the biases within the geometry of the state space, to derive an Equivariant Filter (EqF) for this system, leaving zero linearization error in the navigation states and second-order error only in the biases. We develop an equivariant output model for the DVL, whose update incurs only third-order linearization error, together with a direct pressure output. Monte Carlo simulations benchmark the TG-EqF against a Two-Frame-Group IEKF and a Multiplicative EKF. The TG-EqF reduces error by 18--25\% against both alternatives in each of attitude, velocity, and position. The main benefit is in the covariance it estimates: its Average Normalized Estimation Error Squared (ANEES) stays closer to its nominal value of one than that of the others. Offline analysis on AUV field data corroborates the findings of the simulations, demonstrating reduced position drift.

AI.tldr: Paper introduces TG-EqF for AUV navigation on Lie groups, incorporating biases into state geometry to achieve exact log-linear error dynamics for nav states and reduced linearization error for biases; shows 18–25% accuracy gains and better covariance (ANEES ~1) vs IEKF variants; validated by Monte Carlo and field data.
AI.motivation: Improve consistency and accuracy of AUV navigation without GPS by preserving group structure in state estimation and avoiding bias augmentation that breaks log-linear error dynamics.
AI.method: Develop Tangent-Group Equivariant Filter (TG-EqF) on Lie group state; incorporate IMU biases into geometry; design equivariant DVL output with third-order linearization error; include direct pressure measurement; Monte Carlo benchmarking against Two-Frame-Group IEKF and Multiplicative EKF; field data validation.
AI.result: Attained 18–25% reductions in attitude, velocity, and position errors; ANEES closer to nominal value 1 for TG-EqF; field data shows reduced position drift.
AI.conclusion: TG-EqF yields improved accuracy and covariance consistency for AUV navigation; exploiting symmetry reduces linearization error; results suggest applicability to real-world AUVs and possible extensions to other Lie-group-based navigators.

title: Not All AI Agents Are Equal: Characterizing Resource and Performance Dynamics
summary: LLM-based AI agents process user requests through iterative reasoning and tool execution, often involving the invocation of remote LLM APIs with local tool containers. This execution model can make the optimization of agent serving difficult because latency, local resource demand, and container bottlenecks inter-mix across requests. However, the current agent ecosystem runs without much consideration of resource dynamics, which results in significant waste of the precious resources. This paper analyzes the resource inter-mix of AI agents for three representative tasks: retrieval-augmented question answering, web search, and software coding. To this end, we characterize the latency with respect to the resource dynamics of processing multiple requests and tasks concurrently. Our measurements show that agents have a wide range of behaviors depending on tasks, so that even the same tool can differ substantially in resource dynamics. We also find that running multiple requests concurrently exposes task-dependent bottlenecks in resource dynamics such as CPU, disk I/O, and memory. Furthermore, we uncover that faster LLM responses or more CPU cores do not always accelerate agents. Based on these observations, we demonstrate new optimization opportunities that exploit the resource dynamics of tasks: CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation. Our results show that the latency of CPU-sensitive agent tasks improves $\sim$5.4$\times$, and the average latency across multiple tasks is reduced $\sim$32% compared to native agents.

AI.tldr: Empirical study of resource inter-mix in LLM-based agents across three representative tasks, revealing task-dependent resource bottlenecks and that simply faster LLMs or more CPU do not always help; proposes CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation, achieving substantial latency improvements.
AI.motivation: Current agent ecosystems undervalue resource dynamics, leading to wasted compute and latency. Understanding how CPU, I/O, and memory interact with multi-request, multi-tool agent workflows can enable smarter scheduling and allocation.
AI.method: Empirical measurement of latency and resource usage under concurrent requests for three tasks: retrieval-augmented question answering, web search, and software coding. Analyze variations across tasks and tools, identify bottlenecks, and evaluate CPU-aware admission and task-aware allocation against native agents.
AI.result: Agents exhibit wide, task-dependent resource dynamics; concurrency reveals CPU, disk I/O, and memory bottlenecks not uniform across tasks; increasing CPU or faster LLMs does not universally speed up agents; CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation reduce CPU-sensitive task latency by ~5.4x and lower average latency across tasks by ~32% compared with native agents.
AI.conclusion: Resource dynamics critically influence AI agent performance; targeted, task-aware scheduling can yield substantial latency reductions and better resource utilization; future work should integrate such policies into agent orchestration to maximize efficiency.

title: Past, Future, All at Once: Mitigating Stability-Plasticity Dilemma via Post-hoc JANUS Rectification
summary: Fine-tuning foundation models on new tasks inevitably suffer from catastrophic forgetting. While existing works attempt to mitigate this on the basis of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, they adopted an overly restrictive Subspace Orthogonality condition. In this paper, we introduce a purely post-hoc and tuning-agnostic weight rectification framework that achieves Parameter Space Orthogonality, which is the necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical performance to the first order. By projecting parameter updates into the JAcobian NUll Space (JANUS), our method significantly recovers compromised historical knowledge without interfering with the underlying fine-tuning process. To overcome the local validity of the Jacobian approximation, we further propose a Multi-step Adaptive Rectification mechanism that utilizes the JANUS shift to dynamically verify the valid trust region and adjust step sizes. Coupled with our proposed ghost projection, ghost orientation comparison, and sequence-level singular value decomposition compression techniques, JANUS also achieves great temporal and spatial efficiency. Experiments demonstrate that JANUS seamlessly integrates with various fine-tuning methods, significantly mitigating the stability-plasticity dilemma by recovering historical knowledge while preserving downstream task adaptation.

AI.tldr: JANUS is a post-hoc weight-rectification framework that achieves Parameter Space Orthogonality by projecting updates into the Jacobian Null Space, enabling recovery of historical knowledge during fine-tuning while preserving downstream adaptation; it includes Adaptive Rectification, ghost projection/orientation, and SVD compression for efficiency, and integrates with various fine-tuning methods.
AI.motivation: Catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning and restrictive Subspace Orthogonality assumptions in existing parameter-efficient methods; a tuning-agnostic, post-hoc mechanism is needed to preserve historical knowledge.
AI.method: Post-hoc weight rectification projecting updates into the Jacobian Null Space (JANUS). Multi-step Adaptive Rectification using JANUS shift to verify trust region and adapt step sizes. Ghost projection, ghost orientation comparison, and sequence-level SVD compression for efficiency. Compatibility with different fine-tuning methods.
AI.result: Experiments indicate JANUS significantly mitigates the stability-plasticity dilemma by preserving historical knowledge while allowing effective adaptation to new tasks; demonstrates good temporal and spatial efficiency and compatibility with multiple fine-tuning methods.
AI.conclusion: Parameter Space Orthogonality is the necessary and sufficient condition to preserve historical performance to the first order; JANUS provides a practical, tuning-agnostic framework to achieve this, with efficient mechanisms and broad applicability.

title: GRF-Recon: Global Ray-Field Optimization for Long-Sequence Feed-forward Reconstruction
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026 as a Spotlight presentation
summary: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction provides an efficient paradigm for scene modeling from image sequences. Scaling these models to large monocular scenarios are constrained by excessive GPU memory footprint, degraded local geometry, and long-term trajectory drift. Existing chunk-based optimization strategies provide limited geometric constraints and fail to maintain global consistency over extended trajectories. We present a unified framework for stable and scalable feed-forward 3D reconstruction from long monocular sequences. Our approach builds on coarse-to-fine trajectory alignment augmented by lightweight geometric prior injection. Distilling monocular geometric cues into the feed-forward backbone via LoRA adaptation improves depth accuracy on fine structures while preserving inference efficiency. We introduce a hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization that leverages high-frequency geometric features to guide local point-cloud refinement and enforce consistent inter-frame ray constraints. Unlike prior chunk-based methods, this establishes strong cross-frame geometric coupling while maintaining scalability. Finally, an efficient trajectory stitching strategy with joint ray-error optimization explicitly reduces accumulated drift. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves competitive trajectory accuracy compared with representative SLAM systems, while maintaining globally consistent 3D reconstruction in large-scale scenarios.

AI.tldr: A unified, scalable feed-forward framework for long monocular sequences that achieves globally consistent 3D reconstructions by integrating coarse-to-fine trajectory alignment, LoRA-based monocular cue distillation, a hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization, and joint ray-error trajectory stitching.
AI.motivation: Over long monocular sequences, 3D reconstruction struggles with high GPU memory, degraded local geometry, and accumulated drift. Chunk-based methods offer limited global constraints and poor long-term consistency.
AI.method: 1) Coarse-to-fine trajectory alignment with lightweight geometric priors. 2) Distilling monocular geometric cues into the feed-forward backbone via LoRA adaptation to improve fine-structure depth without sacrificing speed. 3) Hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization leveraging high-frequency geometry to guide local point-cloud refinement and enforce inter-frame ray constraints. 4) Efficient trajectory stitching with joint ray-error optimization to reduce drift.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show competitive trajectory accuracy against representative SLAM systems and globally consistent 3D reconstructions in large-scale scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables stable, scalable feed-forward 3D reconstruction for long monocular sequences by enforcing cross-frame geometric coupling and reducing drift, without sacrificing inference efficiency.

title: LIFD: Anchored Diffusion for 3D-Aware Scene Memory in Robotic Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation under partial observability requires spatial information that extends beyond the current view. Geometry-aware RGB features describe visible structure, but previously observed regions may disappear as the robot or scene moves. Maintaining a useful scene representation therefore requires retaining observation history while inferring missing content without losing its connection to visible evidence. We introduce LIFD (Look, Imagine, Focus, and Do), a framework for persistent, 3D-aware scene memory. LIFD learns a scene-token representation from multi-view agreement and completes it from a single RGB view and recurrent memory. A rectified-flow model generates the tokens while Anchor-Guided Cross-Attention conditions completion on current geometric features. Compact slot features connect this representation to a manipulation policy. Multi-view and geometric supervision are used during representation learning; deployment requires one RGB camera, proprioception, and a task instruction. LIFD (Staged) reaches 91.6% average success on LIBERO and 79.8% on MetaWorld, improving LIBERO average success by 3.1 percentage points over Joint training. On four UR5e task families with ten demonstrations per family, it achieves 56.0% mean success, compared with 40.5% for OpenVLA-7B.

AI.tldr: LIFD is a 3D-aware, persistent scene-memory framework for robotic manipulation under partial observability, using multi-view-derived tokens completed from a single RGB view with a rectified-flow generator and anchor-guided cross-attention, linked to a manipulation policy.
AI.motivation: Robots operating with partial views need memories of previously observed geometry to act robustly; geometry-aware features alone fail when observed regions disappear, so a persistent, test-time-complete scene representation is required.
AI.method: Introduce LIFD (Look, Imagine, Focus, and Do). Learn a scene-token representation from multi-view agreement and complete it from a single RGB view using recurrent memory. A rectified-flow model generates tokens; Anchor-Guided Cross-Attention conditions completion on current geometric features. Slot features connect to a manipulation policy. Train with multi-view and geometric supervision; deployment uses one RGB camera, proprioception, and a task instruction.
AI.result: LIFD (Staged) achieves 91.6% average success on LIBERO and 79.8% on MetaWorld (3.1-point improvement over Joint training) and 56.0% mean success on four UR5e task families (ten demonstrations each) versus 40.5% for OpenVLA-7B.
AI.conclusion: LIFD demonstrates a viable approach to persistent 3D-aware scene memory for manipulation under partial observability, outperforming baselines and enabling robust policy execution from minimal perceptual input.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Agentic AI for Networked Low-Altitude UAVs
comment: Agentic AI, neuro-symbolic AI, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), autonomous decision-making, networked UAV systems
summary: Networked low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) need reliable and adaptive decision-making capabilities to operate under uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity, while many existing agentic systems remain limited by hallucination risks, data dependence, and weak generalization. This article investigates neuro-symbolic agentic AI (NSAAI) as a framework for combining neural grounding, symbolic reasoning, and closed-loop agentic interaction to support more reliable and adaptive UAV autonomy. We first examine its capability foundations in data efficiency, compositional generalization, continual learning, and zero-shot transfer, and then develop a reference architecture integrating task and goal management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification and metacognition, skill execution and network interaction, and shared knowledge and memory. An urban fire-inspection case implemented in LAESim illustrates how a UAV can coordinate sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity, reuse a verified image-delivery skill, and satisfy explicit evidence conditions before completing the mission. The results illustrate the potential of NSAAI to support reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution in networked UAV systems. We further discuss key research directions in uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge and skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation.

AI.tldr: NSAAI combines neural grounding with symbolic reasoning to improve reliability and adaptability of networked UAV autonomy under uncertainty and intermittent connectivity.
AI.motivation: Address unreliable perception, hallucination, data dependence, and poor generalization in UAV autonomy by integrating neural and symbolic components with closed-loop agentic control.
AI.method: Proposes a reference NSAAI architecture with task/goal management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification and metacognition, skill execution/network interaction, and shared memory; analyzes capability foundations (data efficiency, compositional generalization, continual learning, zero-shot transfer) and demonstrates with an urban fire-inspection case in LAESim.
AI.result: Demonstrates potential for reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution in networked UAVs; shows coordination of sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity and reuse of a verified image-delivery skill, with explicit evidence conditions.
AI.conclusion: NSAAI is a promising framework for robust UAV autonomy with reusable skills and grounded decision-making; future work highlighted includes uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge/skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation.

title: EPIG-Tree: Compute-Optimal Branching for Gradient-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reward-based reinforcement learning for language models, exemplified by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), collapses an entire stochastic trajectory into a single scalar reward. This is clean and scalable, but it explores and allocates reward inefficiently: a trajectory may contain many causal decisions, recovery attempts, and environment-randomness events, yet every token or action inherits one trajectory-level advantage. We study tree-based rollout construction as a compute-allocation problem for policy-gradient estimation. Our central claim is that branches should be placed not where the policy is merely uncertain, but where an additional branch most reduces uncertainty about the policy gradient per unit of compute. From a law-of-total-variance decomposition of the local policy-gradient random variable, we derive two allocation laws: new branches reduce decision uncertainty, while repeated suffix rollouts reduce continuation uncertainty. The resulting EPIG-Tree score allocates branches using the already computed rollouts. It estimates occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty, along with a suffix law $n_e \propto w_e \|\nabla_θ\log π(a_e|h_e)\| σ_e / \sqrt{c_e}$. Empirically, EPIG reduces gradient MSE in cloned-state control, winning in all nine dense continuous-control environments of a 13-environment sweep and recovering the reference gradient direction near-perfectly, and it improves frozen-LLM gradient calibration relative to entropy branching. In online single-turn math, tree-local credit beats flat GRPO, while branch placement is secondary to token-level credit assignment. In online multi-turn Wordle, EPIG attains the highest final win rate (0.850), overtaking flat GRPO, which saturates early at 0.790, and entropy branching as training proceeds, confirming that the gradient-estimation advantage transfers to a stateful, large-action setting.

AI.tldr: EPIG-Tree provides a principled, compute-aware tree-based rollout strategy for policy-gradient estimation in language-model RL, deriving two variance-based branch-allocation laws and showing improved gradient accuracy and task performance over GRPO and entropy branching across dense control tasks and stateful, large-action settings like Wordle.
AI.motivation: Address reward-trajectory inefficiency in reward-based LMs training (e.g., GRPO) by allocating compute to rollout branches that maximally reduce gradient uncertainty per unit compute, rather than simply where policy is uncertain.
AI.method: From the law of total variance of the local policy-gradient, derive two allocation laws: (1) add branches where decision uncertainty dominates; (2) reuse suffix rollouts to reduce continuation uncertainty. Propose EPIG-Tree scoring using occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty with an allocation rule n_e ∝ w_e ||∇_θ log π(a_e|h_e)|| σ_e / √c_e. Use previously computed rollouts to place branches. Empirically evaluate on cloned-state control, online single-turn math, and online multi-turn Wordle.
AI.result: EPIG reduces gradient MSE in dense continuous-control environments (9/13 in a sweep) and recovers near-perfect reference gradient direction; improves frozen-LLM gradient calibration vs entropy branching; in online single-turn math, tree-local credit beats flat GRPO; in online Wordle, EPIG achieves final win rate 0.850 vs 0.790 for GRPO and outperforms entropy branching as training continues.
AI.conclusion: A principled, compute-aware tree-branching scheme (EPIG-Tree) improves gradient estimation and downstream performance in both offline control and online, stateful, large-action settings, outperforming GRPO and entropy-based branching strategies.

title: Astronex-World 1.0: Real-Time Interactive World Model Foundation
comment: Technical report. 25 pages, 13 figures, 10 tables. Project page: https://world.astronex.com.cn ; Code: https://github.com/Astronex-Robotics/Astronex-World ; Weights: https://huggingface.co/Astronex-Lab/Astronex-World
summary: We present Astronex-World 1.0, an open controllable video world-model foundation. Given a text prompt (text-to-video) or an initial observation (image-to-video), the model predicts future visual states under frame-aligned camera trajectories, continuous actions, and an embodiment identifier, and accepts text events inserted at a specified position of a rollout. The family provides a bidirectional model for full-context generation and a causal model with block-causal attention and cross-block KV caching for persistent generation, both built on the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B prior. PRoPE injects camera intrinsics and extrinsics, while a 64-dimensional action stream modulates every Transformer layer. A five-stage training path develops bidirectional camera and action control, converts the backbone to block-causal generation, distills a few-step student, restores mixed-domain dynamics, and applies asymmetric DMD/DMD2 distribution matching. The causal model generates 832x480 video at 24 fps. All five training stages run on two NVIDIA L20 48 GB GPUs, and the causal model streams in real time on one. It scores 73.5 on WBench Navi and 70.0 on WBench Full. On Full, this 5B model is above the 13.6B LongCat-Video and the 14B Helios, within one point of the 22B LTX-2.3, and above YUME 1.5, which is post-trained from the same 5B prior on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The reserved action input and output interfaces allow post-training for embodied intelligence and autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: Astronex-World 1.0 is a bi-directional and causal open, controllable video world-model foundation for text/image-to-video tasks, built on a 5B prior, with real-time streaming, embodied interfaces, and competitive benchmarking.
AI.motivation: Fill the need for open, controllable, text-/observation-driven video world models that support embodied control, real-time generation, and post-training adaptation for tasks like autonomous driving.
AI.method: Two models (bidirectional full-context and block-causal) built on the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B prior; PRoPE injects camera intrinsics/extrinsics; a 64-dimensional action stream modulates every Transformer layer; supports text events during rollouts; five-stage training: bidirectional camera/action control, convert backbone to block-causal, distill a few-step student, restore mixed-domain dynamics, asymmetric DMD/DMD2 distribution matching; causal model outputs 832x480 at 24 fps; two NVIDIA L20 48 GB GPUs used for training, causal model streams in real time on one; cross-block KV caching for persistent generation.
AI.result: Delivers 832x480 @24fps video from a 5B prior with real-time streaming; scores 73.5 on WBench Navi and 70.0 on WBench Full; on Full it is competitive with larger models (above LongCat-Video 13.6B and Helios 14B, within ~1 point of LTX-2.3 22B) and surpasses YUME 1.5; includes reserved action I/O interfaces enabling post-training embodied intelligence and autonomous driving tasks.
AI.conclusion: Provides a practical, open foundation for controllable video world modeling with explicit embodied interfaces, enabling post-training adaptation for embodied AI and autonomous driving, with efficient multi-stage training and real-time inference on commodity GPUs.

title: Affective Shared Autonomy: Temporal Affect Dynamics and Subjective Evaluation in Bimanual Teleoperation Tasks
summary: Physical teleoperation integrates human cognitive flexibility with robotic precision, yet demanding manipulation tasks frequently induce severe cognitive workload, acute frustration, and execution breakdown. Conventional shared autonomy paradigms rely primarily on task-based rules, such as spatial error boundaries, which disregard the operator's transient affective state and risk misaligned control interventions. To address this limitation, we propose an affect-aware shared autonomy teleoperation framework that dynamically modulates robotic assistance based on real-time operator state estimation. The system estimates operator affective states from synchronized facial video, cardiac signals, and bilateral arm kinematics, outputting a seven-state affective distribution and a three-category operational abstraction (neutral, productive, adverse). Affect-aware assistance is selectively triggered when the user is detected in a continuous adverse state, preserving task-positive engagement without unnecessary disruption. The empirical user study ($N = 30$) confirms that the proposed affective assistance increases the productive states by up to 39.7% without compromising user agency. The collected dataset represents the first multimodal dataset that provides continuous visual, physiological, and operator's bilateral motion tracking of temporal affective state shifts during bimanual teleoperation. Our multimodal fusion model outperforms zero-shot baselines (Qwen, MiniCPM-V) in tracking temporal state dynamics. This real-world deployment offers a new human-centric framework that integrates visual, physiological, and motion tracking for physical human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: An affect-aware shared autonomy framework for teleoperation uses multimodal signals to estimate operator affect and trigger assistance, improving productive states and preserving agency; introduces a first multimodal dataset and outperforms zero-shot baselines.
AI.motivation: Conventional task-based shared autonomy neglects operator affect; high cognitive workload and frustration hinder performance; need dynamic, operator-state-aware assistance.
AI.method: Real-time affect estimation from synchronized facial video, ECG/PPG heart signals, and bilateral arm kinematics; outputs a seven-state affective distribution and a three-category state (neutral, productive, adverse); adaptively triggers assistance when adverse; collects multimodal dataset; compares a fusion model against zero-shot baselines (Qwen, MiniCPM-V).
AI.result: Productive states increased by up to 39.7% (N=30) without reducing user agency; first multimodal dataset for continuous temporal affective state shifts during bimanual teleoperation; fusion model outperforms zero-shot baselines.
AI.conclusion: Presents a human-centric framework integrating vision, physiology, and motion for physical HRI; demonstrates feasibility of affect-aware shared autonomy and provides a dataset for future research.

title: Customizable and Jointly Optimized Route Planning: A Deep Architecture Enabling Differentiable Shortest-Path Search
summary: With the widespread use of online navigation and ride-hailing services, achieving optimal route planning for diverse user preferences has recently attracted increasing attention. Classic graph algorithms for pathfinding use heuristic cost functions to define edge weight, thus providing no optimality guarantee of route quality. Prior data-driven approaches equating ground truth of the optimal route with user trajectory, which is however moderately influenced by the navigation service, suffers from the feedback loop problem. To address these issues, we propose a deep architecture that is able to jointly optimize cost functions and route-ranking model towards any route preference. First, we run a multi-objective Dijkstra algorithm offline to collect the set of Pareto optimal routes, deeming it as the complete candidate set. Exploiting the property of such a set, we design a neural network structure that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in an end-to-end differentiable manner. Second, we define route preference as a task of constrained optimization of route attributes, and propose a novel loss function that optimizes a single-objective variable, with other variables strictly under constraints. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The results show that our architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in route quality and customizability.

AI.tldr: End-to-end differentiable routing framework that jointly optimizes edge costs and route ranking by first collecting a Pareto-optimal set of routes with offline multi-objective Dijkstra, then using a neural network to emulate shortest-path search and ranking under a constrained optimization loss.
AI.motivation: Tackle the lack of optimality guarantees in heuristic edge costs and the feedback loop in data-driven routing by combining a complete candidate set with differentiable ranking.
AI.method: Offline phase: run multi-objective Dijkstra to obtain the Pareto frontier of routes as a complete candidate set. Model phase: design a neural network that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in an end-to-end differentiable way, constrained optimization of route attributes where a single objective is optimized under constraints for others.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world datasets show the proposed architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in route quality and customization.
AI.conclusion: The approach is promising, offering improved route quality and user-specific customization, with potential scalability considerations and reliance on the completeness of the Pareto set; further analysis on robustness and generalization would be valuable.

title: Dynamic Generalized Gromov-Wasserstein Optimal Transport
summary: Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT) extends classical optimal transport by introducing structure-aware transport cost. This is particularly relevant for spatial transcriptomics, where dynamical reconstruction should preserve tissue structure in addition to matching expression patterns. While static formulations have been widely used for such structure-aware alignment, a general dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories is still missing. We introduce Travelling Pair Dynamical Alignment and Trajectory Estimation (TP-DATE), a theoretical and computational framework to generalize GW-OT dynamically in a simulation-free manner. We formulate a broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) through path actions and prove the static dynamic equivalence. We further develop travelling-pair flow matching, which allows interacting conditional paths and marginalizes their interactions into a single vector field. On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction.

AI.tldr: TP-DATE extends GW-OT to dynamic trajectories via Travelling Pair Dynamical Alignment and Trajectory Estimation; introduces travelling-pair flow matching and static/dynamic QOT; demonstrates improved structure preservation and 3D trajectory reconstruction in spatial transcriptomics.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of a general, simulation-free dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories that preserve tissue structure, beyond static structure-aware GW-OT alignments in spatial transcriptomics.
AI.method: Define Travelling Pair Dynamical Alignment and Trajectory Estimation (TP-DATE). Formulate a broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) using path actions; prove static–dynamic equivalence; develop travelling-pair flow matching to allow interacting conditional paths and marginalize their interactions into a single vector field.
AI.result: Empirically, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction on synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data.
AI.conclusion: TP-DATE provides a general, simulation-free framework to extend GW-OT to dynamic trajectory reconstruction, enabling structure-aware dynamic alignment in spatial omics and related domains.

title: A Free Lunch? Adapting PP-OCRv6 for Historical Text Recognition
summary: Despite impressive reported scores, large vision-language models have seen limited practical uptake in historical automatic text recognition because of their computational cost, dependence on large-scale pretraining, and hallucination. Historical ATR therefore continues to rely largely on compact CRNN line recognizers, which are visually grounded and trainable on modest data. Lightweight recurrence-free recognizers promise the accuracy of larger models with the practical advantages of CRNNs, yet have not been comprehensively evaluated on historical writing. We adapt PP-OCRv6, a recent compact text recognizer without strong language modeling, for historical line recognition and compare it with a conventional CRNN across generalized pretraining, domain-specific training, corpus-level fine-tuning, and manuscript-specific few-shot adaptation on multilingual Latin- and Arabic-script material. While PP-OCRv6 does not consistently outperform the baseline when trained from scratch, heterogeneous pretraining produces markedly better generalization. Comparisons with the Qwen3.5-based Medusa recognizer further show that fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform a large VLM tailored towards historical Latin-script HTR.

AI.tldr: Lightweight, recurrence-free recognizers (PP-OCRv6) can generalize well to historical line recognition with heterogeneous pretraining, and can surpass tailored large LMs like Medusa under fine-tuning, though not always beating CRNN baselines when trained from scratch.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether compact, recurrence-free recognizers can replace or approach CRNNs for historical text recognition, given cost, data, and hallucination constraints of large vision-language models.
AI.method: Adapt PP-OCRv6 (a compact recognizer without strong language modeling) for historical line recognition and compare to a conventional CRNN across: generalized pretraining, domain-specific training, corpus-level fine-tuning, and manuscript-specific few-shot adaptation, on multilingual Latin- and Arabic-script material. Include comparison with Qwen3.5-based Medusa recognizer.
AI.result: PP-OCRv6 does not consistently outperform the CRNN when trained from scratch; however, heterogeneous pretraining markedly improves generalization. Fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform a large VLM (Medusa) tailored to historical Latin-script HTR.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining strategy matters more than model size; lightweight recognizers with appropriate heterogeneous pretraining can rival or exceed large LMs in historical HTR, suggesting practical benefits and a path for future evaluation across scripts and manuscript sizes.

title: HEROIC: Heterogeneous Evidential Reasoning for Open-Vocabulary Identification and Cross-Robot Collaboration
summary: Multi-agent heterogeneous air-ground robot teams are attractive for open world search, with applications for reconnaissance, urban search and rescue missions (USAR), disaster response and recovery, and hazardous environments. These two platforms have different failure modes: aerial robots cover ground quickly but cannot resolve small or occluded targets from altitude, while ground robots can identify objects-of-interest, such as people or hazardous objects, at close range but cover less area. Existing language-tasked teams either have roles fixed prior, or have a language model assign them from hand-written capability tags, so the team is unable to know when within a mission an asset is no longer useful. We present HEROIC, a decentralized heterogeneous multi-agent open-vocabulary search coordination framework that requires agents to communicate in natural language only. HEROIC's initial agent role assignment is derived from sensor properties and a scale law to determine whether targets can be detected with a high confidence. From the mission's natural language prompt alone, this law assigns aerial flight altitudes and sweep spacing. When this calculated height falls below the altitude for safe flight, aerial agents re-task themselves from searcher to aerial triage, escort, and route guide for ground agents. Both robots maintain an evidential belief over the search area (bearing rays for positive evidence, a log-odds posterior for negative evidence) and gate any arrival on close-range verification. In full-stack experiments, HEROIC reaches the target 84% of the time across all 6 scenes, compares to 35-54% for vision-language frontier baselines, frontier-based search, lawnmower, and random-walk running the same perception, all while being 2-4x sooner to arrive at the target.

AI.tldr: HEROIC is a decentralized open-vocabulary coordination framework for heterogeneous aerial-ground robot teams, using natural-language communication to dynamically assign roles and adapt tasks via a scale-law detection criterion; it maintains evidential beliefs and gates actions on close-range verification, achieving substantially higher target discovery rates and faster arrival than baselines.
AI.motivation: Address fixed-role limitations in language-driven multi-agent systems for open-world search, enabling adaptive, language-only coordination without hand-crafted capability tags.
AI.method: Initialize roles based on sensor properties and a scale-law to determine detectability; extract altitude and sweep spacing from the mission prompt; re-task aerial agents to triage/escort/route-guide when safe-flight altitude is insufficient; maintain evidential belief (bearing rays for positive evidence, log-odds for negative) with gated close-range verification; fully decentralized, communicating via natural language.
AI.result: Full-stack experiments show 84% target reach across 6 scenes, versus 35-54% for competitive baselines, and 2–4x faster to reach the target.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that language-only, decentralized coordination can effectively manage heterogeneous aerial-ground teams for open-world search, delivering higher success rates and faster target arrival; confirms the value of adaptive role reassignment driven by a scale-law detection criterion and evidence-based decision gates.

title: E-AVI: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Assessment for Automated Video Interviews
summary: Automated video interview assessment integrates verbal content, acoustic delivery, and visual behavior, yet numerical predictions alone provide limited inspectable support. We present E-AVI, an evidence-grounded framework that extracts timestamped multimodal evidence and integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings for scoring. A shared evidence pool further supports natural-language feedback and follow-up question answering. On RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset, E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation. Ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses characterize the predictive contribution, grounding, and practical utility of the evidence pathway. Together, these results demonstrate that our proposed E-AVI framework improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis.

AI.tldr: E-AVI is an evidence-grounded multimodal video interview assessment framework that extracts timestamped evidence, uses dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings, and provides a shared evidence pool for natural-language feedback and QA. It outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation on RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset, with extensive ablations and analyses supporting interpretability and practical utility.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limited interpretability of purely numerical predictions in automated interview assessment by grounding scores in timestamped multimodal evidence and enabling natural-language feedback and follow-up QA.
AI.method: E-AVI extracts timestamped multimodal evidence (verbal content, acoustics, visuals), applies dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings, and maintains a shared evidence pool to support NL feedback and QA. The system is evaluated on RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset, with ablations (evidence-deletion, bootstrap), human-audit, and QA analyses to characterize grounding and utility.
AI.result: E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation on both datasets. Ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses demonstrate the predictive contribution, grounding, and practical value of the evidence pathway.
AI.conclusion: E-AVI improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis.

title: Correct Now, Insufficient Later: Auditing Update Sufficiency in Context Compression
comment: 20 pages, 9 tables, 2 figures. Code and reproducibility materials to be released separately
summary: A memory can answer a current query correctly while discarding distinctions required by a later update. We investigate this failure with a paired-history audit: two histories have the same current answer, receive a shared future update, and require different subsequent answers. A pilot evaluates 24 history pairs across six synthetic mechanisms, 12 memory conditions, two repeats, and two model backends. A deterministic frontier selector obtains strict reveal accuracy of 96/96 on DeepSeek and 82/96 on GLM; a structured writer obtains 62 successes with one unresolved outcome and 56/96. The configured four-outcome joint contrast has finite-sample identification intervals of [0.521, 0.542] and [0.292, 0.313], not confidence intervals. A record-level audit distinguishes retained-state adequacy, response delivery, and answer-schema compliance without changing those original scores. It finds 26 and 25 well-formed but semantically wrong structured reveal memories, while all 14 GLM frontier reveal failures contain correct values in the wrong wrapper. Tombstone removal produces 16/16 exact replay failures in the targeted mechanism. Identifier renaming then exposes a separate flaw: original frontier late-reference adequacy falls from 8/8 to 94/320 transformed instances. We provide and test a label-equivariant repair, but it preserves only 2/8 original late-reference answers: eliminating a naming shortcut does not solve unknown future relevance. These results support a scoped evaluation methodology and reproducible failure analysis, not general superiority of the repaired algorithm. Paid pilot evidence, retrospective diagnostics, and new offline tests are reported separately; no independent held-out or natural-task validation is claimed.

AI.tldr: A pilot study uses a paired-history audit to diagnose memory-update failures in language-model memories, testing multiple memory mechanisms, audit dimensions, and backends. It reveals diverse failure modes, shows that certain metrics (strict reveal accuracy, finite-sample intervals) are not confidence intervals, and demonstrates that several repair attempts do not generalize; overall results advocate scoped, reproducible failure analysis rather than overall algorithmic superiority.
AI.motivation: To diagnose how memory systems in language models preserve or discard information when future updates require different subsequent answers, using controlled paired histories and targeted diagnostics to reveal failure modes and repair attempts.
AI.method: A pilot with 24 history pairs across six synthetic mechanisms, 12 memory conditions, two repeats, and two model backends. Evaluations include a deterministic frontier selector, a structured writer, and a four-outcome joint contrast. A record-level audit dissects retained-state adequacy, response delivery, and answer-schema compliance. Additional manipulations include tombstone removal and identifier renaming, followed by a label-equivariant repair evaluation. Paid pilot and retrospective diagnostics are reported separately; no held-out natural-task validation is claimed.
AI.result: Deterministic frontier selector achieves strict reveal accuracy of 96/96 on DeepSeek and 82/96 on GLM; structured writer yields 62 successes with one unresolved, and 56/96. The four-outcome joint contrast yields finite-sample intervals [0.521,0.542] and [0.292,0.313] (not CIs). Record-level audit finds 26 well-formed but semantically wrong structured reveal memories; GLM frontier reveals are correct values in the wrong wrapper. Tombstone removal yields 16/16 exact replay failures. Identifier renaming exposes a drop in original frontier late-reference adequacy from 8/8 to 94/320 transformed instances. Label-equivariant repair preserves only 2/8 original late-reference answers; removing a naming shortcut does not fix unknown future relevance.
AI.conclusion: The results support a scoped evaluation methodology and reproducible failure analysis rather than broad superiority of the repaired algorithm. No independent held-out or natural-task validation is claimed; separate reports cover paid pilot evidence, retrospective diagnostics, and offline tests.

title: PointEvent: Rethinking Event-based Tiny Object Detection via Serialized Motion Evidence Accumulation
summary: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity for tiny UAV detection, yet distant targets generate sparse and fragmented events that are easily overwhelmed by clutter and ego-motion. Existing methods mainly rely on dense event representations or local sparse spatiotemporal modeling, resulting in redundant computation or fragmented modeling of motion continuity across distant asynchronous events. To address this limitation, we introduce serialized motion evidence accumulation, which treats motion continuity as an ordered evidence propagation process. Specifically, the same event stream is organized into locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and chronology-preserving temporal paths through the latent complementary serializations. Based on this principle, we propose PointEvent, a lightweight event-wise state-space framework that alternates serialized scans across the complementary orders, progressively consolidating fragmented motion evidence beyond fixed local neighborhoods. A high-resolution event branch preserves fine-grained target responses, while compact context modulation suppresses interference. Experiments demonstrate that PointEvent achieves SOTA with the fewest parameters and fastest measured inference among the compared methods. Code: https://github.com/wzz-z/PointEvent

AI.tldr: PointEvent introduces serialized motion evidence accumulation for event streams to detect distant UAVs; achieves SOTA with minimal parameters and fast inference.
AI.motivation: Distant targets produce sparse and fragmented events; clutter and ego-motion overwhelm detection when using dense representations or local spatiotemporal models. A method that propagates motion evidence over time and space while preserving locality and chronology is needed.
AI.method: Two complementary serializations organize the same event stream into locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and chronology-preserving temporal paths. The model alternates serialized scans across these orders in a lightweight event-wise state-space framework (PointEvent). It includes a high-resolution event branch for fine-grained responses and compact context modulation to suppress interference, progressively consolidating fragmented motion evidence beyond fixed local neighborhoods.
AI.result: Empirical results show state-of-the-art performance with the fewest parameters and fastest measured inference among compared methods; code released (GitHub).
AI.conclusion: Serialized motion evidence accumulation across complementary orders effectively consolidates fragmented motion evidence in sparse, distant event streams, enabling robust tiny UAV detection with real-time efficiency.

title: Vehicle Trajectory Prediction via Neural Fusion of Multiple EKF-Based Trajectory Candidates
summary: Predicting the future trajectories of surrounding vehicles in autonomous driving is important for collision risk assessment and safe ego-vehicle path planning. Conventional neural network-based trajectory predictors typically achieve strong prediction performance by exploiting agent history, dynamic scene graphs, and semantic maps. However, in specific motion regimes such as acceleration, deceleration, and turning, these predictors may fail to reflect physically feasible trajectories. To address this issue, this study proposes a framework that fuses the output of Trajectron++, a neural network-based trajectory predictor, with extended Kalman filter (EKF)-based multiple trajectory candidates at a late stage. On the nuScenes dataset, the proposed method reduces the average displacement error and final displacement error of the Trajectron++ robot baseline by 13.7% and 14.6%, respectively, without modifying the baseline architecture. These results indicate that EKF-based trajectory candidates can effectively complement neural trajectory prediction through learned fusion.

AI.tldr: Fusion of Trajectron++ with EKF-based trajectory candidates improves neural trajectory prediction without changing the baseline model.
AI.motivation: Neural predictors can produce physically infeasible trajectories in regimes involving acceleration, deceleration, or turning; integrating physics-based estimates aims to enforce physical plausibility and enhance accuracy.
AI.method: Generate multiple EKF-based trajectory candidates and perform a late-stage fusion with Trajectron++ outputs, without modifying the underlying neural predictor architecture.
AI.result: On the nuScenes dataset, ADE is reduced by 13.7% and FDE by 14.6% relative to the Trajectron++ baseline.
AI.conclusion: EKF-based trajectory candidates complementary to neural predictions via learned fusion can improve trajectory accuracy while preserving the existing predictor framework.

title: Geopolitical Divisions Across Languages in Large Language Models
summary: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots for news and explanations of world events. But do they receive the same political answers when they ask in different languages? Here we show that the language of a question can change how the same AI systems assess the war in Ukraine. We ask GPT, Claude and Gemini to evaluate twenty statements about the war in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. The balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses differs across languages. When we group responses by countries' official languages, they follow a pattern resembling worldwide political divisions: relatively more Russia-leaning answers correspond to more favourable public views of Russia, less support for Ukraine in United Nations votes, and less aid to Ukraine. The broad pattern recurs across all three models and remains when individual statement pairs are removed. Our findings suggest a possible route through which information warfare may shape the text used to train AI models, which may in turn spread geopolitical biases.

AI.tldr: Language of the query affects political slant in three AI models; across 112 languages and 20 statements about the Ukraine war, responses skew more Russia-leaning in some languages, correlating with public opinion and UN votes; pattern is robust across models and persists when statements are removed, implying possible bias propagation via training data.
AI.motivation: Assess whether multilingual prompts induce political biases in AI chatbots and understand implications for information warfare and training data biases.
AI.method: Query three AI models (GPT, Claude, Gemini) with 20 statements about the war in Ukraine in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. Analyze leanings by language and by countries’ official languages, correlate with public opinion indicators (e.g., UN votes, aid to Ukraine), and perform robustness checks by removing statement pairs.
AI.result: Found language-dependent Russia-leaning vs Ukraine-leaning bias across all three models. Languages tied to certain countries show more Russia-leaning answers, aligning with more favorable views of Russia and less support for Ukraine in UN votes and aid. Pattern recurs across models and persists when individual statement pairs are removed, suggesting a broad, language-driven bias not tied to a single prompt set.
AI.conclusion: Language can shape political bias in AI outputs across multilingual prompts, with potential implications for information warfare and bias propagation through AI training data. Calls for multilingual bias evaluation, debiasing strategies, and monitoring of training data sources.

title: Evaluating Explanation Methods by the Predictors They Induce
summary: Explanations of machine learning models are usually judged by criteria that are hard to compare. We propose a simpler test: if an explanation really describes how a model uses its features, it should be possible to rebuild the model's predictions from it. We turn each explanation into a predictor by reading each feature's effect and adding them up, and measure how well that predictor reproduces the model on unseen data. Nothing is fitted, so the score reflects the explanation itself. The test applies to any explanation that can be written as a function of the features; we demonstrate it on partial dependence plots (PDP), accumulated local effects (ALE), SHAP and LIME. We prove that summing partial dependence curves gives the best possible additive summary of a model when its features are independent, and that this fails when they are dependent. Across 13 real datasets and 9 synthetic designs and four model families, which method scores best depends entirely on feature dependence: where features are independent SHAP is slightly worse than PDP, exactly as the theory predicts; on dependent real data SHAP leads. Some widely used quality metrics even prefer a damaged explanation to an intact one.

AI.tldr: A reconstruction-based test for explanations: convert explanations into predictors by summing per-feature effects and evaluate their ability to reproduce a model’s predictions on unseen data. Applies to PDP, ALE, SHAP, LIME; performance depends on feature dependency; theory shows PDP is optimal additive summary under feature independence, but fails with dependent features; SHAP can outperform PDP on dependent data; some metrics may misrank explanations.
AI.motivation: Explanations are heterogeneous and hard to compare. A universal, model-agnostic criterion is needed to assess whether an explanation truly captures how a model uses its features.
AI.method: Turn each explanation into a predictor by summing each feature's effect. Evaluate on unseen data without fitting to data. This generic approach can be applied to any explanation representable as a function of features (PDP, ALE, SHAP, LIME). Provide theoretical results (independence implies PDP sum is best additive summary) and empirical evaluation across 13 real datasets, 9 synthetic designs, and four model families.
AI.result: Additive reconstruction works as a fidelity test for explanations. For independent features, summing PDPs yields the best additive summary; this breaks under feature dependence. In experiments, SHAP’s performance relative to PDP depends on feature dependence: with independent features PDP slightly outperforms SHAP, while with dependent real data SHAP outperforms PDP. Some common quality metrics can even prefer a damaged explanation over an intact one.
AI.conclusion: The usefulness of explanation methods is contingent on feature dependence; a single metric is insufficient to judge quality. The proposed reconstructibility test reveals when explanations are faithful and highlights that SHAP and PDP have complementary strengths depending on correlation structure. Researchers should consider feature dependencies when evaluating and selecting explainers.

title: G^2RA-NET: Graph-based Cross-Slice Relation Modeling with Attention Gating for Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Medical image segmentation supports quantitative clinical analysis and computer-aided diagnosis. Recent methods for medical image segmentation have improved both local feature representation and volumetric context modeling. However, existing methods still strug- gle to efficiently model cross-slice relations in anisotropic volumet- ric images, limiting segmentation consistency and accuracy. This pa- per proposes G^2RA-Net, a medical image segmentation framework that combines graph-based cross-slice relation modeling with atten- tion gating. Graph-Based Slice Relationship Modeling (GSRM) cap- tures anatomical dependencies across consecutive slices by repre- senting each slice as a graph node and propagating semantic con- text through graph message passing. The Cross-Slice Attention Gate (CSAG) then selects relevant neighboring context and emphasizes target anatomical regions through attention-guided feature modula- tion. Experiments on brain MRI and abdominal CT datasets demon- strate that G^2RA-Net outperforms representative methods in seg- mentation accuracy and boundary quality. Ablation studies further validate the proposed design.

AI.tldr: G^2RA-Net introduces graph-based cross-slice modeling and a cross-slice attention gate to improve segmentation in anisotropic volumetric medical images, achieving higher accuracy and boundary quality on brain MRI and abdominal CT.
AI.motivation: Anisotropic volumes hinder cross-slice dependencies; existing methods struggle to efficiently model cross-slice relations, impacting segmentation consistency and accuracy.
AI.method: Graph-Based Slice Relationship Modeling (GSRM) treats each slice as a graph node; propagates semantic context via graph message passing. Cross-Slice Attention Gate (CSAG) selects relevant neighboring context and modulates features via attention.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on brain MRI and abdominal CT shows superior segmentation accuracy and boundary quality compared to representative methods; ablation studies validate contributions.
AI.conclusion: G^2RA-Net effectively combines graph-based cross-slice modeling and attention gating to improve cross-slice consistency and segmentation performance in anisotropic volumes.

title: RotateIt! Fast and Reliable Single-Arm Garment Unfolding via Online-Adaptive Dynamic Rotation
summary: Robotic garment unfolding is essential for downstream tasks, yet quasi-static methods require repeated actions, while existing dynamic approaches predominantly rely on bimanual flinging. We present RotateIt!, a single-arm framework that uses adaptive axial rotation for dynamic garment unfolding. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first unfolding framework to employ dynamic axial rotation as its primary manipulation primitive. From a randomly initialized tabletop configuration, the robot selects a rotation-effective grasp and rotates the lifted garment about an approximately fixed anchor, generating inertial tension that separates overlapping layers within a compact workspace. A grasp ranker selects the anchor, while an online residual policy adapts the rotation extent and speed, thereby determining the release timing. Across seen and unseen simulated garments and eight unseen real garments, RotateIt! improves success within three attempts by 44.0-61.0 percentage points over quasi-static pick-and-place. The simulation-trained policies transfer zero-shot to the real world, achieving 75.6% success, 41% higher first-attempt coverage, and 26% higher final coverage. The resulting states further enable autonomous robotic folding without manual rearrangement.

AI.tldr: RotateIt! uses a single-arm dynamic axial rotation to unfold garments, outperforming quasi-static methods and transferring from simulation to real without fine-tuning; enabling autonomous downstream folding.
AI.motivation: Quasi-static garment unfolding requires many actions and can be inefficient; existing dynamic methods often rely on bimanual flinging. A single-arm, autonomous approach with dynamic axial rotation aims to reduce actions, handle overlapping layers, and improve success in real-world tasks.
AI.method: From a randomly initialized tabletop configuration, the robot selects a rotation-effective grasp and rotates the lifted garment about an approximately fixed anchor to generate inertial tension that separates overlapping layers. A grasp ranker chooses the anchor, while an online residual policy adapts rotation extent and speed, and determines release timing.
AI.result: In both seen and unseen simulated garments and eight unseen real garments, RotateIt! improves success within three attempts by 44.0–61.0 percentage points compared with quasi-static pick-and-place. The simulation-trained policies transfer zero-shot to the real world, achieving 75.6% success, 41% higher first-attempt coverage, and 26% higher final coverage. The resulting unfolded states enable autonomous robotic folding without manual rearrangement.
AI.conclusion: The work introduces a novel dynamic-axial-rotation primitive for single-arm garment unfolding, demonstrating substantial performance gains and seamless sim-to-real transfer, with states suitable for autonomous folding downstream.

title: FedeRICo: Federated Region-Influenced Coupling for Traffic Flow Prediction
summary: Urban traffic forecasting often relies on information distributed across stakeholders who may be unable to share raw data due to privacy or commercial constraints, motivating federated spatial-temporal approaches. In such federated settings, each client observes traffic over a distinct sensor subgraph with its own spatial topology and temporal dynamics, leading to significant heterogeneity across clients. Existing federated spatial-temporal methods typically rely on model parameter aggregation and provide limited mechanisms for recovering spatial dependencies across client boundaries. This introduces two key limitations. Specifically, parameter aggregation across heterogeneous graph domains tends to dilute client-specific representations, while road network partitioning breaks the propagation of traffic dynamics across client boundaries. To address these challenges, we propose FedeRICo, a federated traffic forecasting framework that combines gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication. FedeRICo employs a dual-branch forecasting architecture in which a globally guided branch captures transferable forecasting structure, while a private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections and incorporates boundary residual signals. The global branch is coordinated through gradient alignment across all clients, enabling collaborative optimisation without destructive parameter interference. To recover cross-client spatial dependencies, boundary messages are extracted through a trend-residual decomposition that suppresses periodic structure and communicates only transient spatial-temporal residual signals between physically adjacent clients. Experiments across four real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that FedeRICo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines while maintaining competitive training runtime.

AI.tldr: FedeRICo introduces gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication for federated traffic forecasting, addressing heterogeneity and cross-border spatial dependencies; it outperforms baselines on four real-world benchmarks while maintaining efficient training.
AI.motivation: Federated traffic forecasting faces privacy- and data-sharing constraints across stakeholders with distinct sensor subgraphs, leading to heterogeneity in spatial topology and temporal dynamics. Parameter aggregation dilutes client-specific information and partitioning impedes cross-client propagation of traffic dynamics.
AI.method: A dual-branch architecture: a globally guided branch captures transferable forecasting structure, and a private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections. Gradient alignment coordinates the global branch across clients. Boundary messages are derived via trend-residual decomposition, suppressing periodic structure to communicate only transient boundary residual signals between physically adjacent clients, enabling cross-client spatial dependency recovery.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on four real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks shows that FedeRICo consistently surpasses state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines, with competitive training runtimes.
AI.conclusion: FedeRICo effectively mitigates heterogeneity and boundary-breaking issues in federated spatial-temporal forecasting by combining gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining privacy and efficiency.

title: MATCH: Model-Aware Tool Learning with Curriculum Scheduling and Hierarchically Gated Rewards
summary: Tool learning enables large language models (LLMs) to use external tools for tasks beyond parametric knowledge. Reinforcement learning can optimize tool-call behavior from feedback, but current methods still face two problems: fixed-threshold curricula can become misaligned with the policy's evolving capability boundary, and additive rewards can leak argument-level credit when the predicted tool is wrong. To address these problems, we propose MATCH, a closed-loop framework for model-aware tool learning with curriculum scheduling and hierarchically gated rewards. Model-Aware Curriculum Learning (MACL) maintains reward-derived sample difficulty that co-evolves with the policy, and each epoch selects samples near the current capability boundary together with a top-k pool of harder cases. Hierarchical Tool-call Gated Reward (HTGR) scores tool name, argument key, and argument value as a gated chain, granting credit at each level only when prerequisites hold. The same HTGR rewards drive both GRPO updates and MACL's difficulty refresh, closing the loop between policy optimization and sample scheduling. On API-Bank and BFCL V3, MATCH reaches 72.19% and 62.87% overall accuracy, outperforming the main supervised and RL-based baselines. Backbone experiments further show consistent improvements across four backbones from two model families.

AI.tldr: MATCH is a model-aware tool-learning framework using curriculum scheduling and hierarchically gated rewards to align tool-use with evolving policy capabilities, reducing credit leakage and improving performance.
