AI.motivation: Two main issues hinder RL-based tool learning: fixed curricula misalign with a policy boundary that shifts as capabilities grow, and additive rewards that unreliably credit a tool when its prediction is wrong.
AI.method: Introduce MACL (model-aware curriculum learning) that selects samples near the current capability boundary plus harder cases, and HTGR (hierarchical tool-call gated reward) that score tool name, argument key, and value in a gated sequence. HKGR rewards guide both GRPO updates and MACL refresh, forming a closed loop that links policy optimization with sample scheduling.
AI.result: On API-Bank and BFCL V3, MATCH achieves 72.19% and 62.87% overall accuracy, outperforming supervised and RL baselines. Backbones across two families show consistent improvement (four backbones).
AI.conclusion: A tightly coupled loop between policy updates and sample difficulty, via MACL and HTGR, yields robust tool-learning improvements and generalizes across models and datasets.

title: A Smaller Transformer in Your Transformer
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the 37th British Machine Vision Conference (BMVC 2026)
summary: Recent findings indicate that Vision Transformers settle into locally similar computational phases, implying a level of depthwise computational redundancy. However, existing methods to exploit this redundancy either fail to reduce inference compute or severely degrade model expressivity. In this work, we formalise a unified view of block redundancy that decouples the geometry from specific surrogate interventions. We then introduce Transformer-Within-Transformer (TWT), a post-hoc method that fuses contiguous groups of redundant layers into a single learned surrogate layer. TWT reduces parameter count and inference compute while remaining competitive with original models using half the depth on natural images, and in several downstream histopathology settings, TWT matches or even improves on the original baseline.

AI.tldr: Transformer-Within-Transformer (TWT) is a post-hoc method that fuses contiguous redundant Transformer layers into a single surrogate layer, reducing parameters and compute while maintaining or improving performance on natural images and histopathology tasks.
AI.motivation: Vision Transformers exhibit locally similar computational phases, indicating redundancy across depth. Existing redundancy-exploitation methods either fail to reduce compute or degrade expressivity. A unified view of block redundancy is needed to decouple geometry from surrogate interventions and enable effective compression.
AI.method: Introduce a unified framework for block redundancy and present TWT, a post-hoc technique that replaces groups of consecutive, redundant layers with a single learned surrogate layer that encapsulates their function, thereby halving effective depth while preserving performance.
AI.result: TWT reduces parameter count and inference compute; achieves competitive results with half the depth on natural images and matches or surpasses the original baseline in several downstream histopathology tasks.
AI.conclusion: TWT demonstrates that structured redundancy in Vision Transformers can be exploited via a post-hoc surrogate layer to compress depth and compute without sacrificing expressivity, offering a general approach for efficient Vision Transformer deployment.

title: TADreamer: Zero-Shot Language-Guided 3D Navigation for Terrestrial-Aerial Bimodal Robots via Video Imagination
summary: Language-guided navigation for terrestrial-aerial bimodal robots requires selecting routes and locomotion modes that match scene context and task intent. Generated videos can represent such motion sequences, but recovering metrically consistent navigation references from them is challenging because of scale ambiguity and axis-dependent geometric distortions. We present TADreamer, a zero-shot framework that grounds video-imagined navigation in measured geometry without task-specific training or fine-tuning. A vision-language model translates onboard observations and instructions into navigation prompts, selects valid generated videos, and provides corrective feedback when regeneration is needed. The selected video is reconstructed into 3D waypoints annotated with terrestrial or aerial modes. A two-stage calibration procedure uses field-of-view constraints to initialize scale estimation, then refines axis-dependent scales, rotation, and translation by registering the reconstructed point cloud to measured geometry. The calibrated waypoints and mode labels guide a planner that incorporates measured geometry for robot execution. Real-world experiments demonstrate navigation across seven indoor and outdoor scenarios. With five candidates per round, usable videos are obtained within two rounds in all seven scenarios. On the calibration observations, our method reduces mean absolute depth error by 87.7% and mean absolute relative depth error by 86.3% compared with NavDreamer.

AI.tldr: TADreamer is a zero-shot framework that grounds video-imagined navigation in measured geometry for terrestrial–aerial bimodal robots, using vision–language prompts to select and refine generated videos, reconstructing them into 3D waypoints, calibrating scale and pose against measured geometry, and guiding execution with a geometry-aware planner.
AI.motivation: Recover metrically consistent navigation references from generated, video-imagined sequences amidst scale ambiguity and axis distortions, without task-specific training for terrestrial–aerial robotics.
AI.method: A vision–language model converts onboard observations and instructions into navigation prompts, selects valid generated videos, and provides corrective feedback. The chosen video is reconstructed into 3D waypoints with terrestrial or aerial mode labels. A two-stage calibration initializes scale from field-of-view constraints and refines axis scales, rotation, and translation by registering the reconstructed point cloud to measured geometry. A planner uses calibrated waypoints and mode labels with measured geometry for execution.
AI.result: Real-world experiments across seven indoor and outdoor scenarios show usable videos are obtained within two rounds with five candidates per round. Depth calibration on observed data achieves an 87.7% reduction in mean absolute depth error and an 86.3% reduction in mean absolute relative depth error compared to NavDreamer.
AI.conclusion: TADreamer demonstrates effective zero-shot grounding of video-imagined navigation to real geometry for terrestrial–aerial robots, enabling robust, geometry-consistent navigation without task-specific training and outperforming a prior approach in depth accuracy.

title: Can Data Attribution Filter Out Subliminal Learning? Not Reliably
summary: Subliminal learning allows language models to transmit behavioral traits through training data with no obvious semantic relationship to those traits, undermining content-based data filtering as a safety intervention. Training data attribution offers an alternative: it identifies the training examples responsible for a given model behavior, independent of their semantic content, and so may apply in exactly the cases where semantic inspection fails. We evaluate three gradient-based attribution methods (GradCos, a contrastive GradCos variant, and EK-FAC) across three models, comparing them against divergence tokens, a strong baseline previously shown to localize subliminal learning (albeit one that requires access to counterfactual teacher models). Filtering at the token level, EK-FAC mitigates a significant part of the effect, the other methods provide little benefit, and all mostly fall short of divergence tokens. Filtering entire samples is less effective for every method, though EK-FAC often gives a stronger signal than divergence tokens in this setting. Success is inconsistent across methods and settings: variants that work well for some model-preference combinations fail for others, and we do not identify a consistent explanation for these differences. Our results suggest that gradient-based attribution can identify data responsible for subliminal learning in some settings, but that some approximations are more reliable than others.

AI.tldr: Gradient-based data attribution shows limited and inconsistent effectiveness for localizing subliminal learning; EK-FAC token-level attribution performs best among the tested methods but often trails the strong baseline of divergence tokens; sample-level filtering is generally less effective.
AI.motivation: Subliminal learning enables transmission of behavioral traits via training data with no obvious semantic cues, undermining content-based filtering. Data attribution offers a content-agnostic way to identify training data responsible for a model behavior, potentially enabling safer filtering when semantic inspection fails. The study benchmarks three gradient-based attribution methods against a strong baseline (divergence tokens) across multiple models.
AI.method: Evaluation of three gradient-based attribution methods—GradCos, a contrastive GradCos variant, and EK-FAC—across three models. Comparisons are made to divergence tokens. Experiments analyze filtering at the token level and at the whole-sample level to locate data responsible for subliminal learning.
AI.result: EK-FAC at the token level mitigates a significant portion of subliminal effects; the other methods provide little benefit and most methods fall short of the divergence-token baseline. Whole-sample filtering is less effective for all methods, though EK-FAC sometimes yields a stronger signal than divergence tokens in this setting. Success is inconsistent across model–setup combinations; no consistent explanation for the differences. Overall, gradient-based attribution can identify responsible data in some settings, but the reliability of approximations varies.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-based attribution can aid in identifying data responsible for subliminal learning in some scenarios but is not consistently reliable; divergence tokens remain a more robust baseline. Further work is needed to understand when and why these methods succeed and to develop more reliable data-attribution techniques.

title: SETTer: Sparse-Encoder Transformer for Long-term Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
summary: Long-term multivariate time series plays a significant role in many application areas such as power systems, trading, etc. However, their accurate prediction is quite difficult for conventional forecasting methods as they often exhibit high dimensionality and complex relationships. Recent works show that transformer-based approaches are quite effective for long-term forecasting thanks to their attention mechanism. However, in the presence of complex high-dimensional inputs, they show evidence of oversmoothing, limited capacity, and opacity. To this end, this paper introduces SETTer, a transformer-based model that addresses these challenges by incorporating novel techniques for decoupled self-attention and hybrid masking. The proposed techniques enable SETTer to effectively capture the dominant short- and long-term patterns across the temporal and channel dimensions. In addition, we enrich the model layers with simple explainable structures that indicate the discriminative pattern of SETTer. We show that with a single-layer transformer architecture, SETTer can effectively model long-term dependencies in the presence of varying data complexities. Extensive experiments on real-word benchmark datasets for long-term multivariate time series forecasting demonstrate that SETTer outperforms state-of-the-art models in 88% of the scenarios.

AI.tldr: Ter transformer SETTer with decoupled self-attention and hybrid masking improves long-term multivariate time series forecasting using a single-layer architecture while enabling explainability, outperforming state-of-the-art in 88% of benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address the challenges of high dimensionality, oversmoothing, limited capacity, and opacity in transformer-based long-term forecasting for multivariate time series.
AI.method: Introduce SETTer, a transformer-based model that uses decoupled self-attention and hybrid masking to capture dominant short- and long-term patterns across temporal and channel dimensions; employ simple explainable structures within layers to indicate discriminative patterns; demonstrate that a single-layer transformer suffices.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world long-term multivariate time series datasets show SETTer outperforms state-of-the-art models in 88% of scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Decoupled attention and hybrid masking enable effective modeling of long-term dependencies in high-dimensional inputs, with added interpretability, using a compact single-layer transformer.

title: AnyviewMeter: Adapting Robotic Reward Models with Camera Geometry and Multi-View Attention
summary: Robotic reward models evaluate task execution from visual observations, but their predictions can change with camera viewpoint and occlusion even when the underlying task state is unchanged. Adapting a pretrained reward model to a local task therefore requires accounting for how that task is observed. We introduce AnyviewMeter, a geometry-conditioned adaptation framework for robotic reward models that represent task progress as a scalar reward signal. It combines low-rank fine-tuning with token-aligned Plucker rays and synchronous block attention: ray conditioning incorporates camera geometry into visual features and attention queries and keys, while block attention fuses synchronized views inside the pretrained decoder. The framework supports both single-view reward prediction and joint multi-view evaluation through parameter-efficient adaptation of a pretrained Robometer model. On PickCube, single-view adaptation improves progress prediction in every camera group and reduces mean absolute error under a changed field of view by approximately 21% relative to RGB fine-tuning. Across simulated manipulation tasks, joint multi-view prediction reduces progress error by 41-69% compared with averaging single-view RGB predictions and improves temporal ordering in approximately 88% of task-camera groups. On real tasks with fixed and wrist-mounted cameras, mean absolute error decreases by approximately 21% relative to averaged RGB fine-tuning. These results support camera geometry and joint visual evidence as useful components of task-specific robotic reward adaptation.

AI.tldr: Geometry-conditioned, parameter-efficient adaptation for robotic reward models (AnyviewMeter) using Plucker ray conditioning and synchronized block attention to fuse multi-view observations, improving single- and multi-view reward predictions under varying camera geometry.
AI.motivation: Robotic reward models' predictions change with camera viewpoint/occlusion even when the task state is unchanged; there is a need for geometry-aware adaptation to local tasks.
AI.method: Low-rank fine-tuning with token-aligned Plucker rays; ray conditioning incorporates camera geometry into visual features and attention queries/keys; synchronized block attention fuses synchronized views inside the pretrained decoder; supports single-view and joint multi-view adaptation of a pretrained Robometer.
AI.result: Single-view adaptation improves progress prediction across all camera groups and reduces MAE under changed FOV by ~21% relative to RGB fine-tuning. Across simulated manipulation tasks, joint multi-view prediction reduces progress error by 41-69% vs averaging single-view RGB predictions, and improves temporal ordering in ~88% of task-camera groups. Real tasks with fixed/wrist cameras show MAE decreased by ~21% relative to averaged RGB fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Camera geometry and joint visual evidence are effective components for task-specific reward adaptation; the framework enables robust reward predictions across viewpoints and supports both single- and multi-view evaluations.

title: Improving Cross-embodiment Transfer in Latent Action Models with Action-Similarity Supervision
summary: As generalist robot policies gain vision and language from web-scale pretraining, demonstrations remain costly to collect and tied to the robot that recorded them. Latent action models (LAMs) address both by learning latent actions from action-free videos that can be shared across embodiments, however, in practice, LAMs are sensitive to background visual noise, and the same motion from two different robots may be encoded with different latents. One solution to the background visual noise is to add an auxiliary loss predicting the robot action from the latent action, further associating the latent action space to the embodiment specific robot action space. We study a different use of the same labels, through action-similarity supervision. The similarity between any two latent actions is trained to match the similarity of the two ground-truth robot action sequences. The ground-truth actions are never predicted by the LAM, so the latent action does not need to encode embodiment specifics. We evaluate cross-embodiment transfer on RoboTwin 2.0 in a controlled setup, two bimanual robots demonstrate disjoint task sets, a policy is trained on all the demonstrations, and each robot is evaluated closed-loop on the tasks only the other demonstrated. With the policy architecture and its hyperparameters, the dataset, and the evaluation protocol fixed, predicting latent actions instead of ground-truth actions more than doubles cross-embodiment success. Given the same ground-truth actions, similarity supervision transfers better than an auxiliary loss that predicts the ground-truth action during the LAM training. Computing the similarities on end-effector motion rather than joint-space motion, and letting the loss compare latent actions across the two robots, gives the best approach of the study.

AI.tldr: Action-similarity supervision for Latent Action Models (LAMs) improves cross-embodiment transfer by aligning latent-action similarities with ground-truth action-sequence similarities; best when using end-effector motion and cross-robot latent-action comparisons, yielding >2x cross-embodiment success on RoboTwin 2.0.
AI.motivation: LAMs allow sharing across embodiments but are sensitive to background noise and embodiment-specific latents. A supervision signal that aligns latent actions across robots can enable robust cross-embodiment transfer without predicting raw actions.
AI.method: Train LAMs with an action-similarity loss that makes the similarity between latent actions match the similarity between corresponding ground-truth robot action sequences. Ground-truth actions are not predicted by the LAM. Similarities are computed on end-effector motion and compared across two robots. Evaluation uses RoboTwin 2.0 with two bimanual robots with disjoint task sets; a single policy is trained on all demonstrations and evaluated on tasks demonstrated by the other robot.
AI.result: Latent-action prediction outperforms ground-truth-action prediction by more than 2x in cross-embodiment success. Similarity supervision surpasses an auxiliary loss that predicts ground-truth actions. End-effector-motion-based similarity with cross-robot latent-action comparison yields the best performance.
AI.conclusion: Similarity-based latent-action supervision reduces embodiment bias and improves cross-embodiment transfer for LAMs. End-effector-based similarity is a particularly effective signal for aligning latent actions across devices.

title: DART: Distillation-Aware Reparameterization for Training-Free LoRA Reuse in Few-Step Video Diffusion Models
summary: Step distillation reduces the cost of video generation, but reusing a LoRA trained for a longer trajectory can alter its functional effect or degrade target quality. Static parameter compatibility offers one perspective on this problem; our observations show that similar measured geometry can coexist with different adapter behavior under a shortened denoising schedule. We propose DART, a training-free method that combines low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule response calibration using forward evaluations and no source training videos. On a four-step Wan2.2 target, DART-F improves the joint quality score from 0.9029 to 0.9227 and changes macro functional retention from -0.4644 to +0.1349. Component analysis shows that calibration accounts for most of the quality improvement, while coordinate transport provides complementary gains when combined with calibration. Adapter-level results reveal positive functional effects for some adapters and strong attenuation with reduced negative functional effects for others. Evaluations on two additional targets show the same aggregate trend. These results motivate evaluating distilled-model LoRA reuse jointly through functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance, without assuming recovery for every adapter.

AI.tldr: DART is a training-free method that preserves functional behavior while reusing distilled LoRAs for video generation by combining low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule calibration, showing improved quality and functional retention across targets without source training data.
AI.motivation: To address degradation and negative transfer when reusing LoRA adapters trained on longer trajectories after step distillation, by evaluating functional preservation and avoiding negative transfer without access to source training videos.
AI.method: DART combines low-rank coordinate transport with forward-evaluation–based target-schedule calibration in a training-free framework, requiring no source training videos.
AI.result: On a four-step Wan2.2 target, DART-F raises the joint quality score from 0.9029 to 0.9227 and shifts macro functional retention from −0.4644 to +0.1349; calibration accounts for most gains, while coordinate transport provides complementary improvements; adapter-level effects vary, with some adapters showing positive functional effects and others greatly attenuated negative effects; two additional targets show the same aggregate trend.
AI.conclusion: Evaluate distilled-model LoRA reuse jointly through functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance, and do not assume recovery for every adapter; a training-free calibration+coordinate-transport framework can improve quality while mitigating negative transfer.

title: CARE-VI: Conservative Adaptive Reliability Estimation for Value Improvement in Off-Policy Actor-Critic Learning
summary: Reliable temporal-difference targets are central to off-policy actor-critic learning. Direct value improvement refines the next-state target with alternative actions, but the reliability of this refinement depends on how candidate actions are ranked, reviewed, and weighted. Noisy rankings may force premature candidate commitment, reusing selection scores may bias target valuation, and fixed enhancement weights may amplify weak evidence. To address these risks, we develop Conservative Adaptive Ranking and Screening (CARS), which retains an ordered candidate prefix within a preset budget and narrows it only when the observed boundary gap exceeds a disagreement-scaled uncertainty radius. Selector-Evaluator Value Assessment (SEVA) uses selector critics to order candidates and a separately parameterized evaluator critic to review the selected value, then caps the reviewed value at the selector reference. Dynamic Adaptive Risk-aware Enhancement (DARE) then regulates each residual correction using candidate reliability, the gap between selector and evaluator signals, and a finite stage factor. Together, CARS, SEVA, and DARE form CARE-VI, an evidence-regulated target construction framework that preserves the backbone interfaces for critic regression and actor updates. The analysis bounds the CARS boundary error, the SEVA selected-value overestimation, and the one-sided deviation of the DARE residual displacement from its population counterpart, and establishes fixed-policy recovery after the finite-stage perturbation ends. Experiments with SAC, TD3, and TD7 on four MuJoCo tasks show that CARE-VI achieves the highest mean return in all twelve settings. Grouped ablations and scalar diagnostics support the roles of the three components in improving target reliability.

AI.tldr: Conservative Adaptive Ranking and Screening (CARS) with SElector-Evaluator Value Assessment (SEVA) and Dynamic Adaptive Risk-aware Enhancement (DARE) form CARE-VI, an evidence-regulated target construction framework for off-policy actor-critic learning that preserves critic interfaces while improving TD target reliability. Theoretical guarantees and strong empirical wins (SAC, TD3, TD7 on MuJoCo).
AI.motivation: Off-policy actor-critic methods rely on reliable TD targets; naive refinement via next-state actions risks unstable or biased targets due to noisy rankings, reused scores, and fixed enhancement weights. A framework that adaptively ranks, reviews, and regulates residual corrections can improve target reliability and learning stability.
AI.method: CARS retains an ordered candidate prefix within a preset budget and narrows it only when a boundary gap exceeds a disagreement-scaled uncertainty radius. SEVA uses selector critics to order candidates and a separately parameterized evaluator critic to review the selected value, capping the reviewed value at the selector reference. DARE regulates each residual correction using candidate reliability, the gap between selector and evaluator, and a finite-stage factor. The three components integrate into CARE-VI, preserving standard critic regression and actor update interfaces.
AI.result: Theoretical bounds: CARS boundary error, SEVA selected-value overestimation, and one-sided deviation of DARE residual from its population counterpart; fixed-policy recovery after finite-stage perturbation. Empirically, CARE-VI achieves the highest mean return across SAC, TD3, and TD7 on four MuJoCo tasks (twelve settings), with ablations and scalar diagnostics confirming component roles.
AI.conclusion: CARE-VI provides an evidence-regulated target construction framework that improves TD target reliability in off-policy actor-critic learning while maintaining standard learning interfaces, backed by theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance.

title: Cross-Modal Attention Acts as a Frequency Filter: Why Verbose Prompts Improve Robustness in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are fragile under image corruption. We find that the wording of the question affects VLMs in two opposite ways. Verbose questions make VLMs substantially more robust---e.g., rephrasing "Is there a cat?" into "Please look carefully and answer: is there a cat?". Conversely, VLMs become more fragile under corruption when the question is semantically complex or finer-grained, e.g., "what colour is the cup left of the chair?" instead of "is there a cup?". Both effects stem from question-conditioned cross-modal attention, which induces a spectral filter over image patches: verbose questions broaden its frequency support, while fine-grained questions concentrate it onto fewer visual scales. The model's answer drifts most when this filter and the corruption sit on the same spatial frequencies. We test the filter view on Qwen3-VL and LLaVA-OneVision across GQA and CLEVR; verbose paraphrasing reduces drift variance by 70--81% on the 8B models. The practical recipe---pad the prompt---further yields measurable gains in accuracy, even under image corruption.

AI.tldr: Verbose question phrasing improves VLM robustness to image corruption, while semantically complex questions can worsen it; a cross-modal attention spectral filter explains both effects; prompting strategies (paraphrase, padding) can mitigate drift and boost accuracy.
AI.motivation: Understand why question wording affects image-language model robustness under corruption and propose a unified lens and practical fixes.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation of VLMs (Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-OneVision) on GQA and CLEVR with varied question wording (short vs verbose vs fine-grained); measure drift under image corruption; analyze cross-modal attention spectra; test prompt padding as a practical fix.
AI.result: Verbose paraphrasing reduces drift variance by 70–81% on 8B models; fine-grained questions increase drift; padding prompts yields accuracy gains under corruption; cross-modal attention acts as a spectral filter whose bandwidth controls robustness.
AI.conclusion: Question-conditioned cross-modal attention governs robustness to image corruption via spectral filtering; design prompts to widen or tailor the attention spectrum can robustify VLMs; padding is a simple, effective recipe.

title: GR2PO: Group Relative Return Policy Optimization for Continuous Robot Control
summary: Actor-critic architecture has been widely used in continuous robot control. However, they rely on learning a value network, introducing additional computational overhead during training. Moreover, policy learning may also be affected by the approximation error of value estimation. Critic-free group relative policy optimization methods provide a simpler training approach by removing the need for a critic. However, they fail to learn long-term action outcomes when directly applying immediate rewards to policy optimization in dense-reward environments. To address these problems, we propose Group Relative Return Policy Optimization (GR2PO), a critic-free reinforcement learning framework for continuous robot control. GR2PO estimates the discounted returns from the parallelly collected trajectories, performs group normalization at each rollout time index, and uses relative advantages and clipped targets to update the policy. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we instantiate it on robot control simulation environments and deploy the model to a real-world edge device. The results show that GR2PO significantly outperforms critic-free baselines that use immediate rewards and performs competitively against state-of-the-art actor-critic methods. Furthermore, GR2PO demonstrates competitive training efficiency. Inference tests on NVIDIA Jetson TX2 demonstrate the feasibility of deploying the learned policies on edge platforms. Further ablation experiments analyze the effects of parallel group size, return estimation methods, and target clipping ratio on learning performance. To support follow-up research, we will make the complete code publicly available after the paper is accepted, including the framework implementation, experimental configuration, and training and evaluation scripts.

AI.tldr: GR2PO is a critic-free RL framework for continuous control that estimates discounted returns from parallel trajectories, uses group normalization, relative advantages, and clipped targets to update policies; it outperforms critic-free baselines with immediate rewards and is competitive with actor-critic methods, with feasible edge deployment and informative ablations.
AI.motivation: Critic-free methods avoid value networks but struggle to learn long-term outcomes with immediate rewards; actor-critic methods incur computational overhead and suffer from value estimation error. There is a need for a critic-free approach that captures long-term returns and is efficient for edge deployment in continuous control.
AI.method: Introduce Group Relative Return Policy Optimization (GR2PO): estimate discounted returns from parallel rollouts, apply group normalization at each rollout time index, and update policies using relative advantages and clipped targets. Evaluate in robot control simulations and on NVIDIA Jetson TX2; perform ablations on parallel group size, return estimation methods, and clipping ratio. Plan to release full code and experimental configuration post-acceptance.
AI.result: GR2PO significantly outperforms critic-free baselines that use immediate rewards and is competitive with state-of-the-art actor-critic methods. It shows competitive training efficiency and feasible edge deployment (Jetson TX2). Ablation studies reveal effects of parallel group size, return estimation methods, and target clipping ratio on learning performance.
AI.conclusion: GR2PO provides an effective critic-free framework for continuous robot control that matches or surpasses critic-based methods while remaining computationally efficient and suitable for edge deployment. The work also commits to releasing code to support replication and future research.

title: MAGMA-GEN: Validated Recovery Supervision from Ambiguous Failures via Counterfactual Re-Execution
summary: Hierarchical robotic systems executing long-horizon manipulation tasks must make high-level semantic decisions that orchestrate stochastic low-level skills. In this setting, failed rollouts are ambiguous: a poor downstream state may reflect an invalid high-level decision, partial observation, or a valid decision whose physical execution failed. Traditional supervised learning lacks data for such recovery states, while reinforcement learning struggles with sparse rewards and non-local credit assignment. We propose MAGMA-GEN, an on-policy data-generation pipeline that converts ambiguous failed rollouts into validated recovery supervision. MAGMA-GEN first uses a privileged coach to hypothesize an early decision-level error and propose localized correction or recovery actions. Because this diagnosis is fallible, candidates are retained only if re-execution from the same state under matched conditions improves downstream progress. This produces supervised examples from the agent's own failure distribution without per-step human demonstrations. Evaluated on interactive long-horizon manipulation tasks, MAGMA-GEN improves task success and recovery capabilities, against distillation and trajectory-repair baselines under evolving task constraints in both simulation and real-robot execution.

AI.tldr: MAGMA-GEN: an on-policy data-generation pipeline that converts ambiguous failed rollouts into validated recovery supervision by using a privileged coach to propose localized corrections, retaining candidates only if re-execution under matched conditions improves downstream progress; enables supervision from the agent's own failure distribution without per-step human demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical long-horizon manipulation faces ambiguity in failed rollouts where poor downstream states can stem from invalid high-level decisions, partial observability, or execution failures. This makes standard supervised learning and reinforcement learning challenging (data scarcity for recovery, sparse rewards/credit).
AI.method: MAGMA-GEN runs an on-policy data-generation loop where a privileged coach identifies potential early decision-level errors and proposes targeted recovery actions. Because the diagnosis may be fallible, proposed corrections are kept only if re-execution from the same failure state under matched conditions yields improved downstream progress. This yields supervised examples sourced from the agent's own failure distribution without requiring per-step human demonstrations.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on interactive long-horizon manipulation tasks shows that MAGMA-GEN improves task success and recovery capabilities compared to distillation and trajectory-repair baselines, and remains effective under evolving task constraints in both simulation and real-robot execution.
AI.conclusion: MAGMA-GEN provides a data-efficient, on-policy source of recovery supervision for hierarchical long-horizon manipulation, bridging the gap between supervised learning and reinforcement learning by leveraging the agent's own failure distribution to generate validated corrections without extensive human demonstrations.

title: QoS-Aware Federated Learning for Multimodal In-Cabin Interaction in Smart Vehicles
summary: Modern smart vehicles leverage multimodal sensors, ranging from high-bandwidth vision systems to low-rate physiological monitors, to provide personalized in-cabin services. However, integrating high-fidelity multimodal fusion with collaborative training is often hindered by the heterogeneous and time-varying Quality of Service (QoS) constraints of vehicular networks. Standard Federated Learning (FL) approaches enforce rigid synchronous rounds that fail to account for these resource asymmetries, leading to safety-critical timing violations and energy exhaustion. In this paper, we propose FedQoS, a novel asynchronous, event-triggered FL framework that decouples local computation from global communication via a two-phase gating mechanism. First, we introduce a resource-aware training gate that initializes local learning only when sensing buffers and energy reserves meet safety thresholds, preventing ML tasks from compromising core vehicle mobility. Second, a QoS-aware transmission policy gates uplink updates based on an efficiency score that balances model novelty against instantaneous latency and energy costs. Locally, clients optimize an objective featuring a staleness-aware proximal term that dynamically adjusts the global anchor strength based on update age. Extensive experiments on multimodal vehicular datasets demonstrate that FedQoS achieves competitive personalized accuracy with only marginal performance loss compared to FedAvg, while substantially reducing QoS violations, cutting communication overhead by 76.7\%, and lowering latency cost by 26.0\%, demonstrating a highly favorable accuracy and efficiency balance for real-world vehicular deployments.

AI.tldr: FedQoS enables asynchronous, event-driven federated learning for multimodal vehicles using a two-phase gating mechanism to respect QoS and energy constraints, achieving near-FedAvg accuracy with major reductions in QoS violations and communication/latency costs.
AI.motivation: Rigid synchronous FL rounds are ill-suited for heterogeneous, time-varying vehicular QoS constraints, risking safety-critical timing violations and energy depletion. A framework that decouples computation from communication and adapts to local resource states is needed.
AI.method: Two-phase gating: (1) resource-aware training gate that starts local learning only when sensing buffers and energy meet safety thresholds; (2) QoS-aware transmission policy that gates uplink updates using an efficiency score balancing model novelty, latency, and energy. Locally, a staleness-aware proximal term adjusts global anchor strength based on update age.
AI.result: On multimodal vehicular datasets, FedQoS achieves competitive personalized accuracy with only minor loss versus FedAvg, while substantially reducing QoS violations and cutting communication overhead by 76.7%, and latency cost by 26.0%.
AI.conclusion: FedQoS provides a favorable accuracy–efficiency balance for real-world vehicular deployments by enabling asynchronous, QoS-aware FL with resilient resource-adaptive gating.

title: Bridging Modalities on the Cortex: Surface-based MRI to PET Translation with a Diffusion Bridge
summary: Cortical hypometabolism measured by Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography (FDG-PET) is a highly sensitive biomarker for dementia diagnosis. However, high costs, radiation exposure, and limited accessibility constrain its clinical utility. While cross-modal synthesis from Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) offers a promising alternative, existing volumetric generation methods do not explicitly account for the highly folded cortical geometry, where disease-related patterns predominantly reside. To address this, we introduce a novel surface-based diffusion bridge framework DB-SUiT for MRI-to-PET translation that operates natively on the cortical manifold. A conditional Spherical U-shaped vision Transformer (SUiT) is specifically designed to model the intricate cross-modal relationships while preserving surface topology. It combines spherical convolutional encoders for multi-scale surface feature extraction with bottleneck Transformers to capture long-range spatial dependencies, while incorporating demographic and subcortical conditions to refine the synthesis. Evaluated on two datasets, including subjects with different dementia types, DB-SUiT demonstrates high-fidelity synthesis that substantially outperforms other baselines. In automated dementia classification, synthesized PET surfaces improve performance over MRI by 14.2% and PET volumes by 11.3%, approaching the performance of real PET surfaces. In a blinded reader study, synthetic PET achieved 85.5% diagnostic accuracy, compared with 75.8% for MRI and 95.2% for real PET. This further demonstrates cross-cohort and cross-pathology generalization, as the model was evaluated without retraining on an external cohort that included a dementia subtype not represented during training. Our code is available at https://github.com/ai-med/DB-SUiT.

AI.tldr: Introduces DB-SUiT: a surface-based diffusion bridge for MRI-to-PET translation on the cortical manifold using a conditional spherical U-shaped transformer, improving dementia diagnosis performance and generalization, with code released.
AI.motivation: FDG-PET is sensitive for dementia but costly and invasive; cross-modal MRI synthesis aims to provide PET-like information without radiation or cost. Existing volumetric methods ignore cortical folding where disease patterns concentrate. The work targets geometry-aware MRI-to-PET synthesis on the cortex.
AI.method: A surface-based diffusion bridge framework (DB-SUiT) operating on the cortical manifold. A conditional Spherical U-shaped vision Transformer (SUiT) uses spherical convolutional encoders, bottleneck Transformers, and incorporates demographic and subcortical conditions. It performs multi-scale surface feature extraction and long-range dependency modeling to translate MRI features to PET surfaces. Evaluated on two dementia datasets, including multiple subtypes, with cross-cohort generalization.
AI.result: DB-SUiT achieves high-fidelity PET surface synthesis, surpassing baselines. In automated dementia classification, synthesized PET surfaces improve accuracy by 14.2% over MRI and 11.3% over PET volumes, approaching real PET performance. In a blinded reader study, synthetic PET achieved 85.5% diagnostic accuracy (MRI: 75.8%; real PET: 95.2%). The model generalizes across cohorts and a previously unseen dementia subtype without retraining. Code available at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: A geometry-aware, surface-based MRI-to-PET translation framework on the cortical manifold can yield PET-like biomarkers with strong diagnostic performance and cross-cohort generalization, offering a viable, non-invasive surrogate for PET in dementia assessment.

title: Feeling Terrain Before Crossing: World Models for Off-Road Navigation
summary: Navigation world models plan by foresight, predicting the future that each candidate action sequence produces and selecting the best, rather than mapping observations to actions directly. Unlike urban settings where a predicted scene is a sufficient proxy, off-road navigation hinges on the robot--terrain interaction, so the prediction must cover not only what the camera will see but what the robot will feel. However, existing scene-focused models do not predict how much the robot will slip, tilt or shake along a planned trajectory. Proprioception captures these dynamics directly and, when used as input, improves the prediction of the physical future. We present Feel-WM, the first off-road navigation world model that conditions on proprioception and predicts what the robot will feel alongside what the camera will see. The physical future takes the form of a future proprioceptive state and a failure risk, both learned from the robot's own experience without human labels. The planner rolls out the physical future alongside the scene and weighs the predicted failure risk against goal similarity in a separable score. Experiments on real off-road data and in simulation demonstrate that Feel-WM outperforms visual-only navigation world models in open-loop planning and closed-loop rough-terrain navigation across wheeled and legged platforms. Deployed on a Husky on mountain trails, Feel-WM plans onboard, predicts rough ground ahead and steers around it, completing courses that an end-to-end policy fails.

AI.tldr: A proprioception-conditioned off-road world model (Feel-WM) predicts both visual outcomes and future proprioception to improve planning; it integrates a predicted failure risk with goal similarity for planning, trained from self-collected robot data without labels, and demonstrates superior performance over visual-only models on wheeled/legged platforms in real and simulated off-road tasks.
AI.motivation: Off-road navigation requires modeling terrain interaction (slippage, tilt, shake) beyond camera-facing scene predictions. Proprioception provides direct information about dynamics, enabling more accurate physical future predictions and safer planning.
AI.method: Introduce Feel-WM, a world model that conditions on proprioception to predict a future proprioceptive state and a failure risk. The planner rolls out both the visual scene and physical futures, combining a separable score of failure risk and goal similarity. Trained from robot experience without human labels. Evaluated on real off-road data and simulation across wheeled and legged platforms; deployed onboard on a Husky.
AI.result: Feel-WM outperforms visual-only navigation world models in open-loop planning and closed-loop rough-terrain navigation, generalizing across platforms. It completed courses that an end-to-end policy failed, by predicting rough ground ahead and steering around it.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating proprioception into world models yields more accurate physical futures and safer, more effective planning for off-road navigation, enabling onboard planning and better performance than vision-only models.

title: WiCleanData: Guaranteeing the Type Consistency of Wikidata by Taxonomy Refinement and Constraint Enforcement
summary: Because of its collaborative nature, Wikidata suffers from errors, in- consistencies, and excessive complexity, such as redundant classes, ambiguity between instances and classes, wrong taxonomic paths, and type constraint violations. The manual curation of these issues is infeasible at scale. To address these challenges, we introduce WiCleanData, a refined version of Wikidata with a consistent tax- onomy and free from type constraint violations. Specifically, we have designed an automated pipeline that first cleans the taxonomy with language model assistance, then simplifies type constraints by hierarchical aggregation, and finally filters facts accordingly. The resulting knowledge graph, free from any type violation, is made publicly available via a Web interface, enabling easy exploration and downstream applications.

AI.tldr: WiCleanData: a refined Wikidata with a consistent taxonomy and no type constraint violations, produced by an automated LM-assisted taxonomy cleaning pipeline and hierarchical constraint aggregation, publicly accessible via a Web interface.
AI.motivation: Wikidata suffers from errors, inconsistencies, and excessive complexity (redundant classes, instance-class ambiguity, wrong taxonomic paths, and type-constraint violations); manual curation is infeasible at scale.
AI.method: An automated pipeline: (1) clean taxonomy with language model assistance, (2) simplify type constraints by hierarchical aggregation, (3) filter facts accordingly; output is a type-violation-free knowledge graph released via a Web interface.
AI.result: WiCleanData is the resulting KB; taxonomy cleaned, constraints simplified; publicly available for exploration and downstream applications.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates feasible scalable KG curation by combining LM-assisted taxonomy cleaning and constraint aggregation, producing a clean, usable knowledge graph and enabling downstream tasks; the public release encourages adoption and benchmarking.

title: Local Sparsity Enables Unsupervised LLM Safety Detection
summary: Deployment-time safety methods for large language models (LLMs) are predominantly supervised and assume access to unsafe training data. Nevertheless, new attacks and harm categories regularly arise, not captured by models trained in such a supervised fashion. An alternative approach is to view this problem through the lens of anomaly detection, namely, to rely solely on modeling safe data and flagging out-of-distribution inputs. However, LLM activations lie in a high-dimensional space, raising concerns about whether anomaly detection is statistically feasible. We show that, under the linear representation hypothesis (LRH), there may indeed be hope. In the LRH concept space, which is typically recovered via a sparse autoencoder (SAE), nearby points share a small common active support. Using this local sparsity insight, we propose a framework for locally masked SAE-based anomaly detection, supported by theoretical justifications. We validate it on various architectures and datasets, including both capability-testing datasets and safety-specific datasets. Finally, when we allow algorithms to use 1% out-of-distribution data for calibration, locally sparse methods achieve near-optimal performance, demonstrating their ability to capture meaningful safety information while using only 1-2% of SAE neurons for computation.

AI.tldr: Locally sparse SAE-based anomaly detection under the Linear Representation Hypothesis enables effective deployment-time safety with minimal calibration data, achieving near-optimal performance while using only a small fraction of SAE neurons.
AI.motivation: Safety for LLMs at deployment requires detecting novel, unsafe inputs without relying on unsafe training data. High-dimensional LLM activations make anomaly detection challenging; the linear representation hypothesis (LRH) suggests a low-dimensional, locally shared active support can be exploited to detect out-of-distribution inputs.
AI.method: Recover a concept space via a sparse autoencoder (SAE) under the LRH. Develop a locally masked SAE-based anomaly detection framework that exploits local sparsity in the concept space. Validate across multiple architectures and both capability-testing and safety-specific datasets. Incorporate calibration with small amounts (as low as 1%) of out-of-distribution data.
AI.result: Locally sparse methods achieve near-optimal detection performance with only 1–2% of SAE neurons active for computation, given just 1% OOD calibration data, and show robust performance across architectures and datasets.
AI.conclusion: LRH-guided locally sparse SAE-based anomaly detection is a promising, data-efficient approach for deployment-time LLM safety, capable of adapting to new danger categories with minimal additional calibration data.

title: Task-Oriented Semantic Feature Transmission for Multi-Task Satellite Remote Sensing over Low-SNR Channels
summary: Conventional satellite remote sensing transmission follows a reconstruct-then-infer paradigm that optimizes pixel-level fidelity, creating an objective mismatch with downstream tasks such as classification and detection, especially at low SNR. This paper investigates a task-oriented framework that bypasses image reconstruction and directly transmits semantic features extracted by a multitask-pretrained backbone. A lightweight channel adaptation module (CAM) compresses feature dimensionality for bandwidth reduction, and a feature restorer recovers task-relevant structure after channel corruption. With the backbone frozen, the CAM and task-specific downstream heads are jointly optimized with task and feature-level supervision under random-SNR training. Under the adopted AWGN setting, experiments on scene classification and object detection show consistent gains over reconstruction-oriented JSCC baselines across different SNR conditions, with the largest improvements in the low-SNR regime.

AI.tldr: Task-oriented semantic transmission for satellite sensing: sends compressed semantic features instead of pixel data, using a channel-adaptive module and a feature restorer; frozen backbone with joint optimization, achieving gains over pixel-reconstruction JSCC, especially at low SNR.
AI.motivation: Pixels may be redundant for downstream tasks. Align communication with task objectives (classification/detection) to improve task accuracy and efficiency under bandwidth and noise constraints in satellite systems.
AI.method: Extract semantic features with a multitask-pretrained backbone; use a lightweight channel adaptation module (CAM) to compress feature dimensionality; a feature restorer recovers task-relevant structure after channel corruption. Train CAM and downstream heads while keeping the backbone frozen, using both task-level and feature-level supervision under random SNR with AWGN channel models.
AI.result: Consistent performance gains over reconstruction-oriented JSCC baselines across SNRs for scene classification and object detection, with the largest improvements in low-SNR settings.
AI.conclusion: Task-oriented feature transmission with joint optimization and channel adaptation improves robustness and efficiency for satellite remote sensing tasks in noisy channels, reducing reconstruction emphasis while maintaining or boosting task performance.

title: Learning Reliable Parking Policies via Offline Reinforcement Learning with Quantized Action Representations
summary: Parking is a routine yet safety-critical task for autonomous vehicles operating in urban environments. However, cluttered and weakly structured parking spaces, compounded by the interactive uncertainty from surrounding vehicles, hinder reliable maneuver generation. To address these challenges, we develop a waypoint-level offline reinforcement learning framework for interaction-aware autonomous parking. Specifically, a dedicated parking dataset is constructed from hierarchical expert rollouts with rotational waypoint augmentation, covering both non-interactive scenarios and interactive ones. The policy is then conditioned on a compact state representation, in which LiDAR-based obstacle features are adapted to the target pose via feature-wise linear modulation. A state-conditioned tokenizer further quantizes continuous waypoint sequences into discrete action tokens, over which conservative Q-learning is performed to suppress value overestimation on poorly supported actions. Extensive closed-loop experiments are conducted in the high-fidelity CARLA simulator. The proposed framework attains the highest parking success rate among all baselines and transfers reliably to unseen parking slots.

AI.tldr: A waypoint-level offline RL framework for interaction-aware autonomous parking using FiLM-modulated LiDAR features and a state-conditioned tokenized action space, achieving strong CARLA performance and transfer to unseen slots.
AI.motivation: Parking in urban, cluttered environments with interaction uncertainty demands data-efficient, safe planning. Traditional planners struggle with weakly structured spaces and multi-agent interactions; offline RL with discrete actions and robust representations can improve reliability and safety.
AI.method: 1) Build a parking dataset from hierarchical expert rollouts with rotational waypoint augmentation to cover both non-interactive and interactive scenarios. 2) Condition the policy on a compact state representation. 3) Adapt LiDAR obstacle features to the target pose via feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). 4) Use a state-conditioned tokenizer to quantize continuous waypoint sequences into discrete action tokens. 5) Apply conservative Q-learning on tokens to mitigate value overestimation for poorly supported actions.
AI.result: Closed-loop experiments in CARLA show the approach achieves the highest parking success rate among baselines and can transfer to unseen parking slots, indicating strong data efficiency and generalization within the test domain.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses clutter and interaction uncertainty in autonomous parking by combining offline RL with a compact state representation, FiLM-based perception adaptation, and discrete-action tokenization, achieving robust performance and transfer in simulation.

title: FCA-Guided Counterfactual Explanations for Multi-Modal Breast Cancer Diagnosis: A Framework Achieving Perfect Validity with Emergent Sparsity
summary: Deep learning models for multi-modal breast cancer diagnosis achieve high predictive accuracy but remain clinically unacceptable without actionable, counterfactual explanations. Attribution-based methods (LIME, SHAP) are categorically inapplicable to this purpose, as they generate no alternative instances and thus cannot be evaluated on counterfactual quality metrics. This investigation provides empirical evidence that FCA-Guided Counterfactual (FCA-CF) framework that uses a Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) concept lattice as a hard structural constraint on counterfactual search, operating over a multi-modal TCGA-BRCA dataset. We benchmark against four genuine counterfactual methods: Wachter-style CF, DiCE, FACE, and NICE, evaluated on 60 benign-predicted TCGA-BRCA instances. The FCA-CF framework achieves Validity = 1.0000 (100% of counterfactuals successfully flip the prediction), Sparsity = 2.37 features changed (best among all valid methods), and Proximity = 0.900 (normalised L2-based, matching NICE as joint best). The classifier achieves Accuracy = 0.980, F1 = 0.976, ROC-AUC = 0.9947. Ablation analysis confirms that the FCA lattice constraint is the primary sparsity driver (removing it increases sparsity by +40%, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.78), while Phase C greedy refinement accounts for the largest individual contribution (+113% sparsity increase when disabled, p < 0.001, d = 5.01). FCA-guided counterfactual generation achieves a clinically important Pareto-dominant outcome; it is simultaneously the sparsest and among the most proximate of all valid methods, with perfect validity. The emergent sparsity property arising from lattice topology rather than numerical penalty terms constitutes a structurally novel contribution to the counterfactual explanation literature.

AI.tldr: FCA-CF uses a Formal Concept Analysis lattice as a hard constraint on counterfactual search for multi-modal breast cancer diagnosis; achieves perfect validity, best sparsity, strong proximity; ablations show lattice drives sparsity; claims emergent structural sparsity from lattice.
AI.motivation: Need for actionable counterfactual explanations in medical DL models; attribution methods insufficient; to provide clinically actionable, evaluable counterfactuals.
AI.method: Construct FCA lattice from data; constrain counterfactual search (hard constraint) to lattice; compare with Wachter CF, DiCE, FACE, NICE on 60 benign-pred TCGA-BRCA instances; evaluate Validity, Sparsity, Proximity; ablation to assess contributions; Phase C greedy refinement.
AI.result: Validity=1.0000; Sparsity=2.37 features; Proximity=0.900; Classifier metrics: Accuracy 0.980, F1 0.976, ROC-AUC 0.9947; Ablation: lattice constraint reduces sparsity by ~40%; Phase C greedy refinement contributes largest sparsity increase when disabled (~+113%); Pareto-dominant: sparse and proximal with perfect validity.
AI.conclusion: FCA-lattice constrained CF provides a novel, structurally driven sparsity mechanism; yields clinically meaningful counterfactuals; emerges from lattice topology rather than numerical penalties; outperforms four genuine methods on the study.

title: Fast-varying Natural Frequencies and Damping Ratio Identification for Linear Time-Varying System
comment: Preprint submitted to Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing
summary: This work proposes a physics-enhanced machine learning approach for the system identification of Linear Time-Varying (LTV) systems under time-varying operating conditions in terms of fast-varying natural frequencies and damping ratios by combining a long short-term memory network with an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). The proposed approach uses vibration data (displacement and velocity measurements), domain knowledge of modal damping ratios, and a physics-based model that can yield an approximate natural frequencies time-dependency model. The approach is validated using synthetic data generated from a finite element model of a 2-blade offshore wind turbine under realistic environmental and operating conditions. This system displays fast time-varying frequencies due to operating conditions, whose identification is particularly challenging because of the wind and wave loading. The robustness of the proposed approach is assessed under assumed incorrect system information (e.g. damping ratio). The proposed approach is evaluated across different environmental and operating conditions to show its applicability to different operating regimes. The results show the approach can accurately identify the selected fast-varying natural frequency, 1st Fore-Aft (FA-1) mode, with a maximum root mean square error of 0.0012 Hz. The results demonstrate that the model trained on EKF estimates depends on accurate damping values, whereas the model trained on physics-based data exhibits robustness to incorrect damping assumptions. The approach is extended to damping ratio identification for the selected mode by estimating the root mean square error between models trained on EKF estimates and physics-based data. The results show that the approach can yield a good approximation of the FA-1 mode damping ratio using grid search, offering an improvement over covariance-driven stochastic subspace identification.

AI.tldr: A physics-enhanced ML framework combining LSTM and EKF for fast-varying LTV system identification, using vibration data and physics-based frequency models; validated on synthetic wind-turbine data; achieves very low RMSE for FA-1 frequency and shows robustness to damping misspecification; damping ratio estimation via grid search outperforms SSI.
AI.motivation: Identify time-varying modal properties under changing environmental/operating loads where pure data-driven or purely physics-based methods struggle; incorporate physics to constrain learning and improve robustness.
AI.method: Hybrid approach: use LSTM to model temporal evolution of dynamics; apply Extended Kalman Filter with a physics-informed time-varying natural frequency model and known modal damping; input includes displacement/velocity data; leverage physics data for training; assess robustness to incorrect damping; extend to damping ratio identification via grid search; compare against covariance-driven stochastic subspace identification (SSI).
AI.result: Accurate FA-1 natural frequency tracking with RMSE up to 0.0012 Hz; EKF-estimate–trained models are sensitive to damping values, while physics-based training shows robustness to damping misspecification; damping ratio approximated well via grid search, outperforming SSI in this aspect.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates promise of physics-informed ML (LSTM+EKF) for tracking fast-varying modal properties in LTV systems under realistic conditions; synthetic validation supports applicability, but real-data validation and robustness to noise/model mismatch remain to be demonstrated.

title: Ischemic Stroke Segmentation and Net Water Uptake Quantification on Multicenter Non-Contrast CT Using Supervised Target-Domain Adaptation
summary:
Objectives: Quantitative assessment of infarct hypodensity on non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT), including net water uptake (NWU), requires manual or semi-manual lesion delineation, often guided by CT perfusion or diffusion-weighted MRI, limiting clinical applicability. Automated segmentation on NCCT could enable efficient biomarker extraction such as NWU but remains challenging across heterogeneous multicenter data. This study aimed to develop and externally test a domain-aware deep learning framework for ischemic stroke segmentation on NCCT and assess its suitability for NWU quantification.
  Materials & Methods: In this retrospective multicenter study of 801 patients from four datasets, an nnU-Net-based model was trained on NCCT scans from the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf and the Acute Ischemic Stroke Dataset. To adapt to new domains, the model was fine-tuned on target-domain subsets from Boston (n=11) and ISLES (n=75), with evaluation on held-out cases not used for fine-tuning. Automated segmentations and NWU values were compared with expert references.
  Results: For lesions $\geq$ 30 mL, median Dice was 0.68 (Boston) and 0.56 (ISLES). Including smaller lesions, which predominated in ISLES, median Dice was 0.54 (interquartile range [IQR] 0.30-0.70) for acute lesion segmentation (Boston dataset) and 0.20 (IQR 0.03-0.41) for NCCT lesion segmentations when compared to post-treatment infarct (primary target of the ISLES challenge). Automated NWU mean absolute error was 1.37 percentage points (SD 1.61, Boston).
  Conclusion: Target-domain adaptation supported NCCT-only infarct segmentation across heterogeneous external cohorts, although performance varied across domains. The approach enabled low-error NWU quantification from baseline NCCT without advanced imaging, supporting further prospective clinical evaluation.

AI.tldr: Domain-adapted nnU-Net enables automated NCCT infarct segmentation enabling NWU quantification across multicenter data; performance varies by domain, but external testing shows potential for NCCT-only biomarker extraction.
AI.motivation: Manual lesion delineation to compute NWU on NCCT is time-consuming and not scalable; automated NCCT segmentation would enable a practical biomarker; however multicenter data heterogeneity hinders generalization; domain-aware adaptation aims to address this.
AI.method: Train nnU-Net on NCCT from two datasets; fine-tune on small target-domain subsets (Boston n=11, ISLES n=75); evaluate on held-out cases; compare automated segmentation and NWU with expert references; include 801 patients from four datasets.
AI.result: For lesions ≥30 mL, median Dice: Boston 0.68, ISLES 0.56; including smaller lesions, Dice 0.54 (Boston acute), 0.20 (ISLES). NWU MAE 1.37 percentage points (Boston). External domain adaptation allowed NCCT-only segmentation with varying performance; NWU quantified with low error.
AI.conclusion: Target-domain adaptation enables NCCT-only infarct segmentation across heterogeneous external cohorts and supports NWU extraction without advanced imaging; promising for prospective evaluation.

title: Learning and Transferring Closed-Loop Robot Software
summary: Closed-loop robot policies require observation processing, state management, and situation-dependent branching, making them costly to design and tune manually. Although coding agents increasingly support control-code generation and optimization, it remains unclear whether implementations improved on source tasks also support policy acquisition for new tasks. We study this question by treating complete closed-loop implementations as reusable execution experience. For each source task, a coding agent generates policy code from a few successful demonstrations and iteratively improves it using simulation feedback. The validation-selected implementations are retained in a software archive. For new tasks, the agent generates and improves policies using archived implementations, target demonstrations, and execution feedback. The resulting policy is then frozen and executes without further model calls. Across four source tasks in RoboCasa, iterative optimization increases mean success from 28.3% to 64.2%. Across nine target tasks and three independent runs, mean success is 45.2% without references, 41.5% with initial source code, and 57.0% with optimized source code. Optimized references outperform initial references in all three runs on the nine-task average, with a mean gain of 15.6 percentage points. These results demonstrate the value of execution-improved software as a resource for acquiring new policies in this setting, although initial references remain better on two target tasks when averaged across runs.

AI.tldr: Reuse complete closed-loop policy implementations as execution experiences to bootstrap and optimize policies for new tasks, achieving substantial transfer gains.
AI.motivation: Designing robust closed-loop policies is expensive and manual tuning is required. It is unclear whether improvements on source tasks transfer to new tasks. The work treats complete closed-loop implementations as reusable execution experience to facilitate policy acquisition.
AI.method: For each source task, a coding agent generates policy code from a few demonstrations and iteratively refines it using simulation feedback, then validates and archives successful implementations. For new tasks, the agent uses archived implementations, target demonstrations, and execution feedback to generate and improve policies, which are frozen and executed without further model calls.
AI.result: On source tasks (RoboCasa), iterative optimization raises mean success from 28.3% to 64.2%. On nine target tasks (three runs): mean success is 45.2% without references, 41.5% with initial source code, and 57.0% with optimized source code. Optimized references outperform initial references by 15.6 percentage points on the nine-task average. Initial references outperform on two target tasks across runs.
AI.conclusion: Execution-improved software can serve as a reusable resource to acquire new policies, enabling transfer and improved performance. However, initial references still excel on some tasks, indicating room for further improvement and task-dependent effects.

title: Marginal utility, matrix factorization, and the Key-Value (KV) cache: a unified information-economic framework for sovereign geo-mining inference
comment: Version 11, 14 septembre 2026. 49 pages, 9 tables. Les valeurs de l'architecture souveraine sont projet{é}es et non mesur{é}es ; le calcul {à} grande {é}chelle est en cours. Soumission pr{é}vue {à} IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence
summary: This paper builds a theoretical bridge between the economic notion of marginal utility and two machine-learning constructs, matrix factorization and the Key--Value cache of transformer language models. The singular value spectrum of a rating matrix is shown to be a diminishing marginal utility schedule for latent factors, the eigenvalue spectrum of the projected covariance operator to be the marginal utility schedule of a model's learned representation, and cache eviction and low-rank cache compression to be instances of constrained utility maximization under a memory budget. The three collapse into a single allocation rule: retain the top dimensions whose eigenvalue exceeds the shadow price of the binding constraint. The framework is applied to the automated extraction of structured information from geo-mining documents, where it motivates a multi-pass inference protocol, a layer-wise TIES model merging procedure, and a selection policy combining extraction quality, localization drift and energy, scalarized with a Conditional Value-at-Risk term on drift. Two empirical contributions are reported. An 11.2-million-parameter hierarchical classifier, trained in about five minutes on a single GPU, reaches 90.0 per cent level-1 accuracy on a held-out test set from a 973-document uranium-exploration corpus, against 92.0 per cent for a proprietary model on a fifty-document human audit of the same corpus, at a latency of 2.62 ms per card against approximately 2,000 ms for the API and at negligible cost. A diagnostic of uniform-density TIES merging exposes a reproducible degenerate mode in which the merged model returns token-identical outputs across five geographically distinct districts while declaring high confidence; re-executing the merge under layer-wise calibrated densities removes that signature on the diagnostic sample. The full-scale extraction benchmark, including LoRA fine-tuning, is reported as projected rather than measured and remains an empirical extension of this work.

AI.tldr: A theoretical framework linking marginal utility to ML constructs (matrix factorization, transformer caches), yielding a single allocation rule to keep top eigen-dimensions above a shadow price; applied to geo-mining info extraction with a multi-pass inference protocol and TIES merging; reports an 11.2M-parameter classifier achieving 90% L1 on uranium corpus, with a diagnostic that reveals a degenerate merge mode mitigated by density calibration; full-scale benchmark is projected.
AI.motivation: To unify economic intuition of marginal utility with spectral ML representations and memory-constrained caching, enabling principled dimension selection and efficient inference for structured information extraction.
AI.method: Establish spectral-marginal utility correspondences: singular values map to latent-factor utility; eigen-spectrum maps to representation utility; cache eviction and low-rank compression as constrained utility maximization under memory budget; derive a single allocation rule: retain top dimensions whose eigenvalue exceeds the shadow price. Implemented in a geo-mining extraction pipeline with a multi-pass inference protocol, layer-wise TIES model merging, and a drift-penalty CVaR scalarization; empirical pipeline includes LoRA fine-tuning and energy-aware selection.
AI.result: Two empirical contributions: (1) an 11.2M-parameter hierarchical classifier trained in about five minutes on a single GPU achieving 90.0% L1 accuracy on a 973-document uranium-exploration corpus; (2) a 50-document human audit showing 92.0% on a proprietary model with 2.62 ms per card vs ~2000 ms for API; a diagnostic reveals a reproducible degenerate merge mode in TIES that is mitigated by layer-wise calibrated densities; full-scale extraction benchmark is projected, not measured, and remains an empirical extension.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a unified allocation principle tying economics and ML constructs under memory constraints, with practical gains for structured information extraction and model merging; highlights potential degeneracy in TIES merges as a challenge to address in future work.

title: QUALS: Corpus Equilibrium for Universal Forecasting via Pattern Quantization and Learnability Synchronization
summary: Ubiquitous time series data across diverse domains enables critical applications in areas such as transportation systems and power grids. Recently, training foundation models on massive datasets to achieve accurate zero-shot forecasting has emerged as a major research focus. However, current studies predominantly prioritize architectural innovations while insufficiently addressing data diversity, often relying on simple data sampling strategies that fail to manage complex data distributions effectively, leading to inefficient use of training data and suboptimal performance. To address this, we propose QUALS, a large-scale time series corpus equilibrium framework. QUALS significantly enhances data efficiency, i.e., enabling existing models to achieve superior performance using only a small fraction of the original training data. Specifically, QUALS operates through two core mechanisms. First, a pattern quantization framework systematically decodes heterogeneous patterns from mixed corpora via vector quantization and uniform binning. Second, a learnability synchronization framework calibrates sampling weights for heterogeneous patterns, bridging the optimization gap between simple and complex motifs to maximize overall training efficiency. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that pre-training on QUALS consistently achieves superior zero-shot performance, even under substantially reduced training budgets.

AI.tldr: QUALS: a large-scale time series corpus equilibrium framework that improves data efficiency for pre-training time-series models by partitioning and balancing heterogeneous patterns via pattern quantization and learnability synchronization.
AI.motivation: Current emphasis on architectural innovations overlooks data diversity and sampling efficiency; naive sampling across mixed time-series corpora leads to underutilization of training data and suboptimal zero-shot forecasting performance.
AI.method: Two core mechanisms: (1) pattern quantization with vector quantization and uniform binning to decode heterogeneous patterns from mixed corpora; (2) learnability synchronization to calibrate sampling weights for patterns, aligning optimization between simple and complex motifs to maximize training efficiency.
AI.result: Pre-training on QUALS yields superior zero-shot performance with substantially reduced training budgets across extensive benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: QUALS advances data-efficient foundation-model pre-training for time series by effectively representing and weighting diverse patterns, enabling strong zero-shot results under constrained data usage.

title: Needles in a Raystack: Ultra-Sparse LiDAR Occupancy Detection for Bat Tracks
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted and presented at the AI4Nature@AVSS 2026 Workshop of the 22nd International Conference on Advanced Visual and Signal-Based Systems (AVSS 2026), Lecce, Italy
summary:
Monitoring flying animals is important for understanding and protecting biodiversity, but nocturnal species such as bats are difficult to observe in the field. Using LiDAR, bat movements at night result in ultra-sparse 3D spatio-temporal data in which standard reconstruction losses tend to predict only background and miss real flight paths. We study this problem as voxel-wise occupancy detection in sensor-centric LiDAR raystacks. A lightweight 3D U-Net is proposed that preserves temporal resolution, uses skip connections for spatial detail, and combines weighted binary cross-entropy with Dice loss to handle the strong class imbalance.
  In real LiDAR recordings of bats over open fields, cross-checked with acoustic monitoring, a reconstruction-based 3D convolutional autoencoder baseline fails to recover foreground trajectories. In contrast, the proposed U-Net recovers sparse foreground occupancy in diagnostic experiments and produces coherent occupancy patterns along bat flight trajectories, providing a practical basis for validation-scale experiments, later clustering of flight tracks, and future integration of bat activity information into biodiversity-aware turbine curtailment strategies.

AI.tldr: Lightweight 3D U-Net for voxel-wise occupancy detection in sparse LiDAR data to recover bat flight trajectories, outperforming a reconstruction-based autoencoder baseline.
AI.motivation: Nocturnal bats are difficult to observe; LiDAR yields ultra-sparse 3D data, making standard reconstruction losses fail to recover real flight paths, hindering biodiversity monitoring and turbine-impact assessment.
AI.method: Sensor-centric LiDAR raystacks; voxel-wise occupancy detection with a lightweight 3D U-Net preserving temporal resolution, using skip connections and a loss combining weighted binary cross-entropy and Dice loss to address extreme class imbalance; comparison against a 3D convolutional autoencoder baseline.
AI.result: The proposed U-Net recovers sparse foreground occupancy and coherent flight trajectories in real bat recordings, whereas the autoencoder baseline fails to retrieve foreground paths; the approach provides a practical basis for validation-scale experiments, clustering of flight tracks, and integration of bat activity into biodiversity-aware turbine strategies.
