AI.conclusion: Occupancy-based recovery in sparse LiDAR data is viable for nocturnal bat monitoring and can support subsequent analyses (tracking, clustering) and application to turbine curtailment; suggests a practical workflow for biodiversity-informed wind energy operations.

title: Distributed Model Predictive Control with Connectivity-based Contracts
summary: Teams of mobile robots rely on continuous communication with their neighbors for coordination, yet most distributed model predictive control (DMPC) schemes assume the communication network stays connected rather than actively enforcing it. Adding such a guarantee is hard since the usual mathematical condition for connectivity is nonconvex and links every agent to every other, which is incompatible with a scalable distributed real-time controller. We propose a DMPC framework in which each agent is assigned a connectivity contract: a local region prescribing where its predicted positions may lie over the prediction horizon. The contracts are designed so that, as long as every agent stays within its own contract, the team is guaranteed to remain connected. Given the maintained contract graph, an agent builds its contract from a single exchange with its immediate neighbors, after which every agent solves its own optimization problem independently. We prove that the resulting closed-loop system maintains connectivity, avoids collisions, and respects local state and input constraints. Simulation and hardware experiments on miniature autonomous car-like robots demonstrate the approach.

AI.tldr: Introduces a decentralized DMPC framework using connectivity contracts to guarantee network connectivity for multi-robot teams while enabling independent optimization.
AI.motivation: Guarantee connectivity in distributed MPC for robotic teams without sacrificing scalability; nonconvex connectivity constraints hinder real-time distributed control.
AI.method: Assign each agent a local connectivity contract defining where predicted positions can lie; maintain a contract graph via a single exchange with neighbors; each agent solves its own DMPC with its contract; proven guarantees on connectivity, collision avoidance, and constraint satisfaction.
AI.result: The framework ensures connectivity, collision avoidance, and adherence to state/input constraints; validated by simulations and hardware experiments on small autonomous car-like robots.
AI.conclusion: Connectivity-contract DMPC provides scalable, provable guarantees for maintaining network connectivity in multi-robot coordination while enabling decentralized optimization.

title: Tailored to you: longitudinal effects of personalising language models
summary: Interest in developing personalised language models is rapidly growing. While personalisation is often viewed as a mechanism to better serve diverse user needs, the effects of sustained interactions with personalised models on people's perception of and behaviour toward AI remain poorly understood. Most critically, downstream consequences outside the immediate human--AI interaction loop, such as effects on users' self-perceptions and interpersonal relationships, remain largely unexamined. In this study, we recruited 992 participants to complete daily advice-seeking interactions with language models over the course of five days, comparing outcomes from a non-personalised baseline against two personalisation approaches: memory-based (conditioned on prior conversational history) and survey-based (conditioned on information collected through a pre-study intake survey). We find that several changes in human-AI interaction over time are driven primarily by repeated exposure rather than personalisation itself. However, participants interacting with personalised models experienced differences in advice-seeking and information-sharing attitudes and behaviours: participants in the memory-based condition engaged in greater self-disclosure and rated the model as less creepy, while participants in the survey-based condition reported higher regret about having shared personal information with the AI. We conclude by highlighting the nuanced effects of different personalisation approaches on interaction outcomes, and discussing the implications of these findings for the responsible design and deployment of personalised AI systems.

AI.tldr: Five-day study on personalised language models shows that repeated exposure drives changes in user behavior; memory-based personalization increases self-disclosure and lowers perceived creepiness, while survey-based personalization raises regret about sharing; many effects arise from repetition rather than personalization per se.
AI.motivation: To understand downstream effects of LM personalization on user perception and behavior, including self-perception and social relationships, beyond immediate task performance.
AI.method: Experimental study with 992 participants over five days, randomized to three conditions: non-personalised baseline, memory-based personalization (conditioning on prior history), and survey-based personalization (conditioning on intake survey). Participants engaged in daily advice-seeking interactions with LMs; outcomes include self-disclosure, perceived creepiness, information-sharing attitudes, regret, and other attitude/behaviour changes over time.
AI.result: Repeated exposure largely drives changes in human–AI interaction; personalization yields distinct effects: memory-based increases self-disclosure and reduces creepiness; survey-based increases regret about sharing.
AI.conclusion: Personalisation effects are nuanced; design should account for different personalization modalities, user privacy, and consent to mitigate adverse psychological responses and to optimize beneficial outcomes in responsible AI deployments.

title: A Noise Optimum in Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning: Isolation, Mechanism, and Scope
summary: Injecting stochastic noise into a consolidation rule can improve a network's retention of earlier tasks up to an optimal level, then degrade it -- an inverted-U in retention vs. noise. This paper isolates what produces that optimum and maps where it holds, entirely in simulation. (1) Phenomenon: the retention inverted-U appears on several related-task continual-learning benchmarks (Split-MNIST, FashionMNIST, continual Yin-Yang). (2) Isolation: a magnitude-matched ladder shows the effect requires coherent restoring toward the consolidated weights -- a random-direction force of identical magnitude produces no optimum, and a coherent force toward the wrong target actively hurts. (3) Active ingredient: most of the optimum is recovered by coupling the anchor gain to the injected-noise variance sigma^2 -- a one-line rule that neither Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Adaptation (fixed gain) nor MESU (posterior-variance gain) implements. A forced Ornstein-Uhlenbeck calculation derives the rising flank and predicts that the optimal noise rises with per-task interference g -- confirmed out-of-sample in direction against pre-existing measurements (the exponent is unresolved at our grid). The barrier-conditioning of the originating Doob h-transform is a low-sigma safety net that bounds forgetting where the coupled gain is too weak. (4) Scope: the optimum requires shared task structure -- it is absent on permuted-MNIST, and a controlled rotated-vs-permuted comparison localizes the boundary to task structure; the precise governing quantity is left open. (5) Length: at matched severity the advantage persists but attenuates with task count, and we show no rotation family can attribute the trend (a compact-group identity). A single-seed BrainScaleS-2 demonstration of the originating rule is reported separately (Howe, arXiv:2607.06924); this paper makes no hardware claim.

AI.tldr: In simulations of continual learning, adding stochastic noise to the consolidation rule yields an inverted-U retention curve; the optimum arises from a one-line rule that couples anchor gain to the injected-noise variance, requires coherent restoration toward consolidated weights, and depends on task structure. It is absent in permuted tasks and does not claim hardware advantages.
AI.motivation: Identify the mechanism that creates the retention optimum under noise in continual-learning networks and map the domain over which it holds.
AI.method: Simulation-based experiments across related-task benchmarks (Split-MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, continual Yin-Yang) with magnitude-matched ladders; comparisons between coherent restoring toward consolidated weights vs random directions; theoretical treatment via forced Ornstein-Uhlenbeck calculations and Doob h-transform; evaluation of task-structure dependence (permuted vs structured tasks); a BrainScaleS-2 single-seed demonstration referenced separately.
AI.result: A retention inverted-U persists across several related-task benchmarks and is abolished by random-direction forces of equal magnitude but preserved when forces coherently target the consolidated weights. The majority of the optimum is recovered by coupling the anchor gain to the injected-noise variance sigma^2, a simple rule not implemented by standard Ornstein-Uhlenbeck adaptation or MESU. The rising flank can be predicted by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck analysis; the optimal-noise level increases with task interference g. Doob h-transform barrier-conditioning provides a low-sigma safety net against forgetting when coupling is weak. The optimum requires shared task structure and is absent in permuted MNIST; boundary localization to task structure is noted but the governing quantity is not resolved. At matched severity, the benefit persists but attenuates with more tasks; rotation-family explanations fail to account for the trend. A separate hardware demonstration (BrainScaleS-2) is reported elsewhere; this paper does not claim hardware results.
AI.conclusion: The dominant driver of the optima is a simple, noise-variance–coupled anchor gain that enforces coherent restoration toward consolidated weights; task structure is essential for the effect, and the precise governing quantity remains open. The results point to a principled rule for noise-assisted consolidation in continual learning, with limitations tied to task structure and scale.

title: MTF-Net: Multi-Modal Temporal Feature Fusion Network for Pedestrian Intention Prediction
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, accepted on International Conference on Cloud and Network Computing
summary: Accurately predicting pedestrian intentions is crucial for ensuring safe and proactive interaction between autonomous vehicles and pedestrians. However, existing approaches often depend on architectures that either model temporal dependencies within individual modalities or fuse modalities only at coarse semantic levels. To address these limitations, we propose MTF-Net, a novel Multi-Modal Temporal Feature Fusion Network that jointly models kinematic, appearance, and contextual cues for pedestrian intention prediction. MTF-Net integrates four complementary modalities-bounding-box dynamics, human pose keypoints, local context, and scene-level semantics within a recurrent fusion framework enhanced by gated linear units (GLUs). These GLU-based modules adaptively regulate cross-modal information flow, enabling interpretable and efficient feature interaction across temporal scales. Through three dedicated temporal encoding branches and an attention-guided fusion head, the proposed model robustly anticipates pedestrian crossing intentions several frames before they occur. Extensive evaluations on the PIE and JAAD benchmarks demonstrate that MTF-Net surpasses recent transformer- and graph-based models, achieving up to 0.95 AUC on PIE and 0.94 AUC on JAAD, while maintaining real-time performance. The results highlight that reliable pedestrian intention prediction arises from principled multi-modal fusion rather than excessive architectural complexity.

AI.tldr: MTF-Net is a multi-modal temporal fusion network for pedestrian intention prediction that combines bounding-box dynamics, pose keypoints, local context, and scene semantics using GLU-based cross-modal fusion across three temporal branches, achieving state-of-the-art AUC on PIE (0.95) and JAAD (0.94) with real-time performance.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches either model temporal dependencies within single modalities or fuse modalities only at coarse semantic levels, limiting multi-modal temporal reasoning for intent prediction.
AI.method: MTF-Net employs four modalities—bounding-box dynamics, human pose keypoints, local context, and scene-level semantics—integrated in a recurrent fusion framework with GLU-based modules that adaptively regulate cross-modal information flow. It uses three dedicated temporal encoding branches and an attention-guided fusion head for robust anticipation several frames before crossing.
AI.result: Outperforms recent transformer- and graph-based models on PIE and JAAD, achieving up to 0.95 AUC on PIE and 0.94 AUC on JAAD, while maintaining real-time performance.
AI.conclusion: Reliable pedestrian intention prediction stems from principled, multi-modal temporal fusion rather than solely increasing architectural complexity.

title: Co-VLA: Consensus-based Federated Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot learning, with performance improving as models and datasets scale. Scaling robot data collection, however, remains challenging because data are naturally distributed across robots, tasks, and locations, making centralization costly or impractical. Federated learning offers a way to train on decentralized robot data, but applying it to VLAs requires accounting for heterogeneous robot client data distributions. We present Co-VLA, which applies consensus optimization using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers~(ADMM) to federated VLA training. We show that the same algorithm supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with both fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters. The name Co-VLA reflects both consensus and collaboration: clients with different local robot datasets collaboratively train a shared model without sharing their data. Our experiments demonstrate that Co-VLA achieves performance comparable to centralized training in both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings.

AI.tldr: Co-VLA uses ADMM-based consensus in federated training to collaboratively train vision-language-action models across decentralized robot data, enabling full-model and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters; achieves centralized-training-level performance without data sharing.
AI.motivation: Centralized collection of diverse robot data is costly and impractical; federated learning can leverage decentralized datasets across robots, but heterogeneity in data distributions poses a challenge for VLA models.
AI.method: Apply consensus optimization via Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to federated VLA training. The framework supports full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, including fixed-rank adapters and rank-adaptive adapters.
AI.result: Empirical results show Co-VLA attains performance comparable to centralized training under both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings.
AI.conclusion: Co-VLA demonstrates effective collaborative learning for VLAs without sharing data, and ADMM-based consensus can mitigate data heterogeneity in federated robotic learning.

authors: Henrique Curi de Miranda e Lourenço Alves Pereira
title: A Proposal for an Agentic AI Architecture to Support Multi-Domain Decision-Making in the Brazilian Armed Forces
comment: This paper was accepted for publication in the XXVIII SIGE (Simpósio de Aplicações Operacionais em Áreas de Defesa)
summary: The growing complexity of multi-domain operational environments (land, aerospace, naval, cyber, and electromagnetic spectrum) has increased the volume and velocity of data reaching command-and-control (C2) centers, straining the observe-orient-decide-act (OODA) decision cycle. Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems currently employed in defense are, in general, reactive and isolated tools that still rely heavily on human operators to integrate information, assess scenarios, and formulate courses of action. This paper proposes a conceptual Agentic AI architecture for AI systems that can plan, access data sources, execute tools, and act autonomously and audibly, aimed at supporting decision-making across the three Brazilian Armed Forces (Navy, Army, and Air Force). Four application fronts are discussed (decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, and countermeasure suggestion), as well as the data and sensor access requirements and the security and permission safeguards necessary for responsible employment across administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical contexts.

AI.tldr: A conceptual Agentic AI architecture is proposed to autonomously plan, access data, execute tools, and act to support decision-making across Brazil’s three armed forces in multi-domain operations.
AI.motivation: Escalating data volume and velocity in multi-domain environments strain the OODA loop; existing defense AI is reactive and human-dependent, necessitating autonomous, proactive, auditable AI capable of planning and action.
AI.method: Conceptual design of an Agentic AI architecture with data/sensor access, tool execution, and autonomous audible action; analysis of four application fronts (decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, countermeasure suggestion) plus data access and security/permission safeguards across administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical layers.
AI.result: A holistic, forward-looking architecture and deployment considerations; explicit requirements for data/sensor access and security controls; outlines four domains of application and governance for responsible use.
AI.conclusion: The architecture could enhance decision support and autonomy for Brazil’s Navy, Army, and Air Force, provided robust data governance, safety, and mission-appropriate constraints are in place.

title: Small Enough to Know Everything: The Fully-Enumerable Transformer as an Instrument for the Science of Delayed Generalization
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. Code and per-seed run records will be released publicly
summary: Tiny transformers trained on fully-enumerable tasks occupy an unusual position in the study of grokking: every input can be evaluated, every generalization ceiling can be computed exactly, and hundreds of seeds cost minutes. We argue this regime is a scientific instrument with four capabilities that approximate settings cannot offer: (a) exact, falsifiable generalization ceilings; (b) task surgery that manipulates one structural variable while provably fixing all others; (c) direct observation of every weight; and (d) survival-time statistics over many seeds that recast "does not grok" as a censored observation. The obvious objection is that laws characterized at 10^4 parameters may not mean anything beyond them. We answer it with a preregistered conservation study: three task-side laws established at 12K parameters -- a recoverability-ceiling law, a role-conflict delay law, and a weight-decay response law -- are re-measured under an identical from-scratch protocol at 12K, 1M, and 50M parameters (a 4,000x span; 360 runs plus a 44-run control arm). The ceiling law and the delay law are conserved (0/144 Holm-corrected ceiling violations; Spearman rho >= 0.75 at every scale, permutation p < 1e-4), while the weight-decay law deforms systematically, steepening with scale. Preregistered controls show the 50M role-conflict deficit survives learning-rate adjustment and a tripled budget. Conservation was tested against criteria frozen before data collection, and one law's deformation shows the test could have failed. These results license the fully-enumerable transformer as a model organism for the task-side laws of delayed generalization: what it measures exactly, larger models largely obey -- and where they deviate, the deviation is itself lawful and measurable.

AI.tldr: Fully-enumerable tiny transformers enable exact, falsifiable generalization ceilings, controllable structural manipulations, complete weight observation, and multiseed survivability statistics; a preregistered cross-scale study shows two task-side laws conserved and one deformed by scale, legitimizing such models as a lab for delayed generalization laws.
AI.motivation: To study grokking and delayed generalization with exact, testable invariants. Fully enumerated tasks and tiny models provide precise measurements of generalization ceilings, the effect of isolated structural changes, and weight-level dynamics across scales.
AI.method: Train tiny transformers on fully enumerated tasks; evaluate every input; perform task surgery by manipulating one structural variable while fixing others; observe every weight; collect survival-time statistics across many seeds; conduct a preregistered conservation study across 12K, 1M, and 50M parameters with identical from-scratch protocol (360 runs plus 44-control); test three task-side laws: recoverability-ceiling, role-conflict delay, and weight-decay response; apply Holm corrections, compute Spearman rho, and permutation p-values to assess invariance across scales.
AI.result: Ceiling law and delay law are conserved across scales (0/144 Holm-corrected ceiling violations; Spearman ρ ≥ 0.75 at all scales; permutation p < 1e-4). The weight-decay law deforms with scale, steepening as parameters increase. The role-conflict deficit persists under learning-rate adjustment and a tripled budget. One deformation instance shows the test could have failed if criteria had differed. Overall, the fully-enumerable transformer behaves as a model organism for delaying generalization, with invariant laws largely preserved and scale-dependent deviations that are themselves measurable.
AI.conclusion: The fully-enumerable transformer framework provides exact, falsifiable measurements of task-side laws governing delayed generalization. Larger models largely obey these laws; where they deviate, the deviations are systematic and measurable, enabling principled study of when and why grokking occurs.

title: MoSSGate: Memory-Modulated State-Space Gating for Skin Lesion Segmentation
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, accepted on International Conference on Cloud and Network Computing
summary: Accurate skin lesion segmentation is crucial for reliable computer-aided dermatological diagnosis, yet existing convolutional and transformer-based models often struggle to jointly capture long-range spatial dependencies and fine boundary details under limited computational budgets. This trade-off between global context modeling and boundary-aware localization frequently leads to over-segmentation, fragmented predictions, or missing thin peripheral structures. To address this challenge, we propose MoSSGate, a plug-and-play module for U-Net that integrates (i) boundary-aware spatial gating to restrict long-range propagation to informative regions, (ii) an external memory modulator that provides sample-adaptive dynamic control, and (iii) parallel 2D state-space modeling for efficient global context aggregation with linear complexity. The proposed design enables adaptive, context-aware information propagation while preserving sharp and accurate lesion boundaries. Extensive experiments on the ISIC 2017 and ISIC 2018 benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy with strong efficiency, achieving 86.3% and 85.9% mIoU and 92.6% and 90.6% Dice, respectively, while requiring substantially fewer FLOPs than most competing CNN-based methods. These results highlight a favorable accuracy efficiency trade-off for high-resolution medical image segmentation.

AI.tldr: MoSSGate: a plug-and-play U-Net module combining boundary-aware spatial gating, an external memory modulator for sample-adaptive control, and parallel 2D state-space modeling to enable efficient global context aggregation with linear complexity, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on ISIC 2017/2018 at lower FLOPs.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between long-range context modeling and precise boundary localization in high-resolution skin lesion segmentation under limited compute; existing CNN/transformer approaches struggle with either coarse context or delicate boundary details, leading to over-segmentation or fragmented predictions.
AI.method: A three-component module (i) boundary-aware spatial gating to limit long-range propagation to informative regions, (ii) external memory modulator for sample-adaptive dynamic control, and (iii) parallel 2D state-space modeling for efficient global context with linear complexity) integrated into U-Net as a plug-and-play component.
AI.result: On ISIC 2017 and ISIC 2018, MoSSGate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: mIoU 86.3%/85.9% and Dice 92.6%/90.6%, with substantially fewer FLOPs than most competing CNN-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The design enables adaptive, context-aware information propagation while preserving sharp lesion boundaries, delivering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for high-resolution medical image segmentation.

title: Execution-Aware Pre-Execution Ranking for Grasp-Conditioned Robotic Placement
summary: A geometrically valid placement can still be difficult to execute because the selected grasp changes the required end-effector pose, collision geometry, and transport motion. Placement is formulated as a pre-execution ranking problem in which supplied grasp-placement candidates are scored before planning. The model combines a typed target-conditioned point cloud with three pose descriptors and hierarchical heads for planning success and execution success conditioned on planning. On a 30-object, 1,235-scene dataset with scene-group-held-out splits, three-seed top-1 success on covered test groups reaches 85.63 +/- 1.08% for joint selection and 79.84 +/- 0.16% for fixed-target ranking. For the designated frozen seed-42 checkpoint, top-1 success improves from 72.84% to 85.78% over full-pool cuMotion for joint ranking and from 59.65% to 79.67% for fixed-target ranking. Frozen transfer to xArm7/MoveIt requires no xArm-specific retraining. Across 27 locked cases, 13 complete end to end (48.15%). Of the 16 cases that pass Top-5 preflight and begin execution, 13 succeed (81.25%). Candidate-level deployment-feasibility prediction reaches 81.25% recall, 85.20% specificity, and 83.23% balanced accuracy.

AI.tldr: A pre-execution ranking approach for grasp-placement candidates improves end-to-end placement success by conditioning on planning outcomes and using a typed point-cloud representation with multiple pose descriptors; achieves strong top-1 and Top-5 metrics on a large dataset and transfers to xArm7 without retraining.
AI.motivation: How to mitigate execution-time changes in end-effector pose, collision geometry, and transport motion by predicting feasibility before planning.
AI.method: Construct typed target-conditioned point clouds, three pose descriptors, and hierarchical prediction heads for planning success and execution success conditioned on planning; evaluate on 30-object, 1,235-scene dataset with scene-group-held-out splits; compare joint ranking and fixed-target ranking; perform frozen-seed and transfer experiments; measure deployment-feasibility metrics.
AI.result: Top-1 success: 85.63% (joint) and 79.84% (fixed-target) on test groups; seed-42 improves from 72.84% to 85.78% (joint) and 59.65% to 79.67% (fixed-target) over cuMotion; 27 locked cases yield 48.15% end-to-end; 16 preflight-pass cases yield 13 success (81.25%); deployment-feasibility recall 81.25%, specificity 85.20%, balanced accuracy 83.23%.
AI.conclusion: Pre-execution ranking conditioned on planning improves end-to-end placement success with transferable, seed-stable performance and modest deployment metrics; further validation on broader robots and real execution would strengthen claims.

title: UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Self-evolving methods reduce the need for human-annotated trajectories by allowing tool-using agents to generate their own training data. Yet existing methods typically separate trajectory generation from evaluation, relying on static verifiers that cannot adapt to emerging failure modes or self-consistency signals that may reinforce errors shared across trajectories. Jointly adapting planning, execution, and evaluation offers a promising alternative, but introduces a fundamental coordination challenge: each component continuously changes the data or feedback used to train the others. We address this challenge with \textbf{UnifiedPlayers}, a cooperative framework comprising a Planning Player that generates tasks, an Execution Player that produces multi-turn trajectories with Python tool calls, and an Evaluation Player that constructs executable verifiers. We design role-specific rewards that coordinate the three players toward a shared learning objective under GRPO. Across two model backbones and twelve reasoning benchmarks, UnifiedPlayers outperforms the strongest prior baseline by at least 3.5\% on mathematical reasoning and 3.9\% on general reasoning tasks. Moreover, the learned verifier achieves 84.2\% adversarial detection accuracy, while its reward signal exhibits 2.03$\times$ higher per-question variance than a self-consistency baseline, providing more discriminative verifications. These results highlight cooperation among specialized players as a promising path toward self-enhanced tool-integrated agents.

AI.tldr: UnifiedPlayers coordinates planning, execution, and evaluation to form self-evolving tool-using agents, yielding improved reasoning accuracy and robust verifier performance.
AI.motivation: Addresses the coordination problem in joint adaptation where data and feedback continually change; static verifiers and disjoint generation/evaluation hamper learning; proposes a unified, cooperative framework.
AI.method: Three specialized agents: Planning Player generates tasks; Execution Player produces multi-turn trajectories including Python tool calls; Evaluation Player builds executable verifiers. Role-specific rewards guide cooperation under GRPO. Evaluated across two model backbones and twelve reasoning benchmarks, with adversarial verification and reward-variance analysis.
AI.result: Outperforms strongest prior baseline by at least 3.5 percentage points on mathematical reasoning and 3.9 points on general reasoning. The learned verifier attains 84.2% adversarial detection accuracy. The verifier’s reward signal exhibits 2.03× higher per-question variance than a self-consistency baseline, indicating more discriminative verifications.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that cooperation among specialized planning, execution, and evaluation agents yields improved performance and robust verification, making unified players a promising direction for self-enhanced tool-integrated agents.

title: Support Thresholds, Not Algorithms, Limit Rare-Association Recovery in Co-Purchase Networks
summary: The support threshold of the Apriori algorithm involves a trade-off in conducting market basket analysis: the associations that occur frequently are noted with high threshold; however, the low ones lead to generating the large amount of rules. The paper compares five methods for co-purchase edge filtration on two grocery datasets: i.e., Instacart (3.2 million baskets) and Dunnhumby (208 thousand baskets), including Apriori, Apriori + lift post-filtering, top-$K$ ranking based on lift, and two methods based on networks, noise-corrected (NC) and disparity filter (DF). The top-$K$ method ensures the maximum average lift, while the NC achieves similar lift level by means of a single value of the significance parameter ($α$). These two methods recover substantially more rare high-lift associations than Apriori (80-100% against 22-28%). NC and top-$K$ select meaningfully different edges (18-29% non-overlapping): NC retains statistically validated pairs, while top-$K$ retains rare pairs with high lift but low statistical significance. A rolling-origin holdout evaluation shows that top-$K$ edges recur at higher rates at every split, but NC edges are ~12 pp more likely to remain statistically significant in the held-out network.

AI.tldr: Comparing five edge-filtration methods for co-purchase networks (Apriori, Apriori+lift, top-K lift, Noise-Corrected, Disparity Filter) on Instacart and Dunnhumby datasets. Network-based methods (NC and top-K) recover far more rare high-lift edges than Apriori and show different edge sets; NC emphasizes statistically validated edges with greater held-out stability, while top-K prioritizes high lift and recurring edges, albeit with lower significance.
AI.motivation: Address the Apriori trade-off between frequent rules and rule explosion; improve discovery of rare but meaningful co-purchase edges and their stability across datasets and time splits.
AI.method: Five filtration methods evaluated: Apriori, Apriori + lift post-filtering, top-K ranking by lift, Noise-Corrected (NC) filtration, and Disparity Filter (DF). Datasets: Instacart (3.2M baskets) and Dunnhumby (208k baskets). Evaluation metrics include average lift, recovery of rare high-lift associations, edge overlap between methods, and rolling-origin holdout to assess recurrence and statistical significance over splits.
AI.result: Top-K achieves the maximum average lift. NC achieves similar lift with a single alpha parameter. Both NC and Top-K recover 80–100% rare high-lift associations, compared to 22–28% for Apriori. NC and Top-K edges have 18–29% non-overlap; NC preserves statistically validated pairs, while Top-K retains rare high-lift edges with low significance. In rolling-origin holdout, Top-K edges recur at higher rates across splits; NC edges are ~12 percentage points more likely to remain statistically significant in held-out networks.
AI.conclusion: Network-based filtration (NC and DF) substantially enhances discovery of meaningful edges beyond Apriori, with NC offering greater statistical stability in held-out data and Top-K offering higher recurrence and lift for rare edges. Method choice should align with goals: NC for robustness and significance; Top-K for discovering rare, high-lift edges that may be less stable yet potentially impactful.

title: A Two-Stage Multi-Scale Attention-Based Network for Weakly Supervised Cataract Fundus Image Enhancement
summary: Cataract is a major cause of vision loss and hinders further diagnosis. However, cataract fundus image enhancement often grapples with challenges such as limited paired cataract retinal images and insufficient recovery of fine details in the retinal images. To mitigate these challenges, we in this paper propose a two-stage multi-scale attention-based network (TSMSA-Net) for weakly supervised cataract fundus image enhancement. Our TSMSA-Net leverages the domain transformation to synthesis paired real-like cataract images, solving the problem of difficult acquisition of paired images. To further extract detailed information from fundus images and reduce the generation of artifacts during the enhancement process, we propose a multi-scale attention-based stage to learn more useful features for cataract image enhancement. Experimental results on Kaggle and ODIR-5K demonstrate that our TSMSA-Net outperforms current state-of-the-art cataract fundus images enhancement even without paired images and exhibits certain generalization ability. Experimental results on Kaggle and ODIR-5K datasets indicate that our TSMSA-Net outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods for cataract fundus image enhancement, even in the absence of paired images. Additionally, it demonstrates a certain level of generalization capability. The enhancement also can improve the performance of vessel segmentation and classification in cataract images.

AI.tldr: Proposes TSMSA-Net, a two-stage multi-scale attention-based network for weakly supervised cataract fundus image enhancement that synthesizes paired real-like cataract images via domain transformation; achieves state-of-the-art results on Kaggle and ODIR-5K without paired data and improves downstream vessel segmentation and classification.
AI.motivation: Overcome scarcity of paired cataract retinal images and limited recovery of fine retinal details during enhancement; enable effective learning from weakly supervised data.
AI.method: Two-stage network TSMSA-Net with multi-scale attention; uses domain transformation to generate paired real-like cataract images; stage-wise attention to extract detailed features and reduce artifacts; trained under weak supervision without explicit paired data.
AI.result: Outperforms current SOTA on Kaggle and ODIR-5K for cataract fundus image enhancement even without paired images; demonstrates generalization; enhancement improves vessel segmentation and classification.
AI.conclusion: TSMSA-Net effectively handles weak supervision in cataract fundus image enhancement; domain-based data synthesis mitigates lack of paired data and preserves fine details, with positive impact on downstream tasks.

title: LapaTrack-3D: 6 DoF pre-operative shape tracking for laparoscopic surgery
comment: This paper has been accepted by IEEE Transactions on Medical Robotics and Bionics (T-MRB)
summary: This work proposes a real-time 6 Degree-of-Freedom (6 DoF) tracking algorithm for monocular laparoscopic surgery. It provides alignment between intra-operative video and pre-operative data (e.g., CT). The 6 DoF tracking offers a solution for accurately locating the internal anatomy of the target organ despite the lack of tactile feedback and transparency. The ORB-SLAM2 framework is adopted and modified for prior-based 3D tracking with four major modifications. First, the primitive 3D shape is used for fast initialization of the ORB-SLAM2 monocular mode. Second, a pseudo-segmentation strategy is employed to separate the target organ from the background for tracking. Third, the 3D shape is incorporated as a geometric prior in its pose graph optimization. Fourth, the Multi-Scale Retinex with Chromaticity Preservation (MSRCP) algorithm is leveraged and modified for image enhancement in challenging illumination scenarios. In-vivo and ex-vivo experiments validate that LapaTrack-3D provides robust 3D tracking and effectively handles typical challenges such as poor illumination, fast motion, out-of-field-of-view scenarios, partial visibility, and ``organ-background'' relative motion. LapaTrack-3D achieves a processing rate of 13 Hz for 1280*720 pixel video.

AI.tldr: A real-time monocular 6-DoF tracking method (LapaTrack-3D) for laparoscopic surgery using ORB-SLAM2 with four priors to align intra-op video to pre-op data, achieving 13 Hz and robust performance under common surgical imaging challenges.
AI.motivation: To address lack of tactile feedback and the need to localize internal anatomy by aligning intraoperative video with preoperative data, enabling improved navigation.
AI.method: Modify ORB-SLAM2 monocular pipeline with: (1) fast initialization using primitive 3D shape; (2) pseudo-segmentation to separate organ; (3) integrate 3D shape as geometric prior in pose-graph optimization; (4) MSRCP-based image enhancement for challenging illumination.
AI.result: In-vivo and ex-vivo experiments demonstrate robust 3D tracking under poor illumination, fast motion, out-of-FOV, partial visibility, and organ-background relative motion; processing rate 13 Hz at 1280x720.
AI.conclusion: LapaTrack-3D delivers robust real-time 3D tracking for monocular laparoscopy and effective alignment between intraoperative video and preoperative data, addressing key surgical imaging challenges.

title: Solving Minimum Span Antibandwidth and Cyclic Antibandwidth Labeling Problems
summary: The Antibandwidth and Cyclic Antibandwidth problems are NP-hard graph labeling problems that aim to maximize the minimum (cyclic) distance between labels assigned to adjacent vertices. Extensive research on these problems has resulted in a variety of mathematical formulations and computational approaches. However, their minimum span perspective, in which a prescribed minimum (cyclic) distance is fixed and the objective is to minimize the label span, has received comparatively little attention. In this paper, we consider this complementary perspective by introducing the Minimum Span Antibandwidth/Cyclic Antibandwidth Labeling (MSABL/MSCABL) problems and developing a unified Boolean Satisfiability (SAT)-based framework for solving them. The SAT-based framework formulates MSABL/MSCABL as a sequence of decision problems and exploits their monotonicity to accelerate the search process. We also consider two SAT solving strategies, parallel and incremental SAT solving: the former examines multiple candidate spans concurrently, while the latter reuses a single SAT instance while progressively restricting the label domain. The proposed approaches are evaluated on benchmark instances from the Harwell-Boeing Sparse Matrix Collection and compared with CPLEXCP, CPLEXMIP, and Gurobi. The results show that SAT-based approaches are highly competitive in solution quality, with the parallel approach performing best overall for MSCABL and the incremental approach for MSABL. With the no-hole constraint, they remain competitive with CPLEXCP and significantly outperform CPLEXMIP and Gurobi, particularly for MSCABL. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of SAT solving as an exact approach for MSABL and MSCABL.

AI.tldr: Introduces MSABL/MSCABL (minimum-span variants of antibandwidth problems) and a unified SAT-based exact framework employing parallel and incremental strategies; evaluative experiments on Harwell-Boeing graphs show SAT approaches are competitive, with MSCABL benefiting most from parallel solving and MSABL from incremental solving, and strong performance under no-hole constraints.
AI.motivation: Fill the gap in the literature for the minimum-span perspective of antibandwidth problems by providing an exact, SAT-based solution framework and enabling efficient search through monotonic decision problems.
AI.method: Formulate MSABL/MSCABL as a sequence of monotone decision problems and solve with a unified SAT-based framework. Implement two strategies: (1) parallel SAT solving that tests multiple candidate spans concurrently, and (2) incremental SAT solving that reuses a single SAT instance while progressively restricting the label domain. Benchmark against CPLEX CP/MIP and Gurobi on Harwell-Boeing instances, with and without the no-hole constraint.
AI.result: SAT-based approaches yield high-quality solutions; parallel solving is best for MSCABL, incremental solving best for MSABL. Under no-hole constraint, SAT methods remain competitive with CPLEX CP and significantly outperform CPLEX MIP and Gurobi, especially for MSCABL.
AI.conclusion: SAT solving is an effective exact approach for MSABL/MSCABL, offering competitive or superior performance to conventional MILP/CP solvers and providing a unified, scalable framework for these minimum-span labeling problems.

title: Robust Federated Q-Learning with Almost No Communication
comment: Accepted at the 2026 American Control Conference (ACC 2026)
summary: We consider a federated reinforcement learning setting involving $M$ agents, all of whom interact with a common Markov Decision Process (MDP). The agents exchange information via a central server to learn the optimal value function. Our goal is to understand to what extent one can hope for collaborative sample-complexity speedups in such a setting, when a small fraction of the agents are adversarial and can act arbitrarily. To that end, we propose Robust Fed-Q}, a federated Q-learning algorithm that blends ideas from both model-based and model-free RL, along with the median-of-means device from robust statistics. We prove that despite corruption, with high-probability, Robust Fed-Q (i) guarantees exact convergence to the optimal value function in the limit of infinite samples, and (ii) enjoys near-optimal finite-time rates that benefit from collaboration. In addition, our approach requires just $\tilde{O}(1)$ rounds of communication to achieve each of the above guarantees, a feature of independent interest in FL where communication is the major bottleneck.

AI.tldr: Robust Fed-Q enables Byzantine-robust federated Q-learning with a hybrid model-based/model-free approach, achieving near-optimal collaborative sample complexity and robust convergence under a subset of adversarial agents, with only polylogarithmic communication rounds per guarantee.
AI.motivation: To understand whether collaborative sample-efficiency is achievable in federated RL when some agents may behave adversarially, and to design algorithms that are robust to such faults while minimizing communication.
AI.method: Propose Robust Fed-Q, a federated Q-learning algorithm that combines model-based and model-free RL components and uses the median-of-means robust aggregation to tolerate adversaries. A central server aggregates updates from M agents, with a small fraction potentially Byzantine.
AI.result: With high probability, Robust Fed-Q guarantees (i) exact convergence to the optimal value function in the limit of infinite samples, and (ii) near-optimal finite-time rates that improve with collaboration. The algorithm requires only ten{	ilde{O}(1)} rounds of communication to achieve these guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Robust Fed-Q achieves Byzantine-robust collaborative RL with fast finite-time rates and minimal communication, making federated RL feasible in adversarial settings and highlighting the value of combining model-based and model-free insights with robust statistics.

title: Scene-Q: Confidence-Aware Coarse-to-Fine Querying of 3D Scenes with Selective VLM Reasoning
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IROS 2026
summary: Indoor mobile robots require open-vocabulary scene understanding that grounds natural-language queries in a consistent 3D map. Many existing systems ultimately rely on cosine-similarity retrieval with contrastive image--text encoders, which is efficient but brittle when labels are near-synonymous or multiple similar instances appear. We present Scene-Q, a confidence-aware coarse-to-fine querying framework that normalizes encoder scores with temperature scaling and selectively invokes a reasoning VLM only for low-confidence cases. High-confidence queries are answered by fast retrieval, while ambiguous ones are reranked over a small top-K candidate set using the original multi-view images and instance bounding boxes, enabling context-aware disambiguation at low cost. Scene-Q improves open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation on ScanNet200 and natural-language 3D instance retrieval on real-world reconstructions, with the largest gains on spatial and relational queries while keeping a substantial fraction of queries on the fast path.

AI.tldr: Scene-Q introduces a confidence-aware coarse-to-fine querying framework for open-vocabulary 3D grounding, combining fast, temperature-normalized retrieval with selective, context-aware reasoning on a small top-K set to balance speed and accuracy; it yields improvements in open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation and 3D instance retrieval, especially for spatial/relational queries.
AI.motivation: Open-vocabulary scene understanding in 3D maps is essential for indoor mobile robots. While cosine-similarity retrieval with contrastive image--text encoders is efficient, it struggles when labels are near-synonymous or when multiple similar instances exist. A system that can disambiguate with higher-level reasoning while maintaining low computational cost is desirable.
AI.method: Normalizes encoder scores with temperature scaling to produce confidence scores. Uses a fast retrieval path for high-confidence queries. For low-confidence cases, invokes a reasoning vision-language model (VLM) to re-rank a top-K candidate set using multi-view images and instance bounding boxes, enabling context-aware disambiguation with modest cost.
AI.result: Scene-Q improves open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation on ScanNet200 and natural-language 3D instance retrieval on real-world reconstructions, with the largest gains on spatial and relational queries while maintaining a substantial fraction of queries on the fast path.
AI.conclusion: A practical framework that balances speed and accuracy by combining a fast, calibrated retrieval with selective, context-aware reasoning. This reduces brittleness in open-vocabulary 3D grounding and is particularly effective for spatial/relational queries.

title: Hybrid Residual Reinforcement Learning for Contact-Rich Robotic Book Insertion
summary: Placing a grasped book into a tight shelf is a compact but difficult contact-rich control problem: millimetre-scale pose error can turn a geometrically valid approach into jamming, failed release, or incomplete seating. We study this final phase after grasp acquisition and global approach, and ask how control authority should be divided between known geometry and learned behaviour. Our method retains a nominal task-space controller for structured insertion and seating, while residual PPO supplies bounded local corrections and decides when to release. Only the brief open-retreat-reclose transition is scripted. For the final policy used on hardware, a deployment-matched simulation evaluation over 512 fixed conditions yields 98.50 percent mean success (0.23 percentage-point sample SD) across three independent training runs, compared with 37.89 percent for nominal control. On the physical xArm7, 60 trials over 30 matched conditions show the same qualitative advantage: residual control raises success from 26.7 percent to 63.3 percent, reduces failures from 22 to 11, and wins 13 of the 15 matched conditions in which the two controllers differ. Robustness tests show that performance remains above 87 percent under initialization perturbations up to 1.5x, while very tight clearances expose the geometric limit of local correction. These results support a hybrid design in which geometry preserves reliable task structure and learning is concentrated on the contact-sensitive behaviour that fixed rules handle poorly.

AI.tldr: Hybrid geometry-learning control for tight-insertion: a nominal task-space controller augmented with a residual PPO policy for local corrections and release decisions significantly improves success rates on both simulation and real hardware, with robustness to perturbations; learning focuses on contact-sensitive behavior while geometry preserves task structure.
AI.motivation: Tight shelf insertion is highly sensitive to millimetre-scale pose errors. Fixed geometry controllers can fail during contact-rich final phases. A hybrid approach can allocate control authority between known geometry and learned behavior to improve reliability.
AI.method: Maintain a nominal task-space controller for insertion and seating; add a residual PPO policy to provide bounded local corrections and to decide when to release. Scripted brief open-retreat-reclose; evaluate on deployment-matched simulation across 512 conditions; validate on xArm7 hardware with 60 trials across 30 matched conditions.
AI.result: Simulation: mean success 98.50% (SD 0.23 percentage points) across three runs vs 37.89% for nominal control. Hardware (xArm7): 60 trials across 30 conditions show success 63.3% vs 26.7% for nominal, with reduced failures (11 vs 22). In 15 matched conditions where controllers differ, the hybrid succeeds in 13. Robustness: performance >87% under initialization perturbations up to 1.5x; very tight clearances reveal geometric limits of local correction.
AI.conclusion: A hybrid geometry-learning design can preserve reliable task structure while learning handles contact-sensitive behavior fixed rules struggle with. The approach yields substantial gains in accuracy and robustness, supporting the strategy of dividing control authority between geometry and learning for contact-rich manipulation.

title: Perception, Layout, and Validation: Calibrated Confidence for Reliable Straight-Through Processing of Financial Documents
summary: Straight-through processing (STP) on extracted key-value fields from financial documents without human review requires a calibrated probability together with a bounded guarantee on the residual error of the auto-approved tier. The emergence of modern Vision Language Models (VLMs) provides an out-of-the-box capability for extracting the key-values, but their verbalized confidence signals are unreliable and weakly track field correctness. This paper introduces a decomposed confidence layer along three interpretable channels, including perception, layout, and validation. Together with a final conformal risk control, the score can be used for reliable STP of financial documents. The method is validated on three public datasets covering real invoices, synthetic invoices, and ad-buy forms, using two different VLM families (Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite). Our decomposed score consistently improves the separation of correct from incorrect extractions, substantially raising the AUROC from 0.54-0.74 for VLM verbalized signals to 0.90-0.99 with contributions from all three designed channels. Crucially for industrial deployment, this enables usable STP. The native VLM confidence signals could clear only 0.1%-7.0% of fields under risk control at a target error of <10%. In contrast, the proposed method auto-approves 49-72% of fields while holding the empirical error of the accepted tier at or below the target.

AI.tldr: A decomposed confidence layer (perception, layout, validation) with conformal risk control improves reliable straight-through processing (STP) of key-value extractions from financial documents, outperforming native VLM confidences across datasets and models.
AI.motivation: VLMs provide extraction but verbalized confidence is unreliable; need calibrated probabilities with bounded residual error to safely auto-approve fields without human review in financial document processing.
AI.method: Introduce a three-channel confidence decomposition (perception, layout, validation) plus a final conformal risk control. Evaluate on real/synthetic invoices and ad-buy forms using two VLM families (Qwen3.6-27B, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite). Assess separation of correct/incorrect extractions (AUROC) and auto-approval rates.
AI.result: AUROC for correct vs incorrect extractions rises from 0.54-0.74 (verbal signals) to 0.90-0.99 (three-channel score). Native VLM confidence clears only 0.1%-7.0% under risk control at target error <10%; the proposed method auto-approves 49-72% of fields while maintaining empirical error at or below the target.
AI.conclusion: The decomposed confidence design with conformal risk control enables usable/stable straight-through processing for financial documents by providing reliable, calibrated confidence signals and substantially higher autonomous approval rates.

title: When Does Retrieval Help Time-Series Forecasting?
summary: Retrieval plug-ins supply a deep forecaster with information its lookback window cannot carry. Published evaluations report consistent gains, and each credits its own mechanism. We show that the benefit belongs instead to the operating point: the relation between window length $S$ and dominant seasonal period $L$, an axis the standard protocol never varies. Stratifying the evaluation by that relation exposes the regime. At $S{=}12$, a simple control that repeats the last observed period beats the six standard backbones, in aggregate, on four of seven benchmarks by $8\%$ to $44\%$ of MSE. It beats the strongest plug-in we run on ETTm1 and matches it on ECL. It is worse by up to $25\%$ on the three datasets whose training-split spectra lack a concentrated, shared period. A controlled synthetic sweep of horizon, period, and window shows the benefit boundary tracks the period (correlation $+0.71$), not the horizon ($-0.23$). A paired control with no phase to recover nearly erases the effect, consistent with phase starvation. Zero-shot pretraining does not escape it: a foundation model trails trained backbones by $22\%$ to $50\%$ on the periodic benchmarks. Within our instrument, exact lookup matches graph diffusion: the payoff is consulting the record, not the machinery on top. Two interpretable statistics, a trend test and a staleness rate, predict the sign of the per-cell benefit at $0.76$ accuracy under leave-one-dataset-out evaluation, a suggestive margin over the $0.69$ majority rule, where a 22-feature stack manages $0.57$. We propose no new plug-in. The contribution is the regime map, the protocol that reveals it, and two statistics that screen it before deployment. Code: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/retrieval-regime.

AI.tldr: Benefits of retrieval plug-ins arise from the S–L regime (window length S relative to dominant seasonal period L), not from the plug-ins themselves. A regime map and simple baselines reveal when gains occur; a last-period repeat baseline can outperform complex backbones in certain regimes; two interpretable statistics predict benefit with good accuracy; code provided; no new plug-in is proposed.
AI.motivation: Question the universal efficacy of retrieval-based forecasters and explain inconsistent reported gains by revealing the operating regime that governs success; provide a practical screening protocol before deployment.
AI.method: Systematic stratification of evaluation by the relationship between lookback window S and dominant seasonal period L. Controlled synthetic experiments varying horizon, period, and window. Paired controls with/without phase to assess phase effects. Zero-shot pretraining versus trained baselines. Benchmark across multiple datasets (ETTm1, ECL, etc.). Compare against six standard backbones and retrieval plug-ins. Introduce two interpretable statistics (trend test, staleness rate) to predict per-cell benefit. Leave-one-dataset-out evaluation. Provide code for replication.
AI.result: At S=12, a simple last-period-repeat baseline beats six backbones on four of seven benchmarks by 8–44% of MSE. It outperforms the strongest plug-in on ETTm1 and matches it on ECL, but underperforms by up to 25% on datasets lacking concentrated shared periodicity. The benefit boundary tracks the period (correlation +0.71) rather than the horizon (-0.23). Phase starvation explains much of the effect; a paired control with no phase nearly erases the benefit. Zero-shot pretraining underperforms trained backbones by 22–50% on periodic benchmarks. Exact lookup matches rival graph diffusion in payoff, indicating the value is in the data record rather than the machinery. Two statistics (trend test, staleness rate) predict the sign of per-cell gain with 0.76 accuracy under leave-one-ddataset-out, versus 0.69 baseline; a 22-feature stack achieves 0.57. No new plug-in is proposed. The contribution is the regime map, an evaluation protocol to reveal it, and screening statistics for deployment. Code provided.
AI.conclusion: The observed gains from retrieval plug-ins are regime-dependent. A regime-aware evaluation reveals when benefits occur, guiding deployment decisions. The main contributions are the regime map, the evaluation protocol, and two predictive statistics for screening; no new plug-in is necessary.

title: SAGE-Yoga: Multi-Cue Learning for Yoga Pose Classification and Joint-Level Correction
summary: Automated yoga analysis requires both accurate pose classification and interpretable feedback on pose execution. However, existing methods often rely on a single visual prediction, struggle to distinguish visually similar poses, and treat pose classification and correction as separate tasks. To address these limitations, we propose SAGE-Yoga, a unified coarse-to-fine framework for yoga pose classification and joint-level correction from a single RGB image. Inspired by how yoga instructors assess posture using multiple complementary cues, SAGE-Yoga first employs a bagging-based ensemble of complementary visual backbones to generate a ranked set of candidate pose classes. Additionally, a margin-based gating mechanism preserves confident visual predictions while invoking geometric verification only for ambiguous cases. Moreover, once the final pose class is determined, SAGE-Yoga retrieves a medoid reference pose and compares the observed joint angles with class-specific distributions to identify misaligned joints. Finally, these deviations are translated into actionable corrective feedback. Empirically, experiments on the Yoga-82 dataset show that the visual ensemble achieves 89.0% Top-1 accuracy, while the complete framework improves performance to 90.7% Top-1 accuracy and 90.1% Macro-F1. These results demonstrate that combining complementary visual evidence with selective geometric verification improves fine-grained pose classification while enabling interpretable, joint-level correction.

AI.tldr: SAGE-Yoga introduces a unified coarse-to-fine framework for yoga pose classification and joint-level correction from a single RGB image, combining a bagging-based ensemble of visual backbones with a margin-based gating mechanism and geometric verification, plus medoid-based reference comparison for actionable feedback. It achieves 89.0% Top-1 on the visual ensemble and 90.7% Top-1 / 90.1% Macro-F1 overall on Yoga-82.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of single-predictionyoga analysis systems that struggle to distinguish visually similar poses and separate classification from correction. The goal is to integrate classification with interpretable, joint-level feedback using multiple complementary cues.
AI.method: 1) Bagging-based ensemble of complementary visual backbones generates a ranked candidate pose class list. 2) Margin-based gating preserves confident predictions and triggers geometric verification only for ambiguous cases. 3) After final pose is determined, retrieve a medoid reference pose per class and compare observed joint angles against class-specific distributions to identify misaligned joints. 4) Translate deviations into actionable corrective feedback.
AI.result: On Yoga-82, the visual ensemble achieves 89.0% Top-1 accuracy; the full framework improves to 90.7% Top-1 and 90.1% Macro-F1, indicating improved fine-grained classification and interpretable, joint-level correction.
AI.conclusion: Combining complementary visual evidence with selective geometric verification enhances fine-grained pose classification while enabling interpretable, joint-level correction.

title: MaskHarness-WAM: Instance-Grounded Harnessing for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires not only stable local visuomotor control, but also continuous target tracking and reliable task progress assessment throughout execution. This challenge becomes particularly critical when multiple objects share identical appearances and must be manipulated in a prescribed order. In such scenarios, relying solely on a limited-horizon manipulation policy is often insufficient to determine which instance should be operated on and when the task should transition to the next stage. To address this challenge, we propose MaskHarness-WAM, an instance-grounded harness for long-horizon manipulation. The proposed system connects high-level task planning with low-level manipulation policies through target masks, while leveraging visual feedback for subtask scheduling and continuous execution. Since each subtask corresponds to a different target instance, the low-level policy requires a newly established initial target mask under the updated scene at each subtask transition. The harness continuously re-observes the environment, generates, and verifies the target mask at subtask boundaries, thereby updating the instance-level spatial condition provided to the low-level policy. Furthermore, the system advances the manipulation process by switching target instances according to the verified completion status of each subtask. Experiments on a real robot platform demonstrate that MaskHarness-WAM substantially outperforms limited-horizon policies on sequential multi-object manipulation, showing its effectiveness in extending local manipulation skills to reliable long-horizon execution.

AI.tldr: MaskHarness-WAM ties high-level task planning to low-level manipulation using dynamic, instance-specific target masks to handle long-horizon sequential manipulation with identical-looking objects, showing significant gains over limited-horizon policies in real-robot experiments.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon manipulation with multiple identical-looking objects requires maintaining instance identity and correct task progression; limited-horizon policies struggle to determine which instance to operate on and when to transition to the next subtask.
AI.method: An instance-grounded harness that links high-level planning with low-level manipulation via target masks. The system re-observes the scene, generates and verifies a new initial target mask at subtask boundaries, and updates the instance-level spatial condition provided to the low-level policy. It switches target instances based on the verified completion status of each subtask, enabling continuous execution across subtask transitions.
AI.result: Real-robot experiments show MaskHarness-WAM substantially outperforms limited-horizon policies for sequential multi-object manipulation, indicating improved reliability and long-horizon execution.
AI.conclusion: MaskHarness-WAM provides an effective framework to extend local visuomotor skills to robust long-horizon manipulation in scenarios with identical-looking objects by tightly coupling planning, perception, and manipulation through dynamic instance-aware target masks.

title: MTVA-Bench: Evaluating the Language Model Inside Cascaded Voice Agents
summary: Generally, most voice agents are cascaded systems, i.e., an ASR model transcribes the caller's audio, a language model reads the transcript and decides what to say and which backend tools to call, and a TTS model speaks the reply. Nearly all of the decision making happens in the language model, but existing evaluations measure it either too broadly or too narrowly. End-to-end voice benchmarks score the full pipeline, so recognition errors and model errors mix into a single number. LLM benchmarks isolate the model but they do not evaluate what makes real phone calls hard, such as transcription issues, caller's voice being split across messages and the requirement that replies follow the language and script specified. We introduce the Multi-Turn Voice Agent Benchmark (MTVA-Bench), which evaluates the language model on the same conditions it faces inside a cascaded system. The caller is played by an LLM following a set of rubrics and tool calls are answered by a mock backend which responds to the arguments the model actually sent. The benchmark contains 49 agents working across 490 reviewed scenarios and supports 7 languages. Scoring is a combination of deterministic checks on tool calls with two LLM judges, one that scores scenario specific rules and one that grades conversation quality without access to the task. Both judges must cite specific messages from the transcript. Task and conversation scores are weighted equally, since a call can complete its task and still go badly for the caller. In a seven-model study, six of the models select the correct tool within 6.4 points of one another, but their overall scores span 24.4 points. Most of the gap comes from argument values, action ordering, rule compliance, and what the model says around its tool calls.

AI.tldr: MTVA-Bench presents a multi-turn voice-agent benchmark that evaluates language models in cascaded ASR-LM-TTS settings using 49 agents, 490 scenarios, and 7 languages; scoring blends deterministic tool-call checks with two LLM judges; results show models align on tool selection but diverge on conversation quality and tool-call execution, highlighting gaps in argument values, action ordering, rule compliance, and speech-context handling.
AI.motivation: Fill the gap between end-to-end voice benchmarks (task-level scores) and isolated LLM benchmarks (model-centric scores) by evaluating LM behavior under realistic, multi-turn, spoken-dialog constraints inherent in cascaded voice systems.
AI.method: Construct MTVA-Bench with caller simulated by an LLM following rubrics; mock backend responds to actual arguments; 49 agents across 490 scenarios in 7 languages; scoring combines deterministic tool-call checks with two LLM judges (scenario-specific rules and general conversation quality) and requires transcript-cited evidence; task and conversation scores weighted equally.
AI.result: In a seven-model study, six models agreement on tool selection within 6.4 points of each other; overall scores span 24.4 points; the largest variance stems from argument values, action ordering, rule compliance, and the content around tool calls.
AI.conclusion: MTVA-Bench reveals that tool-call decision quality and discourse around tool use are major sources of variance even when tool selection is relatively concordant; the benchmark aligns evaluation with real-world voice-agent constraints and identifies specific levers (values, ordering, rule adherence, communicative behavior) for model improvement, with multilingual support and a realistic evaluation protocol.

title: SoftTri: Smooth Triangular Membership Functions for Adaptive Fuzzy Inference Systems
summary: Triangular membership functions (MFs) are widely used in fuzzy systems because of their interpretability, low parameterization complexity, and strong locality properties. However, their inherent nondifferentiability at knot points limits the effectiveness of gradient-based optimization in adaptive neuro-fuzzy architectures, often necessitating subgradient approximations or heuristic smoothing techniques. In this paper, we propose \emph{SoftTri}, a differentiable triangular membership function constructed using a smooth soft-hinge mechanism inspired by Swish-type activations. The proposed formulation preserves the geometric structure and localized behavior of classical triangular MFs while providing $C^\infty$ smoothness with respect to both the input variable and the membership parameters $(a,b,c)$ for any finite sharpness parameter $β>0$. Closed-form analytical gradients are derived to enable efficient and fully differentiable backpropagation-based learning. SoftTri is integrated into a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy neural network with grid-partitioned rules and evaluated on multiple one-dimensional and two-dimensional nonlinear approximation benchmarks as well as a real-world regression task using the Airfoil Self-Noise dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that SoftTri consistently improves optimization stability and approximation accuracy compared with classical triangular membership functions, while achieving performance comparable to or better than Gaussian MFs under identical rule structures and training settings. The proposed approach provides an effective compromise between interpretability and differentiable optimization in modern neuro-fuzzy learning systems.

AI.tldr: Introduces SoftTri, a differentiable soft-hinge-based triangular membership function for neuro-fuzzy networks, enabling backpropagation while preserving locality; shows improved optimization stability and accuracy over classical triangular MFs and competitive performance with Gaussian MFs across benchmarks and the Airfoil Self-Noise dataset.
AI.motivation: Triangular membership functions are popular due to interpretability and locality but are nondifferentiable at knot points, hindering gradient-based learning in adaptive neuro-fuzzy architectures. A differentiable alternative that preserves structure is desired.
AI.method: Define SoftTri using a smooth soft-hinge mechanism (inspired by Swish activations) to make triangular MFs C∞ with respect to input and parameters (a,b,c) for any finite sharpness β>0. Derive closed-form gradients for efficient backpropagation. Integrate into a Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy neural network with grid-partitioned rules and evaluate on 1D and 2D nonlinear benchmarks, plus Airfoil Self-Noise regression data.
AI.result: SoftTri consistently improves optimization stability and approximation accuracy compared with classical triangular MFs, and achieves performance comparable to or better than Gaussian MFs under identical rule structures and training settings.
AI.conclusion: SoftTri offers a practical compromise between interpretability and differentiable optimization in modern neuro-fuzzy systems, enabling effective fully differentiable learning without sacrificing the local structure of triangular MFs.

title: Distance to Class Prototypes: Active Learning for Object Detection
summary: Deploying a deep object detector in a new setting is limited less by architecture than by the cost of annotating data from that setting. Active learning lowers the cost by choosing which images to label, and the choice is only as good as the signal used to score an unlabeled image. That signal is usually the class posterior, which is cheap but poorly calibrated, or the disagreement across several models or several stochastic passes, which is better but multiplies inference over a pool far larger than the labeled set. We propose a signal richer than the posterior yet still read from one forward pass of one network. A supervised contrastive term added to the training objective shapes a per-object embedding space in which distance encodes class membership, and an unlabeled detection is scored by how far it lies from the region occupied by its predicted category, weighted by its confidence. The criterion needs no ensemble, no auxiliary predictor and no repeated inference, and its entire cost is 2.89M parameters, an increase of 8.3% over a bare detector. On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO it beats the posterior of the same detector in every round in which a selection is made, by up to 1.08% mAP50 against run to run deviations of 0.02% to 0.18%, and it stays competitive with ensemble and Monte Carlo dropout criteria costing three to fifty forward passes per unlabeled image. Experiments use the single-stage detector under which the compared criteria report their results, so that the selection decision is isolated from the strength of the detector.

AI.tldr: A lightweight active-learning signal for object detection that uses a supervised contrastive term to shape per-object embeddings, enabling single-pass scoring of unlabeled detections without ensembles; shows improvements over the class posterior on VOC and COCO with modest parameter overhead.
AI.motivation: Deploying detectors in new domains is bottlenecked by labeling cost. Class-posterior uncertainty is cheap but poorly calibrated; ensemble or multiple inference methods improve selection but are expensive. A signal richer than posterior, obtainable in one forward pass, can reduce labeling costs.
AI.method: Introduce a supervised contrastive objective that organizes per-object embeddings so that distances reflect class membership. Unlabeled detections are scored by how far they lie from the region occupied by the predicted category, weighted by confidence. No ensembles, extra predictors, or repeated inferences are required; about 2.89M additional parameters (~8.3% of a bare detector). Works with a single-stage detector.
AI.result: On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO, the method beats the posterior-based selection in every active-learning round, achieving up to 1.08% mAP50 improvement with low run-to-run deviation (0.02%–0.18%). It remains competitive with ensemble and Monte Carlo dropout criteria that incur 3–50 forward passes per unlabeled image.
AI.conclusion: A single-pass, contrastive-signal for active learning in object detection yields consistent gains over posterior-based scoring, with modest parameter overhead and competitive performance relative to heavier ensemble-based strategies.

title: Compliance for Free: Learning Identifiable Impedance via Bilateral Teleoperation
summary: Vision-language-action models tell a robot where to move, but not how hard to push. Contact-rich tasks depend on that second quantity, compliance, yet no widely used demonstration interface records it. The obstacle is identifiability as realized pose and measured force cannot separate the operator's intended equilibrium from their stiffness, so VR controllers, SpaceMouse and handheld grippers cannot supply compliance supervision even in principle. Prior compliance-output policies work around this with hand-specified task structure, privileged simulation contact state, or dedicated force and tactile hardware. Four-channel bilateral teleoperation removes the ambiguity directly by using the leader arm as a separate measurement of the intended equilibrium, making per-axis stiffness identifiable by regression using only the joint-torque sensing already on the manipulator. This yields per-timestep, direction-dependent compliance labels at zero annotation cost, which we use to fine-tune a VLA to emit stiffness alongside pose. On a Franka Research 3 wiping task, ours is the only policy of five whose contact force changes when the instruction asks for a firm wipe rather than a normal one (6.4N (normal) to 9.1N (firm) RMS, Cohen's d = 0.89, p = 0.023

AI.tldr: Four-channel bilateral teleoperation identifies per-axis stiffness from joint torque, enabling zero-cost, per-timestep compliance labeling to train a vision-language-action model to output stiffness alongside pose.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action policies lack compliant control information; identifiability problem arises because pose and force cannot separate intended equilibrium from stiffness; existing interfaces fail to supervise compliance in a principled way.
AI.method: Use four-channel bilateral teleoperation to treat the leader arm as the measurement of intended equilibrium. Perform regression on joint-torque data to identify per-axis stiffness, yielding per-timestep, direction-dependent compliance labels without annotation. Fine-tune a VLA to emit stiffness in addition to pose.
AI.result: On a Franka Research 3 wiping task, the proposed policy is the only one among five that changes contact force when asked for a firm wipe vs a normal wipe (6.4N normal to 9.1N firm; RMS). Cohen's d = 0.89, p = 0.023.
AI.conclusion: Four-channel bilateral teleoperation resolves identifiability without privileged states or extra hardware, providing zero-cost compliance labels that can train VLA models to output both pose and stiffness.

title: PaGNet: A Panel-Aware GBDT--Neural Network for Multi-Target Corporate Tax Avoidance Proxy Forecasting
summary: Forecasting corporate tax avoidance proxies from firm--year panel data is challenging because predictive signals are distributed across short firm histories and related targets, while screening-oriented use requires transparent model behavior. We propose PaGNet (Panel-Aware GBDT--Neural Network), a two-branch hybrid that combines a LightGBM branch using panel-temporal summaries with a Panel-MLP branch using attention-pooled temporal aggregation and shared-trunk multi-task learning. A per-target validation-optimal blender produces both the final prediction and a compact branch-reliance diagnostic without trainable fusion parameters.
