Fine-tuning visual-navigation models on UNI reduces trajectory prediction error by 17.4-24.8% on held-out UNI demonstrations. Evaluation on other navigation datasets shows benefits that vary by dataset and metric. We further demonstrate closed-loop transfer to a powered wheelchair in curb, staircase, and curb-cut scenarios. These results support low-cost physical proxies as a practical source of navigation supervision collected without the target robot.

AI.tldr: UNI is a robot-free data collection paradigm using a rollator and smartphone to collect physically constrained human navigation demonstrations, biasing data toward wheeled-feasible routes; it yields scalable supervision that improves navigation models and transfers to a powered wheelchair.
AI.motivation: To enable scalable, real-world navigation data collection without teleoperating the target robot, addressing cost and scalability barriers.
AI.method: Use a four-wheeled rollator walker and smartphone to collect constrained human demonstrations; rollator constraints bias demonstrations toward wheeled-feasible paths; accumulate 37.2 km of real-world data; recover metric trajectories to supervise goal-conditioned navigation models; fine-tune visual navigation models on UNI; evaluate on external datasets and demonstrate closed-loop transfer to a powered wheelchair in curb, staircase, and curb-cut tasks.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on UNI reduces trajectory prediction error by 17.4–24.8% on held-out UNI demonstrations; benefits on other datasets vary by dataset and metric; demonstrates closed-loop transfer to a powered wheelchair in curb, staircase, and curb-cut scenarios.
AI.conclusion: UNI provides a practical, scalable source of navigation supervision via low-cost physical proxies, enabling data collection without the target robot; demonstrates that constrained demonstrations can effectively supervise navigation models, though the wheeled-bias may limit coverage of non-wheeled paths and stair negotiation.

title: Diagnose, Recover, Certify: Task Readiness under Hidden Dynamics Changes
summary: A deployed control policy can conceal consequential dynamics changes: an actuator may lose effectiveness without affecting the current task when the policy rarely excites it, despite being critical for a future task that has not yet been specified. We introduce task readiness under dormant dynamics drift, a decision problem that unifies active change diagnosis and post-change control recovery under a limited, task-agnostic interaction budget. An agent must identify whether and where local dynamics have changed, use a small number of informative interactions to characterize the change before downstream task identity is revealed, and subsequently provide each candidate task with either a recovered policy and a calibrated lower bound on its achievable return or an abstention decision to a safe fallback. We propose Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport, an intervention-based Bayesian procedure that couples fault localization with estimation of actuator effectiveness through a shared matched-response representation, thereby preserving diagnostic reliability while converting localized evidence into recovery-relevant uncertainty. This uncertainty is propagated to task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification, enabling deployment decisions that explicitly trade off expected performance, confidence, and fallback use. We evaluate the resulting framework on a diverse suite of dormant-actuator benchmarks spanning multiple simulators, under a protocol that separates diagnosis from capability recovery, scores deployment by readiness coverage, selective risk, and interaction cost as well as return, and identifies the fault regimes in which transported evidence is decisive.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian, intervention-based framework for diagnosing and recovering from dormant actuator dynamics changes under a limited interaction budget, delivering readiness-certified deployment decisions and safe fallbacks via a matched-pulse transport procedure.
AI.motivation: Deployed policies can mask consequential actuator degradations that affect future tasks. There is a need to detect if/where dynamics have changed and adapt for downstream tasks without task knowledge, while balancing diagnostic reliability, recovery performance, and interaction costs.
AI.method: Task readiness under dormant dynamics drift with Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport (EG-MPT). An intervention-based Bayesian procedure that localizes faults and estimates actuator effectiveness using a shared matched-response representation. Uncertainty from diagnosis informs task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification, enabling selective abstention to fallback when confidence is low.
AI.result: Evaluated on diverse dormant-actuator benchmarks across multiple simulators. The protocol separates diagnosis from capability recovery and scores deployment by readiness coverage, selective risk, interaction cost, and return, identifying regimes where transported evidence is decisive for recovery and policy selection.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables deployment decisions that explicitly trade off expected performance, confidence, and fallback use, by transporting diagnostic evidence to policy-ready choices and providing safe, ready-to-deploy outcomes under dormant dynamics.

title: How Far Can Sub-3B Open Language Models Go in Zero-Shot Essay Scoring on an 8 GB Consumer GPU?
summary: Zero-shot essay scoring with large language models is usually demonstrated with proprietary API models, yet the settings where automated scoring is most needed, such as public schools grading thousands of essays under strict privacy rules, are often those where sending student writing to a third-party API is unacceptable. We ask how much capability survives when the model must be a sub-3B open model running fully locally in FP16, with a controlled study of four instruction-tuned models from two families (Qwen2.5 at 0.5B/1.5B/3B, SmolLM2 at 1.7B) on all eight ASAP-AES prompts on a single 8 GB consumer GPU, with bootstrap confidence intervals, Holm-corrected paired tests, and deployment-realistic variants of the key design choices. Three findings emerge. (i) Rubric-decomposed prompting beats holistic prompting for every model under batch min-max aggregation (though Qwen2.5-3B drops significantly on one prompt), and under mean aggregation two unrelated families land within 0.01 at the 1.5-1.7B scale. (ii) Mapping trait scores into the prompt range is fragile to grader calibration: one model compresses traits into a narrow low band (2-4 on 0-10) and naive mean aggregation collapses, while the min-max normalization of Multi-Trait Specialization repairs it (macro QWK 0.204 to 0.388) and stays within 0.03 when its statistics are frozen on 30 held-out essays. (iii) Signed error falls with essay length in eleven of twelve configurations, opposite to the verbosity bias reported for large LLM judges; normalized rubric decomposition largely flattens this slope for well-calibrated models. We anchor results honestly: the best local configuration (0.388) remains far below both the human inter-rater ceiling (0.769) and a length-only baseline (0.523), so we position sub-3B local models strictly for formative, human-supervised feedback.

AI.tldr: Sub-3B open LLMs evaluated locally for zero-shot essay scoring; rubric-based prompting outperforms holistic prompting; trait-score mapping requires robust normalization; longer essays reduce signed errors; best local config achieves 0.388 macro QWK, far below human inter-rater ceiling, thus suitable for formative feedback with supervision.
AI.motivation: Address privacy and deployment constraints in automated essay scoring; expand evaluation to open, locally runnable models; compare instruction-tuned models on ASAP-AES prompts.
AI.method: Four models from two families (Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B; SmolLM2 1.7B) evaluated on eight ASAP-AES prompts; batch min-max vs mean aggregation; bootstrap confidence intervals; Holm-corrected paired tests; deployment-realistic variants; single 8GB GPU; fixed prompting design; evaluate rubric-decomposed vs holistic prompts; multi-trait specialization normalization.
AI.result: i) Rubric-decomposed prompting beats holistic prompting across models under batch min-max; (ii) trait-score mapping is sensitive to grader calibration; min-max normalization with Multi-Trait Specialization improves robustness; macro QWK 0.204 to 0.388; stable under 30 held-out essays; (iii) signed error decreases with essay length in most configurations; normalization flattens slope; best local QWK 0.388; still below human inter-rater ceiling 0.769 and length-only baseline 0.523.
AI.conclusion: Sub-3B local models can provide formative feedback under privacy constraints, but current performance lags behind human performance; privacy-preserving deployment is feasible with careful prompting and normalization, but models should be used with human supervision and feedback loops; future work should enhance calibration, expand data, and explore hybrid human-in-the-loop approaches.

title: FreqDINO++: A Frequency-Guided Multi-Task Routing Vision Foundation Model for Universal Ultrasound Analysis
summary: Ultrasound image analysis plays a crucial role in cancer screening and prenatal diagnosis, yet comprehensive assessment requires jointly addressing tasks such as lesion segmentation and benign-malignant classification. While recent vision foundation models have shown remarkable universal representations, unlocking their potential for ultrasound is bottlenecked by the considerable domain gap from natural images. Existing methods typically fine-tune heavy vision encoders for isolated tasks, incurring substantial computational overhead while overlooking the underlying commonalities across heterogeneous tasks. In this work, we propose FreqDINO++, a frequency-guided multi-task routing vision foundation model for universal ultrasound analysis. We first introduce a Multi-task Routing Adapter (MR-Adapter) to support parameter-efficient integration of task-common and task-specific knowledge, a Frequency-aware Feature Enhancer (F$^2$-Enhancer) is then designed to capture the rich multi-scale frequency characteristics of ultrasound images, and a Task-aligned Collaborative Decoder (TC-Decoder) is devised to promote collaboration between dense and global prediction tasks through global-local token interaction. Extensive experiments on large-scale multi-task and external single-task ultrasound benchmarks demonstrate that FreqDINO++ consistently outperforms strong baselines and recent foundation models across 27 diverse clinical task scenarios, while also showing promising generalization to unseen data. The code is at https://github.com/MingLang-FD/FreqDINO-Plus.

AI.tldr: Proposes FreqDINO++, a frequency-guided, multi-task vision foundation model for ultrasound analysis, featuring MR-Adapter, F^2-Enhancer, and TC-Decoder to enable efficient cross-task learning; achieves state-of-the-art performance across 27 ultrasound tasks and generalizes to unseen data.
AI.motivation: Ultrasound analysis requires joint lesion segmentation and benign-malignant classification. The domain gap from natural images limits foundation models. Existing methods fine-tune heavy encoders for isolated tasks, causing high compute and missing cross-task commonalities. A parameter-efficient, task-sharing approach is needed for universal ultrasound analysis.
AI.method: Introduce MR-Adapter for parameter-efficient routing of task-common and task-specific knowledge; design F^2-Enhancer to capture multi-scale frequency characteristics of ultrasound; develop TC-Decoder to enable collaboration between dense (segmentation) and global (classification) predictions via global-local token interaction.
AI.result: Empirical results on large-scale multi-task and external single-task ultrasound benchmarks show FreqDINO++ consistently outperforms strong baselines and recent foundation models across 27 diverse tasks, with good generalization to unseen data.
AI.conclusion: FreqDINO++ is an effective universal ultrasound analysis framework offering efficient multi-task learning, frequency-aware feature enrichment, and collaborative decoding, with code released for reproduction.

title: GPT-6-Astra in a Navigation Workflow: Behavioral Analysis in Zero-Shot Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments
summary: We study GPT-6-Astra in a zero-shot Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) system, where it interprets instructions, assesses its surroundings, and proposes actions. The system uses a common observation--decision--execution workflow with direct model API calls, without a packaged agent harness or navigation-specific fine-tuning. In this workflow, each request receives selected observations, execution feedback, and retained progress records. Evaluation covers the complete system, including context management and action control. We evaluate the system on 50 of the 100 R2R-CE val-unseen episodes used by Open-Nav. It achieves a success rate of 52.0\%, an SPL of 48.9\%, and an nDTW of 70.8\%. Our analysis highlights three findings. First, recorded responses link landmarks and earlier actions to instructions using observations and supplied history. Second, reviews include requests for additional views and revisions of uncertain judgments. Third, the results suggest a gap between task understanding and autonomous completion: an unfinished crossing is recognized while rotation continues. At termination, 36.0\% of episodes succeed with a workflow-accepted STOP, while another 16.0\% meet the distance criterion at the step limit. These results highlight a central challenge: translating correct local judgments into sustained progress and appropriate stopping.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot VLN-CE system (GPT-6-Astra) navigates via instruction understanding, environment assessment, and action via direct API calls, without an agent harness or task-specific fine-tuning, achieving moderate success on Open-Nav’s R2R-CE val-unseen. Key findings show linkage of landmarks to history, frequent requests for additional views/revisions, and a gap between local judgments and sustained autonomous progress, with stopping decisions often unmanaged.
AI.motivation: Evaluate end-to-end capabilities of a large-language-model–based navigation agent in continuous environments without task-specific fine-tuning or packaged navigation harness, including system-level context management and action control.
AI.method: Zero-shot VLN-CE pipeline using a per-step observation–decision–execution workflow with direct model API calls, no dedicated navigator; uses selected observations, execution feedback, and retained progress; evaluated on 50 of Open-Nav’s R2R-CE val-unseen episodes; metrics include success rate, SPL, and nDTW.
AI.result: Performance: 52.0% success, 48.9% SPL, 70.8% nDTW. Termination: 36.0% STOP accepted; 16.0% meet the distance criterion at the step limit. Qualitative findings include responses linking landmarks to earlier actions via observations/history, requests for additional views and revisions of uncertain judgments, and an unfinished crossing ongoing during rotation.
AI.conclusion: Main challenge is translating correct local judgments into sustained progress and appropriate stopping; to close the gap, improvements are needed in global task planning, robust stopping criteria, and better integration of perception, reasoning, and action under a unified, end-to-end workflow.

title: NeuSOGA3D: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Explainable 3D Geometric Reconstruction
comment: Preprint. Community feedback and comments are welcome
summary:
Three-dimensional reconstruction from unorganized point clouds remains a challenging problem in computer vision, geometric modeling, and computer-aided design. While neural implicit methods achieve impressive reconstruction accuracy, geometry is typically encoded in latent representations that limit interpretability and reuse within engineering workflows.
  We present NeuSOGA3D (Neuro-Symbolic Geometric Abstraction in 3D), a hybrid framework that combines learned perceptual priors inherited from NeuSOGA with explicit symbolic geometric reasoning. The method projects point clouds onto principal orthographic planes, constructs symbolic implicit spline representations from the resulting observations, and fuses them through shape-preserving constructive solid geometry operations to generate a coarse visual hull. Additional geometric detail is recovered through cross-sectional decomposition and volumetric reconstruction using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines.
  Unlike conventional neural implicit approaches, NeuSOGA3D progressively transforms observations into explicit symbolic entities, including control polygons, implicit spline fields, cross-sections, and volumetric lofts. Experiments on all forty categories of the ModelNet40 benchmark demonstrate the ability of the framework to recover structurally meaningful and CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud observations. The results highlight the potential of combining learned perception with symbolic geometric reasoning for explainable geometric intelligence.

AI.tldr: A hybrid neuro-symbolic pipeline (NeuSOGA3D) bridges neural implicit geometry with explicit CAD-like symbols to reconstruct CAD-friendly 3D shapes from unorganized point clouds.
AI.motivation: Neural implicit methods deliver accuracy but encode geometry in opaque latent representations, hindering interpretability and reuse in engineering workflows; there is a need for explainable, editable geometry.
AI.method: Project point clouds to principal orthographic planes; derive symbolic implicit spline representations from observations; fuse via shape-preserving constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations to generate a coarse visual hull; recover details through cross-sectional decomposition and volumetric reconstruction using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines; progressively convert observations into explicit symbolic entities (control polygons, implicit spline fields, cross-sections, lofts).
AI.result: Demonstrates on ModelNet40 across 40 categories that the framework can recover structurally meaningful and CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud observations.
AI.conclusion: A neuro-symbolic hybrid approach enhances explainability and CAD compatibility, showing potential for integrating learned perception with symbolic geometric reasoning in 3D reconstruction.

title: Improving Online Reinforcement Learning via Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation
summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms frequently exhibit poor sample efficiency and unstable learning dynamics, stemming from systematic critic estimation errors that are exacerbated by greedy policy updates. Existing behavior-prior reinforcement learning methods attempt to alleviate this issue by relying on offline pre-training to learn behavior models from fixed datasets and using policy priors to constrain online policy updates. However, the limited quality of offline datasets often hinders the ability to provide high-value policies that can effectively guide policy updates. The absence of expert trajectories significantly impairs online policy learning, leading to low sample efficiency and suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we depart from conventional behavior prior approaches and propose a Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation (B2PD) algorithm. B2PD leverages action-value priors to guide a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) in generating a high-value behavior support set. The resulting expert behavior priors are further distilled into the agent, effectively reducing inefficient exploration and enabling stable policy optimization, while establishing a bidirectional knowledge flow mechanism. Empirical evaluations on both state- and pixel-based tasks verify that B2PD substantially improves sample efficiency while maintaining stable policy optimization. More broadly, this work shows that enforcing high-quality behavioral support during online learning effectively mitigates critic-induced error amplification, enabling structured behavior priors to guide policy updates in a principled and sample-efficient manner.

AI.tldr: B2PD uses a bidirectional behavior prior distillation framework with action-value priors guiding a CVAE to produce high-value behavioral supports, which are distilled into the online agent to improve sample efficiency and stability by mitigating critic-induced errors.
AI.motivation: Online RL suffers from sample-inefficiency and unstable learning due to critic estimation errors amplified by greedy updates; offline behavior priors depend on limited-quality datasets and lack expert trajectories, hindering effective online policy learning.
AI.method: Leverage action-value priors to train a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) that generates a high-value behavior support set; distill the resulting expert priors into the agent and establish bidirectional knowledge flow to guide online policy updates and reduce exploration inefficiency.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on state- and pixel-based tasks shows substantial gains in sample efficiency and stable policy optimization, validating that high-quality behavioral support during online learning mitigates critic-induced error amplification.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing high-quality behavioral support during online RL enables principled, sample-efficient policy updates via structured behavior priors and bidirectional knowledge transfer.

title: Fast Cross-Strength Multi-Contrast Brain MRI Translation using Latent Bridge Matching
summary: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) acquired at different field strengths exhibits pronounced variation in noise, resolution, homogeneity, and contrast, which limits comparability across acquisition settings and complicates downstream analysis. We address this with a unified conditional model for controllable field-to-field synthesis, built on the framework of conditional latent bridge matching. Our single model achieves highly competitive results across the validation phase for all three tasks of the MRIxFields2026 challenge without task-specific architectures or training. We achieve fast generation with only a single inference step, producing all modality and field-strength combinations for $30$ axial slices in under $90$ seconds, as well as cross-modality-strength translation for a full volume in under $70$ seconds, on a single NVIDIA A5000 GPU. We further provide extensive ablations regarding different components of our solution. Code: https://gitlab.com/siddharthsrivastava/mrixfields-2026

AI.tldr: A single conditional latent bridge model enables controllable cross-field and cross-modality MRI synthesis, achieving competitive validation results with fast, one-shot inference across modalities and field strengths.
AI.motivation: MRI data from different field strengths vary in noise, resolution, homogeneity, and contrast, hindering comparability and downstream analysis. A unified model avoids task-specific architectures and training.
AI.method: A unified conditional latent bridge matching model for field-to-field MRI synthesis. One-step inference generates all modality and field-strength combinations for 30 axial slices; cross-modality-strength translation for a full volume. No task-specific architectures/training; extensive ablations; GPU-accelerated implementation; code provided.
AI.result: Competitive results across all three MRIxFields2026 tasks on validation. Fast generation: 30 axial slices across all modality/field combos in under 90 seconds; full-volume cross-modality-strength translation in under 70 seconds on a single NVIDIA A5000 GPU. Ablations reported; code available.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the effectiveness and efficiency of a single, unified model for cross-field MRI synthesis, enabling rapid, flexible generation across modalities and field strengths and facilitating standardized comparisons across scanners.

title: VLN on the Fly: An Onboard Vision-Language Navigation Stack for Aerial Robots
summary: Running vision-language navigation fully onboard an aerial robot is hard, since grounding, planning, and control must share limited compute and a single-stage error is difficult to isolate in flight. End-to-end aerial policies fuse these stages into one network, giving up the observability and safety checks a modular stack keeps available. We propose VLN on the Fly, an onboard stack that keeps grounding, planning, and control as separate, inspectable stages. A quantized VLM grounds an instruction to a coarse image cell, depth lifts it to a 3D goal, a fast B-spline planner returns a feasible trajectory, and a pretrained reinforcement learning policy tracks it to motor commands across quadrotors. Across 15 onboard flights over three everyday referents in a controlled indoor volume, the stack reaches the target in 13 of 15 trials with 5.72 cm mean goal error and 39.3% average GPU utilization. In 6 additional cluttered-environment trials, the stack tracks collision-free trajectories under onboard perception gating.

AI.tldr: An onboard, modular VLN stack for aerial robots that preserves grounding, planning, and control as separate stages, enabling interpretable, real-time navigation with limited compute.
AI.motivation: Running vision-language navigation onboard is challenging due to constrained compute and the need to maintain observability/safety checks; modular stacks can isolate errors and enable inspection.
AI.method: A modular onboard stack: a quantized VLM grounds an instruction to a coarse image cell; depth lifting yields a 3D goal; a fast B-spline planner computes a feasible trajectory; a pretrained RL policy tracks the trajectory to motor commands across quadrotors; evaluated in 15 onboard flights over 3 referents in indoor space, plus 6 cluttered trials with perception gating.
AI.result: Reached the target in 13 of 15 trials; mean goal error 5.72 cm; average GPU utilization 39.3%; 6 cluttered-environment trials showed collision-free trajectory tracking under onboard perception gating.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that a modular, onboard VLN stack can achieve accurate and safe navigation on a quadrotor with real-time performance, maintaining observability and safety checks absent in end-to-end policies.

title: Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation: From Natural-Language Traffic Rules to PROLOG
comment: In Proceedings of the International Workshop on Translating Natural Legal Language into Formal Representations (NLL2FR 2025)
summary: Traffic regulations are written for human interpretation and therefore rely on shared background knowledge and flexible phrasing, which inherently introduce ambiguity, context dependence, and semantic underspecification. These linguistic characteristics conflict with the precision required by computational reasoning engines such as Prolog, which demand explicit logical structure. This study evaluates two baseline translation approaches, Natural Language to Prolog ($NL\rightarrow Prolog$) and Logical English to Prolog ($LE\rightarrow Prolog$), and introduces a new reasoning-guided translation framework called Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation ($S4L\rightarrow Prolog$). The proposed S4L framework performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a single guided prompt, enabling direct translation of raw traffic rules into executable logic without human intervention. A benchmark consisting of twenty real-world traffic rules was used to evaluate each approach in terms of syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness. $S4L\rightarrow Prolog$ achieves the highest accuracy, correctly formalizing 75 percent of the rules, while $NL\rightarrow Prolog$ reaches 60 percent and $LE\rightarrow Prolog$ reaches 55 percent. Qualitative analysis further shows that S4L captures implicit causal relations, deontic modality, and exception structure more reliably than the baselines. These results demonstrate that structured reasoning prompts can substantially improve the reliability of natural-language-to-logic translation for legal and safety-critical applications.

AI.tldr: Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation (S4L→Prolog) outperforms NL→Prolog and LE→Prolog in translating traffic rules into Prolog, achieving 75% accuracy on 20 rules by leveraging a single guided prompt that performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between ambiguous natural-language traffic regulations and explicit logical representations required for automated reasoning. Address limitations of naive NL→Prolog and LE→Prolog translations in safety-critical domains.
AI.method: Baseline translations NL→Prolog and LE→Prolog are compared to the proposed S4L framework. S4L performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a guided prompt. Evaluation uses a benchmark of 20 real-world traffic rules, assessing syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness.
AI.result: S4L→Prolog achieves the highest accuracy (75% correct), outperforming NL→Prolog (60%) and LE→Prolog (55%). Qualitative analysis shows S4L better captures implicit causal relations, deontic modality, and exception structure.
AI.conclusion: Structured reasoning prompts enable more reliable NL-to-logic translation in legal/safety-critical contexts, suggesting a viable path to automate executable-rule generation from natural language.

title: Placement Is Free, Composition Is Not: The Latin Square as a Provably-Balanced Construction for Heterogeneous Sequence-Mixer Stacks
summary: Since GPT, most Transformers have repeated the same attention mechanism at every layer. Yet this design is largely a convention rather than a tested conclusion. When multiple sequence mixers are combined in one stack, improvements may arise from mechanism choice, placement, or both, making causal attribution difficult. We introduce Aether-7B-5Attn, a 6.59B-parameter mixture-of-experts model ($\approx$2.98B active) whose 49 layers contain seven sequence-mixing mechanisms arranged as a $7\times7$ Latin square. Because each mechanism appears exactly once in every row and column, the design guarantees balanced exposure across depth while eliminating placement confounds. To evaluate this principle, we build a parameter-matched proxy with four mechanisms arranged as a $4\times4$ Latin square over sixteen layers, matched to 700.9M parameters and trained with eight seeds per arm. The results reveal a clear dissociation. Rearranging a distributed heterogeneous stack into a balanced periodic cycle changes validation loss by only 0.16\%, indicating that exact placement has little effect. In contrast, clustering the same mechanisms into contiguous depth bands incurs a 0.59\% penalty, while replacing the heterogeneous stack with a homogeneous one incurs a 1.68\% penalty. These results indicate that performance depends primarily on heterogeneous composition distributed across depth rather than on any particular permutation. We confirm this finding at 2.16$\times$ larger scale (1.514B parameters), where the homogeneous-stack penalty increases to 2.63\% and removing the SSM-family mechanism produces a 3.20\% degradation. We further report per-mechanism cost profiles, English and Korean evaluations, and a causal-safety audit of all 49 layers. We release model weights, training recipes, training code, logs, and architecture source code.

AI.tldr: Aether-7B-5Attn studies whether layer-wise attention mechanism placement matters in deep transformers by enforcing a balanced, Latin-square exposure of seven mixing mechanisms across 49 layers, and comparing to four-mechanism proxies and homogeneous stacks. Findings: placement has minor effect; distributing heterogeneity across depth drives most performance gains; contiguous depth bands hurt more than reordering; removing a mechanism or scaling reveals penalties up to ~3%. Per-language results (English/Korean) and safety audit included; weights and code released.
AI.motivation: To causally attribute performance gains in deep transformers to the choice vs. placement of heterogeneous sequence-mixing mechanisms, and to test whether balanced exposure across depth confers advantages independent of exact permutation.
AI.method: Develop a 6.59B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Aether-7B-5Attn) with 49 layers, using seven sequence-mixing mechanisms arranged in a 7x7 Latin square to ensure each mechanism appears once per row/column. Build a parameter-matched 4x4 proxy (16 layers) with four mechanisms, trained across eight seeds per arm, for controlled comparisons. Evaluate using validation loss changes across rearrangements (balanced cycle vs. contiguous bands vs. homogeneous stacks) and scale experiments at 2.16x larger parameter count (1.514B). Assess per-mechanism costs, English and Korean evaluations, and conduct a causal-safety audit. Release all artifacts.
AI.result: Rearranging a distributed heterogeneous stack into a balanced periodic cycle changes validation loss by only 0.16%, indicating placement has little effect. Clustering mechanisms into contiguous depth bands incurs a 0.59% penalty, while replacing the heterogeneous stack with a homogeneous one incurs a 1.68% penalty. At 2.16x scale, penalties grow to 2.63% (homogeneous stack) and 3.20% (removing the SSM-family). Per-mechanism cost profiles and English/Korean performance reported; extensive safety audit performed. Model weights, training recipes, code, logs, and architecture source released.
AI.conclusion: Performance in deep, heterogeneous stacks is driven primarily by distributing diverse mechanisms across depth rather than by their exact permutation; balanced exposure (Latin-square) yields little advantage over arbitrary rearrangements, whereas clustering or homogenizing degrades performance. Results hold at larger scale and with/remove a mechanism, underscoring the value of heterogeneity across layers. Release of resources supports reproducibility.

title: EliGSiR: Continual RGB-D Mapping with Gaussian Splatting under Bounded Compute
summary: Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting assumes a closed set of observations and long optimization schedules. Continual RGB-D mapping in contrast poses the problem that new observations arrive online, while previously reconstructed regions must be preserved. We present EliGSiR (Evidence-guided Load-adaptive Incremental Gaussian Splatting with Image Replay), a continual Gaussian mapper that controls how the available optimization budget is used as the reconstruction evolves. Map-Guided View Scheduling filters redundant incoming views and reconsiders retained views according to the current state of the map. Load-Adaptive Fidelity adjusts supervision resolution to the current mapping load instead of following a fixed resolution schedule. Targeted Geometry Growth separates depth supervision from Gaussian creation and adds geometric capacity only where repeated RGB-D observations indicate missing or misplaced structure. Together, these mechanisms adapt which views are optimized, how much image detail is used, and where the representation grows while mapping remains active. We evaluate EliGSiR on Replica, TUM RGB-D, ScanNet++, and real RGB-D sensor sequences, considering both the final reconstruction and the map available throughout acquisition. On TUM RGB-D fr3/long_office_household, EliGSiR reaches 21.52 dB with the same ground-truth mapping poses used by the controlled baselines, compared with 19.42 dB for SplaTAM. In the tracked-pose comparison, EliGSiR with live ORB-SLAM3 poses reaches 23.02 dB in 155.5 s, compared with 20.10 dB in 230.9 s for CaRtGS using its native tracker. We further evaluate reconstruction throughout acquisition and show how EliGSiR adaptive view scheduling, supervision fidelity, and geometry growth improve the use of the available mapping budget.

AI.tldr: EliGSiR is a continual Gaussian mapping framework that adaptively allocates optimization budget for online RGB-D mapping through (1) map-guided view scheduling, (2) load-adaptive fidelity, and (3) targeted geometry growth, achieving higher reconstruction quality and faster mapping than baselines across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting assumes a closed, offline observation set and long optimization schedules. In continual RGB-D mapping, new observations arrive online while previously reconstructed regions must be preserved, requiring adaptive budgeting and view selection.
AI.method: EliGSiR introduces three components: Map-Guided View Scheduling to filter and reconsider views based on the current map; Load-Adaptive Fidelity to adjust supervision resolution to the available mapping load; Targeted Geometry Growth to separate depth supervision from Gaussian creation and allocate geometric capacity where missing or misaligned structure is indicated by repeated RGB-D observations. It also employs image replay and evaluates on Replica, TUM RGB-D, ScanNet++, and real sequences for both final reconstruction and map-throughout-acquisition.
AI.result: Empirical results show improved quality and efficiency: on TUM RGB-D fr3/long_office_household, EliGSiR achieves 21.52 dB vs 19.42 dB for SplaTAM under the same ground-truth poses. In tracked-pose mode with live ORB-SLAM3, it reaches 23.02 dB in 155.5 s vs CaRtGS 20.10 dB in 230.9 s. Additional evaluations demonstrate that adaptive view scheduling, fidelity, and geometry growth lead to better use of the available mapping budget and improved reconstruction throughout acquisition.
AI.conclusion: EliGSiR demonstrates that adaptive budgeting along with view filtering, variable supervision, and selective geometry growth enable effective online continual 3D mapping with higher quality reconstructions and faster mapping compared to strong baselines.

title: Strategic Transformer for Resource-Constrained Multi-Object Navigation in Ultra-Large-Scale Environments
summary: Resource-constrained multi-object navigation in vast indoor environments ($>2,000\text{ m}^2$) poses significant challenges for efficiency and strategic planning. To tackle this, we reformulate the task as a Set Orienteering Problem (SOP), providing an optimization framework under resource constraints where exploitation is governed by the SOP model and exploration is managed by a separate heuristic switcher. Conventional baselines suffer from either rigid planning or myopic behaviors. To overcome these limitations and resolve the NP-hard computational challenges of SOP for real-time navigation, we develop the Strategic Transformer. This lightweight architecture functions as a priority planner that internalizes expert combinatorial logic into a predictable $41.03\text{ ms}$ forward pass while reducing teacher-student information asymmetry. Incorporating geometric attention biases allows the network to effectively model long-range structural dependencies. By coupling the Transformer's macro-plan with a bounded iterative 2-opt local refinement on a capped candidate graph, our framework achieves a $94\times$ speedup compared to heavy meta-heuristics, ensuring bounded-latency inference suitable for onboard deployment. Experiments on ProcTHOR validate that our method successfully bridges the gap between exploration and exploitation, outperforming carefully re-implemented baselines under Progress weighted by Path Length (PPL) and establishing a new benchmark for scalable, resource-constrained navigation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a resource-constrained multi-object navigation method by formulating it as a Set Orienteering Problem (SOP) and solving it with a Strategic Transformer that speeds up planning for onboard deployment, combining macro-planning with local 2-opt refinement; achieves substantial speedups and favorable Progress weighted by Path Length (PPL) on ProcTHOR.
AI.motivation: Efficient, real-time navigation in large indoor environments under resource/latency constraints; traditional planners are either rigid or myopic and SOP is NP-hard, hindering real-time applicability.
AI.method: Formulate navigation as SOP with an exploitation policy guided by SOP and exploration via a separate heuristic switcher. Introduce Strategic Transformer as a lightweight priority planner that internalizes expert combinatorial logic in a 41.03 ms forward pass. Add geometric attention biases to capture long-range structure. Combine macro-plan from Transformer with a bounded iterative 2-opt local refinement on a capped candidate graph to produce a real-time solution with 94x speedup over heavy meta-heuristics.
AI.result: Outperforms re-implemented baselines on PPL (progress weighted by path length) and establishes a new benchmark for scalable, resource-constrained navigation on ProcTHOR; demonstrates bounded-latency inference suitable for onboard deployment.
AI.conclusion: A fast, accurate planner that bridges exploration and exploitation under resource constraints, enabling real-time SOP-based navigation and expanding the practicality of SOP-based approaches for large-scale indoor environments.

title: A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support
comment: Workshop on Qualitative Reasoning 2026 at IJCAI (35th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
summary: Spatial reasoning abilities correlate strongly with performance in STEM fields. Games offer a compelling medium for training these critical skills in developing children who have a natural proclivity for play. However, to facilitate human-like tutoring and player guidance, these games require an AI agent capable of making commonsense inferences from spatial events. Qualitative reasoning (QR) models appear to be a suitable framework for these application domains. As these models reason in symbolic representations, they can seamlessly translate game states into interpretable feedback for human-like player guidance. This paper introduces a hybrid qualitative model designed for Camelot Jr., a block-puzzle game that requires constructing multi-level bridges to connect two avatars stationed on separate towers. The game poses a challenge for the player, who must make platforms stable, plan their path, and ensure they use all the provided blocks. To handle the precise physics required by the domain, we integrate a mathematical center-of-mass stability logic to guide our qualitative solver. Our work facilitates spatial skill training in Camelot Jr. and contributes to the development of human-centric, explainable game-playing agents.

AI.tldr: Hybrid qualitative reasoning with center-of-mass stability logic for Camelot Jr.; enables an interpretable, physics-aware solver to guide spatial skill training.
AI.motivation: Need for human-like tutoring and explainable feedback in spatially demanding games; QR models can translate game states into symbolic, interpretable guidance.
AI.method: Develops a hybrid qualitative model using symbolic representations; integrates a mathematical center-of-mass stability check to handle physics; applies to Camelot Jr. puzzle of building stable multi-level bridges.
AI.result: Claims feasibility and explainable guidance; demonstrates integration of COM with QR for precise physics; results on applicability to Camelot Jr. and training tasks are discussed but not quantified in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Advances human-centric, explainable game-playing agents and spatial-skill training through interpretable, physics-aware qualitative reasoning.

title: Labeled Incidence Structures for Native Transformer Modeling of Text, Knowledge Graphs, and Hypergraphs
summary:
Text, knowledge graphs, and hypergraphs all have elements that play distinct roles within relation instances, structure that is lost when data is flattened into token sequences. We introduce labeled incidence structures (LIS), a uniform representation that encodes each endpoint as $(x_d, s, e)$: content $x_d$, a role or slot $s$, and the relation instance $e$ in which that role appears. Because every data type maps to the same $(x_d, s, e)$ representation without flattening, a single standard transformer can process them all natively, structural differences are carried entirely by the operators, not the architecture.
  LIS assigns a structural address to each endpoint by composing a slot operator and an instance operator, $A(s,e) = R_s R_e$. We characterize when this factorization gives every token a unique, path-independent address. When it does, the natural operator comparing endpoint $j$ to endpoint $i$ is the relative transport $P_{j\to i} = A_i^{-1} A_j$, which gives attention a role- and relation-aware inductive bias without imposing an arbitrary sequence order.
  Additive encodings of the form "position term plus relation term" can miss information that depends jointly on $s$ and $e$. We prove this in a controlled example family: when the journey operator is approximated by the sum of a position-only term and a relation-only term, the approximation cannot capture how position and relation combine, only their separate effects.
  We also analyze persistent knowledge repositories. Identifiers tied to storage locations make models sensitive to storage order, while freely learned identifiers can become harder to control as the repository size $M$ grows relative to the sample size $n$. Computing relation-instance operators from content avoids this storage-order issue and yields a capacity bound independent of $M$, under fixed architectural and Lipschitz assumptions.

AI.tldr: Introduces labeled incidence structures (LIS) to unify text, knowledge graphs, and hypergraphs into a single representation that preserves roles and relations via endpoints (x_d, s, e). A single standard transformer can process all types; structure is carried by operators rather than architecture.
AI.motivation: Preserve structural information across heterogeneous data formats and enable a single transformer to process text, graphs, and hypergraphs without flattening, avoiding loss of relational roles and instance context.
AI.method: Define LIS endpoints as (x_d, s, e) and construct a composite address A(s,e) = R_s R_e using slot and instance operators. Analyze conditions under which this factorization gives each token a unique, path-independent address. Propose the relative transport P_{j→i} = A_i^{-1} A_j as the natural attention operator that is role- and relation-aware. Compare additive encodings (position term + relation term) to joint s,e interactions, proving that sums cannot capture joint effects in a controlled example family. Examine persistent knowledge repositories, showing storage-order sensitivity with fixed storage identifiers, and derive that computing operators from content yields a capacity bound independent of repository size M under fixed architecture and Lipschitz constraints.
AI.result: The framework yields: (1) criteria for when A(s,e) provides unique, path-independent addresses; (2) a natural, role- and relation-aware attention via relative transport P_{j→i}; (3) a formal limitation of additive encodings in capturing joint s-e effects; (4) analysis of storage-order sensitivity and a capacity bound that is independent of M when operators are content-derived under fixed architectural and Lipschitz assumptions.
AI.conclusion: LIS offers a uniform, architecture-agnostic representation that preserves structural nuances across data types, enabling consistent transformer processing and revealing theoretical insights into addressability, attention biases, additive encoding limitations, and storage-related capacity considerations.

title: MM-Future: Multi-Mode Joint World-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous driving involves coupled decision-making and scene evolution under multi-mode uncertainty. To capture this coupling and uncertainty, we introduce MM-Future, a world-action model that generates multiple paired scene-action hypotheses and models bidirectional interaction within each pair. Each hypothesis is initialized from a structured action prior and an independent future scene source, which are then co-evolved through a modality-aware diffusion Transformer. To support efficient multi-mode rollout, MM-Future compresses multi-view video into planning-oriented representations, dubbed MM-Tokens. Finally, a future-conditioned proposal scorer ranks trajectory candidates by shared history context and their paired predicted future. On NAVSIM navtest, MM-Future achieves 94.0 PDMS and 91.5 EPDMS, while attaining a 32.3 HD-Score in zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM. Ablations show consistent improvements over both single-mode and action-only variants, validating the benefit of multi-mode joint world-action modeling.

AI.tldr: MM-Future is a multi-mode world-action diffusion model for autonomous driving that jointly evolves multiple scene-action hypotheses using MM-Tokens for planning; it achieves strong evaluation scores on NAVSIM and HUGSIM and shows ablations favoring multi-mode joint modeling.
AI.motivation: To address coupling between decision-making and scene evolution under multi-modal uncertainty, which single-mode or action-only models struggle to capture; enable efficient multi-mode rollout and better trajectory ranking.
AI.method: Propose MM-Future: generate multiple paired scene-action hypotheses; initialize each from structured action priors and independent future scene sources; co-evolve via modality-aware diffusion Transformer; compress multi-view video into MM-Tokens; use a future-conditioned proposal scorer to rank trajectory candidates using history context and predicted future.
AI.result: Achieves 94.0 PDMS and 91.5 EPDMS on NAVSIM navtest; 32.3 HD-Score in zero-shot closed-loop on HUGSIM; ablations show gains over single-mode and action-only variants.
AI.conclusion: Joint multi-mode world-action modeling with diffusion-based co-evolution and planning-oriented representations improves planning robustness and trajectory quality; MM-Future's architecture validates the benefit of combining multiple future-conditioned hypotheses and learned representations for autonomous driving.

title: LLM-Guided Transformation of Non-Critical Driving Scenes into Safety-Critical Scenarios Using Augmented Reality
summary: Testing Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS) requires realistic safety-critical scenarios, but collecting such data from real-world driving is costly and unsafe. This paper presents an automated pipeline that transforms safe driving scenes into safety-critical scenarios by combining computer vision, Large Language Models (LLMs), and Augmented Reality (AR). The system detects and tracks road users, extracts safety features including distance, velocity, motion direction, and Time-to-Collision (TTC), and assesses scene criticality. Safe scenes are modified by an LLM, which generates realistic collision-inducing objects and behaviors that are integrated into the original scene using AR. The proposed pipeline was evaluated on the nuScenes dataset, achieving 97.52% safety classification accuracy and successfully generating realistic scenarios such as pedestrian crossings, rear overtaking vehicles, and sudden-stop events. The results demonstrate an effective and flexible approach for automated generation of safety-critical scenarios to support the testing and validation of autonomous driving systems.

AI.tldr: Transforms safe driving scenes into safety-critical scenarios by integrating computer vision, LLMs, and augmented reality; evaluated on nuScenes with high safety-criterion detection (97.52%); generates scenarios like pedestrian crossings, rear overtaking, and sudden-stop events.
AI.motivation: Realistic safety-critical ADS test data is expensive and hazardous to collect from real-world driving; automated generation is needed to test and validate autonomous systems.
AI.method: Detect and track road users; extract safety features (distance, velocity, motion direction, Time-to-Collision); assess scene criticality; use an LLM to generate realistic collision-inducing objects/behaviors; integrate into the original scene via augmented reality.
AI.result: Achieved 97.52% safety classification accuracy on nuScenes; successfully generated realistic scenarios such as pedestrian crossings, rear overtaking vehicles, and sudden-stop events.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates an effective and flexible automated pipeline for generating safety-critical scenarios to support testing and validation of autonomous driving systems.

title: Generating Heterogeneous 3D Geological Microstructures from 2D Images via a Stable Diffusion-Adversarial Model
summary:
Characterizing the physical properties of clay and cementitious materials matters across many fields, from materials science to geological waste disposal. Property simulation typically calls for 3D imaging, which is expensive, not always accessible, and technically limited for certain materials. Recent progress in deep generative models offers a way around this, reconstructing 3D volumes from the more easily acquired 2D images.
  Among GAN-based methods for 3D microstructure generation, SliceGAN has shown strong results for homogeneous isotropic and anisotropic systems. It struggles, however, to capture the finer detail of more complex heterogeneous microstructures, which motivates alternative generative frameworks.
  We introduce a hybrid approach that draws on the stability and generation quality of denoising diffusion models. Since no 3D ground truth is available, we replace the standard denoising loss with an adversarial loss, which yields a stable training process in our experiments. We show that the resulting model generates microstructures of varying complexity with minimal slice artefacts and close agreement with ground-truth phase fractions and structural descriptors.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-adversarial hybrid model for 3D microstructure generation from 2D images, addressing SliceGAN limits and enabling accurate phase fractions without 3D ground truth.
AI.motivation: 3D microstructure property simulations are costly; 3D imaging not always accessible; need methods to recover 3D from 2D; diffusion-based generation may yield better detail for heterogeneous materials than GAN-based SliceGAN.
AI.method: Replace denoising loss in a diffusion model with an adversarial loss to enable training without 3D ground truth; combine diffusion model stability with GAN-like adversarial objective; generate 3D volumes with minimal slice artefacts.
AI.result: Generated microstructures across varying complexity, with phase fractions and structural descriptors close to ground truth; reduced slice artefacts; improved fidelity over GAN-based methods for heterogeneous microstructures.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates viability of diffusion-adversarial hybrids for 3D microstructure reconstruction from 2D data; stable training and faithful 3D reconstructions extendable to materials with complex heterogeneity; potential for broader application in materials design and geological waste disposal.

title: Personalising a Cross-User Surface Electromyography Encoder Under a Small Calibration Budget
summary: A myoelectric interface needs calibration from the user before it will function. Earlier work has treated calibration as a quantity, but has not asked the question of what a device should do with the calibration repetitions once they have been collected. This paper views personalizing the cross-user encoder as a design decision with a cost. Four alternative approaches to using exactly the same labeled repetitions were tested from a single cross-user encoder per held-out subject. Prototypical adaptation, linear probes, scaled fine-tuning and full fine-tuning were tested at every budget up to the maximum each database allows, five repetitions on DB1 and four on DB2 and DB5. Comparing four ways to spend a small calibration budget across 77 subjects, full fine-tuning is the most accurate at every budget, consistently enough that there is no exception among subsets of subjects. The result which impacts how one might make an engineering decision however is that a gradient free prototypical rule recovers 52 to 78 per cent of its benefit with no optimiser and no per-user copy of the weights, which makes personalisation something a worn device can do at donning time. The widespread intuition that a good representation only needs a fresh classifier is incorrect here. How well each method may perform relative to a per-user classifier that would be fitted by a clinic will depend on the specific database.

AI.tldr: Full fine-tuning of a cross-user encoder yields the highest accuracy across calibration budgets; a gradient-free prototypical rule recovers 52-78% of its benefit without any optimizer or per-user weight copies, enabling on-donning personalization; the value of representation learning vs per-user classifiers depends on the database.
AI.motivation: Investigate how to use calibration repetitions to personalize a cross-user myoelectric decoder, treating personalization as a design choice with a cost rather than an assumed benefit of calibration.
AI.method: Four strategies using identical labeled repetitions were evaluated: prototypical adaptation, linear probes, scaled fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. Experiments spanned budgets up to the database limits (five repetitions on DB1, four on DB2/DB5) across 77 subjects with a single cross-user encoder per held-out subject.
AI.result: Full fine-tuning consistently achieved the highest accuracy at every budget. The gradient-free prototypical rule recovered 52–78% of its benefit without an optimizer or per-user copies of weights, enabling donning-time personalization. The common assumption that a good representation suffices (only needing a fresh classifier) does not hold here; performance relative to clinic-fitted per-user classifiers varies by database.
AI.conclusion: Personalization of the cross-user encoder can be effectively achieved at donning time, especially with full fine-tuning, while gradient-free prototypical adaptation offers a practical fallback with substantial gains without optimization or per-user weight storage. The optimal choice is dataset-dependent, and implications for engineering decisions should consider calibration budget and operating context.

title: Compact Vision Models for Iris Presentation Attack Detection under Presentation Attack Instrument Shift and Environmental Degradation
comment: Accepted at BIOSIG 2026. This preprint includes minor nomenclature and editorial corrections clarifying the project-specific Patch-ABMIL and Compact-TransMIL variants
summary: Iris presentation attack detection (PAD) is security-critical when a subsystem that appears reliable during development encounters presentation attack instruments (PAIs) or acquisition conditions absent from validation data. We benchmark three compact scratch-trained computer-vision models, each with at most approximately 0.26 million trainable parameters, on the Notre Dame subset of LivDet-Iris 2017 under PAI-driven domain shift and environmental degradation. All models are trained without external pretraining or data augmentation and evaluated over five seeds. A validation-selected threshold is transferred unchanged to the known-attack, unknown-attack, corrupted, and pooled test partitions. From known to unknown attack presentations, Attack Presentation Classification Error Rate (APCER) increases by 17.11-30.47 percentage points and Detection Equal Error Rate (D-EER) increases by 7.38-12.73 percentage points. At the validation-selected threshold, ZACH-ViT obtains the lowest unknown-attack APCER (47.69 +/- 4.84%) and D-EER (38.87 +/- 0.93%), while Compact-TransMIL obtains the lowest Bona Fide Presentation Classification Error Rate (BPCER). ZACH-ViT also gives the lowest unknown-attack BPCER at an APCER limit of 10% (81.29 +/- 1.95%). The high absolute errors show that the comparative advantage of the best compact model does not constitute deployment readiness under unknown PAIs.

AI.tldr: Compact scratch-trained iris PAD models show limited generalization under PAI-driven domain shift; best model not deployment-ready.
AI.motivation: Assess whether small, scratch-trained models can generalize to unseen PAIs and degraded conditions without pretraining or augmentation, using LivDet-Iris 2017 Notre Dame subset.
AI.method: Train three models (~0.26M params) from scratch, no external pretraining or augmentation; five seeds; fixed validation threshold transferred to known/unknown/corrupted/pooled tests; evaluate APCER, D-EER, BPCER.
AI.result: APCER and D-EER degrade considerably from known to unknown attacks (17.11-30.47 pp; 7.38-12.73 pp). ZACH-ViT yields best unknown-attack APCER (47.69±4.84%) and D-EER (38.87±0.93%); Compact-TransMIL yields best BPCER; unknown-attack BPCER best at APCER limit 10% (81.29±1.95%). Overall, absolute errors are high, undermining deployment readiness under unknown PAIs.
AI.conclusion: Compact models exhibit limited generalization to unseen PAIs and degraded conditions; to approach deployment, strategies like external pretraining, data augmentation, broader validation, and threshold calibration across domains are needed.

title: Implementation of Tightly-Coupled SLAM Fusion of GPS, IMU, and LiDAR for Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Autonomous vehicles depend entirely on Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) to navigate safely in unknown environments. However, relying on a single sensory modality introduces critical failure points: LiDAR systems degrade in featureless corridors, Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) accumulate mathematical drift, and GPS drops frequently in urban canyons. This paper presents the implementation of a tightly-coupled SLAM fusion architecture that integrates a Velodyne 3D LiDAR, a high-frequency IMU, and GPS to achieve continuous spatial awareness. Utilizing a phased development methodology, we establish a 2D baseline to validate hardware synchronization and transform geometries before upgrading to a full 3D architecture driven by FAST-LIO2. This advanced approach uses an Iterated Error-State Kalman Filter (IESKF) to process dense 3D laser points alongside continuous inertial data, eliminating motion blur at high speeds. To eradicate long-term drift, a GTSAM pose-graph optimization back-end executes multi-modal loop closures. Evaluated across simulated environments and physical deployments, the results demonstrate that tightly-coupled 3D fusion effectively overcomes individual sensor blind spots to generate highly detailed point clouds, providing the foundational High-Definition (HD) maps required for advanced downstream autonomous planners.

AI.tldr: A tightly-coupled 3D SLAM fusion architecture integrating Velodyne LiDAR, high-rate IMU, and GPS, using an Iterated Error-State Kalman Filter (IESKF) and pose-graph optimization (GTSAM) to produce detailed HD maps for autonomous planning.
AI.motivation: Mitigate reliance on any single sensor by addressing LiDAR featureless environments, IMU drift, and GPS outages; provide continuous, high-fidelity spatial awareness and robust HD maps for planners.
AI.method: Phase 1: develop a 2D baseline to validate hardware synchronization and transform geometries. Phase 2: extend to full 3D mapping powered by FAST-LIO2. Sensor fusion via Iterated Error-State Kalman Filter (IESKF) processing dense 3D point clouds with continuous inertial data. Long-term drift corrected with a GTSAM-based pose-graph optimization that incorporates multi-modal loop closures.
AI.result: Demonstrates that tightly-coupled 3D fusion mitigates sensor blind spots, yielding detailed point clouds and robust HD maps in both simulated and real deployments, suitable for downstream autonomous planning.
AI.conclusion: A tightly-coupled multi-sensor SLAM architecture combining LiDAR, IMU, and GPS with IESKF fusion and pose-graph optimization provides robust, drift-resistant, high-fidelity mapping essential for reliable autonomous navigation.

title: The Organization of Inference: Information, Resource Constraints, and AI Production
summary: The economic value of inference depends on how capacity and task information are distributed across stages of AI production. We study these organizational margins using controlled workflow experiments on externally verified software-engineering tasks. In two matched resource panels, direct execution records the same success rate of 59.6 percent at logical-token ceilings of 12,000 and 24,000, while success under information-constrained planning rises from 36.2 to 51.2 percent. The planning disadvantage narrows by 15.0 percentage points (95 percent task-cluster bootstrap interval: 4.2 to 25.8). A strict read-only planning campaign varies whether the planner sees the task issue. At 12,000 tokens, issue access raises success by about 16 percentage points over issue-hidden planning. Compared with direct execution, task-informed planning is about 10 points lower at 12,000 tokens; at 24,000 tokens, it shows a 29.6-point advantage. In the resource panels, direct execution uses substantially less than either ceiling, while the planning workflow's binding rate falls from 46.2 to 0.8 percent and downstream execution accounts for 89.9 percent of the increase in total use. Scale determines the capacity available to a system; workflow and information structure shape the productive value

AI.tldr: Economic value of AI inference hinges on how capacity and information are distributed across production stages; planning under information constraints improves outcomes with scale, and task-informed planning shows variable advantages over direct execution depending on token ceilings.
AI.motivation: Quantify how organizational margins (workflow structure and information distribution) affect productive value in AI production, using controlled experiments to compare direct execution with information-constrained planning across token ceilings.
AI.method: Controlled workflow experiments with two matched resource panels (token ceilings 12,000 and 24,000). Compare direct execution vs information-constrained planning (with varying visibility of the task issue). Measure success rates, binding rates, and downstream execution; use externally verified software-engineering tasks; bootstrap confidence intervals.
AI.result: Direct execution achieves 59.6% success at both ceilings; planning under information constraints rises from 36.2% to 51.2% success. The planning disadvantage narrows by 15.0 percentage points (95% CI: 4.2–25.8). Read-only planning with issue access increases success by ~16 percentage points at 12k; task-informed planning lags direct execution by ~10 points at 12k but gains 29.6 points at 24k. Binding rate in the planning workflow declines from 46.2% to 0.8%; downstream execution accounts for 89.9% of the total use increase. Scale determines capacity; workflow and information structure shape productive value.
AI.conclusion: Scale (token capacity) sets available system capacity, while how workflow and information are structured (planning vs direct execution, issue visibility) shapes the realized productive value. Proper alignment of capacity distribution with information flow can substantially alter performance outcomes.

title: Intact-to-Amputee Transfer in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding: Training Source and Calibration Budget
summary: A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A systematic review of 1077 studies quantifies where the evidence is thin: amputees appear in about one in six. Here a montage-agnostic cross-user encoder is carried to eleven transradial amputees on a protocol matched to its intact-limb training data. Zero-shot cross-population transfer fails outright: the encoder requires labeled data from the new user before it begins decoding, and it then exceeds the per-user classifier a clinic would fit by 0.190 macro F1 at three repetitions and for every subject in the cohort. Given three labelled repetitions it reaches 0.779 macro-F1 against 0.589 for the per-user pipeline. Training on forty intact subjects produces better transfers to a new amputee than training on ten other amputees, and combining the two produces better transfers than either individually. The prediction pre-registered for this study, which extends the encoder's baseline-strength account with the premise that amputee EMG is less separable, holds true only after a few repetitions become available and after enriching the source pool with additional amputees. At a single repetition, and at every budget under a source matched to the intact-limb comparison, it fails. Thus, it locates the boundary of the proposed account.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot cross-user transfer fails for EMG-based prosthesis decoding; calibration with a few labeled repetitions and diverse source data enables the cross-user encoder to outperform per-user models, delineating the boundary of cross-population transfer.
AI.motivation: To evaluate cross-user generalization of myoelectric decoders, quantify calibration requirements, and understand how source-pool composition (intact vs amputee data) affects transfer to amputees.
AI.method: Train a montage-agnostic cross-user encoder on intact-limb EMG. Test on 11 transradial amputees with a protocol matched to intact data. Assess zero-shot transfer, then three labeled repetitions, comparing to a per-user classifier. Explore effects of source-pool size (40 intact vs 10 amputees) and combination, with pre-registered predictions and an analysis of amputee EMG separability.
AI.result: Zero-shot cross-population transfer fails: new-user labels are needed before decoding. With three labeled repetitions, macro-F1 reaches 0.779, versus 0.589 for the per-user pipeline. Training on forty intact subjects transfers better than training on ten amputees; combining sources yields the best transfer. The pre-registered account holds only after some repetitions and with a richer amputee source pool. At a single repetition (or with budgets under a source-matched intact-limb baseline), transfer fails, defining the boundary of the proposed account.
AI.conclusion: Cross-user encoders can surpass per-user pipelines given labeled calibration and diverse source data, but zero-shot transfer is not viable. Beneficial transfer requires at least a few labeled repetitions and expanded source diversity; the boundary conditions emphasize calibration and source-pool richness to achieve cross-population gains.

title: TouchSight: Bare-Handed Tactile Prediction from Egocentric Video via Generative Visual Augmentation
summary: Tactile signals provide direct contact and force measurements that are essential for understanding physical interactions and enabling dexterous robotic manipulation. However, tactile sensing requires direct measurement at contact interfaces, making large-scale data collection reliant on intrusive, costly, and restrictive instrumentation. We present TouchSight, a monocular egocentric vision framework for dense full-hand contact force prediction that leverages 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and extensive hand-object interaction (HOI) data. To address the appearance gap between gloved training data and bare-hand real-world scenarios, we construct TwinTouch-20H: 20 hours of paired visual data in which generative video models re-render gloved recordings as bare-hand observations against new backgrounds while preserving the original measured tactile labels. TouchSight predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos, outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and improves consistently as glove supervision scales. These results demonstrate that dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone, without tactile instrumentation at capture time.

AI.tldr: TouchSight uses monocular egocentric video to predict dense hand-contact forces, bridging glove-based and bare-hand appearances via a generative re-rendering dataset (TwinTouch-20H), enabling tactile signal recovery without real tactile sensors.
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on intrusive tactile instrumentation by leveraging visual signals and synthetic appearance-matching to enable large-scale dense tactile data collection.
AI.method: Proposes TouchSight: a monocular egocentric framework that learns dense contact force prediction from gloved recordings and generated bare-hand video. It introduces TwinTouch-20H, a 20-hour paired-visual dataset where generative models re-render gloved footage as bare-hand observations on new backgrounds while preserving tactile labels, trained on ~500 hours of pressure-glove data and extensive HOI data.
AI.result: TouchSight outperforms prior contact-prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and shows performance gains with increased glove supervision.
AI.conclusion: Dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone, without tactile instrumentation during capture.

title: RoboFind: Multi-Agent Personalized Object Search for People Who Are Blind or Have Low Vision
summary: Blind and low-vision users often need to locate a specific personal object rather than an arbitrary instance of the same category. The task calls for a robot that can move through the space and reach viewpoints the user cannot, and for an accessible interface where the user says which object is meant and learns whether the right one was found. We present RoboFind, a multi-agent framework in which a smartphone teaches the target and a quadruped robot carries out the search. A Target Teaching Agent converts guided smartphone recordings into a semantic target profile and a reusable multi-view reference bank through an accessible capture flow with AR guidance, speech and haptic feedback, and screen-reader support, so later missions refer to a stored object without repeating the teaching process. At runtime, a Navigation Agent explores the environment and proposes candidate targets, a Verification Agent checks each candidate against the stored references, and a Coordination and Recovery Agent completes the mission or triggers recovery and continued search. Across 32 real-robot missions, RoboFind reaches 85.0% success against 25.0% for a reconstructed sequential first-stop baseline over 20 trials with ten targets, and reduces false success from 75.0% to 5.0%. On six shared targets it succeeds in 10/12 trials, against 5/12 for 12 independently executed GPT-6 Astra-only trials. These results show that the multi-agent design fits the demands of personalized object search, where verifying object identity before declaring completion is what makes the outcome something a user can rely on.

AI.tldr: RoboFind demonstrates a multi-agent system enabling blind/low-vision users to locate a specific personal object via smartphone-based teacher targeting and a robotic search, achieving high real-world success and low false positives.
AI.motivation: Address personalized object retrieval for visually impaired users, requiring user-guided identity specification, robust verification, and accessible teaching interfaces.
AI.method: Introduce RoboFind with a Target Teaching Agent on a smartphone to build a semantic target profile and a multi-view reference bank via accessible capture (AR guidance, speech, haptics, screen-reader). Runtime uses a Navigation Agent, a Verification Agent, and a Coordination & Recovery Agent controlling a quadruped robot. Evaluated across 32 real-robot missions; compared to a reconstructed sequential baseline and GPT-6 Astra-only trials.
AI.result: Achieves 85.0% success across 32 missions versus 25.0% baseline; reduces false success from 75.0% to 5.0%. On six shared targets, 10/12 trials succeeded (vs 5/12 Astra-only).
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent design improves reliability and trust for personalized object search by performing identity verification before completion; supports scalable, user-centered assistive search workflows and suggests robust potential for real-world deployment.

title: SkillAA: Attribution-Guided Skill-Graph Updating with Targeted Validation and Rollback
summary: External skills provide domain procedures without parameter updates, but existing methods often edit skills directly from failed rollouts without structured routing from an observed failure to an editable location; existing skill graphs also underuse semantic boundaries, object addresses, and topological dependencies for skill retrieval, targeted updating, and scoped validation. We introduce SkillAA (Skill Abductive Attribution), a structured skill-optimization framework for frozen language models. It represents skill applicability, execution, and composition in a unified graph, allowing the same structure to support skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation. SkillAA contrasts successful and failed executions to route candidate repairs to specific graph objects, updates only the selected local structure, and uses Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes before commitment. With gpt-5.6-sol, SkillAA reaches 81.5%, 66.7%, and 91.2% on SearchQA, LiveMath, and DocVQA, respectively, and attains the highest observed mean in every main setting. These results support the utility of attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation.

AI.tldr: Structured skill-optimization via SkillAA enables attribution-guided, graph-scoped repair and validation for frozen LMs, yielding strong benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing skill frameworks lack structured routing from failures to editable graph components and underutilize semantic boundaries, addresses, and topology for targeted updates and validation.
AI.method: Introduce SkillAA: a unified graph representing skill applicability, execution, and composition; supports skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation; route repairs by contrasting success vs failure to specific graph objects; update only local structures; employ Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes; evaluate with gpt-5.6-sol.
AI.result: On benchmarks—SearchQA 81.5%, LiveMath 66.7%, DocVQA 91.2%—with highest mean in main settings.
AI.conclusion: Attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation enhance skill retrieval, targeted updates, and reliable validation in frozen-LM skills.

title: A Learning Algorithm for Threshold Boolean Networks with Prescribed Fixed Points
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, to be published in 20th International Meeting, CIBB 2025, Revised Selected Papers
summary: We present a learning algorithm for inferring threshold Boolean networks (TBNs) with a prescribed set of fixed points. The proposed method employs a custom differentiable loss function that jointly enforces fixed point preservation, penalizes spurious attractors, encourages binary outputs, and promotes sparsity through L1 regularization. Applied to the FOS-GRN model of Arabidopsis thaliana, the approach achieved perfect reconstruction (i.e., all 10 desired fixed points and no spurious ones) in 5 out of 30 independent runs, recovering on average 8.53 $\pm$ 0.90 correct fixed points with no spurious attractors. In contrast, standard methods such as the Perceptron and Logistic Regression recovered up to 10 fixed points but introduced between 8 and 31 spurious ones.
