An additional analysis varying the sparsity coefficient ($λ$) confirmed that the method's performance and the structural properties of the inferred networks remain robust within a practical range (up to 0.01) of regularization strengths. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of the proposed algorithm in capturing meaningful network dynamics under prescribed dynamical constraints.

AI.tldr: A differentiable learning framework infers threshold Boolean networks with fixed-point constraints, achieving high fidelity and robustness against spurious attractors, outperforming standard classifiers on the FOS-GRN Arabidopsis model.
AI.motivation: To infer Boolean regulatory networks with guaranteed fixed-point dynamics by enforcing fixed-point preservation while discouraging spurious attractors and promoting sparsity.
AI.method: Train a threshold Boolean network using a custom differentiable loss that (i) preserves designated fixed points, (ii) penalizes spurious attractors, (iii) encourages binary activations, and (iv) applies L1 regularization for sparsity; evaluate on the Arabidopsis FOS-GRN model with multiple runs.
AI.result: In 5 of 30 runs, perfect reconstruction of all 10 fixed points with no spurious attractors; average recovery of 8.53 ± 0.90 fixed points and no spurious attractors; standard methods (Perceptron/Logistic Regression) produced up to 10 fixed points but with 8–31 spurious attractors; robustness observed for sparsity coefficient λ up to 0.01.
AI.conclusion: The proposed loss-guided learning method is effective and stable for capturing critical network dynamics under prescribed fixed-point constraints, offering clear advantages over traditional classifiers in preserving dynamical structure.

title: WeVisDoc: From Coverage to Capability for Robust End-to-End Document Parsing
summary: Document parsing converts document images into structured content and requires reliable performance across diverse layouts and acquisition conditions. Yet training corpora are biased toward common document types and clean digital pages, while expanding coverage alone does not specify how to address a parser's remaining weaknesses. We present WeVisDoc, a two-stage data-centric framework for robust end-to-end document parsing. Stage I broadens semantic, structural, and appearance coverage through heterogeneous data and structure-preserving degradation synthesis. Stage II uses a held-out probe to measure the Stage I parser's residual errors within fixed visual-structural clusters. These diagnostics guide targeted data construction and reallocation of the target-token budget. WeVisDoc-4B achieves an Overall score of 95.38 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and a mean Overall score of 75.54 across the three PureDocBench tracks, ranking first among the compared end-to-end parsers in all four settings. Compared with Stage I, Stage II improves Overall scores for the 2B and 4B models on both benchmarks, with larger gains on the degraded PureDocBench tracks, including a 4.03-point gain for the 4B model on the Real Degraded track.

AI.tldr: Two-stage data-centric framework WeVisDoc for robust end-to-end document parsing; Stage I broadens coverage; Stage II diagnostics guide targeted data construction; achieves state-of-the-art scores on OmniDocBench and PureDocBench.
AI.motivation: Document parsers trained on biased, clean data struggle with diverse layouts and degraded acquisition; need guidance beyond larger corpora to fix remaining weaknesses.
AI.method: Stage I: heterogeneous data and degradation; Stage II: held-out probe metrics residual errors within fixed visual-structural clusters to reallocate target-token budget; Stage II improves over Stage I.
AI.result: WeVisDoc-4B: OmniDocBench v1.6 Overall 95.38; PureDocBench mean 75.54; rank 1 among end-to-end parsers; Stage II yields gains (2B/4B) and +4.03 on Real Degraded track for 4B.
AI.conclusion: Two-stage data-centric framework enhances robustness and performance across varied benchmarks; diagnostics-driven data allocation yields notable improvements.

title: Navi-Agent: Unlocalized Monocular Navigation Agent
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics & Automation (ICRA)
summary: Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires an embodied agent to execute long-horizon instructions in unknown environments. Existing zero-shot VLN-CE systems typically maintain spatial states through geometric localization or coordinate-based representations. Recent geometry-constrained navigation removes depth and globally consistent coordinates, but maintaining persistent spatial awareness for place confirmation, progress verification, and recovery remains challenging. We present Navi-Agent, a zero-shot VLN-CE agent that constructs a coordinate-free spatial state from visual observations and executed motion histories. Navi-Agent organizes this state as a navigation topology, where nodes represent visual places and edges represent motion transitions. This representation enables observation-based approximate self-localization, task progress verification, and visual revisitation-based recovery. Navi-Agent performs closed-loop navigation by decomposing instructions into sub-goals, executing local visual navigation, and verifying visited places through the constructed spatial state. Experiments on zero-shot VLN-CE benchmark and real-world robot platforms show that Navi-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance among geometry-constrained methods while remaining competitive with approaches relying on geometric localization.

AI.tldr: Navi-Agent is a zero-shot VLN-CE agent that builds a coordinate-free navigation topology from visual observations and motion histories to perform observation-based localization, progress verification, and recovery, achieving state-of-the-art performance among geometry-constrained methods.
AI.motivation: VLN-CE requires long-horizon navigation in unknown environments without reliable depth or global coordinates; existing methods struggle to maintain persistent spatial awareness for place confirmation, progress tracking, and recovery.
AI.method: Construct a topology where nodes are visually grounded places and edges are motion transitions; use this to perform approximate self-localization, progress verification, and revisitation-based recovery; decompose instructions into sub-goals, perform local navigation, and verify visited places; closed-loop navigation.
AI.result: Empirical results on zero-shot VLN-CE benchmarks and real-world robots show Navi-Agent outperforms geometry-constrained baselines and is competitive with geometry-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Coordinate-free spatial state via a navigation topology enables robust zero-shot VLN-CE navigation without depth, enabling localization, progress verification, and recovery, with strong empirical performance.

title: How Do Agent Harnesses Create Value? Planning Information and Release Control in Stateful LLM Agents
summary: Agent harnesses supply planning guidance, organize execution, and check completion. We study how these components affect success, erroneous acceptance, and cost in two Retail experiments and an Airline pilot in $τ^2$-bench. The primary comparison pairs prewritten task-specific plans (Fixed) with shuffled policy text matched in word count (Sham), isolating the contribution of guidance content. Across 265 matched cells, Fixed improves oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90\% task-clustered bootstrap interval, 1.15--13.36 points), with gains concentrated in higher-complexity tasks. A read-only terminal verifier rejects 61\% of Retail oracle-invalid episodes while withholding 17\% of correct ones, at less than one cent of additional cost per episode. Which component matters more depends on the loss assigned to erroneous acceptance: at low liability the planning gain dominates; at high liability the verifier's avoided false passes dominate---and a standalone verifier captures nearly all the false-pass benefit of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of its cost.

AI.tldr: Prewritten task plans (Fixed) improve oracle-verified success; a read-only verifier reduces erroneous acceptance; the optimal mix depends on false-pass costs, with verification offering most benefit at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Disentangle the contributions of guidance content (planning) from policy text and assess the separate and combined value of planning vs verification in automated decision agents across retail and airline benchmark tasks.
AI.method: Compare Fixed (prewritten task-specific plans) against Sham (shuffled policy text matched in word count) across 265 matched task–episodes in two Retail experiments and an Airline τ^2-bench pilot; evaluate a read-only terminal verifier; report oracle-verified success gains, false-acceptance/error metrics, and cost implications; bootstrap CIs for robustness.
AI.result: Fixed yields a 7.17 percentage-point increase in oracle-verified success (CI 1.15–13.36); gains are larger for higher-complexity tasks. A read-only verifier rejects 61% of oracle-invalid episodes and withholds 17% of correct ones, at under $0.01 additional cost per episode. The relative importance of planning vs verification depends on the loss for erroneous acceptance: at low liability planning dominates; at high liability the verifier’s false-pass avoidance dominates. A standalone verifier captures nearly all false-pass benefits of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of the cost.
AI.conclusion: Guidance content via prewritten plans provides measurable performance gains; verification can achieve most false-pass avoidance at lower cost, especially under high-liability settings. A modular verifier may largely substitute for the full stack when false positives are the primary concern.

title: Improving Generalization and Robustness in Offline Reinforcement Learning via Boundary-Aware Data Augmentation
summary: Current offline reinforcement learning (ORL) algorithms tend to overfit the training dataset and exhibit poor in-distribution generalization and robustness performance when deployed to real environments, thus compromising their effectiveness. Existing methods typically enhance in-distribution generalization and robustness by leveraging regularization techniques widely used in computer vision. However, due to the high sensitivity of low-level physical signals to distributional shifts, these methods still suffer from notable limitations in in-distribution generalization and robustness, making it difficult to achieve stable performance in complex environments. To address this issue, we theoretically analyze the error bounds of the behavior policy and action-value function trained with random episode interpolation, revealing that the error scales positively correlated with the distance between states. Based on this insight, we propose a method called $\bf{B}$oundary-$\bf{A}$ware $\bf{D}$ata $\bf{A}$ugmentation (BADA), which leverages neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries, enabling the generation of synthetic data that more faithfully preserves the original data distribution. We first conduct qualitative studies in a toy environment, showing that BADA generates mixed samples that preserve desirable policy smoothness while accurately reconstructing multimodal value distributions. Extensive experiments on limited offline datasets further demonstrate that BADA attains state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Boundary-Aware Data Augmentation (BADA) for offline RL; theoretical error bounds show error grows with state distance under random episode interpolation; uses neighboring states to define interpolation boundaries; generates synthetic samples that preserve the original distribution; toy experiments show policy smoothness and multimodal value distributions; achieves state-of-the-art results on limited offline RL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Offline RL models tend to overfit and suffer from poor in-distribution generalization and robustness due to distribution shifts and sensitivity of low-level signals. Existing regularization from computer vision is insufficient. A principled data augmentation that respects the data manifold could improve generalization.
AI.method: Derives error bounds for the behavior policy and Q-function under random episode interpolation. Introduces Boundary-Aware Data Augmentation (BADA) that uses neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries, enabling synthetic samples that stay within the data distribution. Includes qualitative toy-environment studies and extensive offline experiments.
AI.result: BADA achieves state-of-the-art performance on diverse offline RL benchmarks with limited data.
AI.conclusion: Boundary-aware, interpolation-based data augmentation mitigates overfitting and improves in-distribution generalization and robustness in offline RL, enabling more stable performance in complex environments.

title: When Do Language-Grounded Explanations Help? A Graph-Bottleneck for Farm Monitoring Interpretable Sheep Facial Pain
summary: Automated pain recognition from facial expression could make continuous welfare assessment practical in sheep, but adoption depends on trust: a stockperson cannot act on a score that arrives without justification. We ground a model in the Sheep Pain Facial Expression Scale (SPFES) by letting each detected facial region attend over text embeddings of the clinical descriptors and then test whether the resulting explanations mean anything. They do not. Ablating an entire descriptor changes the predicted logit by about $10^{-4}$, and the most-attended cue agrees with the predicted pain level in only $32.6\%$ of regions, although the attention maps, the learned gate, and the generated text all proposed otherwise. We therefore remove the appearance bypass with a concept bottleneck whose classifier reads only SPFES concept scores, supervised by per-region state annotations that image-level pipelines discard. This costs $0.05$--$0.10$ in Cohen's $κ$ but yields concepts that are demonstrably learned: minority pain-indicating states are recovered at $3.5$--$8.3\times$ their base rates, and the ear and eye severity orderings emerge without severity supervision. Removing the supervision alone leaves $κ$ unchanged while concept accuracy falls to $0.109$, showing that architectural necessity does not imply semantic validity. We also show that pooled concept accuracy is misleading under clinical imbalance and provide a cross-validated, protocol-matched benchmark of seven methods on this dataset.

AI.tldr: Attention-based SPFES explanations in sheep pain recognition are not semantically meaningful; a concept bottleneck improves interpretability and minority pain state recovery but incurs a drop in Cohen's kappa; pooled concept accuracy is misleading under imbalance; cross-validated benchmark across seven methods.
AI.motivation: Evaluate trustworthiness of automated pain scoring by validating explanations against clinical descriptors and developing an interpretable model aligned with SPFES concepts; assess explainability modalities under dataset imbalance.
AI.method: 1) Train SPFES-attentive model with text embeddings of descriptors; 2) Evaluate explanation validity and ablations; 3) Remove appearance bypass and use a concept bottleneck supervised by region annotations; 4) Evaluate effect on kappa and concept recovery; 5) Assess effect of supervision removal; 6) Provide cross-validated benchmark across seven methods.
AI.result: Ablating a descriptor causes negligible logit change (~1e-4); most-attended cue aligns with predicted pain in 32.6% of regions; attention maps and generated text disagree with predictions; concept bottleneck yields κ cost of 0.05-0.10 but concepts are learned; minority pain states recovered 3.5-8.3x; ear/eye severity orderings emerge without supervision; removing supervision leaves κ unchanged but concept accuracy drops to 0.109; pooled concept accuracy is misleading under imbalance; cross-validated benchmark on seven methods.
AI.conclusion: Architectural choices strongly affect interpretability and alignment with SPFES; a supervised concept bottleneck improves semantic validity at some cost to clinician agreement; robust evaluation under imbalance and protocol-matched benchmarks is essential for trustworthy welfare AI.

title: Imagine-TAMP: Imagination-Guided Task and Motion Planning in Partial Observability
summary: Robots operating in cluttered environments must often manipulate objects whose locations are only partially observable. A central challenge is deciding whether to acquire another observation or to first manipulate objects that may occlude the target. Conventional task and motion planning (TAMP) approaches typically make this decision using symbolic action costs or expensive geometric planning, neither of which adequately captures how likely an observation is to reveal an occluded target. We introduce Imagine-TAMP, an interleaved planning and execution framework that uses semantic and geometric imagination to compare alternative task-level strategies under partial observability before committing to expensive motion planning. A vision-language model shapes a particle belief over target locations using commonsense relationships between the target and visible objects, while a generative scene model estimates plausible geometry in unobserved regions. Given a target hypothesis and imagined scene, Imagine-TAMP generates multiple symbolic plan skeletons and assigns non-unit costs that approximate both manipulation effort and target visibility from sensing actions, distinguishing a short but poorly informative observation strategy from a longer strategy that first manipulates an occluder to better expose the target. The selected skeleton is then refined into a feasible continuous plan and executed, with new observations updating the belief and triggering replanning when necessary. Experiments show that imagination-guided evaluation improves observation-versus-manipulation decisions: in viewpoint-constrained shelf scenes, non-unit geometric evaluation increases success from 46.0% to 84.0%, while semantic belief shaping further reduces manipulation and replanning. On a real robot, the complete system reduces planning time by 32% relative to a geometry-only ablation.

AI.tldr: Imagine-TAMP interleaves planning and execution by imagining both semantic relationships and plausible geometry to compare observation-first versus manipulation-first strategies under partial observability, before committing to costly motion planning.
AI.motivation: In cluttered, partially observable environments, deciding whether to acquire another observation or manipulate occluders is not well-captured by symbolic costs or purely geometric planners. The paper aims to better estimate information gain and manipulation effort to guide planning.
AI.method: The framework uses a vision-language model to shape a particle belief over target locations via commonsense relations between the target and visible objects, and a generative scene model to hypothesize geometry in unobserved regions. It generates multiple symbolic plan skeletons with non-unit costs reflecting sensing and manipulation effort, selects a skeleton, refines into a feasible continuous plan, executes, and replans as new observations arrive.
AI.result: Experiments show imagination-guided evaluation improves observation-versus-manipulation decisions: in viewpoint-constrained shelf scenes, non-unit geometric evaluation raises success from 46.0% to 84.0%, and semantic belief shaping reduces manipulation and replanning. On a real robot, the complete system reduces planning time by 32% relative to a geometry-only ablation.
AI.conclusion: Imagination-based evaluation enables more effective decision-making under partial observability in TAMP, reducing unnecessary manipulations and accelerating planning, with demonstrated gains in both simulated and real-robot settings.

title: SoL-Pi: Recursively Scaling Auto-Research Loops for Efficient Agent Harness
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Code: https://github.com/NVlabs/SoL-Pi . Project page: https://nvlabs.github.io/SoL-Pi/
summary: As coding agents move from supervised code completion to unattended, around-the-clock exploration, their work expands from isolated predictions into long trajectories of reasoning, tool use, and feedback. Token efficiency therefore becomes important for scaling recursive self-improvement. We take an RSI-inspired approach at the harness layer, scaling auto-research loops across increasingly numerous and diverse environments for harness rollouts. At this scale, the process yields reusable improvements that transfer beyond their development setting, moving automated harness discovery toward production-level outcomes. Four mechanisms survive selection and form SoL-Pi, spanning action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading. On the 51-task EdgeBench evaluation, SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API cost by about one third. In other words, estimated hourly savings are \$8.75-\$13.50 relative to native Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and \$4.36-\$5.71 relative to Pi.

AI.tldr: SoL-Pi extends an RSI-inspired harnessing approach to scale auto-research loops across diverse environments, achieving production-level efficiency by four mechanisms, and matching Pi on EdgeBench while significantly reducing token traffic and API costs.
AI.motivation: Tackle token- and cost-inefficiency in long-horizon, unattended code-search/creation loops; achieve transferable improvements and production-scale outcomes beyond the development setting.
AI.method: Introduce four mechanisms—action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading—then scale harness rollouts across diverse environments (EdgeBench 51 tasks). Compare SoL-Pi to Pi and other baselines (GPT-5.6 Sol, Opus 5) using token traffic, API costs, and performance metrics.
AI.result: SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi on EdgeBench tasks across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5. It reduces recorded token traffic by 44.7–49.0% and API cost by ~33%. Estimated hourly savings are $8.75–$13.50 versus native Codex/Claude Code harnesses, and $4.36–$5.71 versus Pi.
AI.conclusion: Scalable RSI-inspired harnesses can yield transferable, production-level improvements with substantial efficiency gains, enabling more cost-effective unattended auto-research.

title: SAGG: Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating for Robust Multimodal Learning under Heterogeneous Corruption
summary: Multimodal gradient balancing methods modulate encoder gradients with a shared scalar per modality, implicitly assuming that corruption is uniform across the training batch. In practice, corruption is sample-heterogeneous: within a single mini-batch, different samples may have different modalities corrupted. We prove that under this heterogeneous corruption model, any batch-level sample-agnostic linear estimator with a shared modulation parameter incurs an irreducible bias with respect to the clean-data gradient, and that sample-level all-or-nothing gating is the unique unbiased strategy within a natural distribution-free estimator class. Motivated by this result, we propose Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating (SAGG), which makes a binary retain-or-discard decision per sample via an online feature-norm quality test and incorporates a truncation mechanism for variance control. We prove that SAGG-based SGD converges at the standard O(1/sqrt(T)) rate to stationary points of the clean loss without a corruption-dependent error floor, and derive a certified robustness radius for the independent-encoder architecture that connects per-modality Lipschitz constants to the classification margin. Experiments on Kinetics-Sounds and UCF-101 under Gaussian noise injection, partial modality missing, and natural contribution imbalance show that SAGG consistently outperforms ten existing methods, with the largest gains in high-corruption regimes where batch-level bias is most severe.

AI.tldr: Sample-adaptive gradient gating (SAGG) addresses sample-wise corruption in multimodal learning, replacing batch-level modulations with per-sample gating, yielding unbiased optimization, convergence guarantees, and strong empirical gains under noise and missing modalities.
AI.motivation: Batch-wise gradient modulations assume uniform corruption; in reality corruption is sample-heterogeneous, causing irreducible bias with shared modulation. Need unbiased, per-sample strategies.
AI.method: Introduce SAGG: per-sample binary retain/discard using online feature-norm quality test; include truncation for variance control; prove that sample-level all-or-nothing gating is unbiased in a distribution-free class; derive convergence O(1/√T) to clean-loss stationary points; derive certified robustness radius linking per-modality Lipschitz constants to margin; experiments on Kinetics-Sounds and UCF-101 under Gaussian noise, missing modalities, and natural imbalance.
AI.result: Theoretical: batch-level, shared-parameter modulation yields irreducible bias under heterogeneous corruption; optimal unbiased strategy is per-sample gating; SAGG SGD converges to stationary points of the clean loss without corruption floor; robustness radius derived. Empirical: SAGG outperforms 10 baselines, with largest gains in high-corruption regimes; settings include Gaussian noise, partial modalities missing, and imbalance.
AI.conclusion: Sample-adaptive gating effectively mitigates batch-level bias from heterogeneous corruption, delivering convergence guarantees, robustness certification, and superior empirical performance.

title: Cross-Architecture Foundation-Model Distillation for Edge Flood Segmentation
comment: Main paper (17 pages) with supplementary material (11 pages). Submitted to IEEE JSTARS, Special Section on Generalist-Specialist Model Synergy for Remote Sensing: Theories, Methods, and Applications
summary: Geospatial foundation models can provide strong flood-segmentation performance, but their size limits deployment on memory-constrained edge hardware. We distill a 300-million-parameter Prithvi-EO-2.0 teacher, fine-tuned on the 252 manually labeled Sen1Floods11 training scenes, into a 0.7-million-parameter EfficientViT-B0 student. The teacher supervises additional unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery, allowing the student training set to grow without new manual annotations. At the matched budget of 252 scenes, teacher-supervised training is competitive with direct training and improves STURM-Flood performance across tested configurations; a geometry-matched control shows that label source alone does not explain the difference. Scaling the teacher-supervised pool to 2,500 scenes narrows the remaining student--teacher gap: the float student reaches 0.787 water intersection over union on the Sen1Floods11 test split against 0.822 for the teacher, matches the teacher on STURM-Flood under our evaluation protocol, and remains below it on WorldFloods-v2. After activation replacement and quantization-aware training, the student runs as a 1.5-megabyte 8-bit integer (INT8) TensorRT engine on a Jetson Xavier NX at 5.57 milliseconds of graphics processing unit (GPU) compute per 512-by-512 image, with approximately 14 megabytes of runtime device memory. A fixed modified normalized difference water index (MNDWI) threshold is competitive with both models on the two clean external benchmarks, so we interpret those benchmarks as generalization tests rather than as evidence of learned-model superiority over a spectral rule. The results support the conclusion: foundation-model supervision can amplify a fixed manual annotation budget into a substantially larger training set and yield a compact, deployable edge model.

AI.tldr: Distill a large geospatial flood-segmentation model into a tiny edge-friendly student using teacher supervision on unlabeled data, achieving competitive performance with limited manual annotations and enabling deployable on-device inference.
AI.motivation: Overcome memory and compute constraints on edge hardware for flood segmentation by leveraging foundation-model supervision to amplify a fixed annotation budget into a larger, unlabeled dataset.
AI.method: Distill a 300M-parameter Prithvi-EO-2.0 teacher into a 0.7M EfficientViT-B0 student. Use teacher to supervise unlabeled Sentinel-2 data, expanding training beyond 252 manually labeled Sen1Floods11 scenes. Evaluate with 252-scenes baseline, scale to 2,500 scenes, apply activation replacement and quantization-aware training, and deploy as INT8 TensorRT on Jetson Xavier NX (~5.57 ms per 512x512 image, ~14 MB RAM). Compare against fixed MNDWI threshold baselines and on external benchmarks (Sen1Floods11 test, STURM-Flood, WorldFloods-v2). Include geometry-matched controls to isolate label-source effects.
AI.result: With 252 scenes, teacher-supervised training is competitive with direct training and improves STURM-Flood performance; label-source alone does not explain gains. Scaling to 2,500 scenes narrows the gap: student IoU 0.787 on Sen1Floods11 vs teacher 0.822; student matches teacher on STURM-Flood under protocol, but lags on WorldFloods-v2. After optimization (activation replacement, QA training), the student runs as a 1.5 MB INT8 TensorRT engine on Jetson Xavier NX, with ~5.57 ms per 512x512 image and ~14 MB memory. A fixed MNDWI threshold remains competitive with both models on two external benchmarks, implying benchmarks test generalization vs learned superiority. Overall, foundation-model supervision can transform a fixed annotation budget into a larger training set and yield a compact edge model, though teacher advantage varies by dataset.
AI.conclusion: Foundation-model supervision enables scalable, deployable flood-segmentation models by augmenting limited manual annotations with unlabeled data. While the student approaches teacher performance and can operate efficiently on edge devices, performance varies across benchmarks; fixed spectral heuristics may still outperform learned models in some external tests. The approach demonstrates the viability of distillation-driven data expansion for compact geospatial models.

title: Resilient Motion Planning for Free-Flying Space Robots under Actuator Failures
summary: Free-flying robots rely on multiple thrusters to maneuver in space. If one or more of these thrusters fail, the robot may lose control authority and risk mission failure. At the same time, their free-flying nature implies that, even in the absence of actuation, they continue along (locally) straight-line trajectories. In this work we present a probabilistic, proactive, motion planning framework that explicitly accounts for actuator failures in space. We model actuator failure modes as a Markov chain and propagate the probability of successfully reaching the goal along the planning horizon. Precomputed reachable sets evaluate the robot's capabilities of reaching waypoints under potential failures and an RRT$^*$-based planner concatenates these waypoints. The resulting algorithm maximizes the overall target-reaching probability, providing maximally resilient motion plans utilizing free-flying properties. We validate our approach experimentally on a physical free-flyer platform with injected actuator failures.

AI.tldr: Probabilistic proactive motion planning for free-flying robots under actuator failures. Models failures as a Markov chain, precomputes reachable sets for failure-robust waypoint feasibility, and uses an RRT*-based planner to maximize the probability of reaching the goal. Validated experimentally on hardware with injected failures.
AI.motivation: Space free-flyers risk loss of control authority due to actuator failures; their motion is locally straight when unactuated, making resilience planning essential.
AI.method: Model actuator failures as a Markov chain and propagate the probability of reaching the goal over a planning horizon. Precompute reachable sets for waypoint reachability under potential failures. Use an RRT*-based planner to concatenate these waypoints, optimizing the overall target-reaching probability to yield resilient trajectories.
AI.result: Experimental validation on a physical free-flyer platform with injected actuator faults, demonstrating the planner’s ability to produce higher-probability, failure-aware trajectories.
AI.conclusion: A proactive, failure-aware planning framework can produce maximally resilient motion plans for free-flying space robots by integrating probabilistic failure modeling, reachability analysis, and sampling-based planning.

title: FreqCondNorm: Towards Cross-domain Predictive Maintenance through a Frequency-Conditioned Transformer Foundation Model
summary: Deep learning predictive maintenance models suffer from poor transferability across machines and operating conditions, especially when labelled data are scarce and signals span five orders of magnitude in sampling frequency (1 Hz to ~100 kHz). We propose FreqCondNorm, a Transformer-based architecture that introduces a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer to unify heterogeneous time-series within a single model. The architecture is pretrained on five public predictive maintenance datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS) using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling. On fault diagnosis, the model achieves 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 pp over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, demonstrating strong transfer across sampling frequencies. However, the approach does not improve remaining useful life prediction, suggesting a mismatch between pretraining and RUL objectives that warrants future investigation.

AI.tldr: A Transformer-based predictive maintenance model (FreqCondNorm) uses a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization to unify heterogeneous time-series across sampling frequencies, enabling strong fault-diagnosis transfer but not improving remaining useful life (RUL) prediction; pretrained with MAE and contrastive learning on five datasets.
AI.motivation: To overcome poor cross-machine/condition transfer in DL predictive maintenance caused by highly heterogeneous sampling frequencies and limited labeled data.
AI.method: A Transformer architecture with FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization (FreqCondNorm). Pretraining via masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling on five datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS). Evaluation includes fault diagnosis and RUL tasks, with zero-shot transfer to MFPT.
AI.result: Fault diagnosis achieves 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (6.4 percentage points higher than CNN). Zero-shot accuracy on MFPT is 82.1%. Demonstrates strong transfer across sampling frequencies; however, no improvement in RUL prediction.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-conditioned normalization and domain-balanced pretraining enhance cross-condition fault diagnosis and frequency transfer, but misalignment between pretraining and RUL objectives limits RUL gains; further work needed to align objectives or adapt pretraining for RUL tasks.

title: Hypernetwork-Parameterized Spatially Adaptive Neural Operators for PDE Learning
summary: Spatially heterogeneous partial differential equations (PDEs) exhibit location-dependent dynamics arising from variations in geometry and physical coefficients. Existing neural operators improve localized modeling through multiscale features, attention mechanisms, or domain decomposition, yet their update rules often remain spatially shared. Hypernetwork-based methods adapt parameters across PDE instances but typically generate only one global parameterization per instance. Consequently, shared operators may underfit boundaries and high-gradient regions, with these localized errors accumulating during autoregressive rollout. We propose a spatially adaptive neural operator (SANO), which replaces this spatially shared parameterization with a spatially continuous field of location-dependent operator parameters. SANO uses Fourier-encoded coordinates and a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork to generate spatial operator-conditioning codes at sampling points. A Hyper-Neural Element (HNE) mechanism interpolates these codes within local subregions, coupling neighboring operators while allowing their update rules to vary across space, and partition-of-unity weights assemble the overlapping local predictions. Experiments on one-, two-, and three-dimensional PDEs and two perforated-domain elliptic benchmarks show that SANO consistently outperforms competitive neural-operator, hypernetwork-based, and physics-informed baselines.

AI.tldr: Spatially adaptive neural operator SANO replaces spatially shared parameterization with a continuous spatial field of operator parameters, using Fourier-encoded coordinates, a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork, and Hyper-Neural Elements with partition-of-unity, achieving superior performance on PDEs with spatial heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Neural operators often employ shared parameters across space, leading to underfitting at boundaries and high-gradient regions in spatially heterogeneous PDEs. A spatially varying operator can capture location-dependent dynamics and reduce error accumulation.
AI.method: Introduce Fourier-encoded coordinates; a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork generates operator-conditioning codes at sampling points. Hyper-Neural Elements interpolate codes within local subregions, coupling neighboring operators. Partition-of-unity weights assemble overlapping local predictions into a global operator.
AI.result: SANO consistently outperforms competitive neural operators, hypernetwork-based methods, and physics-informed baselines across 1D–3D PDEs and perforated-domain elliptic benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Spatially adaptive operator parameterization improves accuracy for spatially heterogeneous PDEs and scales across dimensions; the SANO framework implements location-dependent updates via local coupling and partition-of-unity fusion.

title: SenseFuse: Label-Free Fusion of Image and Shape Encoders for Open-Vocabulary 3D Instance Segmentation
summary: Open-vocabulary scene understanding is fundamental for robotics, laying the groundwork for spatial reasoning and object manipulation. While closed-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation heavily leverages 3D shape information, state-of-the-art open-vocabulary methods remain predominantly restricted to 2D image features or image-distilled representations during mask labeling. In this paper, we propose SenseFuse, a label-free fusion method that balances 2D image and 3D shape encoders for robust open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation, refining only the mask-labeling stage of existing pipelines. We reveal that 2D image and 3D shape encoders exhibit largely disjoint failure patterns and rarely share identical wrong labels, whereas two 2D image encoders frequently repeat the same errors. This distinct behavior makes the 2D and 3D pair inherently complementary. We introduce an adaptive mechanism that selects a scene-level fusion weight to maximize a label-free sensitivity measure, estimated directly from a single scene's unlabeled proposals in milliseconds. SenseFuse improves labeling accuracy in every evaluated setting across ScanNet200, Replica, and ScanNet++, recovering 67-100% (median 93%) of the gain achievable with an oracle weight, and it raises instance AP in 21 of 22 reported settings. Code is available at https://github.com/hanes1207/SenseFuse.

AI.tldr: SenseFuse introduces a label-free fusion of 2D image and 3D shape encoders to enable robust open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation, using an adaptive scene-level fusion weight derived from a label-free sensitivity measure in unlabeled proposals, yielding near-oracle gains across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation remains bottlenecked by reliance on 2D features or distilled representations; 2D and 3D encoders exhibit largely disjoint error patterns, making them complementary. A label-free fusion that adaptively balances modalities can improve labeling without requiring annotations.
AI.method: Propose SenseFuse, a label-free fusion mechanism that adaptively selects a scene-level fusion weight to maximize a label-free sensitivity measure computed from unlabeled proposals within a single scene (milliseconds). The fusion refines only the mask-labeling stage of existing 3D open-vocabulary pipelines, leveraging the complementary strengths of 2D and 3D encoders.
AI.result: Across ScanNet200, Replica, and ScanNet++, SenseFuse consistently improves labeling accuracy in all settings, recovering 67–100% (median 93%) of the gain achievable with an oracle fusion weight and increasing instance AP in 21 of 22 reported settings; code is released at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: The largely complementary error patterns of 2D and 3D encoders enable effective label-free adaptive fusion at mask-labeling time. SenseFuse offers a lightweight, scalable solution that boosts open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation without additional labeling, performing robustly across diverse datasets.

title: Time-Efficient Iterative Learning Planning for Safety-Critical Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
summary: Autonomous mobile robots require timeefficient planning and safety-critical dynamic obstacle avoidance under constrained onboard computation. While Iterative Learning Planning (ILP) offers lightweight and efficient traversal planning, it lacks explicit mechanisms for dynamic obstacle perception and avoidance. This article extends ILP to safety-critical navigation in dynamic environments by integrating an anticipatory risk-blended control barrier function (ARB-CBF). The extended ILP learns traversal-speed and steering-bias profiles via a fractionalpower update based on local obstacle risk, generating nominal control commands that ARB-CBF modifies at runtime for real-time safety guarantees. Algorithmic analysis demonstrates that the ILP replanning stage scales at O(kN) for k iterations and N waypoints, while ARB-CBF executes with linear complexity. Comprehensive simulations and real-world experiments validate the framework, demonstrating superior temporal efficiency and safety with lower computational overhead compared to optimizationbased baselines, making it highly suitable for resourceconstrained platforms.

AI.tldr: Extends Iterative Learning Planning (ILP) with an anticipatory risk-blended CBF (ARB-CBF) to enable safety-critical, dynamic obstacle avoidance on resource-constrained platforms. ILP learns traversal-speed and steering biases; ARB-CBF vetoes/modifies commands in real time to guarantee safety.
AI.motivation: Address ILP's lack of explicit dynamic obstacle perception/avoidance while maintaining computational efficiency for resource-constrained robots.
AI.method: Integrate ARB-CBF with ILP: ILP outputs nominal controls (speed, steering bias) via a fractional-power update based on local obstacle risk; ARB-CBF adjusts these commands at runtime to ensure safety. Complexity: ILP replanning scales as O(kN) with k iterations and N waypoints; ARB-CBF runs with linear complexity.
AI.result: Simulations and real-world experiments show improved temporal efficiency and safety with lower computational overhead than optimization-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: The framework is well-suited for resource-constrained platforms, delivering real-time, safety-aware navigation in dynamic environments.

title: Refuse, Decompose, Refresh: A Claim-Safe Protocol for Closed-Loop AI Evaluation
comment: 8 pages, 0 figures, 3 tables. The reproducibility artifact is linked in the paper
summary: An AI evaluation can be perfectly reproducible and still support the wrong claim. This risk is acute in closed-loop systems: policy determines visited states, observable components, and which failures leave a measurable trace. We propose a claim-safe protocol with three actions. Refuse: abstain when a clean reference stream or matched runtime comparison lacks support. Decompose: report protocol execution, operational false admission, and structural hypotheses separately rather than as one PASS/FAIL label. Refresh: treat distribution-shift alarms as requests to invalidate and recompute a reference map, not as fault evidence. We instantiate the protocol in an aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, three demand regimes, two fault-mask families, and independent development and heldout seeds. The preregistered heldout contains 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows. Only 55/72 regime-component units were reference-admitted and 54/55 remained runtime-admitted, making abstention part of the result. Stable false admission was 0/20 represented components, with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391 under a frozen 0.20 rule. Within admitted units, affected clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction: across 540 unit-arm rows nested in 20 component clusters, the cell-minus-traffic negative-log-likelihood difference was 0.1264 nats per row, with a 95% component-cluster interval of [0.0593, 0.1918]. A drift log shows why "null" must be reference-relative: clean fault-null streams triggered 15/15, 0/15, and 14/15 alarms across three regimes, while only the middle regime matched the frozen detector reference. Rather than a universal threshold, we contribute an executable contract linking observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims.

AI.tldr: Claim-safe AI evaluation protocol for closed-loop systems; uses Refuse, Decompose, Refresh; instantiated in aggregate simulator; abstention is part of results; provides executable contract linking support, calibration, claims.
AI.motivation: Address the risk that reproducible AI evaluation can support wrong claims in closed-loop AI where policy determines visited states, observables, and measurable failures.
AI.method: Propose a protocol with three actions (Refuse, Decompose, Refresh) and instantiate it in an aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, 3 demand regimes, 2 fault-mask families, and independent development and heldout seeds; preregistered heldout with 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows; measure reference-admitted vs runtime-admitted units; analyze false admissions; use drift logs to assess reference-relative thresholds; deliver an executable contract linking observable support, calibration, and justified claims.
AI.result: Key empirical findings include: 55 of 72 regime-component units were reference-admitted and 54 of 55 remained runtime-admitted; abstention occurred as part of the result. Stable false admission was 0/20 among represented components, with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391 under a frozen 0.20 rule. Among admitted units, the clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction; across 540 unit-arm rows in 20 clusters, cell-minus-traffic NLL difference was 0.1264 nats per row, with a 95% component-cluster interval [0.0593, 0.1918]. A drift log shows null must be reference-relative: clean fault-null streams triggered alarms at varying rates across regimes, with only the middle regime matching the frozen detector reference. The work argues for a shift from universal thresholds to an executable contract that ties observable support, calibration, and justified claims.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose and instantiate a claim-safe protocol and deliver an executable contract that improves the reliability of claims in AI evaluation by ensuring evaluated claims are supported by observable evidence and calibrated references, rather than relying on a single PASS/FAIL label.

title: ZeroHAT: Behavior-Conditioned Zero-Shot Human Activity Trace Generation
summary: Human activity traces record individuals' timestamped visits to points of interest and are essential for applications such as mobility prediction and urban simulation. However, accessing large-scale HATs is challenging due to high collection costs and privacy concerns. Synthetic HAT generation offers a promising way to make such data available and has attracted growing interest from both industry and academia. Although many efforts have been devoted to this topic, most of them rely on real data from a region to generate synthetic data for the same region, which is infeasible for the many regions where real HATs are unavailable. To fill this gap, we propose ZeroHAT, a behavior-conditioned framework that generates synthetic HATs for a target region in a zero-shot manner by transferring behavioral patterns learned from real HATs in source regions and adapting them with publicly available contextual information about the target region. ZeroHAT has three key novel components: (i) a multidimensional consistency-aware intent extractor; (ii) a cross-region behavioral cloning module; and (iii) a behavior-conditioned activity realization module. We evaluate ZeroHAT on a ten-city benchmark, where extensive experiments show that ZeroHAT achieves 4.5-6.4x the normalized downstream utility of the strongest baseline and improves average fidelity by 15.6%-40.8% across target regions.

AI.tldr: ZeroHAT: a zero-shot framework to generate synthetic human activity traces for a target region by transferring patterns from source regions and conditioning on target context; with three modules and strong performance on a ten-city benchmark.
AI.motivation: Overcome high costs and privacy barriers of real human activity traces; enable data-driven applications in regions lacking data by zero-shot synthesis.
AI.method: Three components: (i) multidimensional consistency-aware intent extractor (to infer user intent across dimensions); (ii) cross-region behavioral cloning (transfer patterns from source regions); (iii) behavior-conditioned activity realization (generate activity sequences conditioned on target region context). Uses publicly available contextual information for the target region.
AI.result: On a ten-city benchmark, ZeroHAT yields 4.5–6.4x normalized downstream utility over the strongest baseline and improves average fidelity by 15.6%–40.8% across target regions.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective zero-shot synthetic HAT generation across regions, enabling data availability and potential privacy-preserving data augmentation; performance surpasses baselines; relies on high-quality contextual information; future work may explore robustness to context quality and privacy guarantees.

title: Grounded Product Understanding in Livestream Videos
summary: E-commerce livestreams have emerged as an important channel for presenting products to online consumers, containing multiple products whose information is scattered in different moments. This poses significant challenges for downstream product understanding applications, such as product-centric livestream clipping, where models need to identify the product and its relevant segments for information gathering. However, existing benchmarks for general product understanding typically evaluate product retrieval and temporal localization in isolation, leaving the critical correspondence between product identity and temporal evidence largely unassessed. To address this limitation, we introduce GPUB, a large-scale benchmark comprising 3,000 livestream instances with quality-controlled multi-moment temporal annotations and a catalog of over 31K fashion products. GPUB supports three evaluation tasks: the main task Grounded Product Understanding (GPrU) requires jointly identifying the target product and localizing its supporting moments from a livestream video and a candidate product set; Product Retrieval and Product Moment Localization serve as two complementary subtasks. Evaluation of existing multimodal models shows that GPrU remains highly challenging, with the best-performing baseline achieving only 10.13% Pair mAP@.3. To narrow the performance gap, we further develop UniPro, a unified product understanding model that derives product-aligned and temporally structured representations from shared multimodal encoding, improving Pair mAP@.3 to 21.53% while achieving 37.23% Joint R@1@.3 on GPrU.

AI.tldr: GPUB provides a large-scale benchmark for grounded product understanding in e-commerce livestreams, introducing GPrU and two subtasks; UniPro yields substantial performance gains.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate product retrieval and temporal localization in isolation, neglecting the joint correspondence between product identity and temporal evidence; a dataset with multi-moment temporal annotations and a real product catalog is needed.
AI.method: GPUB contains 3,000 livestreams with quality-controlled multi-moment temporal annotations and a catalog of over 31K fashion products. It supports three tasks: Grounded Product Understanding (GPrU) plus Product Retrieval and Product Moment Localization. UniPro is a unified multimodal model that derives product-aligned and temporally structured representations from shared encoding.
AI.result: Strongest baseline achieves Pair mAP@.3 of 10.13%; UniPro improves to 21.53% Pair mAP@.3 and 37.23% Joint R@1@.3 on GPrU.
AI.conclusion: GPrU is challenging; unified product understanding can significantly narrow the gap, and GPUB enables rigorous evaluation of joint product identity and temporal evidence in livestreams.

title: Spatial-Semantic Uncertainty in VLM-Based Target Search: Balancing Exploration and Identification
comment: Accepted for presentation at IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026) WorkshopRethinking Uncertainty for Modern Robotics Paradigms
summary: Robots searching for a target from a natural-language description must determine not only where to search, but also which observed candidate is the desired target. These decisions reflect two distinct sources of uncertainty - spatial uncertainty over candidate locations and semantic uncertainty over target identity - that are often conflated in VLM-based search systems. We introduce a spatial-semantic uncertainty formulation that maintains separate beliefs over each component and integrates probabilistic VLM evidence into a global target-identity posterior, including probability mass for undiscovered targets. This decomposition allows an information-theoretic planner to independently value candidate discovery and target disambiguation through spatial and semantic expected information gain (EIG), providing an explicit mechanism for trading broader exploration against earlier identification. We evaluate six VLM uncertainty-elicitation interfaces on 500 synthetic targets and show that similar recognition accuracy can conceal substantial differences in calibration and false confidence. In degraded-observation search-and-identify experiments, EIG-based planners reach confident decisions in 75.0%-92.5% of trials, compared with 20.0% for Random search, while different spatial-semantic weightings achieve comparable identification accuracy once confidence is attained. Increasing semantic emphasis reduces unnecessary exploration and VLM queries, demonstrating that explicitly planning over semantic uncertainty can accelerate target resolution without sacrificing decision quality. These results highlight the distinct roles of uncertainty representation and uncertainty-driven planning in embodied VLM systems.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic framework decouples spatial and semantic uncertainty for target search with vision-language models (VLMs), integrating VLM evidence into a joint target-identity posterior and including mass for undiscovered targets. An information-theoretic planner uses spatial and semantic expected information gain (EIG) to trade exploration and identification. Empirical results show EIG planners outperform random searches in reaching confident decisions and that heavier semantic emphasis reduces unnecessary exploration while preserving accuracy, underscoring the value of explicit uncertainty representation and planning.
AI.motivation: Tackle the conflation of spatial (where to search) and semantic (which target) uncertainty in VLM-guided search. Provide calibrated beliefs and a principled planning objective to manage exploration vs disambiguation.
AI.method: Develop a spatial–semantic Bayesian formulation with separate beliefs for candidate locations and target identity, coupled via probabilistic VLM evidence into a global target-identity posterior including probability mass for undiscovered targets. Compute spatial EIG and semantic EIG for decision-making. Evaluate six VLM-uncertainty interfaces on 500 synthetic targets in both standard and degraded-observation conditions to assess calibration, false confidence, and planning efficiency.
AI.result: EIG-based planners reach confident decisions in 75.0–92.5% of trials, versus ~20% for random search. Different spatial–semantic weightings yield similar identification accuracy once confident. Increasing semantic emphasis reduces unnecessary exploration and VLM queries, indicating planning over semantic uncertainty accelerates resolution without sacrificing final decision quality.
AI.conclusion: Separating spatial and semantic uncertainty and planning over both via information gain improves efficiency and reliability of embodied VLM search systems, validating the distinct roles of uncertainty representation and uncertainty-driven planning.

title: Language-model groups overstate consensus when replaying human deliberation on a reasoning task
comment: 37 pages, 4 figures. Preregistration: https://osf.io/5jp7s . Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21318346
summary: Full-consensus rates are often treated as indicators of collective cognition, yet depend on how participation and final states are operationalized. We replayed 100 held-out human Wason groups with matched large language model (LLM) agent groups, seeding one belief-anchored agent per participant's pre-discussion answer and scoring agents and people with the same code. Across human scoring definitions, estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0%; about one fifth of participants never posted, whereas agents almost always did. Agent groups remained more consensual in two post-unblinding sensitivity analyses: the submit-based comparison (n = 98) yielded gaps of 34.0 and 43.9 percentage points for chat and reasoning modes, and the participation-matched comparison (n = 45) yielded gaps of 34.1 and 44.4 points. These complementary routes reduced different measurement asymmetries yet converged within 0.5 percentage points. The gap persisted without early stopping and under a reparameterization removing the memorizable answer; reasoning-mode groups then agreed nearly unanimously, mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy, and belief-anchored agent groups were biased estimators of the human group-outcome distribution in this setting. These analyses provide a scoring-explicit basis for assessing simulated-group estimates of human deliberative outcomes.

AI.tldr: Consensus rates depend on how participation and final states are defined; using matched human and LLM-agent groups shows persistent gaps under different scoring definitions, which converge when combined but differ when memorizable answers are removed; reasoning-mode groups can converge on incorrect answers; simulated consensus misaligns with actual accuracy, and belief-anchored agents bias estimates of human outcomes.
AI.motivation: Quantify how operational choices in measuring consensus affect estimates of collective cognition and evaluate how well simulated groups proxy human deliberation.
AI.method: Replayed 100 held-out human Wason groups with matched large language model (LLM) agent groups. Seeded one belief-anchored agent per participant’s pre-discussion answer; used identical scoring code for humans and agents. Compared submit-based and participation-matched definitions (post-unblinding sensitivity analyses). Also reparameterized to remove memorizable answers to test robustness. Assessed how simulated consensus tracks human outcomes.
AI.result: Human consensus estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0%, with about one-fifth of participants posting zero contributions while agents posted nearly always. Post-unblinding, the submit-based gaps were 34.0 and 43.9 percentage points (chat and reasoning modes); participation-matched gaps were 34.1 and 44.4 points. The two routes converged within 0.5 percentage points. Under a reparameterization removing memorizable answers, reasoning-mode groups agreed nearly unanimously, mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy, and belief-anchored agent groups biased estimators of the human group-outcome distribution.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a scoring-explicit basis for using simulated groups to estimate human deliberative outcomes, highlighting the sensitivity of consensus measures to operationalization and the potential biases introduced by agent-based proxies. It suggests careful, transparent scoring and sensitivity analyses are essential when interpreting simulated-group estimates of collective cognition.

title: EviRec: Continual Evidence Learning for Dual Cold-Start POI Recommendation
summary: Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation is a core task in location-based services, yet most existing methods assume a fixed user population and POI catalog. Through a large-scale data-driven analysis of 10 U.S. cities, we identify substantial POI churn, user turnover, category drift, and decay in static POI memory, motivating the study of continual dual cold-start POI recommendation. To address this setting, we propose EviRec, a continual evidence-learning framework that estimates how much historical evidence should be trusted separately for each candidate POI. EviRec scores each visible candidate from three complementary views: a matching view based on the user's recent mobility profile, a transition-memory view that captures repeated mobility routines, and a lifecycle view that reflects candidate maturity. Because a near-zero transition score may indicate either irrelevance or insufficient observation, EviRec qualifies the evidence using each candidate's observation state and applies a reliability gate to adaptively route between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence. We evaluate EviRec on a full-year, five-city POI check-in dataset containing more than 30,000 users and 684,200 trajectories. Experimental results show that EviRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with the largest gains concentrated on cold-start queries. In particular, EviRec improves NDCG@10 by 20.4\% on Dual-New cases over the strongest baseline. In-depth analyses further confirm that these gains arise primarily from candidate-specific reliability gating while largely preserving previously learned mobility routines.

AI.tldr: EviRec is a continual evidence-learning POI recommender for dual cold-start scenarios, using three views and a reliability gate to adaptively weight evidence, achieving significant gains in NDCG@10, especially for cold-start queries.
AI.motivation: Large-scale POI data shows substantial churn in POIs, user turnover, category drift, and decay of static memory, which undermines static POI recommendation models and motivates continual dual cold-start approaches.
AI.method: Propose EviRec, a continual evidence-learning framework that estimates per-POI how much historical evidence to trust. It scores candidates via three views: 1) matching (recent mobility), 2) transition-memory (repeated routines), 3) lifecycle (maturity). A reliability gate uses observation state to route between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence, enabling adaptive evidence fusion.
AI.result: On a year-long, five-city POI check-in dataset (30k+ users, 684k trajectories), EviRec outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with the largest gains in cold-start (Dual-New) cases; NDCG@10 improves by 20.4% on Dual-New cases. Analyses attribute gains to candidate-specific reliability gating while preserving learned mobility routines.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-guided, multi-view evidence integration enables effective continual dual cold-start POI recommendation, with evidence routing that adapts to data sparsity and POI maturity, yielding robust improvements over existing methods.

title: Automated Goldsmith's Mark Retrieval in Silverware
comment: Accepted at the VISART workshop, ECCV 2026. 18 pages, 8 figures, 1 table
summary: For art historians, goldsmith marks play a critical role in the identification and dating of artifacts. In practice, experts must manually compare a query mark against hundreds of documented examples, a process that is both tedious and highly dependent on specialist knowledge. To address this, we present an AI-assisted retrieval pipeline that combines mark localization with metric-learning fine-tuning across three backbone architectures: an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50, a supervised ViT-S/16, and a self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14. We conduct a systematic evaluation of cropping strategies, where we measure the impact of no cropping, manual ground-truth cropping, and learned detection-based cropping, and assess their interaction with each backbone. Our strongest configuration, DINOv2 ViT-S/14 with manual crop and metric-learning fine-tuning, achieves an mAP of 62.63% and a Top-1 accuracy of 73.74%. Our experiments show that self-supervised pretraining and mark localization are the two most impactful factors, with learned cropping recovering the majority of the gain from manual cropping without requiring ground-truth annotations at inference time. To enable reproducibility and adoption in the digital humanities, we release our manually annotated dataset and codebase, and deploy the system via a public web interface.

AI.tldr: AI-assisted retrieval for goldsmith marks using localization + metric-learning across ResNet-50, ViT-S/16, and DINOv2 ViT-S/14. Best with DINOv2+manual crop+metric-learning: mAP 62.63%, Top-1 73.74%. Self-supervised pretraining and localization are key; learned cropping bridges most of manual-crop gains without GT at inference. Dataset/code released; web interface provided.
AI.motivation: Automate and accelerate the identification and dating of artifacts by reducing manual, expertise-intensive comparison of marks, increasing reproducibility and scalability for digital humanities.
AI.method: Localization + metric-learning fine-tuning across three backbones (ResNet-50, ViT-S/16, DINOv2 ViT-S/14); evaluate cropping strategies (no crop, ground-truth crop, learned crop); assess interactions between backbones and cropping.
AI.result: DINOv2 ViT-S/14 with manual crop and metric-learning achieved mAP 62.63% and Top-1 73.74%. Self-supervised pretraining and mark localization are the most impactful factors; learned cropping recovers much of manual-crop gains without requiring ground-truth at inference. Dataset and code released; deployed via public web interface.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised pretraining and precise mark localization drive performance; learned cropping offers practical gains by reducing annotation needs, aiding reproducibility and adoption in the digital humanities.

title: Visual Sim-to-Real Learning for Robotic Insertion under Geometric Variations: Application to Rebar Installation
summary: Rebar insertion is among the most repetitive and physically demanding tasks on construction sites, and a contact-rich problem at 1.4 mm clearance. The parts, however, vary at two levels: a nominal design per structural member, and fabrication tolerance around each nominal design. Real-world data therefore has to be re-collected as designs and batches change. We present RebarSim, a visual sim-to-real system trained entirely in simulation. A privileged state-based teacher is trained with reinforcement learning over procedurally generated rebar geometries, then distilled into a multi-view student that maps raw RGB and proprioception directly to actions under extensive domain randomization. The student transfers to the real world zero-shot, seating rebars taken from a real factory production run in 91.3% of real-robot rollouts. Underlying that result, geometry diversity and pretraining both bring benefits. Training across a diverse set of nominal designs rather than one lifts the zero-shot success of both the teacher and the student on unseen designs, and the student policy outperforms a single-design specialist on that specialist's own design. A pretrained student then adapts to a new design with 4--6x fewer distillation samples than one trained from scratch. Visual sim-to-real transfer depends on appearance randomization and the DAgger mixture: removing either one sharply lowers success. Videos, code, and task assets are available at https://rebarsim.github.io.

AI.tldr: RebarSim trains a privileged teacher RL policy in simulation on procedurally generated rebar geometries and distills it into a multi-view RGB/proprioception student with domain randomization, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer that achieves 91.3% success in real-robot rollouts; design diversity and pretraining boost zero-shot performance; adaptation to new designs is sample-efficient (4–6x fewer distillation samples); appearance randomization and DAgger are essential components.
AI.motivation: Address the repetitive, physically demanding nature of rebar insertion and its sensitivity to nominal designs plus fabrication tolerances. A robust sim-to-real approach is needed to handle design changes without extensive real-world data collection.
AI.method: Train a privileged state-based teacher via reinforcement learning on procedurally generated rebar geometries. Distill the teacher into a multi-view student that maps raw RGB and proprioception to actions, using extensive domain randomization (appearance, geometry) and a DAgger mixture. Evaluate zero-shot transfer to real hardware with rebars from a factory production run; assess design diversity, pretraining, and adaptation efficiency across unseen designs.
AI.result: Zero-shot transfer yields seating success on 91.3% of real-robot rollouts. Geometry diversity and pretraining improve zero-shot performance for both teacher and student on unseen designs. The student outperforms a single-design specialist on its own design. Adapting to a new design requires 4–6x fewer distillation samples than training from scratch.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates effective visual sim-to-real transfer for a highly contact-rich task under design variability. Key findings are that diverse nominal designs and pretraining boost zero-shot generalization, and that distillation to a vision+proprioception policy with appearance randomization and DAgger is crucial for robust performance.

title: Limits of Confidence in Diffusion
summary: Discrete diffusion, including remasking and uniform-state samplers, generate a sequence by writing multiple token positions per step, drawing each from a per-position distribution and choosing which positions to write from those same distributions. For domains of general interest (pixels, phonemes, or words) there are inherent dependencies between tokens. We show that a step matches the training distribution only when the positions it writes are conditionally independent given the tokens already fixed, that no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group, and that per-position distributions do not determine whether a group is dependent: two joint distributions can have identical per-position marginals while differing in which combinations of values occur. On ScanAndAdd, a synthetic task whose joint distribution is available in closed form, we verify that every group of two or more undetermined positions a confidence ranking writes is dependent, and measure the generated distribution to be $29\times$ the sampling-noise floor total variation while per-sample metrics are $1.0$.

AI.tldr: Per-position factorization in discrete diffusion cannot capture dependencies among tokens, and a step in such methods matches training only under conditional independence. Product of per-position marginals cannot represent dependent groups, even if marginals match. Empirical evidence on a synthetic ScanAndAdd task shows strong dependence across multi-position groups and a large gap between generated distribution and the sampling-noise floor, despite perfect per-sample metrics.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between per-position sampling in discrete diffusion and the inherent dependencies among tokens in realistic domains (pixels, phonemes, words). Establish theoretical limits on when a step can match the training distribution and demonstrate the insufficiency of per-position marginals for diagnosing or capturing dependence.
AI.method: Theoretically prove: (i) a step matches the training distribution only if the written positions are conditionally independent given fixed tokens; (ii) no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group; (iii) per-position distributions do not determine dependence, since two joint distributions can share identical per-position marginals while differ in value combinations. Empirically validate on a synthetic task ScanAndAdd with closed-form joint distribution, analyzing whether undetermined position groups are dependent and measuring distributional distance and per-sample metrics.
AI.result: Analytical results show conditional independence is required for step alignment with training; products of per-position marginals cannot reproduce dependent groups; per-position marginals fail to signal dependence. On the ScanAndAdd task, every group of two or more undetermined positions is dependent; the generated distribution is 29× the sampling-noise floor in total-variation distance, while per-sample metrics remain at 1.0.
AI.conclusion: Discrete diffusion with per-position factorization fundamentally cannot faithfully model dependencies among tokens in domains with joint dependencies. To capture such structure, one must move beyond per-position marginals (e.g., to joint or structured conditionals) to align with the training distribution and avoid underestimating distributional error even when per-sample metrics are perfect.

title: Sharp Reconstruction Bounds for Autoencoders Using the Same Forward Map
summary: We study reconstruction in autoencoders that apply the same forward map before and after setting the observed coordinates to zero. For equal odd input and hidden dimensions $d\geq 3$, among orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms whose Jacobian singular values lie in $[m,M]$, we show that the least uniform reconstruction-derivative error is $\max\{1-M(M-m)/2,0\}$, with affine maps attaining this sharp bound at every prescribed depth. A translated radial rotation can nevertheless reconstruct any prescribed ball exactly with singular values arbitrarily close to one, motivating additional conditions for a finite-data bound. We test this prediction on a 798,452-point terrestrial LiDAR forest scan. At input scale $0.05$, the mean theoretical bound is $0.155$, about $84\%$ of the mean normalized training error $0.185$ across four spatial regions, two depths, and three seeds. At this scale, adding one hidden coordinate reduces the mean reconstruction error below $6\times10^{-6}$.

AI.tldr: Sharp bound on reconstruction-derivative error for autoencoders under zeroed coordinates: for equal odd input/hidden dims (d≥3) and orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms with Jacobian singular values in [m,M], the least uniform reconstruction-derivative error is max{1 - M(M - m)/2, 0}, with affine maps attaining it at all depths. A translated radial rotation can achieve exact ball reconstruction with singular values arbitrarily close to 1. Empirical LiDAR test corroborates theory: at scale 0.05, mean bound 0.155 vs mean training error 0.185; adding one hidden coordinate drives mean error below 6e-6; indicates finite-data bounds require further conditions.
AI.motivation: Characterize fundamental limits of reconstruction accuracy for autoencoders under a common forward map with partial observation, identify optimal map classes (affine) and constructive schemes (translated radial rotation), and validate predictions on real-world 3D data to inform finite-data considerations.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis over orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms with Jacobian singular values constrained to [m,M], for equal odd dimensions d≥3. Derive the sharp bound on the uniform reconstruction-derivative error; prove affine maps attain the bound at every depth. Introduce a translated radial rotation construction that can reconstruct any prescribed ball with singular values arbitrarily close to 1. Empirically test predictions on a 798,452-point terrestrial LiDAR forest scan, comparing the theoretical bound to observed training error across scales, depths, seeds, and regions, and evaluate the impact of adding hidden coordinates.
AI.result: The least uniform reconstruction-derivative error equals max{1 - M(M - m)/2, 0}. Affine maps attain this bound for all depths. The translated radial rotation can reconstruct any ball exactly with singular values near 1. In the LiDAR experiment, at input scale 0.05 the theoretical bound is 0.155, about 84% of the mean training error 0.185 across four regions, two depths, three seeds; adding one hidden coordinate reduces the mean reconstruction error to below 6×10^-6.
AI.conclusion: The bound is sharp; affine maps are optimal under the stated constraints; certain constructions (translated radial rotations) allow exact local reconstruction as singular values approach 1. Empirical data support the theory and show dramatic error reduction with modest hidden capacity, though finite-data guarantees require additional conditions.

title: A Dual-Stream Regulated Reconstruction and Segmentation Network with Hierarchical Artifact-Prior Modeling for Ultra-Low-Field Pediatric Neuroimaging
summary: Automated quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation of multiple structures in $0.064\,\mathrm{T}$ ultra-low-field pediatric MRI are limited by a low signal-to-noise ratio, weak anatomical boundaries, and frequent artifacts. We present a unified framework for the LISA 2026 Challenge that performs all three tasks together within one inference pipeline. A network with two coupled streams, built on a 3D U-Net, first reconstructs an enhanced uLF volume and then combines the original and enhanced images for subcortical segmentation. To improve boundary stability, we add an auxiliary class covering brain tissue outside the target structures, derived from whole brain masks. A head conditioned on an artifact graph predicts the seven artifact ratings from reconstruction residuals and frozen segmentation features. We address the scarcity of dense annotations using diffeomorphic registration from atlas to target for label propagation and to regularize anatomical reconstruction. We report validation results across all three tasks.

AI.tldr: A unified multi-task pipeline for 0.064 T pediatric MRI performing quality assessment, enhancement, and subcortical segmentation in one inference.
