It uses a two-stream 3D U-Net: reconstructs an enhanced uLF volume, then uses combined original and enhanced data for segmentation; an auxiliary boundary class from whole-brain masks improves boundary stability; an artifact-rating head conditioned on an artifact graph predicts seven artifact ratings from reconstruction residuals and frozen segmentation features; atlas-to-target diffeomorphic registration enables label propagation to regularize reconstruction and address sparse annotations. Validation results are reported across all three tasks.
AI.motivation: Low signal-to-noise ratio, weak anatomical boundaries, and frequent artifacts in ultra-low-field pediatric MRI hinder performance; the scarcity of densely labeled data motivates label propagation from atlas and a unified multi-task framework.
AI.method: - Two coupled streams on a 3D U-Net: first reconstructs an enhanced ultra-low-field (uLF) volume; second uses original and enhanced images for subcortical segmentation. - Auxiliary boundary class derived from whole-brain masks to stabilise boundary delineation. - Artifact-rating head conditioned on an artifact graph; predicts seven artifact ratings from reconstruction residuals and frozen segmentation features. - Diffeomorphic atlas-to-target registration for label propagation to create dense supervision and regularize reconstruction. - Joint training across quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation tasks.
AI.result: Validation results are reported across all three tasks, demonstrating feasibility of the integrated approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a unified, end-to-end solution for simultaneous quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation in ultra-low-field pediatric MRI, with mechanisms to handle artifacts and limited dense annotations via atlas-based label propagation.

title: Worst-Case Hidden-Vehicle Trajectory Search in Spatiotemporal Occlusion Regions
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Safe and Defensive Autonomous Driving (SDAD) as an Oral Presentation; Best Paper Award. Workshop website: https://sdad.cc/papers.html
summary: Occlusion creates fundamental uncertainty in autonomous driving. Existing methods often propagate frame-wise hypotheses or optimize ego behavior against prescribed hidden-agent predictions, leaving the worst history-consistent interaction unexplored. We introduce History-Conditioned Minimax Trajectory Search (HC-MTS), which combines temporal occlusion reasoning with response-aware search. First, HC-MTS constructs finite hidden-state modes, each certified by a backward witness satisfying multi-frame visibility, occupancy, semantic-map support, and class-specific kinematic constraints. It then solves a bilevel minimax problem: an inner finite oracle maximizes the ego driving score over destination attainment and ride comfort, while the outer search selects the legal hidden-vehicle trajectory that minimizes this best-response value. Across eight Waymo Open Motion Dataset scenarios, increasing the visibility-memory horizon from K=1 to K=20 reduces the mean per-scenario vehicle, pedestrian, and total retained hidden-seed counts by 18.12%, 21.67%, and 18.45%, respectively. HC-MTS identifies six avoidable counterexamples, while no legal collision-producing attacker is found in the remaining two scenes within the finite search budget.

AI.tldr: HC-MTS proposes a history-conditioned minimax search to handle occlusion in autonomous driving by enumerating finite hidden-state modes with multi-frame constraints and solving a bilevel minimax: inner ego-score maximization, outer hidden-trajectory minimization, yielding reduced hidden-seed retention and revealing counterexamples on Waymo data.
AI.motivation: Occlusion creates fundamental uncertainty in autonomous driving. Frame-wise hypotheses and prescriptive hidden-agent predictions neglect long-horizon, history-consistent interactions, leading to unaddressed worst-case scenarios. A history-conditioned, response-aware approach aims to reason about occluded agents over time.
AI.method: Construct finite hidden-state modes certified by backward witnesses using multi-frame visibility, occupancy, semantic-map support, and class-specific kinematic constraints. Solve a bilevel minimax problem: inner oracle maximizes ego driving score (destination attainment and ride comfort) over possible actions; outer search selects legal hidden-vehicle trajectories that minimize the inner best-response value, within a finite search budget.
AI.result: On eight Waymo Open Motion Dataset scenarios, increasing visibility-memory horizon K from 1 to 20 reduces mean retained hidden seeds for vehicles, pedestrians, and total by 18.12%, 21.67%, and 18.45% respectively. HC-MTS identifies six avoidable counterexamples; among the remaining scenes, no legal collision-producing attacker is found within the finite search budget.
AI.conclusion: History-conditioned minimax trajectory search effectively reasons about occluded agents under finite horizons, reducing retained hidden seeds and exposing actionable counterexamples, suggesting practical improvements for robust planning under occlusion within a bounded computational budget.

title: PAA: The Probabilistic Allen Algebra: A Generative and Complete Probabilistic Extension of Allen's Interval Relations
summary: Allen's interval algebra is a qualitative calculus for temporal relations, but its thirteen base relations are crisp predicates over exact interval boundaries. This is inadequate for temporal information from language, perception, databases, or uncertain histories, where times, durations, and boundaries are uncertain and expressions such as "just before" or "roughly during" have graded meaning. We develop the probabilistic Allen algebra (PAA): a generative and complete extension in which relation probabilities are derived from distributions over interval boundaries rather than assigned as scores. Time points are Gaussian; intervals have Gaussian midpoints and truncated-Gaussian durations. Every relation is a boundary-ordering predicate in one common probability space: point-point relations reduce to error functions, and point-interval and interval-interval relations to multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities induced by linear inequalities. Contact relations (meets, starts, finishes, equals) receive positive measure through a tolerance band, and under a single tolerance the thirteen relations form a true partition that recovers crisp Allen as the tolerance vanishes. The construction derives Allen's taxonomy rather than positing it: coarse predicates such as precedence, overlap, and containment are unions of leaves whose probabilities are leaf sums, and this hierarchy is preserved as intervals collapse to points and thirteen relations reduce to five and then three. Each relation further decomposes into correlation-aware temporal primitives in the spirit of CIDOC CRM. The algebra is scale-invariant and separates graded expressions such as "shortly before" from contact relations. All results are Monte-Carlo validated and shipped as an open, tested Python package.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic, generative extension of Allen's interval algebra (PAA) that models time with Gaussian boundaries, yielding a complete set of relation probabilities and recovering crisp Allen in the limit; validated by Monte Carlo and released as an open Python package.
AI.motivation: Address uncertainty in temporal information from language, perception, databases, and histories by moving from crisp, exact-boundary predicates to graded, probabilistic relations; derive the taxonomy rather than assume it.
AI.method: Represent time points as Gaussian; model intervals with Gaussian midpoints and truncated-Gaussian durations; express all relation predicates as boundary-ordering events within a single probabilistic space; derive probabilities via error functions for point-point relations and via multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities for point-interval and interval-interval relations; incorporate a tolerance band for contact relations (meets, starts, finishes, equals) so that a single tolerance yields a true partition of the 13 relations; show that coarse predicates (precedence, overlap, containment) are unions of leaves and that taxonomy is preserved as intervals collapse to points and as 13 relations reduce to 5, then 3; decompose each relation into correlation-aware temporal primitives in the style of CIDOC CRM; ensure scale invariance and separate graded expressions (e.g., "shortly before"); validate all results by Monte Carlo, and provide an open, tested Python package.
AI.result: The 13 Allen relations form a true partition under a single tolerance; the framework derives the taxonomy rather than imposing it; coarse relations emerge as unions of leaves; the hierarchy persists as intervals shrink to points (13→5→3 relations); each relation decomposes into canonical temporal primitives; comprehensive Monte-Carlo validation supports the approach; implementation available as an open-source Python package.
AI.conclusion: PAA offers a complete probabilistic foundation for qualitative temporal reasoning, enabling graded expressions like 'shortly before' while preserving Allen's taxonomy in the appropriate limit; aligns with CIDOC CRM principles and is scalable via a single, interpretable tolerance parameter; released as open-source software.

title: COMPASS: Ordered Clustered Routing at 100K Scale
summary: Large-scale routing often requires visiting clusters of nodes in a prescribed order, giving rise to the Ordered Clustered Traveling Salesman Problem (OCTSP). Optimizing each cluster independently seems natural, but misses non-local dependencies. We introduce the COMPASS algorithm for OCTSP, which combines search with learning-accelerated routing by orchestrating parallel sub-solvers. COMPASS has no quality ceiling and its solutions keep improving with compute. It exploits the clustered structure, and can reach exact solutions in time exponential in cluster size rather than instance size. Empirically, COMPASS consistently outperforms alternative methods. Unlike common large-scale routing solvers, COMPASS consumes general distance matrices and is not limited to coordinate inputs. We demonstrate scaling to 100K synthetic nodes and to 28.5K real e-commerce nodes. To our knowledge, the latter is the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances, 9x beyond established ATSP benchmarks.

AI.tldr: COMPASS for OCTSP uses parallel sub-solvers and learning-accelerated routing to exploit cluster structure, achieving scalable, improving solutions with compute; reaches exact solutions in time exponential in cluster size; demonstrates large-scale performance on 100k synthetic nodes and 28.5k real e-commerce nodes with asymmetric distances.
AI.motivation: OCTSP requires ordered visitation of clusters; naive per-cluster optimization ignores non-local dependencies and fails on large instances. COMPASS aims to leverage clustering structure and learning to improve routing quality and scalability.
AI.method: Combines search with learning-accelerated routing by orchestrating parallel sub-solvers; exploits clustered structure and non-local dependencies; supports general distance matrices (not limited to coordinates); scalable to large instances.
AI.result: COMPASS consistently outperforms alternative methods; has no quality ceiling; solutions improve with compute; can reach exact solutions with time exponential in cluster size; scales to 100K synthetic nodes and 28.5K real-world nodes (largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances, 9x beyond ATSP benchmarks).
AI.conclusion: COMPASS is a scalable, general-purpose OCTSP solver that leverages clustering and learning to overcome non-local dependencies, scalable to very large and asymmetric-distance instances while using general distance matrices.

title: DocAttriBench: Benchmarking Answer Grounding in Document Visual Question Answering
summary: Answer grounding in document visual question answering remains an open challenge: most benchmarks lack grounding annotations or provide limited-quality labels, while constructing grounded datasets still requires costly manual effort. We introduce DocAttriBench (DAB), a large-scale benchmark for fine-grained, element-level source attribution in Document VQA, grounding answers to specific layout elements such as text blocks, tables, and images. To build DAB, we propose a Mask-based Perplexity-Derived Attribution method (MAPPET) that combines document layout and language modeling to identify the most informative element for each answer. MAPPET measures the increase in perplexity after masking candidate elements and attributes the answer to the element contributing most to model confidence. Applying MAPPET to multiple existing Document VQA datasets yields DAB, with 237k documents and 296k question-answer pairs with element-level grounding. We benchmark grounding-capable multimodal LLMs on DAB, evaluating answer accuracy, attribution accuracy, and overall answer quality. Results show that while larger models generally achieve higher answer accuracy, even the strongest models often fail to localize the supporting elements. DAB provides a scalable benchmark for developing grounded, verifiable, and trustworthy Document VQA models. Dataset and code are available at https://aimagelab.github.io/DocAttriBench/.

AI.tldr: DocAttriBench (DAB) is a large-scale, element-level grounding benchmark for Document VQA built with MAPPET, showing improved QA performance but persistent grounding gaps; DAB contains 237k documents and 296k QA pairs with element-level annotations; code available.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of fine-grained grounding annotations in Document VQA and enable scalable, verifiable grounding of answers to specific document elements (text blocks, tables, images).
AI.method: Introduce MAPPET (Mask-based Perplexity-Derived Attribution) to identify the most informative element by measuring perplexity increase when masking candidate elements; apply MAPPET to existing Document VQA datasets to produce DAB with element-level grounding; benchmark grounding-capable multimodal LLMs on QA accuracy, attribution accuracy, and overall answer quality.
AI.result: DAB comprises 237k documents and 296k QA pairs with element-level grounding; larger models improve answer accuracy but still struggle to localize supporting elements; provides a scalable benchmark for grounded, verifiable Document VQA models.
AI.conclusion: DAB offers a scalable, trustworthy benchmark for developing grounded Document VQA models and facilitates evaluation of both QA performance and grounding accuracy; dataset and code are publicly available.

title: Towards AI-enhanced control: a numerical technique for trajectory smoothing of a parallel robot for pancreatic surgery
summary: The paper presents a numerical approach for the end-effector trajectory smoothing of a parallel robot designed for minimally invasive pancreatic surgery. The approach is tailored for real-time master-slave control architecture and uses a 3D space mouse for command input for velocity control. The trajectory smoothing is achieved by generating S-curves in the end-effector velocity fields, thus controlling the accelerations, which in turn reduces tissue trauma in the minimally invasive procedures. Real-time control is enabled by segmenting the S-curves based on the command inputs from the 3D space mouse. A special case is considered where the acceleration time is constant for all command inputs. Numeric results demonstrate stable transitions (without abrupt changes) in both the end-effector parameter space and in the active joints parameters, thereby validating the proposed approach. Further work aims to test the approach on an experimental model and integrate it into AI-based training modules.

AI.tldr: Numerical trajectory smoothing for a parallel MIS robot using S-curves in velocity space enables real-time master-slave control with a 3D space mouse, showing stable end-effector and joint transitions; experimental validation and AI-driven training integration are planned.
AI.motivation: Minimally invasive pancreatic surgery demands smooth, dexterous end-effector motion to minimize tissue trauma while supporting real-time, intuitive control.
AI.method: Generate S-curves in end-effector velocity fields to bound accelerations; segment curves based on 3D space-mouse inputs for real-time control; analyze a constant acceleration-time special case; evaluate via numerical simulations focusing on end-effector and joint-space transitions.
AI.result: Numerical results show stable, non-abrupt transitions in both end-effector and active joint parameters, validating the trajectory-smoothing approach.
AI.conclusion: The approach is numerically validated and ready for experimental testing; future work includes validating on an experimental model and integrating the method into AI-based training modules.

title: Ownership in AI-Assisted Everyday Tasks
summary: When does work done with AI still feel like ours? As AI becomes woven into everyday tasks, we must examine what happens to our sense of ownership and contribution when a machine shares in producing what we make. We report an exploratory qualitative survey in which participants were asked to describe two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not. We find that felt ownership depends on the process of collaboration: people disown work when they merely approve AI's suggestions, but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite. Ownership can also extend to settings where people own the vision for a project but not the execution; respondents reported high ownership on tasks they could not have completed without AI. Loss of personal voice and a lack of comprehension of the output both erode ownership. Finally, willingness to disclose AI use is often decoupled from actual pride or ownership, and instead shaped by community norms and fear of credit erasure. We propose several research directions as a result of these findings to promote AI development that supports people's sense of authorship over their own lives.

AI.tldr: AI changes perceived ownership; ownership depends on collaborative process and ability to influence, not just using AI; tasks where AI is essential or vision is owned by user retain high ownership; mere approval erodes ownership; disclosure is shaped by norms; directions for future research to support authorship.
AI.motivation: As AI integrates into everyday work, understanding how humans retain sense of authorship and control is crucial for responsible AI design and uptake.
AI.method: Qualitative exploratory survey asking participants to describe two self-selected tasks done with AI: one felt like their own and one did not; analysis of perceived ownership and factors influencing it.
AI.result: Ownership is contingent on collaboration dynamics: disown when simply approving AI suggestions; retain ownership when leading, iterating, or rewriting; ownership can extend when user owns the project vision but not execution; high ownership when AI enables tasks otherwise impossible; loss of personal voice and lack of comprehension erode ownership; willingness to disclose AI use is shaped by norms and fear of credit erasure, not pride.
AI.conclusion: Researchers should explore directions to design AI that supports genuine authorship, such as transparency, controllability, provenance, and collaboration models that keep human authorship salient across tasks.

title: Minimax-Optimal Online Contract Design with Unrestricted Bounded Contracts
summary: We study repeated contract design when a principal observes outcomes but not the actions that generate them. The principal may use any bounded outcome-contingent payment vector, and the agent's best response can make expected profit discontinuous in those payments. For every fixed number $m\ge2$ of outcomes, the minimax regret over $T$ rounds is of order $T^{m/(m+1)}$, up to logarithmic factors. The upper bound allows arbitrary action spaces and agent heterogeneity, without smoothness or monotone-surplus assumptions. Its key is an effective-dimension reduction that the benchmark can be normalized even when fixed tie-breaking is not shift invariant, after which revealed preference yields a monotone response map in payment-difference coordinates. A learning policy built on a Lipschitz parametrization of this map attains the rate using only observed outcome categories. The lower-bound construction accounts for how incentive losses accumulate across outcome dimensions. It shows that each additional contractible outcome creates a precise and unavoidable increase in the worst-case cost of learning.

AI.tldr: Minimax regret in repeated contract design with observable outcomes scales as T^{m/(m+1)} for m outcomes; upper bound robust to arbitrary action spaces, agent heterogeneity, and without smoothness; uses effective-dimension reduction and revealed preference; learning via Lipschitz map on outcome-difference coordinates; lower bound shows each extra outcome increases learning cost.
AI.motivation: To quantify the learning difficulty and limits in a repeated principal–agent setting where the principal only observes outcomes (not actions) and can employ any bounded outcome-contingent payments, accounting for multiple outcome dimensions and potential discontinuities in agent response.
AI.method: Establish a minimax regret bound for fixed m≥2 outcome dimensions. Prove an upper bound using an effective-dimension reduction that normalizes the benchmark even without shift-invariant tie-breaking, then leverage revealed preference to obtain a monotone response map in payment-difference coordinates. Construct a learning policy based on a Lipschitz parametrization of this map and utilize only observed outcome categories. Prove a matching lower bound by showing incentive losses accumulate across outcome dimensions, with each additional contractible outcome increasing worst-case learning cost.
AI.result: Minimax regret over T rounds is of order T^{m/(m+1)} (up to logarithmic factors) for any m≥2. The bound holds with arbitrary action spaces and agent heterogeneity, with no smoothness or monotone-surplus assumptions. The upper bound relies on an effective-dimension reduction and a monotone response map in a transformed space; the learning policy uses a Lipschitz parametrization and observed outcome categories. The lower bound demonstrates that each extra contractible outcome irreversibly increases the learning cost.
AI.conclusion: The number of contractible outcomes fundamentally governs learning difficulty in repeated contract design. The proposed approach achieves near-optimal regret rates under minimal assumptions, revealing how incentive losses accumulate across outcome dimensions and quantifying the cost of additional outcomes.

title: RawSLAM: Online HDR Gaussian SLAM from Linear Radiance
summary: Current dense visual SLAM systems rely almost exclusively on 8-bit tonemapped Low Dynamic Range (LDR) inputs, limiting their robustness in extreme lighting where shadows and highlights trigger tracking drift and mapping collapse. Conversely, existing raw and High Dynamic Range (HDR) reconstruction pipelines operate strictly offline. They depend on Structure-from-Motion preprocessing and are not suited for large inter-frame motion. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first online Gaussian SLAM framework that tracks and maps directly on single-exposure 16-bit linear HDR imagery. Our method rests on three core components: an architecture-agnostic HDR Gaussian Splatting module featuring an MLP-free logarithmic parameterization of Gaussian color features; a Reinhard range-compressed photometric objective; and structure-guided spatial gradient weighting. Combined, these components allow our approach to outperform a direct HDR adaptation of MonoGS in both trajectory and reconstruction accuracy, while rendering natively in linear scene radiance for post-rendering processing. The same formulation runs unchanged on standard 8-bit inputs, roughly halving the MonoGS baseline error. Furthermore, our HDR Gaussian module transfers seamlessly to SplaTAM, Gaussian SLAM, and DROID-W, eliminating all tracking failures these systems suffer on challenging illumination sequences. To enable this research, we introduce RawSLAM: a dataset of 10 real-world indoor sequences featuring 16-bit RAW imagery, aligned depth, IMU measurements, and external OptiTrack poses. Code and dataset will be made publicly available soon.

AI.tldr: Introduces the first online HDR Gaussian SLAM operating directly on single-exposure 16‑bit linear HDR images, with an HDR Gaussian Splatting module, Reinhard photometric objective, and gradient-weighted optimization, achieving state-of-the-art trajectory/map accuracy and robustness under challenging illumination; also releases RawSLAM with 16‑bit RAW data and related code soon.
AI.motivation: Current dense SLAM largely uses 8‑bit LDR inputs, suffering in extreme lighting; offline HDR pipelines are not suited for large inter-frame motion; a real-time HDR-capable SLAM would improve robustness and enable HDR processing directly in the mapping backend.
AI.method: An architecture-agnostic HDR Gaussian Splatting module using a logarithmic, MLP-free parameterization of Gaussian color features; a Reinhard range-compressed photometric objective; and structure-guided spatial gradient weighting. The framework runs online on 16-bit HDR imagery and remains applicable to 8-bit inputs. The approach also enables seamless transfer to other systems (SplaTAM, Gaussian SLAM, DROID-W).
AI.result: Outperforms a direct HDR adaptation of MonoGS in both trajectory accuracy and reconstruction quality. On 8-bit inputs, the method roughly halves the MonoGS baseline error. The HDR Gaussian module transfers to competing systems and mitigates tracking failures on challenging illumination sequences.

title: Integrated Guidance and Control of a Mother-Child UAV-UGV System for Cooperative Missions
summary: Autonomous recovery of a small multirotor onto a hovering multirotor carrier differs from recovery onto ground or shipborne platforms because the recovery surface is itself an actively controlled, thrust-limited aerial vehicle. This paper presents a field-validated autonomy framework for a heterogeneous rover-mothership-child system executing rover supervision, mothership transit, child deployment and sortie, autonomous return, aerial recovery, and synchronized descent. The recovery stack combines jerk-bounded reference generation, disturbance-observer-augmented planar tracking, feasibility-aware vertical control, a discrete-time barrier-based safety filter for relative vertical geometry, and communication-aware carrier-state prediction. The contribution is the coordinated system-level integration of these methods for recovery onto a hovering multirotor and its full-scale outdoor validation. The framework is implemented on a PX4-ROS 2 architecture using RTK-enabled GNSS, IMU, and barometric fusion, with mothership-side 1D lidar used only as an auxiliary near-contact cue. RTK-fixed positioning was maintained throughout testing. Across 20 outdoor cooperative missions, 17 successfully completed deployment, sortie, and recovery, giving an observed mission success rate of 85%. For successful recoveries, mean terminal-alignment time was 6.3 s, mean planar alignment error at acceptance was 0.18 m, maximum terminal planar deviation was 0.32 m within a 0.40 m capture radius, and minimum logged relative vertical separation during coupled descent was 0.41 m. Mothership planar station-keeping RMS error was 0.25 m. The three unsuccessful trials occurred at different mission stages and are analyzed separately. Results demonstrate practical autonomous aerial recovery within the tested outdoor operating envelope.

AI.tldr: Field-validated autonomy framework for autonomous aerial recovery of a small multirotor onto a hovering carrier, featuring rover–mothership–child coordination and safety filters; 17/20 successes (85%).
AI.motivation: Recovery onto a capable, thrust-limited aerial platform is distinct from ground/shipment recoveries due to carrier dynamics and contact constraints; needs end-to-end field validation for reliable deployment, supervision, and recovery operations in autonomous operations.
AI.method: Integrated rover-mothership-child workflow with: (1) jerk-bounded reference generation, (2) disturbance-observer-augmented planar tracking, (3) feasibility-aware vertical control, (4) discrete-time barrier-based safety filter for relative vertical geometry, (5) communication-aware carrier-state prediction; implemented on a PX4-ROS 2 stack with RTK-enabled GNSS, IMU, baro fusion; mothership uses 1D lidar as auxiliary cue. RTK-fixed throughout outdoor tests. Validation across 20 missions including rover supervision, mothership transit, child deployment, sortie, autonomous return, aerial recovery, and synchronized descent.
AI.result: Out of 20 outdoor cooperative missions, 17 completed deployment, sortie, and recovery (85% success). For successful recoveries: mean terminal-alignment time 6.3 s; mean planar alignment error at acceptance 0.18 m; maximum terminal planar deviation 0.32 m within 0.40 m capture radius; minimum vertical separation during coupled descent 0.41 m. Mothership planar station-keeping RMS error 0.25 m. The three failures occurred at different mission stages and were analyzed separately.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates practical autonomous aerial recovery within the tested outdoor envelope, validating the integration of the proposed methods for autonomous recovery onto a hovering multirotor and highlighting the robustness and limitations across the mission stages.

title: Deep Noir: Autonomous Steering Discovery via Architectural Chronometry in Transformer Models
summary: Activation steering modifies LLM behavior at inference time, but identifying where and how strongly to steer remains manual. We introduce Deep Noir, a framework that uses Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to autonomously discover optimal steering parameters. Across three scales (1B x 3, 2-3B x 2, and 7-9B x 4), our engine achieves 16.7 percentage-point improvement on spam at 1B (standard deviation 4.7; 39 runs), with gains increasing to 21 to 42 percentage points at 7-9B across four architectures. On SST-2 sentiment, it achieves a 13.1 percentage-point improvement with zero code changes. Mechanistic grounding enables automated discovery of intervention points that generalize across tasks and architectures. On sentiment, RepE without head masking fails to improve over baseline, while Deep Noir improves all models (p less than 0.01). We further show that steering creates a predictable prompt-injection attack surface whose vulnerability increases monotonically with steering magnitude. This finding is relevant to agent systems deploying steered classifiers.

AI.tldr: Deep Noir automates inference-time steering of LLM behavior using Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to autonomously discover optimal steering parameters, improving task performance across multiple model scales and architectures while exposing a monotonic increase in prompt-injection vulnerability.
AI.motivation: Manual tuning of steering parameters at inference is a bottleneck and may not generalize across tasks/architectures. An automated, mechanistically grounded framework can discover robust steering interventions that transfer across tasks and models, while also highlighting potential security risks.
AI.method: Combine Logit Lens convergence with causal head-level attribution to identify optimal steering points. Evaluate across model scales (1B×3, 2–3B×2, 7–9B×4) and tasks (spam detection, SST-2 sentiment). Compare with RepE and head masking. Assess generalization of intervention points and quantify vulnerability of steering as a function of steering magnitude.
AI.result: Significant performance gains: spam improves by 16.7 percentage points at 1B (SD 4.7; 39 runs); 21–42 points gains at 7–9B across four architectures. SST-2 sentiment improves by 13.1 points with zero code changes. Mechanistic grounding yields intervention points that generalize across tasks/architectures. RepE without head masking fails on sentiment, while Deep Noir improves all models (p < 0.01). Steering introduces a predictable prompt-injection attack surface that grows with steering magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Automated, mechanistically grounded steering can enhance LLM performance across tasks and architectures, while also revealing security tradeoffs. The approach generalizes beyond specific models and tasks, but increases susceptibility to prompt-injection as steering strength grows, informing design considerations for steered classifier and agent-system deployments.

title: Learning Principal-Agent Contracts for Equitable Smallholder Carbon Farming under Moral Hazard and Adverse Selection
summary: Agricultural soils are a major untapped carbon sink. Carbon farming is emerging as a promising practice for tapping this potential. Smallholder farmers, who dominate agriculture across South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, are key to scaling climate mitigation via carbon farming. It is ironic that real-world carbon programs largely fail to reach them. We study this important gap through the lens of contract design. An aggregator offers a single pooled contract to a heterogeneous population of smallholder farmers who have private adoption costs (adverse selection) and exert unobserved effort (moral hazard), with agronomic outcomes evolving over multiple seasons. We formulate this evolving contracting problem as a POMDP and use reinforcement learning to learn a dynamic profit-maximising contract. We analyse the performance of the aggregator under various conditions. We find that a profit-maximising aggregator does not merely inherit the exclusion of smallholders, it amplifies it. On large farms the aggregator realises 87.7% of achievable adoption, against only 8.2% on smallholdings. Per-hectare Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) costs fall as farm size rises, and the aggregator's pooling contract compounds this gradient rather than offsetting it. A counterfactual that makes MRV costs purely area-proportional eliminates this disparity. Our results and simulation can guide contract and policy design that opens carbon income to smallholders while enabling agricultural soils to contribute to climate mitigation at scale.

AI.tldr: Dynamic, pooled contracts for carbon farming disproportionately exclude smallholders; area-proportional MRV could reduce disparity but needs policy design.
AI.motivation: Unlock the large, underutilized potential of agricultural soils as a carbon sink, and scale mitigation by engaging the majority smallholder farmers in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, addressing the mismatch between real-world programs and smallholder inclusion.
AI.method: Formulate the evolving contract design as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) with private adoption costs (adverse selection) and unobserved effort (moral hazard). Use reinforcement learning to learn a dynamic, profit-maximising contract and evaluate performance across scenarios (farm size, MRV costs, pooling vs non-pooled contracts).
AI.result: A profit-maximising aggregator amplifies exclusion: large farms reach 87.7% of achievable adoption, while smallholdings reach only 8.2%. MRV costs per hectare decline with farm size, and pooling contracts exacerbate this gradient. A counterfactual where MRV costs scale purely with area eliminates the disparity.
AI.conclusion: Contract and policy design must address heterogeneity and MRV cost structure to open carbon income to smallholders and enable soil carbon mitigation at scale; interventions could include redesigning MRV to be more area-proportional or offering differentiated contracts to reduce adverse selection and moral hazard.

title: PhGS: Post-Hoc Pruning and Refinement of Single-View Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Reconstructions
summary: Recent single-view feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) generation predicts a fixed number of Gaussians per camera ray, introducing severe spatial redundancy. Most existing compaction strategies target multi-view setups to exploit cross-view consistency and are incompatible with single-image models. Instead of retraining the base feed-forward network to directly output compact representations, our insight is to keep the base models frozen and apply post-hoc pruning and recurrent refinement to the generated Gaussians. Consequently, we propose a backbone-agnostic compaction pipeline for single-view feed-forward 3DGS that couples an importance-score-based pruning mechanism with a trainable, lightweight recurrent refinement module, which iteratively updates the surviving primitives to restore image quality. Our results demonstrate seamless integration with existing baselines while preserving novel-view rendering fidelity and achieving high memory reduction. Furthermore, our method supports flexible inference-time keep ratios for application needs.

AI.tldr: Backbone-agnostic, post-hoc compaction for single-view 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reduces memory by pruning and applying a lightweight recurrent refinement, without retraining the base model, while preserving novel-view fidelity and allowing flexible inference-time keep ratios.
AI.motivation: In single-view 3DGS, each camera ray gets a fixed number of Gaussians, causing spatial redundancy. Existing compaction methods focus on multi-view setups and require retraining; thus there is a need for an efficient, model-free approach to compress representations at inference time.
AI.method: Freeze the base feed-forward 3DGS network. Apply an importance-score-based pruning to select a subset of Gaussians (primitives). Introduce a lightweight, trainable recurrent refinement module that iteratively updates the surviving Gaussians to recover image quality. The pipeline is backbone-agnostic and designed to integrate with existing baselines, enabling adjustable inference-time keep ratios for memory-speed trade-offs.
AI.result: Demonstrates seamless integration with existing baselines, preserves novel-view rendering fidelity, and achieves substantial memory reduction. The method provides flexible inference-time keep ratios, allowing deployment under varying resource constraints.
AI.conclusion: A backbone-agnostic, post-hoc compaction framework effectively reduces memory for single-view 3DGS without retraining, maintaining rendering quality while enabling adaptable inference budgets.

title: Learning Slope-Adaptive Whole-Body Locomotion for Humanoid Robots in Roofing Construction
summary: Roofing requires workers to coordinate locomotion, balance, and work-related body motions on pitched surfaces, creating a challenging application for humanoid robots. Directly retargeted human demonstrations, however, may preserve motion appearance while placing the robot's feet or hands incorrectly relative to the roof. This study presents a task-semantic scene-grounded framework for learning roofer-style whole-body motions on a Unitree G1. Human demonstrations are captured using a tracking system and retargeted to the robot, while a metric roof model supplies the spatial reference unavailable from the tracking system. A trajectory-level optimization grounds inferred support contacts and annotated work relations to the roof, and execution-aware reinforcement learning encourages the resulting policy to preserve these relations under dynamic tracking errors. The framework is evaluated through a multi-motion tracking study, a roof-pitch coverage matrix, a five-way nailgun ablation, cross-task experiments on hammering and lateral pushing, and comparisons with pure reinforcement learning and zero-shot teleoperation. Our method enables the robot to satisfy support, work-clearance, and nonpenetration criteria across all evaluated seeds. Across nailgun, hammering, and pushing, it achieves work-clearance errors between 0.256 and 0.531 cm and 3/3 successful evaluations per task. Physical experiments reproduce uphill walking, nailgun, hammering, and bending motions with mean base-frame motion errors below 80 mm. These findings establish scene-grounded human motion learning as a promising basis for construction-oriented humanoid motion primitives.

AI.tldr: A scene-grounded, task-semantic framework enabling roofer-style, whole-body motions on a humanoid robot by retargeting human demonstrations with roof-aware optimization and execution-aware reinforcement learning to preserve contact semantics and work relations.
AI.motivation: Directly retargeted demonstrations can misplace feet/hands on pitched roofs due to missing spatial references; a roof-aware ground-truth reference is needed to ensure safe, compliant, construct-focused motion primitives.
AI.method: Capture human demonstrations with a tracking system and retarget to a Unitree G1; use a metric roof model as spatial reference; perform trajectory-level optimization to ground inferred support contacts and work relations to the roof; apply execution-aware reinforcement learning to preserve these relations under dynamic tracking errors; evaluate via multi-motion tracking, roof-pitch coverage, nailgun ablation, cross-task hammering/pushing, and baselines (pure RL and zero-shot teleoperation).
AI.result: The framework satisfies support, work-clearance, and nonpenetration criteria across seeds; work-clearance errors range 0.256–0.531 cm with 3/3 successful evaluations per task; physical experiments show mean base-frame motion errors under 80 mm for uphill walking, nailgun, hammering, and bending motions.
AI.conclusion: Scene-grounded, human-motion learning is a promising basis for construction-oriented humanoid motion primitives, enabling safe and accurate roofer-like motions on real robots.

title: Q&A on Any Spreadsheet Requires Interpreting Its Grid Structure
summary: Semantic cell annotation improves chunking interpretability for spreadsheets in LLM-driven RAG systems, aiding answer generation through enriched context rather than improved retrieval accuracy. We propose a novel framework of splitting any spreadsheet into interpretable chunks using cell role annotation. Our framework beats the state of the art, yet it faces a hard ceiling. Spreadsheets are fundamentally two-dimensional unstructured data with continuous relationships and infinite potential cell roles. Because classification models are restricted to finite, pre-defined classes, they cannot perfectly capture this structural nuance, even with human-level annotation. We show that addressing the spreadsheet-to-LLM bottleneck requires moving beyond discrete cell classification. Instead, the field must develop dimensionality-reduction techniques to directly flatten 2D unstructured spreadsheets into 1D unstructured text. Text chunks would be easier for downstream RAG to interpret and generate from.

AI.tldr: Annotating spreadsheet cells with roles aids interpretability but cannot fully capture 2D structure; flattening spreadsheets into 1D text via dimensionality reduction may be needed for LLM-based RAG.
AI.motivation: Enhance interpretability and answer generation in LLM-driven RAG over spreadsheets by providing semantic context through cell-role annotations.
AI.method: Introduce a framework to split spreadsheets into interpretable chunks using cell role annotation; compare to state-of-the-art; analyze the limits of finite-class cell classification in representing 2D structure.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance in chunking/interpretability but faces a hard ceiling due to 2D unstructured, continuous relationships and infinite cell-role possibilities that finite classifiers cannot capture.
AI.conclusion: To overcome the bottleneck, move beyond discrete cell classification and develop dimensionality-reduction techniques to flatten 2D spreadsheets into 1D unstructured text for easier downstream RAG processing.

title: The Bias of Nonlinear Two-Time-scale Stochastic Approximation under Constant Step-Sizes
summary: Two-timescale stochastic approximation (TTSA) is a fundamental tool for analyzing coupled iterative algorithms in reinforcement learning, optimization, and stochastic control. However, finite-time guarantees for nonlinear two-timescale schemes remain difficult to obtain, especially under constant step-sizes. In this paper, we study nonlinear TTSA with step-sizes $α\ggβ$. Under standard stability, regularity, and Markovian noise assumptions, we upper bound the mean-squared error and the bias of both iterates around their limiting equilibria. Our bounds scale as $O(α+β^2/α^2)$, which we prove to be tight when $β\leα^{3/2}$. The analysis separates the contributions of initial conditions, fast-timescale tracking error, Markovian dependence, and timescale coupling, thereby clarifying the origin of the $β^2/α^2$ term. Our results reveal qualitative differences from the linear TTSA setting previously studied, showing that nonlinear dynamics introduce additional finite-time effects that are absent in the linear case.

AI.tldr: Nonlinear two-timescale stochastic approximation (TTSA) with step sizes α ≫ β is analyzed; finite-time bounds on mean-squared error and bias are O(α + β^2/α^2), tight for β ≤ α^{3/2}. The analysis isolates error sources and shows nonlinear dynamics introduce finite-time effects absent in the linear TTSA setting.
AI.motivation: To obtain finite-time guarantees for nonlinear TTSA with constant step-sizes and understand how two timescales interact, including the qualitative differences from the linear case.
AI.method: Consider nonlinear TTSA with α ≫ β under standard stability, regularity, and Markovian noise assumptions. Derive upper bounds on the MSE and bias for both iterates around limiting equilibria, and decompose error into initial-condition, fast-timescale tracking, Markovian, and coupling contributions.
AI.result: Derived MSE and bias bounds scaling as O(α + β^2/α^2); these bounds are tight in the regime β ≤ α^{3/2}. The analysis clarifies the origin of the β^2/α^2 term by separating error sources.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear TTSA exhibits finite-time effects not present in linear TTSA; the results provide near-tight rates and illuminate how nonlinear dynamics contribute to finite-time errors and the coupling between timescales.

title: Refinement Is Inherently Editable: Training-Free Prompt-to-Prompt Image Editing with Generative Refinement Network
summary: Text-guided image editing must introduce the requested changes while preserving unrelated source content. Diffusion-based editors rely on spatial controls whose inaccuracies can leave edits incomplete or alter unrelated regions. Causal autoregressive editors face a further constraint: their fixed decoding order limits revision of earlier decisions. We introduce RefineEdit, a training-free prompt-to-prompt image editing framework built on a Generative Refinement Network. Our key idea is to couple edit localization with content generation through the global refinement of binary image codes, allowing editing evidence to be reassessed as the image evolves. RefineEdit initializes an editing branch from an intermediate source state, reusing the emerging layout. We compare the probabilities assigned by the two branches to the same source-sampled bits, using their signed differences to select editable positions and bits. Selected bits follow editing refinement, while the remaining bits copy the evolving source state. To stabilize editing across refinement steps, adaptive spatial freezing limits unnecessary mask expansion, while finite bit locking keeps recently selected bits editable. The framework requires no additional training, external masks, or attention control. Across nine editing categories of PIE-Bench, RefineEdit achieves the best background-preservation scores in PSNR, LPIPS, MSE and SSIM, together with the highest whole-image and edited-region CLIP scores among the evaluated methods.

AI.tldr: RefineEdit is a training-free prompt-to-prompt image editing framework that refines binary image codes via a Generative Refinement Network to localize edits and update content. It reuses the evolving layout from a source state, uses two branches to compare source-sampled bits and select editable positions, and stabilizes edits with adaptive spatial freezing and finite bit locking. It achieves state-of-the-art background preservation and CLIP scores on PIE-Bench.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based editors suffer from spatial inaccuracies that miss edits or affect unrelated regions, while causal autoregressive editors are constrained by fixed decoding order. A training-free method that dynamically reassesses edits as the image evolves and localizes edits improves fidelity and control without extra training.
AI.method: - Initialize an editing branch from an intermediate source state and reuse the emerging layout. - Introduce a two-branch mechanism that assesses the same source-sampled binary image bits by comparing branch probabilities; use signed differences to select editable positions and bits. - Selected bits undergo editing refinement; remaining bits copy the evolving source state. - Stabilize refinement with adaptive spatial freezing to limit mask expansion and finite bit locking to keep recently selected bits editable. - No additional training, external masks, or attention control required. - Evaluate across nine editing categories of PIE-Bench, reporting PSNR, LPIPS, MSE, SSIM, and CLIP metrics.
AI.result: RefineEdit achieves the best background-preservation scores (PSNR, LPIPS, MSE, SSIM) and the highest whole-image and edited-region CLIP scores among evaluated methods across nine PIE-Bench editing categories.
AI.conclusion: A training-free, prompt-to-prompt editing framework that couples localization and content generation through global binary-code refinement, offering robust, high-fidelity edits with strong preservation of non-edited regions and competitive perceptual quality.

title: OmniMimic: Dynamics-completed Motion Augmentation for Multi-style Omnidirectional Quadruped Locomotion
comment: The project page is at https://OmniMimic.github.io
summary: Animal demonstrations provide quadruped robots with natural and distinctive gait styles that are difficult to specify through hand-crafted rewards. However, their narrow directional coverage leaves little style-consistent supervision for backward, lateral, and turning commands. We present OmniMimic, a training framework that turns directionally limited animal demonstrations into a single multi-gait policy over target per-axis velocity ranges. OmniMimic first combines temporal reversal, constrained dynamics completion, and sagittal reflection to construct robot-specific kinematic and physical supervision beyond the observed directions. It then expands commands progressively from the demonstrated velocity distribution toward the target per-axis bounds, and uses a shared actor with soft-gated, gait-specialized residual experts to balance reusable locomotion skills with gait-specific corrections. Across four gaits in simulation, OmniMimic reduces mean foot-position RMSE at forward and backward reference velocities by 12.9% and velocity-tracking RMSE on a uniform Cartesian command grid by 63.1%, compared with the matched APEX baseline. The project page is at https://OmniMimic.github.io.

AI.tldr: OmniMimic enables a single multi-gait policy for quadruped locomotion from directionally limited animal demonstrations by augmenting supervision and progressively expanding per-axis velocity commands, improving trajectory and velocity tracking versus a baseline.
AI.motivation: Directionally constrained animal demonstrations provide limited supervision for backward, lateral, and turning motions, hindering the learning of consistent multi-gait policies.
AI.method: Combine temporal reversal, constrained dynamics completion, and sagittal reflection to synthesize robot-specific kinodynamic supervision beyond observed directions. Progressively expand command distributions from demonstrated velocities toward target per-axis bounds. Use a shared actor with soft-gated, gait-specialized residual experts to balance reusable locomotion skills with gait-specific corrections.
AI.result: In simulation across four gaits, OmniMimic reduced mean foot-position RMSE at forward and backward reference velocities by 12.9% and lowered velocity-tracking RMSE on a uniform Cartesian command grid by 63.1% relative to a matched APEX baseline.
AI.conclusion: OmniMimic demonstrates effective conversion of directionally limited demonstrations into a robust multi-gait policy, achieving notable gains in trajectory accuracy and velocity tracking across multiple gaits.

title: RAFT: A Stateful Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Industry Track
summary: Effective troubleshooting agents in enterprise customer support depend on retrieving actionable guidance from similar historical cases, yet existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat support cases as static documents and overlook their multi-stage, stateful nature. We introduce RAFT (Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents), a stateful RAG framework that abstracts each closed historical case into a directed chain of timeline entries and retrieves at the entry level, surfacing cases whose intermediate states match the active case and returning the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state; an optional case-level graph links cases through a configurable similarity representation. We evaluate this retrieval layer directly, which, unlike evaluating a full agent system, requires no production deployment. Because public multi-stage troubleshooting data is extremely rare, we pair a synthetic benchmark built from Microsoft Learn Windows Server documentation with real Apache Jira issues carrying human-created duplicate labels. RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress, with statistically significant gains over the strongest baseline; the Jira results provide directional evidence that the advantage transfers to real case histories. We release our benchmark, implementation, and the Apache Jira evaluation set.

AI.tldr: RAFT is a stateful retrieval-augmented framework for troubleshooting that treats historical cases as directed timelines and retrieves at the entry level to surface state-matched trajectories; it optionally links cases via a similarity graph; evaluated on a synthetic Windows Server benchmark and real Apache Jira duplicates; shows improvements over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG; the benchmark and data are released.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of treating support cases as static documents in retrieval-augmented generation; leverage multi-stage, stateful case progress to improve actionable guidance retrieval.
AI.method: Represent each closed historical case as a directed chain of timeline entries and perform retrieval at the entry level to find intermediate states matching the active case; return the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state; optionally connect cases with a case-level similarity graph; evaluate the retrieval layer directly on synthetic and real data; release benchmark, implementation, and evaluation datasets.
AI.result: RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress with statistical significance over the strongest baseline; Jira results provide directional evidence of transfer to real case histories; benchmark and datasets are released.
AI.conclusion: Stateful, entry-level retrieval enables more accurate and actionable guidance in troubleshooting; RAFT demonstrates improved retrieval performance and provides resources for further research through released data and code.

title: SCGFM-ART: Amortized Relational Transport for Structure-Centric Graph Foundation Models
summary: Graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to learn transferable representations across severely heterogeneous graph domains. However, severe domain shifts in topology, graph scale, and feature semantics impede the construction of a unified, domain-agnostic representation space. To address this, we propose SCGFM-ART, a structure-centric GFM framework that aligns arbitrary graphs onto a shared relational atlas via Amortized Relational Transport (ART). The relational atlas serves as a universal coordinate system defined by a finite set of relational landmarks (bases), while ART directly predicts reusable, end-to-end graph-to-base transport plans, bypassing costly runtime Gromov-Wasserstein optimizations. Under this formulation, SCGFM-ART decomposes a graph into a unified representation: globally via its relational response coordinates relative to the atlas, and locally via its node-to-role structural correspondences. These correspondences project disparate node attributes into a canonical role space, resolving structural and semantic heterogeneity within a singular alignment interface. Rigorously modeling graphs and atlas bases as finite measured relational spaces, we establish coordinate fidelity bounds, prove stability under predicted transport plans, and derive an amortized coverage bound that guarantees our learning objective tightly surrogates ideal relational coverage. Benchmarked across 14 cross-domain graph- and node-level classification tasks, SCGFM-ART achieves state-of-the-art transferability, securing superior average ranks of 2.29 and 1.14, respectively. Topological perturbation analyses demonstrate that node-role transport retains fine-grained structural nuances beyond global coordinates. On real-world benchmarks, the amortized formulation yields 44.2 to 85.1 times faster frozen target-domain inference by avoiding iterative alignment at test time.

AI.tldr: A structure-centric graph foundation model (SCGFM-ART) aligns heterogeneous graphs to a universal relational atlas using Amortized Relational Transport (ART), enabling global relational coordinates and local node-role correspondences with theoretical guarantees; it achieves state-of-the-art cross-domain transferability and dramatic test-time speedups by avoiding iterative alignments.
AI.motivation: Severe domain shifts in graph topology, scale, and feature semantics hinder unified, transferable representations. Existing GFMs struggle with costly runtime alignments and lack robust guarantees across heterogeneous domains.
AI.method: Represent graphs and atlas bases as finite measured relational spaces arranged around a shared relational atlas defined by relational landmarks (bases). Use Amortized Relational Transport (ART) to predict end-to-end graph-to-base transport plans without iterative optimization. Decompose graphs into global coordinates (relational response to the atlas) and local node-to-role correspondences, projecting attributes into a canonical role space. Establish coordinate fidelity bounds, prove stability of transport plans, and derive an amortized coverage bound. Validate on 14 cross-domain graph- and node-level classification tasks; analyze perturbations; demonstrate 44.2–85.1x faster frozen target-domain inference at test time by eliminating iterative alignment.
AI.result: SCGFM-ART achieves state-of-the-art transferability across 14 tasks, with superior average ranks (2.29 for graph-level, 1.14 for node-level). Topological perturbation analyses show node-role transport preserves fine-grained structure beyond global coordinates. Amortized inference yields massive test-time speedups (44.2–85.1×) by avoiding iterative alignment.
AI.conclusion: A theoretically grounded, scalable framework for cross-domain graph representation learning that delivers strong transfer performance, stability guarantees, and substantial inference speedups via amortized transport, suitable for heterogeneous graphs and node-level tasks.

title: PROVIA: Procedure State Tracking for Online Mistake Detection in Egocentric Videos
summary: An assistant watching egocentric video should notice a mistake from past frames alone, before the next step begins, and keep working once the person recovers. A mistake changes the state of the work, so every later step has to be read against what was done rather than against the plan. The first-mistake protocol that current online methods report on cuts each recording at its first mistake, so a fixed-time rule that never looks at the video is right on every case. We evaluate on complete trials, where mistakes and recoveries arise naturally, under a validation false-alarm budget and against controls that use timing alone. PROVIA keeps two records apart: a factual state, a learned summary of the steps each actor performed, mistakes included, and the accepted progress, an exact posterior over the state of an automaton induced from correct demonstrations by Bayesian state merging and over the execution status of each actor. Procedure-state transitions occur only in the correct-status branch; the mistake and correction branches retain the source state. A sequential test turns the per-frame mistake probability into alarms. With one filter and one optimization rule, PROVIA ranks mistakes best among the evaluated controlled baselines on CaptainCook4D, IndustReal, HoloAssist and IMPACT-ego. At a validation budget of 0.1 false alarms per minute it recalls .154 against .128 on CaptainCook4D and .034 against .015 on HoloAssist, where it leads at every budget. The pipeline runs at 58-70 frames per second. The source code is available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/PROVIA.

AI.tldr: PROVIA detects mistakes in egocentric procedural video online by maintaining dual state representations and using Bayesian state merging. It outperforms baselines under a low false-alarm budget and runs at real-time FPS; code available.
AI.motivation: Online, state-aware mistake detection in egocentric workflows is essential because mistakes alter downstream states, and prior approaches that cut at first mistake fail to utilize past context or handle recoveries; validated under a fixed false-alarm budget across multiple datasets.
AI.method: Maintain two records: a factual state (steps performed, including mistakes) and an accepted progress (posterior over automaton state). Use Bayesian state merging to induce the correct-demonstration automaton. Transitions occur only on the correct-status branch; mistake/correction branches retain the source state. A sequential test converts per-frame mistake probability into alarms. One filter and one optimization rule drive the detector.
AI.result: PROVIA ranks among the best baselines on CaptainCook4D, IndustReal, Hol oAssist and IMPACT-ego. At a validation budget of 0.1 false alarms per minute, recalls are 0.154 (CaptainCook4D) vs 0.128 (baseline) and 0.034 (HoloAssist) vs 0.015; it leads at every budget. The pipeline runs at 58–70 frames per second.
AI.conclusion: PROVIA provides effective online mistake detection with real-time performance across multiple datasets; source code is available at the provided GitHub link.

title: Walking on the Slope: Stable Bipedal Gaits with Genetic-Algorithm-Optimized Trajectories
summary: This paper presents the kinematic and dynamic modeling, trajectory generation, and stability analysis of an 8-degree-of-freedom (DOF) biped robot walking on flat and inclined terrain. Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) parameters and homogeneous transformations are used to derive the forward kinematics, while closed-form inverse kinematics maps the desired hip and swing-foot Cartesian trajectories, generated with cubic splines, to joint angles. Joint torques are computed using the Newton-Euler iterative algorithm, and dynamic stability is evaluated using the zero moment point (ZMP) criterion. A genetic algorithm (GA) optimizes the hip height, maximum swing-foot lift, and frontal-plane tilt angle by minimizing the work done by the joints subject to a ZMP feasibility penalty. Simulation results in MATLAB show that the nominal 8-DOF model remains ZMP-stable for step completion times down to 0.5 s and for slope inclinations up to 22.5 degrees with the given foot geometry. Beyond these limits, the ZMP leaves the support polygon, and either the foot dimensions or the trajectory parameters must be modified. The results also show that ZMP stability is governed by the mass distribution among the links rather than the total mass of the robot.

AI.tldr: An 8-DOF biped robot model using DH-based kinematics, inverse kinematics for hip/swing-foot, Newton-Euler dynamics, ZMP stability analysis, and GA-based optimization; simulations show stability limits and highlight mass distribution as a key determinant of ZMP stability.
AI.motivation: To enable stable walking of an 8-DOF biped on flat and inclined terrain by integrating kinematic/dynamic modeling, trajectory generation, and optimization, and to identify factors governing ZMP stability.
AI.method: Derive forward kinematics with DH parameters and homogeneous transforms; obtain closed-form inverse kinematics mapping hip and swing-foot trajectories (cubic splines) to joint angles; compute joint torques via Newton-Euler; evaluate stability with ZMP criterion; optimize hip height, maximum swing-foot lift, and frontal-plane tilt using a genetic algorithm with a work-based objective and ZMP feasibility penalty; validate via MATLAB simulations across step times and terrain inclines.
AI.result: Nominal 8-DOF model remains ZMP-stable for step completion times down to 0.5 s and slope inclinations up to 22.5 degrees with the given foot geometry; beyond these limits, ZMP exits the support polygon unless foot dimensions or trajectory parameters are adjusted; also, ZMP stability is governed more by mass distribution among links than by total mass.
AI.conclusion: Mass distribution is a primary design factor for ZMP stability in 8-DOF bipeds; achieving broader stability requires rebalancing link masses or adapting foot geometry and trajectories to keep ZMP within the support area.

title: An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents
summary: Coding harnesses shape how autonomous coding agents translate model capabilities into long-horizon software-engineering performance, yet existing work typically evaluates harnesses as monolithic systems, leaving the effectiveness of individual components unclear. To enable component-level comparisons, we study this question with a lightweight coding harness whose execution loop is fixed while three components are varied: planning, action space, and context management. Across four models evaluated on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1, we evaluate 176 matched settings spanning five context-management strategies, four context-window budgets, and targeted ablations of planning and action space. We find that: (1) Context management becomes increasingly valuable as the context-window budget tightens, with most of its benefit coming from preventing context-overflow failures. (2) Staging rule-based elision before LLM-based summarization provides the strongest overall efficiency among the context-management strategies, whereas making elided content recoverable adds machinery that models rarely use and yields no accuracy gain. (3) Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little change in accuracy. (4) Predefined tools improve performance for models with weaker bash proficiency, whereas bash-capable models can operate effectively with a bash-only interface and achieve substantially lower cost, especially on command-line-centric tasks. Trajectory-level analysis explains these effects: context management extends execution trajectories without substantially altering agent behavior, planning changes where trajectories stop, and the action space changes the granularity at which code is written. These findings inform model- and budget-aware harness design and provide a modular framework for evaluating future harness components.

AI.tldr: A modular study of a fixed-loop coding harness reveals that context management, planning, and action-space choices significantly affect long-horizon code-writing performance and cost, with findings guiding budget-aware harness design and offering a framework for component evaluation.
AI.motivation: Enable component-level comparison of coding-harness components to understand how planning, action space, and context management shape accuracy and efficiency under varying context budgets.
AI.method: Use a lightweight coding harness with a fixed execution loop while varying three components—planning, action space, and context management—across four models evaluated on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1. Assess 176 matched settings spanning five context-management strategies, four context-window budgets, and ablations of planning and action space; perform trajectory-level analysis to relate component choices to behavior.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Context management becomes more valuable as the context-window budget tightens, mainly by preventing context-overflow failures. (2) Staging rule-based elision before LLM summarization yields the strongest overall efficiency; making elided content recoverable adds unnecessary machinery and little accuracy gain. (3) Planning acts as an accuracy scaffold for weaker models, shifting to a cost saver for stronger models with little accuracy change. (4) Predefined tools help models with weaker bash proficiency; bash-capable models can operate effectively with a bash-only interface, achieving substantially lower cost on command-line tasks. Trajectory-level insights: context management extends execution trajectories without substantially altering agent behavior; planning changes where trajectories stop; action space influences the granularity of code generation.
AI.conclusion: The results support modular, budget-aware harness design and provide a reusable framework for evaluating future harness components; practitioners can tailor harness configurations to model capabilities and resource constraints to optimize long-horizon code-writing performance.

title: Seismic Site Response Prediction from Sparse Observations Using Finite-Element-Pretrained Latent Dynamics
summary: Numerical site-response predictions often deviate from observations, yet correcting these discrepancies is difficult because records are limited in both sensor coverage and number of events. This study proposes the Transfer-Enabled Forced Latent Autoencoder for Response Equations (FLARE-T) to improve these predictions by learning and calibrating low-dimensional latent dynamics that connect the base acceleration input to acceleration outputs at multiple depths. FLARE-T learns a low-dimensional response manifold and input-driven dynamics from dense finite-element simulations. It then trains a sparse encoder to map simulated sensor responses into the learned coordinates and uses limited records to calibrate the dynamics within them. A short response window initializes each prediction, while the complete base motion drives the response. The framework was evaluated using a layered-soil centrifuge test and the Lotung field vertical array. Test-set results show that FLARE-T improved multi-depth acceleration histories and 5%-damped pseudoacceleration response spectra relative to the original finite-element models, reducing errors at every evaluated sensor for motions of different intensities and, at Lotung, for both horizontal components. Two Lotung source models with different constitutive parameters achieved comparable test-set accuracy, indicating reduced dependence on precise prior calibration. FLARE-T therefore provides a data-efficient means of combining dense numerical response information with limited field records to improve future site-response predictions.

AI.tldr: Data-efficient FLARE-T learns a latent, input-driven manifold to map base acceleration to multi-depth responses, calibrating with sparse records to improve site-response predictions.
AI.motivation: Numerical site-response models often deviate from observations due to limited sensor coverage and few recorded events; a data-efficient calibration approach that fuses dense simulations with sparse field data is needed.
AI.method: Develop FLARE-T: learn a low-dimensional latent response manifold and input-driven dynamics from dense finite-element simulations; train a sparse encoder to map simulated sensor responses into latent coordinates; use limited records to calibrate the latent dynamics; initialize predictions with a short response window and drive with the full base motion; evaluate on a layered-soil centrifuge test and the Lotung field vertical array; compare two Lotung source models with different constitutive parameters.
AI.result: Improved multi-depth acceleration histories and 5%-damped pseudoacceleration response spectra relative to original FE models; reduced errors at all sensors across motions of varying intensity; comparable test-set accuracy for two Lotung source models, indicating reduced dependence on precise prior calibration.
AI.conclusion: FLARE-T offers a data-efficient framework that fuses dense numerical response information with limited field records to improve future site-response predictions, demonstrating robust performance across sensors and source-model variations.

title: Earth Surface Immune System for Rapid Monitoring of Unknown Anomalies
summary: Earth surface anomalies, driven by escalating climate change, and expanding human activities, are increasing in both frequency and diversity, yet their limited historical data and unpredictability make them fundamentally different from conventional remote sensing targets. Existing methods address specific anomaly categories or stop at localization, leaving a gap between detection and actionable information. Here we present ESIA, an Earth Surface Immune System whose architecture is constrained by three principles from the biological immune system, refined over millions of years against equally diverse and uncertain threats. A non-specific innate immune stage treats anomalies as unobserved changes in time-series satellite imagery, generating binary localization maps at 14.51 km2/s without assuming any anomaly category, surpassing the strongest general baseline by 37% in F1. A specific adaptive immune stage applies negative selection to filter text prompts and matches surviving prompts with localized image patches through a multi-modal foundation model, enabling open-vocabulary recognition of unknown anomaly attributes including category, affected area, and damage severity, with recognition F1 exceeding 80%. A mutation mechanism tunes minimal embeddings at test time, adapting to each scene in 3.26s using a single reference image pair. We validate ESIA on a global-scale dataset covering 19,801.60 km2 across six anomaly categories, comparing against 22 models, and further apply it to quantify degraded farmland in the Dnipro Delta following the Kakhovka Dam collapse and assess burn severity from 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles. This unprecedented flexibility in handling unknown anomalies opens new avenues for real-time disaster response and environmental surveillance.

AI.tldr: ESIA is an immune-inspired, open-vocabulary anomaly detection framework for Earth-surface remote sensing, combining a non-specific innate stage for rapid localization with a specific adaptive stage for open-ended attribute recognition, plus test-time adaptation via minimal embeddings; it achieves strong F1 gains and real-world deployment capabilities.
AI.motivation: Earth-surface anomalies are diverse and increasingly frequent, with limited historical data making them unlike conventional targets. There is a gap between detection and actionable information, especially for unknown categories.
AI.method: Innate stage: a non-specific, time-series-based anomaly detector that yields binary localization maps without assuming anomaly categories. Adaptive stage: negative selection to filter prompts, then matches surviving prompts to localized patches via a multi-modal foundation model for open-vocabulary recognition of attributes (category, affected area, damage severity). Mutation: test-time tuning of minimal embeddings using a single reference image pair to adapt to each scene in ~3.26 s.
AI.result: Localization speed: 14.51 km^2/s. F1 gain over the strongest general baseline: 37%. Recognition F1: >80%. Validation on a global-scale dataset: 19,801.60 km^2 across six anomaly categories, against 22 models. Case studies: degraded farmland in Dnipro Delta after the Kakhovka Dam collapse; burn severity from 2025 Palisades Fire in LA.
AI.conclusion: ESIA offers flexible, open-vocabulary anomaly detection and localization, bridging the gap from detection to actionable information for real-time disaster response and environmental surveillance.

title: Accelerating Visual Policy Learning with Sampling-Based Model Predictive Control
summary: Learning visual policies for locomotion and manipulation requires coordinating contact with the environment and can incur substantial computation and GPU memory costs. First-order policy gradients (FoPG) reduce training cost through differentiable simulation, but local optimization can converge to unintended contact patterns. To address this shortfall, we propose Sampling-Guided Policy Search (SGPS), which couples recurring action-target refinement by sampling-based model-predictive control with first-order policy optimization. Behavior cloning initializes the policy from sampled actions; training then alternates sampling-based refinement with short-horizon FoPG updates under perturbed initial states and randomized dynamics. For visual policy training, we use a decoupled FoPG formulation that excludes rendering from the computation graph, enabling direct learning from depth observations without a state-policy teacher. On a single GPU, SGPS learns policies for locomotion, obstacle traversal, crate pushing, and bimanual carrying on simulated Unitree Go2 and G1 robots. Our experiments further show that refinement improves policy learning beyond initialization and tracking alone. For hardware deployment, the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Go2 and uses onboard depth to autonomously trot, crawl, clear hurdles, and switch between these behaviors.

AI.tldr: Sampling-Guided Policy Search (SGPS) combines sampling-based model-predictive refinement with short-horizon first-order policy gradients to train contact-rich visuomotor policies efficiently, addressing local optima from purely gradient-based learning.
AI.motivation: Reduce training cost and improve stability for visuomotor policies that require precise environmental contact; overcome local optima in FoPG with differentiable simulation; enable direct learning from depth observations without a state-policy teacher.
AI.method: Initialize with behavior cloning from sampled actions; alternately apply sampling-based refinement (MPC-like) and short-horizon FoPG updates under perturbed initial states and randomized dynamics. For visual policies, use a decoupled FoPG that excludes rendering from the computation graph to learn directly from depth observations without a teacher. Demonstrate on simulated Unitree Go2 and G1 robots (locomotion, obstacle traversal, crate pushing, bimanual carrying) with single-GPU training; zero-shot transfer to real Go2 using onboard depth.
