AI.result: SGPS trains policies for locomotion, obstacle traversal, crate pushing, and bimanual carrying on simulated Go2 and G1. Refinement improves learning beyond initialization and tracking alone. The distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Go2, enabling autonomous trotting, crawling, hurdle clearing, and switching among behaviors using depth data.
AI.conclusion: Integrating sampling-based refinement with gradient policy optimization yields more robust visuomotor policies for contact-rich tasks and enables effective sim-to-real transfer with depth-based perception.

title: Training Neural Networks to Approach the Optimum Bayes Estimator in Dense Multi-Emitter Localization
summary: We train neural networks on synthesized frames to approach the optimum Bayes estimator for dense emitter localization. The result justifies the future work on training neural networks to achieve high-throughput large-FOV super spatiotemporal resolution SMLM.

AI.tldr: NNs trained on synthetic frames can approximate Bayes-optimal dense emitter localization, enabling scalable SMLM.
AI.motivation: Improve dense emitter localization in single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM) and enable high-throughput, large-field-of-view (FOV), high spatiotemporal resolution.
AI.method: Train neural networks on synthesized frames with the aim of approaching the optimum Bayes estimator for emitter localization.
AI.result: The approach yields results that justify further work toward scalable NN-based localization for high-throughput, large-FOV SMLM.
AI.conclusion: NN-based approximation of Bayes estimators is promising for dense emitter localization; future work should focus on scaling and efficiency to achieve high-throughput, large-FOV super-resolution SMLM.

title: FunArt: Decoding Functional Structure and Articulation from Generative 3D Latents
summary: To operate effectively in human environments, robots must identify articulated objects, segment their movable and interactive parts, and estimate their kinematic models. Existing articulated scene representations typically recover kinematics from observed interactions, while methods operating on static scans often decouple articulation from functional interactive elements. We present FunArt, a framework that constructs articulation-aware functional 3D scene graphs from posed RGB-D observations captured in a single static configuration. FunArt reconstructs object instances, converts their fused geometry directly into the O-Voxel representation of TRELLIS.2, and exploits its frozen, sparse-compression VAE as a structural prior. A lightweight query-based decoder combines compact object-level latents with dense, surface-aligned features to jointly segment movable parts and functional interactive elements while estimating motion type, axis, origin, and range. On the Articulate3D dataset, FunArt achieves state-of-the-art performance across movable-part segmentation, articulation estimation, and functional-element segmentation, both with and without ground-truth object input. In the end-to-end setting, it outperforms the strongest baselines by 1.5 AP_{50} points for movable parts, 2.8 AP_{50} points under joint origin-and-axis constraints, and 6.7 AP_{50} points for functional elements. These results demonstrate that generative 3D latents encode actionable structural cues that can initialize robotic perception and planning before physical interaction.

AI.tldr: FunArt: articulation-aware 3D scene graphs from a single static RGB-D scan; integrates TRELLIS.2 O-Voxel latent prior and a lightweight query-based decoder to jointly segment movable parts and functional elements and estimate articulation parameters; achieves state-of-the-art on Articulate3D.
AI.motivation: Robots must identify articulated objects and kinematics to operate in human environments. Existing approaches rely on interactions or static scans that separate articulation from functional elements. A single-shot, articulation-aware representation with a structural prior can accelerate perception and planning.
AI.method: Reconstruct object instances from a single posed RGB-D scene, convert fused geometry to the O-Voxel representation of TRELLIS.2, and use its frozen sparse-compression VAE as a structural prior. A lightweight query-based decoder fuses compact object latents with dense surface-aligned features to jointly segment movable parts and functional interactive elements and estimate motion type, axis, origin, and range.
AI.result: On Articulate3D, FunArt achieves state-of-the-art performance in movable-part segmentation, articulation estimation, and functional-element segmentation, both with and without ground-truth object input. In the end-to-end setting, it outperforms strong baselines by 1.5 AP50 points for movable parts, 2.8 AP50 points for joint origin-and-axis, and 6.7 AP50 points for functional elements.
AI.conclusion: Generative 3D latents encode actionable structural cues that can initialize robotic perception and planning before physical interaction, enabling articulation-aware scene understanding from a single static capture.

title: V2-STRep: VLM-Grounded Structured Task Representations for Reusable Robot Skills Acquired from Generated Videos
summary: Human manipulation videos provide rich motion and interaction cues for acquiring robot skills without robot demonstrations. Video generation models synthesize such demonstrations from an initial scene image and task instruction, avoiding the need to record demonstrations for each task. However, the recovered motion captures only one scene-specific realization, leaving task structure, geometric relations, and constraints implicit. We present V2-STRep, a zero-shot framework that converts generated video motion into reusable robot skills through VLM-grounded structured task representations. The representation specifies motion phases, references, and task-relevant constraints, with targets described by minimal geometric structures: points, point-normals, axes, planes, and full 6D poses. VLM-provided 2D image-space cues are lifted into 3D using RGB-D observations to reconstruct task geometry and candidate grasp poses. Geometry-specific rules transfer motion to new scenes, while task-constrained trajectory optimization couples grasp selection with complete robot motion planning. It preserves task requirements while using remaining rotational freedom to accommodate joint limits. Updating deployment grounding and constraints enables reuse under new compatible instructions without generating another video. Experiments on six real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improved execution success over baselines, reliable cross-scene transfer of successfully acquired skills, and adaptation to changed deployment instructions.

AI.tldr: V2-STRep transforms video-generated demonstrations into reusable robot skills by grounding structured task representations from vision-language models, enabling geometry-aware, cross-scene transfer and constrained trajectory optimization without new videos.
AI.motivation: Video-based demonstrations offer rich motion cues but are scene-specific and not readily reusable. A structured, geometry-aware representation is needed to transfer skills across scenes with adherence to task constraints.
AI.method: Propose V2-STRep: use VLM-grounded structured task representations outlining motion phases, references, and constraints. Represent targets with simple geometric primitives (points, normals, axes, planes, 6D poses). Lift 2D VLM cues to 3D using RGB-D to reconstruct task geometry and candidate grasps. Apply geometry-specific rules to transfer motion to new scenes, and perform task-constrained trajectory optimization that couples grasp selection with full robot motion planning while respecting joint limits. Update grounding/constraints to reuse for compatible instructions without re-generating video.
AI.result: Empirical validation on six real-world manipulation tasks shows higher success than baselines, reliable cross-scene transfer of learned skills, and adaptation to altered deployment instructions.
AI.conclusion: V2-STRep enables zero-shot, geometry-aware transfer of robot skills from video-generated demonstrations, reducing the need for new data and supporting robust execution across scenes and instructions.

title: Deep Learning-Based Classification of Cognitive and Resting States Using Electroencephalography Signals
summary: The categorization of cognitive and resting states derived from electroencephalography (EEG) signals is crucial for comprehending fluctuations in brain activity linked to various mental states. EEG provides a non-intrusive approach for documenting brain function in both resting and task-oriented cognitive conditions, whilst deep learning techniques enable the automatic extraction of significant patterns from intricate EEG data. This study presents a deep learning framework to distinguish between resting and cognitive states through EEG records. The proposed framework integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) stacked with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for the extraction of features from EEG signals. Time-frequency analysis is conducted to explore the salient aspects of signals, and the derived features are then assessed utilizing conventional deep learning and machine learning classifiers, including the suggested 2D-Net architecture. The proposed approach and feature extraction strategy outperform the evaluated comparative methods, achieving accuracies of 83.177% for resting-versus-mathematical task classification, 76.107% for resting-versus-memory task classification, and 83.432% for resting-versus-music task classification. The findings illustrate the efficacy of integrating signal processing with deep learning methodologies to discriminate resting from cognitive states utilizing EEG signals.

AI.tldr: A CNN-GRU deep learning framework with time-frequency features distinguishes resting vs cognitive states from EEG, achieving ~76–83% accuracy across tasks and outperforming baselines via a 2D-Net architecture.
AI.motivation: To understand fluctuations in brain activity by automatically distinguishing resting and cognitive states from EEG using deep learning and time-frequency feature extraction.
AI.method: Time-frequency analysis of EEG signals followed by a CNN stacked with a GRU for feature extraction; evaluation using conventional deep learning and machine learning classifiers, including the proposed 2D-Net architecture.
AI.result: Resting vs mathematical task: 83.177% accuracy; resting vs memory task: 76.107% accuracy; resting vs music task: 83.432% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Integrating signal processing with deep learning effectively discriminates resting from cognitive states in EEG, with the proposed approach (including 2D-Net) outperforming comparative methods.

title: Should This Case Be Adapted? Prediction Fragmentation Controls Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Episodic test-time adaptation resets a frozen segmenter to source weights $M_0$ on each case and adapts for a fixed step count. A fixed horizon conflates a cohort-level question, how far to adapt, with an irreducibly per-case one, whether this case should be adapted at all. Cohort means hide that decision: on cross-vendor cardiac MRI the mean $Δ$Dice from adaptation is statistically indistinguishable from zero while 58.7% of cases are individually made worse. We quantify this harm as harmful accepted area (HA), the harmful fraction of the edited area a controller deploys. Held-out tuning gives a stronger baseline than a fixed horizon, but the budget it selects transfers on neither of the two main medical benchmarks, and no global budget can condition on the case. We show that prediction fragmentation---the disagreement geometry between $M_0$ and the adapted mask $M_k$---predicts HA with no labels or extra backward passes at decision time, comparably on three benchmarks (Spearman $ρ$ 0.50--0.60), at a quarter of gradient-norm's latency. A case-level router built on it cuts HA from 0.228 to 0.139 on a benchmark that took no part in its design, with the design frozen and only cut-points recalibrated there. On the cardiac benchmark the design was selected on, the router cuts HA from 0.129 to 0.013 at matched Dice and 1.10 deployed updates, against the retrospective-best budget found post hoc on evaluation labels, and reduces that 58.7% to 20.0%, an upper bound we quantify. Where the retained cases are not net-helped (as on prostate), the router still cuts HA but concedes accuracy, a boundary we report. Thresholds are fit once on a labeled split disjoint from evaluation; decisions use no labels or gradients. The template ports across architecture and domain (nnU-Net$\to$SegFormer, Cityscapes$\to$ACDC) with coordinate, thresholds and per-bucket actions instantiated per domain.

AI.tldr: A case-level router using prediction fragmentation between a frozen segmenter M0 and its adapted mask Mk reduces harmful edits (HA) during episodic test-time adaptation, without requiring extra labels or gradients, and generalizes across architectures and domain pairs.
AI.motivation: Episodic test-time adaptation risks harming many cases while giving little average gain. Fixed adaptation horizons fuse cohort-level adaptation amount with individual-case necessity, leading to cases being worsened. A lightweight, label-free decision mechanism is needed to decide when to adapt on a per-case basis while maintaining efficiency.
AI.method: Define harmful accepted area (HA) to quantify edits. Use prediction fragmentation (disagreement geometry between M0 and Mk) as a label-free predictor of HA. Build a case-level router using this metric; fit decision thresholds on a labeled split, then apply without labels or backprop at decision time. Evaluate across cross-domain benchmarks, compare to fixed-horizon and held-out-tuning baselines, and test generalization across architectures (nnU-Net, SegFormer) and domains (Cityscapes, ACDC, cardiac MRI).
AI.result: Prediction fragmentation correlates with HA (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.50–0.60) with no extra labels or backward passes. The router reduces HA substantially: on the cardiac benchmark, HA drops from 0.129 to 0.013 at matched Dice with 1.10 deployments; overall reduction from 58.7% to 20.0% lid upper bound. It also lowers early HA from 0.228 to 0.139 on another benchmark. The approach generalizes to architectures and domain pairs (nnU-Net→SegFormer, Cityscapes→ACDC) and remains effective even when retained cases are not net-helped, albeit with some accuracy trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: A case-level router based on prediction fragmentation can substantially reduce harmful edits in episodic test-time adaptation without labels or gradients, outperforming fixed-horizon and budget-based baselines, and generalizes across architectures and domains.

title: CoRef-GS: Cooperative Referring Gaussian Splatting for Multi-Agent Scene Understanding
comment: The established benchmark and source code will be publicly released at https://github.com/ruojiruoli17/CoRef-GS.git
summary: Referring scene understanding for embodied robots requires grounding object- and relation-centric language queries from a designated viewpoint. While a local semantic Gaussian map can support such grounding within one agent's observations, cooperative settings require this ability to remain effective after independently reconstructed maps are aligned and fused. In this setting, the referred target or its contextual landmark may come from another agent's observations, while spatial relations must still be interpreted from the querying robot's viewpoint. We formulate this problem as cooperative referring Gaussian grounding over fused maps, which requires geometric alignability, instance-level semantic comparability, and view-conditioned relation reasoning. Existing language-aware Gaussian methods mainly focus on single-map querying, whereas Gaussian registration methods optimize geometric or photometric alignment without preserving language-grounding-oriented semantic compatibility. We propose CoRef-GS, a cooperative referring Gaussian splatting framework. CoRef-GS constructs local open-vocabulary instance-aware Gaussian maps, then aligns partially overlapping maps with a cross-agent alignment module by geometric and semantic consistency, and grounds queries using a view-conditioned mask relation graph. We further introduce CoQuad-Ref, a dual-quadruped benchmark spanning both real-world and simulated indoor scenes. Experiments show that, on simulated scenes, CoRef-GS reduces the rotation error from 2.58° after coarse initialization to 0.15° after refinement, and improves real-world referring mIoU over ReferSplat from 52.6% to 68.8%. The established benchmark and source code will be publicly released at https://github.com/ruojiruoli17/CoRef-GS.git.

AI.tldr: CoRef-GS is a cooperative referring Gaussian grounding framework that enables grounding language queries across fused multi-agent maps through geometric/semantic alignment and view-conditioned relation reasoning; it introduces the CoQuad-Ref benchmark and shows substantial improvements in rotation accuracy and referring mIoU, with public code release.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent robotics, independently built local maps must be aligned and fused while preserving language-grounding semantics. Existing Gaussian methods excel at single-map grounding or generic alignment but neglect cross-map semantic compatibility for language queries.
AI.method: Develop local open-vocabulary instance-aware Gaussian maps, apply a cross-agent alignment module enforcing geometric and semantic consistency on partially overlapping maps, and use a view-conditioned mask relation graph to ground queries. Also introduce CoQuad-Ref benchmark for dual-quadruped settings in real and simulated indoor scenes.
AI.result: Simulated experiments: rotation error reduced from 2.58° (coarse) to 0.15° (refinement). Real-world: referring mIoU improved from 52.6% (ReferSplat) to 68.8%..
AI.conclusion: CoRef-GS enables effective cooperative referring grounding on fused maps, advances language grounding in multi-agent perception, and provides a benchmark and open-source code.

title: Distributionally Robust Federated Learning with Multi-Source Data
summary: Federated learning trains a shared model from private client data. In practice, data-generating distributions may differ, and the true mixture across clients is often unknown, making the underlying group distribution difficult to specify. Existing approaches address cross-client mixture uncertainty by optimizing against the worst-case mixture, yet assume accurate client-wise distribution estimates. However, these estimates can be unreliable when based on finite samples. To handle both cross-client mixture uncertainty and within-client distributional ambiguity, we construct a global ambiguity set as the union of admissible mixtures of local ambiguity sets. The construction allows client-specific ambiguity radii and admits a client-wise separable reformulation. Leveraging this structure, we establish a high-probability out-of-sample performance guarantee. We further develop a federated algorithm for a penalty-based reformulation and prove its convergence under milder regularity conditions. Simulations validate the algorithm's effectiveness.

AI.tldr: Robust federated learning under both cross-client mixture uncertainty and within-client distributional ambiguity by constructing a global ambiguity set as unions of local ambiguity mixtures, enabling client-specific radii and a separable reformulation; provides high-probability out-of-sample guarantees and a convergent penalty-based federated algorithm, validated by simulations.
AI.motivation: Non-iid data across clients and unknown global mixtures complicate FL. Finite samples yield unreliable local distribution estimates. There is a need for robust, scalable methods with performance guarantees that handle both cross-client and within-client uncertainty.
AI.method: Build a global ambiguity set as a union of admissible mixtures of local ambiguity sets with client-specific radii, enabling a client-wise separable reformulation. Derive a high-probability out-of-sample performance guarantee. Develop a federated algorithm for a penalty-based reformulation and prove convergence under milder regularity conditions.
AI.result: Establishes a high-probability performance guarantee and presents a convergent penalty-based FL algorithm. Simulations validate robustness and effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: Addresses dual sources of distributional uncertainty in federated learning by providing a tractable, separable reformulation and a provably convergent algorithm, with empirical validation of robustness.

title: FlowSGS: Improving Flow Matching Priors for Inverse Imaging with Stochastic Interpolants
summary: Flow matching has emerged as the state-of-the-art generative model and has been used for plug-and-play (PnP) priors to solve inverse problems in computational imaging. However, existing flow-based inverse solvers assume linear forward models and/or make simplifying approximations in posterior sampling. To circumvent these problems, we introduce FlowSGS, a flow-based posterior sampling method using Split Gibbs Sampling (SGS) to decompose the posterior into a likelihood step and a prior step. Specifically, we sample from the likelihood step using Langevin dynamics and leverage the Stochastic Interpolants (SI) framework to integrate a pretrained flow model into the prior step. We provide a form for the prior step that uses SI's reverse-time SDE, and show connections to previous PnP methods. Moreover, with the aid of the flow prior's straight probability paths and a novel timestep correction technique for the reverse-time SDE, FlowSGS requires fewer network evaluations in its prior step than plug-and-play diffusion samplers. Our experiments show state-of-the-art performance on a range of inverse problems. For the first time, we provide an experiment on a nonlinear inverse problem (Fourier phase retrieval) for flow-based inverse solvers.

AI.tldr: FlowSGS introduces a flow-based posterior sampling framework using Split Gibbs Sampling to solve inverse problems with nonlinear forward models, combining Langevin dynamics for likelihood and SI-based priors via reverse-time SDE, achieving state-of-the-art results and reduced network evaluations.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of flow-based inverse solvers that assume linear forward models and rely on approximations in posterior sampling; enable nonlinear forward models and plug-and-play priors with learned flow models; improve sampling efficiency.
AI.method: Split Gibbs Sampling decomposes the posterior into a likelihood step (Langevin dynamics) and a prior step (SI-based flow prior using reverse-time SDE). The prior step leverages the Stochastic Interpolants framework with pretrained flow models, and introduces a timestep correction for the reverse-time SDE to reduce network evaluations.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance across a range of inverse problems; first experimental demonstration on nonlinear Fourier phase retrieval for flow-based solvers; reduced network evaluations in the prior step compared to plug-and-play diffusion samplers.
AI.conclusion: FlowSGS provides an effective, efficient flow-based posterior sampling approach for inverse problems, enabling nonlinear forward models, connecting to PnP methods, and offering improved sampling efficiency and broad applicability.

title: Semantic SLAM in Precision Agriculture using Bayesian Inference
summary: This paper presents a real-time semantic world modeling framework specialized for precision agriculture using autonomous robots. The framework combines probabilistic mapping of objects and their semantic attributes, updated through Bayesian inference, with a graph-based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) approach implemented using $g^2o$, a general framework for graph optimization. This integration enables accurate mapping and localization without relying solely on GPS. By leveraging semantic information such as plant type, size, and health, the robot can perform tasks while mapping and localizing itself within a field of crops. The proposed framework was validated through Gazebo simulations and physical experiments on an indoor field with artificial plants using Boston Dynamics' robot dog Spot. A YOLOv8n object detection model was trained to extract object and semantic data from depth camera observations. These simulations and experiments demonstrate that the system can successfully perform real-time mapping of up to at least 400 plants.

AI.tldr: Real-time semantic SLAM for precision agriculture: combines Bayesian probabilistic object mapping with g2o graph SLAM, enabling GPS-independent mapping/localization; validated in Gazebo and indoor Spot experiments with YOLOv8n; achieves real-time mapping of 400+ plants.
AI.motivation: In precision agriculture, reliable localization and semantic understanding are needed in fields where GPS can be unreliable or insufficient. Integrating semantic attributes (plant type, size, health) into SLAM enables autonomous farming tasks with better situational awareness.
AI.method: 1) Probabilistic (Bayesian) mapping of objects and semantic attributes. 2) Graph-based SLAM implemented via g2o for simultaneous localization and mapping. 3) Vision-based perception using YOLOv8n to extract object and semantic data from depth camera observations. 4) Validation through Gazebo simulations and physical indoor-field experiments with Boston Dynamics Spot. 5) Real-time processing to map up to at least 400 plants.
AI.result: Demonstrates real-time, GPS-independent mapping and localization with semantic attributes; successfully maps and localizes a field of 400+ plants in both simulation and physical tests; shows feasibility of integrating semantic information into SLAM for agriculture.
AI.conclusion: The framework proves feasibility and effectiveness of real-time semantically aware SLAM for precision agriculture, enabling autonomous farming decisions without sole reliance on GPS; scalable to larger plant counts and adaptable to other agricultural scenarios.

title: Radio Frequency Detection and Classification of Microplastics in Water
summary: Micro- and nano-plastic particles (MPs/NPs) are ubiquitous environmental contaminants whose increasing abundance and potential health impacts have created an urgent need for rapid, label-free detection methods. As particle size decreases to the low-micrometer range, conventional optical and spectroscopic techniques become increasingly challenging because of limited throughput and/or complex sample preparation. In this work, we present a machine learning (ML)-assisted radio-frequency (RF) dielectric spectroscopic cytometry (DiSC) platform for the label-free detection and classification of MPs. Eight types of $ 10 $ μm nominal-diameter MP particles suspended in deionized (DI) water were characterized at four frequencies spanning $ 0.2\text{-}9\text{ GHz} $. The measured alterations in RF scattering parameters (S-parameters), referenced to the carrier medium, were used to train supervised ML models for material classification, including the identification of MPs in mixed samples and saline-water environments. For eight MP classes suspended in DI water, the proposed method achieved macro-average F1-score, precision, and recall values exceeding $ 0.71 $. Furthermore, PET classification performance was largely maintained in saline carrier media containing $3.3\% $ and $ 6.6\% $ sea salt. These results demonstrate the feasibility of ML-assisted RF DiSC for rapid, single-particle MP classification in aqueous environments. Future work will focus on improving classification performance through enhanced RF calibration, increased spectral coverage, larger training datasets, and validation using environmentally aged and biologically contaminated microplastics.

AI.tldr: ML-assisted RF dielectric spectroscopic cytometry enables label-free, single-particle classification of microplastics in water using S-parameters across 0.2–9 GHz; macro-F1/precision/recall ~0.71 for 8 classes; PET classification robust in saline environments; requires more data/calibration for broader applicability.
AI.motivation: Urgent need for rapid, label-free detection of microplastics (MPs) due to environmental prevalence and potential health impacts. Conventional methods suffer from limited throughput and complex sample preparation; RF dielectric spectroscopy combined with machine learning offers potential high-throughput, label-free single-particle screening in aqueous media.
AI.method: Measure RF scattering parameters (S-parameters) of eight 10 μm MP classes suspended in DI water, across four frequencies spanning 0.2–9 GHz. Reference S-parameters to carrier medium. Train supervised ML classifiers on RF features to identify material class, including mixed and saline conditions. Evaluate macro-average F1, precision, and recall.
AI.result: Eight MP classes achieved macro-average F1-score, precision, and recall exceeding 0.71 in DI water. PET classification remained robust in saline media with 3.3% and 6.6% sea salt.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of ML-assisted RF DiSC for rapid, label-free single-particle MP classification in aqueous environments. Future work: improve RF calibration, expand spectral coverage, increase training data, and validate with environmentally aged and biologically contaminated MPs.

title: ERCPMP-Gx: Endoscopic Image and Video Dataset for Morphological, Histopathological, and Genomic Characterization of Colorectal Polyposis
summary: Hereditary polyposis syndromes can be precursor lesions to colorectal cancer and are associated with a broad spectrum of extracolonic tumors. Early identification and accurate classification of these syndromes are essential for timely diagnosis, individualized patient management, and targeted surveillance strategies for affected families. However, public endoscopic datasets are largely organized around the individual sporadic polyp, and none links the polyposis phenotype to histopathology and germline findings at the patient level. Here, we present ERCPMP-Gx, an endoscopic, histopathological, and genomic dataset developed to support the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the recognition, characterization, and classification of colorectal polyposis. Most procedures were performed using the Olympus EVIS X1 system with white-light endoscopy (WLE), narrow-band imaging (NBI), magnifying NBI (M-NBI), and NBI with near focus modes, yielding 160 images and accompanying video clips. Approximately eighty percent of cases represent clinically and/or genetically confirmed hereditary polyposis syndromes (PG), including familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS), and ganglioneuroma syndrome (GNS), while the remaining twenty percent comprise non-hereditary polyps and polyp-mimicking lesions with overlapping morphological features (Non-PG), included to support differential classification. Each released record is linked, where available, to standardized endoscopic annotations, representative histopathology, and clinically reported germline findings, forming an AI-ready, patient-level annotation framework. The dataset is publicly accessible at Mendeley (https://doi.org/10.17632/nzyfc544bx.2). For the latest updates and further information, readers are referred to the DataBioX website: https://databiox.com.

AI.tldr: Multi-modal, AI-ready dataset (ERCPMP-Gx) linking endoscopic images/videos with histopathology and germline data for hereditary colorectal polyposis syndromes; ~160 images/videos; ~80% PG (FAP, PJS, JPS, GNS) and 20% Non-PG; public release to enable AI-based recognition and classification.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of patient-level, multi-modal endoscopy datasets that connect phenotype, histopathology, and germline findings for hereditary polyposis syndromes, enabling AI-driven diagnostics and surveillance.
AI.method: Data collection using Olympus EVIS X1 across WLE, NBI, M-NBI, and near-focus modes to yield 160 images and video clips; each record linked to standardized endoscopic annotations, histopathology, and germline findings; emphasis on a patient-level annotation framework; public release via Mendeley and DataBioX.
AI.result: Publicly available, AI-ready dataset with standardized, multi-modal annotations linking endoscopy, histopathology, and germline data; distribution includes PG and Non-PG cases.
AI.conclusion: Fills a gap in linking polyposis phenotype with histopathology and germline data at the patient level, enabling AI applications in recognition, characterization, and classification of colorectal polyposis; promotes standardized annotations and reproducibility.

title: Bayesian Continuum Robot Dynamics and State Estimation
summary: Recent factor graph approaches to continuum robot state estimation have been successful for quasi-static applications and spatiotemporal estimation using white-noise kinematic motion priors. However, when inertial effects are significant, these approximations may fail to capture the underlying physics, limiting accuracy during dynamic motions. In contrast, our approach approximates the Cosserat rod dynamics of continuum robots. We write inertia and damping as equivalent applied loads, so that the dynamic balance retains the algebraic form of the static one from prior work with quasi-static robots. Without backbone observations, the framework reduces to a stochastic forward simulation of the robot's motion. Given observations, it jointly refines kinematic and dynamic states and infers external loads, among other states. We validate the approach through simulation and experiments, demonstrating stochastic forward simulation as well as state estimation on tendon-driven continuum robots.

AI.tldr: A dynamic-state-estimation framework for tendon-driven continuum robots that embeds Cosserat rod dynamics into a factor-graph; inertia/damping treated as equivalent loads to preserve static-like balance; enables stochastic forward simulation and joint state/external-load estimation, validated in simulation and experiments.
AI.motivation: Current factor-graph approaches work well in quasi-static settings but fail to capture inertial dynamics, limiting accuracy during dynamic motions.
AI.method: Approximate Cosserat rod dynamics; treat inertia and damping as equivalent applied loads so the dynamic balance retains the algebraic form of the static case; without backbone observations it reduces to stochastic forward simulation; with observations, jointly refines kinematic and dynamic states and infers external loads.
AI.result: Validation through simulation and experiments; demonstrates stochastic forward simulation as well as state estimation on tendon-driven continuum robots.
AI.conclusion: Extends continuum-robot state estimation to dynamic regimes by integrating Cosserat-rod dynamics into a probabilistic forward-model, enabling external-load inference and improved accuracy over quasi-static methods.

title: When EOS Tokens Disagree: Understanding Length Inflation in On-Policy Distillation
comment: 30 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables, code available at https://github.com/UNCSciML/opd-eos
summary: We study length inflation in on-policy distillation (OPD), where student responses can become excessively long and even exhaust the generation budget. We identify \emph{termination-token mismatch} between base students and post-trained teachers as an important source of this behavior. Across Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma, the two models can place their stopping probability on different EOS tokens, even when their declared stopping sets are identical. This mismatch can suppress the student's preferred termination action without reliably transferring the teacher-preferred alternative. We show that aligning the decoding stopping set alone is insufficient, while treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action substantially mitigates mismatch-induced length inflation across all three model families. To further understand how termination behavior evolves over training, we study OPD across different K2-Horizon training stages. This stage-wise analysis shows that termination preferences can shift substantially during training, while also revealing a distinct length inflation late in the OPD run that persists beyond termination alignment. Together, these results identify termination mismatch as an important, but not exhaustive, source of OPD length dynamics. We release an implementation incorporating the proposed termination-handling corrections.

AI.tldr: Termination-token mismatch between base students and post-trained teachers causes length inflation in on-policy distillation (OPD); aligning functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action mitigates the issue across Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma; a stage-wise (K2-Horizon) analysis reveals dynamic shifts in termination preferences; an implementation with termination-handling corrections is released.
AI.motivation: OPD can yield excessively long generations due to misaligned termination signals. Understanding and mitigating termination-related dynamics is essential for efficient, reliable distillation across diverse model families.
AI.method: Empirical analysis across three model families (Qwen3, Llama, Gemma). Examine how EOS/termination tokens are used, identify termination-token mismatch as a source of length inflation, and propose treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action. Conduct stage-wise analysis of OPD across K2-Horizon training stages to observe how termination preferences evolve. Provide an implementation of the proposed termination-handling corrections.
AI.result: Found that simply aligning stopping token sets is insufficient; sharing functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a single semantic stop action substantially reduces length inflation across all three model families. Stage-wise analysis shows termination preferences can shift during training and that a late-stage length inflation persists beyond basic termination alignment. The approach generalizes across multiple architectures and is accompanied by a released implementation.
AI.conclusion: Termination mismatch is an important but non-exhaustive driver of OPD length dynamics. Semantic alignment of EOS tokens is an effective mitigation strategy, though other factors can contribute to length inflation. The work provides a practical correction and resources for replication.

title: Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing
summary: Professional design requires any-color control: the ability to specify an object's target color with any 24-bit hex value for image generation and editing. Prior work has explored color generation, editing, and colorization, but often relies on dedicated color representations or specialized inference procedures. Advances in large language models offer a simpler starting point: even compact models can associate hex values with color semantics. We present Paint-Anything, which learns a shared hex-prompt interface for generation and editing through object-level color supervision. We develop a data pipeline that constructs Paint-500K from real images through object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis. Since shadows make real-image labels only approximate colors, we complement this supervision with pure-color anchors whose pixels exactly match their paired hex values. These anchors are used only at high-noise timesteps, leaving low-noise training to natural images. We further introduce Any Color Benchmark (ACBench), comprising ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit, to measure object-level hex color fidelity across both tasks. On FLUX.2-4B, Paint-Anything improves ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit scores by 85.3% and 28.3%, respectively, relative to the base model, with ablations supporting the training recipe. It also achieves the highest average CompColor score among the compared methods.

AI.tldr: Paint-Anything introduces a hex-color prompting interface to enable object-level any-color control for generation and editing. It constructs a 500k-image dataset (Paint-500K) using object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis, supplemented by pure-color anchors at high-noise timesteps. A new ACBench benchmark (ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit) measures hex color fidelity. On FLUX.2-4B it achieves large gains (≈85% T2I, 28% Edit) and the best CompColor score among peers.
AI.motivation: Provide precise, object-level hex color control in generation/editing without relying on specialized color representations or inference schemes, leveraging the semantic-color associations learned by even compact language-model-backed systems and addressing labeling noise via anchor supervision.
AI.method: Train a diffusion-based model with a shared hex-prompt interface, construct Paint-500K via object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis; introduce pure-color anchors matching exact hex values to be used only at high-noise timesteps to stabilize training; propose ACBench to evaluate hex-color fidelity on both T2I and editing tasks.
AI.result: Quantitative gains on FLUX.2-4B: +85.3% (ACBench-T2I) and +28.3% (ACBench-Edit) over the base model; highest average CompColor score among compared methods, indicating strong object-level hex color fidelity across generation and editing tasks.
AI.conclusion: A simple hex-prompt interface combined with anchor-based supervision enables effective object-level hex color control in generation and editing, with a large-scale dataset and a dedicated benchmark supporting robust evaluation and surpassing existing methods in color fidelity.

title: INSPECT: Learning Robot View Selection from Assistant Use
summary: Robots inspecting an assembly must determine which parts are present and whether they are correctly installed. During egocentric assembly assistance, head motion and workpiece handling reveal evidence for these checks, while spoken state confirmations link observations to procedural outcomes. We introduce INSPECT, which learns robot view preferences from records of a smart-glasses assistant that answers part queries and provides next-step guidance. Presence-Invariant TwinSwap (PI-TwinSwap) calibrates object evidence through paired identity interventions. Claim-indexed supervision separates evidence requirements from camera-reproducible observation changes. Object-centered calibration adapts relative view preferences to robot poses, while clause-level screening checks predicted evidence. The robot selects views using only its current observation and known poses, without candidate images. Evaluation uses annotated assistant-video replay to simulate state feedback, without target-domain view labels for policy training. On images of physical gearbox assemblies, INSPECT achieves the highest view utility among the compared non-oracle policies and raises human-rated full verifiability from 34.8% to 41.7% compared with keeping the current view. On commercial angle-grinder recordings in IMPACT, the transferred relative-view selector increases the correct decision rate from 50.6% to 54.3% with a frozen perception head. The source code is available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/INSPECT.

AI.tldr: INSPECT learns view preferences for robotic assembly inspection from smart-glasses assistant data, enabling efficient view selection; introduces Presence-Invariant TwinSwap (PI-TwinSwap), claim-indexed supervision, object-centered calibration, and clause-level screening; demonstrates improved verifiability and decision accuracy on gearbox assemblies and IMPACT data; code released.
AI.motivation: In egocentric assembly, robots must determine part presence and correct installation, but evidence is view- and pose-dependent. The task requires a view policy that uses only current observations and known poses, without relying on target-domain views or oracle labels.
AI.method: Propose INSPECT with multiple components: Presence-Invariant TwinSwap calibrates evidence under paired interventions; Claim-indexed supervision separates evidence requirements from camera-induced observation changes; Object-centered calibration links relative view preferences to robot poses; Clause-level screening checks predicted evidence; View selection relies solely on the robot’s current observation and known poses, with no candidate images; Evaluation uses annotated assistant-video replay to simulate state feedback without target-domain view labels; cross-domain transfer evaluated on gearbox assemblies and IMPACT data; code provided at repository.
AI.result: On gearbox assemblies, INSPECT achieves the highest view utility among non-oracle policies and improves human-rated verifiability from 34.8% to 41.7% over keeping the current view. On IMPACT recordings, the transferred relative-view selector increases correct decision rate from 50.6% to 54.3% with a frozen perception head.
AI.conclusion: INSPECT delivers a transferable, evidence-aware view planning framework for assembly inspection, improving verifiability and decision accuracy under limited supervision and across domains; code is publicly available.

title: Parallelism, critical windows, and separations among diffusion language models
summary:
A popular selling point of diffusion large language models (dLLMs) is their capacity for parallelism: the ability to generate sequences of text far more efficiently than autoregressive models, which require one forward pass per token. Yet among the many competing paradigms for dLLMs, from masked to uniform to Gaussian diffusion, principled understanding of how these different proposals compare in parallelism remains limited. In this work, we initiate a fine-grained comparison of the capacity for parallelism among these three leading approaches and prove the following:
  - Uniform and Gaussian diffusion can sample in a number of forward passes which scales with the dual total correlation of the underlying distribution, a measure of intrinsic complexity which can be much smaller than the context length. Previously, it was only known how to achieve this using masked diffusion.
  - For a certain family of random empirical measures, we show that $\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{d})$ forward passes are necessary and sufficient to sample using uniform or Gaussian diffusion, yet there exist approximate score oracles for which $\widetildeΩ(d)$ forward passes are needed for masked diffusion. This establishes the first provable separation in parallelism between the three prevailing dLLM paradigms.
  Contrary to popular intuition that masked diffusions are harder to parallelize because they must commit to token values, the latter separation instead comes from the fact that the critical windows in masked diffusion sampling are asymptotically narrower than those in uniform and Gaussian diffusion sampling.

AI.tldr: The abstract provides a theoretical comparison of diffusion-based LLMs' parallel sampling across masked, uniform, and Gaussian diffusion, establishing a first provable separation in required forward passes and linking parallelism to intrinsic complexity measures and sampling windows.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify how different diffusion paradigms affect parallel sampling efficiency in dLLMs, beyond heuristic assumptions.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis leveraging dual total correlation to characterize intrinsic complexity; analyzes sampling complexity under three diffusion schemes; derives asymptotic forward-pass counts; uses random empirical measure models to illustrate worst-case and average behavior.
AI.result:
- Uniform and Gaussian diffusion can sample in a number of forward passes that scales with the dual total correlation of the underlying distribution, potentially much smaller than the context length, extending prior results which only showed this for masked diffusion. 
- For a certain family of random empirical measures, tilde Θ(sqrt(d)) forward passes are necessary and sufficient to sample with uniform or Gaussian diffusion; yet there exist approximate score oracles for which tilde Ω(d) forward passes are needed for masked diffusion. This yields the first provable separation in parallelism among masked, uniform, and Gaussian diffusion. 
- Contrary to the intuition that masked diffusion is harder to parallelize due to committing to token values, the separation arises because the critical sampling windows in masked diffusion become asymptotically narrower than those in uniform and Gaussian diffusion.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a principled separation in sampling parallelism among the three diffusion paradigms, linking efficiency to intrinsic complexity (dual total correlation) and the width of sampling windows, and resolves a common intuition by showing that masked diffusion’s narrower sampling windows drive the observed parallelism gap.

title: FAMOS: Feed-Forward 3D Articulation Modeling from Sparse Observations
summary: Modeling articulated objects from sparse monocular views is challenging because each observation reveals only partial geometry and motion evidence. Most feed-forward methods infer articulation from a single observation and therefore rely heavily on learned category-level shape priors. We present FAMOS, a feed-forward model that predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds. Our model jointly reasons over multiple observations and naturally supports a variable number of inputs, including a single view. To aggregate articulation cues across observations, we introduce a Multi-state Articulation Transformer with alternating state-wise and global attention. We further propose an observed articulation span objective that supervises the motion range each part exhibits across the input observations, encouraging the model to leverage the full observation set. To overcome the limited scale and diversity of existing datasets, we introduce a procedural data generator that synthesizes self-annotated assets during training. Experiments on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K demonstrate consistent improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based baselines. Project page: https://kevinqu7.github.io/famos

AI.tldr: FAMOS enables articulated-object modeling from sparse monocular views by predicting movable-part segmentation and joint parameters with a Multi-state Articulation Transformer, an articulation-span supervision, and a procedural data generator; it outperforms prior feed-forward and optimization-based baselines on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Articulated object reasoning from sparse, unordered observations is challenging due to partial geometry and motion evidence, and existing methods rely on category-level shape priors. A model that jointly aggregates multiple views, handles variable input, and scales to diverse data is needed.
AI.method: FAMOS is a feed-forward model that takes a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds to predict movable-part segmentation and joint parameters. It uses a Multi-state Articulation Transformer with alternating state-wise and global attention to aggregate cues across observations and supports a variable number of inputs, including a single view. An observed articulation span objective supervises the motion range per part across inputs. A procedural data generator creates self-annotated training data to boost scale and diversity.
AI.result: Experiments on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K show consistent improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables robust articulation understanding from sparse views, leveraging multi-observation aggregation and articulation-span supervision, and benefits from synthetic data generation to improve generalization across benchmarks.

title: A Simulation Platform for AUV Fault Recovery: Exploring LLM-Based Diagnostic Strategies
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE/OES Autonomous Underwater Vehicles Symposium (AUV 2026), Southampton, UK. This is the author-accepted manuscript
summary: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) operating beyond reliable communications must recover from failures without human intervention. We investigate an architecture in which conventional deterministic layered control autonomy manages normal operations, while an invokable large language model (LLM) serves as a diagnostic and recovery planner when onboard anomaly detection identifies performance outside expected limits. Because language models are stochastic, rigorous evaluation requires ensemble testing rather than individual demonstrations. We present a closed-loop simulation architecture that couples real-time C vehicle software with a higher-level orchestration layer for physics-based fault injection, structured prompting, language-model interaction, mission file generation, validation, execution, and LLM-judge scoring. The framework, which we call SPAR (Simulation Platform for AUV Recovery), supports evaluation across fault realizations, prompt structures, reasoning models, and mission conditions. We vary these for a mass-shift fault over 480 SPAR trials, evaluating a frontier model and three off-the-shelf locally deployable LLMs. Model choice dominates diagnosis: the frontier model places the CG-shift mechanism in its top three hypotheses in 85-90% of trials, versus 60-78% for the best local model. Reasoning analysis indicates that local-model success is associated with following the complete diagnostic procedure, whereas weaker models often commit prematurely to elevator failure even though the actuator tracks its command. Diagnosis and operational decision performance do not appear to be coupled in this dataset. The contributions are an architecture extending unanticipated-fault recovery from detection to mitigation and an ensemble methodology for evaluating LLM-assisted mission management on low-power AUVs.

AI.tldr: SPAR is a simulation platform that integrates deterministic AUV control with an invokable LLM for diagnostics and recovery planning, enabling ensemble evaluation of LLM-assisted fault management under variable prompts, models, and mission conditions.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AUVs operating with intermittent communications require robust, automated detection, diagnosis, and mitigation of anomalies. LLMs offer reasoning and planning capabilities, but their stochastic nature demands ensemble testing to compare models, prompts, and strategies on resource-constrained platforms.
AI.method: Developed SPAR (Simulation Platform for AUV Recovery) architecture that couples real-time C vehicle software with a higher-level orchestrator for physics-based fault injection, structured prompting, LLM interaction, mission file generation, validation, execution, and LLM-judge scoring. The framework enables evaluation across fault realizations, prompt structures, reasoning models, and mission conditions. The study evaluates a mass-shift fault over 480 SPAR trials, comparing a frontier LLM model against three off-the-shelf local LLMs.
AI.result: Frontier model places the CG-shift mechanism in its top three hypotheses in 85–90% of trials, while best local models achieve 60–78%. Local-model success correlates with following the complete diagnostic procedure; weaker models often prematurely commit to elevator failure despite command-tracking actuator behavior. Diagnosis and operational decision performance appear uncoupled in the dataset.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes an architecture that extends unanticipated-fault recovery from detection to mitigation and presents an ensemble methodology for evaluating LLM-assisted mission management on low-power AUVs.

title: Mitigating Retaliatory Algorithmic Collusion in Repeated Games
summary: Reinforcement learning agents trained to maximize their own reward in repeated interactions can converge to supra-competitive outcomes resembling explicit collusion, without communication or shared design. Existing mitigation approaches are largely tied to specific economic settings, like two-sided platforms and auctions, leaving open how to design interventions for general repeated games. We address this gap by formalizing the connection between empirical observations from prior work on Q-learning collusion and classical theory of Simple Penal Codes (SPCs). We show any non-trivial SPC induces a quantifiable conditional dependence in agents' policies, detectable via the total variation distance between an agent's action distributions across cooperation and defection histories. Building on this connection, we propose CURB (Collusion Unwinding via Reward shaping and Belief injection), a reward-shaping framework that penalizes this Total Variation (TV) distance signal during Q-learning and is guaranteed to convert any SPC fixed point of the dynamics into a trivial one, thus precluding collusive equilibria sustained by punishment threats. Empirically, CURB substantially reduces collusion by Q-learning agents in both Bertrand and Cournot Competition Repeated Games. We further demonstrate that CURB extends to deep Q-network agents in Bertrand competition, suggesting the mechanism generalizes beyond tabular Q-learning.

AI.tldr: CURB is a reward-shaping framework that penalizes SPC-induced policy dependence across cooperation/defection histories (via TV distance) to unwind collusion in repeated games, converting nontrivial SPC fixed points to trivial ones; it reduces collusion for Q-learning and extends to deep Q-networks in Bertrand competition.
AI.motivation: Prevent collusion emergent from RL agents in repeated strategic settings by providing a general intervention not tied to a specific economic environment, linking empirical Q-learning collusion to classical SPC theory.
AI.method: Formalize the link between SPCs and conditional dependence in agents' policies measured by total variation distance between action distributions under cooperation vs. defection. Implement CURB by reward shaping that penalizes this TV-distance signal during Q-learning, with a theoretical guarantee that nontrivial SPC fixed points are converted to trivial ones. Validate empirically in Bertrand and Cournot repeated games with tabular Q-learning and demonstrate extension to deep Q-networks.
AI.result: CURB substantially reduces collusion in Q-learning agents across Bertrand and Cournot repeated games; the mechanism generalizes to deep Q-networks in Bertrand competition, indicating robustness beyond tabular Q-learning.
AI.conclusion: CURB provides a general, theoretically grounded intervention to curb emergent collusion in repeated games by shaping rewards based on policy dependence signals, offering a path toward mitigating collusion in a broad class of learning agents and settings; future work could explore broader game classes and scalability to larger action spaces.

title: SplashSplat: Reconstructing Splashing Liquids from Real-World Multi-View Videos
comment: 18 pages (11 main + 7 supplementary), 14 figures, 12 tables. Project page: https://niko-creater.github.io/splashsplat-web/
summary: A splash lives for a fraction of a second: sheets tear into ligaments and droplets, appearance is view-dependent and nearly textureless, and little persists long enough to track. Reconstruction research has consequently focused on smoke, synthetic liquids, or gently deforming surfaces. To our knowledge, no synchronized multi-view dataset of splashing liquids exists. We therefore introduce a benchmark of 20 real scenes, from coherent streams to violent splashes, captured by seven synchronized, calibrated 4K cameras at 60 fps, with manually refined per-view liquid and container masks and fixed evaluation splits. We further present SplashSplat, built on a single principle: impose physical structure only where the observations can constrain it. Per-frame liquid SDFs fused from the masks provide the geometry, level-set transport between consecutive SDFs yields a coarse velocity field, and Lagrangian carriers advected along this flow, corrected against each new observation and reseeded where coverage is lost, decode local Gaussians for differentiable rendering. SplashSplat outperforms state-of-the-art dynamic Gaussian splatting methods on our real captures and on a synthetic benchmark, with physically more plausible motion and a lower training cost. The same representation supports temporal interpolation and style transfer without re-optimization.

AI.tldr: SplashSplat introduces a synchronized 7-view 4K 60fps real-splash dataset and a physics-informed, differentiable representation for splashes that fuses per-frame liquid SDFs, level-set transport, and Lagrangian carriers with Gaussian splatting.
AI.motivation: Reconstruction of splashing liquids is challenging due to ultra-short lifetimes, view-dependent appearance, and lack of saturated real datasets; existing methods rely on smoke, synthetic liquids, or gently deforming surfaces. A real, multi-view benchmark is needed to enable physically grounded reconstruction.
AI.method: A data-driven framework (SplashSplat) that imposes physical structure only where observations constrain it. It reconstructs per-frame liquid SDFs from masks, propagates a coarse velocity via level-set transport between consecutive SDFs, uses Lagrangian carriers advected by this flow (corrected with new observations and reseeded to maintain coverage), and decodes local Gaussians for differentiable rendering. It also provides a 20-scene benchmark with manual per-view masks and fixed splits.
AI.result: SplashSplat outperforms state-of-the-art dynamic Gaussian splatting on both real captures and a synthetic benchmark, producing more physically plausible motion at lower training cost. The representation supports temporal interpolation and style transfer without re-optimization.
AI.conclusion: A physically structured, observation-constrained representation enables robust, efficient reconstruction and rendering of splashes, with benefits in motion plausibility, cost, and capabilities such as interpolation and style transfer.

title: SmellDiffusion: Diffusion-Based Quadruped Navigation with Olfactory Scene Graphs
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables, submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
summary: A robot sent to a named gas leak must preserve gas identity, estimate the source, and navigate to the resulting goal. We present SmellDiffusion, a simulation pipeline that represents species-specific gas zones in an open-vocabulary olfactory scene graph and shares the selected goal between classical and diffusion planners. Its key components are a peak-local geometric gate for selective source correction and diffusion-based, gas-guided trajectory generation. Among 424 unique source-wind configurations in solved flow, 28 have a concentration peak displaced more than 0.5m from the source. A source-independent geometric gate, calibrated only on the training split and evaluated at the observed peak, detects 9 of 10 held-out displacements at 0.64 precision. Gating a precomputed forward-matching correction reduces mean error on the displaced cases from 1.468m to 0.592m (60%), using matching for only 14/204 cases. All-case mean error falls from 0.205m to 0.180m. All planners receive the same scene-graph source estimate as their goal. In a controlled comparison, best-of-ten diffusion achieves mean gas exposure comparable to gas-guided A* (0.0476 versus 0.0455). A single diffusion proposal takes 41.7ms, compared with 72.3ms for gas-guided A*, although best-of-ten sequential sampling increases total runtime. Plain A* also reaches the same goal and remains the fastest and shortest-path method. Six matched Gazebo runs give mean robot-to-source errors of 0.39m for A* and 0.31m for diffusion.

AI.tldr: SmellDiffusion combines diffusion-based planning with a geometric gate to localize gas sources and navigate to goals in a shared scene graph; achieves competitive exposure to A*, with improved source localization and faster proposals.
AI.motivation: Gas leak response requires preserving gas identity, estimating the source, and reaching the resulting goal under diffusion-affected flows. The challenge is robust planning across diverse source-wind configurations and peak misplacements, which existing planners struggle to handle.
AI.method: An open-vocabulary olfactory scene graph is used, with a shared goal between classical and diffusion planners. Key components include a peak-local geometric gate for selective source correction and diffusion-based, gas-guided trajectory generation. A source-independent geometric gate is calibrated on the training split and evaluated on observed peaks. Gating a forward-matching correction reduces errors. The approach compares best-of-ten diffusion proposals against gas-guided A* and plain A*, with Gazebo validation.
AI.result: Among 424 unique source-wind configurations, 28 exhibit a concentration peak displaced >0.5 m from the source. The gate detects 9 of 10 held-out displacements at 0.64 precision. Gate-based forward-matching reduces mean error for displaced cases from 1.468 m to 0.592 m (60% reduction), using matching for only 14/204 cases. All-case mean error drops from 0.205 m to 0.180 m. In controlled comparisons, best-of-ten diffusion yields mean gas exposure comparable to gas-guided A* (0.0476 vs 0.0455). A single diffusion proposal takes 41.7 ms, faster than gas-guided A* at 72.3 ms, though best-of-ten sequential sampling increases total runtime. Plain A* is fastest. In six matched Gazebo runs, robot-to-source error is 0.39 m for A* and 0.31 m for diffusion.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-guided planning with the proposed gating and shared goals achieves performance on par with or better than gas-guided A*, offering accuracy improvements and faster per-proposal times, while maintaining robust source localization in olfactory navigation.

title: CrystalMO-TuRBO: Multi-Objective Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for High-precision Joint Crystal Structure Refinement
summary: Crystal structure refinement is a fundamental inverse problem in materials characterization, where structural parameters are optimized to reproduce experimental diffraction data. Conventional approaches, such as least-squares and likelihood-based optimization, rely on local search and often struggle with non-convex, noisy, and highly correlated parameter landscapes, particularly when integrating multiple diffraction modalities. Joint refinement of X-ray and neutron data is especially challenging due to their complementary but competing sensitivities, which are typically combined through scalarized objectives requiring manual weighting and leading to suboptimal solutions. We propose CrystalMO-TuRBO, a multi-objective trust region Bayesian optimization architecture for joint crystal structure refinement. The method models X-ray and neutron discrepancies as separate objectives and transforms the problem into a normalized maximization setting. A two-phase optimization strategy is introduced: Phase 1 performs global exploration using parallel trust-region Bayesian optimization across multiple scalarizations to identify promising regions of the parameter space, while Phase 2 conducts localized refinement within a shrinking region to achieve high-precision solutions. This design explicitly separates global search from fine-grained optimization, addressing the unique accuracy requirements of refinement tasks. We evaluate the proposed method on experimentally collected X-ray and neutron diffraction data from single-crystal Ho2Ti2O7. Results demonstrate improved convergence, robustness, and parameter precision compared to classical refinement methods and Bayesian optimization baselines on refinement of a single-crystal pyrochlore material system.

AI.tldr: A multi-objective trust-region Bayesian optimization framework (CrystalMO-TuRBO) for joint X-ray and neutron crystal structure refinement, featuring Phase 1 global exploration across multiple scalarizations and Phase 2 local refinement within a shrinking trust region; demonstrates improved convergence and parameter precision over classical and Bayesian baselines, validated on Ho2Ti2O7 single-crystal data.
AI.motivation: Joint refinement of X-ray and neutron data is challenging due to non-convex, noisy, and highly correlated parameter landscapes, with complementary yet competing sensitivities. Scalarized objectives require manual weighting and can yield suboptimal solutions; there is a need to separate global search from precise local refinement for refinement tasks.
AI.method: A multi-objective trust-region Bayesian optimization framework that models X-ray and neutron discrepancies as separate objectives and normalizes them for maximization. Phase 1 runs parallel TBBO across multiple scalarizations for global exploration; Phase 2 performs localized refinement within a shrinking trust region to achieve high-precision solutions.
AI.result: Empirically, CrystalMO-TuRBO improves convergence, robustness, and parameter precision compared to classical refinement methods and Bayesian optimization baselines in refining a single-crystal pyrochlore system, demonstrated on experimentally collected X-ray and neutron data from Ho2Ti2O7.
AI.conclusion: The two-phase design explicitly separates global search from fine-grained optimization, addressing the accuracy demands of refinement tasks and improving performance in joint X-ray–neutron crystal structure refinement.

title: Can 4D Foundation Models Remember?
summary: Perceiving and remembering the visual world is fundamental to navigating and interacting with our environment. Current 4D foundation models, such as camera-controllable video models or 4D reconstruction models, can perceive and reconstruct dynamic environments, but how well they remember what they have perceived remains an open question. Existing benchmarks largely rely on pixel-level metrics and lack ground truth for objects once they leave the field of view, making them unable to evaluate visual memory in an object-centric manner against references. To fill this gap, we introduce PersistBench, a dataset and metric suite that leverages 360° videos as omniscient ground truth and proposes three evaluation aspects: object permanence, motion continuity, and appearance preservation. Evaluating various models across diverse categories reveals that current models can only maintain short-term consistency that degrades significantly once objects leave the field of view. Our findings highlight the gap between current model capabilities and robust visual memory ("seeing is not remembering"), providing guidance for future development of 4D foundation models. Dataset and code are available on the project page: https://guangzhaohe.com/persistbench.

AI.tldr: PersistBench introduces a dataset and metric suite to benchmark visual memory of 4D foundation models using 360° omniscient ground truth, focusing on object permanence, motion continuity, and appearance preservation. It reveals current models retain only short-term consistency, with memory degrading when objects exit the field of view.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks emphasize pixel-level similarity but lack ground-truth, object-centric memory evaluation, especially for objects after they disappear from view. There is a need to assess true visual memory in 4D perception systems.
AI.method: Construct PersistBench from 360° video data to provide omniscient ground truth. Propose three evaluation axes—object permanence (whether objects can be tracked when occluded or out of view), motion continuity (temporal consistency of trajectories), and appearance preservation (consistency of object appearance across views/frames). Define corresponding metrics and protocols to benchmark 4D models.
AI.result: Evaluations across diverse categories show models retain only short-term consistency; memory quality significantly degrades once objects leave the field of view.
AI.conclusion: There is a notable gap between perception and robust visual memory in current 4D foundation models. PersistBench offers a benchmark and guidance for progress toward models capable of longer-term object-centric memory.

title: RTK-Vision PPO for Autonomous Micro UAV Recovery on an Airborne Carrier
summary: Autonomous recovery of a micro unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) onto a moving airborne carrier enables reusable deploy-mission-recover operation, but couples long-range rendezvous, close-range perception, carrier motion, aerodynamic interaction, and a discontinuous contact event. This paper presents an RTK-vision-guided reinforcement-learning framework in which a child UAV is physically transported by a larger carrier, takes off from the carrier while airborne, executes an independent sortie, returns to the carrier's current position, redocks, and subsequently descends with the carrier. Both vehicles carry RTK-GNSS, and the carrier continuously shares its navigation state with the child. Near the recovery deck, RTK remains active while a downward-facing camera with a fiducial marker detector provides marker-relative alignment cues. A proximal policy optimization (PPO) policy governing the terminal recovery phase is trained in a physics-based MuJoCo simulation environment with explicit sensor noise models, an aerodynamic disturbance surrogate, and marker-latency randomization, then transferred to hardware. PX4 retains low-level stabilization, and a deterministic safety gate authorizes descent independently of the learned policy. The PPO checkpoint achieves 99.55% success over 2,000 held-out randomized terminal episodes, compared with 78.4% for a tuned PD baseline under identical conditions, with a median planar terminal error of 6.62 cm. Across 14 outdoor trials, the full mission succeeds in 13 trials (92.9%), spanning both near-region recovery and recovery after the carrier translates away from the release point. The results demonstrate a complete autonomous aerial deployment-and-recovery cycle rather than an isolated landing maneuver, establishing a practical basis for reusable carrier-child operation in inspection, surveillance, and mobile-logistics applications.

AI.tldr: RTK-vision-guided reinforcement-learning framework enabling autonomous recovery of a micro-UAV from a moving airborne carrier, using PPO in MuJoCo with sensor disturbances; achieves high sim-to-real performance and a complete deploy–mission–recover cycle.
AI.motivation: Enable reusable carrier–child operation by solving the coupled problem of long-range rendezvous, close-range perception, carrier motion, aerodynamic interaction, and contact dynamics within a single autonomous pipeline.
AI.method: RTK-GNSS state sharing between carrier and child; downward-facing camera with fiducial marker detector for marker-relative alignment; a PPO policy trained in a physics-based MuJoCo simulation with explicit sensor noise, aerodynamic disturbance surrogate, and marker-latency randomization; policy transferred to hardware with PX4 handling low-level stabilization and a safety gate governing the descent; real-world deployment using marker cues and continuous navigation state sharing.
AI.result: Simulation: PPO checkpoint achieves 99.55% success over 2,000 randomized terminal episodes, vs 78.4% for a tuned PD baseline; median planar terminal error of 6.62 cm. Outdoor trials: 13/14 successes (92.9%), spanning near-region recovery and post-carrier translation recovery.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a complete autonomous aerial deployment–recovery cycle for carrier–child operation, providing a practical basis for reusable carrier-based missions in inspection, surveillance, and mobile logistics.

title: Recursive Quantum Long Short-Term Memory for Stable Short-Horizon Temperature Forecasting
summary: Quantum long short-term memory (QLSTM) models extend recurrent sequence learning with variational quantum circuits, but their optimization behavior can vary substantially across random initializations and temporal contexts. This paper evaluates a recursive QLSTM architecture against a standard QLSTM for one-step-ahead prediction of daily minimum and maximum temperature. Using daily weather observations from Toronto and identical training settings, we compare convergence, predictive accuracy, and generalization across input windows of 8, 16, and 32 days over 20 random seeds. The recursive model consistently reaches a near-optimal test loss earlier, reduces mean absolute error and root mean squared error, and exhibits a smaller generalization gap. These results indicate that recursive quantum feature transformations can improve stability and out-of-sample performance for compact hybrid quantum--classical temporal models.

AI.tldr: Recursive QLSTM improves convergence, accuracy, and generalization for weather forecasting tasks compared to standard QLSTM.
AI.motivation: Address optimization variability and stability in quantum recurrent models due to random initialization and temporal context; assess whether recursion in quantum feature transformations benefits compact hybrid quantum-classical temporal models.
AI.method: Empirically compare recursive QLSTM against standard QLSTM on one-step-ahead daily min/max temperature prediction using Toronto data, identical training settings, input windows of 8,16,32 days, across 20 random seeds; evaluate convergence (test loss), MAE, RMSE, and generalization gap.
AI.result: Recursive model reaches near-optimal test loss earlier, reduces MAE and RMSE, and shows smaller generalization gap across window sizes and seeds.
AI.conclusion: Recursive quantum feature transformations can enhance stability and out-of-sample performance in compact hybrid quantum–classical temporal models.

title: TraceFlow: Guiding Frozen Flow-Matching Robot Policies with Success and Failure Traces
summary: A vision-language-action (VLA) policy with a flow-matching action expert generates each action chunk (a short command sequence) by integrating a learned velocity field; once its weights are fixed, the success or failure of an earlier rollout cannot change the chunk generated now. Concurrent test-time methods give a frozen policy such an input from retrieved successes, a learned critic, a verifier, or a dynamics model, but none uses the robot's own failed rollouts as negative evidence with nothing but a terminal outcome bit. We introduce TraceFlow, a progress-aligned guidance field that turns the action densities of retrieved successful and failed rollouts into a bounded correction to a frozen flow-matching action expert, using one terminal outcome bit per rollout and no other label. Its TraceBank stores traces, time-ordered state-action records with a terminal label, starts from the target-task training traces, and later admits the deployed robot's own rollouts. On an ordered real-robot packing task the base completes 21 of 50 trials in order, TraceFlow 39, and one stacking round without any weight update 47, with wrong-sequence episodes falling from 20 to 0. In simulation the gain is selective: with per-suite selected settings, TraceFlow raises RoboMemArena Sequence from 78.92\% to 91.50\% task success and Transferring from 54.41\% to 62.00\% at stacking round 2, leaves the 26-task aggregate unchanged, lowers Counting and Occlusion by 1.12 and 1.42 points, and changes LIBERO-Plus (Long) by +1.27 points (p = 0.0733).
