Stacking gains are finite, every branch peaking before round ten, and the bank's success-to-failure ratio predicts no retrieval allocation.

AI.tldr: TraceFlow introduces a progress-aligned guidance field that converts retrieved success and failure traces into a bounded correction for a frozen flow-matching action expert. It stores time-ordered traces with terminal labels in a TraceBank, starting from training traces and incorporating deployed rollouts, yielding substantial gains in real-robot packing and selective simulation tasks, with finite stacking improvements.
AI.motivation: To exploit the robot's own failed rollouts as negative evidence using only a terminal outcome bit, bypassing reliance on external critics, verifiers, or learned dynamics models, and to improve policy guidance without online weight updates.
AI.method: Propose TraceFlow, a guidance field that morphs action densities from retrieved rollouts into a bounded correction to a frozen flow-matching action policy. TraceBank stores time-ordered state–action traces with a terminal label, initialized from target-task training traces and later expanded to include deployed rollouts. The approach uses only the terminal outcome bit per rollout to steer policy corrections without adjusting the base weights.
AI.result: Real-robot packing: base 21/50; TraceFlow 39/50; one weight-free stacking round 47; wrong-sequence episodes reduced from 20 to 0. Simulation (per-suite settings): RoboMemArena Sequence 78.92%→91.50%; Transferring 54.41%→62.00% at stacking round 2; 26-task aggregate unchanged; Counting and Occlusion down 1.12 and 1.42; LIBERO-Plus Long +1.27 (p=0.0733). Stacking gains finite; TraceBank/TraceFlow predict no retrieval allocation.
AI.conclusion: TraceFlow demonstrates that a failure-derived, terminal-outcome-based correction to a frozen policy can yield substantial real-world gains and selective simulation improvements, with finite stacking benefits and no online weight updates during deployment.

title: COIN-GP: Cooperative Online Learning in Networked Distributed Systems with Partial Measurements via Gaussian Process Regression
summary: In this paper, we tackle the problem of jointly estimating the system states and partially unknown dynamics within distributed sensor-equipped networks, particularly in scenarios where only partial state observations are available. To address this issue, we propose an observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework incorporating online distributed Gaussian Process (GP) regression, which enables accurate estimation despite incomplete in measurements and deficient GP models. In addition, a novel data collection strategy is introduced, with theoretical conditions ensuring feasible data acquisition. Moreover, we also derive an error upper bound encompassing state estimation and model estimation, leveraging the deterministic error bounds of GPs. Empirical simulations demonstrate the superiority of our approach compared to existing distributed GP-based methods.

AI.tldr: Observer-based dynamic cooperative learning with online distributed GP regression for joint state and partially unknown dynamics estimation in partially observed distributed sensor networks; introduces a data collection strategy with feasibility conditions; derives an error bound; empirical results show improvement over existing distributed GP methods.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of jointly estimating system states and partially unknown dynamics in distributed sensor networks when only partial state observations are available, where traditional methods struggle due to incomplete measurements and uncertain GP models.
AI.method: An observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework that uses online distributed Gaussian Process (GP) regression. Includes a novel data collection strategy with theoretical feasibility conditions and derives an upper bound on the combined state and model estimation error by leveraging deterministic GP error bounds.
AI.result: Theoretical error bounds are established; data collection conditions are provided; simulations demonstrate superior performance relative to existing distributed GP-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework achieves improved estimation accuracy under partial observability and uncertain dynamics, with provable guarantees and a practical data collection strategy, though real-world validation and scalability considerations remain for future work.

title: SkipVLA: Skipping VLA Steps with Classical Planning for Fast Robot Manipulation
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are a class of generalist robot policies that map camera images and language instructions directly to robot actions. While promising, these models remain slow at test time, particularly for long-horizon tasks that require many queries to the policy. Recent efforts reduce VLA latency by distilling smaller models, overlapping asynchronous action chunks, or pairing the VLA with a fast low-level policy, but still run a learned policy for the entire task. In contrast to VLA, classical motion planners quickly find collision-free motions, but require an explicit goal and have no semantic understanding of the task. In this work, we present SkipVLA, a hybrid policy that combines a pretrained VLA with a classical motion planner, using the planner for free-space motion and querying the VLA only for contact-rich skills such as grasping and placing. SkipVLA reuses the frozen vision-language backbone of the VLA to predict a target pose for each planned motion, and learns this predictor without additional demonstrations introduced into the system by using what was already learnt by the large VLA. We evaluate SkipVLA with three VLAs on 13 LIBERO tasks in simulation and three pick-and-place tasks on a physical 6-DoF YAM arm, demonstrating up to 2.5x faster task completion and significantly lower energy consumption while achieving the same task success rate.

AI.tldr: SkipVLA is a hybrid policy that uses a classical motion planner for free-space motion and queries a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) backbone only for contact-rich skills, predicting target poses for planned motions. It aims to speed up long-horizon robotics tasks while preserving semantics.
AI.motivation: VLA policies enable semantic, language-guided control but are slow at test time, especially for long-horizon tasks. Classical planners are fast but lack semantic understanding and goal flexibility. A hybrid approach can combine speed with semantic capability.
AI.method: Integrate a pretrained VLA backbone with a classical motion planner. The planner handles free-space motion; the VLA predictor determines target poses for each planned motion to enable contact-rich actions (grasping/placing). The predictor is learned without extra demonstrations by leveraging the knowledge embedded in the large VLA. Evaluation spans three VLAs on 13 LIBERO tasks in simulation and three real-world pick-and-place tasks on a 6-DoF YAM arm.
AI.result: SkipVLA achieves up to 2.5x faster task completion and significantly lower energy consumption, with the same task success rate as baselines.
AI.conclusion: Hybridizing VLA with classical planning can dramatically accelerate task execution while maintaining performance. The approach demonstrates practical benefits and generalizes across multiple VLA backbones and tasks.

title: Multi-center Medical Data Mining with FL-Net - A One-stop Shop for Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning enables collaborative training without sharing patient-level data, but most studies remain simulations. Based on five requirements derived from the literature, we analyzed 14 FL frameworks and found that none fully satisfied these requirements. We present FL-Net, a novel federated clinical research framework to fulfill all requirements. It integrates modular data harmonization, data discovery, disclosure control, securely built versioned FL-Net-Tools and containerized federated workflow execution into a persistent network. It enables the re-use of harmonized data and workflows across studies. FL-Net's end-to-end capabilities were evaluated through harmonization, cross-study patient discovery across MIMIC and US-130, and reproducible, audited federated workflows with up to 50 concurrent clients. FL-Net is being developed within the dAIbetes and Microb-AI-ome EU projects and will cover over 800,000 patients across 10 hospitals in 9 countries covering longitudinal and single point in time data, FL-Net provides a practical foundation for interoperable, reproducible, and privacy-preserving multicenter clinical research.

AI.tldr: 14 FL frameworks evaluated against five requirements; none meet all; introduces FL-Net, modular, reusable clinical research framework for harmonization, data discovery, privacy/disclosure control, and containerized federated workflows; validated with MIMIC and US-130; supports up to 50 concurrent clients; aims to enable interoperable, reproducible multicenter research across >800k patients.
AI.motivation: Address gap between simulated FL studies and real-world clinical research needs; lack of frameworks meeting five key requirements for interoperability, privacy, and reproducibility.
AI.method: Compared 14 FL frameworks against five literature-derived requirements; designed and implemented FL-Net with modular data harmonization, data discovery, disclosure control, versioned FL-Net-Tools, and containerized workflow execution; evaluated via harmonization, cross-study patient discovery across MIMIC and US-130, and reproducible audited federated workflows with up to 50 clients; deployment within EU projects.
AI.result: No existing framework satisfied all five requirements; FL-Net fulfills all five; demonstrated end-to-end capabilities, data harmonization, cross-study discovery, reproducible workflows, and scalability to 50 clients; persistent network enabling reuse.
AI.conclusion: FL-Net offers a practical foundation for interoperable, reproducible, privacy-preserving multicenter clinical research; ongoing development in EU projects, covering 800k+ patients across 10 hospitals in 9 countries; will support longitudinal and cross-sectional data.

title: DexTouch-WM: Learning Action-Conditioned Tactile World Models from Human Touch for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
comment: Accept to IROS 2026 Workshop RoBoWoMo (Lightning Talk)
summary: Learning predictive models of contact-rich dexterous manipulation requires dense tactile interaction, but such data are costly to scale on real robots and remain tied to embodiment-specific sensors. We introduce DexTouch-WM, an action-conditioned world model that learns from scalable human touch to jointly predict future RGB observations and bilateral tactile dynamics. Our insight is that human and robot manipulation share transferable contact dynamics when their tactile observations and action spaces are made compatible. We deploy flexible piezoresistive arrays with a shared sensing layout on both human and dexterous robot hands, and retarget human motion into the robot action space so that human interaction can supervise the same dynamics model used for real-robot prediction. DexTouch-WM couples a pretrained video expert with a lightweight tactile expert using anatomy-aware tactile tokens and aligned action conditioning. In human-to-robot scaling experiments, we keep five hours of real-robot supervision fixed while increasing human interaction from 0 to 100 hours, and observe substantial improvements in held-out robot-domain visual, geometric, and contact prediction despite disjoint human and robot task sets. Beyond prediction, we evaluate the world models as surrogate environments for policy evaluation and as generators of synthetic trajectories for real-robot policy learning, showing that scalable human interaction provides a complementary data axis for learning dexterous robot world models.

AI.tldr: DexTouch-WM learns an action-conditioned world model from scalable human tactile data to predict future RGB observations and bilateral tactile dynamics, enabling improved robot contact prediction and policy evaluation with less real-robot data.
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on costly real-robot interaction for dexterous manipulation by leveraging transferable tactile dynamics from human demonstrations and scalable touchscreen data, addressing embodiment gaps between human and robot hands.
AI.method: Use flexible piezoresistive arrays with shared sensing layout on human and robot hands; retarget human motion into robot action space; couple a pretrained video model with a lightweight tactile model using anatomy-aware tactile tokens and aligned action conditioning; train with human-to-robot supervision while keeping a fixed amount of real-robot data.
AI.result: Demonstrates substantial improvements in held-out robot-domain visual, geometric, and contact prediction as human interaction scales from 0 to 100 hours while real-robot data remains fixed at 5 hours; shows the world model can serve as surrogate environments for policy evaluation and as generators of synthetic trajectories for real-robot policy learning.
AI.conclusion: Scalable human interaction provides a complementary data axis for learning dexterous robot world models, enabling better predictive performance and facilitating policy learning with limited real-robot data.

title: Epidemiological Causal Graph Identification: Challenges, Identifiability and Algorithms
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, accepted at the 60th Asilomar Conference on Signals, Systems, and Computers 2026
summary: Causal discovery from observational data is fundamental to statistics and machine learning, yet determining causal direction without interventions necessitates structural assumptions. Existing identifiability research primarily focuses on continuous variables under additive noise models, often neglecting mixed datasets containing ordinal scales, counts, and continuous measurements. This paper investigates causal discovery in Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) where nodes follow either an ordinal distribution (via an ordered logit model) or a regular one-parameter exponential family distribution. We prove that the edge direction between an ordinal and an exponential family node is distributionally identifiable for generic parameter values. Our findings generalize previous Ordinal-Poisson results to the broader exponential family. Computationally, we introduce a score-based exhaustive search and a masked continuous optimization framework using DAGMA for larger graphs. Numerical results validate the theory, recovering edge orientations within a Markov equivalence class that are unidentifiable under classical structural equation models.

AI.tldr: Identifiability of causal direction between ordinal (ordered logit) and one-parameter exponential-family nodes in DAGs; generalizes Ordinal-Poisson results to broader EF; introduces score-based exhaustive search and DAGMA, with empirical validation recovering edge orientation beyond SEM identifiability.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery on mixed data types (ordinal, counts, continuous) is hard; existing identifiability results mostly assume continuous variables with additive noise; need to establish direction identifiability for mixed data to enable reliable causal inference.
AI.method: Theoretically prove that the edge direction between an ordinal node and an exponential-family node is distributionally identifiable for generic parameter values. Generalizes to the broader one-parameter exponential family beyond Ordinal-Poisson. Propose computational approaches: (i) score-based exhaustive search, and (ii) masked continuous optimization framework called DAGMA for larger graphs.
AI.result: Proves distributional identifiability for the specified mixed-variable setting. Extends prior Ordinal-Poisson results to broader exponential families. Numerical experiments show recovery of edge orientations within a Markov equivalence class that are unidentifiable under classical SEMs.
AI.conclusion: Extends identifiability theory to mixed data types in DAGs, enabling reliable causal direction inference between ordinal and EF variables. Provides scalable algorithms (score-based search and DAGMA) and empirical validation, broadening applicability of causal discovery beyond continuous-variable SEM assumptions.

title: HIL-UMI: Bringing Human-in-the-Loop Post-Training of Vision-Language-Action Models to Universal Manipulation Interface
summary: Large-scale vision-language-action (VLA) models provide powerful priors for robot manipulation, yet adapting them to a specific deployment remains challenging. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on task-specific demonstrations provides a step toward deployment, but faces two persistent limitations: static data provide limited coverage of out-of-distribution states, and standard imitation objectives do not distinguish progressing behavior from less useful data. Interactive post-training can address these limitations, but typically requires repeated policy execution and human intervention on a physical robot. We introduce HIL-UMI, a policy-guided Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) framework for robot-free human-in-the-loop VLA post-training. During handheld UMI demonstrations, HIL-UMI queries the current policy on the same observation stream without executing its predictions. The Energy Score compares the human action trajectory with policy inference and triggers collection when their discrepancy indicates an out-of-distribution region. In a separate feedback loop, low online advantage predictions identify essential segments for refining a progress-based advantage estimator. The updated estimator then guides advantage-conditioned behavioral cloning using a balanced mixture of base demonstrations and new policy data. This design preserves the iterative and policy-aware nature of human-in-the-loop learning while decoupling data collection from robot deployment. Experiments on four real-world tasks spanning long-horizon and precise manipulation show that HIL-UMI achieves consistent improvement over SFT and benefits from both targeted collection and advantage refinement. Moreover, HIL-UMI outperforms HG-DAgger on Clean Up Table with lower per-frame collection time, suggesting a scalable path for VLA post-training across operators and locations.

AI.tldr: HIL-UMI introduces a policy-guided, human-in-the-loop VLA post-training framework that collects targeted demonstrations via a handheld interface, guided by Energy Score and a refined progress-based advantage estimator, to improve SFT and outperform HG-DAgger with reduced data collection, across four real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of supervised fine-tuning with static task demonstrations and standard imitation objectives, and enable scalable, policy-aware post-training without requiring repeated robot deployment.
AI.method: Handheld UMI demonstrations where the human and policy do not execute predictions; Energy Score detects out-of-distribution regions by comparing human trajectories to policy inferences; a separate feedback loop uses low online advantage predictions to refine a progress-based advantage estimator; perform advantage-conditioned behavioral cloning on a balanced mix of base demonstrations and new policy data.
AI.result: Experiments on four real-world tasks with long-horizon and precise manipulation show consistent improvement over SFT; performance benefits from targeted collection and advantage refinement; outperforms HG-DAgger on Clean Up Table with lower per-frame collection time.
AI.conclusion: HIL-UMI maintains a policy-aware, iterative post-training paradigm while decoupling data collection from robot deployment, providing a scalable path for VLA post-training across operators and locations.

title: RISC-V and machine learning: a survey
summary: The intersection of open-source processor architectures and machine learning is driving the demand for customizable, efficient, and accessible hardware. This survey examines the state of the RISC-V ISA in machine learning applications, analyzing current capabilities, challenges, and future directions based on recent research. The analysis covers academic and commercial implementations, software frameworks, and real-world applications. The RISC-V machine learning ecosystem is evaluated, from instruction set extensions and core implementations to compiler optimizations and deployment strategies. Key contributions include a unified taxonomy of RISC-V ML implementations, a comparative analysis of performance and design trade-offs, an evaluation of software toolchain maturity, and the identification of emerging trends in instruction set extensions and specialized accelerators. Findings reveal progress in energy efficiency, specialized instruction development, and framework integration, while highlighting challenges in standardization, verification complexity, and ecosystem fragmentation. The analysis proposes four research directions to address current limitations: specialized neural processing extensions, adaptive and modular processor architectures, security frameworks, and energy-efficient multi-domain architectures. These directions provide a roadmap for advancing RISC-V as a foundational platform for next-generation machine learning systems.

AI.tldr: Survey of RISC-V ML ecosystem: taxonomy, performance trade-offs, toolchain maturity, and roadmap with four research directions.
AI.motivation: RISC-V enables customizable ML hardware; need comprehensive understanding of current capabilities, gaps, and future directions to guide design and standardization.
AI.method: Literature and industry survey across academia and industry; develop unified taxonomy of ML implementations on RISC-V; compare performance/design trade-offs; assess software toolchains; identify trends and challenges; synthesize four future directions.
AI.result: Shows progress in energy-efficient designs, specialized instructions, and framework integration; identifies standardization gaps, verification complexity, ecosystem fragmentation.
AI.conclusion: Proposes four research directions: specialized neural processing extensions, adaptive and modular architectures, security frameworks, energy-efficient multi-domain architectures; provides roadmap for RISC-V ML platforms.

title: Learning Foresight without Explicit Trajectories for 3D Diffusion Policies
summary: 3D diffusion policies are strong at generating geometrically grounded actions from current observations, but successful manipulation requires not only knowing what motion is feasible now, but also anticipating where the interaction is heading. Existing policies largely leave such foresight to emerge implicitly from action learning. We introduce Movement Trend Guidance, a simple but effective way to provide this foresight without introducing an explicit plan. From a short observation history, the policy learns a compact latent representation of interaction evolution. During training, sparse future gripper states supervise this representation; at inference, only the latent is retained as future-oriented conditioning alongside the current observation. The latent provides global conditioning for action generation, while an additional gated FiLM branch is used only at the UNet bottleneck. Despite adding only 3.52% more parameters to DP3, our method preserves the original dense-action and receding-horizon formulation and consistently improves upon DP3 across RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-40, and DexArt. It reaches 62.8% vs. 56.1% in 50-task RoboTwin2.0 mixed training, 71.93% vs. 37.08% on LIBERO-40, and 72.0% vs. 49.0% on five real-robot tasks. These results show that a diffusion policy can benefit substantially from knowing where an interaction is heading, without being told exactly where to move.

AI.tldr: Movement Trend Guidance adds a lightweight latent forecast of interaction evolution to diffusion-based manipulation policies, improving foresight with minimal parameter overhead.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation requires anticipating future interactions; existing policies lack explicit foresight, relying on implicit learning from data.
AI.method: From short observation history, learn a compact latent representation of interaction evolution; train with sparse future gripper states; at inference, use latent as future-oriented conditioning alongside current observation; use a gated FiLM branch at UNet bottleneck; adds 3.52% more parameters to DP3.
AI.result: Empirically improves DP3 across RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-40, and DexArt: 62.8% vs 56.1% in RoboTwin2.0 50-task; 71.93% vs 37.08% LIBERO-40; 72.0% vs 49.0% on five real-robot tasks.
AI.conclusion: A diffusion policy can benefit substantially from knowing where an interaction is heading without being told exact movements; the approach preserves dense-action and receding-horizon formulation while adding foresight.

title: Don't Mask the Environment: Observation Supervision Changes How Agents Explore Under RL
summary: Agent trajectories record what an agent does and what happens next. Yet standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) applies loss only to agent-authored action tokens, using environment observations as context but not as prediction targets. We ask whether this convention provides the best initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning. We introduce ActObs, which also supervises the observation tokens already present in each trajectory. Although deployed agents never generate observations, learning to predict them encourages the policy to model action consequences without adding data, parameters, sequence tokens, or forward passes. The methods perform similarly after SFT but diverge after GRPO. On Qwen3-4B, GRPO from ActObs achieves higher pass@k at every evaluated sampling budget than its action-only counterpart on Terminal-Bench 2.0. On Qwen3-8B, it trades some pass@1 reliability for higher pass@k (+3.4 pp at pass@16) and solves more distinct tasks. The advantage extends to cross-domain code editing on aider-polyglot (+4.2 pp at pass@1 at 4B), whose tasks are unseen during SFT and RL. ActObs retains more entropy during RL while requiring less policy movement, leaving the final policy closer to its SFT initialization. Our analysis traces this difference to SFT: action and observation gradients rapidly become orthogonal, while action-only training leaves a large residual observation gradient and degrades environment prediction below the base model. Joint supervision prevents this one-sided specialization, preserving consequence prediction and preparing the policy for downstream exploration.

AI.tldr: ActObs adds supervision of observation tokens to standard action-focused fine-tuning, improving downstream RL performance by preserving environment prediction and enabling better exploration across multiple models and tasks, including cross-domain code editing.
AI.motivation: Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains only on agent actions using observations as context, potentially leaving the model ill-prepared for RL where environment prediction and outcome modeling are crucial. ActObs hypothesizes that predicting observations alongside actions can regularize the policy toward understanding action consequences without adding data or parameters.
AI.method: Introduce ActObs to jointly supervise action and observation tokens within agent trajectories. This does not require new data or forward passes during deployment. After SFT, assess performance with GRPO (and baselines) on large LMs (Qwen3-4B/3-8B) and cross-domain tasks (aider-polyglot). Compare to action-only baselines using pass@k metrics across budgets.
AI.result: ActObs and action-only training perform similarly after SFT, but diverge after GRPO. On Qwen3-4B, ActObs GRPO achieves higher pass@k at all budgets than the action-only baseline on Terminal-Bench 2.0. On Qwen3-8B, ActObs yields slightly lower pass@1 but higher pass@k (+3.4 pp at pass@16) and solves more tasks. In cross-domain code editing with aider-polyglot, ActObs improves pass@1 by +4.2 pp. ActObs maintains higher policy entropy during RL with less policy movement, keeping closer to the SFT initialization. This is linked to SFT dynamics: action and observation gradients tend to become orthogonal under action-only training, leaving a residual observation gradient and degrading environment prediction; joint supervision mitigates this and preserves consequence prediction for exploration.
AI.conclusion: Joint supervision of actions and observations during SFT (ActObs) yields RL-ready policies that retain environment-predictive capability and exploration potential, improving downstream performance across domains and model scales. This approach mitigates one-sided gradient specialization and suggests integrating observation prediction into SFT schedules for better RL initialization.

title: MAGNETAR: Multipath-Guided Spatial Posteriors for Transmitter Pose Inference in the Upper Mid-Band
summary: Robots that localize a radio transmitter need more than a point estimate: in cluttered rooms, one measurement is often consistent with several transmitter locations and, because upper-mid-band antennas are directional, several headings. We present MAGNETAR, which infers a joint posterior over planar transmitter position and heading from a single asynchronous radio-frequency (RF) multipath snapshot, represented by angle-of-arrival and signal-to-noise-ratio estimates, given the room layout and receiver pose. Among our five neural scorers, MAGNETAR adopts a shared 2D U-Net conditioned on each candidate heading, jointly normalizing scores over a discretized position-heading grid. Training uses real-to-sim-calibrated 10 GHz simulations and a small measured subset. Grid-based joint posteriors outperform parametric ones on held-out simulations, the heading-conditioned scorer transfers best to robotic measurements, and fusing joint posteriors improves on fusing position-only marginals.

AI.tldr: MAGNETAR builds a grid-based joint posterior over transmitter position and heading from a single RF snapshot using a heading-conditioned 2D U-Net; trained with real-to-sim calibrated 10 GHz data plus a small measured subset; grid posteriors outperform parametric posteriors; heading-conditioned scoring transfers best to robotic measurements; joint posteriors fusion beats position-only fusion.
AI.motivation: In cluttered indoor environments, a single RF measurement can be consistent with multiple transmitter locations and headings due to multipath and directional antennas. A joint position–heading posterior can disambiguate hypotheses and improve localization for mobile robots.
AI.method: A joint posterior over planar transmitter position and heading is inferred from an asynchronous RF snapshot (AoA and SNR) given room layout and receiver pose. MAGNETAR uses five neural scorers; a shared 2D U-Net is conditioned on each candidate heading and scores a discretized position-heading grid, normalizing across the grid. Training combines real-world measured data with simulations calibrated at 10 GHz (real-to-sim).
AI.result: Grid-based joint posteriors outperform parametric posteriors on held-out simulations. The heading-conditioned scorer transfers the best to real robotic measurements. Fusing joint posteriors yields improvements over fusing position-only marginals.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling position and heading in a discretized grid with a heading-conditioned neural scorer provides robust, transferable RF localization in multipath environments, enabling better disambiguation and fusion of hypotheses compared to position-only approaches.

title: Video DeltaNet: A Video-Native Hybrid Attention for Livestream Video Generation
summary: Video diffusion models repeatedly process long spatiotemporal token sequences during denoising, making attention a major computational bottleneck. Linear attention offers an appealing alternative and has been widely adopted in recent large language models, but directly applying it to video models often fails to preserve the fine-grained interactions required for high-quality generation. We present Video DeltaNet (VDN), which combines local Softmax attention with bidirectional linear memory for long-range video context. Its linear branch introduces Video Delta Attention (VDA), which updates memory once per frame by jointly incorporating its spatial tokens. Separate output projections and learnable gates calibrate the two branches, while a staged teacher-alignment recipe progressively introduces the new pathway into pretrained models. We instantiate VDN on MiniMax H3, applying the hybrid to video-to-video interactions while retaining Softmax for interactions involving text or audio. With eight-step distillation and an optimized SGLang serving stack, VDN-H3 completes DiT denoising for a 14.3-second, 768p video in 6.70 seconds on eight NVIDIA B200 GPUs, corresponding to a 14.5x speedup over the 50-step dense H3 baseline on the same GPU count.

AI.tldr: Hybrid attention for video diffusion: Video DeltaNet (VDN) fuses local Softmax attention with a bidirectional linear memory (Video Delta Attention, VDA) to handle long-range video context, enabling fast denoising with teacher-alignment distillation; achieves ~14.5x speedup on 8 GPUs.
AI.motivation: Attention is the main computational bottleneck in long spatiotemporal video diffusion; linear attention helps with scalability but often degrades fine-grained interactions. A hybrid approach seeks to preserve quality while enabling long-range context.
AI.method: Introduce Video DeltaNet (VDN) with two branches: a local Softmax attention branch and a linear memory branch that uses Video Delta Attention (VDA) updating memory once per frame with joint spatial-token integration. Use separate output projections and learnable gates to fuse branches. Apply a staged teacher-alignment to progressively inject the new pathway into pretrained models. Instantiate on MiniMax H3, maintaining Softmax for text/audio interactions, eight-step distillation and optimized SGLang serving stack.
AI.result: VDN-H3 enables DiT denoising for a 14.3-second, 768p video in 6.70 seconds on 8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs, achieving ~14.5x speedup over the 50-step dense H3 baseline on the same hardware.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid attention design effectively preserves fine-grained video interactions while delivering substantial speedups, with distillation-based integration supporting compatibility with pretrained models. Potential benefits include scalability to longer videos and richer multi-modal interactions; limitations may involve residual trade-offs between memory-based context and precision.

title: Towards Scaling Marine Perception with Synthetic Data
summary: Scalable machine learning in challenging underwater environments is strongly limited by the lack of labeled real-world training data. This data is often expensive and laborious to gather, making large-scale real-world data challenging to gather and curate. However, simulated data can help close the gap, enabling many learning-based tasks for underwater perception. In this work, we extend OceanSim, an IsaacSim-based underwater perception simulator, with a Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) pipeline for training models to be used in underwater scenarios. The proposed pipeline enables users to generate large, automatically labeled, photorealistic datasets with configurable scene appearance, structure, and sensor settings. We evaluate the pipeline on a real-world sea urchin detection task and study how different forms of synthetic scene variation affect sim-to-real performance. Based on these experiments, we discuss findings on our results, main limitations of the current pipeline and identify future directions for improving underwater rendering fidelity, scene diversity, and the evaluation of sim-to-real generalization. The open-source code can be found at https://github.com/umfieldrobotics/OceanSim.

AI.tldr: A scalable synthetic data pipeline for OceanSim-based underwater perception enables large, automatically labeled, photorealistic datasets to improve sim-to-real performance, evaluated on sea urchin detection, with analysis of how synthetic variations affect transfer and open-source release.
AI.motivation: Addresses the scarcity and cost of labeled real underwater data; synthetic data can bridge the gap for perception tasks, but requires fidelity and diversity to enable robust sim-to-real learning.
AI.method: Integrates a Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) pipeline into OceanSim (IsaacSim-based) to generate large, automatically labeled, photorealistic underwater scenes with configurable appearance, structure, and sensor settings; evaluates on a real-world sea urchin detection task and studies the effect of synthetic scene variation on sim-to-real performance; discusses limitations and future directions; open-source code available.
AI.result: Provides insights into how synthetic scene variation influences sim-to-real transfer in underwater perception; identifies current bottlenecks and avenues for improving rendering fidelity, scene diversity, and evaluation of generalization; releases the code for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The OceanSim SDG pipeline advances scalable underwater ML by enabling large labeled datasets and systematic study of sim-to-real transfer, while highlighting key limitations and proposing future work to enhance fidelity, diversity, and generalization.

title: Calibrated RF-Fingerprinting Under Interference With Heterogeneous Transmission Protocols
summary: Radio Frequency(RF)-Fingerprinting is a spectrum monitoring technique that identifies specific transmitters based on hardware impairments imprinted within the emitted signal. Although widely researched, studies almost exclusively consider scenarios where only one transmitter is emitting at a time, limiting real world applicability. In this work, we further the study of RF-Fingerprinting by considering co-channel interference, with multiple emitted signals interfering with each other, overlapping in time and frequency. Specifically, we formulate this problem as a multi-label classification problem and employ a 1D convolutional neural network (CNN). Furthermore, the models are calibrated such that the confidence thresholds for the label probabilities are derived, with guarantees on the upper bound on the average number of False Negatives, providing a degree of confidence in not missing a true spectrum policy violation. The proposed method is validated using real world data from the POWDER 5G testbed on devices transmitting 802.11a(Wi-Fi), 4G LTE, and 5G NR waveforms. The results show accuracy as high as 97% and as low as 73% after calibration depending on channel conditions. Also calibrating for various average false negatives upper bounds achieves micro recall scores of approximately (1 - calibrated false negatives) with the calibration robust to out-of-distribution interference, demonstrating the potential of the proposed method in a realistic high contention wireless environment

AI.tldr: A multi-label RF fingerprinting approach using a 1D CNN to handle co-channel interference, with calibrated confidence thresholds and upper-bound guarantees on average false negatives; validated on POWDER 5G data with Wi-Fi, LTE, and 5G NR signals, achieving 97% to 73% accuracy depending on channel conditions; calibration yields robust recall and out-of-distribution interference resilience, enabling reliable spectrum policy enforcement in high contention environments.
AI.motivation: RF fingerprinting typically assumes a single active transmitter; practical deployments must cope with co-channel interference where multiple devices transmit simultaneously. Providing reliability guarantees on not missing true policy violations is essential for spectrum monitoring systems.
AI.method: Formulates the problem as multi-label classification. Uses a 1D CNN to extract features from the transmitted signals (likely raw I/Q or time-domain representation). Implements calibrated probability thresholds for each label, deriving upper bounds on average false negatives (FN) to ensure a controllable miss-rate. Validates on real-world POWDER 5G testbed data containing 802.11a, LTE, and 5G NR transmissions.
AI.result: Achieves accuracy ranging from 97% (favorable conditions) to 73% (poorer channel conditions) after calibration. Calibration aligns micro recall with (1 - calibrated FN rate) and remains robust under out-of-distribution interference, indicating practical viability in high-contention wireless environments.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates the feasibility of calibrated multi-label RF fingerprinting under co-channel interference and offers confidence guarantees on detecting policy violations. Real-world performance varies with channel conditions, suggesting further enhancements in feature extraction, calibration techniques, and generalization to more devices and waveform types.

title: Custom PX4 firmware for autonomous hybrid aerial-marine missions
comment: Accepted to I-RIM 3D 2026 and it will be published in SPAR series
summary: Mapping and monitoring aquatic environments can benefit from hybrid aerial-amphibious drones able to combine flight and water-surface navigation within the same mission. This paper presents a PX4 firmware extension for such platforms, introducing manual and autonomous marine navigation modes integrated with the standard PX4 mission pipeline and QGroundControl interface. The proposed framework preserves existing flight functionalities and safety mechanisms while enabling unified planning and execution of hybrid aerial-marine missions with differentiated aerial and marine waypoints. Simulated case studies validate the implementation and demonstrate stable surface navigation under calm and wavy conditions.

AI.tldr: A PX4 firmware extension enables hybrid aerial-marine missions via manual and autonomous marine navigation modes integrated into the PX4 mission pipeline and QGroundControl, preserving flight safety; validated in simulation with calm and wavy water.
AI.motivation: enable unified planning and execution of hybrid aerial–marine missions for environmental monitoring and data collection using a single platform and mission pipeline.
AI.method: Develop a PX4 firmware extension adding marine navigation modes that integrate with the standard PX4 mission planner and QGroundControl, allowing differentiated aerial and marine waypoints while preserving safety mechanisms; ensure compatibility with existing flight functionalities.
AI.result: Simulated case studies validate the implementation, showing stable surface navigation under calm and wavy conditions and seamless integration with the standard flight stack and mission pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of a unified hybrid aerial–marine mission framework; preserves existing capabilities while enabling water-surface navigation; future work could include hardware experiments and more dynamic marine conditions.

title: PosteriorBench: From Point Estimates to Posterior Matching in Evaluating Generative Inverse Solvers
comment: 32 pages, 10 figures, 21 tables; the code is available at https://github.com/neuraloperator/PosteriorBench
summary: Generative models are increasingly used to solve scientific inverse problems, but existing evaluations still focus primarily on whether a method can produce a single plausible reconstruction. This is insufficient for ill-posed problems, where multiple solutions may be consistent with the same sparse or noisy observations. In these settings, a method can achieve strong pointwise accuracy while still failing to capture the true posterior through mode collapse, overconfident uncertainty, or averaging incompatible solutions. We introduce PosteriorBench, a benchmark for evaluating the distributional accuracy of generative inverse solvers. PosteriorBench evaluates four physics-based inverse problems: Darcy flow inversion, Poisson source recovery, carbon capture and storage, and light transport material inference. For each task, we construct high-fidelity reference posteriors using computationally heavy but established procedures such as rejection sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo, enabling direct assessment of whether solvers recover the full set of solutions rather than the single best sample. We pair these references with a five-metric posterior evaluation suite: posterior-mean error, posterior-standard-deviation error, maximum mean discrepancy, sliced Wasserstein distance, and radially averaged power-spectrum error. These metrics assess pointwise accuracy, marginal uncertainty, distributional alignment, and global frequency fidelity. The benchmark spans sparse sensing, low-resolution observations, nonlinear forward models, varying noise levels, and multimodal priors, with a unified pipeline for distribution matching and uncertainty quantification. Our experiments reveal substantial distribution-matching gaps across current solvers, while showing that neural operators improve resolution robustness, and guidance weights and generation noise are key to posterior-variance calibration.

AI.tldr: PosteriorBench benchmarks the distributional accuracy of generative inverse solvers across four physics-based problems using high-fidelity reference posteriors and a five-metric evaluation suite.
AI.motivation: Ill-posed inverse problems admit multiple plausible solutions. Current evaluations focus on pointwise accuracy, failing to assess whether solvers capture the full posterior. There is a need for a benchmark that assesses distributional fidelity and uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: Construct high-fidelity reference posteriors via rejection sampling and MCMC for four tasks (Darcy flow inversion, Poisson source recovery, carbon capture and storage, light transport material inference). Evaluate solvers with a five-metric suite: posterior-mean error, posterior-standard-deviation error, maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), sliced Wasserstein distance (SWD), and radially averaged power-spectrum error. Provide a unified pipeline for distribution matching and uncertainty quantification and analyze factors such as neural operators, guidance weights, and generation noise.
AI.result: The evaluation reveals substantial distribution-matching gaps across current solvers. Neural operators improve resolution robustness, and properly tuned guidance weights and generation noise are critical for calibrating posterior variance.
AI.conclusion: PosteriorBench offers a unified framework for distributional evaluation of generative inverse solvers, revealing limitations of existing methods and guiding future improvements (e.g., neural operators and uncertainty calibration via guidance and noise) to better capture the true posterior.

title: HOPHY: A Hierarchical Hypergraph Representation for Off-Road Path and Mission Planning
summary: Mission-level autonomy for disaster response, search and rescue, and tactical UGV operations requires repeated path and mission planning as terrain conditions, agent types, and objectives change. Pixel-grid search is costly for repeated kilometer-scale queries, while semantic abstractions must maintain valid costs and connectivity as conditions change. We present HOPHY (Hierarchical Off-Road Planning using Hypergraphs), a reusable hierarchical terrain representation that organizes map-scale terrain into geometrically connected semantic regions (GSNodes), connectivity-preserving critical regions (Coarse Regions), and typed hyperedges for terrain, agent, and weather context. Hyperedge intersections select affected regions and incident edges for state updates without rebuilding the hierarchy. Across real off-road maps spanning kilometer-scale areas, HOPHY achieves 100% planning success and less than 0.01% median cost deviation from the oracle (pixel A*), with substantially lower query and replanning latency than the evaluated pixel and abstraction baselines. Applied to a multi-robot task-allocation (MRTA) problem, these gains reduce total computation by 79x over pixel A* and 7.2x over the fastest abstraction baseline, with mission makespan comparable to pixel A*. Finally, we demonstrate HOPHY on a physical Clearpath Jackal that successfully executes a 1.5-km, eight-task mission across mixed-surface outdoor terrain and a blockage-triggered replanned route.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical hypergraph-based terrain planner (HOPHY) enables fast, scalable off-road planning with connectivity-preserving semantic regions and typed hyperedges; achieves near-oracle performance and large MRTA speedups on real maps and a 1.5-km robot mission.
AI.motivation: Address high cost of pixel-grid planning and fragility of abstracted costs by maintaining valid costs/connectivity while enabling reusable representations for dynamic terrain, agents, and weather.
AI.method: Construct GSNodes (geometrically connected semantic regions), Coarse Regions (connectivity-preserving critical areas), and typed hyperedges encoding terrain, agent, weather context. Use hyperedge intersections to selectively update affected regions/edges, avoiding hierarchy rebuilds. Validate on kilometer-scale real maps and MRTA; demonstrate on a physical robot.
AI.result: 100% planning success; median cost deviation < 0.01% vs pixel A*; lower query/replan latency than pixel/abstraction baselines; 79x MRTA computation reduction vs pixel A* and 7.2x vs fastest abstraction; mission makespan comparable to pixel A*; physical 1.5-km eight-task mission across mixed surfaces with a blockage-triggered replanning.
AI.conclusion: HOPHY provides a reusable, hierarchical, connectivity-preserving terrain representation that enables fast, robust planning for disaster response and mixed-terrain UGV operations, with strong real-world validation.

title: Score Centering Stabilizes Off-policy Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models is notoriously sensitive to small differences between training and inference engines, often referred to as the training-inference mismatch (TIM). However, completely eliminating TIM is impractical, as it would come at a major cost to rollout efficiency. In this paper, we show that the instability of RL under TIM is primarily caused by drift: a persistent bias between training and inference engines that accumulates with every training step. We derive an additive "score centering" correction term that stabilizes RL under TIM by canceling drift. When training models from 0.6B to 30B parameters, score centering alone matches or outperforms methods based on importance sampling under quantization, with the gap growing as the mismatch becomes more severe. Because the correction is additive, score centering also composes with importance sampling -- their composition outperforms pure importance-sampling baselines in our staleness experiments.

AI.tldr: Additive score-centering stabilizes RL under training‑inference mismatch (TIM) by canceling drift, achieving competitive or superior performance to importance sampling (IS) across 0.6B–30B parameter models, and is composable with IS for further gains.
AI.motivation: TIM introduces instability in reinforcement learning for large language models; completely eliminating TIM is expensive and reduces rollout efficiency. The work seeks a lightweight corrective mechanism to mitigate drift and stabilize RL under TIM.
AI.method: Derive an additive score-centering correction term that cancels drift between training and inference engines; apply it across a training range from 0.6B to 30B parameters; compare against IS-based methods under quantization; test composability with IS in staleness experiments.
AI.result: Score centering alone matches or outperforms IS-based methods under quantization, with the advantage growing as TIM worsens; the additive correction composes with IS, and their combination outperforms pure IS baselines in staleness scenarios.
AI.conclusion: An additive score-centering correction provides a simple, scalable remedy for TIM-induced instability in RL of large language models, performing well relative to IS methods and enabling safe composition with IS to further improve robustness under drift.

title: MoWAM: Explicit Future Motion Prediction for Efficient World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robot policy learning by incorporating future dynamics, yet explicitly generating future videos at inference introduces substantial computational overhead. Removing future generation improves efficiency, but leaves future dynamics only implicitly encoded in observation features, which can limit robustness under distribution shifts. We propose MoWAM, an efficient WAM that replaces future video generation with explicit future motion prediction. Instead of reconstructing the complete future scene, MoWAM models structured robot motion as a compact abstraction of the future, capturing how the robot is expected to evolve under the current scene and interaction constraints. A Mixture-of-Transformer architecture learns future visual dynamics during training while jointly predicting motion and action, allowing video generation to be removed entirely at inference while retaining an explicit representation of the future. The compact motion representation further enables efficient inference-time scaling by sampling multiple candidates of motion and action pairs and selecting among them with a motion-aware task-progress verifier. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that MoWAM achieves strong in-distribution performance, improved out-of-distribution robustness, and higher average real-world success than representative WAM baselines. In addition, performance improves as more candidates are explored, demonstrating that explicit future motion provides an effective and efficient basis for inference-time scaling.

AI.tldr: MoWAM replaces future video generation in World Action Models with explicit, compact future motion predictions via a Mixture-of-Transformer, enabling efficient, scalable inference without sacrificing performance.
AI.motivation: Address the substantial computational overhead of generating future videos at inference in WAMs and the robustness limits when future dynamics are only implicitly encoded in observation features under distribution shift.
AI.method: Introduce MoWAM: a Mixture-of-Transformer that predicts structured future motion and actions, removing video generation at inference. It uses a compact motion abstraction to represent future dynamics, trained to model future visual dynamics while jointly predicting motion and action. A motion-aware task-progress verifier supports selecting among multiple motion/action candidates during inference, enabling sampling-based scaling.
AI.result: Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world manipulation tasks, MoWAM achieves strong in-distribution performance, improved out-of-distribution robustness, and higher average real-world success than representative WAM baselines. Performance improves as more motion/action candidates are explored, demonstrating the efficacy of explicit future motion for inference-time scaling.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, structured future motion can provide an efficient, scalable, and robust basis for WAM-like policy learning. MoWAM demonstrates that replacing future video generation with a compact motion representation maintains performance while enabling effective inference-time candidate selection.

title: Underwater Visual Target Tracking with Target-Specific Depth Estimation and Adaptive Model-Fusion Predictive Control
summary: Vision-based underwater target tracking is challenged by unreliable depth measurements and unknown target motion. This paper proposes a stereo visual-servoing framework for an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV). For perception, the framework derives a stable 3D relative state from stereo images through target-specific depth extraction and Kalman filtering. It constructs a target-depth mask from color, disparity, and temporal cues to select reliable target pixels, and then filters the resulting depth measurement and detected image center separately. For control, the framework decouples yaw regulation from translational control, avoiding computationally expensive coupled multi-DOF optimization and enabling real-time translational MPC. The translational controller employs adaptive model-fusion predictive control, combining constant-velocity and zero-velocity target models to accommodate different target-motion patterns. It updates the model weights using historical prediction errors and computes translational commands subject to actuation, following-distance, and field-of-view constraints. Through simulations and real-world experiments, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and show it has better performance than existing frameworks.

AI.tldr: A stereo vision-based underwater target-tracking framework enabling real-time control via adaptive model-fusion MPC and Kalman-filtered 3D perception; shows improved performance over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Unreliable depth measurements and unknown target motion in underwater vision hamper robust target tracking; a unified perception-control framework is needed for real-time AUV operation.
AI.method: Derives a stable 3D relative state from stereo images using target-specific depth extraction and Kalman filtering; constructs a target-depth mask from color, disparity, and temporal cues to select reliable pixels; filters depth and image center measurements separately; decouples yaw regulation from translational control; employs adaptive model-fusion predictive control combining constant-velocity and zero-velocity target models; updates model weights via historical prediction errors; computes translational commands under actuation, following-distance, and field-of-view constraints.
AI.result: Simulations and real-world experiments validate the framework and indicate better performance than existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed stereo visual-servoing framework provides real-time, robust perception and control for underwater target tracking, with demonstrated effectiveness in both simulation and practice.

title: MILER: Semantic Mid-Level Representation for Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning in Unstructured Autonomous Driving
summary: Reinforcement learning constitutes a promising approach owing to its potential for superhuman performance and self-learned policies. However, its application to real-world autonomous driving remains scarce, particularly in unstructured environments, because of the challenges associated with sim-to-real transfer for unstructured environments. In this work, we present MILER, an end-to-end policy framework with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. During offline training, we employ a custom semantic mid-level representation (MLR) simulator and train the policy network using reinforcement learning, with its control outputs applied directly to a bicycle model. During deployment on the real vehicle, camera and LiDAR data are processed by BEVFusion to generate a semantic bird's-eye-view representation consistent with that of the MLR simulator. The actions generated by the policy network are not applied directly to the real vehicle. Instead, we employ a trajectory-alignment strategy that enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of both perception and control. We extensively evaluate the proposed framework on a diverse test track comprising numerous challenges, including various obstacles, hairpin curves, velocities of up to 33.6 km/h, and off-road sections. In total, we drove 17.3 km with two different vehicles on a 3.0 km test track without human intervention, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, the entire software stack runs on a Jetson AGX Orin.

AI.tldr: MILER presents a zero-shot sim-to-real pipeline for autonomous driving in unstructured environments using a mid-level representation (MLR) simulator and a trajectory-alignment strategy, enabling policy outputs to be transferred from offline RL in simulation to real cars via BEVFusion-generated semantic BEV and a non-direct control application on real hardware.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving in unstructured environments with reliable sim-to-real transfer is challenging due to perception and control gaps between simulation and reality; achieving zero-shot transfer reduces data collection and real-world testing burden.
AI.method: Offline RL training with a dedicated semantic mid-level representation (MLR) simulator; policy outputs mapped to a bicycle model; deployment uses BEVFusion to produce a semantic BEV aligned with MLR; actions are not applied directly but converted via a trajectory-alignment strategy for zero-shot transfer.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation on a diverse test track with obstacles, curves, speeds up to 33.6 km/h, and off-road sections; 17.3 km driven autonomously on a 3.0 km track using two vehicles; software stack runs on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for end-to-end RL in unstructured driving through alignment of perception representations and trajectory-based execution, while highlighting practical vehicle deployment constraints.

title: OPTED: On-Policy Fine-Tuning for End-to-End Driving using a Render-Free Teacher
summary: As scaling pre-training data alone yields diminishing returns, post-training is becoming increasingly important across physical AI domains such as autonomous driving. End-to-end driving policies are pre-trained in open loop with behavior cloning on human demonstrations. However, compounding errors during closed-loop deployment can take the vehicle outside the training data distribution, increasing the risk of safety-critical incidents. Closed-loop post-training can mitigate this risk but requires costly simulation for sensor-based policies. We propose OPTED (on-policy fine-tuning for end-to-end driving) which decouples reinforcement learning from the post-training of the end-to-end policy: a privileged teacher is trained using RL on vectorized inputs (HD-map and bounding boxes). This teacher then provides supervision to the pre-trained student during closed-loop post-training. We apply OPTED to two camera-based models, TransFuser and VaVAM, and fine-tune them in AlpaSim, using neural reconstructions (3DGS) of real driving logs. Driving scores increase by factors of 1.6$\times$ and 9.5$\times$, respectively. In controlled experiments OPTED matches closed-loop performance with approximately three orders of magnitude fewer simulator interactions than direct RL post-training, while staying closer to the human prior. Project page: https://01dami23.github.io/opted/

AI.tldr: OPTED decouples RL-based post-training from pre-trained end-to-end driving by using a privileged teacher trained with RL on vectorized inputs to supervise the student during closed-loop post-training. It improves driving scores substantially (1.6x and 9.5x) and achieves close-to-RL performance with ~1000x fewer simulator interactions, while staying close to human priors.
AI.motivation: Diminishing returns from scaling pre-training data; high risk of compounding errors during closed-loop deployment; sensor-based RL requires costly simulation; need data-efficient, human-aligned post-training for end-to-end driving in physical AI domains.
AI.method: Train a privileged teacher via reinforcement learning using vectorized inputs (HD-map, bounding boxes). The teacher provides supervision to the pre-trained student during closed-loop post-training. Evaluate on two camera-based models (TransFuser, VaVAM) fine-tuned in AlpaSim using 3DGS reconstructions of real driving logs.
AI.result: Driving scores increase by 1.6x for TransFuser and 9.5x for VaVAM. OPTED achieves close-to-RL closed-loop performance with approximately three orders of magnitude fewer simulator interactions than direct RL post-training, while remaining closer to human priors.
AI.conclusion: A separated, privileged-teacher RL framework for post-training can dramatically improve sample efficiency and safety alignment in end-to-end driving, offering a practical and scalable approach for physical AI domains.

title: Agile-WAM: An Agile Tactile World Action Model for Contact-Rich Robot Control
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) advance beyond conventional visuomotor policies by jointly predicting future world states and robot actions, enabling the policy to learn physical dynamics that support effective control. However, recent tactile WAMs often rely on large-scale pretrained generative backbones to capture contact-rich physical dynamics, which limit their inference efficiency and flexible deployment. In this paper, we present \ABBR{}, an agile tactile World Action Model for contact-rich robot control. \ABBR{} encodes visual and tactile observations into a shared latent that serves as the source of a direct vision-tactile-to-action flow-matching process, which can jointly generate latent representations of action chunks and future visual/tactile latents. A key observation is that vision and tactile signals evolve at inherently different timescales: adjacent visual frames are often highly similar, whereas tactile signals can change abruptly upon contact. We therefore introduce multi-horizon multimodal prediction in \ABBR{}, which provides supervision for visual latent at a larger temporal offset while predicting the tactile latent in the next frame to capture fine-grained contact dynamics. Across nine simulated and five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, \ABBR{} demonstrates strong and robust performance, outperforming the strongest baseline in success rate while maintaining low inference latency. In particular, in five real-world experiments, \ABBR{} yields a relative gain of $\textbf{29.4\%}$ in overall success rates while achieving inference latency of $\textbf{11.9 ms}$. These results demonstrate that multimodal WAM can be achieved with an agile architecture suitable for precise and high-frequency robot control. More details are available on our project page: https://hanchuzhou.github.io/TARO_project_page/.

AI.tldr: A lightweight tactile World Action Model (TARO) jointly predicts future world states and actions using a shared vision-tactile latent, with multi-horizon predictions to respect different timescales; it achieves strong real-world performance with low latency, outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Current tactile WAMs rely on large pretrained generative backbones, which hinder inference efficiency and flexible deployment. There is a need for agile architectures that can handle contact-rich dynamics at high frequency.
AI.method: Encode visual and tactile observations into a shared latent; use a direct vision-tactile-to-action flow-matching process to generate latent representations of action chunks and future visual/tactile latents; implement multi-horizon prediction by predicting tactile latent in the next frame for fine-grained contact dynamics while forecasting visual latent at a larger temporal offset.
AI.result: Evaluated on nine simulated and five real-world tasks; TARO outperforms the strongest baseline in overall success rate and maintains low inference latency; in five real-world experiments, achieves a 29.4% relative gain in success rate with an inference latency of 11.9 ms.
AI.conclusion: An agile, multimodal WAM can be realized with a lightweight architecture, enabling precise and high-frequency control in contact-rich robot manipulation.

title: Coding Agents with an Obstacle-Aware Harness for Safe Robot Manipulation
summary: Coding agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot manipulation: a language model writes the robot controller as a program, and agents built in this way now operate robots without robot-specific training.Whether this paradigm is also safe, however, has not been asked. We evaluate coding agent under a safety constraint, where each task pairs a manipulation goal with an obstacle the robot must not touch. The agent pursues the goal but collides with the obstacle in most cases, treating task completion as its sole objective while neglecting safety. The agent reasons about the obstacle in its traces, and the prompt already forbids touching it, so neither perception nor instruction is at fault; the fault lies in the planning, where the stated constraint never becomes a priority. By decomposing manipulation into a route phase and a contact-rich moment, we locate the source of the failure. Along the route, the model cannot prioritize the safety constraint, having no notion of a clearing route and none of replanning once a chosen route becomes infeasible. At the contact, it is unaware that contact execution is bounded by the same constraint. To close this gap, we present SafeHarness, which equips the model with two obstacle-aware harnesses that enable it to prioritize the safety constraint. Obstacle-aware route planning grounds the objects as bounding boxes and draws candidate routes over them as sequences of waypoints. The agent then plans a route in advance, verifies it, replans when necessary, and only then executes it. Obstacle-aware contact execution instead selects the contact position so that the contact itself avoids the obstacle. SafeHarness attains 71.9% task success and 87.5% collision avoidance, surpassing the previous SOTA by 6.5% and 27.0%, respectively. These results are $2.3\times$ and $1.5\times$ those of the same agent without harnesses.

AI.tldr: SafeHarness equips coding agents with obstacle-aware route planning and contact execution to enforce safety constraints in robot manipulation, achieving 71.9% task success and 87.5% collision avoidance, outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Safety constraints are not automatically prioritized by coding agents; current planning neglects safety, leading to collisions despite explicit prohibitions.
AI.method: Two obstacle-aware harnesses: (1) obstacle-aware route planning grounds objects as bounding boxes and generates candidate routes as waypoint sequences; plans, verifies, and replans before execution. (2) obstacle-aware contact execution selects contact points to ensure contact itself avoids the obstacle. Integration guides the agent to prioritize safety during both planning and contact.
AI.result: SafeHarness achieves 71.9% task success and 87.5% collision avoidance, surpassing previous SOTA by 6.5% and 27.0%, respectively; results are 2.3× and 1.5× those of the same agent without harnesses.
AI.conclusion: Obstacle-aware harnesses effectively prioritize safety constraints in coding agents for manipulation, improving both safety and task success and closing the gap to a safety-aware baseline.

title: GeoAAC: Geometry-Based Adaptive Action Chunking from Denoising Trajectories in VLA Policies
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
summary: Action chunking is widely used for action generation and execution in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, yet existing approaches commonly use a fixed action horizon. During a rollout, different task stages may require different levels of action continuity, control precision, and closed-loop feedback, making a fixed horizon unable to accommodate changing control requirements. We propose \textbf{GeoAAC}, a geometry-based adaptive action chunking method for flow-based VLA policies that adjusts the action horizon according to the reliability of the current action prediction. We show that the geometry of Flow Matching denoising trajectories provides process-level information for characterizing prediction reliability, with geometric variation across action prefixes remaining positively correlated with predictive uncertainty. GeoAAC uses this prefix-wise geometry to construct a horizon-wise geometric profile and adaptively determine the action horizon from a single generation without additional training. Experiments with GR00T N1.5 and π0.5 on LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa365, and real-world manipulation tasks show consistent improvements over fixed-action-horizon baselines and existing adaptive methods, including up to 8.7 percentage points in simulation and an increase in average real-world success rate from 53.3\% to 74.4\%.

AI.tldr: GeoAAC is a geometry-based adaptive action chunking method for flow-based Vision-Language-Action policies. It adapts the action horizon during rollouts by analyzing the prefix geometry of denoising trajectories, enabling single-generation horizon adaptation without retraining. It outperforms fixed-horizon baselines and existing adaptive methods, with notable simulation gains and real-world success rate improvements.
AI.motivation: Fixed action horizons in VLA policies fail to match varying control requirements across task stages, leading to suboptimal continuity, precision, and feedback. There is a need for horizon adaptation informed by the reliability of current action predictions.
AI.method: Leverages the geometry of Flow Matching denoising trajectories to quantify prediction reliability. Constructs a prefix-wise geometric profile to form a horizon-wise policy that adaptively determines the action horizon from a single generation, with no additional training.
AI.result: Shows consistent improvements over fixed-horizon baselines and prior adaptive methods across simulators LIBERO/LIBERO-Pro and RoboCasa365, as well as real-world tasks. Reported gains include up to 8.7 percentage points in simulation and an increase in average real-world success rate from 53.3% to 74.4%.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive horizon selection using trajectory geometry enhances flow-based VLA policies, enabling better action continuity and control precision without extra training. The approach generalizes across simulators and real-world tasks.

title: StageGuard: Learning Stage Transitions for Long-Horizon Robot Tasks via Agentic Distillation
summary: Hierarchical planning frameworks combine skills from multiple robot control policies for long-horizon task execution, where determining when to terminate the current skill and advance to the next subtask is essential. Existing approaches often rely on pre-designed completion signal checkers that are hard to obtain in real-world execution. Large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) offer strong reasoning capabilities, but their decision boundaries are not inherently aligned with task completion criteria, while cloud deployment and lengthy reasoning introduce substantial latency, limiting real-time monitoring. We propose StageGuard, an agentic distillation framework for accurate and efficient stage-transition decisions. StageGuard combines teacher-model reasoning with demonstration trajectories to generate structured explanations of subtask completion and policy switching. A lightweight student VLM uses these explanations to generate compact self-explanations, which are used for supervised fine-tuning. We evaluate stage-transition prediction on trajectories from two benchmarks and assess closed-loop task success through integration into hierarchical robot control on BEHAVIOR-1K, with further validation on real robots. Results show substantial improvements in stage-transition prediction while supporting efficient online monitoring.

AI.tldr: StageGuard distills teacher reasoning and demonstrations into compact explanations to guide a lightweight student VLM for precise, real-time stage-transition decisions in hierarchical robot control.
AI.motivation: Need reliable completion signals for long-horizon planning; pre-designed checkers are hard to obtain in real-world settings; while large vision-language models offer reasoning, their decision boundaries may misalign with task criteria and they incur latency for cloud-only solutions.
AI.method: Agentic distillation: generate structured explanations of subtask completion and policy switching from teacher reasoning and demonstration trajectories; train a lightweight student VLM to produce compact self-explanations; use supervised fine-tuning on these explanations; apply explanations to predict stage transitions for online monitoring; evaluate on BEHAVIOR-1K and real robots.
AI.result: Substantial improvements in stage-transition prediction; improved closed-loop task success when integrated into hierarchical robot control on BEHAVIOR-1K; validated on real robots; demonstrates efficient online monitoring.
AI.conclusion: StageGuard enables accurate and efficient stage-transition decisions in hierarchical robot control by explanation-guided distillation, aligning VLM decisions with task completion criteria and supporting real-time monitoring.

title: Workspace Models: Lightweight Robotic Memory via Saliency-Driven Supervision
summary: Complex robotic manipulation tasks frequently require a long-term memory of past events and actions. As conditioning on full histories renders policies prone to spurious correlations and degrades performance, many approaches to policy memory involve compressing historical information through expensive VLM queries in-the-loop to process only task-salient information. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach in which computationally intensive VLM queries are made during train-time to learn a lightweight latent memory that can be efficiently queried at deployment time. Our representation, which we call the \textbf{workspace token}, is trained by (1) using a VLM to identify current and historical information necessary for completing a task, then (2) distilling these into the workspace token using a set-reconstruction decoder loss. In both simulation and hardware, we show that the workspace token can be used as a drop-in replacement for observations during deployment, enabling policies to solve memory-intensive tasks without the need for VLM reasoning in-the-loop. Interestingly, we found that workspace tokens are not only more lightweight but also lead to better policy performance.

AI.tldr: Offline, VLM-guided distillation of a compact workspace token yields a memory-efficient, deployable observation representation for long-horizon robotic manipulation, achieving equal or better performance than VLM-in-the-loop baselines.
AI.motivation: Full observation histories degrade policy performance due to spurious correlations and impose heavy computation via in-the-loop VLM queries; a lightweight, train-time-learned memory is needed for deployment.
AI.method: Train-time: use a vision-language model to identify task-relevant current and historical information. Distill this information into a lightweight 'workspace token' via a set-reconstruction decoder loss. Deployment: use the workspace token as the observation, eliminating VLM reasoning in-the-loop.
AI.result: The workspace token serves as a drop-in replacement for observations in both simulation and hardware, enabling memory-intensive tasks to be solved without online VLM queries; tokens are lightweight and yield equal or improved policy performance compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Training-time VLM-guided distillation can produce compact, effective memory representations (workspace tokens) that enable efficient deployment for complex robotic manipulation without sacrificing performance.
